concepts/abwehr.title: The Abwehr
concepts/abwehr.content:
The Abwehr
The Abwehr was the German military intelligence service, the secret service of the Reichswehr and later of the Wehrmacht, and the great espionage apparatus of the Second World War. Its name — literally “defence” — was the cover under which it gathered intelligence, planted agents and carried out sabotage and counter-espionage. From his headquarters at the War Department in the Bendlerstrasse in Berlin, the service was directed for most of the war by Admiral Wilhelm Canaris, whom the wartime chronicler Kurt Singer called the mystery man of German espionage. Under Canaris the Abwehr wove a web of spy centers across the world, from the harbors of Europe to the Near East and the deserts of Asia, and stood at the centre of the secret war this wiki records.
The service and its chief
The Abwehr’s headquarters could not be concealed as successfully as its chief’s personality. Canaris shared quarters with the War Department at 14 Bendlerstrasse, in the very heart of Berlin; in March 1935 he had a private entrance constructed, and he entered and left by a staircase exclusively his. Of the thousands who frequented the enormous building, only a few ever saw him face to face. The service was the organized expression of his own method — mass espionage, built on the belief “that the laborer is worthy of his hire,” with pay rolls of hundreds of sub-agents beneath each principal. Under Canaris the German consuls and ministers, whose offices were strangely placed near the harbors of Europe, were frequently members of the Naval Intelligence Service, and beneath them worked the hundreds of agents on the Admiral’s pay roll.
The machinery of the secret war
The Abwehr’s techniques were the espionage of a modern industrial state. Its agents were placed at the chokepoints of the enemy’s world: German consulates stood at the harbors of Sweden, Finland and Denmark, with sub-agents from harbor pilots to lighthouse keepers; observation instruments were installed in the consulates to watch the southern Swedish fortifications; no boat passed the Gulf of Bothnia unobserved. Its operations, as Singer recounted them, reached into the highest councils of the enemy — the theft of the French navy’s complete mobilization orders before they had even been signed by Admiral Darlan, and the seizure of the British plans for the co-ordination of air force and army. It ran the spy who signalled the U-boat that sank the Royal Oak at Scapa Flow, the weather-station outposts of the Arctic and Greenland, the illicit radio stations of the war of the airwaves, and the saboteurs and fifth columns that prepared the way for invasion.
The European and world networks
The Abwehr’s reach defined the geography of the secret war. In Scandinavia its chief was Horst von Pflugk-Hartung, the murderer of Rosa Luxemburg, who by 1940 had marshalled seven hundred and fifty assistants across Norway, Sweden and Denmark and whose Nazi spy web in Copenhagen was among the service’s most celebrated creations. In neutral Ireland two agents conferred with Canaris at the German Embassy and received instructions, codes and orders for action whenever war should break out. In the Near East his agents furnished the Arabs with arms and urged revolt against England, and his trusted agent Dr. Fritz Grobba, once German Minister to Afghanistan and later to Iraq, assembled a fifth column that produced the Iraq uprising of 1941. From Athens, in the latter part of 1941 and into 1942, Canaris set up new espionage headquarters from which his agents covered British-held territory from Syria into the Mongolian desert, with communication maintained by desert caravans equipped with modern ultra-short-wave receivers.
The fall of the network
The same war that made the Abwehr’s reputation undid it. The Allies learned to read its methods and to turn its agents: Singer recounts that the British and American intelligence services, working independently, both caught the Abwehr’s desert trick of relayed code messages, and that a counter-espionage screen of doubled and watched agents (“a screen of twittering canaries”) was raised against the enemy nets. The individual cases that fill his chapters — the sabotages, the weather-station battles in Greenland, the spy who had to be shot at, the fake refugees and the parachutists in Ireland — trace a service fighting harder and finding less as the war turned. Above all the Abwehr stood in the shadow of the party’s own police, and the rivalry between the military service and the SS was to strip it of its functions and its chief.
The rivalry with the party
The Abwehr was never the only German secret service, and the history of the war is in part the history of its struggle with the political police. Canaris’s service belonged to the military establishment, while the SS and its chief Heinrich Himmler built a rival apparatus of their own; the two stood in suspicion and rivalry throughout the war. Canaris himself, in Singer’s account, was a man who had served his country’s espionage since 1914 and had even posed as a Jew under the aliases Otto Seliger and Moses Meyerbeer in America during the First World War, and whom Singer judged an enigma — the greatest organizer of espionage the world had known, and at the same time a man whom the party mistrusted. It was that rivalry, and the rivalry of the services, that would ultimately undo the Abwehr and its chief.

concepts/agrarian-question-spain.title: Agrarian question in Spain
concepts/agrarian-question-spain.content:
Agrarian question in Spain
The agrarian question in Spain was the problem of the land — the maldistribution of the soil between a few great proprietors and the mass of the landless, and the poverty that flowed from it — which the Republic of 1931 inherited as the most ambitious problem facing the new regime. Agriculture was the base of the national and social life of Spain, and the obstacle it raised was the inseparable companion of a defective political system: the latifundist countryside of the south, where vast estates lay in the hands of a small class while day-labourers, the braceros, went without work for half the year, stood against the smallholding north, and upon this inequality the whole social peace of the country turned. The Republic’s answer, the agrarian reform, was intended to break the latifundio and settle the landless; but it came late, was timid in content and application, and in the effort it both raised the expectations of the countryside and alienated the great proprietors, so that the land question became one of the forces that carried Spain to civil war.
The latifundist countryside
The social world of the Spanish field was divided between the great estates of the south and the small properties of the north. In the latifundist provinces of Andalusia and Extremadura a few families held enormous holdings worked by a numerous class of landless labourers, who lived from the harvest and starved in the months of idleness. The growing population and the impact of the world economic crisis of the early 1930s made the problem urgent: the economic depression, arriving in Spain later than elsewhere but with grave social consequences, threw yet more labour onto a market that could not absorb it. To the labourer the land reform meant work and bread; to the proprietor it meant the loss of the estate. The Republic came to power amid this expectation and this fear, and the question of the land was the question on which its relations with a large part of the population would turn.
The reform
The agrarian reform was the most ambitious measure the new regime attempted. It appeared before the constitution was drafted, and it confronted a multisecular problem made urgent by the crisis. Yet the reform that was finally passed and applied was a timid thing — hedged about with compensation, with exceptions and with delays — and even that timidity was decisive in alienating a large part of the population. To the right, any expropriation of the latifundio was an attack on property and on the social order; to the left, the reform’s slowness and insufficiency proved the Republic’s bad faith. The reformist biennium was consumed in this contradiction: it could neither satisfy the landless, who grew impatient and occupied the land on their own account, nor reassure the proprietors, who joined the enemies of the Republic. The social agitation in the countryside — the strikes, the occupations, the burnings — accompanied the reform at every step and turned the field into a theatre of the class war.
The question in the Republic
The agrarian question lay behind the political oscillations of the Republic. The conservative biennium that followed 1933 halted and reversed the reform, and the countryside of the south swung to the right of the proprietors even as the landless pushed toward revolution. In the spring of 1936, with the Popular Front returned to power and the reform restored, the agitation of the field quickened: the occupation of estates, the tension between the rural labourers and the great proprietors, became one of the motors of the polarisation that carried Spain toward the rising of July 1936. When the war came, the land question was fought out on both sides of the line — the revolution in the republican zone swept up the land alongside the factories, while in the rebel zone the latifundist aristocracy, which had stood with one side from the beginning, held what the reform had threatened. The deep division that the war opened between the two Spains was in part a division of class, and at its heart lay the land.

concepts/bloc-national.title: The Bloc National
concepts/bloc-national.content:
The Bloc National
The parliamentary majority and coalition that governed France in the five years after the Great War, from the legislative elections of 16 November 1919 to the triumph of the opposing Cartel des Gauches in May 1924. The Bloc national — the National Bloc — was the postwar political expression of the France of victory and reconstruction, a coalition in which the parties of the Right and the conservative centre swept away the prewar republican majority, and whose brief and troubled life defined the first chapter of French politics after 1918. Its story is told, from opposite ends of the political divide, by the Socialist deputy-historian Alexandre Zévaès and the electoral geographer André Siegfried: the one writing in 1926, the other in 1930, both measuring the Bloc against the France it had displaced and the France that displaced it.
The victory of 1919
The elections of November 1919 were the first consultation of the peace, held under a new system of proportional representation that had displaced the old single-member scrutiny. The Chamber they produced, Zévaès writes, was moderate by majority, acquired to what was called the Bloc national — a coalition composed, for the largest part, of clericals, nationalists, progressists, republicans of the Alliance démocratique and national radicals. Departments whose representation had been entirely or largely radical or socialist — Savoy, Haute-Savoie, Haute-Saône, Côte-d’Or, and others — elected the lists of the Bloc. In Paris, Millerand, who twenty years earlier had been one of the leaders of parliamentary socialism and the man of the Saint-Mandé discourse, had become, with Maurice Barrès, the most qualified representative of the Bloc.
Siegfried gives the same victory its analytical reading. The Bloc, victor on 14 November 1919, pretended to reunite all Frenchmen in a national interest of reconstruction, as the country had concentrated itself wholly in the union sacrée against the invader. But it was a degenerate form of that sacred union: the new bloc insensibly allowed itself to slide from national union to conservative union. The new Chamber was the most right-wing France had elected since the Assembly of 1871 — with 180 deputies of the Left, 216 of the Centre and 221 of the Right, the added forces of centre and right were crushing, and the political axis of the assembly passed at the intersection of the left republicans and the progressists, in sum at the centre-right. Never, Siegfried remarks, had the influential political circles contained more men of a temperament so little republican, however beyond doubt their republican loyalism.
The temper of the Bloc
The Bloc, Siegfried insists, was nonetheless a faithful representation of a France still warm from the war — a country impatient to raise its ruins, extraordinarily susceptible the moment one touched the Treaty of Versailles or trimmed its “sacred” right to reparations. This tangle of very different tendencies, he argues, kept France so long on the defensive before the League of Nations, carried Millerand the consul to the Élysée, and Poincaré into the Ruhr, while the reconstruction, without any counterpart in reparations, drove the pound sterling up in March 1924 to the then-record level of 138 francs. The political year of the Bloc was thus an affair of the past as much as of the present: a defensive nationalism resting on the treaty and the reparation, a conservatism that the peace had rendered respectable, and a financial crisis that the reconstruction, paid for out of the French pocket, only deepened.
Zévaès’s account of the Bloc in office is that of a majority growing steadily more conservative and subjecting itself to the financial powers. The ministries of Georges Leygues, Aristide Briand and Raymond Poincaré governed the three last years of the legislature, from 1921 to 1924. Meanwhile the presidency of the Republic passed through its most grotesque interlude: Clemenceau, the “Father of Victory,” was passed over for the Élysée in favour of Paul Deschanel, the son of a proscribed republican of the Deux-Décembre who had spent his life flirting with the parties of the Right — Deschanel, stricken with madness, climbing the trees of the Élysée garden and throwing himself from the carriage of a train, to be replaced within months by Millerand. The Bloc, victorious in the name of order and national reconstruction, was nevertheless a regime of precarious ministries, financial difficulty and a presidency that could not hold its own dignity.
The fall of the Bloc
The turning came with the elections of 11 May 1924. Against the Bloc, which had taken on an ever more conservative character and had subjected itself to the financial powers, there rose under the impulse of Painlevé and Édouard Herriot a Cartel des gauches — a Cartel of the Left formed of the radicals, radical-socialists, socialist republicans and united socialists. Siegfried calls the election a bifurcation, an essential turning of our political history since the war — an election of opinion, whose result, unexpected at the time, appears easily explicable in retrospect. The intervention in the Ruhr had troubled the spirit of peace and an opinion instinctively hostile to it; the growing organisation and concentration of industry and the bank offended the jealous individualism of the democracy; opinion believed, wrongly, that it saw an alliance forming between nationalism and capital, just when the business world was beginning to understand that it would have more to gain than to lose in a policy of pacific compromise; and the crisis of the franc in March 1924, with its heavy new taxes and its decree-power over the administration, had driven the threatened fonctionnaires into passionate opposition.
The Cartel triumphed on the whole line in 1924, counting some 320 of its own in the new legislature. Millerand, who at the Élysée had wished to keep a militant attitude and who, months before the elections at a ceremony at Évreux, had pronounced a resounding discourse in praise of the Bloc national, was directly struck by the ballot. The radicals and socialists demanded his resignation, evoking the precedent of the republican majority of 1877 and declaring that Millerand was no longer qualified to name the president of the Council; the Senate by 154 votes against 144 and the Chamber by 320 against 214 refused all communication with any ministry he formed. Millerand bowed, Gaston Doumergue was elected president, and Herriot formed a ministry on the policy of the Cartel. The Bloc national was dead, and the republic had turned, as Zévaès closes his narrative, from one coalition of impotence to another — for Bloc national and Cartel des gauches, face to face with the same difficulties, bore witness, he writes, to the same powerlessness.

concepts/catalan-question.title: Catalan question
concepts/catalan-question.content:
Catalan question
The Catalan question was the problem of the place of Catalonia within Spain — the demand of a distinct people, with its own language and its own economic life, for the recognition of its national personality and the government of its own affairs. It was, in the judgment of one observer, perhaps the most difficult but also the most fertile of the questions of the regional resurgence that Spain carried into the twentieth century, and for the Republic of 1931 it was the test of the new regime’s will to answer the plurality of the peninsula. The Republic answered it with a statute of autonomy and a Generalidad that governed Catalonia; and when the autonomy was suspended after the insurrection of October 1934, the question returned in the form of a constitutional crisis that the Republic could neither resolve nor escape, and that drove the statesman who had led the Republic at its height to the ships of his detention off Barcelona.
The national fact
The Catalan question rested on a distinct nationhood. At the beginning of the nineteenth century the national spirit of Catalonia was dead — the peasantry kept the language, and a corruption of it reigned among the urban crowd — but the century of industry and the Catalan resurgence reawakened it, and by the twentieth century Catalonia was a modern nation with a language, a literature and an economic life that the rest of Spain did not share. The regionalist movement had pressed the matter in the Cortes of the monarchy — the Lliga of Cambó, the statutes of the Mancomunidad — but it was under the Republic that the claim came to its head. The psychological and historical aspects of the question were interwoven: the Catalanist read the common past as his own, and the demand for autonomy was at once a demand for justice, for language and for the recognition of a distinct personality that no central government of Madrid had ever conceded.
Autonomy under the Republic
The Republic proclaimed in April 1931 had promised to answer the plurality of Spain, and Catalonia was the first and the largest of the claims upon it. In the first days of the regime, the general in command at Barcelona, Francesc Macià, proclaimed the Catalan State in the name of the people of Catalonia, and the provisional government of the Republic negotiated the concession of a statute of autonomy in its place. The statute was carried through the constituent Cortes, and Catalonia received a Generalidad — a government and parliament of its own — with the competence over the language, the schools and the agrarian life of the country. The statute was the fruit of the partnership of the Catalan republicans with the government of Azaña, who made the reconciliation of the Republic and Catalonia one of his first and most personal works.
October 1934
The Catalan autonomy did not outlive the first biennium. When the conservative coalition of 1933 turned the Republic to the right, and when in October 1934 the CEDA entered the government, the Generalidad — alarmed that the turn to the right would destroy the statute and the land law it had enacted — joined the socialist protest and proclaimed, on the night of 6 October, the Catalan State within the Spanish Federal Republic. The Republic’s government answered by declaring a state of war and crushing the revolt under martial law; the statute of autonomy was suspended and the Generalidad’s leaders were imprisoned. The rebellion was the turning of the Catalan question into a constitutional crisis: Azaña, who happened to be in Barcelona and had had no part in the rising, was arrested on 8 October and held on the ships off the city, and his own account of those days, Mi rebelión en Barcelona, was written from the prison ships to answer the charge that he had instigated the rebellion he had in fact deplored. The episode split the Republic: the repression of October, and the campaign that sought not to defeat Azaña but to annihilate him, poisoned the remainder of the conservative biennium.
The question in 1936
With the victory of the Popular Front in February 1936, the suspended statute of autonomy was restored and the Catalan prisoners, including the Generalidad’s president Lluís Companys, were released. The Catalan question seemed for a moment answered; but the summer of 1936 carried the Republic into civil war, and the autonomy of Catalonia was swallowed by the war itself. In the republican zone Catalonia became one of the great theatres of the revolution and of the internal politics of the Popular Front, and the Generalidad of Companys governed beside the armies and the committees that the war had thrown up. The Catalan question, which the Republic had set out to settle in the years of its peace, ended by being settled by the war — dissolved in the revolution of the republican zone, and then abolished by the dictatorship of Franco, which made the unification of Spain and the suppression of the Catalan language part of the founding work of its regime.

concepts/corporate-state.title: The Corporate State
concepts/corporate-state.content:
The Corporate State
The corporate state (stato corporativo) is the organisation of the Italian Fascist state by which the economy and the professions were regrouped, not as free associations of capital and labour in conflict, but as organs of the nation itself. Under this conception the employers and the workers of each branch of production were brought together into a single body — the corporation (corporazione) — whose task was not to arbitrate a struggle between two hostile classes but to direct the whole branch toward the national interest, under the guidance of the state. The regime presented the corporate order as the fulfilment of its revolution: the replacement of the class war and of liberal laissez-faire by a unified, disciplined and organic economy. The two principal sources of this wiki, Volpe’s History of the Fascist Movement and Pini’s Storia del Fascismo, describe the building of this order in the years after 1925, with the syndical law of 1926 and the Labour Charter at its core.
Syndicalism and the state
The corporate state grew out of the Fascist movement’s own syndicalism. Even before the seizure of power, the Fasci had begun to organise labour not against but across the line of class, and Volpe’s History records the Fascist syndicalism and the Confederations — the Lavoro d’Italia, founded in April 1922 and directed by the syndicalist Edmondo Rossoni — through which the movement sought to draw the workers into the national community. The intention was to overcome the division of society into hostile classes, the very division upon which both liberal economics and Marxist revolution rested. Pini’s chronicle, in its chapter on the conquest of the state, treats the Fascist economy and the syndical organisation as part of the same work of reconstruction by which the regime, after the decisive act of 3 January 1925, remade the institutions of the country. The corporate idea, in these accounts, is the positive programme of that reconstruction: not the suppression of the workers but their incorporation, as Italians, into the organs of the nation’s productive life.
The syndical law of 1926 and the Labour Charter
The juridical foundation of the corporate state was laid in the years 1926–1927. Volpe, in his chapter on the reform of the state, describes the syndical law of 3 April 1926 — drawn up with Giuseppe Bottai — by which the state recognised a single syndicate (one trade union) for each category of employers and workers, and through which the Corporations were constituted. The same law established the National Council of Corporations, authorised to bring together the representatives of the syndicates under the eye of the state. The Labour Charter (Carta del Lavoro), proclaimed in 1927, set out the principles of the new economic order: labour in all its forms is a social duty; the nation is the end and the means of production; and the state, as the organ of the nation, supervises and directs the economy. Pini treats both measures in his chapter on the conquest of the state, as the central documents of the Fascist economy and the syndical organisation. In the regime’s own framing the Charter and the law together replaced the class struggle with a corporate discipline in which the interest of each trade was subordinated to the interest of the nation.
The accord of liberty and authority
Volpe presents the corporate structure as an accord between liberty and authority. The corporations were not, in his account, a mere state command over the economy, but a reconciliation: the liberty of the syndicates to organise their own category was preserved, yet it was bound within the authority of the state, which held the whole in a unity that the conflict of classes had made impossible. The result was an economy conceived as an organic body — each corporation a member, the state the directing head — rather than as a battlefield of opposed interests. This is the sense in which the regime could claim the corporate state as a “revolution”: it had transcended the two great errors of the modern world, the liberal atomisation of society and the Marxist division of it into classes, and had substituted the nation. Volpe, writing in 1936, counts the corporate organisation of 1933–34, which carried the structure to its full development, as the chief accomplishment of the two years that had passed since his original study.
The fulfilment of the revolution
In the sources the corporate state appears not as a separate department of the regime but as the consummation of Fascism itself. Pini’s chronicle closes with the Fascist state as the latest-formed of the European states, already realising its imperial future; the corporate order is presented as the form that Fascism gave to Italian life, the proof that the movement had done more than seize power — it had built a new national constitution of society. Volpe’s final chapter offers the corporate state to Europe as the model of the new order that the other nations must learn from Fascism. The Labour Charter and the Corporations are thus the regime’s answer to the question of what Fascism was for: the unity of the nation made flesh in the ordering of its work. What the sources describe is the regime’s own ideal of itself — the corporate state as the triumph of the organic national community over both the class war and the individualist market.

concepts/cult-of-personality.title: The Cult of the Personality
concepts/cult-of-personality.content:
The Cult of the Personality
The cult of the personality (культ личности, kul’t lichnosti) is the devotion paid to the leader in the Soviet order of the Stalin era — the public veneration of Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin as the disciple and successor of Lenin, the architect of socialism, and the Supreme Commander who led the Soviet people to victory. The two sources gathered here are themselves instruments of that devotion: the official Short Biography of 1948, issued by the Institute of Marx–Engels–Lenin under the Central Committee and closing with the encomium that “Stalin is Lenin today,” and the collected volume of Stalin’s wartime addresses, orders and toasts, which presents the war as the work of the leader and of the people who were one with him. In the official self-account this veneration is not a personal vanity but the natural and fitting honour owed to the man who embodied the party, the doctrine and the nation.
The leader and his life
The Short Biography gives the cult its form by making Stalin’s life identical with the history of the party. Born in Gori, schooled at the Tiflis theological seminary, converted to Marxism in his youth, and driven into the underground by arrest and exile — the biography traces him through the congresses of the underground party, the work on Pravda and in the Duma faction, and the years in the Turukhansk region, until the October Revolution and the civil war brought him to the centre of power. Through every stage he appears as the faithful builder of the Bolshevik party of a new type and the closest collaborator of Lenin; after Lenin’s death and illness the biography presents his succession as the continuation of Lenin’s work and his defeat of the oppositions — the Trotskyists, the “rightists,” the Bukharinists — as the defence of the Leninist line against its enemies. The biographical portrait is thus a political statement: the leader is not a man among men but the incarnation of the general line, and to honour him is to honour the cause.
Stalin is Lenin today
The biography reaches its fullest expression in the closing encomium of the Stalin era, the formula that “Stalin is Lenin today” (Сталин — это Ленин сегодня). The phrase gathers up the whole cult: the leader is the living successor of the founder, and the revolution that Lenin began is continued and completed in the person of Stalin. The same portrait extends the veneration to every sphere of his activity — he is the author of the doctrine in practice, the organiser of industrialisation and collectivisation, the architect of the 1936 Constitution, the teacher of the party, the friend of the peoples of the USSR, and, in the war years, the Generalissimo. The cult, in these pages, is total: it joins the personal and the political, the military and the ideological, the Russian and the universal, into a single image of the leader as the necessary and sufficient cause of the Soviet achievement.
The leader and the nation at war
The wartime volume, On the Great Patriotic War of the Soviet Union, carries the same devotion into the years of danger. Every order of the Supreme Commander is signed “Верховный Главнокомандующий, Генералиссимус Советского Союза, И. Сталин,” and the collection frames the war as the struggle of the Soviet people under their leader against the fascist aggressor. In the address of 9 May 1945 Stalin salutes the Soviet people as the true bearers of the victory — “a people of extraordinary patience” — and in the toast speech of 24 May 1945 he raises his glass to the Russian people as “the most outstanding nation of all the nations forming the Soviet Union.” The cult here fuses the leader with his people: the victories are his orders and their sacrifices together, and the reverence for the leader and the pride of the nation are one movement. It is this union — of leader, party, doctrine and people — that the concept names, and that the official sources of the period present not as a cult but as the natural devotion of a grateful and victorious people to the man who embodied their cause.
The concept in its era
The cult of the personality, as the sources embody it, is the highest development of the theme that runs through all the Stalin-era accounts of Soviet history: the leader as the necessary agent of the revolution. It is inseparable from the doctrine of Marxism–Leninism, which the Short Course presents as the science of the party, and from the party of a new type, which the biography shows Stalin building in the underground; it is the personal face of the party’s leadership, just as the five-year plans are its economic face. In the official self-account of the years before any qualification of the cult, the veneration of Stalin is the crown of the whole construction — the recognition, by a people who had built socialism and won a great war, of the man who led them. The concept is thus best understood as the regime understood it: not as a departure from Marxism–Leninism but as its fulfilment in the person of the leader.

concepts/era-of-tyrannies.title: Era of Tyrannies
concepts/era-of-tyrannies.content:
Era of Tyrannies
The era of tyrannies (l’ère des tyrannies) is the name the French historian and liberal philosopher Élie Halévy gave to the age that, in his reading, opened in August 1914 and came to dominate the interwar decades — the age of Italian Fascism, German National Socialism and Russian Bolshevism, the three great dictatorial movements that together transformed the modern state. The phrase, drawn from his closing essay of 1936 and given to the posthumous volume of 1938, holds that these regimes were not, as they were often presented in the democracies, simple reactions against the French Revolution and its liberal inheritance. They were continuations and radical transformations of the very era of revolutions, reshaped by the total war and total revolution of 1914–1918 into something the nineteenth century had never known: the “organised” state, and in Russia the totalitarian state, which mobilises the whole nation for war and revolution alike.
The dating of the age
Halévy dated his era precisely. “L’ère des tyrannies date du mois d’août 1914” — the era of tyrannies dates from the month of August 1914 — he declared at the outset of the lecture he delivered to the Société française de Philosophie, and the words gave the collected volume of his essays its title. The dating mattered, for it located the origin of the new tyranny not in any single coup or seizure of power — not in the March on Rome of 1922, not in the appointment of the German Chancellor in January 1933 — but in the outbreak of the First World War, the event that by its strain and its total character set loose the twin forces of total war and total revolution. It was the war, in Halévy’s analysis, that broke the constitutional order of the European states, that strained every government into mobilising its whole population and its whole economy, and that produced, in Russia, the first great revolutionary rupture of the age. The movements that came after — Fascism, National Socialism, and in its own fashion Bolshevism — were the heirs of that rupture, not the enemies of everything the eighteenth century had begun.
Continuation, not reaction
The heart of the thesis was the insistence that the tyrannies belonged to the revolutionary tradition rather than against it. Against the common view of the democracies, which regarded Fascism and National Socialism as the liquidation of the French Revolution’s legacy of liberty, equality and fraternity, Halévy argued that they were continuations of the “era of revolutions” itself. Socialism, which had begun in the nineteenth century as the enemy of the state, the critic of its power and its wars, had ended in alliance with a strengthened and dictatorial state; the revolutionary energy that had once been directed against governments was now channelled through governments of a new and terrible kind. In this the great movements of the twentieth century recalled the old tyrannies of antiquity and the revolutionary dictatorship of 1793 — the France of the Committee of Public Safety and of the Terror, which had also fused revolutionary fervour with the concentration of state power. The difference was the scale and the completeness made possible by total war: where the revolutionary state of 1793 had mobilised France against Europe, the tyrannies of the twentieth century organised entire peoples, their economies, their thought and their very souls, behind the single will of the movement.
War and revolution together
The synthesis of Halévy’s analysis lay in the mutual reinforcement of war and revolution. In his interpretation of the world crisis of 1914–1918, which the volume places immediately before the closing essay, he traced two movements that fed each other: the movement towards revolution, by which the strain of the war drove the European states, and above all Russia, towards the overthrow of their old orders, and the movement towards war, by which the crisis of the pre-war decades and the war itself produced the conditions in which totalitarian movements could arise. War drove revolution, and revolution in turn demanded war — or at least demanded the permanent mobilisation of the nation that war had made habitual. The organised state of the twentieth century was the product of this convergence: it was a state built for war, that maintained the discipline of war in time of peace, and that treated its own people as a resource to be commanded for the struggle. This is why Halévy saw the era of tyrannies as a distinct and new phenomenon, born of the fusion of total war and total revolution, and not as a simple replay either of the old absolutisms or of the liberal constitutionalism of the nineteenth century.
The three tyrannies
The three movements that embodied the era presented themselves, from their own sides, in exactly the language of mobilisation and totality that Halévy diagnosed from without. In Italy, the movement of the camicie nere (the blackshirts), as its own chroniclers recounted it, had been forged in the intervention crisis and the war itself — the Rivoluzione fascista of Alberto Businelli told the story of the young Fascists, veterans of the trenches and of the Futurist arditi, who carried the war’s energies into the struggle against the postwar order and marched on Rome in 1922 to seize the state for the nation. In Germany, the programme of Mein Kampf made the state an instrument of race and of the movement, rejected the parliamentary order in the name of the leader-principle, and demanded the total organisation of the people behind the Führer; the official record of the seizure of power presented the year 1933 as the conquest and consolidation of a wholly new state, and the völkisch enthusiasm of a tract such as Die Seele des Dritten Reiches hailed the revolution as a renewal of the whole German soul. And in Russia, as the third and most complete case, the revolutionary state that the Bolsheviks had built out of 1917 carried the logic of total organisation furthest of all, becoming in Halévy’s terms the totalitarian state proper. From the vantage of the liberal democracies, which the collection’s French essays defended, all three stood as warnings of what the modern state became when it was put wholly in the service of war and revolution.
The meaning of the era
For Halévy, who died in 1937 before the second war that his analysis had foreseen, the era of tyrannies was above all a question posed to the democracies and to the liberal tradition he had spent his life studying. The growth of the state, which he had traced through English history and English socialism, had culminated in a state that consumed society; the reconciliation of the classes by peaceful reform, the English way that he set against the continental pattern of revolution, now stood against the European tide. The essay thus functions, within this wiki, as the democratic diagnosis of the very forces that the Russian, German and Italian sources celebrate from within — the liberal account of the totalitarian state, written on the eve of the Second World War, against which the revolutionary self-narratives of the three movements are measured.

concepts/espionage-wwii.title: Espionage in the Second World War
concepts/espionage-wwii.content:
Espionage in the Second World War
Espionage — the secret gathering of an enemy’s military and political knowledge by concealed agents, the secret war fought alongside the visible one — was raised by the Second World War to an instrument of mass organization. The wartime chronicler Kurt Singer, who had tracked Axis agents as a newspaperman since 1933 and was consulted by Allied agencies, presented the secret services of both sides as great organized systems as much as collections of individuals. Modernized espionage, he wrote in 1945 while the conflict was still ending, had become a war of its own, and he warned that no victory would ever disband it: “There will always be human material for spies and traitors.”
The war behind the war
The espionage of the Second World War differed from that of the First in scale and technique. Where the earlier war had rested on individual agents — the dancer Mata Hari, in Singer’s telling, was recruited by the young naval officer who would become Admiral Canaris — the new war was waged by standing services of the great powers, each with its networks, its radio, its saboteurs and its counter-espionage screens. Singer’s chapters follow the German Abwehr under Admiral Wilhelm Canaris, the Soviet secret service at Lubianka Street under Lavrenti Beria, the Japanese networks reaching across the Pacific, and the counter-intelligence of the Allies in the United States, Britain, Ireland, Denmark, Scandinavia and Africa. The methods were modern: mass espionage built on pay rolls of hundreds of sub-agents, weather-station outposts in the Arctic, illicit radio stations and the war of the airwaves, sabotage by parachutists and planted explosions, and the fifth columns that prepared a country for occupation from within.
The German Abwehr and Canaris
The thread that runs through the whole book is the German secret service under Canaris, whom Singer called “the mystery man of German espionage” and perhaps the greatest organizer of espionage the world had known. Canaris’s network reached across Europe and far beyond: German consuls stationed near the harbors were often submarine commanders and agents of the Naval Intelligence Service, with hundreds of sub-agents on his pay roll; his hand extended to the Near East, where his chief agent in Iran was the archeologist Max von Oppenheim and his trusted agent Dr. Fritz Grobba poisoned Iraq with anti-British propaganda, and to Athens, whence his agents covered British-held territory from Syria into the Mongolian desert, communicating by desert caravans fitted with ultra-short-wave receivers. The Abwehr’s individual exploits, as Singer reported them, ranged from the theft of the French navy’s complete mobilization orders at Munich in 1938 to the sinking of the battleship Royal Oak at Scapa Flow in October 1939, engineered by a trusted agent posing as a Swiss watchmaker.
The networks in the neutral north
The secret war was fought nowhere more intensely than in the neutral and occupied countries of the North. The Abwehr’s Scandinavian chief was Horst von Pflugk-Hartung, who had worked with Canaris in Spain during the First World War and had shot Rosa Luxemburg in the revolution of 1919; by 1940 he had marshalled seven hundred and fifty assistants across Norway, Sweden and Denmark, “from harbor pilots to fishermen, from shipowners to lighthouse keepers.” In neutral Ireland enemy agents were parachuted in to spread mischief and to work upon her neutrality; in the Baltic the Russians entered Estonia as the espionage of both sides crowded its ports, and in the Arctic German weather stations fought a lonely battle for information on which the submarines depended. The Nazi spy web in Denmark was only the most celebrated of these northern nets, and its collapse marked the turning of the secret war against Germany.
The secret services of the other powers
Opposite the Abwehr stood the secret services of the Allies and of the Axis’s other partners. The Soviet service, centralized under Beria at Lubianka Street in Moscow, had been built by purging and re-inspecting its network across Europe through the 1930s; its spies pursued the strengthening of Russia’s military position against the coming war. The Japanese, Singer recounted, landed saboteurs in the United States and ran their agents even in Harlem, and attempted the same fifth-column work in the lands they drove toward. Against them the Allies raised counter-espionage screens, caught and turned German agents, and in Africa used Free French agents in the campaigns of 1943. Singer, writing under wartime censorship, concealed the names of Allied agents still at work and declared openly that some incidents and dialogue had been reconstructed where documentary proof was wanting; ninety-five per cent of the names and incidents, he insisted, were taken from well-substantiated documents, court records and official statements.
The secret war and the wider conflict
The espionage of the war was not a sideshow but a continuous action interwoven with the campaigns this wiki records: the abwehr’s networks operated across the very countries of interwar Europe — Spain, where Canaris’s agents searched for the vanished Maurice Mercier, the neutral Iberia and the Arab world, Denmark and the Baltic, the Atlantic and the Arctic. For the states that waged it, espionage was the instrument that prepared war, fed the battlefronts with intelligence and carried sabotage into the enemy rear; for the German regime it was inseparable from the political police, and Canaris’s service was to fall to that rivalry. In Singer’s closing warning, the secret services would survive the peace, and the free nations would need to keep their guard against the postwar underground already being planned.

concepts/etrange-defaite.title: L'Étrange Défaite
concepts/etrange-defaite.content:
L’Étrange Défaite
The “strange defeat” — the phrase and the diagnosis of Marc Bloch, the medieval historian and co-founder of the Annales school, for the collapse of France in May and June 1940. Written in a fury in the weeks immediately after the disaster, between July and September 1940, and published posthumously in 1946, L’Étrange Défaite is at once an eyewitness narrative of the rout, an analysis of its causes reaching into the deepest structures of the French army and French society, and a moral examination of conscience. Bloch declared that he wrote not his memoirs but a procès-verbal, an official report of the year 1940, intended for the future researchers who would one day again enjoy the freedom of thought and judgment; and it is as such a report, by a citizen-soldier of the republic’s academic elite, that it stands for this wiki — the French case from the side of the victim and the analyst, the internal diagnosis of the catastrophe from the very regime that the German, Italian and Russian sources present from the totalitarian side.
The witness
Bloch presents himself in the opening chapter with his état civil (civil status) as a witness. To write and teach history, he says, has been for some thirty-four years his trade; and the first duty of the historian, in the phrase of his master Pirenne, is to be interested in life — for without bending over the present it is impossible to understand the past. He was twice a soldier. In August 1914 he began the first war as a sergeant of infantry, almost at the level of the simple soldier, and rose through chef de section and officer of intelligence to captain; in 1939, twenty-one years later, he was mobilised again into the Intelligence staff of the 1st Army. A testimony, he writes, is worth only fixed in its first freshness; and so he writes now, though the pages will long be known only sous le manteau (under the cloak), for his children and for the friends who may one day read them. His heroes are the common people of France — the miners of the Nord and the Pas-de-Calais, whom he names the best warriors of 1914–1918, an aristocracy of honesty and courage.
The deposition of a defeated man
The second chapter, the longest, written first and in the heat of the moment, recounts the collapse as Bloch saw it from within the Intelligence staff. “We have just suffered an incredible defeat. Whose fault is it? The parliamentary regime, the troops, the English, the …” — so the chapter opens, listing the rival recriminations that at once flew up after the disaster. Bloch refuses the facile assignation of blame. His account of the rout is that of a professional historian applying to the present the same habits of criticism, observation and honesty he had brought to old documents: the unreadiness of the high command, its extraordinary slowness to grasp the nature of the war the Germans were fighting, the confusion, the collapse of communications and command, the breakdown of the army as a fighting institution. The Germans had transformed war — the motorised columns, the armoured thrust, the war of movement that devoured distance — and the French command, thinking in the categories of the last war, had not understood it in time. The “strange” of the strange defeat is precisely this gap: a defeat not of courage but of understanding, of preparation, of a military and national mind still fixed in the forms of 1918.
The examination of conscience
The third chapter, written with greater distance after the armistice, turns from the army to the nation, and it is here that Bloch draws the concept to its full reach. In a nation, he writes, no professional body is ever alone responsible; the states-majors worked with the instruments the country had furnished them, lived in a psychological atmosphere they had not entirely created. So the testimony of the soldier must be prolonged into an examination of conscience of the Frenchman. He will be constrained, speaking of his country, not to speak of it only in good terms — it is hard, he says, to have to discover the weaknesses of a sorrowing mother. The arrière (the rear) had much sinned; and what arrière was there, in the old sense? The bombing aircraft and the war of speed had thrown disorder into the whole order of peril, eating distance, and the ordinary man of the rear went on believing in the distinction of the kinds of war. The warnings had not been lacking — the atrocious images of Spain in ruins, the martyred Polish cities — but the propaganda of the enemy had turned even the fear of bombardment to its account, and Paris might perhaps have been defended had the superstition of open cities not so hampered the operations.
Bloch’s indictment is total and measured at once. The professional military caste, the political class, the bourgeoisie with its vieux démon (old demon), the educational system, the whole society that had not prepared itself for total war — all had their part. He refuses the fatal legend of the stab in the back, so propitious to “redressments à rebours and pronunciamientos,” and he measures the defeat against the long history of a nation he refuses to abandon. The manuscript closes at Guéret-Fougères in the Creuse, in July–September 1940; the Testament of 18 March 1941, appended to the volume, affirms, in the face of death, that he was born a Jew, that he felt himself during his whole life above all and very simply French, and that he died as he had lived, a good Frenchman. Bloch himself did not survive the war: stripped of his chair by the Vichy racial laws, he entered the Resistance, was captured, tortured, and shot by the Germans on 16 June 1944 near Lyon.
The meaning of the concept
The strange defeat is thus not merely an account of a military collapse but a diagnosis of a regime and a society — the last judgment of the Third Republic by one of its finest minds. It is the concept that answers, from the moment of catastrophe, the chronicle of drift that Daniel Halévy had written in 1938: the pratique du rien (practice of nothing) of the ruling republic had refused to choose, to prepare, to believe in the force it named as the condition of survival, and the strange defeat was the price of that refusal. Yet Bloch’s is not an indictment of France but of the failure of a particular France to be equal to the war of the twentieth century; his indictment of the regime is inseparable from his faith in the people and in the republic. The strange defeat, for the future researchers to whom he addressed his report, is the witness of a historian who loved truth above all — whose device was Dilexit veritatem, he loved truth — and who understood that only by the severe and honest diagnosis of the disaster could the nation be rebuilt. The concept has become the enduring name of the French collapse of 1940, and of the wider failure of the old parliamentary republic to face the era of total war and total revolution.

concepts/falange-espanola.title: Falange Española
concepts/falange-espanola.content:
Falange Española
The Falange Española (Spanish Phalanx) is the name of the fascist movement that José Antonio Primo de Rivera founded in Spain in the autumn of 1933, and the formation to which the regime that triumphed in the Civil War was to attach its single-party line. Born in the republican years as one among several small groups of the extreme right, it was the Spanish expression of a wider European temper — the cult of the nation, the exaltation of violence, the hostility to parliamentary democracy — yet it remained, through the whole life of the Republic, a marginal and divided force. Its founder, the eldest son of the general who had ruled Spain from 1923 to 1930, supplied the personal symbolism that the other more or less fascist groups lacked; his execution in the first months of the Civil War made him the movement’s martyr; and the Falange’s incorporation into the unified state party of Franco carried his name and his cult into the dictatorship that arose after his death.
The Founder and the Founding
José Antonio Primo de Rivera came to the founding of the Falange by way of his father’s memory. The dictator’s eldest son, born into a family that for three generations had given itself to the army, chose instead the law, and Madariaga, the liberal exile writing from Buenos Aires, found in him an attractive and contradictory man — brave, intelligent, idealistic, with an acute and irrepressible humour that exceeded what a dictator needed, “delicado y en el fondo escéptico,” delicate and at bottom sceptical. His vocation for public life arose, in Tusell’s account, above all from a desire to vindicate the memory of his father, whose regime he saw as a hesitant germ of the fascist ideal he wished to impose upon Spain. Tusell notes that José Antonio interviewed the Italian Duce barely ten days before founding the Falange, and that in the final republican period the movement received a monthly subvention of 50,000 lire through the Italian embassy in Paris.
The Falange Española was founded in October 1933, in an act that appeared in the press as one of “Spanish affirmation” but passed almost unnoticed. Madariaga records it in the same breath as a fact of the republican years and offers his private conviction — never made public by José Antonio — that the founder, unlike the great majority of his followers, thought the final triumph of communism inevitable and judged it best to advance toward it by the authoritarian road of fascism. The movement absorbed the Juntas de Ofensiva Nacional-Sindicalista of Ledesma Ramos, though the union was always conflictive: Ledesma, who wished to radicalise the movement leftward and preferred Garibaldi’s red shirts to Mussolini’s black ones, saw in the Falange only rich young gentlemen, officers retired by the Azaña law, and provincial landowners, and separated from it at the end of 1935.
Movement, Party and Contradiction
The Falange presented itself as more than a party: in the manner of the European fascisms it claimed to be a movement and a faith, the instrument of the nation’s youth against the corruption of the old political world. Tusell stresses, however, that the contradictions of the founder were those of the party. Proclaiming a revolutionary will and a programme of social transformation, it kept patent connections with the high classes: its two 1933 deputies were nobles elected by the most conservative sectors of Cádiz, it was subsidised by monarchists, and the founder himself valued his title of nobility, his knighthood in a military order and the life of the upper classes. Its internal life was marked by divisions, indiscipline and schism from both its left and right wings. Like the far left, the fascist extreme in Spain was a tiny world: Tusell places the Falange at the start of 1936 as a force even more marginal than the communists, its one real success lying in university student circles.
Violence and the Street
The Falange, however hesitant it may have been in taking up systematic violence, became during the second, conservative biennium one of the principal parties practising it. Its language was violent and provocative — provocative precisely because the image of what was happening in other latitudes already existed in Spain — and its street confrontations with the Left could reach murder. The first dead among the Falangist press readers and distributors fell in January 1934; only in June of that year did the Falangists themselves kill, but the possibility existed from the beginning, the membership cards asking whether the applicant had or had not a “bicicleta” (bicycle) — that is, a pistol. Within the movement there was a sector that saw violence as its very reason for being, an armed wing of the Right with no objection to its use. Madariaga, for his part, reads the movement’s character through the founder: José Antonio was too fine, too much the gentleman, too timid at bottom to be a chief, let alone a dictator, and the Falange shared his hesitations. Yet both historians agree on the place of the movement in the approach to catastrophe: fascism and communism, the two totalitarian extremes, could not by themselves have provoked the Civil War; the war arose instead from the collision of the two great Spanish institutions, the army and the workers’ organisations, that embodied the nation’s tradition of violent intervention in politics.
The Martyr and the Unified Party
José Antonio Primo de Rivera was caught in the collapse of the Republic’s order after the rising of July 1936. Imprisoned in Alicante, he remained a prisoner while the war ran its course; Tusell records that the Germans showed little disposition to rescue him and that the Falange’s own influence could not free him. He was executed in November 1936, in the first months of the conflict. His death made him the Falange’s martyr: the removal of his ashes from Alicante to the Escorial, carried across half of Spain, reminded Madariaga of the days when the remains of Queen Isabella had been borne toward Granada, and their burial at the foot of the Escorial’s high altar gave the bishops much to think about, as a symptom of a new spirit not so respectful of traditional Spanish values as it proclaimed. With the unifier of the parties under Franco, the Falange Española Tradicionalista y de las JONS, José Antonio’s name passed into the cult of the new state, his founder’s mystique serving the regime that had arisen after his death and that claimed his movement’s single-party inheritance for its own line.

concepts/fasci-di-combattimento.title: The Fasci di Combattimento
concepts/fasci-di-combattimento.content:
The Fasci di Combattimento
The fighting bands founded at Milan on 23 March 1919 — the founding institution of Italian Fascism and, from the first, its deliberate negation of the party form. The Fasci di combattimento (fighting fasci), from which the whole movement and later the Partito Nazionale Fascista took their name, were created by Benito Mussolini in the hall in Piazza San Sepolcro as an “anti-party,” in Volpe’s phrase — a reaction against the whole mass politics of the postwar, built on youth, impulse and faith rather than on programme or discipline. Where the interventionism of 1914–15 was the moral root of the movement, the Fasci were its first organisation: the banding together, in the ruin of the peace, of the interventionists, the ex-servicemen, the Arditi and the Futurists who had made and fought the war, and who now refused to wait on the liberal state to save the nation.
The anti-party
The Fasci were born in the months when the victory of 1918 seemed to be dissolving into defeat. The demobilised soldiers returned to a country of rising prices, triumphant Socialism and a government at Paris apparently surrendering what the war had been fought to win. Farinacci’s party history of 1919 opens its account with the “collapse of the ruling class” — the verbose and irresolute Orlando at the peace conference, the League of Nations as the “ideal instrument of an iniquitous peace,” the strength of the country diminished and offended by its own government. Against this paralysis, Volpe writes, Mussolini deliberately created an “anti-party”: not a disciplined organisation but a movement, a “policy of the masses” answered with the passion of the few. The word fascio — a band or bundle, drawn from the Latin fasces — was chosen to suggest union and force rather than the machinery of a parliamentary party.
On the morning of 23 March 1919, in the meeting-room in Piazza San Sepolcro, the founders came together: a few hundred interventionists, ex-servicemen, officer-students, Futurists and Arditi. Businelli, himself a young squadrist who had served under Marinetti in the Roman days of 1919, calls it the adunata of Piazza San Sepolcro — the constituent assembly of interventionism, the first victory of the movement. Farinacci stresses the episodes that had convinced the war-veterans that only force could answer the red wave: the occupation at Dalmine, the metalworkers’ seizures in the early months of 1919, and the intervention of the Arditi. From the meeting issued a programme at once revolutionary and national — anti-monarchical in its republicanism, anti-clerical, hostile to the great landowners and the banks, insistent on the rights of the war-winners, demanding a constituent assembly. What held it together, Volpe insists, was not doctrine but the conviction that the old ruling class had failed and that the generation that had made the war must remake the state.
A movement, not a party
The Fasci were deliberately formless — a mood and a weapon rather than an organisation. Volpe’s chapter on the Fascist movement sets out the character of the thing Mussolini had created: youth, impulse, faith, pragmatism, the spirit of the demobilised officers and officer-students, the reaction against the occupation of the factories. From the first the Fasci placed themselves against both the red internationalism of the Socialists and the timid moderation of the liberal ministries. Pini and Bresadola, in their chapter on the founding, frame the birth between “troubled months” and “the defeat at Versailles” — a movement struck out of the double humiliation at home and abroad.
The weeks after San Sepolcro made the bands felt in the streets. In April 1919 came the first open collision in Milan: the assault on the offices of Avanti!, the Socialist daily — an act Farinacci records as the beginning of the civil war and the “prologue of the long drama,” the moment the Fasci answered the insult of defeat with force. The elections of November 1919 were a disaster for the movement — a single deputy, Mussolini himself, elected in Milan against the Socialist flood — yet the chroniclers insist that the seed had been sown. The Fasci were not a parliamentary force but a revolutionary one; their field was the street and the province, not the Chamber.
From band to squadre
The turn of 1920–1921 transformed the Fasci from a Milanese coterie into a nationwide movement. The red biennium — the strikes, the occupation of the factories, the agrarian unrest of the Po valley — supplied the Fasci their opportunity and their mission. Volpe records the reaction against the occupation of the factories as the turning point that drove the middle classes and the ex-servicemen against the red movement for good. Businelli’s “tragic year of recovery” narrates the same season: the red wave, the Fascist reaction, the second adunata of the Fasci. As the Socialist state collapsed into itself at Livorno, the Fasci multiplied, and out of them grew the squadre d’azione — the action squads that carried the punitive expeditions across the provinces. Farinacci, the Cremona ras, was the leader of this provincial squadrism; his account of 1919 is the account of the movement from within its most violent and decisive phase.
The Fasci remained for years what they had been at San Sepolcro — an anti-party, an armed current of opinion rather than a disciplined organisation. Only in 1921, as the movement grew into a mass force, did the decision to transform it into a party come, and even then it was contested. Volpe’s account of the passage from “movement” to “party” centres on the internal strife between the two Mussolinis — the statesman who wanted to build an organisation and the revolutionary who let the squadre loose. The Popolo d’Italia of 2 February 1922 set the course toward a national party, and in October 1922 the Fasci, now hundreds of thousands strong, marched on Rome. Yet in the Fascist self-understanding the party was always a reluctant, secondary form of the founding band: the Fasci di combattimento were the essence, the seed from which the whole state was to grow. The very name of the regime’s institution — the party as fascio, the bundle — preserved the memory of the few hundred believers in the hall at San Sepolcro.

concepts/fascism-italian.title: Italian Fascism
concepts/fascism-italian.content:
Italian Fascism
Fascism (Fascismo) is the movement, the doctrine and the regime that rose in Italy from the interventionism of the First World War and seized power with the March on Rome of October 1922. The name comes from the fascio (bundle), the Roman symbol of strength in union, which the first militants adopted for their bands — the Fasci di combattimento (combat groups) founded at the Piazza San Sepolcro in Milan on 23 March 1919. The four Italian sources in this wiki — the movement-insider origin-story of Alberto Businelli, the academic regime history of Gioacchino Volpe, the official party chronicle of Giorgio Pini and Federico Bresadola, and the exhaustive documentary history of the Cremona boss Roberto Farinacci — together present Fascism as it understood itself from within: a revolution, not a change of government, born of the war, directed against the liberal and socialist order, and carried to power by the energy of its young blackshirts under the will of Benito Mussolini.
The war and the Fasci
All four narratives root the movement in the First World War and the interventionist crisis. Volpe’s History of the Fascist Movement opens the story with the interventionist split of 1914–15, when Mussolini, the editor of Il Popolo d’Italia, broke with the Socialist party and its neutrality to carry the campaign for Italy’s entry into the war. Businelli’s Rivoluzione fascista, prefaced by the futurist Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, recounts the same turn from the Balkan powder-keg of 1912–1914 through the declaration of Italian neutrality in August 1914 and the founding of Il Popolo d’Italia, and celebrates the young Futurist-squadrist energies that answered the call. Farinacci, writing from the radical wing, casts the whole crisis year of 1919 as the collapse of the ruling class — the corruption of the liberal governments and the diplomatic humiliation at Paris — against which the Fasci were the patriotic answer. The war is not, in these accounts, a catastrophe to be repented but the furnace in which the new Italy was forged; the demobilised officers and officer-students whom Volpe names among the movement’s founders carried its temper into the postwar.
The Fasci di combattimento, founded at Milan on 23 March 1919, are treated by every source as the decisive act. Mussolini himself, in these accounts, presented the new formation not as a party but as an “anti-party” — an instrument of the youth, the impulse and the faith that the old political world had lost. Volpe stresses this character of the movement as against the party: it was defined by energy, pragmatism and devotion to the nation rather than by a fixed programme, and its programme, drawn up at the congress of Florence, remained subordinate to the action itself. Farinacci devotes his first volume to the year of the founding, tracing the creation of the Fasci, the assault on the offices of the socialist daily Avanti!, and the place of the Arditi and the interventionists in the new formation. The national humiliation over Fiume and the Adriatic, denied to Italy at the peace conference, supplies the patriotic grievance that the Fasci take up.
The movement, squadrism and the March on Rome
The passage from the parliamentary-political phase of 1919 to the violent phase of 1920–1921 is the turning of the story. Confronted with the red tide of the biennio rosso — the strikes, the agrarian unrest and the occupation of the factories of September 1920 — the Fasci answered with the squadre d’azione (action squads), the armed bands of blackshirts whose punitive expeditions (the spedizioni punitive) broke the Socialist and the labour organisations in the Po valley and the cities. Pini’s chronicle devotes a chapter to the camicie nere and to squadrism, telling how Fascism organised itself in the provinces against the collapse of the liberal order; Farinacci, in the second volume of his Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, presents the “Victory of the Fasci” as the patriotic, anti-Bolshevik answer to the “Red Insurrection” of 1920, and defends the squads as a surgical necessity forced on the nation by the impotence of the state. The movement’s own historians do not soften this violence; they vindicate it, casting it as the reassertion of Italianness against the foreign and the red, and the “drip of blood” (the stillicidio di sangue) of the martyrs as the price of the resurrection.
The March on Rome of October 1922 is the climax every source narrates. Businelli’s sixth chapter, “The Year of Victory,” describes the plan of insurrection, the gathering of the Fasci at Naples on 24 October, and the concentration of the columns upon the capital; Farinacci’s third volume carries the account through the fall of the Giolittian, Bonomi and Facta ministries to the King’s refusal to order a military response and the entry of the blackshirts into Rome on 28 October. Volpe, soberly, records the quadrumvirate of action — Bianchi, De Vecchi, Balbo and General De Bono — given a dictatorial mandate, the massing of a hundred thousand blackshirts, and the King’s summons of Mussolini, who rose to power “by revolutionary means.” In every telling the March is the victory not of an election but of the movement’s own will, the nation’s ideal revolt against a state that could no longer govern.
Fascism at the helm
The sources present the years after 1922 as the consolidation of the regime and the building of a new state. Volpe’s chapter “Fascism at the Helm” records the restoration of order, the return of the state budget to balance, the public works and the agricultural campaign (the battaglia del grano), and the advance of Italy’s place among the nations; Pini’s later chapters carry the story through the “proof” of the Matteotti murder and the Aventine secession of 1924, and then the “Conquest of the State” of 1925–1927 — the dictatorship of 3 January, the works of the regime, the Fascist economy, the syndical organisation and the Labour Charter. The theme, in every account, is that Fascism did not merely hold office but transformed the state: it replaced the old parliamentary liberalism with a unified national order, expressed in the Fascist militia, the party reform, and ultimately the corporate organisation of the economy. Volpe, in his Author’s Note of 1936, surveys what two further years had added — the new cities, the land reclamation, the colonial development, and above all the corporate structure — as the natural fruit of the same revolution.
A doctrine of action
What the sources give is less a doctrine than a temper. Fascism appears as the party of the nation against the parties, the faith of the young against the old, action against talk, sacrifice against interest. Businelli calls the movement’s energy a “bollente fede italiana” (a burning Italian faith); Pini ascribes the state’s formation to popular adhesion, the dedication of martyrs and “the genial and victorious will of Benito Mussolini”; Volpe presents Fascism as a “revolution” that offers itself to Europe, a civilising mission the other nations must learn from. Farinacci, the most polemical, frames it as the revenge of the honest and the patriotic upon a corrupted ruling class. Across all of them runs the conviction that Fascism was not one more party contending for office but the awakening of the Italian nation itself — the latest-formed of the European states, in Pini’s closing words, certain of its imperial future.

concepts/five-year-plans.title: The Five-Year Plans
concepts/five-year-plans.content:
The Five-Year Plans
The five-year plans (пятилетки, pyatiletki) are the national economic programmes by which the Soviet state carried out the socialist industrialisation of the country — the deliberate transformation, within fixed periods of five years, of a backward agrarian land into a great industrial power. In the official account given by the Short Course of the History of the VKP(b), the biography of Stalin and the school textbook of the history of the USSR, the plans are the central acts of the years of socialist construction: the first five-year plan adopted in 1929 and fulfilled in four years, the second plan fulfilled ahead of schedule, and the collectivisation of agriculture that ran beside them. Together they are presented as the material foundation of everything the Soviet order achieved, and as the proof that a planned economy directed by the party could outpace the spontaneous development of capitalism.
The struggle for industrialisation
The background to the plans, in every source, is the decision to industrialise “in historically the shortest possible time” — the phrase the biography of Stalin uses for the years 1926–1929. After the devastation of the civil war and the partial recovery under the New Economic Policy, the party faced the question of whether the Soviet country, encircled by a hostile capitalist world, could build the industry it needed. The Short Course treats this as the period of the “struggle for socialist industrialisation” (социалистическая индустриализация), in which the party had to overcome the difficulties of a backward economy and to defeat those within its own ranks — the Trotskyist-Zinovievist bloc and the Bukharin-Rykov group — who either despaired of the pace or clung to the market. The answer was the plan: to set the whole economy to the single task of building heavy industry — the factories, the power stations, the metallurgical works — that alone could arm and equip a socialist state.
The first five-year plan (первая пятилетка) was adopted amid this struggle, and the Short Course records its launching together with the offensive against the capitalist elements in town and country and the beginning of socialist emulation (социалистическое соревнование) — the competition of workers and brigades to overfulfil their quotas. The plan is presented not as a bookkeeping exercise but as a summons: it mobilised the whole people, and its fulfilment ahead of schedule, “in four years,” is celebrated as a national triumph. The biography of Stalin places this achievement at the centre of its portrait of the leader as the architect of industrialisation, and the school textbook brings the same story to the classroom under the heading of socialist industry and the building of a land of socialism.
Industry, agriculture and the Stakhanovite movement
Industrialisation did not stand alone but demanded the remaking of agriculture. The Short Course narrates the struggle for the collectivisation of agriculture (коллективизация сельского хозяйства) in the years 1930–1934 — the transition from the policy of restricting the kulak elements to the policy of liquidating the kulaks as a class, the gathering of the peasants into collective farms (the kolkhozes), and the opening of political departments at the machine-tractor stations to guide the movement. In the official account this was the indispensable complement of industry: only a collectivised agriculture, organised by the state and served by machinery, could feed the growing industrial cities and release the labour and grain that heavy industry demanded. The school textbook, in its chapters on the USSR as the land of victorious socialism, pairs socialist industry with the collective farms as the two pillars of the new order.
The second five-year plan carried the work forward, and its fulfilment ahead of schedule is recorded by the Short Course alongside the rise of the Stakhanovite movement (стахановское движение), named for the miner who overfulfilled his shift’s quota many times over and became the model of the socialist worker. In these accounts the plan, the cadres and the movement of the workers themselves converge: the Short Course stresses the significance of cadres — of trained people — and presents the masses, once released from the fetters of the old order, as eager to outdo the plan. The years of the second plan are shown bringing the reconstruction of agriculture to completion, the rise of popular welfare and culture, and, crowning the whole construction, the adoption of the new Constitution of 1936, which proclaimed the USSR a land of victorious socialism.
The meaning of the plan
Across all three sources the five-year plans carry the same meaning: they are the proof that a people guided by a Marxist-Leninist party could accomplish in a decade or two what capitalism had taken centuries to build. The plans are thus not merely economic programmes but the demonstration of the superiority of the socialist system — the material base of Soviet power, of the “great friendship of the peoples,” and ultimately of the strength that would be tested in the war to come. The biography of Stalin closes this period with the leader at the head of the whole construction; the school textbook ends its account with the USSR as a land of socialism and its 1936 Constitution. In the official self-account the five-year plans are the hinge of Soviet history — the bridge between the October Revolution and the powerful, united, socialist state that the later pages of these same works describe.
