concepts/four-year-plan.title: Four Year Plan
concepts/four-year-plan.content:
Four Year Plan
The Four Year Plan was the economic programme proclaimed by the Führer’s decree of 18 October 1936, by which the National Socialist state undertook to make the German economy — and above all German armament — independent of the world market within four years. It was the second great plan of the regime’s economic policy, and its object, in the official language of the year, was autarky (self-sufficiency): the independence of a great nation from the world economy. The decree named Hermann Göring to direct the plan, and the measures that followed in the closing months of 1936 — the regulation of prices under a Reich Commissioner for Price Formation, the law against economic sabotage, and the penal tightening of the economic order — show the plan to have been as much an instrument of command and control over the national economy as a programme of production.
The reordering of the economy
The Four Year Plan belongs to a sequence of economic measures that the official documentary volumes of the regime record under the heading of the rebuilding of the economy. The same section of the volume covering 1936 gathers, beside the Führer’s decree of 18 October, the speech in which Göring proclaimed the plan to the people from the Berlin Sportpalast on 28 October, the currency declarations of the Reichsbank president Schacht, and the law of 29 October appointing a Reich Commissioner for Price Formation. The logic of the plan was that a nation of the Reich’s size could not leave the provision of its food and its raw materials to the hazards of foreign trade and foreign exchange, and that the machinery of the state must therefore stand behind the effort to produce at home. In this the plan continued the course that the earlier volumes had already recorded — the organic construction of the economy prepared in 1934 and the regulation of foreign trade by the state — but it carried that course much further, making the rearmament of the Reich the explicit and overriding purpose of economic life.
Autarky and rearmament
The year 1936 saw the outward assertion of the regime on every front, and the Four Year Plan was the economic face of that assertion. In the same year the Reich remilitarized the Rhineland, repudiated the treaty of Locarno, staged the Olympic Games as the spectacle of the new order, and sought in the Anti-Comintern Pact a counterweight to the Soviet system; the official commentaries justified the new economic order as a self-defence against the pressure of the world economy and of a hostile world. The plan was framed to answer the question of war-readiness: it bound the whole economy — industry, agriculture, labour, prices and the currency — to the single task of making Germany strong within four years. The instrument was thus not a budget but a command, and the law against economic sabotage of December 1936 made the obstruction of the plan’s fulfilment a crime against the state. Within the same programme the colonial demand acquired its economic point: Schacht, in an essay that the volume records, argued that Germany’s need for raw materials and for land to feed its people could not be satisfied within the borders left to it by the peace, and that the colonial question was therefore a question of the people’s bread and of its economic existence.
The war economy
What the plan launched in 1936 reached its logical and grimmer consummation in the war years, when the same machinery of economic direction was turned wholly to armament. It is this later development that Speer, as the armaments minister from 1942, records from the inside — the organization of the whole economy for the production of war material, the rivalries of the party chiefs over the direction of industry, the improvisations by which output was forced upward, and the technical war in which the state’s command over the economy, first proclaimed in 1936, was exercised to its extreme. The plan of 1936 thus stands at the head of a road that leads from the economic reconstruction of the peace years to the armaments economy of the war; in the regime’s own telling it was the act by which the economy was subordinated to the political will of the Führer, and by which the Reich prepared, within the span of four years, to hold its own against the world.

concepts/francoist-dictatorship.title: Francoist Dictatorship
concepts/francoist-dictatorship.content:
Francoist Dictatorship
The Francoist dictatorship (la dictadura de Franco) is the regime that Francisco Franco established over Spain with the victory of the Nationalist side in the Civil War and that ruled the country from the last war bulletin of 1 April 1939 to the dictator’s death in November 1975. The Spanish historian Javier Tusell, who wrote the definitive scholarly synthesis of the regime, treats it as a dictatorship without making it a Spanish peculiarity: Franco’s conceptions and behaviour, he argues, expressed a wider European type rather than a unique national path. The regime had three subjects, in Tusell’s framing — the person of the dictator, the regime as a dictatorship, and the society that lived under it — and it passed through long phases: the fascist temptation and wartime foreign policy of 1939–51, the years of consensus and economic opening of 1951–65, and the tardofranquismo, the last decade of 1966–75 dominated by the aging dictator’s decline. Madariaga, writing from exile in the early years, called the period covered by his closing book “lo que va de mal vivir la dictadura del General Franco” — so far of the hard living under General Franco’s dictatorship.
The Dictator and the Type of the Regime
Against the tendency to reduce the regime to a psychological portrait of its founder, Tusell sets Franco’s biography and his long political practice, neither inflating the regime into pure personalism nor dissolving it into impersonal structure. Franco, a career officer who had made his name in the Moroccan wars, rose during the Civil War from a general among generals to the single head of the national movement, and at the head of the state he had won he ruled as a personal dictator. The regime he founded is defined, in Tusell’s analysis, as a dictatorship of a distinct European type — authoritarian and personal, drawing on the fascist forms of the age but never identical with them, its fascistisation always incomplete. The traits that the regime itself made the centre of rumour and expectation — the cult of the Caudillo (leader), the single party, the control of press and association — were real, but they expressed a personal and traditionalist authoritarianism as much as a totalitarian ambition.
Victory, Repression and Exile
The regime opened, on the night of 1 April 1939, with the reading of the last official war bulletin — “cautivo y desarmado” the Red Army, Franco’s troops at their last objectives — and the vivas to the exterior allies of the three preceding years, Portugal, Italy and Germany. Its foundation was a victory won by force of arms, and it never lost that character. Tusell records the torrents of blood that the “Año triunfal” chose to forget, the destruction of wealth, and the sediment of rancour; on the defeated, after 1 April 1939, fell a repression that marked the whole first decade of the regime. The exile of 1939 was, in his judgment, a rupture in Spanish history — larger, longer and more severed from the reality of the interior than any earlier Spanish emigration. Madariaga’s threefold account of the dictator’s task — to remake the national soul, to remake the national body, and to carry the ship of state on a dangerous course — captures the interior labour of those years.
The Fascist Temptation and the Postwar
The first long phase of the regime, from 1939 to 1951, was what Tusell calls the period of tentación fascista, the fascist temptation. From the end of the war to the summer of 1940 Spain drifted toward homologation with the Axis — adhesion to the Anti-Comintern, abandonment of the League of Nations — while its “fascistisation” remained incomplete; from 1940 to 1942 came the interventionist temptation of entry into the world war, against which the actual wartime neutrality of the dictator must be read. After 1945 the regime faced simultaneous dangers: the uncertainty of its internal course, an opposition aiming at rupture or peaceful transition, and an external isolation born of its wartime stance. It responded with what Tusell calls the cambio cosmético — a cosmetic change without substantial transformation — and passed through the “noche oscura” (dark night) of autarky and rationing in the 1940s, an economic isolation whose first postwar pressure only began to lift with the early-1950s growth of national income and the end of the ration book in 1951.
Consensus, Apogee and Decline
The central years, 1951 to 1965, were for Tusell the years of consensus and the apogee of the regime — a dictatorship stable enough that passive social acceptance could be called consensus, explained by repression and the dismantling of the opposition, and consolidated abroad by the Concordat with the Holy See and the pacts with the United States of 1953, which ended the international isolation. The last decade, 1966 to 1975, was dominated more than any earlier phase by Franco’s person in decline. The regime named Juan Carlos as successor, adopted a Press Law and loosened its controls in the apertura (opening) without transforming itself; the aging dictator, past seventy-five, increasingly failed in his old arbitral role among the families of the regime, presided over the governments of Carrero Blanco and then Arias Navarro, and obstinately remained in power until his death in November 1975. Madariaga’s early verdict, that the regime’s foreign policy proved in its whole less bad than its interior policy, stands as the contemporary liberal judgment on the first phase of a dictatorship that was to outlive the world war by three decades.

concepts/fuhrerprinzip.title: The Führerprinzip
concepts/fuhrerprinzip.content:
The Führerprinzip
The leadership principle — the doctrine, set out in Hitler’s Mein Kampf and analysed by his contemporary biographer Konrad Heiden, that authority flows downward from an absolute chief and that every subordinate answers to his superior while being relieved of responsibility toward those below. The Führerprinzip (leadership principle) is the organising idea of the National Socialist movement and, once power was seized, of the state itself: the negation of the parliamentary and majority principle in favour of personality, absolute command, and unconditional obedience. It is at once a theory of authority and a machine for binding men together — the doctrinal form of the relationship between Hitler and his followers that Heiden anatomises as “the age of irresponsibility.”
Personality against the majority
The doctrine of the Führerprinzip is laid down in the second volume of Mein Kampf, above all in the chapter “Persönlichkeit und völkischer Staatsgedanke” (Personality and the völkisch Idea of the State). Hitler sets the principle of the majority against the principle of personality. The parliamentary-democratic state, he argues, rests on the rule of the majority — on numbers, averages and mediocrity — and in so doing dissolves leadership and responsibility into the anonymous vote. The völkisch state, by contrast, rests on personality: the creative individual who perceives the goal, decides, and takes responsibility, and the absolute authority that is conceded to him. Where democracy says that decisions are made by the counting of heads, National Socialism says they are made by the leader’s will.
This is not merely an organisational preference but a doctrine of the racial world. In Mein Kampf the state exists to preserve and advance the racial people, and the preservation of the race is the work of its best — the creative personalities in whom the people’s spirit is most fully present. Authority is therefore not a burden to be shared but a force to be concentrated in the man who embodies the people’s will. The Führer is the representative of the race, not the delegate of a constituency; he owes his authority not to election but to his perception of the goal and his power to command. The mass, in this doctrine, is not the source of authority but the material on which the personality acts — to be led, moulded and saved.
The movement as the machine of obedience
In the movement itself the Führerprinzip was the form of organisation. Mein Kampf insists that a worldview, once accepted, must conquer the state through an organisation bound to it — and that organisation is built on the absolute authority of the leader, descending in an unbroken chain of command to the last man. Each subordinate answers to his superior and to him alone; each is absolved of responsibility for the whole, obeying the command that comes from above. The party Hitler built embodied this: the storm troopers of the SA, the brown-shirted Sturmabteilung (storm detachment), the district leaders (Gauleiter) bound to the Munich centre, the whole structure radiating downward from the Führer. The spoken word, which Mein Kampf makes the primary instrument of the movement, is the voice by which the leader’s will reaches the mass.
Heiden, who observed the movement from its meetings in 1922, gives the sharpest contemporary account of what the Führerprinzip actually meant in practice. In the chapter of his biography devoted to “Propaganda und Organisation” he describes the art of the movement’s growth — wit, logic and insolence, the symbols, the listener made into a collaborator — and locates the leadership principle at its centre. His gloss is devastating: the Führerprinzip meant, for everyone, “relief from responsibility through an absolute supreme authority — security and moral comfort.” The subordinate obeyed and was comforted; he had no need to think, decide or answer for the consequences. But, Heiden insists, when responsibility downward was abolished, responsibility was abolished altogether: the chain of absolute command ended in the absolute ruler, who answered to no one, and the system of uncontrolled authority issued in despotism and the rule of favourites. What the doctrine promised as security was, in his reading, the very abdication of responsibility that made the “age of irresponsibility” possible.
From movement to state
The Führerprinzip, born in the party, became the principle of the state once power was seized in 1933. The official documentary record of the regime presents the rebuilding of state, economy and law in the language of the leadership principle — the law on the formation of the state, the Gleichschaltung (coordination) of the Länder under Reich governors, the concentration of authority in Hitler’s person. The completion of the process was the union of the offices of President and Chancellor in Hitler’s own person on the death of President von Hindenburg in August 1934, when Hitler took the title Führer und Reichskanzler and the Wehrmacht swore its oath to him — the moment at which the leadership principle of the movement became the constitution of the state. The Reichstag, which had voted its power away in the Enabling Act of 1933, was reduced to an echo; the chain of absolute command ran from the Führer to the last official of the Reich.
Heiden closes his biography with the cost of that concentration. The state built on the Führerprinzip was, he writes, an “unplanned dictatorship” that ended in the bloody settling of accounts of 30 June 1934 — the purge of the SA chief of staff Ernst Röhm and the shootings of Schleicher and Gregor Strasser, in which Hitler, contradicting himself, moved with armoured cars and pistol against his own following. The absolute authority that relieved men of responsibility had ended by taking the responsibility of deciding who should live and die into the hands of one man. Heiden’s final image is the urn of ashes handed to the brother of a Munich lawyer shot on the evening of 30 June — “the ashes of the unknown German who fell victim to the highest responsibility assumed on 30 June.” The Führerprinzip, in his reading, was the doctrine that transferred all responsibility to a single man, and that man answered to nothing but his own will.
The principle and its meaning
The Führerprinzip stands at the centre of National Socialist doctrine as the negation of everything the Weimar Republic represented. Against the majority principle of parliament it sets the personality of the leader; against the diffusion of responsibility in democratic government it sets absolute, concentrated command; against the freedom of the citizen it sets obedience and relief from the burden of choice. Hitler’s own text gives it the form of a racial and völkisch necessity; Heiden gives it the form of a social pathology — the security and moral comfort of the man who has given up his responsibility. Both are necessary to understand it: the doctrine as it presented itself, and the doctrine as its opponents experienced it. It is the principle by which a mass movement was bound to a single will, and by which that will was afterwards let loose on the state.

concepts/gleichschaltung.title: Gleichschaltung
concepts/gleichschaltung.content:
Gleichschaltung
Gleichschaltung (coordination — literally the bringing of the state, the people, the economy and the law into the same gear as the party) was the forcible alignment of every institution of German public life with the National Socialist movement in the years 1933–1934. The word names not a single law but a process: the dismantling of the federal and parliamentary order of the republic and its replacement by the one-party, leader-state that the official documentary record of the regime presented under the heading of the Neuordnung von Staat, Volk, Wirtschaft, Kultur und Recht — the reordering of state, people, economy, culture and law.
The end of the party state
The process opened within months of Hitler’s appointment as Reich Chancellor on 30 January 1933. The decree for the protection of people and state, issued in the aftermath of the Reichstag fire, suspended the constitutional guarantees upon which opposition could rest; the election of 5 March returned a Reichstag in which the new government commanded a majority; and on 23 March the assembled Reichstag passed the Enabling Act, by which the government received the power to legislate itself. From that point the documentary record of the first volume of the official Dokumente der deutschen Politik traces the progressive extinction of plural politics. The law against the formation of new parties of 14 July 1933 made the National Socialist German Workers’ Party the sole bearer of political will in the state; the offices and organizations of the old order were drawn into the movement or dissolved; and the Reichsstatthalter law of the same spring placed the administration of the Länder, the member states of the Reich, under commissioners answerable to the central power. What the editor of the volume framed as the conquest of power was, in administrative terms, the end of the party state.
The new constitution of the Führer-state
The second year of the regime completed what the first had begun, and the theme of the second volume of the official series is accordingly the construction of the leader-state itself. The law on the reconstruction of the Reich of 30 January 1934 transferred the sovereign rights of the Länder to the Reich; the Reichsrat, the old upper house of the federal states, was abolished in February; and the administration of justice was drawn up into the Reich. In the same consolidation the office of the head of state passed, on the death of Reich President Hindenburg in August 1934, to the Führer and Reich Chancellor, and the plebiscite of 19 August asked the German people to ratify the union of the two offices in one man. The Gleichschaltung of the law was sealed by the oaths of soldiers, civil servants and ministers sworn to Hitler personally, and by the Heimtückegesetz of December 1934, which made malicious attack upon the state and the party a punishable offence. The volumes present each of these acts not as the abolition of an old order but as the positive construction of a new one — the building of the Reich’s unity out of the fragments of the federal republic.
People, economy and culture
The same movement reached into the social body. The labour constitution was rewritten by the law for the ordering of national labour of January 1934, which set the employer at the head of the enterprise and the whole of the working class beneath a leader in the figure of the German Labour Front; the trustees of labour, the Treuhänder der Arbeit, had been introduced already in the first year of the regime to regulate the wage and the work-place. The economy was to be brought into organic construction by the law of February 1934, which prepared the grouping of German industry into estates under the state, while the peasantry was bound to the soil by the agrarian laws and the battle for production. Culture was gathered into the Reich Chamber of Culture under the law of September 1933, and the constitution of German art of February 1934 made the party’s taste the measure of what might be shown or sung. Even the churches and the schools were drawn into the reordering. Across all these fields runs the formula that titles the third part of each Friedrichs volume — the reordering of state, people, economy, culture and law — and it is this formula, repeated year after year, that gives the concept of Gleichschaltung its official shape: not a single decree but the comprehensive alignment of a whole society with the movement, understood by the regime as the fulfilment of its program.

concepts/holocaust.title: The Holocaust
concepts/holocaust.content:
The Holocaust
The Holocaust — the Shoah, the systematic persecution and extermination of the Jews of Europe by the National Socialist state — was the catastrophe that closed the interwar history this wiki surveys. It had no single beginning but a chain of legal and administrative acts: the racial definition of the Jew as a non-citizen, his exclusion from the economy and the professions, his removal from the community of the people, and at the last his deportation and murder in the extermination camps of which Auschwitz became the name. Within this collection the catastrophe is documented from two opposite ends: the regime’s own record of the racial laws by which it legalized the exclusion, and the testimony of Primo Levi, an Italian Jew deported to Auschwitz in February 1944, who survived to write its human meaning.
The legal consummation of the racial program
The exclusion began as law. The Nuremberg racial laws of 15 September 1935 — the Reichsbürgergesetz, the law on the citizen of the Reich, and the law for the protection of German blood and German honour — translated into the fundamental law of the state the racial doctrine the movement had proclaimed in its program of 1920: that only a Volksgenosse of German blood can be a citizen, and that no Jew can therefore be a citizen. The first implementing ordinance of November 1935 drew the consequence, that the Jew could not be a citizen of the Reich and was deprived of the rights that citizenship conferred. The party’s own documentary compilation, Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich, assembled in 1943 to prove that the program had been fulfilled, reproduces the whole chain of instruments by which the boundary drawn at Nuremberg was carried into every department of life.
The exclusion from the economy
The Nuremberg laws marked the boundary; the ordinances that followed converted the status of the Jew as an alien into a systematic expulsion from the economic life of the nation. The record gathered by the compiler Büttner runs from the Reichsbürgergesetz and the blood-protection law through the law on Jewish cultural associations of March 1938, the ordinance of October 1938 on the identity cards and passports of Jews, the ordinance of November 1938 against the possession of arms by Jews, and the ordinance excluding Jews from German economic life of 12 November 1938 with its implementing ordinance of the same month. By these measures the Jew was driven out of trade, industry and the professions, barred from the carrying of arms, marked by the identity card and the stamped passport, and reduced — in the language the regime itself used — to a guest in Germany under the law of aliens. The regime presented this as the fulfilment of its program; for the Jews it was the foundation on which the later deportations would rest.
The deportation
What the regime of 1933–1940 did not yet record, the survivor’s testimony supplies. Primo Levi’s account of his deportation records the journey that awaited the Jews who had been marked and stripped. In mid-February 1944 the Italian Jews in the transit camp at Fossoli were about six hundred; on the 20th the Germans inspected the camp, and on the morning of the 21st it was known that the next day the Jews would leave — all, no exception, children, old people, the sick. They were loaded onto lorries and taken to the station of Carpi, where the train and its escort awaited them. The wagons were twelve, the people six hundred and fifty; in Levi’s own wagon there were forty-five, in a small one. “Here then, before our eyes, under our feet, was one of those famous German transports, the ones that do not return… freight wagons, closed from the outside, and inside men, women, children, compressed without pity, like merchandise by the dozen, travelling toward nothingness.”
Auschwitz
The deportation’s end was Auschwitz, which Levi records “had no name, then and for us; but it must correspond to a place on this earth.” The arrival stripped the deportees of everything, beginning with their names: the shaving and the showers, the rags, the wooden-soled shoes, and then the tattooing — “Häftling: I have learnt that I am a Häftling. My name is 174517.” The camp was a square of about six hundred metres a side, ringed by two barbed-wire fences, the inner one charged with high-tension current, made up of sixty wooden barracks. Here the systematic murder of the program’s legal end reached its climax: in the summer of 1944 the Hungarian transports arrived and the crematoria worked at full capacity, and on 20 October 1944 came the great selection in which a quarter of the camp’s prisoners were sent to the gas chamber. Levi was saved, by the chemistry examination that won him a laboratory post in the Buna works; the drowned and the saved, as he called them, were divided by the accident of a privileged post.
The meaning of the catastrophe
Levi’s testimony draws from the catastrophe its warning. In his Preface he insists that the book is not a new accusation but “documents for a calm study of certain aspects of the human soul,” and that none of the facts is invented. Yet the warning is explicit: it may happen to many individuals and peoples to believe that every stranger is an enemy; this conviction usually lies latent, an infection, manifesting only in sporadic acts — but when the unspoken dogma becomes the major premise of a syllogism, then at the end of the chain stands the Lager. “The history of the death camps should be understood by all as a sinister danger signal.” The racial laws, which the regime celebrated as the consummation of its program, ended in the gas chambers that Levi survived to describe; the Holocaust is the chain that runs from one to the other.

concepts/interventionism.title: Interventionism
concepts/interventionism.content:
Interventionism
The movement that carried Italy into the Great War — and the founding temper of Fascism itself. Interventionism (interventismo) is the name given to the campaign, running from the declaration of Italian neutrality in August 1914 to the “radiant days of May” 1915, for Italian entry into the war on the side of the Entente. The Fascist historians of the movement agree in treating it not as a mere foreign-policy quarrel but as the moral birth of the new Italy: the moment when a minority of the nation, against the neutrality of the official parties and of the parliamentary state, willed the country’s passage from a pacific, liberal past into the storm of the century. What the interventionist minority set in motion, in their telling, the Fascist movement would complete after the armistice.
The neutrality and the split
The war came upon Italy undecided. Bound by the Triple Alliance to the Central Powers, Italy declared itself neutral in August 1914, and the three years of Balkan crisis that Businelli traces from the Congress of Berlin to Sarajevo left the country at a fork. On one side stood the neutralists — the official Socialists of Avanti!, the Giolittians, the mass of the parliamentary and commercial world, who held that Italy had nothing to gain and much to lose from entering the conflict. On the other stood a minority that Volpe presents as the true voice of the nation’s destiny: those who saw in the war the occasion for Italy to take its place among the great powers and to finish the work of the Risorgimento. The split, Businelli writes, was not only between parties but within them — a division of the national conscience itself.
The man who broke the neutrality front was the revolutionary socialist editor Benito Mussolini. In the autumn of 1914 he turned from the neutrality his own party preached, founded Il Popolo d’Italia, the newspaper that became the organ of the interventionist cause, and was expelled from the Socialist party he had helped to lead. Volpe sets this rupture beside the interventionism of Bissolati and the Radicals, insisting that Mussolini’s was something more than the nationalism of the old parties: it carried a social and revolutionary content, the conviction that the war would not only make Italy great but would transform her from within. Businelli records the founding of the paper, the campaign that followed, and Mussolini’s arrest for the agitation. The same energy that turned against the Avanti! of his old comrades made him, in the eyes of the movement, the man who answered the neutrality with action.
The radiose giornate
The interventionist campaign ran through the winter of 1914–15 as a war of agitation and of the word. It was conducted by the few against the many, and it drew its strength from the young, the students, the artists and the patriots of the cities — the Futurists of Marinetti, the nationalists, the men who had volunteered for the colonial wars, and the circle gathered around Il Popolo d’Italia. Pini and Bresadola, in the chapter of their chronicle devoted to interventionism, present it as a bridge between a past and a future, the prelude to the years of war and then to the founding of the Fasci. The movement, they insist, was not the work of the parliamentary majority but of a resolute minority that dragged the people along — the same minority, in their telling, that had carried Italy into the Libyan war and that would later carry the Fascist revolution.
The crisis came to a head in May 1915, in the days the Fascist tradition remembers as the radiose giornate di maggio — the radiant days of May. The interventionists poured into the piazzas of the great cities, demanding war against the irresolute government; the country seemed to hang between the will of the streets and the caution of the parliament. Volpe’s account stresses the patriotic and social content of this moment: it was not a passing of the general staff but a movement of the whole nation’s better self, the hour in which Italy, as he puts it, was solicited by the war to become herself. On 24 May 1915 Italy entered the war against Austria-Hungary. The interventionists had won — and the victory, in the Fascist reading, belonged to them, not to the liberal state that had resisted them to the last.
The meaning of the intervention
The Fascist historians do not treat interventionism as an episode that ended in 1915 but as the first act of the revolution. The war that followed tested and transformed the interventionists. Businelli devotes his second chapter to Mussolini and the war, to the corporal of the trench — “i galloni di caporale erano sufficienti alla mia ambizione” (the corporal’s stripes sufficed to my ambition) — and to Il Popolo d’Italia carrying the patriotic word through the years of Caporetto and Vittorio Veneto. Volpe’s collected wartime journalism in Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo records how a professional historian of the national school wrote for the interventionist and Fascist press from the middle of the war: the essays on Prussian militarism, on the duties and rights of the nation, on Wilson and America, on the soldiers of the VIII Armata. The war, in this body of writing, is the school of the new Italy — the furnace in which the trincerocrazia, the aristocracy of the trenches, was forged.
Interventionism thus supplied Fascism with its first great moral capital: the claim, repeated through the whole Fascist chronicle, that the movement was the heir of those who had willed and fought the war, and that the neutrality of 1914 and the pacifism of the postwar were the same enemy in two disguises. When after the armistice the country seemed to be losing the peace it had won, the interventionists became the nucleus of the new movement. Volpe opens his History of the Fascist Movement with the interventionist split and the Fasci d’azione that grew out of it; the Fasci di combattimento of March 1919, Businelli writes, were the constituent assembly of interventionism — the survivors of the intervention and of the trenches gathering, against a state that had betrayed the victory, to complete what May 1915 had begun. The interventionism that carried Italy into the war is therefore, in the eyes of its own historians, the root from which Fascism itself grew: the first assertion that a determined minority, speaking for the nation, might override the neutrality and the weakness of the liberal state.

concepts/la-pratique-du-rien.title: La Pratique du Rien
concepts/la-pratique-du-rien.content:
La Pratique du Rien
The phrase of Daniel Halévy, in his chronicle of the crisis year 1938, for the governing art of the Third Republic in its last age of drift — the practice of doing nothing, the pratique du rien, as the regime’s response to the accumulated financial, social and diplomatic problems of the late 1930s. It is not a programme but the negative of a programme, the systematic inaction by which the parliamentary republic, unable to choose between the policies of the left and the right, between the defence of the League and the accommodation with the new tyrannies, let the year 1938 run its course from the January opening of the Chamber to the Munich Agreement. For this wiki it stands beside Marc Bloch’s Étrange Défaite as one of the two great contemporary verdicts on the republican regime — the one a diagnosis of its inaction before the disaster, the other an examination of the disaster itself — and it supplies the civilian, moderate-liberal record of the French crisis from within, at the moment before 1939.
The drift of the regime
Halévy opens his account of the year in the winter of the Popular Front’s collapse. The January reopening of the Chamber found Herriot re-elected its president, a “powerful nightingale” in the chair, closing his speech of thanks with the plea that every difficulty could be mastered by a common will to wisdom. And then, Halévy writes, hasten our pace: enumerate the withdrawals, the refusals, the vain attempts that are to succeed one another over the coming days. Herriot, asked by President Lebrun to form a ministry, refuses — for he aimed, at fourteen months’ distance, at the presidency of the Republic, and would not compromise himself in the mêlée. So vanishes, a second vanishing, the great man of the Radical party. Georges Bonnet, active and young, is called in his turn, but the Socialists launch against him an exclusion as a false brother, and the intimidated Radicals dissuade him from the adventure: so vanishes, a third vanishing, the Radical party entire. Then Léon Blum is summoned. Since he had so much power to prevent, one should put him to the test.
This is the rhythm of the year Halévy records — a succession of men who refuse, ministries that cannot form or that form only to drift, a parliament that postpones every decision. The practice of nothing is not the work of wickedness but of a system that has exhausted men and things. This same parliamentarism, Halévy writes, which has worn out so many things and beings, which has given rise to this sort of nothing, has also given rise to practitioners of nothing, very skilful in their employment. Chautemps is of that race, and one of the best — a remarkable creator of delays, who would govern five weeks not by governing but by tacking, assailed by the difficulties of the treasury and by strikes, powerless against revolutionary summons, a spectator of the scandal of the Marseille longshoremen who refused to work beyond their exact forty hours and let the Algerian produce rot. To the question of what is to be done, the regime answers with the creation of delay.
The refusal of policy
The climax of Halévy’s diagnosis is the great parliamentary warning of the end of February, when Flandin and Reynaud sought to rouse the Chamber from its discouraged torpor. Yvon Delbos, the foreign minister, had pronounced uncertain words in which the name of the defunct Society of Geneva returned like a refrain; Flandin confessed he had not understood Delbos’s discourse. “The League of Nations is dead,” he said; “the Russian armies are a phantom. Mr. Neville Chamberlain has understood this and has modified his policy. When will France do as much?” The absence of policy, the absence of action, he declared, which characterise the discourse pronounced that morning by the minister of foreign affairs, conduct either to humiliation or to war. He knew, he added, that the necessity of sparing the majority imposed intermediate solutions, and that Chautemps would say there could be no other majority; but the events unfolding in Europe posed new questions to which it was impossible to answer with old formulas. If you wish to negotiate, you need force; if you wish to run the risk of war — and he did not believe they wished it — you will need force too; not only the force of armies, but the force of finances, of economies, of morale. And he closed with the warning that, even if the choice between the two policies were postponed, a moment would come when it could no longer be made — for by waiting, every day hastened the risk of humiliation, of war, of the ruin of the regime.
Reynaud, whose plan was not Flandin’s — he believed in the validity of the Polish, Czech, Rumanian and Russian alliances, and would not have France withdraw from central Europe — agreed on the essential: the condition of all foreign policy was a transformation of domestic policy. If Italy shows us insolence, he said, it is because she no longer believes in our force. And it was not a matter only of arms: the state of mind of England had been influenced by what her friends believed of the French economy, the French finances, the French money. From the restoration of French force depended the equilibrium of Europe; and for that force there must be union, the union sacrée renewed. The two speeches were greeted by applause from the right and the centre, and the Chamber went on. Chautemps, whose duty was clear — to concentrate his vigilance on the outside and to warn the chiefs of Parliament — did instead the contrary: he interested himself in financial questions, invented a Caisse autonome de la Défense nationale, thought of the economic redressment of the country, and asked for full powers — which the Socialists would grant, they said, only if they were to exercise them themselves. So he asked no more, and prepared his resignation. The practice of nothing had refused the very force it named as the condition of survival.
The balance of the year
The concept draws its meaning from the year it describes, which closes in the aftermath of Munich. Halévy’s chronicle records the summer of illusion — the deceptive calm between the Anschluss of March and the Sudeten storm — the mounting crisis of the autumn, the September mobilisations, and the flight of the Czechoslovak question toward the brink of war, before the Munich Agreement of 29–30 September postponed the catastrophe. The practice of nothing had not chosen; the choice had been made for it by the force of events and the accommodation of the powers. Bloch, writing two years later in the fury of defeat, gives the same diagnosis its terrible confirmation: the France that had practised nothing found at the hour of trial nothing to oppose to the total war of the enemy. His examination of conscience indicts the regime and the society for the same refusal — the refusal to prepare, to choose, to believe in the force that only a decided polity could have mustered. The pratique du rien is thus the civil, parliamentary name for what the historian of the defeat called the strange defeat: the inaction of the ruling republic in the face of a world that had chosen to act, and that would not wait.

concepts/lebensraum.title: Lebensraum
concepts/lebensraum.content:
Lebensraum
Living space — the demand, set out in the closing foreign-policy chapters of Hitler’s Mein Kampf, that the German people must win territorial living-space in the East, by conquest if need be, as the foundation of its racial and national future. The word Lebensraum (living space) is the hinge of the book’s programme: against the colonial and commercial policy of the old Reich, which sought markets and oversea possessions, Hitler poses a continental policy of European conquest — the acquisition of land in the East at the expense of Russia and her subject peoples. It is the doctrine by which the race-theory of the first volume becomes a foreign policy of expansion, and the term that joins the racial doctrine of National Socialism to the territorial programme of the German century.
The foundation in race
The demand for living space grows directly out of the racial doctrine of Mein Kampf. If the state exists to preserve and advance the racial people, then the people’s future depends on the land it can command — the soil on which it lives, multiplies and keeps its blood pure. Hitler’s argument begins from the peasant: the German peasant is the foundation of the people, and the German who has lost his rootedness in the land — the rootless, the urban, the uprooted — has lost part of his racial being. A people’s greatness is bound to the territory it possesses, and a people that is cramped upon too little soil will either starve or be forced into a desperate struggle for existence.
From this follows the rejection of the two policies that had governed German expansion before the war. Colonial policy, the acquisition of oversea possessions, is rejected: it disperses the people, mingles it with alien races, and in the end is lost when the sea-power that guards it fails. Commercial and trade policy — the attempt to live by buying and selling in the world economy — is rejected still more firmly: it makes the people dependent on strangers and on money, and money, in the racial argument, is the instrument of the Jew. Against both Hitler sets a third course: the conquest of land in Europe itself, on the continent, at the expense of the peoples who hold it. The German people, in his words, must seek its future not in colonies but in the land of the East.
The programme of the East
The foreign-policy chapters at the close of Mein Kampf — “Deutsche Bündnispolitik nach dem Kriege” (German Alliance Policy after the War), “Ostorientierung oder Ostpolitik” (Orientation toward the East or Eastern Policy), and “Notwehr als Recht” (Self-Defence as a Right) — turn the racial doctrine into a programme of conquest. Hitler rejects the prewar German policy of alliances, which had sought to balance England and Russia against each other, and lays down the two alliances Germany must seek: with England and with Italy. The war of the future, he argues, must be fought against Soviet Russia — against the “Asiatic” threat that Marxism had raised up in the East — and its prize must be the land of Russia and her border states, the great territory that he holds the German people requires.
The demand is argued in the language of nature and right. A people, Hitler writes, has the right to the land it can hold and people; self-defence (Notwehr) is the justification of the movement’s methods and of the nation’s expansion alike. The old borders of the Reich are not sacred; the aim is not the restoration of 1914 but the acquisition of living space. The East is named without hesitation: the destruction of Soviet Russia and the conquest of its territory would free the German people from the “Asiatic” pressure and give it the land on which a greater Germany could live. In the same breath Hitler rejects a return to the Eastern alliance of the past, the old policy of “orientation toward the East” (Ostorientierung) as friendship with Russia, in favour of the new Eastern policy (Ostpolitik) of conquest. The land of the East is to be German, and the peoples who live on it are to give way.
The völkisch meaning of the land
The demand for living space is inseparable from the racial and völkisch doctrine of the whole book, and it reappears in the racial-mystical voice of the movement’s own adherents in the months after the seizure of power. Geisow’s tract of February 1933, Die Seele des Dritten Reiches, closes with the conviction that the German’s struggle for his Lebensrecht (right to life) is “a piece of religion” — the word Lebensrecht carrying the same root as Lebensraum, and binding the people’s right to life and land to its blood and soul. For Geisow the German people’s health lies in its own inherited being, in the soil and life-sap from which it draws its strength; the renewal of life is a work of education and of blood, and the struggle for the people’s existence is a religious struggle. The racial doctrine that justifies living space in Mein Kampf is, in Geisow’s tract, the soul of the Third Reich.
The connection matters for understanding the concept. Lebensraum is not, in these sources, a mere appetite for territory — a colonial grab or a commercial ambition. It is presented as the natural and racial right of a people to the land its blood requires, the foundation of its greatness and the guarantee of its future. The state exists for the race, and the race requires soil; the foreign policy of conquest is the other side of the domestic policy of racial purity. The two halves of the doctrine — the racial state within and the territorial programme without — are one.
The concept and its place
Lebensraum is the point at which the ideology of Mein Kampf becomes a programme for the world. The first volume had argued the racial doctrine and traced the collapse of 1918; the second volume builds the völkisch state and then, in its final chapters, turns that state outward — toward the alliances of England and Italy, the war against Soviet Russia, and the conquest of the East. It is the term by which the racial theory of the movement was carried from the domestic to the foreign sphere, and the promise on which the regime would later act. As the official documentary compilations of the 1930s would show the territorial recovery of the Saar, Austria and the Sudetenland in the language of national right, the deeper demand set out in Mein Kampf was for the living space of the East — the conquest that the racial doctrine made not merely desirable but necessary to the German people’s survival and greatness.

concepts/marxism-leninism.title: Marxism–Leninism
concepts/marxism-leninism.content:
Marxism–Leninism
Marxism–Leninism (марксизм-ленинизм, Marksizm-leninizm) is the doctrine of the Bolshevik party, the theory of the working class and of the socialist revolution that the Short Course of the History of the VKP(b) and the Marxist survey of M. N. Pokrovsky together present as the science of history and of politics. The name unites the two sources of the doctrine: the materialism of Marx and Engels, understood as the scientific law of the development of society, and the teaching of Lenin, who carried that science into the conditions of Russia and built upon it the party of a new type. In the official account the doctrine is not one more opinion among many but the revealed truth of the revolutionary movement — the standpoint from which the whole Russian past, and the whole party’s history, can be read as the struggle of classes and of the working people for their liberation.
The materialist foundation
The foundation of the doctrine, as the sources present it, is historical materialism (исторический материализм): the thesis that society and its history are governed by law, and that the law is ultimately economic. Pokrovsky’s survey opens its general concepts of history with exactly this science — why we need to know the past, the changeability of the world and of human life, knowledge of the past as power over the future, and the “laws of history” that the historian must master. At the base of history, he insists, lies not nature but labour: class struggle is the development of history, classes and economy are its subject, and materialism is the method that sees through the words of kings and churchmen to the real movement of production and exchange. Against the bourgeois view of history, which presented the past as a record of great men and accidents, Marxism sets the understanding that humanity makes itself through work and through the conflict of classes. The whole of Pokrovsky’s Russian history is written in this key — from the slave-owning princes and the feudal boiars to the commercial capital that built the Muscovite state and the industrial proletariat that was to bury the old order.
This materialism is dialectical as well as historical. The Short Course devotes a chapter of its account of the Stolypin reaction — the years when the doctrine had to be defended against every deviation — to “dialectical and historical materialism” (диалектический и исторический материализм), the method by which the party understands that nothing is fixed, that everything develops through internal contradiction, and that the working class is the force destined to overturn the capitalist order. Dialectics is not a scholastic ornament in this telling but the very logic of the revolution, the proof that what exists bears within it the seeds of its own passing.
The party of a new type
The decisive novelty of Marxism–Leninism, and the heart of the whole account, is the party of a new type (партия нового типа). The introduction to the Short Course frames the study of the party’s history as the study of the struggle of the revolutionary proletariat, and the distinctive achievement of Lenin was to understand that the working class could not be left to develop its consciousness spontaneously but required a disciplined, centralised organisation of professional revolutionaries to lead it. In this the Bolsheviks broke with the looser, parliamentarian social democracy of Western Europe and with the internal currents of “economism,” which held that the workers needed only economic improvement, not a fighting party. Lenin’s What Is to Be Done?, which the Short Course treats at length, supplied the ideological foundations of this party; his One Step Forward, Two Steps Back supplied its organisational foundations. The party, in this doctrine, is not the whole working class but its vanguard — the most conscious and devoted part, bound by iron discipline, guided by the theory, and strong precisely because it is united and armed with science.
The history of the party as the Short Course narrates it is the history of this new-type party fighting for the correct line against every internal opponent — against the economists, the Mensheviks, the liquidators and otzovists, the Trotskyists, the “rightists” and the Bukharinists. Each deviation is presented as an error of theory before it is an error of politics: the Mensheviks misunderstood the alliance of workers and peasants, the liquidators despaired of the underground, the Trotskyists broke the discipline of the party. The doctrine, in other words, is the standard by which all these are judged, and the party’s victories are the victories of a correct theory in action. The conclusion of the Short Course draws the lessons: the working-class party is the leading force of the revolution, it grows strong by cleansing itself of opportunist elements, and it is strong through its bond with the people — the source of its strength, as the “Antaeus” parable of the party’s own teaching puts it.
Theory and the people
What unites the party doctrine and the historical survey is the conviction that theory is the servant of the people’s liberation, not a possession of the learned. Pokrovsky’s volume carries Lenin’s own letter praising the projected “history in the briefest outline” as a work “worthy of our attention,” and the survey itself is addressed not to the seminar but to the worker and the school; Shestakov’s companion textbook, in the same folder, brings the same periodisation to the elementary grades. Marxism–Leninism, in the official self-account, is the science of the masses, the weapon by which the working people come to understand their own past and therefore to master their future. It stands as the intellectual ground of the whole Soviet order that the Short Course and its companions describe — the doctrine without which neither the party of a new type, nor the industrialisation and collectivisation it directed, nor the cult of the leader who embodied it, can be understood.

concepts/national-socialism.title: National Socialism
concepts/national-socialism.content:
National Socialism
The ideology and political movement that seized power in Germany in 1933 — at once a racial doctrine, a theory of the state, and a mass organisation built on the leadership principle and the spoken word. National Socialism (Nationalsozialismus) is named in the title of its party, the National Socialist German Workers’ Party (NSDAP), a name Hitler chose to unite the nationalist and the socialist currents of postwar Germany. Its doctrinal foundation is laid out in Hitler’s own Mein Kampf; its critical anatomy in Konrad Heiden’s contemporary biography; and its racial-mystical voice, in the weeks after the seizure of power, in Hans Geisow’s völkisch tract. The three sources together show an ideology that presents itself as the opposite of the liberal and Marxist world that preceded it, built on race, blood and the leadership principle.
The doctrine of race and the völkisch state
At the core of National Socialist doctrine, as Hitler sets it out in Mein Kampf, stands the race. The state is not, as in liberal or Marxist thought, a contract among citizens or an instrument of class, but the means by which a people preserves its racial being. The chapter “Volk und Rasse” (People and Race) lays down the hierarchy of races, the creative power of the superior race, and the duty of the state to keep the blood pure. The Jew appears as the contrary principle — the force that dissolves race, undermines the state, and stands behind both Marxism and the liberalism that National Socialism attacks. Hitler’s political awakening, he insists, was his discovery in Vienna of the “Jewish question,” and the whole doctrine turns on it: the history of Germany’s collapse in 1918 is told as the work of the “November criminals” and the Jewish-Marxist influence that stabbed the army in the back.
The state that follows from this doctrine is the völkische Staat (völkisch state). The second volume of Mein Kampf gives it its form: race as the foundation, the rejection of the democratic and parliamentary state in which numbers and majorities rule, and a division of the people into subjects and citizens on racial grounds. The citizen is not the man who happens to live within the borders of the state but the man of the right race who is willing and able to serve it. The state’s purpose is the preservation and advancement of the racial people, and every institution — law, economy, education, culture — is to be bent to that end. This is the doctrine that the official documentary compilations of the regime would later present as realised in law: the citizenship law of July 1933, the rebuilding of state and economy, the racial policy that Geisow’s tract exalts as the “soul” of the new Reich.
The movement and its meaning
National Socialism is not only a doctrine but a movement — and the movement is prior to the state. Mein Kampf distinguishes Weltanschauung (worldview) from party and insists that the worldview, once accepted, must conquer the state through an organisation bound to it. The party Hitler built was the instrument of the doctrine: a mass organisation of the spoken word, held together by the Führerprinzip (leadership principle) by which authority flows downward from an absolute chief and every man answers to his superior while being relieved of responsibility toward those below. Heiden, who attended National Socialist meetings from 1922, offers the sharpest contemporary reading of what this meant. The movement, he writes, offered the German middle classes “relief from responsibility through an absolute supreme authority — security and moral comfort”; it gathered the failed, the resentful, and the credulous into a community that promised to reverse their ruin and restore the nation’s pride.
Heiden’s picture of the movement is the critical counterpart to Hitler’s own. Where Mein Kampf presents a doctrine of racial renewal, Heiden shows a machine built of oratory, symbols and the cultivation of mass feeling — wit, logic and insolence, the hammering repetition of a few propositions, the listener made into a collaborator. “Hitler always says the same thing,” Heiden quotes, and the sameness was the instrument. The movement’s growth from the tiny German Workers’ Party, which Hitler entered as its seventh member in the Munich of 1919, to the mass party of the early 1930s was the work of this propaganda and organisation — the red banner, the Hakenkreuz (swastika), the storm troopers of the SA, the twenty-five-point programme. Heiden’s biography traces the “steps to power”: the Beer Hall Putsch of 1923, the seven years of reconstruction and electoral advance after 1925, and the capture of the state in 1933.
The völkisch soul of the Third Reich
The racial doctrine that Mein Kampf argues is given a theological-racial form in Geisow’s tract of February 1933, written in the weeks after Hitler’s appointment as Chancellor. Die Seele des Dritten Reiches (The Soul of the Third Reich) presents the National Socialist revolution as “a piece of religion” — the awakening of the German people’s inherited being against the foreign, dismembering forces that had corrupted it. Geisow’s opening chapter, “Weltenwende” (Turn of the Age), holds that history is a piece of nature and that the forces of race and blood, not political arrangement, are the true currents beneath events. The Volksgemeinschaft (national community) that overcomes class divisions is the goal; the enemy is liberalism — that alien, artfremd way of viewing life born of the French Revolution and carried by Jewish-masonic forces — and with it the individualist, dismembering order that had dissolved the people into its parts.
Geisow applies the doctrine across the whole of life: thought itself is race-bound (arteigen), and the German must think out of his own inherited being rather than in alien categories; the economy must be restored to its bond with the people, not left to liberal world-economy; the family is the innermost cell of the people’s life; the church must grasp the blood-bound, God-given order of the people. The tract closes as it opens, with God making world history through the nature and blood He gives to men and peoples — to be German is to be a whole man, and the German’s struggle for his right to life is a piece of religion. Where Mein Kampf gives National Socialism its political and racial argument, Geisow gives it its soul — the conviction of the movement’s own adherents in its first months that the revolution was not a change of government but the reawakening of a race.
National Socialism as doctrine and power
The sources agree on the shape of the whole, whatever their standpoint. For Hitler, National Socialism is the true doctrine of the German people, the worldview that must conquer the state and prepare the nation’s racial future — including the demand for Lebensraum (living space) in the East that the closing foreign-policy chapters of Mein Kampf set out. For Heiden, writing from the critical-democratic side, it is “the age of irresponsibility” made flesh — the reactionary revolution of a middle class that had abandoned responsibility and found, in the leadership principle, relief from the burden of freedom. For Geisow, from within the movement, it is the soul of the German people awakened against the alien. The three voices together — the founder’s doctrine, the opponent’s anatomy, the adherent’s faith — give the fullest contemporary portrait of the ideology that shaped the German century.

concepts/nuremberg-racial-laws.title: Nuremberg racial laws
concepts/nuremberg-racial-laws.content:
Nuremberg racial laws
The Nuremberg racial laws were the two statutes laid before the Reichstag summoned to the party congress at Nuremberg on 15 September 1935 — the Reichsbürgergesetz, the law on the citizen of the Reich, and the law for the protection of German blood and German honour. Together they translated the racial doctrine of the movement into the fundamental law of the state, defining the German citizen by blood and separating the Jews, as aliens under the law, from the community of the people. For the National Socialist order they were not a novelty but the legal consummation of a program; for the Jews of Germany they were the beginning of a systematic exclusion that would reach, in the years that followed, into every department of economic and civil life.
Blood and citizenship
The doctrine on which the laws rested was the oldest layer of the movement’s creed. In Mein Kampf Hitler had set the race at the foundation of the state: the state exists, on this account, not as an administrative convenience but as the means of preserving the purity of the blood of a people, and citizenship is accordingly not a formal status but a racial qualification. The chapter on subject and citizen drew the line that the law of 1935 would trace in positive form — a distinction between the mere subject of the state and the full citizen, who alone enjoys political rights. The racial law of the spring of 1933 had already pointed in this direction by legislating upon German citizenship in racial terms; but the Reichsbürgergesetz of September 1935 was the decisive act. It declared that a citizen of the Reich is only that subject of German or kindred blood who by his conduct shows himself willing and fit to serve the German people and the Reich, and it made the citizen’s political rights the privilege of that citizenship alone. The first implementing ordinance of November 1935 drew the consequence: the Jew could not be a citizen of the Reich, and was to be deprived of the rights that citizenship conferred.
The protection of German blood
The companion statute, the law for the protection of German blood and German honour, made marriage and extramarital intercourse between Jews and citizens of German or kindred blood criminal offences, and forbade the employment by Jewish households of German women of childbearing age and the display of the German flag by Jews. Where the citizenship law redefined the citizen, this law policed the boundary of the people itself, treating the mixture of blood as the gravest injury that could be done to the nation. The official record of the year gathers these acts under the heading of racial and population policy together with the law for the protection of the hereditary health of the German people of October 1935, which carried the same logic into the regulation of marriage and reproduction, and with the decree of September 1935 that established separate schools for Jewish children. Taken together the measures of the autumn of 1935 completed, in the language of the regime, the racial and population policy that the movement had announced in its program.
The exclusion from the economy
The Nuremberg laws marked the boundary; the ordinances that followed over the next years converted the status of the Jew as an alien into a systematic exclusion from the economic life of the nation. In the compilation that Büttner drew up to show the fulfilment of the party program, the laws of 15 September 1935 stand at the head of a chain of instruments that runs through the law on Jewish cultural associations of 1938, the ordinance of October 1938 on identity cards and passports of Jews, the ordinance of November 1938 against the possession of arms by Jews, and the ordinance excluding Jews from German economic life of 12 November 1938 with its implementing ordinance of the same month. By these later measures the Jew was driven out of trade, industry and the professions, and the definition first laid down at Nuremberg was carried to its social and economic conclusion. For the regime the Nuremberg laws were the fixed point — the legal realization of the fourth and fifth points of the program of 1920, that only a Volksgenosse of German blood can be a citizen and that the non-citizen lives in Germany only as a guest under the law of aliens.

concepts/popular-front-spain.title: Spanish Popular Front
concepts/popular-front-spain.content:
Spanish Popular Front
The Spanish Popular Front was the coalition of the republican left, the socialists and their allies that fought and won the general election of February 1936 and governed the Republic in the months that led to the Civil War. It was not a party but a pact — an agreement to present a common front against the parties of the right in the first election of the Republic after the conservative biennium, and to restore the reforming legislation of the first years. In power it proved unable to hold together the forces it had assembled: it revived the programme of the first biennium and released the prisoners of October 1934, but it also opened the quickening of social and political conflict that carried the Republic down what has been called an inclined plane toward the rising of July 1936. And when the war came, the very name became the label under which the republican zone, and the divisions within it, fought on.
The recomposition of the left
The Popular Front grew out of the failures of the second biennium. The conservative coalition of the Radicals and the CEDA had governed since 1933, but its course and the repression that followed the insurrection of October 1934 discredited it and left the parties of the right quarrelling among themselves. On the left, the republican position associated with Azaña, though it had been volatilised in seats in 1933, had kept a substantial body of votes, and it now recomposed itself into a common front with the socialists and their allies. The result was an electoral pact that, unlike a government, did not require the parties to govern together, only to appear together before the electorate and to share a programme of amnesty, of the restoration of the suspended autonomy and of the reforms of the first years. It was a coalition of the ballot, and the ambiguities of that construction were to mark everything that followed.
The election of February 1936
The election of 16 February 1936 gave the Popular Front the victory. Opinion had been swinging back to the left through the oscillations of republican politics — opinion changed, but, as time was to prove, it did not change as much as appearances suggested. The result returned the Republic to the parties that had made the reformist biennium, and Azaña formed the new government at the head of a cabinet drawn from the republican middle of the coalition. The government’s first acts answered its electoral pledges: the amnesty released the prisoners of October 1934, the agrarian and social reforms of the first biennium were restored, and the suspended statute of Catalan autonomy was put back into effect. But the government of the republican middle was not master of the streets. The return of the left had raised expectations among the workers and the peasantry that the cabinet could neither satisfy nor control, and the spring of 1936 passed in a mounting agitation of strikes, land occupations and political violence.
In power
The Popular Front in government was not a united government. Beneath the cabinet of Azaña’s republicans lay the socialists, who were themselves split between the reformists gathered around Indalecio Prieto and the revolutionaries who followed Francisco Largo Caballero, and beyond them the anarchists and the communists, who had accepted the pact but were not of it. The Republic was carried, in the view of one liberal witness, through a third phase toward the left in which the extremists of each side grew bolder. The government sought to hold the centre, but the accelerating polarisation — the strikes, the burning of churches, the clashes in the streets, the assassinations that answered one another — pushed the country down the inclined plane toward catastrophe. It could have been avoided until nearly the last moment, but it was not; in July 1936 the military rising in Morocco split Spain in two.
In the war
Once the war had begun, the Popular Front became the name of the whole republican zone. Its first result, like the first result of the rising on the other side, was the fragmentation of political authority: the government lost control of the revolutionary masses who rose to meet the rebellion, and its chief task through the whole war, in the retrospective verdict of Azaña, was to reduce those masses to discipline. The coalition governed through a succession of cabinets — Largo Caballero’s, and then Juan Negrín’s, which Azaña and Prieto had brought into being — and it fought a war at once against the enemy at the front and against its own internal divisions. The conflict between the anarchist and communist-influenced currents tore the republican rear-guard, the communists grew in power as Soviet aid grew, and the end came in 1939 when the fall of Catalonia brought the surrender of a Popular Front that had long ceased to be united, its sectors acting in sensibly different ways and its last months better read as a phenomenon of disintegration than as an interweaving of conspiracies.

concepts/saar-question.title: Saar question
concepts/saar-question.content:
Saar question
The Saar question was the territorial dispute over the Saarland, the small industrial basin on Germany’s western border that the Treaty of Versailles separated from the Reich and placed for fifteen years under the government of the League of Nations, and whose final fate was to be decided by a plebiscite of its own inhabitants. The question united in a single territory the two great grievances of the German national movement after 1919 — the loss of German land and the exploitation of the German economy by the victors — and its answer came on 13 January 1935, when the Saar population voted by an overwhelming majority for reunion with the Reich. For the National Socialist regime the recovery of the Saar was the first great outward proof of its claim to have undone the injustices of Versailles.
The mandated territory
The Treaty of Versailles had cut the Saar out of the Reich against the current of the national demand. Its coal mines were ceded to France in reparation; the government of the basin was placed under a Governing Commission appointed by the League of Nations; and the whole arrangement was to run for fifteen years, at the end of which the population was to choose among three courses — the maintenance of the treaty’s status quo, union with France, or union with Germany. The years of the mandate were years of estrangement. The German population of some eight hundred and fifty thousand kept its national feeling in the face of a foreign administration; the French troops, though the treaty required their withdrawal, remained until 1927; and the plan for a Franco-German economic approach to the Saar, agreed in principle at Thoiry in 1926, collapsed and left the questions of the mines and the administration unresolved. When the fifteen years drew to a close, the territory and the world knew that the question was to be settled not in the chancelleries but at the ballot.
The two nations’ bid
The campaign that preceded the vote was fought on the ground of the territory. Hitler had proposed in his Reichstag speech of 30 January 1934 that Germany and France settle the Saar in advance of the ballot, arguing that it was the only territorial question still open between the two states, but the offer came to nothing. In the territory itself the parties that demanded the return to the Reich drew together into the German Front, the Deutsche Front, dissolving their separate organizations in the face of a great common duty, and campaigned under the cry that put an end to party quarrelling — “Schluß mit allem Parteihader! … Es lebe die Deutsche Front!” (an end to all party quarrelling … long live the German Front). Against it stood the status-quo camp and the pro-French camp, and the émigré circles abroad who worked against the German return. The campaigners themselves, before the ballot, reckoned on at least eighty-five per cent of the electorate for the immediate return; the vote of 13 January 1935 surpassed their expectation. Bürckel, the campaign’s victorious leader, gave the figures on the radio: some 528,000 valid votes had been cast, and of these 89.05 per cent declared for Germany.
The return to the Reich
The formal reincorporation followed on 1 March 1935. A law of 30 January had already provided for the provisional administration of the Saarland, and on 1 March the protocol recorded Germany’s reintegration into the government of the territory, with Bürckel installed as Reichskommissar under the Führer’s authority; Frick, the Reich Minister of the Interior, spoke at the reunion, and the Reich bought back the mines and folded the basin back into the Reich administration. For the official record of the National Socialist state the recovery of the Saar was the first of the reunions by which the German people were gathered back together, and it was celebrated as the precondition of the steps that followed — the proclamation of conscription in March and the rearmament that the return made possible. In the party’s own programmatic history the Saarland stands at the head of the first point of the program of 1920, the reunion of all Germans in a Greater Germany; and for the nationalist press that had fought the campaign, the vote closed a chapter that the treaty of 1919 had opened, and reopened the question that would in the years to come carry the movement from the Saar to the Rhineland, to Austria and beyond.
