concepts/second-spanish-republic.title: Second Spanish Republic
concepts/second-spanish-republic.content:
Second Spanish Republic
The Second Spanish Republic was the democratic regime proclaimed in Madrid on 14 April 1931 and endured, through reform, crisis and civil war, until the end of the war in 1939. It arose out of the capitulation of the monarchy of Alfonso XIII, which the municipal elections of 12 April 1931 had brought down, and it brought to power for the first time in the history of Spain the mass participation of the people in public life — an experience that the dictatorship of Primo de Rivera had hidden and then made abrupt. Unlike the parliamentary liberalism that had preceded it, the Republic set out to change the social and territorial foundations of the country, and in doing so it gathered against itself every force that the old order commanded. Its brief life was the Spanish democratic experience par excellence before 1977, a republic that governed between two anti-republican extremes and ended, in July 1936, in the military rising that split the country in two.
The fall of the monarchy
The Republic was not proclaimed to a people taken by surprise. At the beginning of 1930, with the dictatorship of Primo de Rivera already fallen and the king’s authority spent, the monarchy was in mortal danger; the pact of San Sebastián had joined republicans, socialists and catalanists in a common enterprise, and the attempt to return to constitutional government under Berenguer and then the Aznar ministry had only hastened the end. The municipal elections of 12 April 1931 gave the republican-socialist coalition an overwhelming victory in the cities, and although the monarchy had the legal ground to hold on, the king drew the conclusion and left the country rather than provoke a conflict in the streets. On the evening of 14 April the Republic was proclaimed and the provisional government was installed at the ministry of the Interior. Those first days were one of the rare moments of the revolutionary calendar that was clean — a joy, in the words of one liberal witness, spontaneous as nature in springtime, untainted by the excesses that usually mar dramatic hours. The task that lay before the new regime was nevertheless immense, for it had inherited a country whose social and economic structure was unequal and whose political habits were those of the old oligarchy.
The constituent experience
The regime’s founding act was the election of a constituent assembly, held on 28 June 1931, and its meeting in Madrid on 14 July — a delicate homage to the French Republic. The assembly brought together what one observer called the idealists and the unrealists who were to shape the Republic’s course, and it produced in 1931 a constitution of the left, which separated church and state, dissolved the territorial and social arrangements of the old order, and laid down the rights of the worker and of the citizen. The constitutional debate fixed the terms on which the Republic would be governed: the religious question imposed a new governing formula and opened what has been called the reformist biennium, directed by Manuel Azaña, under whom the constituent Cortes continued to legislate after the constitution had been voted. The Republic, in short, was not merely a change of regime but the advent of the masses to public life, and its leaders were aware that they were making a democracy in a society that had not been democratic.
The reformist biennium
The first two years of the Republic were given over to the great reforming programme that the constituent Cortes set in train. The military reform under Azaña restructured an over-large officer corps and an army that had grown accustomed to intervening in politics; the religious reform separated the Church from the state and provoked the sharpest clerical–anticlerical cleavage of the republican years; the agrarian reform confronted the most ambitious problem facing the new regime, the latifundist countryside of the south, though even in its timid content and application it was decisive in alienating a large part of the population; and the social legislation touched labour, wages and insurance. On the periphery, the Republic had to answer the regional and linguistic pluralism of Spain, above all the Catalan and Basque questions. Azaña’s government carried the programme, but it governed between two enemies. The Republic was held, in a famous image, in a pincer — between the monarchists of the right, who never accepted its existence, and the anarchists of the left, who rejected the state altogether. From opposite directions the two extremes pressed on the democratic experiment, and the reformist government exhausted itself.
The conservative biennium
The elections of November 1933 ended the reformist biennium and turned the Republic to the right. The centre-left coalition that had governed disintegrated, and power passed to the collaboration of the Radical Party of Alejandro Lerroux with the CEDA, the Confederación Española de Derechas Autónomas, the confederation of the Catholic right founded by José María Gil Robles, which had grown strong during the first two years of the Republic more through the errors of the left than through its own virtue. The second biennium reversed much of the reforming legislation and drew the anti-republican forces of the right into a position of growing ascendancy. Its course was an interminable agony, marked by social conflict and by the constitutional crisis of October 1934, when the entry of the CEDA into government provoked a socialist and Catalan insurrection that was crushed under martial law and that drove Azaña, who had had no part in it, to the ships of his detention off Barcelona. The repression and the suspension of the Catalan autonomy statute poisoned the remainder of the biennium, and through 1935 the radical–cedista coalition slowly fell apart.
Toward 1936 and war
The elections of February 1936 returned the Republic to the left under the banner of the Popular Front, a coalition that the recomposition of the republican left made possible and that won the day. The new government set out to restore the reforms of the first biennium and to release the prisoners of October 1934, but its coming provoked a quickening of social and political conflict, an accelerating polarisation and violence that carried the Republic down an inclined plane toward catastrophe. It could have been avoided until nearly the last moment; but in July 1936 the military rising, led from Morocco, split Spain in two and turned the Republic’s democratic life into a civil war. For the republican zone the war brought the social revolution and the repression of the rear-guard, the long defence of Madrid, the internationalisation of the conflict, and the internal politics of a Popular Front that quarrelled and divided even as it fought. The end came in 1939: the fall of Barcelona in February, the recognition of the rebel regime by France and Britain, and the surrender that closed the Republic’s corta vida y larga muerte — its short life and long death.

concepts/short-course-official-history.title: The Short Course as Official History
concepts/short-course-official-history.content:
The Short Course as Official History
The Short Course (Краткий курс, Kratkii kurs) is the canonical history of the Bolshevik party issued under the direct editorship of the Central Committee of the CPSU(b) and approved by it in 1938, reprinted here in the 1945 printing of OGIZ / Gospolitizdat. The History of the CPSU(b). Short Course — История ВКП(б). Краткий курс — became for decades the obligatory text of party and civic education, and with it is paired in this folder the Short Course of the History of the USSR of A. V. Shestakov, the school textbook approved by a government commission for the elementary grades. Together these “short courses” define the official form of Soviet history in the Stalin era: the compressed, authoritative narrative that fixed the periodisation of the national past and of the party’s struggle, and made that narrative the common property of the educated people of the USSR.
The form of the Short Course
The Short Course of party history is built as a continuous story from the rise of Russian social democracy to the completion of socialist construction. Its introduction frames the study of the party’s history as the study of the struggle of the revolutionary proletariat and of the party of a new type; its twelve chapters carry the narrative from 1883 — the years of the narodnik movement and Plekhanov’s Emancipation of Labour group, and the beginning of Lenin’s activity — through the formation of the RSDRP and the Bolshevik-Menshevik split, the first Russian revolution of 1905, the Stolypin reaction, the imperialist war and the February revolution, the October socialist revolution, the civil war and foreign intervention, the restoration and the New Economic Policy, and the struggle for industrialisation and collectivisation, to the completion of socialist society and the adoption of the new Constitution of 1936. The conclusion draws the chief lessons of the party’s path: that the working-class party is the leading force of the revolution, that it grows strong by cleansing itself of opportunist elements, and that it is strong through its bond with the people, the source of its strength. The whole is written from a strict Bolshevik standpoint, presenting the party’s history as the victory of the Marxist-Leninist line over its internal opponents and its external enemies.
The companion school textbook of Shestakov, published in a print run of five million copies, reduces the same story to the compass of the elementary grades. Its introduction, “Our Motherland,” sets the patriotic and materialist premises; its fifteen chapters run from the remote past and the Kievan state through the Tatar-Mongol yoke, the formation of the Russian national state, the empire of the landlords and merchants, the growth of capitalism, the revolutions of 1905 and 1917, the civil war, and the transition to peaceful work, to the final chapter on the USSR as the land of victorious socialism and the new Constitution. The two short courses therefore cover the same ground from two stations — the party history for the adult student, the national history for the schoolchild — and together they extend the official narrative to the whole educated public.
The authority of the canon
What makes the Short Course a concept rather than merely a book is its claim to authority. The party history was approved by the Central Committee in 1938 and issued by the commission of the Central Committee, and it carried the direct imprint of Stalin’s editorship; the school textbook was approved by the All-Union Government Commission for the compilation of the history textbook. These are not ordinary publications but the official determinations of what the history of the party and the country was — the fixed periodisation adopted throughout the Stalin era, against which every other account was measured. The twelve-chapter structure of the party course became the authoritative scheme of Soviet history, and its judgments — on the economists, the Mensheviks, the Trotskyists and the “rightists,” on the kulaks and the “enemies of the people” — became the standard language of the period. The short course is thus the intellectual form of Stalinist history itself: brief not because it is slight but because it is settled, the narrative compressed to the essentials that every loyal citizen was to know by heart.
The two short courses in this folder are also linked, in the official account, to the wider historiographical tradition the same folder preserves. They stand at the end of the development that the Marxist survey of Pokrovsky, published a few years earlier and endorsed by Lenin, had carried forward in the 1920s and early 1930s — the reading of Russian history as the record of class struggle — and they give that reading its definitive, simplified and canonised form. In the period of their authority the short course and the textbook together made the official history a public possession: the story that the worker, the student and the schoolchild learned as the truth of their own country and party.

concepts/spanish-neutrality-wwii.title: Spanish Neutrality in World War II
concepts/spanish-neutrality-wwii.content:
Spanish Neutrality in World War II
Spanish neutrality (neutralidad española) is the name given to Spain’s standing apart from the Second World War — a status that was never static, that ran from a clearly pro-Axis non-belligerency to a growing Allied-leaning neutrality, and that the three witnesses in this wiki describe from three different vantage points: the American ambassador who worked to keep Spain out of the Axis, the Spanish scholar who saw the regime’s foreign policy as the least bad part of its course, and the historian of the dictatorship who periodised the whole war-time drift. From the German victory over France in the summer of 1940 to the closing months of the war, Spain remained formally at peace while the world’s belligerents competed for her, and the question of which side she might join was one of the great uncertainties of the European war.
The Dual Commission
The American ambassador, Carlton J. H. Hayes, arrived in Madrid in May 1942 under what he describes as a double commission: to counteract the pressure of the Axis on Franco’s Spain and to keep Spain out of the war, while at the same time encouraging it to resist any German advance across the Peninsula — a matter vital for the planned invasion of North Africa. Hayes’s memoir is the record of how, over three years, Spain granted the Allies an increasing number of facilities, at first under severe German threats and later more readily as the Allied victory became certain. He is the Allied voice on the Spanish state that the Nationalist and regime sources treat from within, and his account frames the whole problem of Spanish neutrality as a contest of pressures: the Axis working upon Madrid to draw it into the war or at least to deny the Allies its ports, the Allies working to detach it and to extract from it the supply of its minerals.
Non-Belligerency and the Axis Temptation
The word that Spain herself used for her early wartime posture was not neutrality but no-beligerancia (non-belligerency) — a status looser than neutrality, adopted by a power that favoured one belligerent while staying out of the fight. Tusell, writing with the detachment of the modern historian, rejects the claim of the late-franquista propaganda that Germany pressed and Franco resisted. He holds instead that from the German victory over France there was an absolute identification of the Spanish leaders with the Axis cause, prolonged with nuances into 1944. The period from the end of the Civil War to the summer of 1940, when the world war seemed decided and Fascist Italy entered it, saw Spain’s internal and institutional drift toward homologation with the Axis — its adhesion to the Anti-Comintern and its abandonment of the League of Nations — even as that “fascistisation” of the regime remained incomplete. The years 1940 to 1942 were those of what Tusell calls the tentación intervencionista, the interventionist temptation, with the internal struggle within the regime, the influence of Serrano Suñer, and the repeated German overtures toward a Spanish entry into the war.
The Hesitant Road to Neutrality
After the turn of the war, Serrano Suñer’s displacement and the arrival of Jordana at Foreign Affairs marked the beginning of what Tusell calls “un titubeante camino hacia la neutralidad” — a hesitant path toward genuine neutrality. Through the years 1942 to 1945 the Spanish government still gave assurances to the Axis while its actual policy shifted toward the Allies. It is precisely this period, from Hayes’s arrival in 1942 to his departure in January 1945, that the ambassador’s memoir records in its nine chapters: the early struggles with Spanish non-belligerency, the winning of facilities for the Allies, the opposing currents of Axis agents and Allied mission in Madrid, the progress of Spanish neutrality as the war turned, the crisis over tungsten, and at last Spain’s “benevolent neutrality” toward the Allies as victory approached. Hayes’s account of the facilities — the use of Spanish territory and ports, the easing of restrictions, the opening of the frontier — shows neutrality as a negotiated and shifting condition rather than a fixed principle, and the wolfram crisis as the moment when the Allies pressed hardest upon the Spanish government to cut off the crucial tungsten exports that fuelled German industry.
Foreign Policy as the Regime’s Better Part
Madariaga, writing from the liberal exile in the early years of the regime, judged Franco’s foreign policy in its whole as “menos mala que su política interior” — less bad than his interior policy. His chapter on the foreign policy of the General between the Civil War and the world war insists on its limits and its determining forces: a Spain exhausted and ruined, unable to enter a great war, and a dictator whose foreign course, whatever his sympathies, was constrained by the nation’s weakness and by the shifting fortunes of the belligerents. This is the contemporary liberal verdict on the neutrality, delivered before the outcome of the war was certain, and it complements Hayes’s American view of the same course. The Spanish case thus stands in the wiki beside the other neutral and near-neutral powers of the war: a state that remained at peace, not from principled abstention, but from a calculation of interest and weakness that evolved with the war itself.

concepts/squadrism.title: Squadrism
concepts/squadrism.content:
Squadrism
Squadrism (squadrismo) is the armed phase of the Fascist movement — the organisation and action of the squadre d’azione (action squads), the bands of blackshirts who, in the years 1920–1921, carried the Fascist counter-offensive against the socialist and labour movements of Italy. The word names at once the squads themselves and the style of politics they embodied: the punitive expedition (spedizione punitiva), the beating of opponents, the burning of the offices of socialist newspapers, the ejection of elected councils, and the claim of blood and martyrdom as the proof of the nation’s faith. The sources of this wiki — Businelli’s origin-story, Pini’s party chronicle, Volpe’s regime history, and above all Farinacci’s party history of the red biennium — present squadrism from within, as the movement itself understood it: the patriotic and anti-Bolshevik reaction of a people defending its Italianness against the red tide.
The squads and the red tide
The squadre d’azione grew out of the confrontation between the Fasci and the workers’ and peasants’ movement of 1919–1920. The postwar years had brought the biennio rosso (the red biennium): waves of strikes, agrarian unrest in the Po valley, the seizure of factories by the metalworkers in September 1920, and the dominion of the Socialist and labour leagues over wide provinces. Businelli’s Rivoluzione fascista narrates the turn as the “tragic year of recovery” — the strikes and the red wave, the occupation of the factories, and the Fascist reaction that followed. Farinacci, in the second volume of his Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, subtitled L’Insurrezione Rossa e la Vittoria dei Fasci, presents the same months in two parts: first the “Red Insurrection” of the workers and peasants, and then the “Victory of the Fasci” that answered it. For him the squads were not aggressors but the necessary response to anarchy — the nation’s armed defence against a revolution that the liberal state, from Nitti to Giolitti, was too weak or too cowardly to stop. The movement’s own historians never disavow the violence; they justify it as the reassertion of order and of the national will.
The punitive expeditions
The characteristic action of squadrism was the punitive expedition — the spedizione punitiva in which a column of blackshirts descended upon a town or a quarter to break the strength of the red organisations. Farinacci’s chapter on the action squads and the reprisals (Le squadre d’azione e le rappresaglie) records the multiplication of the Fasci, the end of the strength of the state, and the punitive expeditions launched against the revolutionary organisations, which he describes as a “surgical necessity” — a phrase that captures the movement’s own reading of its violence as a healing act. The same chapter tells of the rising of Trieste against the arrogance of Slavs and Socialists, the burning of the Balkan socialist Lavoratore, the barricades and massacres of the Venezia Giulia, and the devastation of the red strongholds. Pini’s chronicle, in its chapter on the camicie nere, recounts the same campaign in the provinces — the battles of Sarzana and Modena, the exhaustion of the liberal government — as squadrism organising itself into a force that could no longer be resisted. The stillicidio di sangue, the drip of blood that the movement’s martyrology counted in its fallen, is treated in every account as the sacrificial currency of the resurrection: blood called to blood, and each martyr made the faith more certain.
The conquest of the localities
Squadrism was, above all, a local conquest. The squads did not merely fight the reds in the streets; they seized the communes. Volpe’s History of the Fascist Movement records the “battles of local expurgation” by which the blackshirts ejected the Socialist mayors and communal councils and installed Fascist administration, and notes how the party and the squadre became one — the Party and the squads as a single organism. Farinacci’s account of the “epicentre” of the Fascist resurgence — the province of Bologna, the capital of what he calls agricultural Bolshevism — tells the same story in detail: the massacre of Molinella, the dominion of the red leagues over the proprietors, and the tragic episode of the Palazzo d’Accursio in Bologna, where the installation of the new communal council ended in the killing of a Fascist and the sounding of the tocsin. The expulsion of the legitimate socialist councils was in many provinces the decisive Fascist act before the March on Rome; by the time of the national elections of May 1921, into which the Fascists entered as part of the National Blocs, the movement had already reconquered the countryside commune by commune.
The civil war and its meaning
The sources treat the years 1920–1921 as a civil war — and they say so openly. Farinacci speaks of a “phase of the civil war” in the electoral struggle of 1921, of assassinations and reactions, of the law of the talion and of a “bloody dripping” (un sanguinoso stillicidio), and of the rovent (glowing) atmosphere of the battle. Businelli calls 1920 the “bloody Christmas” and the year of martyrdom; Pini entitles his treatment of 1920 the convulsione insanguinata (the blood-stained convulsion). Yet in every one of these accounts the violence is narrated as the nation’s self-defence and self-renewal: the squads are the camicie nere (the blackshirts) of the new Risorgimento, the armed conscience of Italy against a state that had abandoned it. The meaning the movement attached to squadrism was not terror but resurrection — the reassertion of Italianness, of the land, and of national honour against the foreign and the red. That is why the same sources who record the burnings and the beatings also record the martyrs’ names, and why the squadrist, with his black shirt and his dagger, stands at the centre of the Fascist origin-story as the type of the new Italian.
From squads to the regime
With the March on Rome of October 1922 the squads had conquered the state, and their place in the movement changed. Volpe records how the party, the militia and the quasi-constitutional union of the new government drew the armed energies of squadrism within the state, and how the restoration of order became the task of the regime. The squadrist temper did not vanish — Farinacci, the most unrepentant of the ras, remained a force in the party through the Matteotti crisis and the consolidation of 1925 — but the squads were progressively absorbed into the institutions of the Fascist state, the party and the Militia. The sources present this as the consummation of squadrism rather than its suppression: the violence that had made the nation again was now the authority that ruled it. The squadre d’azione had done their work, and the movement that had armed them took up the governance of the corporate state.

concepts/sturmabteilung.title: The Sturmabteilung (SA)
concepts/sturmabteilung.content:
The Sturmabteilung (SA)
The Sturmabteilung (storm detachment), abbreviated SA, was the brown-shirted storm-troop organisation of the National Socialist movement — the street-fighting force that carried the movement’s terror in its years of struggle and that Hitler destroyed as an independent power in the purge of 30 June 1934.
The movement’s fist
The SA grew out of the armed following the movement gathered in the years after the First World War — the veterans and fighters who formed the early storm troops under men like Ernst Röhm. In Heiden’s biography of Hitler the SA appears as the “iron fist” of the movement’s early years, the instrument of propaganda and terror by which National Socialism fought its way into the streets of the republic. It was the SA’s street-fighting, its brawls with the Communists and its marches through the towns of Germany, that made the movement’s presence felt in the years of reconstruction and electoral advance after 1925. As the movement grew, the SA grew with it, into a mass organisation of hundreds of thousands of brown-shirted men under the Stabschef (chief of staff) Röhm.
The rival to the state
By the moment of the seizure of power in 1933 the SA had become the movement’s principal armed body — a mass of men who had fought for the revolution and who expected its rewards. Röhm dreamed of making the SA the foundation of a people’s army that would absorb or stand beside the Reichswehr, and this ambition brought him into conflict with the army leadership and with the more cautious Hitler. The documentary record of 1934 records the resolution of that conflict: in the purge of 30 June 1934 the SA leadership was destroyed, Röhm shot, and the organisation reduced to a tamed instrument under his successor Viktor Lutze. The destruction of the SA’s power was the condition of the army’s trust in the new regime, and it marked the subordination of the movement’s revolutionary force to the state that Hitler was building.

concepts/third-republic-france.title: The French Third Republic
concepts/third-republic-france.content:
The French Third Republic
The parliamentary republic that governed France from the fall of the Second Empire in September 1870 until the military collapse of 1940 — the longest-lived regime France had known since the Revolution, and the frame within which the political, social and moral life of the interwar years was lived. Born of the defeat at Sedan and consolidated only after a decade of monarchist crisis, it is the very model of the Latin parliamentary republic of the centre that this collection of sources sets against the revolutionary and totalitarian states of Russia, Germany, Italy and Spain. Three of the five French sources that ground this wiki tell its story from within — Alexandre Zévaès, a Socialist deputy who had sat in the Chamber from 1898 to 1914; André Siegfried, the electoral geographer writing in 1930; and Marc Bloch, the historian of the Annales school who drew the regime’s balance in the ruin of 1940 — and between them they give the republic as its defenders and its critics saw it, from its birth to its death.
The birth of the regime
The republic was proclaimed on the 4th of September 1870, in the week of the catastrophe of the Second Empire. Zévaès, writing as a man of the Left, opens his history with the empire of the césarisme of Soulouque — the police-ridden, censored state of fashionable Paris, the muzzled press and the ubiquitous mouchard (spy) — whose gaudy luxury masked the rot that Sedan exposed. The proclamation of the republic in the Hôtel de Ville followed the surrender of the Emperor, and the new government, the Government of National Defence, at once confronted the war against Prussia and the negotiation of the peace. Within the year the regime passed through its most terrible trial: the insurrection of the Commune in the spring of 1871, its bloody repression, and the election of a National Assembly in which a monarchist majority threatened to undo the republic in its cradle. The republic of the first decade hung on the hazard of events — the republican campaign of Gambetta, the fall of Thiers on the Vingt-quatre mai, the Ordre moral of Marshal MacMahon and the duc de Broglie with its religious pilgrimages and its veiled royalism — before the Constitution of 1875 fixed the republican form in law.
The constitution gave France a president and two chambers, a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies elected by universal suffrage; and it is this parliamentary frame that Siegfried, the geographer, takes as the permanent object of his analysis. Writing in 1930, he treats the regime not as a recent construction but as the political expression of a national character already complete by the end of the eighteenth century — peasant and artisan, individualist, “hard as what is old,” formed before the industrial age that was now closing around it. The parties of the republic, in his reading, issue from two revolutions: the French Revolution, which set the fundamental division of the political spectrum, and the Industrial Revolution, which laid a newer social-economic fault across it. And the temperament underneath, he insists, is intimate contradiction — the Frenchman is politically on the left but socially conservative; his heart is on the left and his pocket on the right.
The consolidation of the republic
The republic that had so narrowly survived its first years became, after 1879, the settled form of French government. Zévaès carries the narrative through the great crises that tested and ultimately confirmed the regime: the Boulangist danger, when the Republic seemed momentarily to hang on the popularity of a single general; the Panama scandal, which exposed the corruption of parliamentary finance; and above all the Dreyfus affair, which for years split France into two camps and, in its resolution, produced the consolidation of the republic under Waldeck-Rousseau and the ministry of Combes — the law on associations, the dispersal of the religious congregations, and in 1905 the separation of Church and State. The republic of the radicals, in Zévaès’s sympathetic account, was the regime of the working class and the small producers of the civisme (civic-mindedness) that Siegfried names as a permanent trait of the French character. Its great legislative age, from the 1880s to the eve of the war, was the age in which the republic made itself a social state.
The war of 1914–1918, which the republic carried through the union sacrée (sacred union) of all parties, left it victorious but exhausted. The treaties were signed, the peace won; and yet Zévaès, closing his history in 1926, draws a sombre balance. The immense problems of the peace — the application of the treaty, the restoration of the devastated regions, the crushing debts and the ruinous rise in the cost of living — confronted a political class of evident infirmity. He evokes the spectacle of a life stripped of grandeur, the rivalry of ambitions and vanities in the multiplied groups of the Chamber, and, behind the paravent of the great war in which fifteen hundred thousand men had fallen for Right and Civilization, the furious unloosing of appetites and cupidities. The politics of the Directory and the morals of the Directory: such is the portrait he leaves of the postwar republic at the moment his own narrative ends.
The character of the regime
Siegfried, writing four years later, gives the regime its analytical anatomy. Its permanent spirit, he argues, is made of three persistences and three reactions. The persistences are the affirmation of popular sovereignty, declared irrevocable; an incorrigible penchant for absolutism, the tenacious virus of the past that reappears nine times out of ten in those who administer or govern — for, as Alain’s maxim runs, power is always monarchical; and the Bonapartist spirit, a nostalgia for power in a regime that systematically enervates it, whence a latent antiparliamentarism in a country that precisely willed parliamentarism to be everything. Because the people wish to be everything, their elected delegate becomes the essential piece of the system: the supremacy of the deputy, of universal suffrage. And because government is enervated by its very nature, the republic lives in a constant oscillation of ministries, majorities and scrutins (division votes).
This is the regime whose end Halévy’s chronicle and Bloch’s indictment record. Daniel Halévy, writing the year-by-year diary of 1938, finds in the practice of the parliamentary republic a governing art of drift and inaction — the pratique du rien, the practice of nothing, as he names it. Bloch, writing in the fury of 1940, draws the same regime to its account. His examen de conscience (examination of conscience) of a Frenchman indicts not the republic alone but the whole society that had failed to prepare for total war — the military caste, the political class, the bourgeoisie and its “old demon,” the educational system. Yet even at the moment of death Bloch does not abandon the regime’s deepest claim. In the clandestine essay he wrote under Vichy, Pourquoi je suis républicain, he makes his confession: the republic is the form of power that leaves the citizen the object of a mature choice, the community that does not impose itself upon man. The regime that governed France for seventy years died not because it had always been false but because, at the crisis, the society that should have defended it had ceased to believe in it. That is the strange defeat, and the balance-sheet of the Third Republic, as its own historians and witnesses drew it.

concepts/three-franciscos.title: The Three Franciscos
concepts/three-franciscos.content:
The Three Franciscos
The Three Franciscos is the name Salvador de Madariaga gives to his interpretation of the Spanish Civil War in the eighth chapter of the second book of his España: Ensayo de historia contemporánea — “la batalla de los tres Franciscos,” the battle of the three Franciscos. It is not a story of three men who fought one another in the field, but a frame for understanding the war’s deep Spanish nature against the international struggle that the world projected upon it. The three Franciscos are Francisco Largo Caballero, the revolutionary labour leader; Francisco Franco, the general of the rising; and Francisco Giner de los Ríos, the educator who had died two decades before the war. The first two embodied, in Madariaga’s telling, the tradition of violent intervention in Spanish public life; the third embodied the opposite tradition of reasonable transaction and mutual accord — and was the victim of the other two.
The War of Blood and the War of Ink
Madariaga opens the chapter with a contrast between two wars. The conflict fought with blood in Spain, he writes, was reflected in the West “en un cielo de papel” — in a paper sky — as a war of ink, a controversy among foreign disputants that turned the Spanish struggle into a debate about Europe. The intricacy of that paper war owed much to the fact that most of the disputants forgot the deeply Spanish nature of the conflict to emphasise its international aspect. Foreigners did so, Madariaga thought, perhaps from ignorance and innocence; the majority of the Spanish participants deliberately induced that forgetting, moved by the desire to obtain foreign support against their national adversaries. In its essence, he judged, the Civil War was among other no less lamentable things an “orgía de donjulianismo” — an orgy of donjulianismo, a word he coins from the legendary count Julián, the Spanish renegade who invited the Moors into Spain, to name the readiness of Spaniards to summon foreigners against their own countrymen.
The Double Manoeuvre
The begging of foreign help demanded a double propaganda. For the war to be waged by proxy, it was necessary that the right convince the fascist world that the left was communist, and that the left convince the democracies that it was not. Each of these manoeuvres provoked its contrary — a campaign to show that there was no communism in the left, or alternatively that there was no fascism in the right. In this double propaganda, Madariaga observes, the negative assertion was more serious than the affirmative one: both sides spent their energy denying the true character of the enemy. And yet neither the Russian communism nor the Italo-German fascism, however great their interest in the Spanish war and however early they bestirred themselves in it, could claim to have caused it. The war owed itself, he insists, to the combined effect of two pronunciamientos a la española — two Spanish pronunciamientos in the nation’s own tradition.
Largo Caballero and Franco
The two pronunciamientos were those of the two violent Franciscos. The first was that of Francisco Largo Caballero, the caudillo of the revolutionary wing of the Unión General de Trabajadores, who was not a communist; the second that of Francisco Franco, the caudillo of what Madariaga ironically calls the Unión General de Oficiales — the general union of officers — who was not a fascist. In July 1936 these two men, he writes, incarnated the Spanish tradition of violent intervention in public affairs, each at the head of one of the two great disciplined institutions of the nation: the workers on one side, the military on the other. Neither the Russian nor the German nor the Italian ideology had then the least possibility of provoking a civil war in Spain, even had it tried; that power resided exclusively in the two bodies that combined collective or class spirit, mass, discipline and strategic situation in the national organism — the officers of the army and the workers. The war was thus strictly Spanish in its origin, its two initial protagonists the most castizo (most authentically Spanish) of men.
The Third Francisco
Against the two violent Franciscos Madariaga sets the third, the true and great one. Francisco Giner de los Ríos, the founder of the Institución Libre de Enseñanza, had cultivated the tradition of reasonable transaction and mutual accord that Azaña, too late, thought of incarnating in the republican leadership. In this battle of the three Franciscos, Madariaga concludes, the real Francisco — the great one, the creator, the one who was Spain’s hope — was the victim of the violent action of the other two. And yet, although still too unorganised to make itself heard, the true Spain was with don Francisco Giner. The device serves Madariaga as a whole reading of the war and of the national character: the tragedy lay in the triumph of the two traditions of force over the one tradition of agreement. Read against Tusell’s scholarly history, which stresses that the war was not inevitable and could have been avoided until nearly the last moment, the three Franciscos stand as the contemporary liberal diagnosis of why the Republic failed — a diagnosis written from the exile of the victor’s enemies, before the international framing of the conflict had hardened into the categories of the cold war.

concepts/totalitarian-state.title: Totalitarian State
concepts/totalitarian-state.content:
Totalitarian State
The totalitarian state (l’État totalitaire) is the modern form of government in which the state — and the single movement that governs it — claims authority over the whole of life: the economy, culture, education, thought and the soul of the people, and not merely over the outward acts of citizens. The concept as this wiki’s sources present it was named and analysed by the French liberal historian Élie Halévy, who applied it above all to Soviet Russia, and was at the same time given practical embodiment, in different keys, by the three great revolutionary regimes of the interwar years — Italian Fascism, German National Socialism and Russian Bolshevism. Where the old absolutism had commanded the obedience of subjects, the totalitarian state commands their entire existence, treating the whole nation as a single organism to be organised, mobilised and remade behind the will of the movement. It is the distinctive political form of the “era of tyrannies,” the state that total war and total revolution together called into being.
The organised state
Halévy’s account of the new state distinguished the “organised” from the “totalitarian” form, while treating the two as the same family. Every one of the tyrannies, he argued, was an organised state — a state in which the whole nation was systematically organised for a single end, whether that end was war, revolution, or the glorification of the race and the movement. This organisation reached into every sphere that liberal constitutionalism had left to the individual or to society: the economy was to be directed, the classes were to be reconciled by force or fused into a single community, culture and education were to be bent to the service of the state. The totalitarian state, in Halévy’s strict use of the term, was the furthest development of this tendency, and he reserved the word above all for Russia, where the revolutionary state had set out deliberately to remake man and society according to a single doctrine. The distinction mattered to him because it kept the concept analytical: Fascism and National Socialism might fall short of the complete totalitarianism of the Soviet model, but they shared its logic of total organisation, and they belonged to the same era.
The leader and the people
The new state rested on a relation between the leader and the people that inverted the liberal order. In the German sources the state was grounded not in a constitution or in the rights of citizens but in the Führer (the leader) and the Volk (the people), fused into one. The programme of Mein Kampf set out this doctrine at length: race was the foundation of the state, citizenship was a racial qualification, the parliamentary principle of majority rule was rejected in favour of the authority of the single personality, and the state existed as the means of preserving the race and realising the movement. The individual counted only as a member of the people; his liberties were subordinate to the organic whole. The völkisch enthusiasm of the German tracts carried the same idea to its emotional extreme, presenting the revolution as the renewal of the German soul and the achievement of a Volksgemeinschaft (national community) in which the old divisions of class were abolished. In Italy the same relation appeared in the figure of the Duce and in the cult of the nation, the movement and the blackshirt veterans who had seized the state for it. In all three, the leader was not a servant of the state but its embodiment, the living will in which the people’s unity was made real.
The conquest of the state
The totalitarian state did not grow by itself; it had to be seized, and its construction was a work of conquest and consolidation. The official record of the German year 1933 presents this process step by step as the “conquest of power” — the appointment of the Chancellor on 30 January, the decree for the protection of people and state in the aftermath of the Reichstag fire, the election of 5 March, the Enabling Act of 23 March by which the government received the power to legislate itself, the law of 14 July making the party the sole bearer of political will, and the Gleichschaltung of the Länder under Reichsstatthalter. What the editor of the volume framed as the revolutionary transformation of the state was, in administrative terms, the abolition of the party state and the party’s absorption of the whole machinery of government. The Italian case, as its own chroniclers told it, had been different in method but the same in end: the Rivoluzione fascista of Alberto Businelli narrated the movement’s march from the intervention crisis and the war, through the Fiume rebellion and the biennio rosso, to the March on Rome of 1922, when the blackshirts seized the state that they then set about remaking. In both countries the seizure was presented not as the destruction of an old order but as the positive construction of a new one.
The whole of life
The distinctive claim of the totalitarian state was its reach into everything. It was not content with obedience to law; it demanded the alignment of the economy, the culture and the very mind of the people. The German official record grouped its work under the formula of the Neuordnung (the reordering) of state, people, economy, culture and law: the economy was to be brought into organic construction and bound to the people, labour was to be organised under the leadership of the enterprise and the German Labour Front, culture was gathered into the Reich Chamber of Culture, education was to be a work of the renewal of the German people, and even the churches were to be drawn into the reordering. The völkisch tracts applied the same totality to race and soul, holding that thought itself was race-bound and that the German must think out of his own inherited being. The state, in short, claimed the inner life as well as the outer — the soul of the people as much as its property and its work. This is what made the new form distinct from all earlier tyranny, which had commanded obedience without demanding the whole man.
The model and its warning
Read across the sources, the totalitarian state appears as both a programme and a warning. Within the wiki it unites the three revolutionary regimes that the Russian, German and Italian sources each celebrate from their own side, and it supplies the concept that the French liberal analysis of Halévy opposes to them. He saw the totalitarian state as the product of the convergence of total war and total revolution — the state organised for war that maintained the discipline of war in peacetime, and that treated its own people as material for the struggle. It stands at the centre of the era of tyrannies, the political form that defined the decades between the wars and that the democracies were forced to understand as the twentieth century’s answer to the growth of the state.

concepts/volkisch-ideology.title: Völkisch ideology
concepts/volkisch-ideology.content:
Völkisch ideology
Völkisch ideology (from das Volk, the people) was the racial-mystical world-view that supplied National Socialism its deepest intellectual foundation: the conviction that the German people is a community of blood, bound by race and soul into an organic whole, and that its renewal requires the casting off of liberalism, individualism and every alien mode of thought. It is the body of ideas that the völkisch tracts of the movement’s adherents, and the canonical texts of its leaders, set against the rationalist inheritance of the French Revolution — an order of nature, blood and race in place of an order of contract, majority and equality. In the Germany of 1933 it was both the doctrine of a party and a mood of an age, and it supplied the vocabulary — blood, race, the organic people, the enemy — in which the National Socialist seizure of power presented itself to its own public.
Race and blood
At the centre of the völkisch world-view stands the racial idea. In the tract that Hans Geisow published in the weeks after Hitler’s appointment, history is a piece of nature whose path is never straight, and the forces of race and blood are the deep currents beneath political events; the present age is diseased, and the roots of the German people’s health lie in its own inherited being. The same author reads the history of mankind in the light of Nordic prehistory, finds the creative spirit to be the chief psychic mark of the Nordic man, and holds that thought itself is race-bound — that the German must think out of his own inherited being rather than in alien categories. In Mein Kampf the doctrine is carried into the theory of the state: the state exists to preserve the purity of the blood of a people, races stand in a natural hierarchy, and the Jewish people appears as the contrary principle, the force that dissolves the racial order. On this ground the völkisch thinker erects the organic people as against the mere sum of individuals — a community of blood and soul, bound together as the family is bound, and capable of being led as a whole.
Against liberalism
The polemical counterpart of the racial idea is the war upon liberalism. Geisow’s most extended chapter is devoted to the attack upon it: liberalism is presented as an alien and artfremd (foreign to the kind) way of viewing life, an instrument of Jewish and masonic forces behind the French Revolution, and the trinity of freedom, equality and fraternity is exposed as a deception by which the organic people was dismembered into a mass of competing individuals. Against it is set the conception of the people as an organic unity, in which the economy exists for life and not life for the economy, the family is the innermost cell of the people’s life, and the state is bound to the blood-bound, God-given order of the nation. The same rejection of liberal individualism runs through Mein Kampf, which repudiates the parliamentary and majority state in the name of the Führer principle — the authority of personality against the principle of the number — and denounces Marxism as the great enemy on the other flank. The völkisch ideology thus defines itself against both poles of the modern political world at once: against liberalism and its individualism, and against Marxism and its internationalism, in the name of a third thing, the people as a racial and organic whole.
The soul of the people
Because the renewal is a matter of blood and soul rather than of laws and institutions, the völkisch programme is above all an education of the German people. Geisow argues that the renewal of life is the work of the education of the people, that the artist and the school must find again the soil from which they spring, and that the church must grasp the blood-bound order of the people; and he closes with the conviction that God, not man, makes world history, and that the German’s struggle for his right to life is a piece of religion. It is this theological-racial quality that makes the völkisch ideology more than a politics — it is a confession, a claim upon the soul as well as the state. In this light the racial laws of the state, and the whole ordering of the Third Reich, appear to the movement’s own thinkers not as administrative measures but as the working-out of a spiritual law: the realization, in law and education and art, of the racial and organic conception of the German people that the völkisch authors set down in the months and years of the revolution.

concepts/weimar-republic.title: The Weimar Republic
concepts/weimar-republic.content:
The Weimar Republic
The German republic born of the revolution of November 1918, given its constitution at the National Assembly at Weimar in 1919, and carried through a decade of crisis and consolidation before its death in the autumn of 1930. Named for the Thuringian town in which its constitution was drafted, it is the political frame within which the National Socialist movement grew — the democratic state whose fall the movement both exploited and accomplished. The left-socialist historian Arthur Rosenberg, writing in exile in 1935, and the journalist Konrad Heiden, writing a year later, tell the story from opposite ends of the political divide, but they agree that the republic was the work of the working class and that it died because the classes that had made it were too divided to save it.
The birth of the republic
The republic was not proclaimed by a leader or a party but born of the collapse of the imperial order in the last weeks of the war. The revolution of 9 November 1918, Rosenberg writes, came from below — from the sailors, soldiers and workers who, in the face of the fleet’s last order to put to sea, refused the sacrifice and turned on their officers. In Berlin the workers’ and soldiers’ councils elected the new republican government in the Circus Busch on 10 November, the day after the monarchy fell. The first government, the Council of People’s Deputies (Rat der Volksbeauftragten), ruled with dictatorial power, composed of the three Social Democrat (SPD) and the three Independent (USPD) deputies of the revolutionary movement, governing through the winter of 1918–19 while the old order dissolved.
The revolution was not a single act but a contested one. In January 1919 the Spartacus League, which had founded itself as the Communist Party of Germany at its congress of 30 December 1918, rose against the republic it judged bourgeois, and the new government under its minister Gustav Noske suppressed the rising by force. The murders of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht in the suppression, Rosenberg writes, left a wound on the German left that never fully healed — a division between social democracy and communism that ran through the whole life of the republic. The republic, born of the working class, was from its first weeks fought over by two working classes.
The constitution at Weimar
The republic gave itself a legal form in the first months of 1919. Elections to a National Assembly were held on 19 January 1919, and the Assembly met not in stormy Berlin but in quiet Weimar, summoned — as Rosenberg puts it — to give the revolution its constitution and to show it new paths. The constitution drafted there made Germany a parliamentary democracy with a president elected by the people, a Reichstag elected by proportional representation, and the federal structure of the old Reich reshaped into a unitary state, guaranteeing the classic rights of the citizen and the social claims of the age — the right to work, to education, to welfare — as the product of a revolution made in the name of the people.
The constitution was the achievement of the democratic centre, above all of the Social Democrats and the democratic parties that had come to the front in November 1918. Rosenberg’s central point is that this legal structure rested on a social foundation that was already cracked: the bourgeois parties, which had governed imperial Germany, either fought the republic or supported it lukewarmly; the army, the bureaucracy and the great landowners remained monarchist at heart; and the working class that had made the revolution was divided between the social democrats who defended it and the communists who denounced it. The constitution was real, but the will to defend it was concentrated in a minority.
The crises of the early years
The republic spent its first five years in a state of siege. In March 1920 the counter-revolution struck in the Kapp Putsch — the attempt of nationalist officers and civil servants, led by the East Prussian official Wolfgang Kapp, to seize the state and undo the republic. The putsch failed not because the republican government defended itself but because a general strike of the workers, called by the trade unions and the Social Democrats, paralysed the country and forced the conspirators out. Rosenberg draws the lesson: the republic was saved by the working class acting outside the state, while the state’s own forces — the army, the bureaucracy — had stood aside or gone over.
The early 1920s were dominated by the burden of the Entente’s demands. The period 1920–1922 Rosenberg calls the era of the “Catholic democracy” (katholische Demokratie), when the Centre party and its democratic-Catholic partners held the balance and the reparations question pressed on every government. The pressure culminated in 1923, the republic’s worst year. The French occupied the Ruhr; the Reich, under the shipping magnate Cuno who had replaced the fallen Wirth, answered with a policy of passive resistance; and the currency collapsed in the catastrophic inflation that devoured the savings of the middle classes. Rosenberg’s account of 1923 is of a republic dissolving under the double burden of foreign occupation and internal ruin — the year in which the nationalist Right, and with it the young Hitler’s movement, drew its first serious strength.
The stabilisation under Stresemann
From the wreckage of 1923 the republic was rebuilt under Gustav Stresemann. The currency was stabilised, the passive resistance ended, and the Dawes Plan brought American money and a new settlement of the reparations question. The years 1924–1928 were the republic’s period of consolidation, when the crisis receded and the republic seemed to have survived. Rosenberg, writing from the left, gives the era a sharper edge: it was the period in which the American financial power that had emerged from the war as the first power of the earth underwrote the republic, and in which the generals and the capitalists, who had never accepted the democratic state, waited and worked for its reversal.
Heiden’s biography fills in the other side of the same years. The republic of the mid-1920s was a state in which the National Socialist movement, shattered by the Beer Hall Putsch of 1923, was refounded and rebuilt through the legal channels the constitution made available. Hitler’s decision after the putsch — that power was not to be stormed but awaited, through the state and the ballot — was a judgment on the republic as a machine that could be captured by its own forms. The years of relative quiet were the years in which the movement gathered the strength the crisis of 1929 would release.
The death of the republic
The end came swiftly after the crisis of 1929 turned the republic’s stabilisation into ruin. The collapse of the American financial system cut off the money on which the republic had rested, and the depression brought unemployment and despair to the masses the constitution had promised to protect. The National Socialists, twelve seats in the Reichstag of 1928, became the mass party of protest — a hundred and seven seats in the elections of 14 September 1930. Rosenberg fixes that election as the death of the republic. In the autumn of 1930 the Reich government under Brüning was set up as a presidential cabinet governing by emergency decree, no longer resting on a parliamentary majority; and on 18 October 1930 the Reichstag, summoned to vote, capitulated and passed the emergency measures. Rosenberg calls this “the death-hour of the Weimar Republic” (die Todesstunde der Weimarer Republik).
The republic died, in Rosenberg’s reading, because its fate was entrusted to the bourgeoisie while a divided working class could not save it. The men who governed it from 1930 — Brüning, and after him Papen, Schleicher and finally the National Socialists — were the men of the classes that had fought the republic from its birth. The constitution was suspended from within, by legal means, before it was abolished; the Reichstag voted its own power away in the Enabling Act of 1933, and the republic born in revolution perished without a revolution to defend it. For Rosenberg and Heiden alike, it is the cautionary term of the interwar age — a democracy made by a divided people, whose division was the instrument of its death.

entities/alfonso-xiii.title: Alfonso XIII
entities/alfonso-xiii.content:
Alfonso XIII
The Adolescent King
Alfonso XIII assumed the throne of Spain on 17 May 1902, the day he turned sixteen, and in that accession closed the regency of his mother, María Cristina. The Monarquía restaurada (restored monarchy), which the coup of General Martínez Campos had re-established in 1874 under his grandfather Alfonso XII, now passed to a boy who, in Madariaga’s phrase, prepared to assume the regal duties on the very day of his majority. Fernández Almagro’s chronicle of the reign opens with the king’s first ministry under Sagasta, and with the enmities that surrounded the young sovereign from the outset — the palatine intrigues, the enemies of the régime, and a socialism just entering politics. What both sources agree upon is that the reign was to be read as an effort to make the modern awakening of Spain penetrate the national consciousness; Madariaga interprets it precisely as “el esfuerzo para hacer penetrar en la conciencia del pueblo español las lecciones del despertar intelectual y económico” of the second half of the nineteenth century. The task, in the liberal reading, was to reconcile the two Spains — the society that was renewing itself and a State that followed different paths — along what Fernández Almagro called an ascending line of wealth and enlightenment.
The King’s Moderating Power
Throughout the reign the king stood at the centre of the constitutional machinery, exercising what the age called the poder moderador (the moderating power). The chronicle of the reign is a succession of governments — Maura, Canalejas, Romanones, Dato, García Prieto — each crisis resolved in the palace. Fernández Almagro records the royal interventions in the crisis of the “papelito,” the difficulties of forming ministries, the king’s journey to France and England, the attempt against him in Paris, and the marriage that followed. The Moroccan question hung over the whole reign, from the Algeciras conference through the Semana trágica of 1909 in Barcelona and the execution of Francisco Ferrer Guardia, to the disaster of Annual in 1921. When the Great War came, Spain remained neutral; the king worked to keep it so against the strains of German and French pressure, the sinking of Spanish ships, and the “neutralidades que matan” that divided opinion. The wartime years also brought the Juntas de Defensa (defence committees) of the officer corps, the revolutionary strike of August 1917, and the regionalist questions, all of which the moderating power was called upon to absorb.
The Dictatorship and the Crown
The military coup of 13 September 1923 brought the reign to its decisive turn. Madariaga’s chapter on the dictatorship opens with the reflection that governing is not easy for a king, and that Alfonso XIII “hubiera preferido ser el verdadero dictador de la nueva situación” — would have preferred to be the true dictator of the new situation. The king accepted the pronunciamiento (military coup) of General Primo de Rivera, and the Crown came to rest on the Dictatorship. Fernández Almagro, in his Part V, follows the whole course of that association: the Military Directory, the dictator’s journey to Rome and his encounter with Mussolini, the Unión Patriótica, the settlement of the Moroccan war by the landing at Alhucemas and the surrender of Abd-El-Krim, the National Consultative Assembly, and the slow erosion of the régime through the depreciation of the peseta, the student strikes, the exile of Sánchez-Guerra, and the abortive pronunciamientos against the dictator. By 1930 the monarchy itself had been compromised. The kingship that had shared the Dictatorship’s power could not disown its acts when the Dictatorship collapsed; the presidents of the Senate and Congress reminded the king, after the coup, of his personal responsibility, as Madariaga records, for accepting a military dictatorship over the constitution he had sworn to uphold.
The Capitulation
The fall came through the municipal elections of 12 April 1931. Fernández Almagro’s final part, “La Monarquía, sitiada,” narrates the capitulation: the abortive revolutionary movements, the military rebellion at Jaca and the execution of Captain Galán and García Hernández, the Pact of San Sebastián, the republican propaganda and the general abstention of the old parties, the last government of Admiral Aznar, and the consultation to the country. When the municipal elections returned a republican-socialist triumph in the cities, the monarchy was evicted. The last Council of Ministers met, the provisional government of the Republic proclaimed itself at the ministry of Gobernación, and Don Alfonso departed Spain. Madariaga’s phrase for the whole process — “la realidad puede más que la realeza,” reality prevails over royalty — summarises the end of a reign in which, in his judgment, the king had lapsed into the daily struggle of parties and sects. Alfonso XIII went into exile without abdicating, and died in Rome in 1941, outliving the Dictatorship that had bound the Crown to its ruin.

entities/azana.title: Manuel Azaña
entities/azana.content:
Manuel Azaña
The Prime Minister of the Republic
Manuel Azaña, a liberal republican intellectual and the most prominent statesman of the Second Republic, became the central figure of its first, reformist phase. Elected after the fall of the monarchy in 1931, he directed the reformist biennium as minister of War and then as president of the Council — the government that gave the Republic its character. Tusell’s account of the military reform under Azaña emphasises the prestige his ministerial work earned him and the restructuring of an over-large officer corps, while the religious question, dividing the provisional government in the Cortes, imposed a new governing formula and opened what Tusell calls the reformist biennium, directed by Azaña. In Madariaga’s narrative of the Republic’s idealist opening, Azaña belongs to the idealists who were to shape the regime’s course, the man of the Constituyente of 14 July 1931 and of the Constitution that followed. It was the “España, en aquellos primeros días esplendorosos de la República” — the idyll of spring 1931 — that Azaña did most to embody.
The Reformer at the Helm
The Republic Azaña directed undertook the great reforms that defined the Spanish democratic experiment: the military reform, the agrarian question, the religious settlement, the regional autonomy statute for Catalonia, and the social legislation of the early thirties. Tusell notes that the agrarian reform was the most ambitious problem facing the new regime and, with the religious question, decisive in alienating a large part of the population; even the timidity of its content confronted a multisecular problem made urgent by the economic crisis and a growing population the labour market could not absorb. Azaña himself, in the parliamentary speech gathered in Mi rebelión en Barcelona, defended the Republic’s government and its relation to the Catalan law of land-cultivation contracts. The reformist momentum exhausted itself in the crisis of 1933; Azaña’s republican-left position was volatilised in seats, if less in votes, in the elections of November 1933 that ended the biennium and brought the conservative radical-cedista coalition to power.
The Accused of October 1934
The conservative biennium that followed turned on the insurrection of October 1934, and Azaña into its most celebrated prisoner. When the CEDA entered the government in October 1934, the socialists and the Catalan Generalidad rose; in Barcelona the Estado Catalán was proclaimed within a Spanish federal republic, and the Republic’s government crushed the revolt under martial law. Azaña, who had arrived in Catalonia in July for his health and was present when the rising broke, was arrested on 8 October 1934 and charged with instigating the rebellion. His own memoir, Mi rebelión en Barcelona, written from the ships of his detention — first the Uruguay, then the Ciudad de Cádiz and the Barcaiztegui — is his answer to the indictment, a defence of his conduct through the autumn of 1934 and a rebuke to the campaign against him. The open letter prefacing the book, signed by public men who were not his co-partisans, protested that what was done against him was not opposition but persecution: “No se aspira a vencerle, sino a aniquilarle.” Azaña’s preference, Tusell records, was for “el rey y sus ministros” against the rebels, and the legal appendix of the volume reproduces the Supreme Court’s sobreseimiento libre — the free dismissal of his case for want of evidence.
The President of the Republic
The Popular Front victory of February 1936 restored the left, and with it Azaña, who was named president of the Republic. Madariaga’s article on Azaña of 20 March 1935, gathered among the appendices to España, had already defended him in the hour of his persecution. As the “inclined plane” of spring and summer 1936 carried Spain toward the military rising of July, and the Civil War broke, Azaña stood at the head of a state that he watched being torn apart. Tusell’s account of the revolution that followed the rising opens with Azaña’s retrospective verdict: the republican government faced both the military movement advancing on Madrid and the insurrection of the proletarian masses who, without directly attacking the government, did not obey it — who wished to make a syndical revolution against fascism — and whose chief task through the whole war was to “reduce those masses to discipline.” Throughout the war Azaña was the true author, with Prieto, of the political resolution of the Popular Front’s crises: he deplored Largo Caballero’s presence in power, judged his performance in the harshest terms, and was decisive in selecting Juan Negrín, in whom he saw a “tranquil energy.” As the Republic collapsed, Azaña crossed into France in February 1939 and died there in 1940, in the exile that closed the life of the man who had been the Republic’s leading spirit and its president in its agony.

entities/badoglio.title: Pietro Badoglio
entities/badoglio.content:
Pietro Badoglio
The Marshal of the Regime
Marshal Pietro Badoglio was the army’s first soldier under the Fascist regime, the Chief of the General Staff who led the Italian conquest of Ethiopia, and the man who, in July 1943, succeeded Mussolini as Head of the Government at the King’s bidding. His own memoir of the Second World War, written at Cava dei Tirreni in the summer of 1944 and published in English in 1948, is at once an apologia for his conduct and a denunciation of the regime’s political and military leadership that he held responsible for Italy’s ruin — the account of Fascism’s fall told from within by the military commander who turned against it. He declares at the outset that he has written “because I believe that the Italian people have the right to know the course of events which led to their ruin,” disclaiming any wish to justify himself.
His memoir places him from the first at the heart of the regime’s highest decisions. In April 1939 Mussolini sent to Hitler a memorandum in his own hand, copies of which were forwarded to the King and to Badoglio, setting out the thesis that a war was inevitable between the rich and the poor nations — between those with a high birth-rate and a shrinking population, between those well supplied with raw materials and those deficient — and that the choice lay between fighting and dying of suffocation. Yet Badoglio’s portrait of the regime’s diplomacy is one of a Duce who kept the Crown ignorant. He records that Mussolini never informed the King of his intention to form the alliance with Hitler, and that it was only when the agreement was concluded and signed that he decided to notify the monarch. Article 5 of the Constitution read that executive power appertains exclusively to the King, who declares war and makes treaties of peace, alliance and commerce; the King showed his deep resentment and his anger at such a violation, but observed that it was not possible to undo what had been done without causing serious difficulties.
War and the Resignation
Badoglio’s record of the war is a chronicle of accumulating disaster over which he had ever less control. He contested Mussolini’s rush into the conflict — opposing the attack on France, which he judged wrong on both technical and moral grounds, and resisting the command of the forces in the field until the King’s sanction made it unavoidable. By the eve of the coup d’état, as he reconstructs the military situation from the reports of General Ambrosio, Chief of the General Staff, it was “absolutely deplorable”: the resources poured into the colonies had disappeared, Libya had engulfed almost all the scanty reserves, two-thirds of the army sent to Russia and practically all its equipment had been lost, the Air Force had been almost wiped out, the mercantile marine lost, and the Navy badly hurt in cruisers and destroyers. It was this ruin, and the dispersal of the forces by Mussolini, that drove him at last to countenance the removal of the Duce. The resignation of Badoglio as Chief of the General Staff — the “dictatorship in extremis,” as he titles the chapter — had come earlier, and his memoir leaves the impression of a man who watched the catastrophe from the side while the regime’s leadership refused to face it.
The Coup d’État
The conspiracy to remove Mussolini took shape between Badoglio and Ambrosio. In his account the two men agreed on two objectives to be achieved as rapidly as possible: the arrest of Mussolini and half a dozen leading Fascists, and the neutralization of the Fascist Militia, especially the armoured division then in the neighbourhood of Rome. Ambrosio thought it would take a month to collect the necessary forces in the capital without arousing suspicion. The overture came on the night of 24–25 July 1943, when the Fascist Grand Council met and, as Badoglio relates, the discussion continued to a very late hour; on the morning of Sunday 25 July came the sensational news that the Grand Council had demanded Mussolini’s resignation, with his most bitter assailants said to be Ciano, Grandi, De Bono and Bottai. The proceedings were summed up in a resolution — Grandi’s, whose original text Badoglio reproduces — which saluted the combatants, and which “invites the Government to beg the King, to whom the whole nation looks with loyalty and confidence, that he should for the honour and safety of the country assume the effective command of the Army, Navy and Air Force” and take the supreme initiative of command, “the glorious heritage of the House of Savoy.” Nineteen members signed for it, seven voted against, Farinacci’s rival resolution was not put, and Suardo abstained.
The King summoned Mussolini. When the Duce declared that he believed the resolution was not in order, Badoglio — present at the audience — answered that he did not agree; the Grand Council was an organ of State which Mussolini himself had created by a law passed by the Chamber and the Senate, and every decision of the Council was therefore valid. “Then according to Your Majesty I ought to resign,” said Mussolini with considerable violence. “Yes,” the King answered, “and I forthwith accepted his resignation.” When he heard this, Badoglio records, Mussolini collapsed as if he had been struck over the heart, muttering hoarsely, “Then my ruin is complete.” Taking leave of the King, he went out, and finding his car gone was directed to where it stood “in the shade at the side of the Villa” — and suddenly found himself surrounded by secret police who asked him to get into a motor ambulance. Asked where he was being taken, he was told, “To a place where you will be quite safe,” and was conveyed to a Carabinieri barracks.
The Head of the Government
The King then asked Badoglio to become Head of the Government. He accepted, “very conscious of my lack of political experience,” and put forward a list of politicians of the parties that had promised to collaborate — Bonomi, Casati, Soleri, Bergamini, Einaudi among them. The King was entirely opposed to the plan. He insisted that Badoglio must act with great rapidity and energy, internally and in relation to the Germans, and must not be surrounded by politicians; “You must have a Ministry of experts,” he said, “who will carry out your orders efficiently.” Badoglio demurred that he would be cut off from public opinion, but the King was determined to have his own way, assuring him that the whole country was with him, and so he agreed. The two proclamations announcing that the war would go on had already been printed, drawn up with the help of Senator Vittorio Orlando; the decision was taken that in view of the precarious position Italy could not announce that she would ask for peace, which would have provoked an immediate and violent German reaction. As he left his house that night an enormous and delirious crowd made it difficult for him to get in. At two in the morning he was summoned to the Ministry of War, where General Galbiati, Chief of Staff of the Fascist Militia, had apparently decided to resist; Badoglio’s peremptory order to place himself under the command of General Armellini had the desired effect, and Galbiati resigned. So, at the head of a military government that had arrested its own predecessor and promised to continue the war, Badoglio took up the task whose end he narrates through the armistice of 8 September, the flight to Brindisi, the cobelligerence, and the liberation of Rome in June 1944.
