entities/balbo.title: Italo Balbo
entities/balbo.content:
Italo Balbo
The Young Squadrist of Ferrara
The regime’s historians present Italo Balbo as the incarnation of the provincial squadrista — the man of the squadre d’azione (action squads) — who rose out of the agrarian struggle of the Po valley to stand, still a young man, among the founders of the state. Volpe’s history of the Fascist movement singles him out among the leaders who gave coherence to the masses of the postwar years: in Ferrara, the stronghold of the red agrarian movement, Balbo was “only a little more than twenty years of age, a war volunteer and ‘Alpino,’ a follower of Mazzini and a fascist,” one of the outstanding men of the province at a moment when the whole region had become the capital of agricultural Bolshevism. Pini’s chronicle places him at the same point of the story — in the counter-offensive of 1921, when Fascism passed from the parliamentary hopes of 1919 to the violent organization of the provinces, the young ras (provincial boss) of Ferrara embodied the will that the movement would not submit to the red dominion of the land.
Averse to the Peace
When the leaders of the movement sought to moderate the violence, Balbo was among those who refused. Volpe records that at the time of the Pacification Pact of the summer of 1921 — the patto di pacificazione by which Mussolini, under pressure, attempted a truce with the Socialists — the Communists refused to treat, and even in some places the Fascists refused to make peace, “such as in the greater part of Romagna, Emilia, Tuscany and the Veneto”; Balbo and Grandi were averse to it. It was, in Volpe’s judgement, a grave moment for Fascism, almost the beginning of a rupture. The same narrative records Balbo’s instinct for the movement’s symbolic continuity with the Fiume undertaking: his proposal to send a greeting to D’Annunzio was accepted unanimously and became a bridge between Fascism and the Fiume movement, and between Fascists who were not in complete accord. When the squadrist reaction was at last given a unified form, it was Balbo who signed it: on 22 November 1921, following an agreement between Italo Balbo and the Fascist general Gandolfo at Oneglia, there was created a General Command for the constitution and discipline of the squadre — the military arm of the movement placed, under the leadership of the man of Ferrara.
The Quadrumvir of the March
Balbo’s decisive hour was the March on Rome. Volpe’s fifth chapter reconstructs the Milan meeting of the Fasci of 16–18 October 1922, at which, around Mussolini, were present Bianchi, De Vecchi, Balbo, General De Bono — the Commandant of the squadre — and the Generals Fara and Ceccherini. It was decided to nominate a quadrumvirato (quadrumvirate) with full powers to prepare for revolutionary action; the four were Bianchi, Balbo, De Vecchi and De Bono. In the meantime Balbo, De Bono and De Vecchi were instructed to work out a scheme of mobilisation and to fix the points of concentration for the different columns that would advance on Rome — the columns of Blackshirts assembled twenty or thirty kilometres from the capital, massed in the end, a hundred thousand strong, in the Villa Borghese as the old order hesitated. Pini’s chronicle of the same days tells it in the same language: at the house of the Fascio of Milan on 16 October, with De Bono, Italo Balbo, De Vecchi, Michele Bianchi and the generals Fara and Ceccherini around Mussolini, a revolutionary Quadrumvirato was created, composed of Bianchi, De Vecchi, De Bono and Balbo, and the military modalities of the insurrection were studied. In the chronicles of the regime, Balbo’s name stands therefore not among the statesmen of the later consolidation but among the men of action who made the seizure of power — the young provincial boss whose squadre had broken the red hold on the Po valley and whose column marched on Rome.
The Later Man of the Regime
The English text of Volpe’s history, brought down to the mid-1930s, records what the consolidated regime made of the squadrist of the March. The author’s note, written two years after the original study appeared, reviews what the intervening years had added to Fascism — and among the achievements it lists is the Balbo squadron flight: “there has been another Atlantic flight, from Italy to the United States, by a squadron under Balbo.” For Volpe the feat belongs to the same register as the Littoriali of culture, the land reclamation and the corporate organisation — the demonstration of Fascism’s vitality in the service of the state. The once-revolutionary quadrumvir had become one of the regime’s celebrated men, his name attached to the aerial undertakings that carried Italian prestige across the ocean. In the arc the historians trace — from the young Mazzinian volunteer of Ferrara through the refusal of the peace, the command of the squadre and the quadrumvirate, to the Atlantic flight of the consolidated state — Italo Balbo is the figure who passed from the violence of the movement’s rise to the glories of its maturity without ever ceasing to be the man of the squadre.

entities/bloch-marc.title: Marc Bloch (1886–1944)
entities/bloch-marc.content:
Marc Bloch
Marc Bloch (1886–1944) was a French medieval historian, co-founder of the Annales school, who served as a soldier in both world wars and, in the weeks immediately after the collapse of France in 1940, wrote L’Étrange Défaite — the celebrated eyewitness examination of the disaster by one of the republic’s finest minds. Stripped of his chair by the racial laws of the Vichy regime, he entered the Resistance and was shot by the Germans in 1944; the report he left behind, addressed to future researchers, became the enduring witness of the defeat from the side of the defeated.
The historian as witness
Bloch opens his account with his état civil (civil status) as a witness. To write and teach history, he declares, has been for some thirty-four years his trade; and the first duty of the historian, in the phrase of his master Pirenne, is to be interested in life — for without bending over the present it is impossible to understand the past. He was twice a soldier. In August 1914 he began the first war as a sergeant of infantry, almost at the level of the simple soldier, and rose through chef de section and officer of intelligence to captain; in 1939, twenty-one years later, he was mobilised again into the Intelligence staff of the 1st Army. A testimony is worth only fixed in its first freshness, and so he writes now, though the pages will long be known only sous le manteau (under the cloak), for his children and for the friends who may one day read them. He writes, he insists, not his memoirs but a procès-verbal, an official report of the year 1940, intended to lie hidden until the day France should again see the freedom of thought and judgment blossom. His heroes are the common people of France — the miners of the Nord and the Pas-de-Calais, whom he names the best warriors of 1914–1918, an aristocracy of honesty and courage.
The deposition of a defeated man
The longest chapter, written first and in the heat of the moment, recounts the collapse as Bloch saw it from within the Intelligence staff. “We have just suffered an incredible defeat. Whose fault is it? The parliamentary regime, the troops, the English, the…” — so the chapter opens, listing the rival recriminations that at once flew up after the disaster. Bloch refuses the facile assignation of blame. His account of the rout is that of a professional historian applying to the present the same habits of criticism, observation and honesty he had brought to old documents: the unreadiness of the high command, its extraordinary slowness to grasp the nature of the war the Germans were fighting, the confusion, the collapse of communications and command, the breakdown of the army as a fighting institution. The Germans had transformed war — the motorised columns, the armoured thrust, the war of movement that devoured distance — and the French command, thinking in the categories of the last war, had not understood it in time. The étrange of the strange defeat is precisely this gap: a defeat not of courage but of understanding, of preparation, of a military and national mind still fixed in the forms of 1918.
The examination of conscience
The closing chapter, written with greater distance after the armistice, turns from the army to the nation, and it is here that Bloch’s diagnosis reaches its full measure. In a nation, he writes, no professional body is ever alone responsible; the states-majors worked with the instruments the country had furnished them and lived in a psychological atmosphere they had not entirely created. He will be constrained, speaking of his country, not to speak of it only in good terms — it is hard, he says, to have to discover the weaknesses of a sorrowing mother. The indictment runs over the professional military caste, the political class, the bourgeoisie with its vieux démon (old demon), the educational system, the whole society that had failed to prepare for total war. He refuses the fatal legend of the stab in the back, so propitious to redressements à rebours and pronunciamientos, and he measures the defeat against the long history of a nation he refuses to abandon. The manuscript closes at Guéret-Fougères in the Creuse, in juillet–septembre 1940.
The Testament and the clandestine writings
To L’Étrange Défaite proper the volume appends Bloch’s Testament of 18 March 1941, dated at Clermont-Ferrand, and his posthumous Écrits clandestins. In the testament he leaves the care of his funeral to his wife or children — purely civil obsequies, with no Hebrew prayers despite their cadences having accompanied so many of his ancestors; his device is Dilexit veritatem (he loved truth), and he holds complaisance in lying the worst leprosy of the soul. But it would be more odious still, he affirms, that any see in this act of probity a cowardly renunciation: born a Jew, he never sought to deny it and found no reason to be tempted to do so, and throughout his life he felt himself above all and very simply French — he dies, as he lived, a good Frenchman. The clandestine essays, written under the Vichy regime that had abolished the Republic, carry the confession further: Pourquoi je suis républicain declares the republican faith of a man who held the form of power an object of mature choice, and the notes on the reform of education demand that every national misfortune begin with an examination of conscience and a total recasting of history teaching. The regime’s racial laws had already cost him his chair at Montpellier. He entered the Resistance under the pseudonym “Narbonne,” was captured, tortured, and shot by the Germans on 16 June 1944 near Lyon — the fate that makes his report of the strange defeat, in the words of his friend Altman, the voice of a great civilian martyr who died without ever having doubted the dawn.

entities/blum.title: Léon Blum (1872–1950)
entities/blum.content:
Léon Blum
The Socialist in Power
Léon Blum, the leader of the French socialists, stood at the head of the Popular Front through its triumph and its agony — the first Socialist statesman to govern the Third Republic as president of the Council in 1936, restored to the same office in the ruinous spring of 1938, and the man who, in the closing months of the year, had to watch the movement he had made founder in the quarrels of its own parties. He had given the regime its governing experiment and its legend; the two great days of June 1936, the fausses grandes journées (the false great days) of the sit-down strikes and the social laws, had marked the French people in their usages and in their beings, as the conservative-liberal chronicler Daniel Halévy acknowledged even while deploring them. The front had shortened the working week, created the paid holiday, given the worker his two Sundays of rest and his August of deliverance — a mark on the habits of a nation that no later recovery of the state could wholly efface. But it had been made, Halévy insisted, by intellectuals jostled by demagogues, everything done against time and in the false; and Blum stood first among those who had “injected into the blood of the French people a drop of a very harmful morphine” from which it would be painful to be cured.
The Practice of Nothing
Halévy gave this chapter of drift and inaction the title la pratique du rien (the practice of nothing) — the art of governing by doing nothing practised by the parliamentary creators of delay, among whom the weary Chautemps was one of the best. By January 1938 the Popular Front was in its death-throes, and the chronicle of the year opens on the night of 13 January with the parliamentary scene of its collapse. Chautemps, president of the Council for seven months, was attempting the impossible task of limiting the damage of the Popular Front without breaking it, of succeeding Blum without pushing him aside. For Blum had retreated only a step: he had yielded the presidency of the Council, retaining the vice-presidency, always ready to know everything, to supervise everything and, if need be, to stop everything. Through the interminable night, as the Chamber drifted from suspension to suspension, it was Blum who held the soudure (the weld) of the two revolutionary parties together — the alliance of Socialists and Communists that he refused on any terms to see separated. When Chautemps finally broke with the Communists and the Socialists carried their resignations, Blum, summoned to the Palace-Bourbon “like the chief of an army compromised on the battlefield,” refused to admit the separation, and Chautemps, abandoned, left power.
The Statesman and the Crisis
The Austrian crisis exploded on Vienna in March, and it was then that Blum’s character was put to the test of the greatest public question. Hitler took Austria while Blum, in Halévy’s acid portrait, preoccupied himself with rendering presentable his “baroque Harlequin, crimson, red and pink” — a ministry in the image of the Popular Front, into which he sought to bring even a piece of the C.G.T. Behind all his combinations, Halévy detected a single dominant preoccupation: the accession of the Communists to government, that he might compromise these intimate and cruel rivals of his party by a share of responsibility. Of the national interest, the chronicler judged, there was no place in these calculations. And Blum, recalling his own famous self-definition — “I am not a Socialist man of state, I am a Socialist man of state,” the phrase he had coined at the tribune of the Senate in August 1936 — proved it once more. While the National deputies gathered, the veterans demanded a government of Public Safety, and the Chamber seethed with the sense that “Blum is keeping France waiting,” he remained closeted at the Quai Bourbon, conferring late with the Communist leaders Thorez and Duclos. When at last he proposed his National Rally to the National deputies, they listened in glacial silence, persuaded that he meant to make them accept a war dictatorship whose master would be his party, and rejected his demand by two hundred votes to three. Blum recalled the worn-out team of 1936 and took possession of the ministries.
The failure of the National Union attempt had a second political meaning. Blum’s party, once in office again, would never abandon the direction of the Front; and when the Chamber told him “Go away!” he remained, in a “lamentable persistence” that, Halévy judged, only heaped odium on his person and increased the discredit of France in Europe. The Senate waited to receive his first projects only to reject them and thus rid the country of his presence. When on 3 April 1938 Blum published his programme — an open inflation of ten milliards, a levy on fortunes, and the institution of multiple controls over the banks, the monopolised industries and the exchanges — he obtained in the Chamber no more than 310 votes against the 385 that had acclaimed him in June 1936. Wishing to retire, he was counselled by his own to go to the Senate and be beaten there, and the “socialist man of state” bowed. On 8 April the Senate, in the person of the old financier Caillaux — “the Senate is the assembly of the peasants; the Senate will reject your projects!” — rejected them, and the Blum government was done. His fall, which he had wished to make a resounding electoral declaration for the future, left the stage to Daladier.
The Era of Tyrannies
Blum’s fall in 1938 closed the last attempt of the Popular Front to govern. The movement had been a phenomenon of the era that the liberal historian Élie Halévy — the brother of the chronicler — diagnosed in his famous lecture L’ère des tyrannies (The Era of Tyrannies, 1936) as the age of the organised and totalitarian state, born of the convergence of total war and revolution since August 1914. The socialist movement, which Halévy had spent his life studying in England and France, had begun as the enemy of the state and ended, in the age of the war and the dictatorships, face to face with the question whether parliamentary democracy and socialism could be reconciled at all. Blum, the socialist who governed within the parliamentary republic while his Communist rivals pressed for the revolutionary road, incarnated that dilemma. In the closing weeks of 1938, after Munich, Blum adopted the idea of the indivisibility of peace and war — the Soviet idea — and the Socialists, meeting in congress on 25 December, divided over it; the chronicler left the year suspended, with the summations of the future gathering.
For Siegfried, writing in 1930 of the fan of parties, the socialists and radicals of the left had stood at the heart of the Third Republic’s unstable equilibrium, their balance struck between a heart on the left and a pocket on the right; for Zévaès, the narrative history of the republic closed in 1926 with the Cartel des Gauches in which the socialist and radical left had struggled against the same crushing problems as the Bloc National. Blum inherited that whole parliamentary tradition and carried it to its last and most desperate phase. His Socialist statesmanship, Halévy’s chronicle suggests, had been the final effort of the old parliamentary Left to govern a France it had itself demoralised; when it failed in April 1938, the way lay open to the restoration of authority that Daladier would attempt, and beyond that to the total war the era of tyrannies portended.

entities/bruning.title: Heinrich Brüning (1885–1970)
entities/bruning.content:
Heinrich Brüning
Heinrich Brüning, the leader of the Catholic Centre, was Chancellor of Germany in the years of its deepest collapse, from March 1930 to May 1932 — the man who governed the republic by the Notverordnung, the presidential emergency decree, when parliament could no longer form a government. He was at once the republic’s last responsible statesman and the gravedigger of its parliamentarism: a man of icy austerity, a former machine-gun officer of the war, a “half dictator and by no means a man of the people,” as the critical exile observer Konrad Heiden put it. His fate was to preside over the transformation of the German state into a presidential regime, to crush the wages and living standard of the working class in a deflationary siege, and then to be toppled by the very forces — the Reichswehr, the junckers and Hindenburg — that had raised him. Rosenberg, writing from the socialist left, dates the death of the Weimar Republic to the moment the Reichstag capitulated to Brüning’s dictatorship in October 1930; Heiden shows how the same man, by trying to hold the state together with decrees, opened the way to Hitler.
The presidential chancellor
Brüning came to power in 1930, when the coalition government of the Social Democrat Hermann Müller fell into the crisis. On the instigation of the Reichswehr leadership, Groener and Schleicher, Hindenburg withdrew his confidence from Müller and summoned Brüning. The Centre leader found no majority in the Reichstag and erected “a kind of half-dictatorship, resting on the authority of the old Hindenburg”: he dissolved the Reichstag and hoped his energetic new leadership would impress the voters and bring the parties that supported him many votes. But the electorate saw only Brüning’s energy without understanding it; the Chancellor remained a stranger to the people. Rosenberg’s analysis cuts deeper. The Weimar constitution had provided that where President and Reichstag irreconcilably disagreed, the people should decide — by referendum, or by new elections. The use of Article 48 to govern by presidential emergency decree in place of the Reichstag’s normal legislation had, Rosenberg insists, nothing in common with the constitution; the triumph of this decree-dictatorship under Brüning was the end of the republic. He dated its death precisely: the Reichstag’s capitulation of 18 October 1930, when the parliament resigned itself to a government it could not unseat, was “the death-hour of the Weimar Republic.”
Brüning’s policy was a programme of deliberate strangulation. He had set himself the task of proving practically the impossibility of the reparations burden; he drove down wages, sought to reduce prices, and lowered the general standard of living. The reparations system collapsed about him and was practically abolished in 1932 — the political fruit of his method — but the cost was borne by the German people in unemployment and misery. Seven million were without work by the winter of 1932. Brüning was the technician of this catastrophe, the man who managed the decline of a state rather than its salvation.
The man between the fronts
Brüning stood between forces that would not let him live. The Social Democrats, whose votes alone made his decrees endurable, “fled to him and did everything he demanded” after their own exclusion from power; yet they grew weary of a toleration that yielded them nothing. The National Socialists rode the misery he created. When Brüning travelled through the German east in 1931, stones were thrown at him in a Silesian town, and the Hugenberg news service that dominated the press reported that “the people receive Brüning with stones,” and that his ministers had crept through the country at night behind curtained windows, in fear, in the railway carriage. Hitler meanwhile soared over Germany in an aeroplane, spoke three times a day to crowds of a hundred thousand, and mocked the Chancellor to his face in the Reichstag: “And if you declare a hundred times that we stay at any price — I answer: we shall overthrow you in any case.”
Brüning’s deeper danger was the junckers, the class of East Elbian great landowners who surrounded Hindenburg. He and some of his ministers planned the partition of unviable great estates into peasant farms; the minister Schlange-Schöningen, himself a great landowner, drew up an excellent plan. When it became known, the great agrarians were filled with furious indignation — “agrarian Bolshevism,” they called it. Hitler, who had written in Mein Kampf that settlement on German soil was nonsense and cowardice, and who had promised the Prince Eulenburg that “national” great estates would be spared, suddenly appeared as the junckers’ protector. Heiden records how the reserve army of the junckers, the thirteen thousand great proprietors whose interests dominated the state, went over to Hitler and placed at his disposal one of the best-filled political chests in Germany, that of the Reich Land League. Brüning, by threatening their estates, had signed his own sentence.
The fall
The machinery of Brüning’s destruction was the same Reichswehr that had made him. Schleicher had decided to break him and to govern through his own creature, Franz von Papen. The intrigue unrolled in five acts through the spring of 1932: Schleicher’s desertion of the cabinet over the proposed SA ban; his negotiations with Röhm and his choice of Papen; the feeding to Hindenburg of material against the constitutional Reichsbanner militia; the junckers’ assault at Neudeck during the Whitsun holidays; and finally, on 29 and 30 May 1932, the interview in Hindenburg’s office. The old President, his thoughts no longer clear, read from scraps of paper in tall letters: “You shall have ministers with Bolshevik plans in your cabinet, that will not do.” “I request you to bring me no more emergency decrees for signature.” It was dismissal. Brüning, who still commanded a majority in the Reichstag, could not and would not govern against Hindenburg and the Reichswehr; at five minutes to noon on 30 May 1932 he declared his resignation. At four in the afternoon Hitler and Göring were received by Hindenburg and told that Brüning had been sent away and that Papen would be Chancellor.
Heiden’s portrait of Brüning is that of a man at once principled and self-defeating: he was the “gentleman” of the crisis who refused the one expedient — a real appeal to the people against the President — that might have saved the republic, because the republic was already so far gone that the working class no longer believed in it. Rosenberg, who wrote from exile and from the left, gave the verdict of a whole tradition: the republic of 1918 had been the work of the working class, and it perished because its fate was entrusted to the bourgeoisie while the workers, three-quarters of the people, were too divided in ideals and in tactics to save it. Brüning embodied that trust in the very classes that destroyed him. He outlived the republic he had governed into the ground, dying in 1970, the austere Catholic statesman of a state that had died with him.

entities/calvo-sotelo.title: José Calvo Sotelo
entities/calvo-sotelo.content:
José Calvo Sotelo
The Monarchist Orator
José Calvo Sotelo, the former minister of the dictatorship of Primo de Rivera, returned to Spain in 1933 from exile to become the most commanding voice of the monarchist right in the Cortes of the Republic. Tusell traces his formation to the integrists of Spanish Catholicism — the circles of Acción Española, whose journal gathered the intellectuals of a national-Catholic reconstruction — and suggests that biographical factors, joined to the experience of exile, carried him toward dictatorial solutions. From 1934 he exercised the effective leadership of the Alfonsine monarchists, and he did not hide his aim of directing Spain toward “una reforma totalitaria del Estado” — a totalitarian reform of the state. The model he followed, in Tusell’s judgment, was less Hitler or Mussolini than the French Maurras, the doctrine of an authoritarian restoration against the parliamentary Republic. A coordination office with the Carlists, TYRE, was created in 1933, and Calvo Sotelo, once elected deputy, played a role of first importance in the parliamentary debates. Political historians have called the party he came to lead a paradox in appearance, a “conservador subversivo” — a conservative and subversive at once.
The Column of the Patria
Calvo Sotelo’s great theme was the Army and the nation. He gave currency to the phrase that the Army was “la columna vertebral de la patria” — the backbone of the fatherland — an image Gil Robles, the leader of the CEDA, never used but which summed up the right’s conception of the armed forces as the ultimate guardian of order. Madariaga, who had known the young Calvo Sotelo before his rise, recalls him in those final months as still a relatively young man, recently returned from exile on his election in the Popular Front elections of February 1936, whose vigorous temperament and fiery eloquence had won him a place in the first rank of the Chamber. In the Cortes he spoke “en términos de violencia y protesta” — in terms of violence and protest — the ex-monarchist minister who, even without being a member of the Falange, served in the parliament as its portavoz, its spokesman. He tried to draw the whole of the right with him toward a dictatorship implanted with the aid of the Army, and his aggressive parliamentary leadership threatened the older leadership of Gil Robles within the conservative camp.
The Imprudence and the Climate
As the spring of 1936 advanced and the Republic descended the inclined plane toward war, Calvo Sotelo’s oratory grew more reckless. Madariaga records that he too delivered a speech that, though within what a deputy had the right to say, was “imprudente en extremo” — imprudent in the extreme — for a man of his opinions in that heated atmosphere. The streets of the Republic filled with violence from both sides; Madariaga’s chronicle lists the assassinated and the wounded, the political locales destroyed, the strikes general and partial, the numberless cases of violence. In such a climate a leading monarchist who preached totalitarian reform and called the Army the backbone of the fatherland made himself a target. Calvo Sotelo himself felt the danger: for weeks, Madariaga notes, he changed his bed daily for want of the elementary security of a man living in a civilized country.
The Murder of 13 July 1936
On the night of 12–13 July 1936 Calvo Sotelo was seized and murdered by guards of the republican police, and the deed set the spark to the already prepared rising. That very day a lieutenant of the Assault Guard, the leftist Castillo, had been shot dead on the pavement; that same night, Madariaga records, Calvo Sotelo slept at home for the first time in weeks. At three in the morning a number of Assault Guards in uniform appeared at his house and ordered him to dress and give himself prisoner. Calvo Sotelo invoked his parliamentary immunity, but the Captain Moreno, one of the intruders, insisted in a tone that admitted no reply. When Calvo Sotelo tried to telephone the minister of the Interior, he was told the line was cut: “Es inútil. Hemos cortado el teléfono.” He went with the uniformed guards, who were after all government police, and was carried away in an official vehicle of the Assault Guard corps, number 17; his body was taken to the cemetery and handed to the keeper. Madariaga’s account renders the horror of the deed with the plainness of the witness.
The Consequence of the Crime
The assassination of Calvo Sotelo, which came as reprisal for the killing of the lieutenant Castillo, was for many contemporaries the decisive push toward the war. Tusell’s analysis is careful: its gravity lay not in that Calvo Sotelo had been assassinated by the government — which no one at the time affirmed and which is historically false — but in the fact that the government gave no impression of controlling part of its own agents, who acted from partisan convictions and outside the law. The crime did not prove the revolutionary menace of the left, but the enormous fragility in which the bad management of the government had left the republican state. Nevertheless a part of Spain felt itself threatened by the other and, in the words Tusell repeats, “por impaciencia y falta de templanza” — by impatience and lack of temperance — committed the error, never justifiable, of rising against the Republic. The murder widened the extent of the conspiracy and terrorized the right further; five days later, on 18 July, the military rising broke out across Spain. In Madariaga’s phrase the Republic was to pay dearly for the deed, for the assassination handed the right its martyr and the revolution its pretext, and the monarchy it had served was never restored. Calvo Sotelo’s fate — the parliamentary orator of the extreme right struck down by the state’s own agents — became one of the founding justifications of the Nationalist cause and one of the deepest grievances of the war.

entities/canaris.title: Wilhelm Canaris
entities/canaris.content:
Wilhelm Canaris
Admiral Wilhelm Canaris — Singer gives him in full as Walter Wilhelm Canaris — was the chief of the German Secret Service in the Second World War, the head of the Abwehr, the military intelligence service. The wartime chronicler Kurt Singer called him the mystery man of German espionage, perhaps the greatest spy of his time and certainly the greatest organizer of espionage the world had known. More than any other important Nazi, Singer wrote, Canaris cultivated obscurity: deliberately he reduced his personality to a cipher, never appeared at the great Nazi mass meetings, never spoke on the air, and was never mentioned in the German press. Few cameras ever caught his likeness, and he renounced all public glory.
The admiral who never wears a uniform
Canaris was promoted to Admiral on the historic morning of 1 September 1939, the day German troops poured across the border into Poland; the modest civilian who walked down Berlin’s Wilhelmstrasse that morning, whom the officer at the door addressed as Admiral, was the new head of all German espionage. He was small and of slight build, with a colorless, sallow skin like that of men who work at night, prominent cheekbones that lent his face a more Slavic than Teutonic cast, and a slight hunch of the shoulders. The name Canaris is Greek; his grandparents were of Greek stock and had emigrated to Germany. He invariably dressed as a civilian, walked with a furtive droop of the head, and was described by the few who met him as neurotically alert — a man who considered no situation harmless, who took care to face you and let the wall guard his back. His home was a secret in the suburb of Zehlendorf, surrounded by a flower garden he loved but had no time to tend; his headquarters at the War Department in the Bendlerstrasse had a private entrance and a staircase exclusively his.
The spy of the First World War
His career as a spy began in 1914. At twenty-five he was already commander of the cruiser Dresden; the outbreak of war found him on the high seas, with no hope of returning to a German port, so he brought his ship to neutral Chile, where he and his crew were interned. A German secret-service officer in the guise of a Red Cross visitor contacted him in the internment camp and planned a daring escape: once free, Canaris was to enter the Imperial Intelligence Service and go to the United States to work under Franz von Papen, organizing anti-American espionage and sabotage. The escape was managed with ease, and in 1916 an unremarkable smallish man with prominent cheekbones came to New York calling himself Otto Seliger, a Polish Jew; under the further alias of Moses Meyerbeer, claiming to be a nephew of the composer, he organized the dynamiting of the Canadian Car and Foundry Company. Singer notes the strangeness that Canaris, whom he calls pathologically anti-Semitic, twice posed as a Jew.
In Spain, to which he was ordered weeks before the United States entered the war, he met the woman who was to play a fateful role in his life — Margarete Gertrude Zelle, the dancer known as Mata Hari. Ostensibly a military attaché, Canaris was in reality preparing bases for German submarines along the neutral Spanish coast, conducting harbor espionage against Allied shipping, planting agents at the Spanish court, and smuggling German agents across the Pyrenees into France. He recruited Mata Hari to go to Paris and become his key agent there, and she became for him only Agent No. H-21; it was to his Intelligence Service, Singer recounts, that her whereabouts were reported when she was betrayed. She gave her life, in Singer’s phrase, to purchase advancement for the career of Canaris.
The conspirator of the Republic
The German Revolution left Canaris jobless with the rank of lieutenant commander, but not inactive. Singer records that on his own initiative he organized counter-revolution against the Weimar Republic, helped conceal the arms the Inter-Allied Control Commissions were hunting for, helped establish the Free Corps that stood in the forefront of the Putsches that shook the Republic, and planned several of them himself. He was a collaborator of Hitler in the Beer Cellar Putsch of 1923, and had it succeeded, he was to have taken over the northern seacoast of Germany. Around 1926 he sank out of sight, working obscurely in a tiny office at the War Ministry whose door read “Department for Naval Transport” — which meant exactly nothing — toiling away at Naval Intelligence in preparation for “Der Tag.” A scandal over the seven-million-mark financing of the militaristic Phoebus film corporation, which he answered only with “Secret funds,” sent him off to Spain, where the secret rearmament was going on; he saw to the building of U-boats in the Echeveria shipyard, was a frequent guest of the Spanish munitions king Juan March, and set up an espionage system against British and Italian shipping.
The servant of the party
In 1929 von Papen introduced Canaris to Hermann Goering; the two Junker officers liked each other from the start, and Canaris offered to bring the intelligence facilities of the German army to the aid of the Hitler movement. His first job for it was a simple personnel report — a file on all German officers indicating their political leanings, finances and moral attitudes. He was instrumental, with von Papen, in deposing Chancellor Kurt von Schleicher, whose post fell free for Hitler after Canaris stole a compromising document from Schleicher’s private desk. As chief of the Abwehr from 1 September 1939 he wove a huge web of spy centers across the world: German consuls near the harbors were submarine commanders and naval agents under his pay roll; his hand reached to the Near East through Dr. Fritz Grobba, to Ireland, to Denmark through Horst von Pflugk-Hartung; his agents seized the French navy’s mobilization orders at Munich in 1938 and signalled the U-boat that sank the Royal Oak at Scapa Flow. Singer presents him as the enigma at the centre of the secret war — the greatest organizer of espionage the world had known, and at the same time a man whom the party’s own police mistrusted, whose service would fall before the rival apparatus of the SS.

entities/chaves-nogales.title: Manuel Chaves Nogales (1897–1944)
entities/chaves-nogales.content:
Manuel Chaves Nogales
Manuel Chaves Nogales (1897–1944) was the Sevillian liberal journalist — editor of the republican daily Ahora in the first months of the Spanish Civil War — whose nine stories of the war, written in exile in Paris in 1937 and gathered as A sangre y fuego: Héroes, bestias y mártires de España, give this wiki its literary testimony of the conflict from the “third Spain” that refused solidarity with the assassins of either side.
The liberal editor in the revolution
Chaves Nogales was a journalist of the liberal centre who had made his newspaper a voice of the Republic. When the war broke out in July 1936 and the government departed for Valencia, his paper was seized by a workers’ committee (a consejo obrero); Chaves Nogales served the workers of the paper with the weapon of his trade, and then, when there was nothing left to save, went into exile. His prologue, dated at Montrouge in January–May 1937, is the manifesto of the “small bourgeois liberal,” antifascist and antirevolutionary alike — a man who had fought fascism with the tools of his profession and who refused the choice between the two fanaticisms he likened to an “abyssinian” (Franco’s Spain) and a “Western Kirghiz” (Bolshevism). His only truth, he wrote, was an insuperable hatred of stupidity and cruelty.
The nine stories of the war
The nine novelas that follow — ¡Masacre, masacre!, La gesta de los caballistas, Y a lo lejos, una lucecita, La columna de hierro, El tesoro de Briesca, Los guerreros marroquíes, ¡Viva la muerte!, Bigornia and Consejo obrero — are, by the author’s own NOTA, drawn faithfully from rigorously veridical facts, each hero a real person veiled only by the proximity of the events. They record the aerial bombing of a town, the cavalry charge of gentleman-soldiers against the revolutionaries, the anarchist Iron Column and its treatment of fascist prisoners, the salvage of Castilian art under fire, the Moroccan soldiers of Franco’s forces and their meeting with the Spanish milicianos, the fascist parade in the Plaza Mayor of Valladolid, and the tank-driver Bigornia who carries a terrified mother and her children to the hospital in Madrid. Set beside the regime histories and the military chronicles, they supply the war’s lived texture from the liberal middle — the human cost that the victors’ and the revolutionaries’ accounts alike pass over.

entities/companys.title: Lluís Companys
entities/companys.content:
Lluís Companys
President of the Generalitat
Lluís Companys, president of the Generalitat of Catalonia from the death of Francesc Macià, was a very different Catalanist from the founder he succeeded. Tusell notes that he lacked the personal charisma Macià had possessed, especially beside men whose biographies were more bound to the Catalanist cause, such as his “conseller” of the Interior, Dencás. Madariaga, the liberal historian, describes him as a lawyer of anarcho-syndicalist lineage who had succeeded Macià, a man who needed the popular vote and courted it assiduously. When Catalonia hesitated between Gassol and Companys after Macià’s death — Gassol being the true spiritual heir who had proclaimed the Estat Català from the balcony of Barcelona’s town hall on 14 April 1931 — it preferred Companys precisely because he was a man of less accentuated Catalanism, who had always expressed himself in Castilian and who commanded the support of the anarcho-syndicalist masses, indifferent and even hostile to Catalanism. Madariaga’s verdict is harsh: Companys was, in his eyes, a demagogue. Yet the same historian insists, with equal firmness, that Companys did not betray Spain in October 1934 as was then said and afterwards repeated: he was a Spanish patriot who at a grave moment of his political activity did what he could according to his lights and in good faith — Spanish Catalanist but also Catalan Spaniardist. The accusation of treason he calls a scandalous injustice; the accusation of breaking the constitution he does not deny.
The Law of Cultivation Contracts
The conflict that brought the Republic to crisis in 1934 grew out of an agrarian question that, Tusell observes, might have been resolved without any institutional clash. The rabassa morta was a Catalan contract governing the cultivation of the vine, under which the tenant, or rabassaire, paid the landowner a proportional share of his harvest. The Law of Cultivation Contracts, approved by a Catalan parliament in which the Esquerra held the majority, was intended to let the rabassaires accede to property under certain conditions; its purpose was not merely acceptable but coincided with the agrarian policy of the radical-cedista governments. The problem was complicated by a question of jurisdiction between the state and Catalan parliaments over the interpretation of the Statute of Autonomy, civil legislation belonging to Catalonia and social legislation to the central state. A part of the Catalan landowners appealed to the Tribunal de Garantías Constitucionales, which, acting on purely legal criteria and against the opinion of its radical-leaning members, declared the law unconstitutional. When the Generalitat refused to accept the ruling, the question, its agrarian origins forgotten, became a quarrel about autonomy itself. As the Catalan left-moderate Hurtado later wrote, the Esquerra had used the rabassaire question “as a mere pretext,” and this was “a genuine misfortune both for Catalonia and for the Republic.” Azaña, defending the Republic’s government before the Cortes in June 1934, took up this very ground, arguing the case of the Republic’s ministers against the Catalan law; and in his Barcelona address to the Catalan republicans in August 1934 he warned against the course on which the Generalitat seemed set.
The Proclamation of the Catalan State
The precipitating cause of the October rising was the entry of the CEDA into the government, which a part of the Left treated as a betrayal of the Republic. In the emotionally charged aftermath of the formation of that government, Companys, as Tusell narrates, was overtaken by the more extreme Catalanism of his own counsellors without apparently measuring the consequences of his acts. On the night of 6 October 1934, from the balcony of the Generalitat, he proclaimed “the Catalan State within the Spanish Federal Republic.” Turning to those who had reproached his lack of Catalanism, he told them, “ya no diréis que no soy catalanista” — now you will not say I am no Catalanist. The declaration, Azaña insisted, was manifestly unconstitutional — the Republic of 1931 was not federal, and the Generalitat had no power to convert it into one. Azaña, who had counselled the Catalan leaders prudence, later wrote that they did not listen, above all because Companys lacked the courage to be prudent. The revolt itself, Tusell shows, was far more a political gesture than an insurrection: part of the CNT and the extreme-left tendencies had proclaimed a strike against the government, not in favour of the Generalitat, and the two most important syndical forces, the official CNT and the rabassaire syndicate for whom the conflict had begun, stood aside. The Generalitat soon surrendered to General Batet, a republican soldier who had no doubt where legality lay; his prudence avoided many deaths, and the mere presence of troops in the street sufficed to defeat the rising.
Condemnation, Amnesty, and War
Madariaga, weighing the repression that followed, judged the juridical responsibility of Companys and of Largo Caballero at least as grave as that of Sanjurjo in 1932 — and noted the disproportion: Sanjurjo was condemned to death while Companys, condemned to imprisonment, could always count, as events justified, on Spain being the land of amnesties. Of the thirty death sentences pronounced in consequence of the 1934 events, only two were carried out, and Companys was not among them. He returned to the presidency of the Generalitat after the Popular Front’s victory in 1936. During the Civil War his position grew difficult as the central government, under Negrín, concentrated power and moved its seat to Barcelona. The letter Madariaga appends to his history — from Companys to President Juan Negrín — shows him protesting, as President of Catalonia, against abuses in the republican rear guard: the entering of the Figueras reformatory by government forces with machine-guns, without notice to the Generalitat; the discovery of nineteen corpses at Sitges that had been prisoners of the Villa de Madrid; the arming of dubious individuals by police commissars who carried out detentions, searches, abuses and shootings; nearly a hundred death sentences in a single week. He wrote that, as power was concentrated and absorbed, “la Generalidad ha quedado convertida en una institución sin relieve” — the Generalitat had been left an institution without relief. Azaña, writing his prison memoir, had already insisted, against the accusation that he had instigated Companys, that a subversive act in which the Generalitat took part could only lead to catastrophe for Catalonia and the Republic. Companys survived the war to fall into Franco’s hands; the Republic that had treated him as a rebel was gone, and the regime that had arisen from rebellion executed him, though on this occasion, Madariaga notes pointedly, Companys had stayed within the law.

entities/d-annunzio.title: Gabriele d'Annunzio
entities/d-annunzio.content:
Gabriele d’Annunzio
The Poet and the Gesture
Gabriele d’Annunzio, the poet and ardito — the man of the assault corps — is the figure through whom the regime-side histories of Fascism read the Fiume undertaking of 1919. He had been the most famous man of letters in Italy before the war, and during it a volunteer of spectacular, performative courage. Pini and Businelli present him as the hero of the gesture against a state that would not defend the nation’s claims: when the peace settlement seemed about to deny Italy the Adriatic city of Fiume, it was d’Annunzio who gave the national protest its dramatic form. In the movement’s own telling he is the precursor of the Fascist impulse — not yet a Fascist, but the man who showed how a resolute minority could act against the timidity of the government. The histories treat him as both a national champion and a warning, a force that the state was unwilling or unable to master.
The March of Ronchi and the Occupation
The undertaking itself is narrated by both Pini and Businelli as the impresa di Fiume — the enterprise of Fiume. On 12 September 1919 d’Annunzio led the legionaries, with units of the Army that had refused to stand down, out of Ronchi on the march to Fiume, and entered the city to proclaim its annexation to Italy. The movement’s historians set this against the conduct of “official Italy”: the cowardice of the Nitti government, the inertia of the state, the diplomacy that had bound Italy at Paris and at London. Farinacci, treating the same events from the party side, calls the ideal origin of the undertaking the Wilsonian utopia and the violations of Italian right. D’Annunzio’s Fiume was a state within the state, holding out against the government that could not bring itself either to support it or to crush it. For the year and more of its existence it became the magnet of the Italian interventionist and nationalist youth who would later form the Fascist movement.
The Carta del Carnaro and the Natale di Sangue
The revolutionary city produced its own constitution, the Carta del Carnaro (Charter of Carnaro), drawn up with the syndicalist Alceste de Ambris — a document of a corporative, national and social republic that the movement’s historians record as one of the inspirations of the corporate state. The occupation could not last. The government of Giolitti, determined to end the impasse, negotiated the Treaty of Rapallo with Yugoslavia in November 1920, which confirmed Fiume as an independent city, and when d’Annunzio refused to yield, ordered the Army to force him out. The Natale di sangue (Bloody Christmas) of late December 1920 — the bombardment of the city by the Italian fleet and the fighting on the streets — ended the undertaking. D’Annunzio left Fiume, and the legionaries dispersed. Pini presents the episode as a gesture that failed in its immediate object yet succeeded in its deeper purpose: the demonstration that a resolute national minority could defy the state, the rehearsal of the techniques of revolt, and the preparation of the ground on which Fascism would build.
The Precursor of Fascism
In the movement’s own history, d’Annunzio stands as the bridge between the war and the Fascist seizure of power. The Fiume undertaking is narrated not as an episode closed in 1920 but as the proof of what a patriotic minority could do, and its veterans, its rhetoric, and its model of the legionary state flowed into the Fascist movement. Businelli treats the enterprise as one of the key steps in the “epic struggle” that led from the interventionist crisis to the March on Rome; Pini’s chronicle gives it a full chapter of its own and presents the legionaries’ devotion and the poet’s oratory as anticipations of the Fascist style. D’Annunzio himself remained something of a rival and an embarrassment to the movement — too individual, too literary, too insubordinate to be a party man — and yet the sources agree in reading his Fiume as the first draft of the Fascist revolution, the moment when the nation’s poets and soldiers moved ahead of its statesmen. When the regime came, it honoured him; the histories of its rise had already made him one of its prophets.

entities/daladier.title: Édouard Daladier (1884–1970)
entities/daladier.content:
Édouard Daladier
The Man of the Radicals
Édouard Daladier, the leader of the Radical-Socialists, came to power in April 1938 as the man who had to repair what the Popular Front had destroyed — the figure on whom, in the crisis year, the restoration of the authority of the state and the conduct of foreign policy both devolved. After Blum, Halévy’s chronicle records, Daladier governed; his accession was expected, and he received every concurrence. “His name had never appeared in the dirty stories”; his person had something salutary and aired about it, and when he crossed the corridors of the Chamber it seemed that some shepherd of the Camargue passed through. He was recognised as a man of upright intentions and of national sense, of certain goodwill; his will, strictly speaking, remained to be tested, for his past had shown him capable of hesitations and retreats. The Socialists and Communists remembered that he had sworn the oath of the Popular Front in 1935, and would not release him from it by showing hostility. It was thus that he obtained the unanimity of votes — a success, Halévy warned, that enveloped manoeuvres and prepared weaknesses.
The Restoration of Authority
The new minister sought to restore the state after the ruinous experiments of the Front. Of the full powers voted him, Daladier would in fact make little; his decree-laws of July contained nothing of the recovery of which so much had been spoken. This was no surprise, for Daladier was paralysed by the very unanimity that had welcomed him. The recovery of the country presupposed a rupture with the Popular Front; but Daladier had not broken, he respected the fiction. The week of the forty hours and of the two Sundays was to remain sacred for him, the abuses that devastated the state were to be spared. His attention turned rather to the outside, to that new Europe which had become the focus of anxieties — and it was high time, for the balance of force had shifted catastrophically. When France had promised aid to Czechoslovakia, her armies stood at the gates of Frankfurt, two hundred leagues from her ally; in 1938 the French army lay at Metz, confronted by a fortified line practically impassable, its sixty divisions facing a young army of a hundred and ten. The engagements of the past had not been revised; Daladier and his foreign minister Bonnet had at least the merit of not eluding the problem.
At London on 29 April 1938 Daladier recalled to the English statesmen the engagements of France. The English were at first resistant — “this Czechoslovakia is an absurd, indefensible country” — but Daladier maintained that if Hitler invaded Czechoslovakia as he had invaded Austria and the blood flowed, France could not remain a spectator. Chamberlain at last answered: if you are drawn into the peril, we will not leave you alone; but let us conduct the affair. There followed the good weeks of the Franco-British entente; on 20 May England made known to Berlin in the most energetic manner that she would have no violence in central Europe, and the dangerous days passed without trouble.
The August days gave an astonishing spectacle. In Germany, orders alerted the population by the hundred thousand, sent to the armies and the fortification works; meanwhile the French were going on their paid holidays — that manna fallen from heaven, the gift of the Popular Front — and not a single aeroplane was delivered to the Air services. Daladier, informed of the perils, watched this senseless gaiety. About the fifteenth the franc wavered on the exchange; Daladier seized the pretext to speak to the country, and for Sunday the 21st he announced a broadcast address. All France listened and heard an indignant man, who showed this people that seemed to wish to ignore it the new Europe — the war raging in Spain and the Far East, the great states of the centre proving their forces with no real limit to service or labour. The weakness of French production, he said, was a national shame; it was urgent to return on the law of the forty hours. He closed with a formula that made a sensation: “Let us put France back to work” (remettons la France au travail). Many were touched and knew he had spoken true, but the response that rose was the cry of the Front’s newspapers that he had insulted the working class. Two ministers, Frossard and Ramadier, watching for his fall, withdrew; the Communists demanded the convocation of the Chambers. For three days Daladier listened to the anathemas of the Communists, the harsh criticism of the Socialists, the uneasy complaint of the Radicals, and succeeded in eluding the assault — always in possession of his weak power, he began negotiations of which some were very useful, notably in the mining industry.
Munich and the End of the Year
The preliminaries were suddenly suspended by an event that imposed itself by its grandeur: the September crisis. France remained a spectator of the prodromes of the drama, all conducted between Chamberlain and Hitler; at last the French and English statesmen took the measure of the peril, and the war was in view. On 24 September the English fleet, the Czechoslovak army and the French army were mobilised; and this mobilisation, Halévy insists, was the national fact — for four days France was touched to its last hamlet, the community of the peril restored the community of beings, and the people, thus called, gave a very good response. There was no enthusiasm, only an astonishment wrapped in silence; but the acceptance was entire, and there were no absentees. “France has shown its strength,” wrote the young political writer Louis Salleron; “she has shown her army, which exists. She has shown her policy, which does not exist.”
On 27 September everything seemed to glide toward the abyss; on the 28th Chamberlain and Daladier met Hitler and Mussolini at Munich, and peace was saved. Daladier and Chamberlain were received on their return as triumphants; yet they had obtained nothing, save for Czechoslovakia the economy of blood. The Germans reserved to themselves the right to take everything, the industrial equipment as well as the arms; they seized three thousand cannon, convoyed and turned at once on the lines of the Rhine. “Was it necessary,” Halévy asks, “that the signatures of France and England should figure at the foot of such a treaty?” For the first instant nothing was felt but the benefit of peace; but the relief was short, and reality reappeared very quickly with its hard contours.
Daladier seized the reawakening that followed. He convoked the Chambers; on 4 October they sat, he exposed the events of September, obtained an approval, and then demanded the full powers in order to go this time to the bottom of the evils the crisis had shown. The night of the full powers repeated the night of 13 January; the clienteles were menaced, and it was a matter of manoeuvring Daladier, of binding him, of surrounding him with traps. Toward midnight the rumour of a dissolution drew the Communists and Socialists together — “the instinct of self-preservation draws us together,” wrote Blum — and Herriot at last interposed and appeased the conflict; Daladier accepted that the full powers be diminished by promises and limited to 15 November instead of 31 December. The year closed with the general strike fixed by the C.G.T. for 30 November. Daladier, breaking with the habits of a culpable tolerance, sent in the mobile guard which after a long nocturnal combat drove the mutinous strikers from the Renault works; and when the strike came it aborted — the post, the transports, the schools all worked, and the French state issued from the day victorious. Daladier had made himself responsible for everything and was given credit for everything. Yet he stood on a soil sown with traps: he carried by 315 votes against 250, and on 22 December escaped a fall only narrowly, 291 against 284. “Seven votes of majority,” he said on being told; “six more than necessary!” A rectification brought the number to four. There they stood, in the lottery of numbers.
Marc Bloch, writing as a defeated soldier and citizen two years later, judged the whole regime with a severity that embraced Daladier’s France: the ministers and the assemblies had prepared the country badly for war, the presidents of the Council had had to demand the full powers as a confession that the constitutional machine grated, and these full powers themselves had not served to reinforce governmental practice. The paralysis of the old parliamentary republic that Daladier had restored by force of will was, for Bloch, the deeper cause of the strange defeat.

entities/de-bono.title: General Emilio De Bono
entities/de-bono.content:
General Emilio De Bono
The Soldier of the Squadre
Among the leaders of the Fascist movement who gathered for the seizure of power, General Emilio De Bono held a singular place: he was the professional soldier who lent the army’s craft to the revolutionary force. Volpe’s history of the Fascist movement, describing the preparation of the March on Rome, names him with a precise office — “the General De Bono who was Commandant of the squadre.” Where the other men of the movement’s leadership were the young provincials of the squadrist war in the Po valley, De Bono brought to the revolution the rank and the habits of the regular officer, the man whose signature on the order of mobilisation gave the Blackshirts the discipline of an army. The regime’s historians present this as the indispensable complement to the ardour of the young: the squadre d’azione (action squads) that had broken the red hold on the countryside of Emilia and Romagna required, when the hour of decision came, a military hand to direct them.
The Quadrumvirate of the March
De Bono’s name is bound in the official histories to the quadrumvirate that led the March on Rome. Volpe’s fifth chapter reconstructs the meeting of the Fasci at Milan of 16–18 October 1922, at which, around Mussolini, were present Bianchi, De Vecchi, Balbo, the General De Bono — Commandant of the squadre — and the Generals Fara and Ceccherini. It was decided to nominate a quadrumvirato (quadrumvirate) with full powers to prepare for revolutionary action; the four chosen were Bianchi, Balbo, De Vecchi and De Bono. In the same account De Bono is joined to Balbo and De Vecchi in the working out of the scheme of mobilisation and the fixing of the points of concentration for the columns that would advance on Rome — the concentration points established twenty or thirty kilometres from the capital, while a hundred thousand Blackshirts massed in the Villa Borghese. Pini’s chronicle of the same hour tells it in the same terms: at the house of the Fascio of Milan on 16 October, with De Bono, Italo Balbo, De Vecchi, Michele Bianchi and the generals Fara and Ceccherini gathered around Mussolini, who declared that the revolutionary moment could no longer be delayed, a revolutionary Quadrumvirato was created, composed of Bianchi, De Vecchi, De Bono and Balbo, and the military modalities of the insurrection were studied.
The Officer at the Seizure of Power
The chronicles record De Bono’s role as that of the technician of the insurrection, the man who gave the revolutionary plan its military form. Where Balbo embodied the provincial squadrist ardour and De Vecchi the Piedmontese monarchist of the Fasci, De Bono stood for the conversion of the regular army’s art to the service of the movement — a conversion the regime’s historians present as the marriage of the two Italies: the Italy of Vittorio Veneto and the Italy of the squadre. The presence of the serving or retired generals at the Milan meeting — Fara and Ceccherini as well as De Bono — was itself, in Volpe’s framing, evidence that the movement had passed from the spontaneous violence of the provinces to a considered and militarily prepared insurrection, entrusted to a command in which the general sat beside the young ras of Ferrara. When the March on Rome came in the last days of October, and the King refused to authorize the military response, the columns whose concentration De Bono had helped fix converged on the capital under the direction of the quadrumvirate.
The Place in the Regime’s Memory
The histories of the Fascist rise give De Bono a settled place in the canonical story of the movement’s origins: he is one of the four names — Bianchi, Balbo, De Vecchi, De Bono — repeated without variation in every account of the October days. The quadrumvirato was the moment at which Fascism, in the telling of its own historians, ceased to be a movement and became an insurrectionary state in miniature, and De Bono’s inclusion in it acknowledged the debt the revolution owed to the professional officer. In the same narrative his earlier command of the squadre linked him to the whole arc of the violent reaction — the convulsione insanguinata of 1920 and the counter-offensive of 1921 by which the Blackshirts had re-occupied the provinces. For Volpe, the soldier of the squadre who helped plan the march belongs to the same category as the young Balbo and the monarchist De Vecchi: the men of the movement who, when the old order faltered before the anarchy it had allowed, gave it the discipline and the determination to take Rome.

entities/farinacci.title: Roberto Farinacci
entities/farinacci.content:
Roberto Farinacci
The Ras of Cremona
Roberto Farinacci (1892–1945) was the ras — the provincial Fascist boss — of Cremona, one of the two dominant figures, with Italo Balbo, of the squadrist violence of the Po valley, and from 1925 to 1926 Secretary of the National Fascist Party. He is the author of the movement’s most exhaustive party history, the Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, published in three volumes by the press of his own home province, the Stabilimento Tipografico «Cremona Nuova», at Cremona in the years 1937–1939. Where the academic Volpe wrote the official narrative of the revolution and Businelli the young educator’s origin-story, Farinacci wrote its documentary history from the inside of its most violent and decisive phase. The trilogy is at once an account of Fascism’s rise and a document of how the radical-squadrist wing of the regime understood its own victory — accusatory, polemical, and addressed to the party it had built by force.
The Collapse of the Ruling Class
The first volume, Il 1919 (1937), treats the single crisis year of the Fasci’ founding. Its two parts announce its argument: Lo sfacelo della classe dirigente (The Collapse of the Ruling Class) and La disfatta diplomatica (The Diplomatic Defeat). Farinacci indicts the liberal governments of Orlando and Nitti, the “Messia americano” (American Messiah) Wilson and the Paris Peace Conference, the Socialists, and the moderates for the national humiliation that, in his telling, made the Fascist reaction necessary. The state of mind of the country after the victory, the compliance of Orlando before Wilson’s League of Nations, the Russian revolution and its repercussions, the split among the interventionists — these fill the first part. The second moves from the assault on Avanti! and the constituent assembly of interventionism through the Caporetto inquiry, the Fiume undertaking, and the elections of 16 November, closing with the equivocal action of the moderate Socialists. Throughout, the Fascist answer to the “ineptitude” of the rulers is presented as the patriotic and necessary one.
The Red Insurrection and the Victory of the Fasci
The second volume, L’Insurrezione Rossa e la Vittoria dei Fasci (1938), covers 1 January 1920 to May 1921, the “red biennium” and the squadrist reaction. In the Avvertenza Farinacci states that he follows an ideal rather than chronological criterion — each chapter develops a single argument or historical moment — and that the Fascist congresses and doctrinal discussions are deliberately omitted for a later volume. Part I, L’Insurrezione Rossa, sets out the “revolt without ideas and without leaders”: the economic and revolutionary strikes, the episode of Cremona, the occupation of the factories and its tragicomic collapse under workers’ management, the agrarian riots in the countryside, the massacre of Molinella, the killings at Palazzo d’Accursio in Bologna. Against the background of the Nitti and then Giolitti ministries, Farinacci mounts his accusation: the cowardice of the ruling class, the “dictator and corrupter of political struggle in Italy” that Giolitti was in his eyes, the pacifism of the moderate Socialists. Part II, La Vittoria dei Fasci, narrates the riscossa — the Fascist resurgence — from the burning of the Lavoratore at Trieste and the rising of the bulwark of Italianness in Venezia Giulia, through the punitive expeditions of the squadre d’azione (action squads), the bloody electoral struggle of May 1921, and the victory of the National Blocs.
The March on Rome
The third volume, La Marcia su Roma (1939), completes the trilogy, carrying the story from the May 1921 elections to October 1922. Part I, La fine del sistema giolittiano (The End of the Giolittian System), opens with the electoral results and the fall of Giolitti, then moves through Mussolini’s hopes and purposes, the Bonomi ministry with the bloodshed of Sarzana and the pact of pacification, and the crisis of development in which Fascism transformed itself into a party. Part II, La Marcia su Roma itself, treats the formation of the National Fascist Party, the comparison of democratic and revolutionary socialism, the catastrophe of the Italian economy, the Facta ministry, and finally the state of mind of October 1922 — the Congress of Naples, Mussolini’s proclamation, the March on Rome, the conduct of the King in refusing the military response, and the “victory of the Blackshirts.” Farinacci thus carries the party’s own history from the Piazza San Sepolcro through the violent years to the moment of power, closing with the formation of the Fascist government.
A Party Historian at the Height of the Regime
Written and published at the height of the Mussolini regime, the trilogy is a primary document of how the squadrist wing of Fascism narrated its own rise. Its tone throughout is that of the organizational boss who had been at the centre of the events — confident, accusatory, and unapologetic about the violence it records. The volumes bear the marks of the Fascist-era state: the press of the ras’s home province, the copies held by the Biblioteca Civica di Varese stamped with the library of the Scuola di Mistica Fascista “Sandro Italico Mussolini.” For the historian of the period they are the fullest self-account of the movement written by one of its principal men of violence, the counterpart to the more measured academic narrative of Volpe and the compact origin-story of Businelli.

entities/franco.title: Francisco Franco
entities/franco.content:
Francisco Franco
The Soldier of the Moroccan Wars
Francisco Franco, a career officer of the Spanish Army, made his name in the long Moroccan campaigns of the reign of Alfonso XIII. The wars against the Rif cabilas, in which Fernández Almagro’s chronicle places the officers who were to dominate Spain’s next quarter-century, gave him his reputation for energy and severity and the rank that carried him to the top of the Army’s command structure. By the years of the Republic he had become one of the most prominent generals in a service that the reformist government of Manuel Azaña was deliberately reducing. Tusell’s biography of the dictator stresses that Franco’s rise during the Civil War was the decisive passage of his career: from a general among generals to the single head of the national movement. The conspirators who plotted against the Republic in 1936 recruited him late; Madariaga, in his personal appendix, records his own error in believing the Republic could not come without a military conspiracy, an error the age was to reverse.
The Generalísimo of the Civil War
The military rising of 18 July 1936 made Franco, who flew from the Canaries to take command in Morocco, the chief of the Army of Africa, and the course of the war carried him to supreme command. Aznar’s authorized military history, written from the victor’s staff, records the decisions and the campaigns that made Franco Generalísimo de los Ejércitos and head of state by the end of 1936 — the crossing of the Strait, the relief of the Alcázar of Toledo, the failed direct assault on Madrid in November 1936, and the turn to the flanking and northern campaigns that, in Tusell’s analysis, resolved the war at its “critical point.” Aznar’s Tomo III renders the final year as “la gran batalla de Franco,” the Aragon offensive, the Ebro and the Battle of Catalonia, the final maneuver of the Generalísimo, and the destruction of the Red army. Throughout, the portrait is of a war directed by a single military mind. Tusell adds the political dimension: a high degree of unity was achieved in the rebel zone without bloodshed, explained by the peculiar mentality of the rebels, who sought above all to prevent the triumph of a revolution they felt as imminent — a preventive counter-revolution whose result was a revolution of disparate contents. On 1 April 1939 the last war bulletin, number 982, announced the victory: “cautivo y desarmado” the Red Army, Franco’s troops had reached their last objectives.
The Dictator and the Falange
At the head of the state he had won, Franco ruled Spain as a personal dictatorship. Tusell defines the regime of 1939–1975 as a dictatorship without making it a Spanish peculiarity, Franco’s conceptions expressing a wider European type rather than a unique national path. The early years were those of the failed “fascistisation” and the fascist temptation: internal drift toward homologation with the Axis, adhesion to the Anti-Comintern, exit from the League of Nations. Against the late-franquista claim that Germany pressed and Franco resisted, Tusell holds that from the German victory over France there was an absolute identification of the Spanish leaders with the Axis cause, prolonged with nuances into 1944, with internal struggle within the régime and the interventionist temptation of 1940–42. Madariaga, from the liberal exile, judges the dictator’s task as threefold — to remake the national soul, to remake the national body, and to carry the ship of state on a dangerous course — and finds that his foreign policy proved in its whole less bad than his interior policy. The repression that fell on the defeated after 1939, the exile of 1939 as a rupture in Spanish history, and the “noche oscura” of autarky and rationing in the 1940s mark the regime’s first decade.
The Caudillo and the War Years
During the Second World War Franco steered Spain through a precarious non-belligerency. Hayes, the American ambassador from 1942 to 1945, records the struggle to keep Spain from joining the Axis and to extract Allied facilities, the wolfram crisis over the crucial tungsten exports to Germany, and the progress of Spanish neutrality as the war turned — until by 1944 the régime’s “benevolent neutrality” toward the Allies accompanied the certainty of Allied victory. Tusell periodises this as a “titubeante camino hacia la neutralidad” — a hesitant path toward neutrality after Serrano Suñer’s displacement and Jordana at Foreign Affairs, still giving Axis assurances while policy shifted. After the war the regime faced external isolation born of its wartime stance, adapting only cosmetically, and Franco’s Spain remained an authoritarian exception in Western Europe. Madariaga’s closing chapters, “lo que va de mal vivir la dictadura del General Franco,” written in the early years of the regime, stand as the liberal verdict on the first phase of a dictatorship that was to outlive the world war and run until the dictator’s death in November 1975.

entities/giolitti.title: Giovanni Giolitti
entities/giolitti.content:
Giovanni Giolitti
The Old Liberal Statesman
Giovanni Giolitti, the old Piedmontese statesman who had dominated Italian politics before the war and governed again in the postwar crisis, appears in the Fascist sources as the representative of the liberalism that Fascism set out to destroy. The movement’s historians are unanimous in seeing in him not a tyrant but the emblem of the parliamentary system in its decadence. Farinacci, whose party history treats the Giolitti ministry at length, is the harshest: for the Cremona ras, Giolitti was the “dictator and corrupter of political struggle in Italy,” the master of manoeuvre who kept a decadent system alive by astuteness and opportunism. Pini and Businelli, more measured, present him as the skilled parliamentary manager who misread the age — the man who thought the old methods of compromise, pressure and the distribution of favours could still hold the state together against the rising tide of class war and nationalism.
The Return to Power
The sources date Giolitti’s return to the autumn of 1920, when the Nitti government collapsed and he was called back to the ministry he had held before the war. Pini’s chronicle marks the reappearance as the beginning of the resurgence — but a resurgence that Giolitti himself could not control. Farinacci’s second volume treats the “Giolitti al potere” at length, indicting his programme as peace at any cost and a policy of accommodation. It was Giolitti who confronted the red insurrection of 1920: the strikes and the occupation of the factories, which he neither suppressed by force nor allowed to succeed, preferring to let the wave break against its own impossibility. The sources are contemptuous of this passivity. Farinacci presents the occupation of the factories as a test that the government failed, the workers’ management collapsing from its own technical incapacity while Giolittian opportunism sacrificed the interests of all to the maintenance of a “demagogy of changed colour.” For the movement, the old statesman’s caution was the abdication of the state.
The Policy of Accommodation
Giolitti’s method, in the Fascist telling, was to hold the ring between the extremes and let them exhaust one another. The parecchio — the “good deal” or “something,” the phrase with which he was said to promise that Italy would get a good deal at the peace — became in the polemic a byword for his readiness to settle for less than the nation claimed. Against d’Annunzio’s Fiume he was patient, and finally ruthless: it was under Giolitti that the Treaty of Rapallo was signed with Yugoslavia in November 1920 and the Natale di sangue (Bloody Christmas) forced the poet’s legionaries out of the city. The sources do not forgive him the suppression of the enterprise that had seemed to embody the national will. At the same time he tolerated the rising Fascist squads, hoping to use them against the Socialists, and even brought them into the National Bloc of 1921. The Fascist historians hold this against him twice over: he both abandoned Fiume and miscalculated the force he had released.
The End of the Giolittian System
The elections of May 1921, fought within the National Bloc that Giolitti had constructed, returned thirty-five Fascists to the Chamber and marked the point at which the movement ceased to be his instrument. The sources see the dissolution of the Chamber and the electoral struggle as Giolitti’s last manoeuvre — Farinacci calls the dissolution the “extreme attempt,” the “perfect field of manoeuvre,” the work of seduction — and its result as the failure of the old politics. Within weeks Giolitti abandoned power, and the ministries that followed, of Bonomi and Facta, proved unable to govern. The third volume of Farinacci’s history names this whole collapse La fine del sistema giolittiano — the end of the Giolittian system — and presents the March on Rome of October 1922 as the settlement of the account opened by his return. The old statesman’s liberalism, in the movement’s verdict, had been shown to be a system of palliatives that neither defended the nation nor governed it, and Fascism came as its successor and its negation.
