entities/goebbels.title: Joseph Goebbels
entities/goebbels.content:
Joseph Goebbels
The Young Man of the New Movement
When he appeared in the National Socialist movement, Joseph Goebbels brought to it something the beer-hall veterans conspicuously lacked: the cultivated intelligence of the German university. Heiden, who followed the party from within, describes the young man who arrived as a member of Gregor Strasser’s northern circle — a product of the lecture rooms, with the manners and the literary tastes of the Berlin literary world, a man whose natural habitat, Heiden suggests, was the Feuilleton page of the liberal Berliner Tageblatt rather than the rowdy meeting hall. It was an irony the biographer presses hard: this most radical of propagandists was, in Heiden’s judgement, “a failed philosemite rather than an antisemite,” a man who had once defended the Soviet Union in print and called Lenin a national liberator, until Hitler personally set his head straight in the spring of 1926. The antisemitism he later made the engine of the party’s appeal was, in Heiden’s account, not conviction but instrument — “he does not take antisemitism seriously, but only uses it as a means of propaganda.”
The turning point of his early career was the rupture with Strasser. Heiden tells the story of the Bamberg conference of February 1926, when the northern leaders had come to vote against the princes’ property, only to find themselves a lost opposition before Hitler’s southern majority. Goebbels, watching the material poverty of the Strasser circle against the apparatus and prosperity gathered around the Führer, saw where success lay and turned. Rising to speak, he declared that the Führer was right in everything, that he had pointed such fundamentally new ways that it needed no Damascus to follow him. The SA leader Pfeffer von Salomon told him afterwards that it was an unheard-of betrayal of his friends; Heiden records the moment as the desertion of Strasser that made Goebbels the man of the Führer. In the same year Hitler appointed him Gauleiter of Berlin, answerable to him alone. Heiden traces the campaign that followed — the battle for Berlin, the establishment of the party’s newspaper the Angriff (the Attack), the fight against Strasser’s northern press and against Gregor Strasser’s power — carried on, in the biographer’s phrase, with all the ambition of the newly converted.
The Instrument of the Word
Goebbels’s whole art lay in the word. Where Hitler held the crowd with repetition and insolence, Goebbels managed the tone — the Pathos of the mass meeting, the attack of the polemical article, the calculated whisper of the publicist. Heiden’s portrait shows him as a man who lived through words and images, drawn to the film studios and the newspaper palaces of Berlin, a creature of the very “asphalt democracy” he was sworn to destroy. He kept his own diary, from which Heiden quotes to catch the party’s moods — the despair after the 1930 losses, the defection of nerve in the crisis of the presidential year, the mounting confidence as the republic failed. When the party had to be held together, it was often Goebbels who rallied it; when a rival had to be ruined, it was Goebbels who administered the poison.
His role in the movement’s growth was matched by his place at Hitler’s side. Heiden groups him with Göring as the two “revolutionaries” who pressed for street action and the intensification of public unrest in the final crisis of the republic, against the more cautious course of Schleicher and the cabinet makers. On 13 August 1932, when Hitler was refused the chancellorship and turned down the stairs of the presidential palace, it was Goebbels who answered the rebuff with a furious article blaming the Jews. Heiden singles the episode out as characteristic: no one had suspected Jewish influence at the Reich offices, and the sharpest antisemites of the party had not thought of it — but Goebbels had, because for him the accusation was a weapon to be drawn at need. It was the same man, Heiden adds, whose wife was the adoptive daughter of a Jew and whose marriage bore the traces of a milieu the party execrated. The contradictions did not trouble him; he lived, in the biographer’s summing-up, as the instrument of the Führer’s will, the ornament and the brain of the propaganda that carried the movement to power.
The Minister of Public Enlightenment
The seizure of power in 1933 made Goebbels a minister and put the whole apparatus of public speech under his hand. The official documentary record collected by Friedrichs shows him at work from the first weeks: the Reichspropagandaleiter (Reich propaganda leader) of the party opening the electoral campaign in the Berlin Sportpalast on 21 February 1933, his call for the “day of the awakening nation,” his speeches in the months that followed as the new government imposed itself. The Reich Ministry for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda, established in March 1933, gathered into one office the direction of press, radio, film and culture — the state’s monopoly over the means by which Germans learned of their own country. Goebbels’s speeches of that spring, preserved in the documentary volumes, mark out the field: the address against the “un-German spirit,” the speech at the burning of unwanted books, the declarations on art and the state, on the tasks of the press and the rebuilding of German culture. The Reichskulturkammer (Reich Chamber of Culture) law of 22 September 1933 placed the whole of artistic life under the new order.
Within the leadership his position grew with his office. Heiden notes the alliance of the two “revolutionaries” — Goebbels and Göring — against the SA and against Gregor Strasser, and the fateful conjunctions of 1933: the Reichstag fire, which Heiden’s sources lay at the door of Göring and Goebbels, who were said to have proposed the burning as a “Wahlbombe” and to have used the young Dutchman van der Lubbe as a decoy. The documentary record of 1934 confirms his reach: his “Day of the Saar” speech in the Saar campaign, his speeches to film and press, his voice in the rebuilding of culture and in the plebiscite campaign of August 1934 that confirmed Hitler’s assumption of the head-of-state office after Hindenburg’s death. By the end of the second year of the regime Goebbels was no longer merely a propagandist but a principal of the state, the man who gave the dictatorship its voice — and, in Heiden’s critical portrait, the man who had understood from the first that in the age of the masses, the command of the spoken and printed word was itself a form of power.

entities/goering.title: Hermann Göring
entities/goering.content:
Hermann Göring
The Aviator of the Movement
When Hermann Göring came to the National Socialist movement, he brought it something the beer-hall agitators never had: the laurels of the war and the manners of the world. Heiden describes him in the early years as the former captain of the air service — Hauptmann Göring, briefly a student of the university — who stood among the handful of respectable men the movement could show to society. He was present in the inner circle of the abortive putsch of 1923, one of the leaders who walked in the march to the Feldherrnhalle; wounded in the collapse, he fled abroad and spent the years of the movement’s dissolution in exile, in Italy and Sweden. At the trial of the putschists, Heiden records, the witness Göring conducted himself with an arrogance that bordered on defiance — shouting down his interrogators, the man whose place in the movement made him “lord over life and death” in the proceedings. The exile, however, cut him off from power while the party rebuilt itself, and it was not until the amnesty of 1926, granted at Hindenburg’s wish, that he could return.
Back in Germany, Göring found himself without office or fortune. Heiden’s account of his return is that of a man who had to earn his living — through business with the aircraft-engine industry, with the firms of Heinkel and the Bavarian Motor Works — until the election of 1928 brought him a seat in the Reichstag and its six hundred marks of monthly pay. He settled in Berlin, lived elegantly on borrowed money, and formed the close friendship with Goebbels that the biographer traces through the party’s internal wars. The two of them, Heiden notes, began a systematic undermining of Gregor Strasser and his circle, making Göring a valuable weapon in Hitler’s struggle for the mastery of the party. It was the beginning of the role that would define him: the Diplomat of Hitler, the man of the world who could speak to generals, princes, industrialists and foreign ambassadors in a language the movement’s street-fighters did not possess.
The Man of Power in 1933
The year 1933 made Göring a master of the state. The official documentary record compiled by Friedrichs shows him everywhere in the first months of the regime. As President of the Reichstag he presided over the chamber that Hitler dominated; as Reich Minister without portfolio and then Prussian Minister-President he wielded the police power of Prussia, the largest of the German states. Heiden’s account of the Reichstag fire places him at its centre: the Ernst document, which Heiden analyses at length, holds that Göring first conceived the idea of a great “Wahlbombe” — an incendiary that would shatter the republic’s order — and that Goebbels proposed the Reichstag as the target, with the young Dutchman van der Lubbe as a decoy. The documentary record itself is more guarded, but it shows Göring’s hand in the measures that followed: the calling out of the SA and SS as auxiliary police in Prussia, the arrests of the communists, the broadcast of 1 March 1933 in which he denounced the communist insurrection attempt. By the terms of the documentary volumes he had become, with Hitler, the effective master of the state’s coercive power before the Reichstag fire itself made the terror popular.
His elevation continued through 1934. The Friedrichs volume on the construction of the Führer-state records Göring’s growing array of offices — his correspondence with Hitler on uniting the Prussian and Reich interior ministries, his speech before the Academy for German Law, his part in the rebuilding of state and law. But it was the purge of 30 June 1934 that fixed his place in the regime. Heiden’s account of the Night of the Long Knives shows Göring at the centre of the killings in Berlin, his office the ante-room through which the doomed passed to the left or the right — one way death, the other life. The scene with Prince August Wilhelm, whom Göring confronted with a list of names and a recorded telephone conversation, threatening him into a quick departure for Switzerland, is told by Heiden as a dark comedy of the new power. Göring had been, Heiden notes, “cheated of his hopes” when Hitler withheld from him the command of the SA, and the purge gave him at last his satisfaction against the men who had displaced him. When the law of 3 July declared the killings of 30 June Staatsnotwehr (state self-defence), Göring stood as one of the two or three men on whom the completed dictatorship rested.
The Marshal and the Second Man
In the years that followed, Göring became the most visibly powerful of Hitler’s lieutenants, the man of the new Reich’s pomp. The documentary record of 1936 shows him as the plenipotentiary for the Four Year Plan, entrusted by the Führer’s decree with the central direction of the German economy — responsible for the production of domestic raw materials, the distribution of resources, the deployment of labour, agricultural production, price formation and currency affairs, with authority to give orders to the highest Reich offices and the agencies of the party. His Sportpalast speech of 28 October 1936, preserved in the documentary volume, proclaimed the second Four Year Plan to the nation. By then he was already Generaloberst and, shortly after, would be promoted to Reichsmarschall, the highest rank in the state. Heiden’s portrait of the earlier years — the “ornament of the movement,” the friend of princes, the collector, the man of display — had given way to a figure of actual command.
Speer’s memoir, written from inside Hitler’s circle, fills in the Göring of the later years with the eyes of a man who knew him in office. Heiden had called Göring “the Diplomat of Hitler”; Speer records him as a force in the daily politics of the regime — the collector of paintings who stripped the occupied territories, the rival and ally who jostled with Goebbels, Bormann, Himmler and Keitel for the Führer’s ear. In the early war years Göring still stood as the “second man in the state”; Speer’s account of his assumption of the Armaments Ministry in 1942 shows Göring present and watchful at the seat of power, threatening resignation when his authority seemed challenged. But the same memoir traces the decline of the Reichsmarschall as the war turned: the illusionism and self-deception that Speer places at the centre of the later Göring, the man whose belief in his own air force and his own legend outran the reality, who by the autumn of 1943 was being written off by the circle around him. From the man of 1933 who had held the police power of Prussia to the decaying satrap of the final years, Göring’s arc was the arc of the regime itself — the triumph of 1933, the consolidation of 1934 and 1936, and the long collapse that Speer records from within.

entities/gregor-strasser.title: Gregor Strasser (1892–1934)
entities/gregor-strasser.content:
Gregor Strasser
Gregor Strasser was the organiser of the National Socialist movement and the man who, after Hitler, was its acknowledged leader — the voice of its “socialist” left, the builder who made the party a national power while Hitler remained its prophet. A former Freikorps officer of massive frame and organising genius, he commanded the anti-capitalist longings of the ruined middle classes in the crisis years, and came within a hair of taking the chancellorship out of Hitler’s hands in the winter of 1932. In the end he was undone by his own temperament and by the betrayal of his closest lieutenants, and on 30 June 1934 the party he had built murdered him. Heiden, who followed the movement from inside, treats Strasser as the party’s true maker in the north and the one Nazi leader whose name might have spared Germany the ruin Hitler was bringing — and who chose, at the decisive hour, to walk away.
The maker of the northern movement
When Hitler was released from Landsberg and refounded the party in 1925, it was Strasser, with his brother Otto and the young Goebbels, who carried it into the north. Two weeks after the founding assembly Strasser gave his grudging declaration that he would be Hitler’s collaborator, went to Berlin, and founded what must be called the Strasser movement — the north German wing that recognised Hitler as leader but had almost nothing organisationally to do with the Munich party, and possessed its own press independent of the Völkischer Beobachter. He and his brother scraped together their private fortunes, bought a bankrupt völkisch publishing house, and threw a dozen newspapers across the land. Strasser lay day and night on the railway, speaking literally every other evening — now Essen, now Halle, now Heidelberg, now Chemnitz. In the years 1925 to 1928, supported by his brother Otto and seconded by Goebbels, he created the National Socialist party in its new form for Hitler. He was the genuine founder of the party in North Germany, and by 1932 North Germany had long since become the movement’s base, no longer Bavaria.
Strasser’s socialism was real enough to alarm the party’s right. He gave the slogan of the “anti-capitalist longing” (antikapitalistische Sehnsucht) to a Germany that ninety-five per cent of whose people, he told the Reichstag, were filled with it. His programme of economic levelling, sketched with Feder, won millions of the desperate and the credulous: he promised the German peasants ten milliards of support, promised the workers the smashing of capitalism, and was on the point of snapping the free trade unionists away from Social Democracy. The heavy industrialists who financed Hitler took fright and cut off their subsidies after Strasser’s speeches; the struggle for the state treasury became a fight to the death. In Hitler’s own circles the name of Gregor Strasser was spoken as the future — the Vice-Chancellor, perhaps the Chancellor, the leader of a German national community “from Strasser to Severing,” the new great calm star rising over the horizon as the mad comet Hitler fell.
The break with Hitler
The break came in the party’s blackest hour. Through the autumn of 1932 the National Socialists lost ground; the party was bankrupt, its SA begging in the streets with collection boxes, its leaders frantic. Chancellor Schleicher, seeking to split the party from within, offered Strasser the Vice-Chancellorship of a cross-party cabinet. Hitler wavered, unable to decide, while Göring and Goebbels — who had deserted Strasser for Hitler at the Bamberg party congress of February 1926 and in Berlin in 1931 — intrigued against the plan. On 3 December the party lost nearly half its votes in Thuringia; the comet was falling. Strasser put an ultimatum to Hitler: Schleicher’s offer, yes or no? Hitler could not accept it, for Strasser’s acceptance would have made him greater than the Führer.
Then Strasser gave way to a fatal emotion. On the morning of 8 December 1932 he sat down in his room at the Hotel Excelsior and wrote Hitler a great letter of renunciation, enumerating the party’s mistakes, reviling Goebbels and Göring, and declaring that Hitler’s road led into chaos and a German ruin. He threw all his party offices at the Führer’s feet, paid his bill, left his suitcase at the Anhalter Bahnhof, and disappeared — sitting out the afternoon over a glass with an old friend, the military official Moritz, then taking the evening train to Munich and south to Bozen with wife and child. The party waited for him, Hitler paced his hotel room frantic, ready to make it up; but Strasser, exhausted by the wild year, wanted only his rest. His letter reached the Kaiserhof at noon and shattered Hitler, who told Goebbels that if the party collapsed he would make an end with his pistol in three minutes. When morning came and Strasser was gone, Hitler breathed again. Strasser’s following was left leaderless; his whole apparatus was smashed, his aide Schulz dismissed, his organisation divided; the party leadership condemned Strasser in a written declaration that many, like Feder, signed only under threat. Hitler wept before the assembled leaders over the friend who had betrayed him, and Streicher, long humiliated by Strasser, cried out from his place in the background against the man who could “do such a thing to our Führer.”
The last struggle
Strasser’s hour returned in January 1933, as the republican winter drew toward its close. He came back to Berlin on the evening of 3 January, rested and ready to fight again; on the same evening Hitler slipped away to Cologne to meet Papen. The two recipes for the crisis confronted each other — Schleicher’s, built on Strasser as Vice-Chancellor, and Papen’s, built on Hitler as Chancellor. For a moment the Strasser plan still lived; he had continued his undermining work in the party and could have counted on a great number of leading comrades if he had come forward with a new party. But Schleicher, frightened by the staged Lippe success, let his courage fail and dropped Strasser. In dropping Strasser, Schleicher gave up himself, and the Papen recipe triumphed. On 30 January 1933 Hitler became Chancellor, and Strasser — who had glimpsed and then lost the chance to become the great moderating star of a “national community from Strasser to Severing” — retired into an unpolitical life as director of the chemical works Schering-Kahlbaum. The revolution had passed him by.
It did not leave him alive. On the noon of 30 June 1934, as the purge raged, five officials of Göring’s Geheime Staatspolizei, the secret state police, called at Strasser’s private flat and fetched him, on the pretext of a house-search for suspected high treason; they handed him over to an SS detachment that drove him away. What happened then was never exactly established — until the following Sunday, when his widow Else received an urn filled with ashes, bearing the number 16 and the inscription: Gregor Strasser, born 31. V. 92 at Geisenfeld, died 30. VI. 34. Secret State Police Office Berlin. Strasser had two sons whose godfather was Adolf Hitler himself, boys of the Hitler Youth; when a neighbour asked one of them, a little later, what he now thought of Hitler, the boy swallowed, looked straight ahead, and answered: “And he is still our Führer!” Hitler’s own justification named Strasser in a single sentence — he had been “drawn in” — and Heiden, weighing the evidence, concluded that the alleged conspiracy of Schleicher, Strasser and Röhm had never existed. Strasser’s was the murder of a rival, of the one man who had stood beside and against the Führer, and whom the Führer could not allow to outlive his eclipse.

entities/herriot.title: Édouard Herriot (1872–1957)
entities/herriot.content:
Édouard Herriot
Édouard Herriot (1872–1957) was the great man of the French Radical Party and, with the collapse of the Bloc National, the head of the Cartel des Gauches that governed France in the mid-1920s — the statesman who, by the late 1930s, had become the living symbol of the old parliamentary Republic of the centre that the totalitarian movements of the age were pressing from both sides.
The leader of the Cartel des Gauches
Herriot was the parliamentary embodiment of radicalism — the party of the pays légal, the small proprietor and the anti-clerical tradition of the Revolution. When the Bloc National fell after the elections of 1924, it was Herriot who formed the Cartel des Gauches government, the coalition of radicals and socialists that the postwar electoral cycle produced. The Zévaès history of the Third Republic records this turn in the chapter on the after-war: the swing from the conservative Bloc to the Left Cartel, and Herriot’s emergence at its head. The Tableau des partis of Siegfried, written in 1930, treats Herriot as one of the decisive figures of the postwar cycles — the radical who embodied the permanent contradiction of the French political temperament, at once the heir of the revolutionary tradition and the guardian of the petty-bourgeois order.
The dean of the Chamber
By the end of the 1930s Herriot had become the senior figure of the parliamentary Republic. In the January 1938 reopening of the Chamber that Daniel Halévy chronicles, Herriot, re-elected president of the Chamber of Deputies, thanks his colleagues in a speech at once animated and charming — “musical as a song,” a “powerful nightingale in the chair,” in Halévy’s portrait — closing with the plea that every difficulty can be mastered by a common will to wisdom. Halévy, the conservative-liberal observer of the Republic’s decline, presents Herriot as the living type of the old parliamentary France: the radical leader, rooted in the provinces and the parties of the centre, whose reassuring competence stood in the Chamber while the crisis of 1938 gathered beyond it. In this he appears as the embodiment of the regime itself — the Republic of the deputies and the committees that the “practice of doing nothing” (la pratique du rien) was, in Halévy’s diagnosis, slowly emptying of decision.
Herriot and the fall of the Republic
The French sources of this wiki present Herriot not as a prime mover of events but as the fixed centre of the parliamentary system in its last years — the Radical statesman who, from the Cartel of 1924 to the eve of the war, stood for the permanence of the Third Republic. He belongs in the same frame as Blum and Daladier, the parliamentary figures of the regime that the totalitarian sources of the German, Italian and Russian sides confront, and whose collapse the defeat of 1940 would bring down with it.

entities/himmler.title: Heinrich Himmler
entities/himmler.content:
Heinrich Himmler
Der Reichsführer SS
Of all the men who rose around Hitler, none carried the terror of the state so quietly as Heinrich Himmler. He came to the movement not from the street-fighting of Röhm’s SA but from the Schutzstaffel, the SS — the protection detachment that began as a bodyguard of black-shirted men and grew under his hand into a state within the state. As Reichsführer SS, Himmler gathered into one organisation the security police, the intelligence service and the concentration camps, and he pursued his work with the method of a bookkeeper rather than a soldier. Where the old fighters of the SA boasted of their wounds, Himmler built files, registers and prisons; where Röhm dreamed of a people’s army, Himmler built a racial elite that guarded the purity of the German blood and the order of the Führer-state. The regime’s own documents celebrated this transformation as the reordering of state, people, economy, culture and law — and at the centre of that reordering stood the man who policed it.
Chef der deutschen Polizei
The decisive step came in 1936, the year of the regime’s great consolidation. On the seventeenth of June the Führer issued a decree creating the office of Chef der deutschen Polizei — Chief of the German Police — and named Heinrich Himmler to it. With that single act the entire police power of the Reich was concentrated in the hands of the SS leader, who now stood over the uniformed police and the political police alike, independent of the ordinary administration of the Interior Ministry whose portfolio he was entrusted to exercise. The official compilation of the year records the decree as a document of state-building, one among the laws and speeches that carried Germany from the humiliation of the post-war years to the assertion of her great-power standing; but contemporaries understood it as the completion of a different work. Henceforward the police were not the guardians of the republic that had been, but the instrument of a racial order. In the terms of the party’s program, as the documentary compilation of the NSDAP set them out, only the man of German blood could be a citizen, and those outside the Volksgemeinschaft lived in Germany only as guests under the law; the police under Himmler were the servants of that blood-law.
Die Schutzstaffel im Staat
Within the new order the SS took on the tasks the party assigned to the guardianship of the race. Himmler’s men enforced the racial legislation that the state enacted from 1935 onward — the laws that defined the citizen by descent and excluded the Jew from the life of the people and the economy, as the party program demanded and the Nuremberg laws accomplished. The documentary record of the road to the National Socialist Reich presents these measures as the fulfilment of the founding program of 1920, point by point; and it was the apparatus Himmler commanded that carried them out. Around the police power grew the economic enterprises of the SS, the camps, and the vast machinery of surveillance that penetrated the daily life of the Reich. In the halls of power the black uniform came to stand for the ultimate sanction of the Führer-state — the instrument that could reach any man, however high.
Himmlers Drohung
The man who ran the terror was never a figure of the limelight. The architect Albert Speer, who moved in Hitler’s circle for a dozen years, remembered Himmler as a presence of menace beneath the surface of the entourage — a man whose threat (Himmlers Drohung, in Speer’s own phrase) hung over the rivals of the Führer’s favour. When the war turned and the leadership closed in on itself, Himmler’s power only grew. He pressed into the rocket research at Peenemünde, extending his empire into the technological heart of the armaments effort; he planned an SS economic concern that would own the labour and the factories it supervised; and when the conspirators of July 1944 struck at the Führer’s headquarters, it was Himmler who stood beside Goebbels in the hour of the counter-action. In the last year of the war, as the generals lost the Führer’s confidence, Himmler’s advance seemed to carry him toward the very succession — until the whole structure collapsed in the spring of 1945 and the architect of the police state fled west and took his own life before the victors could judge him. The state he built outlived him in its ruin; the camps and the files and the concentration of power that he perfected remained among the darkest legacies of the Third Reich.

entities/hindenburg.title: Paul von Hindenburg
entities/hindenburg.content:
Paul von Hindenburg
The Father of the Field
By the time the Republic turned to him, Paul von Beneckendorff und von Hindenburg was already a monument. The East Prussian field marshal who had commanded the German armies through the First World War — the victor of Tannenberg, the figure whom the official eulogy of the regime would later call the “national myth of the German people” — had ended the war a shattered man, leading the armies home through the collapse of November 1918. The regime’s own commemorative text, published on his death in 1934, gives him a place in the founding of the Reich itself: as a young officer he had stood in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles when the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871, and forty years later he was still “the quiet pole in the flight of appearances,” the symbol of German duty to which the nation clung when all else seemed to fall. Heiden, the exile biographer of Hitler, is more astringent, but the contemporary record is unanimous on one point: the old field marshal’s name was not a policy but a myth, and for that reason both the failing republic and its enemies sought to hold it.
After the war he retired, and seemed destined to end his days in the East Prussian quiet of Neudeck. But the republic was in search of a symbol. When President Ebert died in 1925, the parties of the Right — including, Heiden notes, the National Socialists, who had put up Ludendorff and seen him crushingly defeated — united on the old field marshal as their candidate. In the second ballot Hindenburg beat the Catholic leader Marx and the Communist Thälmann without commanding a majority of the whole electorate; under the rules of the constitution he was declared elected. Heiden remarks that this choice of a man of seventy-seven, who had spent his life in the army and had no experience of parliamentary government, was in reality the final installation of the Reichswehr at the centre of the state, for as President Hindenburg was also the supreme commander of the armed forces. The army, the “state within a state,” was now practically withdrawn from the interference of parliament and government. It was, Heiden concludes, a magnificent long-term speculation for Hitler, who had urged his followers to vote for the field marshal as the man in whom “the freedom-will of our people is paired with the rightness and uprightness of the greatest models of our history.”
The President and the Agitator
The presidency of Hindenburg spans the whole crisis of the Republic, and Heiden traces a widening gap between the old man and the political world around him. Surrounded by the East Prussian Junkers, the great landowners who bought him the estate of Neudeck and made his son Oskar its registered owner, the field marshal became the instrument of the agrarian and military interests that clustered at his ear. Heiden’s account of the “sham struggle against Hindenburg” in 1932 shows how the president’s authority became the terrain on which the last battles of the Republic were fought. Hitler, who had once courted him, now ran against him for the presidency. The campaign had a strange, almost chivalrous tone imposed by the challenger: Hitler publicly asked the old man to “fence chivalrously,” to treat the contest as not entirely serious, and then turned harsh — “Go aside, old man, for we do not wish to strike you, but those who hide behind you.” In the first ballot Hindenburg received eighteen million votes to Hitler’s eleven. The old man had won, but the duel itself had done the work: it made Hitler the acknowledged claimant to power and turned the field marshal’s entourage into a party of brokers.
Through 1932 the president disposed of chancellors and governments. Heiden’s narrative of these months is one of a state governed by the favour of the old man — the fall of Brüning, whom he dismissed at the urging of Schleicher and the Reichswehr; the appointment of the outsider Papen, whom the president “had taken a fancy to”; the shifting alliances of generals and landowners behind the scenes. On 13 August 1932, at the height of the crisis, Hitler came before the president to claim the chancellorship and was refused, sent down the stairs at the Palais by a man who distrusted the “Bohemian corporal.” Yet the very refusal was a step toward the transfer of power, for it bound the National Socialists into the game of cabinets and presidential confidence. The old field marshal remained, in Heiden’s phrase, “the Lord President,” the last authority of a disintegrating state, and every faction — the Reichswehr, the Centre, the Social Democrats, the Junkers, and finally Hitler himself — sought to stand under his protection.
The Opening of the Gates
On 30 January 1933 the culmination came. Hitler and Papen stood before the old man at noon; Papen reported that the national concentration had been achieved, and Hitler placed his hand in Hindenburg’s and swore his oath as Chancellor of the German Reich. The regime’s own documentary record gives the act its official meaning: on 30 January the president “opened the gates of the Reich for the young National Socialist movement,” and in trusting confidence handed responsibility to the hands of German youth, building “the bridge from yesterday to tomorrow.” Heiden’s account of the same scene is framed by the old man’s dwindling power — the joke of the entourage that Papen would rule in reality, the dream of taming the National Socialists from within. But Hindenburg’s role did not end with the appointment. His name remained the one independent authority left in the state, and his signature and person still lent the new government its constitutional cover.
The events of 1933 and 1934 unfolded under the presidency of the dying field marshal. The Reichstag fire, the Enabling Act, the end of the party state — all passed over his signature or under the shadow of his authority. In the summer of 1934, as the regime moved against the SA leadership, Hindenburg’s telegrams of 2 July thanked Hitler and confirmed the action, and the law of 3 July retroactively legalised the purge of 30 June as Staatsnotwehr (state self-defence). The old man was by then failing. His political testament, dated 11 May 1934 and delivered by von Papen on 15 August, addressed “the German people and their Chancellor,” recalling his 1919 legacy of duty and calling for the restoration of the old German spirit through the furnaces of suffering. On 2 August 1934 he died at Neudeck, at nine in the morning. The Reich government’s proclamation to the people announced that “Hindenburg is dead,” and Hitler, renouncing the title of president out of respect, took the offices of head of state and chancellor together as Führer and Reichskanzler. The Wehrmacht swore its oath to him; the field marshal was laid to rest with ceremony in the memorial at Tannenberg, his last service to the regime he had let into the Reich.

entities/hitler.title: Adolf Hitler
entities/hitler.content:
Adolf Hitler
The Austrian Before the Age
Adolf Hitler was born at Braunau am Inn, on the Austrian side of the border, in the first half of 1889. The family name carried a dark tail — Schicklgruber — that the biographer Konrad Heiden, writing from exile in the third year of the Third Reich, turns over at length, though the man himself insisted on his true descent from the Hitler line of the Waldviertel. His father Alois, a customs official risen from the peasantry, wanted the boy to follow him into the civil service; the boy wanted to paint. He failed the examination of the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and sank, in his own telling, into years of poverty in the men’s hostels of the imperial capital, earning a meagre living as a draughtsman. Vienna taught him, he later wrote, the two lessons that became the axis of his thought: the bankruptcy of the multi-national Habsburg state, which he watched choke on its many peoples, and the “Jewish question,” which he claimed to have discovered in the streets, the press, and the working-class movement of the city. Heiden, more sceptical, notes that in those lost years Hitler drifted, attended by failure, without plan or connection — a “great inferior one” waiting for an age that would confer greatness on him.
The war of 1914 rescued him from aimlessness. Heiden calls it “the war as redeemer.” Hitler volunteered and served as a runner (Meldegänger) in a Bavarian regiment on the Western Front, was decorated with the Iron Cross, and found in the trenches the home he had never had. The collapse of November 1918 struck him, in his telling, at the hospital at Pasewalk, where he lay blinded by gas; there, he said, he resolved to take up politics and redeem the Germany betrayed by the November criminals. Heiden treats the Pasewalk revelation as myth rather than memory, but the vocation itself was real enough. After the war, posted in Munich as an instructor for returned soldiers, he attended a meeting of a small splinter group, the German Workers’ Party, and entered it as the seventh member — the moment at which, by his own account and Heiden’s, the movement begins.
The Orator and the Führerprinzip
What Hitler brought the tiny party was not doctrine but voice. In the beer halls of Munich he discovered that he could hold a crowd, and the crowd, not the programme, was his instrument. Heiden, who attended National Socialist meetings from 1922 and followed the movement from within, records the art: wit, logic and insolence, the hammering repetition of a few propositions, the listener made into a collaborator. “Hitler always says the same thing,” Heiden quotes, and the sameness was the point. He gathered around him the veterans and adventurers of postwar Munich — Dietrich Eckart, the poet who sensed a leader was needed; Ernst Röhm, the army captain of the “iron fist” who was already collecting weapons and Freikorps fighters; the young officers of the SA, the brown-shirted Sturmabteilung (storm detachment) that grew under his hand. The party adopted a flag and a symbol — the red banner with the Hakenkreuz (swastika) — and a programme of twenty-five points that Hitler himself would later quietly gut.
The organisation he imposed on the movement rested on the Führerprinzip (leadership principle): authority flows downward from an absolute chief, and every subordinate answers upward while being relieved of responsibility toward those below. Heiden offers the sharpest contemporary gloss on the idea. It meant, he writes, “for everyone relief from responsibility through an absolute supreme authority — security and moral comfort” — but it also meant that when responsibility downward was abolished, responsibility was abolished altogether, and the system of uncontrolled authority ended in despotism and the rule of favourites. Hitler’s own text supplies the doctrinal form: in Mein Kampf the state is the servant of the race, the parliamentary majority is rejected, and personality stands over the majority principle. The spoken word, he insists, is the force that sets the great historical avalanches rolling; propaganda is judged only by its success. Written in the fortress at Landsberg after the failure of the Beer Hall Putsch of November 1923 — the march on the Feldherrnhalle that collapsed under police fire — the book was at once a settlement of accounts with the age and a programme for seizing it.
The Seven Years on the Magic Mountain
The putsch of 1923 broke the movement, and Heiden traces Hitler’s long gamble on legitimacy through the years he calls “seven years on the magic mountain.” Hitler, tried before a sympathetic Munich court and imprisoned only briefly, decided that power was not to be stormed but awaited. The party was refounded; he withdrew to Haus Wachenfeld on the Obersalzberg and let the years do the work of the crisis. Two men rose beside him: Gregor Strasser, the Reich organisation leader who built the party’s machine in the north, and his young lieutenant Joseph Goebbels, whom Hitler, in 1926, made Gauleiter of Berlin, answerable to him alone. Inside the party, Hitler crushed the “Strasser-Goebbels front” that had plotted to unseat him, smashing the northern opposition at the Bamberg conference and binding the party to the unchanging twenty-five points under the absolute control of his Munich base. Outside, he courted money and respectability — the salons, the heavy industry, the conservative press — while Goebbels and Göring, returned from exile, fought the party’s internal battles for him.
The age repaid him. The crisis of 1929 and the collapse of the economy turned the small party into a mass one: from twelve seats in 1928 to a hundred and seven in 1930, then to the millions of the presidential year. Heiden’s account of the 1932 duel with Hindenburg is the pivot of the story. Hitler, who had once urged his followers to vote for the old field marshal, now ran against him, bidding the eighty-four-year-old president “go aside, old man.” Hindenburg won eighteen million votes to Hitler’s eleven in the first ballot, but the real victory was positional: the election made Hitler the recognised claimant to the state, and the men around the president — Schleicher, Papen, the East Prussian Junkers — began to bargain with him. In January 1933, after the fall of Schleicher and Gregor Strasser’s despairing resignation, the deal was struck. On 30 January, at noon, Hitler stood before Hindenburg and took the oath as Chancellor of the German Reich. Heiden notes the tears he shed when he came back to the Kaiserhof to Röhm, Goebbels and Göring.
The Break-In and the Absolute State
The seizure of power that followed was, in the official documentary record collected by Friedrichs, presented as a “national socialist revolution.” Hitler’s first steps combined legality and terror. The Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933 — which Heiden’s sources, in the Ernst document, lay at the door of Göring and Goebbels, who proposed the burning as a “Wahlbombe” and used the young Dutchman van der Lubbe as the decoy — produced the decree “for the protection of people and state” that suspended the guarantees of the constitution. The SA and SS were called in by Göring as auxiliary police, and the practical power of the state was taken into Nazi hands beyond the law. In the March elections the party won its plurality; in the first Reichstag of the Third Reich Hitler answered the Social Democrat Otto Wels and carried the Enabling Act, which delivered legislation into the hands of the government. The party state was dissolved; by July the NSDAP was the only legal party in Germany.
Hitler’s power was completed, as the regime’s own documents record, over the following year. The end of the party state, the Gleichschaltung (coordination) of the Länder under Reich governors, the rebuilding of economy and law under the new leadership — all flowed, in the official telling, from the Führer’s hand. The last obstacle to absolute rule was removed on 30 June 1934, in the action against the SA chief of staff Ernst Röhm, whom the regime charged with a treacherous plot. Heiden, writing a year later, gives a very different colour: an “unplanned dictatorship,” the purge of the SA leadership, the shooting of Schleicher and Gregor Strasser, Göring’s handling of the prince, the bloody settling of accounts across the Reich. The regime legalised the killings retroactively as Staatsnotwehr (state self-defence). Two months later, on the death of President von Hindenburg, Hitler united the offices of President and Chancellor in his own person and took the title Führer and Reichskanzler; the Wehrmacht swore its oath to him. Heiden closes his biography with the ashes of a Munich lawyer, shot on the evening of 30 June — “the ashes of the unknown German who fell victim to the highest responsibility assumed on 30 June.”

entities/jose-antonio-primo-de-rivera.title: José Antonio Primo de Rivera
entities/jose-antonio-primo-de-rivera.content:
José Antonio Primo de Rivera
The Son of the Dictator
José Antonio Primo de Rivera, the founder of the Falange Española, was the eldest son of the general who had ruled Spain from 1923 to 1930. Tusell, placing him at the head of Spanish fascism, stresses that the Falange owed to him what the other groups of more or less fascist significance lacked: a known leadership and a personal symbolism. Born into a family where, for three generations, the men had devoted themselves to the army, he might naturally have taken that profession, but he became instead a lawyer with a practice of some prestige, jealous that his worth be recognised. His personality — attractive even to some of his adversaries — was a mixture of barely compatible elements, what Ledesma Ramos called “contradicciones de tipo irresoluble,” contradictions of an insoluble kind. Though the leader of an antiparliamentary party, he was at ease in the debates of the Cortes; sometimes timid and withdrawn, at others a choleric streak burst out and drove him to violent aggression. He often scorned the skills of the professional politicians of his own doctrine — “serviría para todo menos para Caudillo fascista,” I would serve for everything except as a Fascist Caudillo, he said of himself — and his vocation for public life arose above all from a desire to vindicate the memory of his father, whose regime he saw as a kind of hesitant germ of the fascist ideal he wished to impose on Spain. Madariaga’s portrait is gentler and more ironic: brave, intelligent and idealistic, with an acute and irrepressible humour that exceeded what was needed for a dictator, he was “delicado y en el fondo escéptico,” delicate and at bottom sceptical — in Unamuno’s phrase, which both historians quote approvingly, “demasiado fino, demasiado señorito y, en el fondo, tímido” to be a chief, let alone a dictator.
The Founder of the Falange
The Falange Española was founded in October 1933, in an act that appeared in the press as one of “Spanish affirmation” but passed almost unnoticed. Madariaga records that José Antonio, a son of the general Primo de Rivera, had founded the Falange Española, a fascist organisation — and offers his own private conviction that José Antonio, unlike the great majority of his followers, thought the final triumph of communism inevitable and judged it best to advance toward it by the authoritarian road of fascism, a conviction he did not make public. Tusell notes that José Antonio interviewed the “Duce” only ten days before founding the Falange, and that in the final republican period the movement received through the Italian embassy in Paris a subvention of 50,000 lire monthly. The movement incorporated the JONS of Ledesma Ramos, though relations with that group were always conflictive: Ledesma saw in the Falange only “muy ricos señoritos, militares en retiro por la Ley Azaña y terratenientes de provincias” — rich young gentlemen, officers retired by the Azaña law, and provincial landowners — and wished to radicalise the movement leftward; he preferred, he said, Garibaldi’s red shirts to Mussolini’s black ones. The JONS separated at the end of 1935. The contradictions of the founder were those of his party: proclaiming a revolutionary will and social transformation, it kept patent connections with the high classes — its two 1933 deputies were nobles elected by the most conservative sectors of Cádiz, it was subsidised by monarchists, and the founder himself valued his title of nobility, his knighthood in a military order and the life of the upper classes.
Violence and the Street
The Falange, however hesitant it may have been in taking up systematic violence, became one of the principal parties practising it during the second, conservative biennium. Tusell traces its use of violent and provocative language, which was provocative precisely because the image of what was happening in other latitudes already existed in Spain, and a tactic of street confrontation against the adversary of the Left that could reach murder. The first dead among the Falangist press readers and distributors came in January 1934; only in June did the Falangists themselves kill, but the possibility existed from the beginning, as the membership cards carried the question of whether the applicant had (or had not) a “bicicleta” — that is, a pistol. Within the Falange there was even a sector that saw violence as the movement’s very reason for being and had no objection to its use as a pure armed wing of the Right. The movement’s electoral fortunes were negligible — Tusell insists that Spanish fascism at the start of 1936 was a force even more marginal than the communists, its one success being in university student circles — and it spent the republican years in divisions, indiscipline and internal schism from both its left and right wings.
The Martyred Founder
José Antonio Primo de Rivera was caught in the collapse of the Republic’s order after the outbreak of the Civil War. He had been imprisoned, and remained a prisoner in Alicante; Tusell records that the Germans showed little disposition to rescue him, and that the Falange’s own influence was likewise unable to free him. He was executed in November 1936, in the first months of the war. Madariaga notes that even before the war’s end Franco revealed, in a discourse of July 1938, that José Antonio had sent him a patriotic letter in the autumn of 1934 appealing to him to confront the danger of revolution. His death made him the Falange’s martyr. The removal of his ashes from Alicante to the Escorial, carried across half of Spain, reminded Madariaga of the days when the remains of Queen Isabella had been borne through Spain toward Granada; but their burial at the foot of the Escorial’s high altar gave the bishops much to think about, as a symptom of a new spirit not so respectful of traditional Spanish values as it proclaimed. With the unifier of the parties under Franco, the Falange Española Tradicionalista, José Antonio’s name passed into the cult of the new state, his founder’s mystique serving the regime that had arisen after his death.

entities/kirov.title: Sergei Mironovich Kirov
entities/kirov.content:
Sergei Mironovich Kirov
The Leader of the Leningrad Organisation
Sergei Mironovich Kirov, the leader of the Leningrad party organisation and one of the foremost figures of the Soviet party in the early nineteen-thirties, enters the official history of the Stalin era most fully at the moment of his death. In the Short Course of the history of the CPSU(b) he is commemorated in the chapters on the collectivisation of agriculture as the victim of the “villainous murder” of 1934; in the biography of Stalin, in the chapter covering the years 1929 to 1934, the murder of S. M. Kirov and the measures that the party took to strengthen Bolshevik vigilance in consequence stand at the close of the period of the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Congresses. The party history treats those years as the high tide of the construction of socialism — the offensive against the capitalist elements, the struggle with the distortions of the party’s policy in the collective-farm movement, the reconstruction of all branches of the national economy, the results of the fulfilment of the five-year plan in four years and the victory of socialism on the whole front. It is against this background of achievement, and of the party’s work in building the collective-farm system, that the figure of Kirov, a leading organiser of the party in that period, is set, his murder coming precisely as the party was completing the transformation of the countryside.
The Seventeenth Congress and the Turning Point
The murder of Kirov marks, in the official periodisation, the sharpest turning point of the decade. The Short Course places it within a chapter that is also the account of the degeneration of the party’s internal enemies: the degeneration of the Bukharinites into political double-dealers, and the degeneration of the Trotskyist double-dealers into a “White-guard band of murderers and spies,” of which the villainous murder of Sergei Kirov was the work. The official narrative does not present the killing as an isolated act of a single assassin but as the revelation of a conspiracy against the party and the Soviet state — a conspiracy of wreckers, spies and traitors whose exposure demanded the strengthening of Bolshevik vigilance. The biography of Stalin, recounting the same period, makes the murder of Kirov and the vigilance that followed the immediate ground for the measures by which the party cleansed itself of its enemies. In both accounts the death of Kirov is bound to the enemies of the party that the earlier chapters had described: the double-dealers who, routed in open struggle, had concealed their hostility and finally struck down a leader of the party.
The Strengthening of Bolshevik Vigilance
The response of the party, as both sources present it, was the intensification of vigilance. The murder served, in the official account, to expose the true character of the opposition that had been defeated in open struggle years before — the double-dealers who, having been routed at the Fifteenth Congress and in the years that followed, had concealed their hostility behind a mask of loyalty, and whose methods had degenerated from political opposition into espionage, wrecking and murder. The measures taken in the years that followed are narrated in the closing chapters of the Short Course as the liquidation of the remnants of the Bukharinist–Trotskyist spies, wreckers and traitors to the motherland, and in the biography of Stalin as the political trials and the liquidation of the “enemies of the people.” The party history places these measures within the preparation for the new Constitution of 1936 and the elections to the Supreme Soviet that followed, presenting the cleansing of the party as a condition of the completion of socialist construction.
The Memory of Kirov and the Lesson of the Party
In this telling the memory of Kirov is bound to the vigilance that his murder demanded, and to the chief lessons of the party’s history as the Short Course sets them out: that the party of the working class is the leading force of the revolution, and that the party grows stronger by cleansing itself of opportunist elements. The murder of Kirov is thus made to illustrate the second of these lessons — the necessity of guarding the party against the internal enemy who, once an open opponent and then a double-dealer, had become a murderer and a spy. The commemoration of Kirov within the official literature stands as a warning against that enemy and a vindication of the party’s watchfulness over the cause for which he had worked and died. As the party, in the account of its own history, met the death of its leader by strengthening its vigilance and sweeping away the enemies of the people, so the memory of Kirov was made to serve the defence of the Soviet state against the conspirators who had struck him down.

entities/largo-caballero.title: Francisco Largo Caballero
entities/largo-caballero.content:
Francisco Largo Caballero
The Trade-Union Man of the Party
Francisco Largo Caballero, the man who came to preside over the Republic’s government in the first year of the Civil War, stood at the head of the oldest and most syndical tradition of Spanish socialism. Tusell, sketching the leadership of the PSOE at the founding of the Republic, sets him against the party’s doctrinaire thinkers: where Fernando de los Ríos embodied a reformist, “humanist” socialism of the seminar room, Largo Caballero, an old estuquista — a man risen from the plasterer’s trade — represented the party’s union tradition. His working life, Tusell observes, closely resembled that of Pablo Iglesias, the founder of the socialist movement: indefatigable and methodical in his labours, limited in his formal learning, yet possessed of a kind of sixth sense for the mood of the working class and for placing himself at its head. Madariaga, the liberal exile, remembered him likewise as one of the political reserves of the Spanish future, a lifelong friend and acquaintance of the liberal centre as well as of the Left. What his admirers and his critics both concede is that his turnings had less to do with doctrine than with the drift of the labouring masses he served.
Collaboration and Its Reversal
That instinct first carried Largo Caballero toward collaboration with the Republic. Madariaga records that under his “opportunist direction” the socialists had even come to terms with the Dictatorship of Primo de Rivera before turning full circle into opposition, and in the early days of the Republic Largo Caballero was among the most enthusiastic of collaborators. As Minister of Labour in the reformist governments he drove through a wide body of social legislation — Tusell credits him with giving a decisive impulse to the labour and social-reform programme of the first biennium, the bienio reformista, and notes the speed with which the measures of his ministry were put in hand precisely because he presided over it. Yet the same man abandoned the collaborationist course abruptly. The turn came immediately before or at the very moment the socialists left power, and clearly preceded the entry of the CEDA into government. Largo Caballero proclaimed himself a revolutionary and was dubbed the “Lenin español” — the Spanish Lenin — a figure, in Tusell’s analysis, who personified a tendency latent in the socialist masses, above all in the socialist youth and in a segment of the intelligentsia. The maximalist tide was fed from outside by the journalist Luis Araquistain, his collaborator in the Labour ministry and later ambassador in Berlin, who had concluded from the collapse of German socialism before Hitler that two Spains that could not coexist were inevitable and who preached the need to anticipate the adversary.
The Revolutionary Maximalist
The radicalisation of Largo Caballero did not survive the test of power’s approach. Tusell insists that the events of the thirties proved Largo Caballero no Lenin, nor his mentor Araquistain one either; his revolutionary maximalism was, in large measure, a weapon for imposing himself on his adversaries within the party without ever breaking definitively with his own past. Madariaga, weighing the October 1934 insurrection, judged the juridical responsibility of Largo Caballero and of Lluís Companys at least as grave as that of General Sanjurjo in 1932 — yet while Sanjurjo was condemned to death, Largo Caballero went free after a trial in which, as Madariaga wryly notes, he did not cover himself in glory. The general strike of October 1934, of which the PSOE was the essential protagonist, found the party wanting in preparation and revolutionary habit; in Madrid it produced little more than incidents and shootings by syndical masses that had few arms and no strategy for using them. Throughout the crisis, Madariaga records, Largo Caballero “iba y venía” — came and went — announcing the dictatorship of the proletariat as the sole remedy for Spain’s ills, the “separatism of the socialists” set beside the separatism of the Catalans.
Prime Minister in a Revolutionary War
The outbreak of the Civil War in July 1936 brought Largo Caballero to the presidency of the government and the conduct of the war. His government, Tusell shows, was dominated entirely by his person: he held not only the Presidency but the Ministry of War, and placed two socialists of his own tendency, Álvarez del Vayo and Galarza, in the decisive ministries of State and of the Interior, while the communists were left with responsibilities of inferior moment in Agriculture and Public Instruction. The anarchists of the CNT, who had hesitated to enter because of his excessive pretensions, joined in November when the military situation grew dramatic; one minister came to take up his post carrying a rifle, as the anarchist councillors had presented themselves in the Catalan Generalitat. Largo Caballero’s own newspaper had declared that “the Republic of 14 April is dead,” and his enthusiasm for the collectivisations and for the militia army drove not a few left-republicans into exile or into diplomatic posts abroad. Yet Tusell reads the man beneath the revolutionary rhetoric: the moment he reached power he began to speak of respecting republican legality. His revolutionism was, in the end, epidérmico — superficial — while reformism had been the habitual practice of his whole career. Now, aware of the needs of the moment, he tried to win the war by centralising political power and building a military machine, clipping the juntismo (the local revolutionary committees) that delighted his anarchist allies, suppressing such bodies in Valencia, and imposing on the Council of Aragon a wider, non-anarchist composition. It was Largo Caballero who protagonised the militarisation of the militias into the Popular Army, though his own daily paper had initially opposed it.
The Fall
The limitations of Largo Caballero became apparent early. Tusell records that he was incapable of preventing the programmatic, even armed, confrontations of the coalition he presided over, and by the spring of 1937 he had lost the confidence that might have let him impose his will. When the communist ministers walked out of the Council of Ministers to provoke the crisis of May 1937, they were joined by many other factors: Largo Caballero’s wish to mount an offensive in Extremadura set him against Miaja and the Soviets; his desire to build a cabinet from the two syndical centrales alone, UGT and CNT, presumed a popularity already dissipated and marginalised major political forces. Azaña, who had deplored his presence in power, judged his performance in the harshest terms — “ineptitud delirante aliada con la traición,” delirious ineptitude allied with treachery — and noted in his diary, “siete meses de obrero a la cabecera. Diagnóstico: impotencia” — seven months of a worker at the bedside; diagnosis, impotence. Prieto made clear to him that the communists’ withdrawal made the crisis inevitable. In the end Largo Caballero himself conceded that, given his clashes with communists and anarchists and his own temper, he was not “el hombre de las circunstancias,” the man of the hour, and stepped aside in favour of Juan Negrín. His influence waned thereafter; his caballerismo shrank to a mere personalism, unable even to hold the leadership of the UGT, which passed to former “centrists,” while the communists who had once praised him now reproached him with a “dictatorial” position and lack of support at the front and in the rear. He spoke publicly in his declining influence of “casos verdaderamente desgraciados… de personas hechas desaparecer” — truly unfortunate cases of persons made to disappear — and of communists who had “constituted a State within the State.”

entities/lenin.title: Vladimir Ilyich Lenin
entities/lenin.content:
Vladimir Ilyich Lenin
The Founder of the Bolshevik Party
Vladimir Ilyich Lenin, the founder of the Bolshevik party and the leader of the October socialist revolution, stands at the head of the party’s history as the official literature of the Soviet era narrates it. The Short Course of the history of the CPSU(b) opens with the conditions out of which he arose: the abolition of serfdom, the growth of industrial capitalism in Russia, the appearance of the modern industrial proletariat, and the spread of Marxism through the workers’ movement. The Marxist historian Pokrovsky, surveying the same ground from the standpoint of class struggle, treats the rise of the proletariat and the first social-democratic circles of the 1880s and 1890s as the preparation of the revolution in which Lenin would act. Against the narodniks — the populist revolutionaries who put their faith in the peasant commune — and against the “legal Marxists,” Lenin, in the account of the Short Course, advanced the idea of the alliance of the working class and the peasantry and the construction of a party of a new type. In the Petersburg Union of Struggle for the Emancipation of the Working Class and then in the newspaper Iskra (“the Spark”), he gathered the forces of the first congresses of the Russian Social-Democratic Workers’ Party.
The Party of a New Type
The central achievement of Lenin’s theoretical work, in the official telling, was the creation of the Marxist party. His book What Is to Be Done? supplied the ideological foundations, answering the opportunism of the “economists” who would have confined the movement to the trade-union struggle. At the Second Congress of the RSDRP the party adopted its programme and statute and was formed as a united organisation, but disagreements at the congress divided it into two currents, the Bolsheviks and the Mensheviks. The Bolsheviks — the “majority” who, under Lenin’s leadership, held to the necessity of a disciplined revolutionary party — were opposed by the Mensheviks, whom the Short Course presents as the opportunist wing seeking to loosen the party’s revolutionary character. Lenin’s One Step Forward, Two Steps Back supplied the organisational foundations of the Marxist party, and his Two Tactics of Social-Democracy in the Democratic Revolution its tactics. Through the Russo-Japanese War, the first Russian revolution of 1905 and the reaction of the Stolypin years, the party matured; at the Prague conference of 1912 the Bolsheviks formed themselves into an independent Marxist party, free of the liquidators and the anti-party blocs that Lenin had combated, among them the machinations of the Trotskyists.
The Two Revolutions
The imperialist war of 1914 and the second revolution in Russia were, in the Short Course’s periodisation, the proving ground of Lenin’s strategy. The February revolution of 1917 overthrew the tsar, and on Lenin’s return to Russia in April the party set its course for the socialist revolution. Against the Provisional Government and the Menshevik and other parties that supported it, the Bolsheviks prepared the armed uprising; after the defeat of the Kornilov plot and the transfer of the Soviets of Petrograd and Moscow to the side of the Bolsheviks, the October armed uprising of 1917 placed Soviet power in the hands of the workers and peasants. The consolidation of that power demanded the Brest peace with Germany, which Lenin carried against those who opposed it, and the building of the new state through the years of foreign intervention and civil war. Pokrovsky, writing in the third part of his history of the revolutionary period, frames the October Revolution as the defence and completion of the great Russian revolution that had begun in 1905; his survey of the revolutionary era is, in his own account of it, the history of his own time.
The Co-operative Plan and the Succession
With the transition to peaceful construction after the civil war, the party adopted the New Economic Policy and created the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. In his last years, as the Short Course records, Lenin set out his co-operative plan — the programme of drawing the peasantry into socialism through co-operation — and considered the difficulties of the party’s future direction. His illness and death left the succession to the party he had founded; the Twelfth Congress and the discussion on the trade unions are treated in the official account as the ground on which the party, under its new leadership, defended the general line. The slogan that closed the chapter in the school textbook of Shestakov — “Lenin is dead, but his cause lives on” — bound the founder’s legacy to the party that followed him. In the official biography of Stalin, the claim of succession is explicit: Stalin is presented as the disciple and successor of Lenin, the continuation of the work that Lenin began.

entities/ludendorff.title: Erich Ludendorff (1865–1937)
entities/ludendorff.content:
Erich Ludendorff
Erich Ludendorff (1865–1937) was the celebrated German commander of the World War who, as the aged field marshal of the patriotic Right, lent his name and his prestige to the völkisch war-leagues of Bavaria and marched beside Hitler in the Beer Hall Putsch of November 1923 — the figure whom the collapse of that attempt separated, for good, from the leader he had helped raise up. To the biographer of the age of irresponsibility, he appears as the relic of the old military Germany whose authority the revolutionary movement of the postwar years first borrowed and then left behind.
The marshal of the national army
The biographer Konrad Heiden, writing from exile in 1936, meets Ludendorff already as “the aged field marshal” — the name from the Great War, the strategist who had shared the laurels of the eastern commands with Hindenburg and carried into the postwar years the prestige of a commander who would not accept the defeat. In the ruined Germany of 1923, with the Ruhr occupied and the currency dissolving, that name stood at the head of the patriotic leagues that refused the republic and turned their arms against the “inner enemy” of Marxism. When the militant war-leagues came together at Nuremberg on 2 September 1923, the anniversary of Sedan, they formed a loose cartel, the Kampfbund (battle league), over which the aged field marshal Ludendorff presided while Hitler stood darkly beside him. Where Hitler supplied the voice and the organisation, Ludendorff supplied the military legitimacy — the figure round whom the armed following of the Bavarian Right could gather. On 25 September the league leaders met in Munich and, after Hitler spoke to them for two and a half hours, elected him political leader of the whole armed following; the man who yesterday had been the orator of a noise-party was today master of the strongest armed force in Bavaria, with the old marshal’s name as its banner.
The head of the national army
The putsch of 8–9 November cast Ludendorff into the very centre of the rising. When Hitler burst into the Bürgerbräukeller, fired his shot at the ceiling and forced on the assembled Kahr, Lossow and Seißer the shape of a new government, the offices fell out with the field marshal at their head: a Bavarian regency under Kahr, Pöhner as minister-president with dictatorial powers, Ludendorff at the head of the national army, Lossow as Reichswehr minister, Seißer as police minister, and Hitler as the political leader of the provisional national government. “Reich government Hitler, national army Ludendorff,” Hitler thrust out — the partnership of the two men reduced to its formula, the former chief of the wartime army as the military arm of a revolutionary state that did not yet exist. For a few hours the alliance of the old and the new Germany seemed sealed in the smoky hall of the citizen brewery: the marshal who would command the armies the new order claimed, and the agitator who would rule it.
The march and the acquittal
On the morning of 9 November the columns moved up from the Bürgerbräu through the centre of Munich, the swastika banners to the fore, Ludendorff in his general’s greatcoat at the head of the second rank, marching on the Feldherrnhalle in the old gesture that was to carry the city and the army with it. At the closed line of state police across the Odeonsplatz a volley rang out; Hitler, his arm linked with a fallen comrade, went down with a dislocated shoulder and the column dissolved. Some threw themselves flat, some ran, while the army and police swept up the prisoners. Ludendorff, taken with the rest, was tried before a sympathetic Munich court early in 1924 and acquitted on his own plea — the military grandeur of his name shielding him where the “Bohemian corporal” had to answer for high treason from the dock, and the collapse itself, in Heiden’s telling, the point at which the old marshal’s day in the movement was already ending.
The separation from Hitler
The collapse began the rupture that the two men would never repair. Heiden’s chapter on the aftermath is titled “The Return to the Lord President,” and among its record of the attempted suicide, the judicial comedy of the trial and the writing of Mein Kampf behind the comfortable walls of Landsberg stands the separation from Ludendorff. Where Hitler drew from the failure the tactical conclusion that power was not to be stormed but awaited, through the state and the ballot, Ludendorff, acquitted, receded into the nationalist agitation of the völkisch Right — his name, once the banner of the leagues, ceasing to be a standard of the movement that grew out of the wreck. The putsch that made Hitler a national figure left Ludendorff behind it; the prestige he had lent the rising had passed, and the old field marshal’s later course would run ever further from the Führer’s. In the critical biography of the age of irresponsibility, Ludendorff stands as the last representative of the old military Germany whose authority the revolutionary movement used and then outgrew — the commander of the lost war turned figurehead of a lost revolution.

entities/matteotti.title: Giacomo Matteotti
entities/matteotti.content:
Giacomo Matteotti
The Deputy of Rovigo
Giacomo Matteotti was the socialist deputy whose murder in the summer of 1924 became the gravest crisis of the young Fascist regime. The regime’s own chroniclers, writing from within the movement, are at once eager to condemn the deed and anxious to deny that it touched the state. Pini and Bresadola present him as the deputy of Rovigo, a man of an “anima di setfario” (the soul of a sectary) already revealed during the war, when he refused all subsidy to the families driven from the Altipiani by the enemy offensive of 1916, and in the postwar years as the untiring anti-Fascist propagandist who, freshly returned from France and England where he had made contact with subversive and Labour elements, spoke against the government “in an acutely hostile tone.” In the Regime’s telling his intransigence set him apart even among the opposition: a journalist hostile to Fascism had the presumption to ask, on the publication of a book of Matteotti’s, how much the socialists had paid him for it. The majority in the Chamber was Fascist, the chroniclers record, but the parliamentary poison was beginning to infect it.
Volpe, the academic historian of the regime, describes Matteotti as “one of the most rabid and bitter opponents of Fascism,” killed “in a mysterious way on the outskirts of Rome” in the stormy days of May and June 1924 when the new Chamber opened in tempestuous sittings marked by verbal battles and personal encounters. The account both historians share is that the crime was the work of determined individuals. Pini writes that on 10 June Matteotti was attacked and sequestrated by men seemingly resolved to ask him to account for his activity, and that when he fought back and struck one of his aggressors, he was killed by that man — an assassination, the chronicler insists, “not more deplorable than so many others” in which the victims had been the men of the other side.
The Crime and the Storm
The murder did not remain an isolated crime. Pini records how, in vain, the Duce uttered words of execration against the assassins from the tribune — “Only an enemy who had thought something diabolical against me through long nights could have committed this crime” — and how the Fascists unanimously deplored the deed. In vain: the opposition would not let such an occasion slip. The death of Matteotti became a pretext for unleashing all the anti-Fascist hatred that smouldered beneath the ash of the political and journalistic world of Rome and Italy; a “venomous and lying campaign” spread through the newspapers and the sympathising groups, the more damaging because, as Pini concedes, the moral reprobation was general and he can point to no counter-voice. “Matteotti is only a pretext,” he writes; the real aim was to overthrow Mussolini and Fascism.
Volpe, more measured, admits what Pini minimises: that members of the Fascist Party were accused of the crime, “an accusation which was afterwards proved,” and that the whole movement, from its leader to its last-joined member, became the object of defamation and abuse. The crime was exploited at home and abroad to destroy the credit and power of Fascism. The response of the opposition was the secession of the Aventine: a hundred deputies from the various branches of the opposition withdrew from Parliament in protest, hoping to lower the legal status of the Chamber and impede its functioning — “It was the Aventino against Montecitorio,” as Volpe names it, invoking the ancient plebeian withdrawal to the Aventine hill against the seat of the modern legislature. The perturbation throughout the country was enormous. Volpe concedes a “profound moral oscillation in the mass of the people,” quoting Mussolini himself, and records the bewilderment among Fascists and their sympathisers, the beginnings of a break-away, the panic, and a real check in the moral and numerical development of the movement.
The Resolution of January 1925
The crisis drew out through the year 1924, but the regime gathered itself. Volpe observes that the excess of the defamatory campaign contributed to the revival of Fascism, as the factional motives of those who had instigated it could not be concealed: in striking at Fascism they struck at Italy, now not easily separated from it. On 3 January 1925, in a speech to the Chamber, Mussolini showed himself ready to take again the helm and to engage in a decisive battle; illusions were dispelled, the uncertain were stimulated, and the provincial Fascism that had shown a desire to refuse discipline and to begin the warfare anew was pacified. Pini records how the day of 3 January had been awaited with the presentiment of a historic sitting, and how the Duce spoke, as his habit was, “right and decided,” opening with a reference to his speech of 13 December and setting out a whole programme. Fascism came through the strain, in Volpe’s phrase, “somewhat attenuated, but more homogeneous and reinforced by decision and will”; the line between Fascism and what was not Fascism was now clearly drawn. The Ministry became entirely Fascist, the liberals turned Fascist or disappeared from view, and many implacable enemies left the country or were compelled to. The murder of Matteotti, which for a season had shaken the regime to its foundations, was thus absorbed into the consolidation that followed the Aventine and the January speech — the moment when the last restraints of the old liberal order fell away.
