entities/mola.title: General Emilio Mola
entities/mola.content:
General Emilio Mola
The Soldier Placed in the Conspiratorial Post
General Emilio Mola, a career officer of the Spanish Army who had served the monarchy in Africa and passed into the service of the Republic, became the central figure of the military conspiracy of 1936 almost by accident of posting. The republican authorities, suspecting the generals, had scattered the most dangerous among them to peripheral commands: Franco to the Canaries, Goded to Palma de Mallorca, and Mola, “punto menos que en calidad de desterrado” — little short of in exile — from Morocco to the military governorship of Pamplona in Navarre. Aznar’s military history observes that the republican power could never have given a better gift to the rising than to set a young brigadier general in a post where every circumstance allowed him to work “intensa, segura y eficazmente como jefe del Alzamiento dentro de la Península.” The officers of the Pamplona garrison received him with open satisfaction — “ya tenían jefe,” they congratulated one another — and the brigadier soon stood at the head of the nuclei of the conspiracy. With Sanjurjo banished to Portugal and Franco set apart in the Canaries, there was, as Aznar puts it, no one more obvious to take the immediate command.
The Director of the Rising
From Pamplona, from the spring of 1936 onward, Mola directed the preparation of the alzamiento (the rising) across the Peninsula. Tusell, whose synthesis of the Republic’s last months describes Navarre as “el centro inspirador de la conspiración,” names Mola its “mente rectora” — the rector mind of the plot. The conspirator-general worked through the winter and spring weaving together the heterogeneous enemies of the Republic: the Falangists of José Antonio Primo de Rivera, the Carlists of the Communion Traditionalist, and the monarchist circles. His relations with the Carlist leadership were always stormy; the projects of the Carlist chiefs, who dreamed of restoring the old regime about the Carlist Monarchy, had little in common with Mola’s own designs, which a Carlist leader dismissed as “disparates republicanos.” The general built his strength upon the Navarrese requetés — the Carlist volunteers who offered him a reserve of magnificent soldiers, calculable in the aggregate at thirty thousand, of whom Mola in his confidence of a short war never expected to use more than eight or ten thousand. He shared the prevailing belief of the officers in a guerra corta y triunfal (a short and triumphant war) decided by a few strokes of audacity and attack before the government could arm itself.
The Pact with Sanjurjo and the Carlists
As the moment of action approached, the exiled General Sanjurjo pressed his influence upon the conspirators from Portugal. In the second week of July 1936 the Carlists brought Mola a letter from Sanjurjo declaring himself for the bicolor flag as “cosa sentimental y simbólica” and for discarding the liberal and parliamentary system. Mola, not without serious resistance, at length bound himself vaguely to accept the general lines of Sanjurjo’s indications, and a written programme passed between them — the famous letter of 9 July in which Sanjurjo set down the political formula for the rising. In practice Mola negotiated directly with the Navarrese Carlists, over the head of their delegate Fal Conde, securing the requetés on his own terms. The preparation of the movement, in Aznar’s reconstruction, was a tissue of secret journeys, personal emissaries and written compromises of which the correspondence between Mola and Sanjurjo was the thread that gave the scattered plotters their common political ground.
The Rising and the Command of the Northern War
When the Movimiento of 18 July 1936 broke out, Mola’s Navarrese columns of requetés and regulars carried the war in the north, marching on Madrid from the north-east even as Franco’s Army of Africa crossed the Strait. Aznar records him as “director del Movimiento en la Península desde el mes de mayo de 1936,” the military hand that prepared the general rising within the Peninsula while Sanjurjo, the nominal head, was to enter Spain to assume the supreme command. The death of that nominal head in the first days of the rising, together with the consolidation of command around Franco, left Mola to conduct the operations in the north. In the decisive northern campaign of 1937 he was, until his own death, “el responsable de la dirección de las operaciones por parte de los sublevados,” disposing of the seasoned brigadas navarras that had become by their quality a sort of shock force of the national army. At the end of May 1937, a few days before the rupture of the iron ring around Bilbao and the fall of the Biscayan capital, Mola died in an accident of aviation. His death removed the last rival general from the command the war had gathered into the hands of Franco, and the northern campaign that he had directed was brought to its end by his successor.
The Place in the Nationalist Memory
In the authorized military history of the victorious side, Mola stands as the organizer of the rising and the director of the war in the north, the general who gave the alzamiento its plan while the future Generalísimo was still in the Canaries and the nominal leader in exile. Aznar’s narrative of the summer of 1936 turns repeatedly upon his figure — the Pamplona command, the secret correspondence, the thirty thousand requetés he prudently declined to count upon, the short-war confidence the war itself was to disappoint. For the liberal and scholarly accounts, Mola’s significance lies in the fact that he embodied the conspiracy as it actually was: a military plot woven among the enemies of the Republic by a professional soldier of no party, who held together in his single hand the monarchists, the Carlists and the Falangists until the hour of action, and whose direction of the war in the north was decisive in resolving the conflict at its critical point.

entities/mussolini.title: Benito Mussolini
entities/mussolini.content:
Benito Mussolini
The Interventionist Turning Point
Benito Mussolini, the founder of the Fasci di combattimento (fighting bands) and, from 1922, head of the Italian government, is the central figure of the Fascist revolution as every regime-side source in this wiki narrates it. The movement’s own historians begin not with his birth in the Romagna but with his rupture from the Socialist party over the war. In 1914, against the neutrality that the official Socialists preached, Mussolini raised Il Popolo d’Italia, the newspaper that became the organ of the interventionist cause, and was expelled from the party he had once led through the ranks of its revolutionary wing. Businelli records that the founding of the paper and the campaign for Italian entry into the war drew the young interventionists of the cities, and that Mussolini was arrested for his trouble; the same energy, turned against the Avanti! of his old comrades, made him in the eyes of the movement the man who broke the neutrality front. The war itself he served as a corporal in the trenches — “i galloni di caporale erano sufficienti alla mia ambizione” (the corporal’s stripes sufficed to my ambition), Businelli quotes him — while Il Popolo d’Italia carried the patriotic word through the years of Caporetto and Vittorio Veneto.
The Founding of the Fasci
The armistice of 1918 left the interventionists masters of a victory that the peace seemed to be squandering. On 23 March 1919, in the meeting-room of the Circolo degli Industriali at Piazza San Sepolcro in Milan, Mussolini gathered the Fasci di combattimento into being — an “anti-party,” in Volpe’s phrase, deliberately formless, a movement of youth and impulse rather than a disciplined organisation. The programme of that first adunata (assembly) was part revolutionary socialism, part nationalism: a republic for some, the monarchy for others, expropriation alongside the vindication of the nation’s claims at Fiume and on the Dalmatian coast. What held it together was not doctrine but the conviction, as Volpe presents it, that the old ruling class had failed and that the generation that had made the war must remake the state. Farinacci, writing his party history from the Cremona perspective, dates the whole revolution from this Piazza San Sepolcro moment and from the fatti di Milano of April that followed, when the Fascists and the Arditi fell on the offices of Avanti!. The elections of November 1919 were a defeat for the Fasci, but the movement was already passing from the Milanese rooms into the provinces.
The Leader of the Squadre
The turn of 1920–1921 made Mussolini the head of a violent, nationwide movement. Volpe presents the man as two figures in contention — the statesman who wanted to build a party and the revolutionary who let the squadre d’azione (action squads) loose on the Socialist and Popolare organisations of the Po valley. It was the provinces that supplied the strength. Farinacci’s second volume records the red insurrection of 1920 — the strikes, the occupation of the factories, the agrarian unrest — and the Fascist answer: the punitive expeditions of the squadristi, the burning of the Lavoratore at Trieste, the reprisals at Bologna and Ferrara. Through this phase Mussolini spoke, organised the regional congresses, and at the same time tried to bind the movement to legality, signing the Pacification Pact of summer 1921 that the provincial ras refused to honour. The ambiguity was deliberate. Volpe’s account of the transformation from “movement” to “party” centres on the internal strife between these two Mussolinis, resolved only when the Popolo d’Italia of 2 February 1922 set the course toward a national party and a claim on the state itself.
The March on Rome
The seizure of power came in October 1922. Volpe narrates the Milan meeting of the Fasci of 16–18 October, at which Mussolini met with Bianchi, De Vecchi, Balbo, General De Bono and the generals Fara and Ceccherini, and the appointment of the quadrumvirato — the quadrumvirate of action invested with dictatorial mandate — to direct the insurrection. As the columns of Blackshirts gathered at concentration points twenty or thirty kilometres from the capital, and as the Naples adunata of 24 October proclaimed the revolution, the King refused to sign the decree of martial law, and the marching columns entered Rome. On 31 October the order for demobilisation went out as 100,000 Blackshirts massed in the Villa Borghese. Mussolini, who had remained in Milan during the march itself, came to Rome to receive from the King the office of head of the government — power, as Volpe insists, taken by revolutionary means yet confirmed by the Crown. Pini’s chronicle renders the same days as the “ideal revolt” and the collapse of the political system, the moment the liberal state handed itself over.
The Duce and the Corporate State
At the helm, Mussolini’s work was the reconstruction of the state. Volpe’s account of Fascism at the helm and of the reform of the state sets out the programme: the re-establishment of order, the restoration of the balance of the budget, the battaglia del grano (battle for grain) and the public works, the strengthening of the office of head of the government by the law of 24 December, the syndical law of 3 April 1926 drawn up with Giuseppe Bottai, and the building of the corporate structure as “an accord between liberty and authority.” The dictatorship hardened through the crisis of May–June 1924, when the murder of Giacomo Matteotti drove the opposition onto the Aventine and Mussolini answered with the new intransigence of 3 January 1925. Pini’s closing chapters present the conquest of the state: the party reform, the Carta del Lavoro (Charter of Labour), the Circolare ai prefetti, and the reorganization of the armed forces and the syndicates. In the official narrative the Duce appears as the “genial and victorious will” that gave the Italian people a state at once national and imperial.
The Fall
The war of 1940 undid him. Badoglio, the marshal who had served the regime and then overthrew it, supplies the counter-narrative. He records Mussolini’s memorandum of April 1939 to Hitler on the war between the rich and the poor nations, his decision of June 1940 to enter the war on the side of Germany, and the accumulating disasters that followed — the reverses in Greece and North Africa, the invasion of Sicily, the dictatorship “in extremis.” By the summer of 1943 the regime had lost the King and the hierarchy. The Grand Council met on the night of 24–25 July 1943 and voted against him; the King dismissed him, had him arrested, and appointed Badoglio in his place. The man who had marched on Rome in 1922 was carried off the stage by the same Crown that had installed him. Badoglio, writing in 1944, casts his own conduct as the necessary salvage of the nation from the ruin to which, in his telling, the Fascist political and military leadership had condemned it.

entities/negrin.title: Juan Negrín
entities/negrin.content:
Juan Negrín
The Physician of the Republic
Juan Negrín, the last prime minister of the Spanish Republic, belonged to a very different generation and temper from the union men who had governed the Left before him. Tusell, introducing him as Largo Caballero’s successor, stresses that his ideological formation had little that was revolutionary or even Marxist about it: he was young, hard-working, cultured, one of those intellectuals trained abroad through the Junta de Ampliación de Estudios whose antimonarchist radicalisation in the early thirties had carried him into the PSOE. A catedrático of physiology whose school formed many of the best Spanish biologists, he had opposed the October 1934 insurrection, and he had even opposed Largo Caballero’s presence in the presidency of the government, remarking that it amounted to “perder Getafe” — losing Getafe, a town on the edge of Madrid — while the adversary was still far from the capital. He had no sympathy for the caballerismo within the party, repudiated the militiamen and disliked being called “camarada.” Madariaga, listing the leaders of the Left, numbers him among the political reserves of the Spanish future, a lifelong friend of the liberal as well as the socialist world. His language at the head of government was not the language of revolution but the language of the democratic constitution of 1931.
The “Tranquil Energy”
Negrín came to power in the political crisis of May 1937, and he owed his selection less to any party than to Manuel Azaña and Indalecio Prieto. Azaña, who had deplored Largo Caballero’s presence in power and judged his performance with the harshest words, was decisive in choosing Negrín, in whom he saw a “tranquila energía” — a tranquil energy — against the “altibajos” and “repentes,” the ups and downs and sudden starts, of Prieto. Prieto had made clear to Largo Caballero that the communists’ withdrawal from the cabinet meant the inevitable crisis, and then himself stood aside from the presidency. Negrín’s personality, Tusell writes, augured a turn toward order, authority and centralisation: his initial declarations showed a decided will to maintain the Republic of 1931, foreshadowing the thirteen points that would later define his position before the conflict. He did not turn back the collectivisations nor grant real freedom of worship, but he identified the Republic with the democratic norms of its constitutional text. His work, both military and political, was directed to the normalización of the republican zone — that is, to centralisation and the achievement of efficiency without which victory was unattainable. In August 1937 he dissolved the Council of Aragon, using military units, principally communist-led; in October the Cortes met at Valencia in large numbers, testifying before international opinion to the parliamentary and democratic character of the institutions; and the transfer of the capital to Barcelona was intended to draw Catalonia more effectively into the common struggle. Neither the Teruel offensive, nor the defence of the Maestrazgo, nor the subsequent battle of the Ebro would have been imaginable without the new perspectives opened by his assumption of the presidency.
The Concentration of Power
Negrín’s government drew increasing protest as its power grew. Tusell traces the growing communist influence in the republican zone to this period, and notes that the conduct of the war after the northern front’s fall came to depend heavily on the communist-organised forces. Negrín, once considered a manageable man, became indispensable, if only by his own will to hold power and the incapacity or unwillingness of others to replace him amid a harvest of defeats. He came to consult the parties and the President of the Republic ever less; his comment on the Cortes during a crisis — “la charca política se ha agitado mucho; francamente da un poquito de asco” — the political swamp has stirred a good deal; frankly it turns one’s stomach a little — Tusell cites as testimony of megalomania and of an incapacity to take account of the opinions of others. His thirteen-point programme of 1938 was intended to resist, but also to show a will to transact and to respect the values of democracy before France and Britain, possible mediators of a peace. In the April 1938 crisis, after Prieto abandoned the Ministry of Defence convinced the war was lost, Negrín argued rightly that no one who believed the war lost could be Minister of Defence, and he imposed resistance at all costs. His three decrees of August 1938 — militarising the war industries and creating a Chamber of Justice in Catalonia and special courts of military justice — provoked the resignation of the Catalan and Basque ministers and a storm of opposition, Azaña accusing him of attempting a coup d’état; Negrín finally withdrew the last, manifestly unconstitutional proposal, but remained in power.
Resistance to the End
Negrín’s central conviction, expressed to the military commanders at Los Llanos in February 1939 after the fall of Catalonia, was that “as the enemy will not make peace, the only solution is to resist.” His own memoirs and those of his adversaries show the depth of the division this provoked. Colonel Casado, the defender of Madrid, admired Negrín’s intelligence and valour but called him “desequilibrado,” unbalanced, and judged prolonging resistance “a crime against humanity,” describing the Popular Front zone as “a dictatorship in the service of a foreign power,” Russia; Casado had since late 1938 contemplated replacing the government and had made contact with the “fifth column.” Negrín’s decision to change the military command, replacing non-communists such as Casado and Matallana with commanders in large part communist — the only party that at this point seemed disposed to resist — produced immediately the decomposition of the Popular Army, even though the change never took effect. In the March 1939 coup, the Cartagena rising against his government collapsed in confusion, and on 4–5 March Casado formed the National Defence Council in Madrid, its manifesto drafted by Besteiro denouncing the “catastrophist fanaticism” of the head of government, who had already left the country. The communists’ attempt to resist the coup was crushed, and Negrín, without authority and abroad, saw the war end under a government that was not his. Franco, who wanted to finish not only the communists but the whole Popular Front, refused to negotiate with Casado’s council, and the war ended in unconditional surrender.

entities/nitti.title: Francesco Saverio Nitti
entities/nitti.content:
Francesco Saverio Nitti
The Man of the Ruling Class
The chronicle of the Fascist rise treats the premiership of Francesco Saverio Nitti as the emblem of everything it set out to overturn — the Governo senza fede (Government without Faith), the title the authors give the year 1919–20. When the Orlando cabinet fell in June 1919, Nitti, an economist and man of the southern provinces, succeeded it. The regime’s historians concede the welcome he received: he enjoyed a reputation for intellect and culture, and it was believed he also possessed the energy that Italy so needed after the strain of the war. Pini’s chronicle records that in such a moment a Government able to speak a word of faith could have steadied the nation, and that many hoped the new premier was capable of it — only to watch, within a few weeks, every illusion collapse. “To Francesco Nitti,” the chronicle concludes, “there lacked absolutely the faith in the destinies of Italy”; an arid mentality of the bad economist, he stood discouraged before the enormous liabilities of the war. Farinacci, writing the authoritative party history a decade later, finds the same verdict in the record of the summer of 1919: after Caporetto Nitti had invoked a “greater sense of reality” (maggior senso di realtà), which the Fascist historian dismisses as merely the more cautious variant of the Giolittian parecchio — the readiness to cede whatever the enemy and the Allies demanded, so long as peace was preserved.
The Illusions of the First Weeks
The chronicles dwell on how quickly the first reputation faded. In the assessment of the regime’s historians, Nitti’s cunning was after the method of the old Giolitti, yet where Giolitti, in his way of handling men, never abandoned the dignity of the statesman, in Nitti the same astuteness was ready to decline into gross attempts at corruption and shameless mendacity. The test came almost at once. At the end of July 1919 the Socialist party ordered a great general strike, which Nitti faced with an enormous deployment of force, for a moment winning himself the fame of an energetic man and a full applause in the Senate; it was afterwards understood that the measures had been solicited privately by many of the Socialist parliamentary group, with whom Nitti was on excellent personal terms. The Italian Socialists, the chronicle observes, began to fear they would have to run the real risk of making the revolution in earnest. To the Fascist historians this intimacy between the premier and his declared enemies was not a sign of balance but of the very collapse of the state. Farinacci’s account of “Nitti al Governo” is built on the same indictment: the “blackmail-note” of Wilson, the programme of peace at any price, the prayers of a Prefect, and the massacre of via Nazionale in Rome, where the state’s own weakness issued in blood in the capital.
The Months of Shame
It was the Fiume undertaking that fixed Nitti’s place in the Fascist narrative. Pini titles the chapter of his ministry “The Gesture of D’Annunzio — Months of Shame” and treats the Adriatic crisis as the moment when the premier’s prudence was exposed as something worse. Farinacci’s Chapter “Fiume contro Roma” — Fiume against Rome — names its theme directly as “the cowardice of Nitti,” set against the epic of Ronchi and the march of the Legionaries. In this telling the Government of official Italy could respond to the burning city of the oltraggiata Fiume only with inertia, while the man at its head, cautious “up to cowardice” in his action of command, was outmatched by the greatness of events; his indifference, once derided, now sounded as an outrage to the men of the war. Businelli’s movement narrative records the same indignation from within the Fascio: on 9 June the Fascio of Milan admonished the Italian delegates at the conference of Paris to follow a line intransigently Italian and placed its veto on the return of Nitti and of Giolitti; when Orlando abandoned power and Nitti succeeded him, Fascism was not yet strong enough to impose its decisions, but it was no longer weak enough to accept the accomplished fact.
The Fall and the Legacy
The second volume of Farinacci’s history, treating the “red insurrection” and the victory of the Fasci, devotes its eighteenth and nineteenth chapters to “Nitti al Governo” and “La caduta di Nitti” — the fall of Nitti. The Fascist historian presents the ministry’s agony as the slow transformation of minds and the sad agony of the ruling class, the premiere of the bourgeois chief whose policy of peace at any price surrendered the national honour while the country drifted into the anarchy of the biennio rosso. When the premiership passed in June 1920 to the returned Giolitti, the chroniclers saw the substitution as the exchange of one failing system for another. For the men who wrote the regime’s history, Nitti stood for the entire generation of statesmen who had won the war and then lost the peace — the classe dirigente whose sfacelo (collapse) the first part of Farinacci’s work is organized to demonstrate, and against which the Fasci di combattimento had been founded as the patriotic answer. It is precisely this portrait — the intelligent, faithless economist governing through caution and accommodation while D’Annunzio held Fiume and the reds gathered in the Po valley — that the Fascist historiography held up as the negative image of its own revolution.

entities/petain.title: Philippe Pétain (1856–1951)
entities/petain.content:
Philippe Pétain
Philippe Pétain (1856–1951) was the Marshal of France who, in the disaster of 1940, became the head of the French state that asked for the armistice with Germany — the figure around whom the collapse of the Third Republic crystallised, and whom Marc Bloch’s L’Étrange Défaite confronts from the side of the defeated army’s own historian.
The Marshal of the armistice
In the account of the fall of France written in the weeks after the catastrophe, Bloch’s deposition of a defeated man from the Intelligence staff of the 1st Army records the rout and the breakdown of command without making any single man its author. Pétain enters the French sources of this wiki as the Marshal to whom the stricken Republic turned in June 1940 — the victor of Verdun in the earlier war, called back in old age to head the state at the moment of its supreme defeat, and the man who signed the armistice and established the government at Vichy. Bloch, writing “en pleine rage” in the summer of 1940, indicts not the Marshal alone but the whole structure of a France that had failed to prepare for total war: the professional military caste, the political class, the bourgeoisie and its “vieux démon,” the educational system, the entire society. In that examination of conscience, Pétain stands as the terminal figure of the regime’s collapse — the symbol of the old military France whose methods and mental timidity, in Bloch’s diagnosis, had helped bring on the defeat that now placed the Marshal at the head of a dismembered state.
The divided verdict of the defeat
The sources present Pétain without a verdict of their own, recording the role the defeated nation assigned him. Bloch’s Testament and his clandestine essays, written under the Vichy regime that Pétain headed, show the other pole of the division: the republican who refused the regime’s authority, “above all and very simply French,” affirming in the face of death that he was born a Jew. The Marshal of the armistice is thus set against the France that would not accept the defeat or the regime that followed it — the France of Bloch himself, who went into the Resistance and was shot by the Germans in 1944. Within this wiki’s sources Pétain appears as the man of the armistice and of Vichy, the figure the fall of 1940 raised up and the republicans of Bloch’s persuasion could not follow.

entities/primo-de-rivera.title: Miguel Primo de Rivera
entities/primo-de-rivera.content:
Miguel Primo de Rivera
The Pronunciamiento
Miguel Primo de Rivera, a general of the Spanish Army, entered Madrid in the autumn of 1923 carrying the resolution to make himself dictator. The pronunciamiento (military coup) of 13 September 1923, which he had long been preparing from his command, found a country exhausted by the social war in Barcelona, by the trauma of the disaster of Annual in Morocco, and by a parliamentary system that seemed to produce only short-lived ministries. Fernández Almagro’s account of the last constitutional government records the general’s impatience, the denounced conspiracies, the sedition in Málaga, and the Central Staff memorandum, until “Primo de Rivera on the way” resolved the crisis by marching. The King accepted him; the constitution was suspended, and the Dictatorship began under a Directorio militar (Military Directory) in which the general ruled with the collaboration of generals and, later, of civilian ministers.
The Military and Civil Dictatorships
The Dictatorship ran in two phases. The first, from 1923 to 1925, was the Directorio militar, a purely military government. Fernández Almagro follows its measures: the first decrees, the appointment of Martínez Anido to Gobernación, the courtship of the socialists against the politicians, the confinement of Unamuno, the Unión Patriótica (Patriotic Union) as the régime’s single movement, the exile of the Marqués de Cortina, and above all the Moroccan question. The dictator’s great triumph was the liquidation of the Rif war: the Hispano-French cooperation, the landing at Alhucemas in 1925, and the final surrender of Abd-El-Krim, which erased the nightmare of Annual and gave the Dictatorship its one unqualified success. Madariaga’s judgment, however, is that even this success did not redeem the régime: in his balance-sheet the Dictatorship left Spain in a situation equal to or worse than that which it found — “En lo esencial, la dictadura dejó a España en una situación igual o peor que la que encontró.” The second phase, from 1925 to 1930, was the government of civilian collaborators under the dictator’s presidency, culminating in the Asamblea Nacional Consultiva (National Consultative Assembly) of 1927 and the draft of a new constitution that the Crown and the country were unwilling to receive.
The Encounter with Mussolini
The Dictatorship was the Spanish instance of the interwar turn toward authoritarian government, and Primo de Rivera himself sought the parallel. Fernández Almagro records the dictator’s journey to Rome and the encounter with Mussolini, the meeting that linked the Spanish directorio to Italian Fascism in the imagination of contemporaries. The personal affinity was real but the regimes differed; the Italian visit gave the Dictatorship an aura of European currency, of belonging to the movement of the age, even as its substance remained a Spanish military paternalism. The Unión Patriótica was a state party rather than a fascist militia, and the Dictatorship made its peace with the Church and the established interests more readily than any revolutionary movement would have done. The Roman episode nevertheless fixed Primo de Rivera in the wiki’s European pattern of the crisis of liberal order, a Spanish variant beside the Italian and later German cases.
The Erosion and Fall
From 1928 the Dictatorship visibly decayed. Fernández Almagro narrates the accumulating signs: the social question and the schools, the socialists already thinking of the Dictatorship’s end, the exile of Sánchez-Guerra, the artillery pronunciamiento that failed, the dissolution of the Artillery corps, the death of Queen María Cristina, the student strike against Article 53 of the University Statute, the depreciation of the peseta. Madariaga’s chapter on the liquidation insists that no exact judgment of the Dictatorship is possible without a balanced opinion of the régime that it had pleased to call “ancient,” and that the collapse of the one brought down the other. When the Dictatorship fell in January 1930, Primo de Rivera resigned and the King returned to constitutional government under General Berenguer, but the monarchical machinery was too damaged to recover. The dictator, who had bound the Crown to his experiment, went into exile in Paris, where he died a few weeks later, in March 1930 — Fernández Almagro records his “last official note” and the account of the end of the Dictatorship that followed.

entities/primo-levi.title: Primo Levi
entities/primo-levi.content:
Primo Levi
The Chemist of Turin
Primo Levi was an Italian Jewish chemist of Turin, a partisan, and the author of Se questo è un uomo (If This Is a Man), the first edition of which appeared in 1947 and became the most celebrated Italian testimony of the Holocaust. Born in Turin in 1919 into a liberal Jewish family, he took his degree in chemistry in the summer of 1941 — under the racial laws of 1938, which had already barred Jews from academic employment, so that he could not pursue the career his science promised. After 8 September 1943, with the armistice and the German occupation, he joined the resistance; arrested in the Val d’Aosta in December 1943, he was sent to the transit camp at Fossoli near Modena, and from there, with the other Italian Jews, he was deported to Auschwitz in a freight train on 22 February 1944. He was liberated in January 1945. In his own words, written in the opening of the book, “for my good fortune I was deported to Auschwitz only in 1944” — after the German government, pressed by the growing scarcity of labour, had decided to lengthen the average life of those to be eliminated, granting appreciable improvements in the standard of living and suspending at least for a time the arbitrary killings by individuals.
The book was written, as its Preface from prison declares, not to formulate new accusations — “it might rather provide documents for a calm study of certain aspects of the human soul” — and it insists that none of the facts is invented. Levi explains the book’s fragmentary character: the chapters were written not in logical succession but “in order of urgency,” first of all for the purpose of inward liberation, the need to tell the “others” having become, before and after the liberation, an immediate and violent impulse that rivalled the other elementary needs. The dedicatory poem with which it opens, Voi che vivete sicuri (You who live secure), gives the book its title and its summons: “Considerate se questo è un uomo / Che lavora nel fango…” — consider whether this is a man who works in the mud, who knows no peace, who fights for half a loaf, who dies for a yes or a no.
The Deportation
The journey is the book’s first chapter of horror. Levi records that in mid-February 1944 the Italian Jews in the camp at Fossoli were about six hundred, with a hundred or so interned Yugoslav soldiers and some others considered politically suspect. The arrival of a small detachment of German SS might have warned even the optimists, yet the announcement of the deportation still found the spirits unprepared. On the 20th the Germans inspected the camp with care and made public, lively remonstrances to the Italian commissioner over the defective kitchen service and the scanty firewood; but on the morning of the 21st it was known that the next day the Jews would leave. All — no exception: children, old people, the sick. Prepare for fifteen days of travel; for each one missing at the roll-call, ten would be shot. Only a minority of the naive and the deluded clung to hope; those who had spoken long with the Polish and Croatian refugees knew what it meant to depart. Levi evokes the night in which every man took his leave of life in his own way — some praying, some drinking beyond measure, mothers watching with tender care over the food for the journey, washing the children, preparing the baggage — and the dawn that came “like a betrayal.”
The Germans made the roll-call with the absurd precision to which the prisoners would later have to accustom themselves. “Wie viel Stück?” asked the marshal, and the corporal answered with a click of the heels that the “pieces” were six hundred and fifty, and all in order. They were loaded onto lorries and taken to the station of Carpi, where the train and its escort awaited them; there they received their first blows — “so new and senseless that we felt no pain, neither in the body nor in the soul; only a deep astonishment: how can one strike a man without anger?” The wagons were twelve, the people six hundred and fifty; in Levi’s own wagon there were forty-five, and it was a small one. “Here then, before our eyes, under our feet, was one of those famous German transports, the ones that do not return… Exactly so, point by point: freight wagons, closed from the outside, and inside men, women, children, compressed without pity, like merchandise by the dozen, travelling toward nothingness, travelling downwards, toward the bottom.” Auschwitz: “a name without meaning, then and for us; but it must correspond to a place on this earth.”
Häftling 174517
The arrival stripped the deportees of everything, beginning with their names. Levi records the shaving and the showers, the rags thrust into their hands, the wooden-soled shoes, the barefoot run through the cold blue snow of the dawn; and then the tattooing. “Häftling: I have learnt that I am a Häftling. My name is 174517; we have been baptised, we will carry as long as we live the mark tattooed on the left arm.” The camp was a square of about six hundred metres a side, encircled by two barbed-wire fences, the inner one charged with high-tension current, made up of sixty wooden barracks called Blocks. Out of this stripping of the person the book draws its famous distinctions — the drowned and the saved, the “Prominents” who survive by privileged posts and the mass who drown. Levi, as a chemist, was steered toward a laboratory post in the Buna works, and the examination of chemistry that won it is among the book’s chapters, the accident that helped carry him toward survival. In the summer of 1944 the Hungarian transports arrived and the crematoria worked at full capacity; on 20 October 1944 came the great selection, in which a quarter of the camp’s prisoners were sent to the gas chamber — and Levi was saved. The closing chapter of the 1947 edition, Storia di dieci giorni (story of ten days), recounts the ten days between the Germans’ abandonment of the camp and the arrival of the Red Army, with the sick left in the infirmary, the Ka-Be, and Charles and Levi for a time alone among the dying.
The Voice of the Victim
Levi’s testimony stands at the far end of the interwar history this wiki surveys — the endpoint of the racial laws and deportations that the Fascist and Nazi regime sources celebrate. Where Pini, Volpe and Businelli narrate the march of Fascism to power and Badoglio its collapse, Levi writes as the one the system consumed, a prisoner in the Lager; his book is the Italian-Jewish voice of the Holocaust, the counter-testimony to the self-congratulation of the regime’s own accounts. In the Preface he draws the warning that gives the work its moral force: it may happen to many individuals and peoples to believe, more or less consciously, that “every stranger is an enemy”; this conviction usually lies latent, an infection, manifesting only in sporadic and incoherent acts — but when the unspoken dogma becomes the major premise of a syllogism, then at the end of the chain stands the Lager. “The history of the death camps should be understood by all as a sinister danger signal.” That warning, and the single human life — 174517 — that survived to tell it, are what Levi’s testimony contributes to the record of Fascist Europe.

entities/queipo-de-llano.title: General Gonzalo Queipo de Llano
entities/queipo-de-llano.content:
General Gonzalo Queipo de Llano
The Conspirator-General of Andalusia
General Gonzalo Queipo de Llano entered the summer of 1936 as an unlikely chief of insurrection. His republican past set him apart from the plotters who had spent their careers in the service of the monarchy: Tusell records that Queipo de Llano had been an antimonarchist conspirator under the government of Berenguer, had held high military office in the republican years, and was related to Niceto Alcalá Zamora, the first president of the Republic. He was Inspector General of the Corps of Carabineros, and among the republican authorities it was wholly unexpected that this servant of the regime should prove disloyal when the hour came. Charged with raising the region of Andalusia, he discovered on his first contacts few points of support among the garrisons; in Málaga, where one of his daughters lived, the garrison upon which he counted failed him. Yet it was precisely this republican-general-turned-conspirator who performed what Aznar’s military history calls the decisive miracle of the southern rising.
The Conquest of Seville
The fate of the insurrection in the south turned upon Seville, and there Queipo de Llano achieved his great feat. Aznar presents him “prácticamente solo, frente a unos mandos hostiles” — practically alone, against hostile commanders and in the midst of a population that included fierce communist and anarchist masses — yet winning in the Andalusian capital a victory decisive for the future course of the national war. Tusell’s analysis of the same days is more precise: Queipo conquered Seville with some three thousand soldiers of the garrison “a base de una combinación entre audacia y bluff” — a combination of audacity and bluff. His victory was won by the prompt occupation of the central zone of the city, the hesitation of the republican loyalist officers at Tablada, the disorientation of the popular adversary, distracted by burning churches and lacking leadership. Only on 23 July could he consider liquidated the resistance of those who, for days, had controlled two-thirds of the population of the Andalusian capital. The consequences were strategic: only the victory of Queipo de Llano in Seville explains how the Army of Africa could cross the Strait and become the key to all subsequent operations. What the Popular Front authorities had dismissed as impossible — that Queipo in a very precarious situation could do more than defend himself — proved in the event the first great triumph of the rising.
The Voice of Radio Sevilla
With the capital won, Queipo de Llano made himself the voice of the national movement in the south. Aznar’s chronicle captures the paradox of those first days: the general, in the station of Radio Sevilla, “refiere la victoria de las armas nacionales” — announces the victory of the national arms — “pero la verdad es que suenan los tiros en los barrios obreros sevillanos,” while in truth the shots still rang out in the working-class quarters of Seville and all the Andalusian countryside burned like an immense progressive bonfire fanned by communist fury. The broadcasts from Radio Sevilla, blending the report of victory with the menace of reprisal, became the characteristic instrument of Queipo’s command, the radio voice that carried the terror of the national zone across Andalusia even as his slender columns fought to secure the roads. Aznar notes that the general could arm not even two hundred men in the first two days to secure himself in the capital, so thin were the forces with which he held the city and then set out, little by little, to reconquer the whole campiña — the Andalusian plain — exploiting his local triumph to assure the communications between Granada, Córdoba and Seville.
The Lord of the South
From the conquest of Seville, Queipo de Llano ruled Andalusia as its military chief. His columns, Tusell observes, had an aspect as picturesque and motley as the anarchist militias of the region — the war in Andalusia was irregular and hard — but, reinforced after the crossing of the Strait, they showed a combat efficiency vastly superior. His position in the south grew more comfortable as the war advanced; he left the province of Málaga in a precarious situation, with no exit but the road to Almería, making the attack upon it entirely foreseeable, and the fall of Málaga in February 1937 was in large measure the work of the southern command he had established. The character of his rule was as striking as his military audacity: the blend of bluff and terror with which he had taken Seville marked his whole governorship of the Andalusian rear, and his radio voice remained through the war one of the most distinctive and feared instruments of the national cause. For the Nationalist historians Queipo is the audacious conqueror who saved the south; for the scholarly account he is the antimonarchist general converted to the rebellion, whose capture of Seville made possible the entire military course of the war.
The Place in the Rising
Queipo de Llano stands among the four principal military figures of the rising of 1936 — Mola the director of the conspiracy, Sanjurjo its nominal head, Franco the future Generalísimo, and Queipo the lord of the south. His republican past made him in some ways the most anomalous of the rebel generals, yet his conquest of Seville in those first days was arguably the most decisive single stroke of the opening of the war. Where Mola prepared the plot and directed the north, Queipo seized and held the great city whose port and aerodrome received the Army of Africa; where the nominal leader died in the first days, Queipo survived to become the enduring voice and fist of the national zone in Andalusia. The audacity and bluff by which he took Seville, and the radio voice by which he announced it, remain the two poles of his memory in the histories of the war.

entities/ribbentrop.title: Joachim von Ribbentrop
entities/ribbentrop.content:
Joachim von Ribbentrop
Der Mann von außen
The man who came to direct German foreign policy in 1938 was an outsider to the old diplomatic service — a businessman of good family who had sold wine in London and Paris before the war, a man whose service to the party had been rewarded with the trust of the Führer rather than with the respect of the Wilhelmstraße. Joachim von Ribbentrop attached himself to Hitler in the early years of the movement’s rise, and he made himself indispensable as the regime’s man for the great negotiations of the middle thirties. He was sent to London as ambassador, where he pressed the German claim to equality among the powers and carried the Berlin view to the British; he conducted the negotiations with Japan that produced the Anti-Comintern front, the pact of the powers arrayed against the Bolshevik danger that the regime made the keystone of its foreign policy; and he spoke for Germany in the committees and councils of the European capitals. The official documentary volumes of the state record his voice again and again — in the London council chamber, at the table of the Non-Intervention Committee, before the assembled powers — always advancing the same demand: that Germany, the great power of the centre, must have her place.
Vor dem Komitee
In 1937, the year the regime called the passage from great power to world power, Ribbentrop stood before the London Non-Intervention Committee, in July and again in October, to state the German case in the Spanish war. The committees of the powers had been formed to keep the Spanish conflict from spreading into a general war, and the question of volunteers and control divided them; Ribbentrop’s speeches before that body, as the official record preserves them, defended the German position and protested against the interference of the other powers in a struggle Germany saw as her own against the Communist danger. In the same year he carried the German colonial demand before the world — the claim, set out in the Führer’s speeches and pressed in the documents, that Germany, robbed of her colonies by the settlement of 1919, must regain her place among the colonial powers and her share of the raw materials of the earth. Ribbentrop spoke on the Four-Year Plan and world trade, linking the autarky of the German economy to the claim for living-space and markets that the regime made in every forum. It was the same argument he would carry into the chancelleries of Europe: the German people, great and growing, had been denied their rightful measure, and the denial could not stand.
Der 4. Februar 1938
The office came to him in the crisis that remade the German command at the beginning of 1938. On the fourth of February, in the shake-up that followed the fall of the War Minister Blomberg and the army commander Fritsch, the Führer struck at the old order of the state. A Secret Cabinet Council was created to advise him; the Foreign Minister of the old school, Freiherr von Neurath, was dismissed with a letter of thanks; and the official announcement went forth that Joachim von Ribbentrop had been appointed Reichsaußenminister — Reich Foreign Minister. The German ambassadors in London, Rome, Tokyo and Vienna were recalled at the same hour, clearing the diplomatic service of its old men to make way for the new. It was a personal victory for Ribbentrop, who had long coveted the office, and a sign of the age: foreign policy was to be conducted no longer by the cautious professionals of the Kaiser’s school but by the trusted man of the party, whose loyalty to the Führer was absolute. The documentary volume of 1938 sets the appointment at the head of the year’s record, among the decrees by which the state reordered itself for the great events to come.
Das Amt
The year that followed gave Ribbentrop’s ministry its great test and its great triumph. Within weeks of his appointment the Reich annexed Austria, and the Foreign Minister’s office was busy with the notes, the protocols and the congratulations that attended the reunion; in the autumn the Sudeten crisis brought Europe to the edge of war, and the Munich settlement of September yielded the Sudeten German lands to the Reich. Ribbentrop’s radio addresses as Foreign Minister, his notes to the neutral powers, his declarations in Paris — all preserved in the official record — show the new style of German diplomacy: peremptory, confident, speaking the language of power. Where the old Wilhelmstraße had counselled caution, Ribbentrop urged the Führer onward, certain that the age belonged to the strong and that the democracies would yield rather than fight. In the year of Grossdeutschland he stood at Hitler’s side as the man who had broken the encirclement of Versailles and led Germany to the height of her power — the last of the great Foreign Ministers of the Reich, whose office would carry the German demand to the very threshold of the general war.

entities/roehm.title: Ernst Röhm
entities/roehm.content:
Ernst Röhm
Der Hauptmann und die eiserne Faust
When the movement first reached for power in Munich, the strong arm that struck for it belonged to a captain of the old army. Ernst Röhm had come out of the war as a professional officer who refused to believe the war was over; in the Freikorps and in the secret depots of the Black Reichswehr he stored arms and men for a Germany that would rise again. The journalist who watched the party from inside for a decade remembered him as the eiserne Faust — the iron fist — that stood behind the young Hitler, the man who made the streets safe for the speakers and the banners. In those early years the movement’s cry was Brechung der Zinsknechtschaft, the breaking of the bondage of interest, a slogan of revolt against the money and the speculators of the Weimar years; and Röhm embodied the revolt in its most soldierly form. He was not a politician. He was the organiser of force, the man who could say, with a wink to his cronies, that a political movement without arms was a debating society. Where the party spoke, Röhm made certain that it could act.
Der Stabschef
Röhm’s life in the party was a series of departures and returns. After the failure of the Beer Hall Putsch of 1923 the movement dissolved around its imprisoned leader, and Röhm quarrelled with Hitler and went his own way — to Bolivia, to a staff appointment in a foreign army, out of the German story for a season. But the movement he helped build could not do without him. In the years when the republic collapsed into parliamentary paralysis, when cabinets fell and the streets filled with brown columns, the SA — the Sturmabteilung, the storm detachment of the National Socialists — grew into a mass army of its own, and it was Röhm who returned to command it. As Stabschef, chief of staff of the SA, he turned a corps of street-fighters into a force of three million men, uniformed, disciplined, and in his own eyes the true army of the revolution. He overthrew Brüning, or so the entourage boasted: the republic’s last chancellor of the old school fell because the brown legions had made the state ungovernable. The Bohemian corporal whom the officers once mocked had become, by 1933, the Chancellor of Germany — and at his side stood the captain who had carried the weapons.
Der zweite Revolutionär
The triumph of 1933 settled nothing between the two men. Röhm believed that the National Socialist seizure of power had only begun the work: that the revolution must now be completed against the old army, the old officialdom, the industrialists, the whole reactionary world that Hitler was courting. His SA, swollen to its millions, demanded a place in the state, a militia that should stand beside or above the Reichswehr — the professional army of the republic, which the officers jealously guarded. The generals who had tolerated the brown shirts in the street would not tolerate them in the barracks. Around the Führer the voices of the army’s friends gathered, and against Röhm they pressed the argument that the revolution must end where the state began. Heiden, writing in exile, called the affair the 30th of June, the day the unplanned dictatorship at last understood itself; the Führer, Heiden wrote, contradicted himself on the knife’s edge between the army and his old comrade.
Der 30. Juni 1934
The blow came at the end of June 1934, in the year the Führer-state was being completed. On the night of the 30th Hitler flew to Munich, and by his own order Röhm was deposed and expelled from his office, the Stabschef who had been his companion since the beginnings arrested at the Bad Wiessee where the SA leadership had gathered. The official record of the state, collected in the documentary volume of 1934, presents the deed as an act of necessity: a decree deposing and expelling Röhm, letters and commands to his successor Viktor Lutze, telegrams exchanged with the aged Reich President Hindenburg, and on the third of July a law declaring the whole affair a measure of state emergency, Staatsnotwehr, the right of the state to defend itself. Before the Reichstag on the thirteenth of July Hitler laid the account before the nation, naming those the purge had taken and binding the army to himself with the blood of his old friend. Heiden’s account is grimmer and more intimate: the armoured cars in the streets, the shooting, the hunt for the homosexuals of the SA leadership, Göring and the prince gone to ground, the bloodbath — and at its close the story of a Dr. Glaser of Munich, shot on the evening of the 30th by three SS men, whose urn of ashes was handed to his brother: the ashes of an unknown German who had fallen victim, in Heiden’s bitter phrase, to the highest responsibility assumed that day.
Die Nachfolge
The purge did not dissolve the SA; it tamed it. In the years that followed, the brown shirts marched under the new Stabschef Viktor Lutze, disciplined and silent, and the storm detachment that had once threatened the army became an instrument of celebration and civic order. Before the diplomatic corps in 1936 Lutze expounded the nature and tasks of the SA — the parade-ground virtue of the old fighter absorbed into the Führer-state, its revolutionary edge drawn. The man who had been the iron fist of the beginnings was gone, and with him the second revolution; the army he had threatened kept the state, and the SS rose in the place his SA had once claimed. Röhm’s name remained a warning to every man who sought a revolution beyond the one Hitler had chosen to make.

entities/sanjurjo.title: General José Sanjurjo
entities/sanjurjo.content:
General José Sanjurjo
The Soldier of the Monarchy and the Republic
General José Sanjurjo was a professional officer of the Spanish Army whose career spanned the transition from monarchy to Republic. He had been, in Madariaga’s account, an early accomplice of the conspiracy of Primo de Rivera that had installed the dictatorship in 1923, and in 1931 he commanded the Civil Guard — the Guardia civil. When the Republic was proclaimed, Sanjurjo, at the head of that force, gave the king to understand the gravity of the situation; Alfonso XIII abdicated and left for Cartagena, and the general who had helped decide the fall of the monarchy thus passed, in his own person, from the service of the crown to the service of the new regime. Madariaga, the liberal analyst, judges him a “soldado bravo, sin talento alguno ni político ni militar” — a brave soldier without political or military talent — who had played an important part in the advent of the Dictatorship and in the transit from Monarchy to Republic, and was then to become a cause of grief for the Republic.
The Sanjurjada of August 1932
Sanjurjo’s first rupture with the Republic came in August 1932, in a rising that bore his name. Tusell explains that the greater influence over the general, “cabecilla y animador” of the movement, was exercised by old constitutionalist politicians of the former turno parties, who found the evolution of the new regime too radical. Sanjurjo, “soldado valiente pero ignorante y candoroso” — whom Azaña described as an old piece of furniture — let himself be persuaded to undertake a movement in the old style, whose content was not specifically antirepublican. Like the pronunciamientos of the nineteenth century, he attributed to himself the representation of the national will and hoped to win power without much bloodshed, through a psychological struggle with those who held it. The rising was planned at several points of the peninsula but took real effect only in Seville, where Sanjurjo held power for a few hours, and in Madrid, where a handful of officers tried in vain to occupy the Ministry of War. Defeated, he fled toward the coast but fell into the hands of civil guards, his former subordinates, who delivered him to the authorities. Azaña faced the crisis with his customary calm and passed the matter to the tribunals, which condemned Sanjurjo to death; but, supported by a numerous sector of opinion, he commuted the sentence, subjecting the general in prison to the common regime. The defeat of the Sanjurjada, in Tusell’s account, allowed the agrarian reform to advance rapidly and brought Azaña the confiscation of the property of the entire Spanish Grandeza.
Amnesty and the Return to Conspiracy
The general was later freed by an amnesty that cost President Lerroux his premiership, as Madariaga records in his personal appendix, where he confesses his own part in securing it. Sanjurjo then passed into exile in Portugal, where he remained through the spring of 1936, the nominal head around whom the gathering conspiracy revolved. His prestige among the plotters was obvious: in May 1936 the traditionalists incorporated him into their ranks, his military past and his earlier conspiratorial activity giving him “una preeminencia obvia entre los militares.” In the first conspiratorial movements of March 1936 Franco figured only “en una posición de segundo de a bordo, tras Sanjurjo” — in a second position behind Sanjurjo — and from the beginning the future Generalísimo was the second of the rising after its exiled head. The general’s politics, for all his monarchist affiliations, were vaguer than the Carlists wished; a Carlist leader found him “un tanto…” in his convictions, and Sanjurjo himself, in the letter he sent to Mola, declared for the bicolor flag as “cosa sentimental y simbólica” and for discarding the liberal and parliamentary system.
The Letter and the Nominal Leadership
Sanjurjo’s political programme for the rising was set down in his letter of 9 July 1936, addressed to Mola and carried by the Carlists. In it he declared himself for the bicolor monarchical flag as a sentimental and symbolic thing, and for the rejection of the liberal and parliamentary system — the formula that was to give the Nationalist cause its political color even as the military command remained in other hands. Mola, not without serious resistance, accepted the general lines of Sanjurjo’s indications, and the written compromise that passed between the two generals bound the scattered conspirators to a common programme. In the preparations reconstructed by Aznar, Sanjurjo appears as the authority in exile whose blessing and programme gave the rising its political legitimacy, while Mola in Pamplona conducted the military preparation and the Junta of the Carlists worked at San Juan de Luz. When the rising was fixed for July, Sanjurjo, the nominal head of the whole movement, was to fly from Portugal to Spain to assume the supreme command.
The Death at the Outset
At the very outset of the rising Sanjurjo met his death. Setting out from Portugal in the first days of the alzamiento to take command of the movement he nominally headed, he died in an accident of aviation — the air crash that removed the nominal leader on the threshold of the war he had been chosen to lead. The consequence was to leave the supreme command to be gathered, in the course of the conflict, into the hands of Franco, who had been only the second of the rising. For the liberal account, the death cut short the career of a brave but untalented soldier whose earlier rising had already cost the Republic dear; for the Nationalist military history, it removed the symbolic head and left the conduct of the movement to the generals who actually directed it. Sanjurjo thus stands in the histories as the would-be chief of the rising whose death, at its very birth, reshaped the command of the Spanish Civil War.

entities/schleicher.title: Kurt von Schleicher (1882–1934)
entities/schleicher.content:
Kurt von Schleicher
General Kurt von Schleicher was the political brain of the Reichswehr, the German army of the republic, and for five years the unseen manager of its fall. A witty, cynical, officer-casino conversationalist sharpened by thirty years of service, he was the man the press called the “power behind the throne” long before he ever held office. He had made and unmade chancellors from the shadows; when at last he took the chancellorship himself in December 1932, he found himself the prisoner of the same intrigues he had so long directed, and in a month he was gone. On 30 June 1934 the men he had helped to power repaid him with a bullet at his own villa door. Heiden, watching him from the democratic side, judged Schleicher the cleverest man in the game of 1932 — and the most overconfident, a man who played at politics as at cards and believed he could always lay down the winning hand.
The kingmaker
Schleicher’s power rested on the Reichswehr and on his hold over President Hindenburg. As the most important political head in the Reichswehr ministry he arranged the republic’s governments at will; “Schleicher can do anything with Hindenburg,” the National Socialists themselves knew. It was on Schleicher’s instigation, with the then Defence Minister Groener, that Hindenburg in 1930 withdrew his confidence from the Social Democrat Müller and summoned the Centre leader Heinrich Brüning to rule by emergency decree. For two years Schleicher tolerated Brüning while Brüning drove the country’s wages and living standards down in the service of proving reparations impossible — and then he resolved to break him. The five acts of the overthrow played out through the spring of 1932: Schleicher’s sudden abandonment of the cabinet over the SA ban, his private negotiations with the SA chief Ernst Röhm, his choice of the pliable nobleman Franz von Papen as chancellor, the junckers’ manoeuvres at Neudeck, and finally, on 30 May, the dismissal of Brüning. Schleicher meant to rule through Papen as he had ruled through others, invisibly, and to cut Hitler to pieces at leisure.
But Schleicher misread both his creatures. He had sought in Papen a “fool,” and underestimated the man’s ambition and his gift for unscrupulous intrigue; and he had counted on keeping Hitler weak, only to find the National Socialists swelling into the strongest party in the Reichstag. In August 1932 Schleicher’s double game nearly caught him: he had let Hitler believe the chancellorship was within reach, then stood by while Hindenburg, on his walking-stick, refused the “Bohemian corporal” the whole power. The rebuff to Hitler on 13 August was a blow Schleicher had half engineered and could not control. As the year ran out, Schleicher’s own position crumbled. He urged Papen to resign, set a trap for Hitler that Hitler refused to enter, and then — believing he had the Nazi leader on his knees — took the chancellorship himself.
The general as Chancellor
On 2 December 1932 General von Schleicher became Reich Chancellor, at the head of a cross-party “cabinet from the reasonable National Socialists to the reasonable Social Democrats,” as he put it. His scheme was to split the National Socialist party from within: he would make Gregor Strasser, Hitler’s great rival and the party’s organiser, his Vice-Chancellor, and so draw off the party’s best parts into a government of national concentration; then he would dissolve the Reichstag and grind Hitler in the elections. The plan was not absurd. The party was bankrupt, its SA begging in the streets with collection boxes, its leaders quarrelling, its comet visibly falling after the Thuringian losses of December. Schleicher’s mistake was that he made the offer to Strasser and then, when the first tremor came, let his courage fail him. In the Lippe election of January 1933 Hitler threw the whole strength of his movement into one rural district and recovered twenty per cent of the vote; Schleicher let himself be impressed by this staged success, dropped Strasser, and so abandoned the only force that could have saved his cabinet. Heiden’s verdict is exact: in dropping Strasser, Schleicher gave up himself.
The cabinet of Hindenburg had meanwhile chosen between the recipe of Schleicher and the recipe of Papen. Schleicher’s recipe — parts of the party and parts of the Social Democrats, Strasser as Vice-Chancellor, the Reichstag dissolved, Hitler ground in the poll — was rejected; Papen’s recipe — the whole party supporting the government, Hitler as Chancellor, no dissolution — was accepted in the presidential household of Oskar Hindenburg, Meissner and Papen himself. The old President had grown distrustful of his general, who had unguardedly let slip that the Reichswehr was not bound to the capitalist system “for life and death,” and who had let the Osthilfe scandals of the junckers detonate. On 28 January 1933 Schleicher, refused the power to dissolve the Reichstag without fresh elections, resigned. Two days later Hitler was Chancellor. The Reichswehr, which “had always ruled from a distance and threatened, never dared to intervene on the street,” was forced in the person of Schleicher to the most humiliating capitulation.
Schleicher against “the criminals”
Out of power, Schleicher did not keep quiet. He had no more to lose, and he raged. “I know that rogues and criminals govern Germany,” he told a society gathering, “but in six months they will no longer be at the helm.” In a tailor’s shop, invisible in a fitting cubicle, his voice booming, he cursed the “rubbish, criminals, greasy catamites” who ruled, and promised that the gang would soon be “serviced” — a threat the Gestapo remembered. Around the assumption that Hindenburg must soon die, circles both inside and outside the government drew up lists of a new cabinet: Hitler again Chancellor, but with Schleicher as Vice-Chancellor, Gregor Strasser at economics, and Röhm at the war ministry. Heiden, scrupulous here, notes that these lists may have been provocation work; yet Schleicher’s indiscretion made it easy to gather enough of his utterances to hang him ten times over.
On 30 June 1934, as Hitler flew to Munich to destroy the SA, six men in civilian clothes drove up before Schleicher’s villa, forced their way in, and shot the General dead before his wife’s eyes; a bullet struck Elisabeth von Schleicher, who died half an hour later. The official communiqué claimed Schleicher had resisted arrest with a weapon; Hitler, in his Reichstag justification, said he had had Schleicher shot because the General had spoken with the French ambassador François-Poncet “about the weather and old coins.” Heiden assembles the contradictions to show that no conspiracy of Schleicher, Strasser and Röhm had ever existed. Within months the army itself quietly reversed the verdict: at the Linden Opera in January 1935, before the highest Reichswehr officers, Schleicher was rehabilitated and his shooting admitted a fearful blunder, and the old Field Marshal von Mackensen spoke of him among the comrades who had died honourably. No one spoke for Röhm or Strasser. The kingmaker who had made Hitler had been disposed of like a stale card.

entities/speer.title: Albert Speer
entities/speer.content:
Albert Speer
Beruf und Berufung
The man who would build for Hitler came to architecture without politics and was drawn into the movement almost by accident of talent. Albert Speer was a young architect of the middle class, a Swabian by descent, trained in the severe discipline of Heinrich Tessenow and married before the great events of the age had touched his profession. In the slump of the early thirties there were no commissions to be had; he walked the country roads, an architect without work, while the political storm gathered. After the election of September 1930 he heard the National Socialists for the first time, in the Sportpalast, in a hall roaring with a thousand throats, and in the weeks that followed he joined the party. In his own account it was not the program that moved him but the spectacle and the man — the conviction, formed in that crowded hall, that here was a force that would rebuild a humiliated Germany. By 1933, in the first flush of the seizure of power, he was designing the May Day demonstration, and soon he was rebuilding the party’s district house and the new Propaganda Ministry. Hitler, who saw himself as a frustrated builder, took the young architect into his confidence, and there began an association that would carry Speer to the heart of the regime.
Der Architekt des Führers
Hitler was a building client of an obsession the age had not seen. He wanted not offices but monuments, architecture that would outlast its makers and speak for a thousand years. Speer gave him the new Nuremberg party-grounds, the great Zeppelinfeld with its tribune of light; he developed the theory of ruin value, the Theorie vom Ruinenwert — the doctrine that a building should be so conceived that, in its decay, it would still be beautiful as a ruin, a cathedral of the German future testifying to the grandeur of the state that raised it. Around the Zeppelinfeld he threw the Lichtdom, the dome of light, a hundred and thirty searchlights standing about the assembly like a hall of pillars in the night sky. In Berlin he planned the rebuilding of the whole city as a world capital: a grand avenue, a triumph-bow, a great hall that would seat a hundred and forty thousand men, the largest structure the world had known. In 1938 the new Reich Chancellery rose, and through its doors passed the ambassadors and the heads of state of an Europe the Reich was redrawing. On the Obersalzberg, at Hitler’s table, Speer sat among the confidences of the inner circle — the quarrels of the entourage, the tea-table conversations of the Führer, the figure of the eccentric Heß, the radical energy of Bormann and Goebbels.
Das neue Amt
The war that began in 1939 put an end to the great works, though not to the scale of the ambition. When Hitler’s favourite builder, Fritz Todt, died in an aeroplane crash in February 1942, Speer succeeded him as Reich Minister for Armaments and War Production. In a war of material, in which the factories had to match the workshops of the enemy, Speer brought to the armaments economy the same organising energy he had brought to building. He called it organisierte Improvisation — organised improvisation — a system of self-responsibility that gave the industrialists a free hand within the armaments programme and squeezed more tanks, more guns, more steel from a country under bombardment. The ministry fought the party apparatus for scarce labour and scarce raw materials; it confronted Göring, whose air force had failed to shield the Ruhr; it contended with Bormann, who guarded the Führer’s will against every rival, and with Himmler, whose SS reached into the armaments economy and the rocket works at Peenemünde. Speer’s own account of these years is of a war won and lost on the factory floor, of bombs falling on Hamburg and Berlin, of the intelligence that the war was lost while the leadership spoke of wonder-weapons, of the moral catastrophe at the end of the road when the labour of the concentration camps was pressed into the service of production.
Walküre und der Untergang
In July 1944 the bomb that was meant to kill the Führer threw the leadership into its most violent crisis. Speer, at the centre of the counter-actions in Berlin, watched the conspirators of the Bendlerstrasse arrested and the army purged; his own name, he recorded, stood on the ministerial list of the men of the twentieth of July. In the last year the fabric of the regime came apart. Speer flew from front to front, outwitting the orders of destruction that Hitler in his bunker hurled at the industrial plant of the Reich; he was among the last to see the Führer, and his account of the final weeks is of a world closing in, of the suicide of the responsible men, of the flight to Rechlin and the surrender of the fragments of government. At the end he fell into the hands of the victors, and was tried at Nuremberg for the crimes of the state he had served; sentenced to twenty years, he passed them in the fortress of Spandau. It is from that prison that his account comes — the memoir of the highest technocrat of the Reich, who built its monuments and ran its war economy, and who wrote of his own part in it with a scepticism that the historians of the age would debate for decades after his release in 1966.

entities/ss.title: The SS (Schutzstaffel)
entities/ss.content:
The SS (Schutzstaffel)
The Schutzstaffel (protection detachment), abbreviated SS, was the black-shirted organisation that began as Hitler’s bodyguard in the early years of the movement and grew, under Heinrich Himmler, into the police and security apparatus of the Third Reich — the instrument by which the state carried out its racial programme and policed the Führer-state.
From bodyguard to police power
The SS stood in the movement’s history beside the older Sturmabteilung (storm detachment, the SA), from whose street-fighting ranks the movement’s first armed force had been drawn. Where the SA under Röhm remained a mass of brown-shirted fighters, the SS was from the start the smaller, more exclusive elite of black-uniformed men chosen to guard the person of the Führer. Its decisive elevation came in the year of the regime’s great consolidation. On 17 June 1936 the Führer created the office of Chef der deutschen Polizei (Chief of the German Police) and named the Reichsführer SS Heinrich Himmler to it, concentrating the entire police power of the Reich in the hands of the SS leader — over the uniformed police and the political police alike, independent of the ordinary administration of the Interior Ministry. Henceforward the police were the servants of a racial order, not the guardians of the republic that had been.
The instrument of the racial order
Within the National Socialist state the SS took on the tasks the party assigned to the guardianship of the race. Its men enforced the racial legislation enacted from 1935 onward — the laws defining the citizen by descent and excluding the Jew from the life of the people and the economy, as the party programme demanded and the Nuremberg laws accomplished. The documentary record of the road to the National Socialist Reich presents these measures as the fulfilment, point by point, of the founding programme of 1920; and it was the apparatus Himmler commanded that carried them out. Around the police power grew the camps, the economic enterprises of the SS, and the vast machinery of surveillance that penetrated the daily life of the Reich. In the halls of power the black uniform came to stand for the ultimate sanction of the state — the instrument that could reach any man, however high.
The SS in Hitler’s circle
The architect Albert Speer, who moved in Hitler’s circle for a dozen years, remembered the SS as a presence of menace beneath the surface of the entourage — a threat that hung over the rivals of the Führer’s favour. As the war turned and the leadership closed in on itself, the SS’s power only grew: it pressed into the technological heart of the armaments effort, planned an economic concern that would own the labour and the factories it supervised, and stood beside Goebbels in the hour of the counter-action against the conspirators of July 1944. The state the SS had built outlived it in its ruin; the camps and the concentration of power that it perfected remained among the darkest legacies of the Third Reich.
