entities/stalin.title: Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin
entities/stalin.content:
Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin
The Georgian Revolutionary
Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin, the head of the Communist party and, from 1945, Generalissimus of the Soviet Union, is presented in the official literature of his own lifetime as the disciple and successor of Lenin and the architect of Soviet power. The short biography issued by the Institute of Marx–Engels–Lenin opens with his birth on 21 December 1879 at Gori in Georgia, in a family of peasant and artisan origin, and his schooling at the Gori religious school and then the Tiflis theological seminary. It was in the seminarist years that the future leader was converted to Marxism, drawn to the cause at fifteen by the spread of the new doctrine through the Transcaucasus, and it was from the Mesame-dasi (the “Third Group”), the Georgian social-democratic organization, that he entered the revolutionary underground. Expelled from the seminary in 1899, he passed into a life of prison, exile and escape. The Short Course of party history, whose own periodisation the biography follows, sets this activity within the general labour of creating a party of a new type in Russia; the biography records the successive arrests and exiles of the young organizer and his work of building the underground of the Caucasus. Escaping from exile in January 1904, he worked through the 1905 revolution in the region and attended the Stockholm and London congresses, at which the party was reorganised after the split.
Disciple of Lenin and Organiser of the Party
Through the decade between the two revolutions the biography presents Stalin as the builder of the Bolshevik party of a new type in the conditions of underground. He worked on Pravda and with the Bolshevik faction of the State Duma, and took part in the Prague conference of 1912, at which the Bolsheviks formed themselves into an independent Marxist party. The reaction years under the tsarist state meant more arrest, more exile; the biography records his banishment to the Turukhansk region, whence the February revolution of 1917 released him. On Lenin’s return to Russia in April 1917 the party set its course toward the armed uprising, and the October socialist revolution of 1917 was prepared and conducted under its leadership. When, after the seizure of power, the question of peace with Germany divided the new state, Stalin defended the strategy and tactics of the party against the position advanced by Trotsky, who, in the official account, would not accept the necessity of the Brest peace. Through the years of foreign military intervention and the civil war that followed, the biography presents him as an organiser of defence and of the Red Army on the key fronts, engaged in the rout of the intervention and of the White armies.
The Succession and the Struggle Against the Oppositions
With the close of the civil war the party turned to peaceful construction, the restoration of the national economy and the New Economic Policy, and the formation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. It was in these years, after Lenin’s illness and death, that Stalin emerged as the leader of the party. The Short Course narrates this transition within the frame of a party that grows stronger by cleansing itself of opportunist elements; the biography presents Stalin as the leader who carried Lenin’s work forward against the oppositions that sought to turn the party from the general line. Against him stood, in this official telling, the Trotskyists and the “rightists,” the Zinovievists and the Bukharinists, all of whom the party defeated. The biography’s portrait of the period is that of the model leader of party and people, the man who inherited the cause and defended it.
The Construction of Socialism
The decisive work of the Stalin era, as both the biography and the Short Course present it, was the reconstruction of the country on socialist foundations. In the struggle for socialist industrialisation in “historically the shortest possible time,” the party launched the first five-year plan and the offensive against the capitalist elements of the old economy, while Stalin addressed the question of the national and colonial peoples and the “great friendship” of the nations of the USSR. At the close of 1929 he turned the party to the collectivisation of agriculture — the gathering of the peasant economy into the kolkhoz (collective farm) — and to the liquidation of the kulaks as a class. The Sixteenth and Seventeenth Congresses marked the progress of this transformation. The Short Course records in these same chapters the degeneration of the Trotskyist double-dealers into a “White-guard band of murderers and spies” and the villainous murder of Sergei Kirov in 1934, and the measures the party took to strengthen Bolshevik vigilance in consequence. The years that followed brought the fulfilment of the second five-year plan, the Stakhanovite movement, the reconstruction of agriculture and the completion of collectivisation, and the adoption of the new Constitution of 1936, by which the land became, in the official phrase, a land of victorious socialism. The trials of the middle and late thirties appear in this account as the liquidation of the remnants of the Bukharinist–Trotskyist spies, wreckers and traitors to the motherland.
The Supreme Commander
The German attack of 22 June 1941, violating the non-aggression pact of 1939, turned the country to war, and Stalin to the conduct of it as Supreme Commander-in-Chief. The collected volume of his wartime utterances, On the Great Patriotic War of the Soviet Union, gathers the radio address of 3 July 1941, the parade speech on Red Square of 7 November 1941, and the orders of the People’s Commissar of Defence and Supreme Commander issued through the war. In these documents the war is framed as a just, patriotic struggle of the Soviet people against the fascist aggressor, set against the historic defeats of the “invincible” armies of Napoleon and of the Kaiser. The orders mark the defeat of the German plan for a blitzkrieg, the counter-offensive at Stalingrad, the rout at Kursk and the Dnieper, the expulsion of the enemy from Soviet territory, and the entry of the Red Army into the war of liberation of the peoples of Europe. The address of 9 May 1945 salutes the Soviet people as the true bearers of the victory over Germany, and the final order of 3 September 1945 closes the war with Japan. Each order is signed in the persona of the war years — “Supreme Commander-in-Chief, Generalissimus of the Soviet Union, I. Stalin.” The biography closes this account with the post-war reconstruction, the elections to the Supreme Soviet of February 1946, and the encomium of the era: “Stalin is Lenin today.”

entities/sturzo.title: Luigi Sturzo
entities/sturzo.content:
Luigi Sturzo
The Priest of the Popolare
The name of Don Luigi Sturzo enters the histories of the Fascist rise bound to the party he founded — the Partito Popolare Italiano (Italian Popular Party), the Catholic political formation that arose in the confusion of the postwar. Volpe’s history disposes of him, at the end of the volume, in a short glossary of names and terms: the Partito Popolare is defined as a party intermediate between the Communist and the Socialist; its founder and leader was Don Sturzo; it was repudiated by the Holy See and was dissolved by the Fascist government in 1925. That compressed entry, set among the names and doctrines of the movement’s own history, fixes Sturzo’s place in the regime’s account — the clerical politician whose party stood as one of the forces the revolution swept away, and whose fate (repudiated from Rome, dissolved by the state) left him, in the memory of the movement, an isolated man.
The Birth of the Popular Party
The party Sturzo led was born before the Fasci themselves were consolidated, out of the attempt of a part of Italian Catholicism to enter political life. Farinacci’s history of the revolutionary year treats its founding in the chapter on the split among the interventionists and the offensive of the neutralists, and its judgement is harsh: the attempt at renewal was called the “Partito Popolare Italiano,” and it was, in the Fascist historian’s phrase, “the most viscid and poisonous work that an Italian mind ever created against the Patria in the last hundred years.” Yet even Farinacci allows what the party’s partisans claimed for it — that it had the ardour to speak of Christ without shame and without reticence, that it set the spiritual education of Italians as the first and fundamental duty of political life, and that it might even be counted among the beneficent fruits of the victory. The venom of the portrait is directed not at the faith but at the politics: in Farinacci’s reading the Christianity of the Popular Party could be nothing but clericalism — the positive and negative political interest of the Catholic Action — and in the regions of the south it drew in the conservatives who had the terror of the reds, while in the Veneto and the Cremonese it emulated the Communists with promises to the peasants and the exercise of violence and threats, “a true Bolshevik party in Catholic mask.”
The “abilissimo don Sturzo”
In the accounts of the movement, Sturzo appears as the tactician of that clerical politics. Farinacci’s narrative of the founding brings him forward by name at the moment of decision, side by side with the lay leadership of the Catholic world: “The new great Party must not be endangered,” affirmed with admirable concord both Count Della Torre and the “most able Don Sturzo” (abilissimo don Sturzo); they would not put a sure victory at risk for the spiritual crises of some maniac, nor lose the support of the Church. The portrait is of a cautious and skilful founder, shaping the party to hold the Catholic vote without breaking with the Vatican. Volpe’s continuous narrative adds the later political note: in the struggles of the parliamentary system after the war, the party of the popolari were ambitious to be the arbiters of the situation, and its leader Don Sturzo was “so meddlesome and exigent” as to impose himself on the unstable coalition politics of the postwar chamber. In the elections of November 1919, where the Popular Party ran against the war and presented its programme — a programme reported to the party congress by Sturzo himself — it emerged one of the great forces of the new chamber, and its priest-leader took his place among the men the Fascist historians held responsible for the sfacelo of the old order.
The End of the Clerical Party
The fate the regime reserved for Sturzo’s creation was dissolution. Where the other parliamentary forces were broken by the seizure of power and the laws that followed, the Popular Party was singled out: the Fascist government dissolved it in 1925, and the Holy See had already repudiated it, so that the priest-founder saw his party renounced by the Church whose political arm it had claimed to be and then suppressed by the state whose growth he had opposed. For the historians of the movement the episode rounded the argument of the revolutionary years: the clerical attempt to plant a Catholic party in the Italian state had failed before the vigour of Fascism, and Don Sturzo — the abilissimo tactician who had built the party on the support of the Church and the conservatism of the south — was left with neither. The glossary’s flat lines carry the whole judgement: his party was not part of the Fascist Italy that the volume celebrates, but one of the obsolete formations it had dissolved.

entities/trotsky.title: Leon Trotsky
entities/trotsky.content:
Leon Trotsky
The Opponent of Leninism
Leon Trotsky, the leader of the opposition within the Soviet Communist party and the defeated rival of Stalin, appears in the official history of the party of the Stalin era as the type of the internal enemy — the man who, from the early years of the movement, set himself against the Leninist line. The Short Course of the history of the CPSU(b) treats the whole of Trotsky’s political career as a series of attempts to turn the party from the path of Marxism-Leninism, each one in turn defeated by the party and its leadership. Where Lenin laboured to build the party of a new type, the disciplined revolutionary organisation of the Bolsheviks, Trotskyism is presented as the doctrine that would have dissolved it into looseness and opportunism, subordinating the proletarian party to adventurism and faction. The official account begins with the anti-party August bloc, the coalition that Trotsky gathered together in the years of the Stolypin reaction, when the tsarist state had driven the revolution underground and the party’s enemies hoped to break it apart. Against this bloc the Bolsheviks, under Lenin, fought through the reaction years, and the Prague conference of 1912, at which the Bolsheviks formed themselves into an independent Marxist party, broke it. Throughout the whole history, the Short Course returns to Trotskyism as the standing threat to party unity — opposed by the Bolsheviks at every congress and in every period, from the years of the first revolution to the construction of socialism.
The Opposition After the Revolution
In the official narrative Trotsky’s opposition did not cease with the seizure of power, and the Short Course follows it through the whole of the Soviet period. At the moment of the Brest peace, when the young Soviet state, exhausted by war and civil conflict, had to accept peace with Germany in order to survive and consolidate, Trotsky, in the account of the Short Course and of the biography of Stalin, advanced a position that would have refused the peace and exposed the revolution to destruction; it was Lenin and the party who carried the peace against him. After the civil war the struggle passed into the discussions of the restoration period, and the Short Course records the party’s defeat of the opposition in the discussion on the trade unions, at the Tenth Congress, and the strengthening of the party’s unity under its leadership. The party history presents these defeats as the purification by which the party grew stronger — the cleansing of the opportunist elements that threatened it from within. In this same period the Short Course records the formation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics and the turn to the New Economic Policy, measures that the opposition resisted in the name of positions that the party rejected.
The Struggle for Socialist Construction
The decisive confrontation came in the years of socialist construction, when the party, in the struggle for the socialist industrialisation of the country, had to overcome an opposition that sought to turn it from the general line. The Short Course devotes the tenth chapter to this struggle. The difficulties of the period of socialist industrialisation were, in the official account, seized upon by the enemies of the party, who gathered themselves into a new coalition; the chapter narrates the formation of the Trotskyist–Zinovievist anti-party bloc, the anti-Soviet pronouncements of the bloc, and the defeat of the bloc at the hands of the party under the leadership of the Central Committee. The Fifteenth Congress, which set the party’s course on the collectivisation of agriculture, and the rout of the Trotskyist–Zinovievist bloc that followed, completed, in this telling, the defeat of the open opposition. Where the bloc had predicted the failure of industrialisation and the collapse of the party’s plan, the first five-year plan was fulfilled, industry was built, and the country began the mass movement toward the kolkhoz (collective farm) that was to transform its agriculture.
Double-Dealing and Degeneration
The distinctive charge that the Short Course levels at Trotskyism is that of political double-dealing. Defeated in open struggle, the Trotskyists did not, in the official account, abandon their opposition; they concealed it, masquerading as loyal members of the party while working against it from within, so that the struggle against them had to be waged on new ground. The same is said of the Bukharinites, whose degeneration into political double-dealers the Short Course narrates in the same chapters; the “rightist” group of Bukharin and Rykov, which had opposed the party’s course on industrialisation and the offensive against the kulaks, is presented as having likewise concealed its hostility. In the account of the years after the Seventeenth Congress the process is carried to its conclusion: the degeneration of the Trotskyist double-dealers into a “White-guard band of murderers and spies,” the villainous murder of Sergei Kirov in 1934, and the measures that the party took to strengthen Bolshevik vigilance in consequence. The party history makes the connection explicit — the double-dealers who had once argued as opponents within the party became, in the official telling, the wreckers and traitors who served the enemies of the Soviet state.
The Liquidation of the Enemies of the People
The liquidation of the remnants of the Bukharinist–Trotskyist spies, wreckers and traitors to the motherland, recorded in the closing chapters of the Short Course and in the biography of Stalin, closes the history of the opposition. The party history presents this as the necessary cleansing by which the party, in the lesson of its own history, grows stronger — the expulsion of the enemies of the people who had sought to destroy Soviet power from within, and the vindication of the vigilance that the murder of Kirov had demanded. In the official literature Trotskyism thus stands as the great negative example of the party’s history: the opposition that opposed Leninism at its birth, opposed the party after the revolution, and finally degenerated into the band of traitors that struck down a leader of the party and was itself swept away. The defeat of Trotsky is presented not as a personal triumph of any man but as the victory of the party over its internal enemy, by which the cause of the working class was preserved.

entities/victor-emmanuel-iii.title: Victor Emmanuel III
entities/victor-emmanuel-iii.content:
Victor Emmanuel III
The King at the March on Rome
King Victor Emmanuel III of the House of Savoy stood at both ends of the Fascist era — the sovereign who received the March on Rome and the sovereign who, twenty years later, dismissed its Duce. In October 1922 the fate of the liberal state turned on his decision, and the regime’s own chroniclers present him as the arbiter who chose Fascism over civil war. On the evening of Friday 27 October, as Pini records, the ministry of Facta, without awaiting the King, proclaimed a state of siege (stato d’assedio) under pressure from the ministers most hostile to Fascism; for a moment it was believed the King had given his assent and that blood was about to flow, with cannon on Monte Mario and chevaux-de-frise on the bridges of the Tiber. But the King, returning to Rome, found that the Ministry presented him together with its resignation the already-promulgated decree of the state of siege, and he refused to sign it, ordering the measure at once revoked. Businelli, the movement-insider, tells the same story from the Fascist side: the Facta ministry, after resigning, “with a purely anti-constitutional gesture proclaimed the state of siege throughout Italy; but the King opposed a clear and energetic refusal, and the decree was immediately revoked.” Volpe adds that the state of siege was proclaimed in the certainty that the King would sign, but he did not follow his Ministers, and at noon on 28 October the Agenzia Stefani announced its withdrawal.
The King made his motive explicit. Pini records that he summoned the Fascist De Vecchi to the Quirinale and told the soldier, choked with the passion and emotion of the hour: “I want Italians to know that I did not wish to sign the state of siege.” In Volpe’s account the King, better informed than his Ministers, had hastened back to the capital on the evening of the 27th, been acclaimed by both Nationalists and Fascists on his arrival at the station, and accepted the resignation of the Facta Cabinet. As soon as his decision was known in Rome there was a wave of enthusiasm for him, and Fascist and Nationalist squadre began to circulate freely. An attempt to form a Salandra–Mussolini ministry came to nothing because of Mussolini’s refusal, and the task of government fell to Fascism itself.
The Collaboration of the Crown
On 29 October the King instructed Mussolini to form a ministry. Businelli, writing from within the movement, frames it as an act of collaboration offered to the revolution: the ministry of Facta having fallen and the Salandra–Mussolini combination failed, on the 31st His Majesty called Mussolini to Rome, and the collaboration began with the words the Duce addressed to the throne — “I ask pardon of Your Majesty for presenting myself in a Blackshirt. Returning from the fortunately bloodless battle that had to be fought, I bring Your Majesty the Italy of Vittorio Veneto, re-consecrated by the new Victory. And I am a faithful servant of Your Majesty.” Pini likewise records the salute — “I bring to Your Majesty the Italy of Vittorio Veneto, re-consecrated by the new victories” — and tells how the legions of Blackshirts entered Rome, filed past the King on the Piazza del Quirinale, and departed “with order and admirable discipline.” Volpe describes the culmination of 31 October: before the order for demobilisation was issued, a hundred thousand Blackshirts massed in the Villa Borghese, filed past Mussolini in review, advanced to the Altare della Patria, and marched to the Quirinal to salute the King, who, with Armando Diaz and Thaon di Revel at his side, stood for five hours watching the passing of “this river of youth,” amid Garibaldian veterans among the Blackshirts. In all three accounts the Crown’s acceptance of the March is the seal of the revolution: the King refused the state of siege, entrusted government to Mussolini, and watched the columns salute the monarchy, binding Fascism and the House of Savoy together.
The Crown and the Collapse
Two decades later the same King unbound the knot. Badoglio’s memoir, written from inside the last acts, shows the monarch’s uneasy relation to the regime’s arbitrary power throughout the war. When Mussolini concluded the alliance with Hitler and only notified him once it was signed — a violation of Article 5 of the Constitution, under which executive power appertains exclusively to the King, who declares war and makes treaties — the King, Badoglio records, showed his deep resentment and his anger at such a violation, but observed that it was not possible to undo what had been done without causing serious difficulties. The April 1939 memorandum to Hitler had been forwarded to the King among the first copies, but the alliance itself was presented to him as a fait accompli.
It was to the King that the Fascist Grand Council turned when it moved against Mussolini. The resolution passed on the night of 24–25 July 1943, whose text Badoglio reproduces, invited the Government “to beg the King, to whom the whole nation looks with loyalty and confidence, that he should for the honour and safety of the country assume the effective command of the Army, Navy and Air Force” and take the supreme initiative of command, “the glorious heritage of the House of Savoy.” When Mussolini came to the royal villa and insisted the resolution was not in order, the King answered that it was valid, and when the Duce demanded whether he ought to resign, replied simply, “Yes — and I forthwith accepted his resignation.” Badoglio, present, watched Mussolini collapse “as if he had had a blow over the heart.” The King then appointed Badoglio Head of the Government, insisted on a Ministry of experts rather than politicians, showed him the two proclamations already printed announcing that the war would go on, and stood as the authority behind the arrest of the Duce. Victor Emmanuel, who in 1922 had chosen to admit the revolution rather than fight it, in 1943 chose to dismiss its chief rather than share its ruin — the sovereign who had twice resolved the crisis of the Italian state, each time by accommodating the force that stood before the throne.

entities/von-papen.title: Franz von Papen (1879–1969)
entities/von-papen.content:
Franz von Papen
Franz von Papen, a Westphalian nobleman and career officer turned diplomat, entered the centre of German politics in the spring of 1932, when the sickly republic was already staggering, and left it only after he had handed the chancellorship itself to Adolf Hitler. He was the man Schleicher drew “out of the dark” because he wanted “a fool” behind whom he might rule unseen — and the man who, by his own ambition and skill at unscrupulous intrigue, outplayed his maker. A lifetime’s contempt for the parliamentary parties, a talent for the concealed bargain, and a courtier’s intimacy with the aged President Hindenburg made him the indispensable bridge by which the National Socialists crossed from opposition to power. The republican press of the day dubbed his first government the “cabinet of barons,” the Kabinett der Barone; the phrase caught him exactly.
The cabinet of barons
Papen was the candidate of the General Kurt von Schleicher, the Reichswehr’s political brain, who had resolved to overthrow Chancellor Heinrich Brüning and to govern the republic himself through a pliant front man. Papen, a Centre deputy of no great standing, a “bon vivant of old nobility” recently gilded by marriage into the half-French Boch industrial family of the Saar, a professional diplomat whose clumsy hand he had already shown as military attaché in Washington during the war, seemed ideal: a rich, Catholic, aristocratic worldling who could silence the rumours of Hindenburg’s hostility to the Church, and a man without a parliamentary following of his own, who would never threaten his creator. The intrigues of May 1932 — Schleicher’s sudden desertion of the cabinet over the SA ban, the whisperings at Neudeck, the junckers’ cry of “agrarian Bolshevism” against Brüning’s settlement plans — were mounted on Papen’s behalf, and on 30 May the President dismissed Brüning and named Papen Chancellor. On 1 June 1932 the Reichswehr had its chancellor.
Papen governed without a parliamentary majority, dissolved the Reichstag, and struck at the republic’s last great stronghold. On 20 July 1932, invoking the state of emergency, he deposed the Prussian government of Otto Braun and Karl Severing in the Preußenschlag, the coup against Prussia, and proclaimed himself Reich Commissioner. Severing, summoned to the Chancellery and told to consider himself deposed, answered that he would yield to force alone; that evening the police occupied the ministry. The passive Social Democrats, anxious not to endanger the July elections, counselled submission. Papen thus delivered the largest state of the republic, with its police, into the hands of the right, clearing the road before Hitler — the very prize the National Socialists had been unable to take for themselves. He remained Chancellor through the late summer, survived Hitler’s angry demand for the chancellorship on 13 August, and rode the Potempa affair, when his courts-martial sentenced the murderers of a Polish worker to death and Hitler publicly called them “my comrades.” But Papen had no majority, the country was dissolving into a grey winter of seven million unemployed, and the Reichstag brought his government down in September. On 17 November 1932 Papen resigned, with a parting document urging a “national concentration” that would rest on Hitler.
The Cologne alliance
Out of office, Papen did not withdraw. He kept the state apartments of the Reichskanzlei, where the ailing Hindenburg lodged beside him during the rebuilding of the presidential palace, and from this intimacy he worked to unseat his own successor, Schleicher, and to return — this time as the maker of Hitler. The two old enemies buried their feud. On the morning of 4 January 1933 Hitler, ostensibly travelling to an election meeting in Lippe, slipped away to the house of the banker von Schröder in Cologne, where Papen awaited him. The reconciliation was sealed: Hitler acknowledged that only Papen could smooth the old President’s path to him, and renounced the threatened “night of St Bartholomew” and the cry of “street free for the SA”; Papen undertook to talk Hindenburg out of his loathing for the “Bohemian corporal.” The same evening Gregor Strasser returned to Berlin from his southern holiday, ready to fight again; but it was Papen’s recipe, not Strasser’s, that prevailed. Papen’s plan, laid before Hindenburg, was to give Hitler the chancellorship with the National Socialists supporting the government as a whole and the Reichstag left undissolved. The German Nationalists and the Stahlhelm would surround him; Papen himself would be Vice-Chancellor and the true regent.
On 28 January Schleicher, refused the power to dissolve the Reichstag, resigned, and on 30 January 1933 the seventy-eight-year-old President, persuaded that Papen “had” Hitler, received the new Chancellor. Papen, who had forced the final bargain when the cautious Hugenberg balked at conceding fresh elections, stood beside Hitler before the old man and reported the “national concentration” accomplished. He was Vice-Chancellor and believed himself the government’s real master — “the man who brought Hitler to power,” as his enemies and friends both styled him. The official documentary record of the regime preserves his part: in the Friedrichs compilation of the seizure of power, the address of 4 January between Hitler and “the retired Chancellor von Papen” at Cologne opens the narrative of the new year, and Papen appears as Reich Commissioner for Prussia, corresponding with Hindenburg and Göring before yielding the Prussian ministry to the latter in April 1933. He served Hitler, he believed, in order to contain him.
The Marburg speech and its price
The fantasy of control lasted a year. Hitler outgrew his patrons; Papen found himself a Vice-Chancellor “without influence,” betrayed by Hitler and brutally pushed to the wall by Göring. Around him gathered a circle of conservative men — the Catholic Action leader Erich Klausener, the publicist Edgar Jung, his private secretary von Bose, the aristocratic von Detten — who believed the time of defensiveness was over and that a new crisis could sweep the Nazi chiefs away. On 17 June 1934 Papen struck. At the University of Marburg he delivered the Marburger Rede, the Marburg speech, drafted by Jung: the situation was grave, he said, the laws had their defects, violence and injustice were being practised, and one must end the false beautification of the regime; doctrinaire fanatics should fall silent, and false personality-worship was un-Prussian — a lash against Goebbels and Göring. The speech roused the bourgeoisie, and Hindenburg, to whom Papen was still the trusted channel, sent a warm telegram of congratulation, before which even Hitler for a moment bowed.
But the Marburg speech signed the death-warrant of Papen’s circle. On 30 June 1934, while Hitler flew to Munich to massacre the SA leadership, Göring’s police struck in Berlin and Prussia at “the reaction.” Jung was taken from his flat, wrote the word Gestapo in pencil on his bathroom wall, and was never seen alive; Klausener was shot dead in his ministry office with his hat on; Bose and von Detten and a ring of Papen’s collaborators were executed. Göring, who dared not touch Papen himself for fear of the Reichswehr and of Hindenburg, shot the whole garland of his helpers away and left him standing “like a mournful king of the alley.” Papen lived, and served Hitler further — as ambassador to Vienna, as the man who staged the annexation of Austria in 1938. He who had brought Hitler to power outlived the republic he had helped to bury, and died in 1969, an old man of the counter-revolution, the agent of his own defeat.

events/anglo-german-naval-agreement-1935.title: Anglo-German Naval Agreement (18 June 1935)
events/anglo-german-naval-agreement-1935.content:
Anglo-German Naval Agreement (18 June 1935)
18 June 1935 — Germany and Great Britain concluded the Anglo-German Naval Agreement (deutsch-englisches Flottenabkommen), under which the future strength of the German fleet was fixed at thirty-five per cent of the total tonnage of the members of the British Commonwealth. For the National Socialist state the agreement was the first formal recognition by a great power of its rearmament.
The London negotiations
The agreement arose from discussions held in London in the days preceding its signature. Representatives of the government of the German Reich and of the government of His Majesty in the United Kingdom met with the principal aim of preparing the ground for a general conference on the limitation of naval armaments. The British government announced its formal acceptance of the proposal that had been under discussion, whereby the future strength of the German fleet should stand in the ratio of 35 : 100 to the total fleet strength of the members of the British Commonwealth. Great Britain described the proposal as an extraordinarily important contribution to the future limitation of naval armaments, and declared that the agreement concluded with the German government was to be regarded as a permanent and final settlement between the two governments from that day onward, and one that would facilitate the conclusion of a future general agreement on naval limitation among all the sea powers of the world.
The ratio and its limits
The declarations of the German representatives, summarised in the agreement, bound the ratio in several ways. The 35 : 100 proportion was to be a permanent one — the total tonnage of the German fleet was never to exceed thirty-five per cent of the total tonnage of the treaty-defined sea forces of the British Commonwealth, or, if no treaty limits should exist, of the actual total tonnage. Germany declared that it would stand by the 35 : 100 ratio under all circumstances, and that the ratio was not to be influenced by the building programmes of other countries; but if the general balance of naval strength were violently disturbed by abnormal building measures of other powers, the German government reserved the right to ask the British government to examine the new situation. Germany favoured a system dividing warships into categories, with a maximum tonnage and gun calibre fixed for the ships of each category, and expressed itself ready to apply the thirty-five per cent ratio to the tonnage in each retained category, subject to the safeguards agreed.
The building programme
On the strength of the agreement, the Reich government announced on 8 July a naval building programme to bring the Kriegsmarine (navy) up to the thirty-five per cent of the British displacement fixed in the agreement. Laid down or to be laid down during 1935 were two armoured ships of 26,000 tons displacement each with 28-cm guns; two cruisers of 10,000 tons with 20-cm guns; sixteen destroyers of 1,625 tons with 12.7-cm guns (already on the slips in 1934 and 1935); twenty submarines of 250 tons, the first of which entered service on 29 June, two more being already afloat; six submarines of 500 tons and two of 750 tons. The building of the first aircraft carrier, and the plans for the battleships to be laid down in 1936 and later years on the principle of qualitative equality, were in preparation. The agreement was completed by a second naval treaty of July 1937.
Place in the rearmament
In the official record of the year the naval agreement was presented as a new contribution to the European peace, the more notable because it formally acknowledged for the first time the German rearmament that the proclamation of conscription in March had begun. The sea rearmament it sanctioned belonged to the same programme as the army built on the Wehrgesetz and the air force protected by the Air Protection Law of 26 June. That Great Britain — the leading sea power — should grant the Reich a permanent naval equality, if only at the ratio of 35 : 100, stood in the regime’s telling as proof that Germany’s restoration to the community of powers was being recognised, and it bound the very powers that had protested the reintroduction of conscription into an agreement with the rearming Reich.

events/anschluss-1938.title: Anschluss of Austria, 1938
events/anschluss-1938.content:
Anschluss of Austria, 1938
12–13 March 1938.
The March into the Ostmark
On 12 March 1938 German troops crossed the frontier into Austria, and the following day the German government proclaimed the law of reunion by which the Republic of Austria was joined to the German Reich. The Anschluß (reunion, literally “connection”) — the union of the two German states that the treaties of Versailles and St. Germain had forbidden and that every German nationalist current had demanded since 1918 — was accomplished in a weekend and without a shot. The official documentary record of 1938, compiled by Hans Volz for the Dokumente der deutschen Politik, sets the event at the centre of its account of the establishment of Greater Germany: the entry of the Wehrmacht on 12 March, the law of reunion of 13 March, the Reich governor’s administration, the ordinance introducing the Nuremberg race laws into Austria, and the plebiscite of 10 April, by which the regime submitted the accomplished fact to the Austrian people.
The immediate occasion was the collapse of the Austrian government. For years the Austrian state, an independent republic carved out of the rump of the Habsburg Empire, had been a bone of contention between its own factions and the Reich. The National Socialists of Austria, linked to Hitler’s movement, had agitated for union; the authoritarian governments of Dollfuss and Schuschnigg had sought to hold the country independent of Berlin. In February 1938 Hitler summoned the Austrian Chancellor Schuschnigg to the Berghof and forced upon him an agreement; when Schuschnigg, seeking to escape, announced a plebiscite on Austrian independence, the Reich moved. The Austrian National Socialists, led by Seyss-Inquart, took over the government, and on 12 March German troops entered to restore, in the official phrase, order and to accomplish the reunion.
The Law of Reunion
On 13 March 1938 the law of reunion was published. It declared Austria a province of the German Reich under the name of the Ostmark (Eastern March), the historic name of the border march of the medieval German kings. The Reich appointed a governor (Reichsstatthalter) — Seyss-Inquart — to administer the new province, and the laws of the Reich, including the Nuremberg race laws of 1935, were extended to Austria by ordinance. The plebiscite of 10 April, held under the pressure of the accomplished fact and the occupation, returned an overwhelming majority for the union. In the German record the Anschluss was the fulfillment of the first point of the party programme — the reunion of all Germans in a Greater Germany on the basis of national self-determination — and the triumphant completion of a claim that reached back to the end of the First World War.
The party-authorized compilation of Büttner gives the historical depth of the claim. Its first section, devoted to the reunion of all Germans, assembles the documents of the Austrian question from the very beginning: Emperor Karl’s manifesto of October 1918, the proclamation of German-Austria of November 1918, the notes of the Allied powers forbidding union, the failed customs-union plan of 1931, and Hitler’s speech at Linz of 12 March 1938, delivered in the city of his youth as the German troops moved into Austria. In this telling the Anschluss was no sudden conquest but the delayed fulfillment of a national demand that the peace settlement had unjustly denied — the reunion of the German people that Versailles and St. Germain had split in two.
The Making of Greater Germany
The Anschluss transformed the map of Europe and the standing of the Reich. Austria’s independence, guaranteed by the treaties of 1919 and the protocols of the League of Nations, was extinguished, and the Reich’s frontier was carried to the Alps and to the borders of Italy, Hungary and Yugoslavia. The population of the German Reich grew by some six million; Vienna, the fallen imperial capital, became a German city again; and the strategic position of the Reich in central Europe was immeasurably strengthened. The powers of Europe — France and Great Britain — protested in words but did not act, and the Reich learned the lesson that the year was to confirm at Munich: the Western democracies would not fight for the revision of the peace settlement.
The Anschluss was the first of the great annexations of 1938, and it opened the way for the rest. Within six months the Sudeten crisis brought the Reich to the brink of war with Czechoslovakia; within nine months the Sudetenland was ceded at Munich. Volz’s volume, organized around the establishment of Greater Germany, records the two annexations as the two acts of the same process — the reunion of the German lands that the treaties of 1919 had severed. The law of reunion of 13 March was the model for the law of 21 November on the Sudeten territories, and the administration of the Ostmark, with its governors and its imported Reich laws, the pattern for the incorporation of the Sudetenland.
The Anschluss of 1938 was, in the German record, the supreme triumph of the Führer’s policy of reunion — the recovery of the German people’s old capital and the completion of the unity that Bismarck’s Reich of 1871, having excluded the Germans of Austria, had left unfinished. The march into the Ostmark on 12 March, the law of 13 March, and the plebiscite of 10 April stand in the official account as the moment when the Third Reich ceased to be merely the German state and became the Greater German Reich — the Großdeutsches Reich — that the party programme had promised and the age had come to deliver.

events/anti-comintern-pact-1936.title: Anti-Comintern Pact, 1936
events/anti-comintern-pact-1936.content:
Anti-Comintern Pact, 1936
25 November 1936.
The Compact Against the International
On 25 November 1936 Germany and Japan signed at Berlin the pact against the Communist International, the Antikominternpakt (Anti-Comintern Pact), by which the two powers bound themselves to a common defense against the subversive activity of the Third International. The instrument was signed by Ribbentrop for the Reich and the Japanese ambassador for the Empire of Japan, and its text, with the accompanying protocol and the declarations of Goebbels and Ribbentrop, was published at once as one of the principal state documents of the year. In the German official record compiled by Friedrichs, the pact closes the sequence of 1936 — after the remilitarization of the Rhineland in March, the German–Austrian agreement of July, the recognition of Italian Abyssinia and of Franco’s government in the autumn — as the Reich’s alliance with the farthest of the world’s powers against the common enemy of the Communist International.
The pact rested on a diagnosis of the age. In the official German view the Comintern was not a party among parties but an international engine of revolution, operating through the world’s communist movements to subvert the established order; against such an engine the individual states were helpless unless they combined. Germany and Japan, standing at the two ends of Eurasia, each faced the Communist movement on their own frontiers — Germany across its eastern border against Soviet power, Japan against the communism of the East — and the pact joined them in a common front. The declarations that accompanied the signature presented the step as a defensive act: the two powers, the official voice insisted, sought no territory and no conquest but only the peace of the world against the international revolutionary conspiracy.
The Axis of the Far East
The pact of 25 November was the first formal treaty of the alliance that was to grow into the Rome–Berlin–Tokyo axis. Its significance lay not only in what it did but in the direction it gave to German foreign policy. The Reich, having secured its western flank and its southern border, now reached across the world to Japan, and in so doing ranged itself on the side of the revisionist and anti-communist powers against the order of the Western democracies and the Soviet Union. The pact was followed a year later by the adherence of Italy — the protocol of 6 November 1937 by which Rome joined the German–Japanese agreement — and by the end of the decade the loose compact against the Comintern had hardened into the wartime alliance of the Axis powers.
The official German documents of the following year, compiled by Volz, record the growth of this alignment: relations with Japan and Manchukuo, the recognition of Manchukuo, and the strengthening of the common front of Germany, Italy and Japan. The Anti-Comintern Pact was the seed of this system. It bound Germany to Japan in a way that no exchange of ambassadors could have done, and it committed the two powers to regard the international communist movement as a common adversary to be met by common means. In the regime’s own telling the pact was the recognition of a simple fact — that the Communist International threatened all nations alike and that only the cooperation of the threatened states could contain it.
The Front Against Bolshevism
The pact was presented in Germany as a front not merely diplomatic but ideological. Goebbels and Rosenberg had made the world struggle against Bolshevism the central theme of the party congress at Nuremberg in September 1936, and the pact with Japan carried this theme into the sphere of foreign treaty. The German official narrative of the year, from the Reichstag speech of March through the two-year service decree of August, had described the rearmament and the tightening of the German state as self-defense against Soviet imperialism; the Anti-Comintern Pact gave this self-defense an ally. Japan, in the German account, was the power of the East that had understood the same necessity and had resolved to stand against the same enemy.
The immediate consequence was a sharpening of the line between the Reich and the Soviet Union. The Reich had already answered the Franco-Soviet pact by the remilitarization of the Rhineland and the repudiation of Locarno; the Anti-Comintern Pact declared openly that Germany and the Soviet Union stood on opposite sides of the central divide of the age. Yet the pact was also, characteristically, a document of double face: its public text spoke only of defense against the Comintern’s subversive activity, while its secret protocol — which would in time come to light — looked toward the far East and the rearrangement of the region. For the German public and the German record of 1936, however, the pact was presented as an act of peace and self-defense, the alliance of two great powers against the revolutionary international that threatened the world.
The Anti-Comintern Pact of 25 November 1936 stands in the German record as the closing of the Reich’s circle of alliances. In the single year 1936 Germany had recovered the Rhineland, made its agreement with Austria, recognized the new regimes of Abyssinia and Spain, and bound itself to Japan. The year that had opened with the restoration of sovereignty over the German border country closed with the forging of a world front against Bolshevism — a front that pointed, though the record of 1936 did not yet say so, toward the coalition of the Axis and the war to come.

events/armistice-of-1940.title: The Armistice of 1940 and the Establishment of Vichy (22 June – 10 July 1940)
events/armistice-of-1940.content:
The Armistice of 1940 and the Establishment of Vichy (22 June – 10 July 1940)
22 June – 10 July 1940
The armistice of 22 June 1940, by which France surrendered to Germany in the forest of Compiègne, and the establishment in its train of the regime of Vichy — the truncated, disarmed French state that the victor left at the head of the unoccupied part of the country, and that on 10 July 1940 the National Assembly, summoned in the spa town of Vichy, invested with full powers in the aged Marshal Pétain. The two acts — the military capitulation and the political settlement that followed it — together dissolved the Third Republic and founded the État français (the French State) that was to govern France under the German occupation. Marc Bloch, writing the report of the year 1940 in the weeks after the catastrophe, and then, under the new regime, the clandestine essays in which a republican historian measured what had been lost, is the witness from the side of the defeated for both the surrender and the new order.
The surrender
The military defeat of May–June 1940 had been swift and total, and by the third week of June the government, fled from Paris to Bordeaux, confronted the decision that the collapse had imposed. The cabinet chose to seek an armistice rather than continue the war from the empire, and on 22 June 1940 the French emissaries signed the German terms in the railway carriage at Compiègne — the same place where, in November 1918, the German delegates had signed the armistice that ended the First World War. The choice of the site was deliberate, a reversal of the verdict of 1918 imposed upon the vanquished. The armistice of 22 June provided for the cessation of hostilities on 25 June, the German occupation of the north and the Atlantic coast of France, and the demobilisation and disarmament of the French army, leaving the French government at the head of an unoccupied southern zone and of the vast colonial empire. Two million French soldiers passed into captivity as prisoners of war. For France, the war was over in six weeks.
The choice of Pétain
The armistice was signed by the government that the defeat had brought to power. On 16 June the cabinet of Paul Reynaud, which had wished to continue the struggle from North Africa, gave way to a ministry under the Marshal Philippe Pétain — the victor of Verdun in the previous war, the most venerated soldier of France, called to office in the catastrophe as the man who could negotiate with the conqueror and spare the country further destruction. Pétain’s ministry, formed at Bordeaux and then removed to Vichy in the unoccupied zone, embodied the decision to accept the German terms. Bloch, writing in the aftermath, records the great exode (exodus) of June 1940 — the roads choked with the fleeing civilian population ahead of the advancing columns — and the abdication of the will to continue that the armistice expressed. The decision, in his judgement, was not only a military surrender but the abandonment of the war by the leaders of a nation that had not willed to fight it.
The dissolution of the Republic
The armistice settled the war; the political settlement that followed settled the regime. On 10 July 1940 the two chambers of the French parliament, the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, were summoned to Vichy, and the National Assembly voted by an overwhelming majority to confer full constituent powers on Marshal Pétain. The vote dissolved the Third Republic: the constitution of 1875 was set aside, and the Marshal was empowered to promulgate a new constitutional order by his own decree. Thus was founded the État français, the “French State” of Vichy — a regime that replaced the parliamentary Republic with the personal authority of the victor of Verdun, pledged to a national renewal on the ruins of the defeat. For the republicans of the old France the act of 10 July was the revolution of the defeat: the Republic that had governed France since 1870 was abolished by its own elected representatives in the panic of the catastrophe.
The new order
The regime that the vote established set itself against everything the Republic had represented. The motto of the Republic — liberté, égalité, fraternité — gave way to the threefold device of the new order, travail, famille, patrie (work, family, fatherland); the government pursued a policy of collaboration with the occupying power; and the racial laws soon followed, excluding the Jews of France from the civic life of the state. It was under this regime that Marc Bloch, the professor of history, was deprived of his chair at Montpellier by the Vichy statutes — the act that drove the veteran of two wars, who had affirmed that he was born a Jew and had never sought to deny it, into the Resistance. In his Testament, written at Clermont-Ferrand on 18 March 1941, Bloch made his confession against the new order: a stranger, he wrote, to all confessional formalism as to all supposedly racial solidarity, he had felt himself during his whole life above all and very simply French, and he died, as he had lived, a good Frenchman. The establishment of Vichy thus completed, in his own person, the arc of the defeat: the Republic was abolished, the racial principle entered the law of France, and the historian of the strange defeat prepared to spend his last years in clandestine resistance to the regime that had risen from its ruins.
A witness of the year 1940
Bloch wrote the account of the collapse — and measured the political settlement that followed — in the weeks between July and September 1940, that the record might be preserved against the day when France again saw the freedom of thought and judgment blossom. His testimony closes the account of the year 1940 as a procès-verbal (official report) left for future researchers: the narrative of the military defeat, the analysis of the responsibility for it, and the judgement of the new order that the defeat had brought into being. The armistice of 22 June and the vote of 10 July appear in his pages not as the end of the war but as the beginning of a new and darker chapter of French history — the chapter that the republicans of the old France, and Bloch among them, were to spend the following years fighting.

events/armistice-of-8-september-1943.title: The Armistice of 8 September 1943
events/armistice-of-8-september-1943.content:
The Armistice of 8 September 1943
8 September 1943
Italy’s surrender to the Allies, announced from the Rome broadcasting station on the evening of 8 September 1943, five weeks after the fall of Mussolini. By a secret armistice signed at Fairfield Camp in Sicily on 3 September, and published by General Eisenhower’s demand six days early, the government of Marshal badoglio passed Italy from the German to the Allied side of the war — a change of policy kept secret from the Germans until the moment of its announcement, and followed within hours by the German reaction that the new government had dreaded and could not meet. The armistice ended Italy’s war against the Allies and opened at once a war against her former partner; within days the King and the government would abandon Rome for Brindisi, leaving the capital to the Germans.
The secret negotiations
Within days of taking office the Badoglio government resolved that Italy must change sides, while professing to Berlin that the war would go on. The negotiations had to be kept so secret that they could not even be discussed in the Cabinet. On 29 July the new Minister of Foreign Affairs, Guariglia, the Ambassador returned from Turkey, arrived in Rome and entirely agreed that as few people as possible should know of them; he had already let it be known, through the Turkish Foreign Minister, that Italy was on the point of changing her policy. Communication with the Allies was the first difficulty: the British Minister to the Holy See had only a very old code almost certainly known to the Germans, and the American Chargé d’Affaires had none. It was agreed to reassure both sides at once — to accept a German invitation to a conference, and to send officials of the Foreign Office to Lisbon and Tangier to explain to the Allies that Italy accepted it only to lull the suspicions of the Germans. The conference met at Tarvisio on 6 August, in an atmosphere of doubt and suspicion, and reached no decisions; the Italian request, supported by General Ambrosio, to bring home the divisions in Russia and the Balkans was rejected. The only positive success was that the Allied press and wireless hardly mentioned the meeting.
The terms and the signing
For the actual negotiation, General Ambrosio proposed General Castellano, accompanied by a Foreign Office official who spoke perfect English, and it was agreed that a special train leaving for Lisbon on 12 August should carry the military mission. At Lisbon on 17 August the Allied staff chiefs handed him the terms of the armistice “to be accepted or rejected.” He returned to Rome on 28 August, and Badoglio spent a day examining terms that seemed to him very harsh and in some instances impossible to carry out, before laying them before the King. Castellano was instructed to explain that Italy, her armed forces so much weaker than the German, could not carry out the terms as they stood, and that the Government would conclude an armistice when the Allies had landed at least fifteen divisions in a suitable locality. General Bedell Smith replied that the terms communicated in Lisbon could not be altered — the Government could only accept or reject them; three or four divisions would first disembark on the mainland to draw off the German forces, followed a few days later by the fifteen divisions elsewhere; and if the terms were not accepted, all the cities, including Rome, would be razed to the ground. On 1 September Badoglio, Guariglia, Ambrosio and Castellano were all in favour of accepting; Badoglio went to the King for his orders, and Castellano returned to Sicily to sign. It was laid down that the date of the armistice would be between 10 and 15 September, probably 12 September; the documents were brought to Rome on 5 September, and the Allied High Command supplied a radio set with an American secret code, so that from 29 August the government was in constant touch with Allied Headquarters in Algiers.
The eve of 8 September
The plans for the day rested on the assumption that Rome could be held. Rome had been declared an “open city” (città aperta) — but the declaration was unilateral, never accepted by the British and Americans, though the military headquarters were moved outside a protected zone about seventeen miles round the city. Five divisions and the elements of two others, under General Carboni, were concentrated round the capital, and instructions had been drawn up for all commanding officers on their line of conduct in the event of an armistice. It had also been settled with Castellano and the Allied staffs that on the night of the armistice an airborne division should be landed on the outskirts of Rome and an armoured division at the mouth of the Tiber. But on the night of 7 September the plans began to break. About two in the morning of 8 September Carboni arrived at Badoglio’s house with the American General Taylor, who had come to arrange the landing of the airborne division and told Badoglio that, contrary to what had been said, the armistice was imminent and would perhaps be declared that very day. Badoglio objected that the airborne division could only begin its landing on the night of 9 September and could not coincide with the principal landing; Carboni said he would need days to complete the issue of ammunition and petrol. Badoglio drafted a telegram to General Eisenhower insisting that the armistice be postponed to 12 September, and during the morning General Rossi left at once by air for Allied Headquarters.
The announcement
At 5.30 p.m. on 8 September a telegram in code signed by General Eisenhower arrived requiring the Italian Government to declare the armistice at 8 p.m. — and declaring that if this was not done, the armistice signed on 3 September would no longer be valid and the negotiations would be broadcast from Algiers and London. Badoglio was astounded. He learned much later that the Allied High Command, well informed of the situation in Italy, had feared that his government would be overthrown by the Germans and had wished to expedite matters. “It was a decision which entirely upset our plans and brought us to the brink of ruin.” Eisenhower admitted later that evening, hearing from General Rossi the reasons for the request for postponement, “I am inclined to believe that I have made a mistake, but all that matters now is to collaborate to the best of our ability in our common interest.”
Badoglio went at once to the King with the ministers of the Army, the Navy and the Air Force, the Chiefs of the General Staff, Carboni and Major Marchesi. Ambrosio explained that the anticipation of the armistice found the troops in the act of taking up new positions; the Minister of the Army and Carboni, doubting that the British and Americans would keep their undertakings and fearing a violent German reaction, were in favour of rejecting it; Major Marchesi pointed out the serious harm of repudiating the conditions signed on 3 September; Guariglia declared that now more than ever it was essential to “go on to the end.” Badoglio set out the only two courses — the King might publicly repudiate what he had done and dismiss him, or they must accept the conditions whatever the consequences; and the King expressed the view that a change of policy was out of the question and that they must acquiesce. Meanwhile the information service warned that the B.B.C. had broadcast that Italy had asked for an armistice and that Eisenhower had declared that the Allied governments had agreed. It was not possible to delay a moment. The meeting broke up, and Badoglio went at once to the Rome broadcasting station and made the announcement: recognizing the impossibility of continuing the war in face of the overwhelming strength of the enemy, and in order to save the nation from further and even greater disasters, the Italian Government had asked General Eisenhower for an armistice; the request had been acceded to; all hostilities by the Italian armed forces against the British and American forces must cease, though they would repel attacks from whatever quarter they might come. The communiqué was recorded and repeated at frequent intervals, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs arranged to inform Berlin, Budapest, Bucharest and Sofia by telegram.
Aftermath
The armistice had been declared, but the German reaction that the government had so long feared was immediate. Within days the King, Badoglio and the government fled Rome for the Allied lines at Brindisi, leaving the capital — whose defence the plans of early September had been meant to secure — to the Germans, in the flight that forms the subject of Badoglio’s next chapter, “From Rome to Brindisi.” Italy’s passage from the German to the Allied side was complete in form, but the price was the German occupation of the peninsula and a new war, fought on Italian soil, that would last until the liberation of Rome in June 1944.

events/battle-of-france-1940.title: The Battle of France (10 May – 25 June 1940)
events/battle-of-france-1940.content:
The Battle of France (10 May – 25 June 1940)
10 May – 25 June 1940
The German conquest of France in May–June 1940 — the six weeks in which the Wehrmacht broke through the Ardennes and the Meuse, cut off the Allied armies in the north, drove the French army before it in a rout of extraordinary speed, and forced the government to sue for the armistice that surrendered the country. The drôle de guerre (the phoney war) of the winter ended on 10 May with the German offensive against the Low Countries and France; within days the collapse was under way, and by mid-June the capital had fallen and the government had fled. Marc Bloch, writing as a captain of the Intelligence staff of the 1st Army in the weeks immediately after the disaster, called it the étrange défaite (the strange defeat) — an incredible defeat whose fault, the rival recriminations insisted, lay variously with the parliamentary regime, the troops, the English, and every other suspected cause. His testimony, the report of a professional historian set down “en pleine rage” (in a fury), is the most lucid contemporary account of how the French army, which had held the line for four years in the previous war, collapsed in six weeks.
The opening of the offensive
The war in the West had opened in the autumn of 1939, after the German invasion of Poland, and had fallen into a winter of strange inaction — the drôle de guerre, the phoney war, in which the French and British armies sat on the fortified frontier while no great battle was fought. Bloch was mobilised in the autumn of 1939, twenty-one years after he had begun the first war as a sergeant of infantry, and joined the Intelligence staff of the 1st Army. When the German offensive opened on 10 May 1940 against the Netherlands, Belgium and France, it came not where the Allies chiefly expected it — through Belgium, where the French and British advanced to meet it — but through the Ardennes, where the massed panzer divisions broke across the Meuse near Sedan. The Allied plan, which had committed the best of the armies to the Belgian plain, was outflanked before it could be completed, and the German columns, driving for the Channel, cut off the northern armies from the rest of France.
The deposition of a defeated man
Bloch’s account of the collapse, written in the heat of the moment as the “deposition of a defeated man,” records the war from within the shattered command. He saw at first hand the extraordinary slowness of the French command to grasp the nature of the war the Germans were fighting — the war of movement, of massed armour and air power, of decision sought in days rather than in the grinding years of the previous conflict. The high command, in his judgement, was unready; the communications broke down; the confusion and the rout of the units, the collapse of the army as a fighting institution, unfolded before him through May and June. He measured the “strange defeat” against the standards of military history and of the German conduct of war: the enemy had understood that the modern battle was one of speed and of the concentration of force, and the French, with their careful doctrine of the continuous front and the methodical battle, had prepared to fight a war that the Germans had already left behind.
The fall of Paris and the rout
Through June the German advance swept south and west. Paris fell in mid-June, declared an open city as the government abandoned the capital for the provinces, and then for Bordeaux, ahead of the advancing columns. The government of Paul Reynaud gave way to a ministry under the aged Marshal Pétain, the victor of Verdun in the previous war, called to save what could be saved of France; and on the roads the armies and the civilian population fled together in the great exodus of June 1940. Bloch, who had lived the collapse from within the staff and then across the retreating country, records the spectacle with the eyes of the historian: a whole society in flight, an army that had ceased to fight as a coherent institution, and a nation whose leaders had decided that the war could no longer be sustained.
The examination of conscience
The third chapter of Bloch’s report, written with greater distance after the armistice, turns from the army to the nation — the examen de conscience (examination of conscience) of a Frenchman who refuses the facile explanation. In a nation, he insists, no professional body is ever alone responsible. The fault lay, in his judgement, not in the troops — the common people of France, whom he honoured as he had honoured the miners of the Nord and the Pas-de-Calais, the best warriors of 1914–1918 — but in the professional military caste, whose routine and mental timidity had prepared the army for a war it did not fight; in the political class, which had governed without preparing the nation for total war; in the bourgeoisie, with its vieux démon (old demon) of complacency and its attachment to the comfortable past; and in the whole society and its educational system, which had failed to form the citizens and the leaders that the total war demanded. It is a judgment that reaches from the immediate failure of June 1940 into the deepest structures of the Third Republic — the indictment of a regime that, in Bloch’s eyes, had not willed to meet the age of total war.
The end of the battle
By 22 June the French government had accepted the German terms, and the armistice was signed in the forest of Compiègne; on 25 June the fighting ceased, and the battle of France was over. The defeat was total: the German armies occupied the north and the Atlantic coast of France, the government was left at the head of a truncated and disarmed state, and nearly two million French soldiers passed into captivity. Bloch wrote his testimony in the weeks that followed, at Guéret-Fougères in the Creuse, between July and September 1940, that the record of the year might lie hidden until France again saw the freedom of thought and judgment blossom, and the researchers of a future day might profit from “ce procès-verbal de l’an 1940” (this official report of the year 1940). The strange defeat, in his telling, was not a stroke of fate but the judgement of a history — the collapse of a nation and its army that had not understood the war that was being fought against it, and that the armistice, sealing the military catastrophe, left to confront the consequences.

events/battle-of-guadalajara-1937.title: The Battle of Guadalajara, March 1937
events/battle-of-guadalajara-1937.content:
The Battle of Guadalajara, March 1937
8–23 March 1937.
The Third Offensive on Madrid
In March 1937 the Nationalist command made its third and last attempt to close the encirclement of Madrid. After the stalemate of the direct assault in November and the bitter drawn battle on the Jarama in February, Franco conceived, in the words of his historian Aznar, “a plan that is in itself a true technical perfection”: to drop a highly mobile striking mass on the northeast and east of the capital, its axis the highway from Zaragoza toward Guadalajara and Alcalá de Henares, while the battalions fresh from the Jarama forced the Tajuña, broke through in the Arganda zone, and closed the ring hermetically. The honour of the main assault fell — at the Italians’ own insistence — to the Cuerpo de Tropas Voluntarias, the Corpo Truppe Volontarie, the volunteer corps that Italy had sent to the war: four divisions, some 30,000 men, their generals confident after the easy victory at Málaga in February that the same technique would again prevail. Beside them marched the Spanish Division of Soria under General Moscardó.
The Alcarria
The theatre was the high, barren plateau country of Guadalajara province — the alcarria, the region of open mesas cut by deep erosion valleys, “a country of plateaus strongly eroded and of witness-hills,” fragrant with thyme, rosemary and lavender, and bound in winter by enormous mires of clay that made all movement off the roads impossible. Three rivers traverse it — the Henares, the Badiel and the Tajuña — and down the valley of the Henares ran the great carretera de Francia, the magnificent highway from the French frontier through Zaragoza to Madrid. The red army’s defensive system was, Aznar concedes, “the most solid and the best technically disposed that had been produced since the beginning of the war,” directed by the Spanish lieutenant-colonel Vicente Rojo, assisted by the Hungarian Kleber and the German Hans Beimler. Against it, on the road from the north, the offensive was to open on 8 March.
The Advance and the Storm
The secret of the offensive leaked badly — even the frontier papers of France published its details, and Miaja, forewarned, ordered field fortifications thrown up between the Henares and the Tajuña. When the Divisions of Soria and the Italian corps advanced on 8 March, they broke the first defensive system completely; but the weather turned against them. A dense fog covered the horizon, the cold deepened, showers of nearly-frozen rain gave way to an uninterrupted storm of water and hail, the temperature fell several degrees below zero, and the clay of the Alcarria became a morass. The volunteer corps, whose aircraft could not rise from the sodden fields of Soria, found the sky left to the red air force; men and batteries crowded and jammed upon the narrow road; tanks that left the highway were buried in the mud. By the 10th the advance had nonetheless carried some thirty kilometres, and on the 10th the reds occupied Brihuega, their powder magazine blown up in the abandonment, the volunteers entering the still-sleeping streets and pressing a kilometre beyond. Trijueque fell on the 11th. Yet the resistance stiffened daily, the machine-gun and artillery fire thickened, and Moscardó’s conquest of the Jadraque passes on the right flank, for all its brilliance, did not ease the stricken centre.
The Counter-Offensive
The red command, its intelligence intact, had determined to fix its front and pass to the counter-attack. On the night of 11–12 March, under a storm of rain and wind, two International Brigades fell upon Trijueque and retook it; the decision of the battle was to come on the road from Brihuega to Torija and in the wooded grounds of the Palace of Ibarra. The reds, Aznar records, “carried their whole power of penetration to its limits” — but barely had they won two or three local successes than they renounced larger enterprises, content with what served their propaganda. For the volunteers the weather and the strain were overwhelming; the war correspondent of the Soviet and Comintern camp, whose report Aznar quotes, watched “the evident failure of the offensive and the truly appalling weather demoralizing the enemy, a demoralization skilfully reinforced by our propaganda with proclamations and loudspeakers.” The Nationalist tactical circle of Madrid was broken, and though the city’s situation remained precarious, Miaja kept a secondary network of roads by which the capital still communicated, however badly, with the government at Valencia.
The Consequences
Politically and psychologically the disappointment of Guadalajara had a profound international effect. The communist organisations of the world, carried away by an evidently exaggerated propaganda, believed in the victory of the Spanish Popular Front and reinforced their aid and their solidarity; but that same propaganda, in Aznar’s reading, “inflicted a stupid affront on Italy” — and given the psychology of the Duce, it achieved the opposite of its intention, confirming Mussolini’s resolve to support Nationalist Spain to the last day of victory. Tusell groups Guadalajara among those battles — the crossing of the Strait, the defence of Madrid, Franco’s maritime hegemony — that cannot be understood without the foreign aid that the poorly equipped Spanish armies required. The conclusions drawn by every Popular Front in the world about the value of the Italian army were, Aznar maintains, exaggerated, as the rest of the Spanish war would show; “the Italian volunteers fought with a heroism worthy of praise.” The battle taught the Nationalist command a plainer lesson — that against militia masses improved in organization it needed regular troops, officers from the academies, and time to drill and harden them. The road to the north, and to the war’s decisive campaign, now lay open.
