events/battle-of-stalingrad-1942-43.title: The Battle of Stalingrad (19 November 1942 – 2 February 1943)
events/battle-of-stalingrad-1942-43.content:
The Battle of Stalingrad (19 November 1942 – 2 February 1943)
19 November 1942 – 2 February 1943
The battle of Stalingrad was the decisive battle of the Soviet-German front, in which the Red Army, halting the German advance at the walls of the city on the Volga in the autumn of 1942, passed to the counter-offensive on 19 November and, encircling and destroying an enormous picked German army, seized the initiative of the war and began the mass expulsion of the enemy from the Soviet land. In the official account, set down in the orders of the People’s Commissar of Defence and Supreme Commander Stalin, the battle at Stalingrad was the greatest battle in the history of wars — the turning point at which the German-fascist army met its sunset and the Soviet people saw the beginning of their victory. The order of 7 November 1942, on the twenty-fifth anniversary of October, announced the transition of the initiative to the Red Army, and the order of 28 February 1943, on the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Red Army, recorded the destruction of the German forces at Stalingrad and the beginning of the mass expulsion of the enemy.
The summer crisis of 1942
The summer of 1942 had brought the deepest crisis of the war. The order of 7 November 1942 recalled how the Red Army, in the winter period, had beaten off the German attack on Moscow, taken the initiative into its hands and driven the German troops to the west, liberating a whole series of regions of the country. In the summer, however, the position on the front changed for the worse. Taking advantage of the absence of a second front in Europe, the Germans and their allies swept together all their reserves and threw them onto the Soviet front, breaking it at heavy cost and advancing in the south, placing Stalingrad, the Black Sea coast, Grozny and the approaches to the Transcaucasus under threat. The plan of the German command, as the order explained, had been to pass round Moscow from the east, cut it off from the Volga and Ural rear and then strike at the capital; the advance to the south, toward the oil regions, had the auxiliary purpose of drawing off the principal Soviet reserves and weakening the Moscow front. The firmness and courage of the Red Army frustrated the plan for the outflanking of Moscow. The enemy was halted at Stalingrad; but, halted there and already laying down tens of thousands of his soldiers and officers, he threw new divisions into battle, straining his last forces, and the struggle on the Soviet-German front grew ever more intense. On the outcome of this struggle, the order declared, depended the fate of the Soviet state, the freedom and independence of the Motherland.
The enemy halted at Stalingrad
In this decisive moment, the order of 7 November 1942 was addressed to the army and the people on the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Great October Socialist Revolution, celebrated “in the full swing of the cruel struggle against the German-fascist invaders.” The order drew the balance of the first year of the war: the calculations of the German imperialists on the disintegration of the Soviet state had failed completely; socialist industry, the collective-farm order, the friendship of the peoples of the country and the Soviet state itself had shown their firmness and indestructibility, and the whole rear worked selflessly for the needs of the front. The Red Army, bearing the whole weight of the war against Hitler’s Germany and its accomplices, had learned to beat the enemy for certain; the heroic defenders of Moscow and Tula, of Odessa and Sevastopol, of Leningrad and Stalingrad had shown examples of selfless bravery, iron discipline, firmness and the ability to conquer. In the course of the war the Red Army had put out of action over eight million enemy soldiers and officers, and the Hitlerite army, diluted with Rumanians, Hungarians, Italians and Finns, had become far weaker than in the summer and autumn of 1941. The order set the immediate tasks — to defend the line of the front steadfastly, to exhaust the enemy and destroy his men and material, to strengthen iron discipline and unity of command, and to prepare a shattering blow — and closed with the certainty that the day was not far off when the enemy would know the force of new blows of the Red Army. “There will be a holiday on our street as well,” ran the celebrated closing.
The counter-offensive of 19 November
The counter-offensive at Stalingrad opened on 19 November 1942. Three months after the order of 7 November, the order of 28 February 1943 recorded that the troops of the Red Army had begun the offensive on the approaches to Stalingrad, and that since then the initiative of military operations had been in their hands, while the tempo and striking power of the offensives did not slacken. Advancing in the severe conditions of winter along a front of fifteen hundred kilometres, the Red Army attacked almost everywhere with success — at Leningrad, on the Central front, on the approaches to Kharkov, in the Donbas, at Rostov and on the shores of the Azov and Black seas. In three months it liberated from the enemy the territory of the Voronezh and Stalingrad regions, the Chechen-Ingush, North-Ossetian, Kabardino-Balkarian and Kalmyk autonomous republics, the Stavropol and Krasnodar territories, and almost the whole of the Rostov, Kharkov and Kursk regions. “The mass expulsion of the enemy from the Soviet country has begun,” the order declared, and it asked whence such serious failures of the Germans had come and what had changed in these three months — the question answered by the record of the encirclement and destruction of the German forces at Stalingrad.
The destruction of the encircled army
The encirclement and liquidation of the German forces at Stalingrad was the decisive result of the counter-offensive. The order of 28 February 1943 recorded the encircling and liquidation of an enormous picked German army of three hundred and thirty thousand men at Stalingrad, the capture of over three hundred thousand enemy soldiers and officers in the winter campaign, and the destruction of a vast quantity of enemy men and material; only a correct strategy of the command of the Red Army and the flexible tactics of its commanders, the official verdict insisted, could have brought about so outstanding a fact as the encirclement and liquidation of so large an army. The order of 7 November 1943, surveying the completed year, fixed the scale of the battle: the battle of Stalingrad had ended with the encirclement of the three-hundred-thousand-strong German army, its rout and the capture of about a third of the encircled troops; to give an idea of the unprecedented carnage that had played itself out on the fields of Stalingrad, it recorded that at the end of the battle 147,200 killed German soldiers and officers and 46,700 killed Soviet soldiers and officers had been gathered up and buried. “Stalingrad was the sunset of the German-fascist army,” the order concluded; after the Stalingrad massacre, the Germans could no longer recover. By the beginning of February 1943 the liquidation of the encircled army was complete, and the city on the Volga, held through the summer and autumn, had become the symbol of the turning of the war.
The turning of the war
The battle of Stalingrad was the turning point of the Great Patriotic War. From Stalingrad the Red Army never again let the initiative out of its hands; its blows throughout the following summer became ever stronger and its military skill increased with every month. The order of 7 November 1943 fixed the verdict that, from a purely military point of view, the defeat of the German forces by the end of that year had been predetermined by two most important events — the battle of Stalingrad and the battle of Kursk. The attempt of the Hitlerite command to take revenge for Stalingrad by a counter-offensive in the region of Kharkov, designed to arrange a “German Stalingrad” for the Soviet troops, failed; and the winter campaign of 1942–1943 showed that the offensive power of the Red Army had grown. In the official account the battle at the walls of the Volga city stood as the greatest battle in the history of wars — the battle in which the German-fascist army, halted, encircled and destroyed, met its sunset and in which the Soviet people first saw the coming victory of their just war.
Sources

events/battle-of-teruel-1937-38.title: The Battle of Teruel, 1937–1938
events/battle-of-teruel-1937-38.content:
The Battle of Teruel, 1937–1938
15 December 1937 – 22 February 1938.
The Offensive in the Snow
In mid-December 1937, with the northern front at last extinguished and observers beginning to think the war nearly over, the Republican army struck in Aragón. The objective was Teruel, the provincial capital thrust forward like a bastion into the red-held east, and the offensive was thrown in as a diversion to break the threatened Nationalist drive — that “permanent temptation to the imagination of the Generalísimo,” as Aznar puts it — toward the Mediterranean and the division of the red zone. The city was encircled, its communications with Zaragoza severed on 15 December, and the ring closed. What followed was a battle fought in the depths of an appalling winter. On 1 January 1938 the snow covered and immobilised the Nationalist guns and columns on the heights north and northeast of the city; the men, wrapped in blankets, could not take a step nor drag their machine-guns; the airmen flew at thirty and forty degrees below zero, forever alert against the ice forming on their wings. A foreign correspondent, Pariset, wrote of the “enormous white necropolis” of the plain, half a metre of snow over the fallen: “In this polar landscape, men and machines are so many columns of ice.”
The Fall of the City
The garrison, commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Rey D’Harcourt, held out within the city while the Nationalist relief columns of Varela and Aranda fought toward it through the blizzard. But the siege was hopeless. Mines exploded unceasingly beneath the last redoubt, the dead lay unburied and the hundreds of wounded cried out unattended; Rey D’Harcourt, who had lost all capacity for command and organization, and who persuaded himself that for the first time in the war the offensive power of Franco had met a defence it could not break, opened negotiations. The hospital and the convent of the Clarisas had burned with their defenders; in the Seminary, where an armistice had been pledged for the evacuation of women, children and the wounded, the red vanguards poured in as soon as the fire ceased and took the garrison prisoner. On the surrender of the Military Command, the red command was able, for the first time since 18 July 1936, to announce to the world that its troops had taken a provincial capital — Teruel. For the first time, also, a Nationalist force had surrendered, against the orders of resistance its chief had received from the Caudillo.
The Battle of the Alfambra
The loss of the city was not accepted. Through January the Nationalists, their heads at Zaragoza, regrouped for a decisive reconquest, and the blow fell not on Teruel itself but on the red positions to the north, on the far bank of the Alfambra. On 5 February 1938 Franco launched the great manoeuvre that Aznar calls a model of the military art: a force fixed the enemy in the centre, before Villarquemado and Singra, while two converging wings struck out — on the left the Moroccan corps of General Yagüe toward Portalrubio and Perales, on the right the Galician corps of General Aranda toward Celadas and Alfambra; once the rupture was achieved, a mass of cavalry under General Monasterio was to irrupt through the gap toward Lidón and Visiedo. Surprise was half lost when four deserters of the San Quintín regiment gave the reds full knowledge of the plan, but the massed artillery of the whole force — including nearly all the batteries of the Italian corps — and the iron discipline of the assault divisions carried the day. In the first day’s fighting the Navarrese divisions broke the front, took Pancrudo and Corbatón, and the Galician divisions pierced the enemy line at the Lustal vertex; the wings swung and the red Army of the East was caught in the open.
The Reconquest
The Alfambra battle was one of the great disasters of the red army in the war. Sixteen divisions were shattered; the retreating masses, in the words of a red correspondent Aznar quotes, poured back “as on the road from Málaga to Almería.” Turning south, the Nationalists struck for Teruel itself, and on 22 February the city fell once more into national hands, the red garrison of Carabineros and of “El Campesino’s” division abandoning it. Franco himself stood in the first line of the advance, reaching the edge of the recaptured cemetery. Aznar’s tally of the red losses — some 17,000 prisoners, 14,000 dead, 20,000 wounded and sick, over 50,000 casualties in all, approaching half the mass of manoeuvre — is a Nationalist reckoning, but the strategic scale of the defeat was real: twenty batteries, a hundred aircraft, forty tanks, 1,600 square kilometres of territory and fifty villages passed to Franco, and the government of Barcelona lost the mass of manoeuvre of the Levante. The Times of London, in a comment Aznar reproduces, summed it up on 23 February: “the battle of sixty days around Teruel has ended in an overwhelming defeat of the republican army.”
The Prolongation
Teruel, however, was not the end. Tusell reads the battle in the larger frame of the war’s strange prolongation: everything, after the fall of the north, seemed to favour Franco — the rebel material and military superiority on land, the Soviet supplies hindered by Italian submarines and by the fall of Blum’s government in France, the republican fleet acting strictly on the defensive after the loss of the Jaime I — yet the fighting was dragged out. The German ambassador twice wrote to Hitler that the Spanish conflict had no military solution, and at Teruel and later at the Ebro the Popular Army, thrown back and reconstructed, went on fighting. Teruel closed the first chapter of 1938, the winter battle won in the snow; the spring would bring the great offensive that carried the Nationalist armies at last to the Mediterranean.

events/battle-of-the-ebro-1938.title: The Battle of the Ebro (25 July – 16 November 1938)
events/battle-of-the-ebro-1938.content:
The Battle of the Ebro (25 July – 16 November 1938)
25 July – 16 November 1938
The last great offensive of the Republican army of the Spanish Civil War, in which the newly rebuilt Popular Army crossed the lower Ebro in strength and, for nearly four months, fought the Nationalist forces of the Generalísimo to a standstill on a front that swallowed both armies’ reserves. The Red strategic diversion against the Nationalist drive on the Mediterranean, opened on 25 July 1938 and closed on 16 November when the last Republican troops recrossed the river, was the most prolonged and destructive single battle of the war — the effort that revived the desire to resist in the republican zone and, at the same time, exhausted the army that was to collapse with it in Catalonia.
The diversion on the Ebro
The battle arose out of the crisis of the spring of 1938, when the Nationalist offensive through Aragon had split the republican zone in two and driven toward the sea. While the National operation pressed on toward Sagunto and Segorbe, the republican command prepared a counterstroke. Aznar’s military history renders the Red plan through the Orden general de operaciones número 2 — the general order of operations by which the republican high command set in motion the great crossing of the Ebro. The design was a strategic diversion, an offensive thrown across the lower river to cut the Nationalist communications and force the Generalísimo to weaken the drive toward the Mediterranean and the capital of Valencia. It was the republican answer to a moment when, to any observer, the war seemed all but decided against the Republic.
The instrument of the offensive was the rebuilt Army of the Ebro. In the months of the Maestrazgo campaign the Popular Army, which had seemed near disintegration after the Aragon disaster, had reconstructed its organisation and its effectives. Tusell stresses how much this reconstitution owed to the new intakes that had filled the ranks — seventeen quintas, the conscript levies, against Franco’s twelve, drawing on the eighteen-year-olds of the so-called quinta del biberón, the “bottle-fed levy,” and reaching back to reservists past forty. The Army of the Ebro was rebuilt on strict discipline, and a discipline that was necessarily political: as Manuel Azaña observed, with the emphasis of a man who watched his own side with despair, «casi todo el Ejército del Ebro es comunista» — nearly the whole Army of the Ebro is communist — the command of Modesto and the temper of the units reflecting it. It was this force, hardened in the reconstruction, that threw itself across the river in the last days of July.
The crossing and the two armies
On the night of 24–25 July 1938 the Army of the Ebro forced the river at several points, taking the Nationalist defenders by surprise and establishing bridgeheads on the south bank. The crossing, conducted with an audacity and organization that surprised even the victors’ chronicler, carried the battle onto the far bank and, for a time, threatened the Nationalist rear. The opening weeks belonged to the offensive: the republican troops drove inland, seeking to break through toward Gandesa and to sever the communications on which the southern campaign depended.
Franco’s response, by Aznar’s account, was to meet the diversion with the full weight of the Nationalist army, abandoning nothing of the strategic plan. The battle of the Ebro became a war of attrition fought over a narrow strip of the river country, the great crossing followed by the phases of desgaste — the wearing-down — that Aznar’s seventh chapter of Tomo III narrates as the third and fourth phases of the battle: the systematic grinding of the republican bridgeheads under artillery and air power, and then the Nationalist counteroffensive that drove the exhausted defenders back toward the water. As the summer turned to autumn the battle resolved itself into a long, terrible siege in the open, fought on ground that neither side could abandon.
The decision at the river
Through the autumn the battle consumed the reserves of both armies. In the course of the fighting, Tusell records, the German ambassador wrote twice to Hitler that the Spanish conflict had no military solution — a judgment delivered in the very months when the Ebro was bleeding both sides — while the two armies, and above all the republican one, paid for the struggle in irreplaceable men and material. The Nationalist air and artillery superiority, and the inexhaustible capacity of the Generalísimo’s army to feed the battle, slowly turned the balance. The counteroffensive of the autumn, pressed forward step by step, recovered the ground the river had yielded; the republican bridgeheads contracted; and on 16 November 1938 the last troops of the Army of the Ebro recrossed the river, ending the great battle in the position from which it had begun.
The strategic diversion had failed in its object. The drive on the Mediterranean was resumed and completed; but the cost, measured against the end it served, was the destruction of the army that had made the crossing. The Battle of the Ebro showed the Republican state at its most stubborn — the reconstituted army revived the will to resist at a moment when the war seemed lost — and left that army so spent that the collapse of Catalonia, when it came two months later, found it without the strength to fight again. The modest offensive that, in Tusell’s judgement, had shown its “inconsistency” while reviving the desire to resist, had consumed the last great instrument of the Republic.

events/beer-hall-putsch-1923.title: The Beer Hall Putsch (8–9 November 1923)
events/beer-hall-putsch-1923.content:
The Beer Hall Putsch (8–9 November 1923)
8–9 November 1923
The attempt by hitler and the völkisch war-leagues of Bavaria to seize power in Munich and march on Berlin — the shot fired in the Bürgerbräukeller, the forced capitulation of the Bavarian triumvirate, the collapse of the march on the Feldherrnhalle under police fire, and Hitler’s flight. The failure broke the movement in the short run and made Hitler a national figure in the longer; in the fortress at Landsberg he wrote Mein Kampf, the settlement of accounts (Abrechnung) that the future would measure against the event.
Bavaria on the edge
The putsch grew out of the ruin of 1923. The occupation of the Ruhr had bankrupted the Reich, the currency was collapsing, and the republic seemed to be dissolving from within. In September the Reich government under Stresemann abandoned the passive resistance of the Ruhr war, a surrender the nationalist Right refused to forgive. In Bavaria the struggle was cast not as rebellion against the Reich but as the defence of the state against Marxism — the old war against the “inner enemy.” The militant leagues had come together at Nuremberg on 2 September, the anniversary of Sedan, in a loose cartel, the Kampfbund (battle league), over which the aged field marshal ludendorff presided while Hitler stood darkly beside him. On 25 September the leaders of the league met in Munich and, after Hitler spoke to them for two and a half hours, elected him political leader of the whole armed following — yesterday the orator of a noise-party, in Heiden’s phrase, today master of the strongest armed force in Bavaria.
The Bavarian government, fearing exactly this, had already answered. On 26 September it declared a state of emergency and set a dictator over the land, the Generalstaatskommissar (state commissioner-general), the former prime minister Gustav von Kahr. Kahr’s brief was to absorb the patriotic excitement and, if need be, to meet Hitler with force. The Reichswehr in Bavaria stood under General von Lossow, a cautious soldier who would march only when the odds were clearly with him; cornered by the league leaders, Lossow cried out the word that Heiden records as the moment’s signature — “I want to march, good God, I want to march, but only if I have a fifty-one percent probability.” Hitler, meanwhile, had broken with the Reichswehr over the autumn, and was casting about for some stroke before the winter closed in.
The coup in the Bürgerbräukeller
The stroke came on the evening of 8 November. Kahr had been persuaded to address a large patriotic meeting in the Bürgerbräukeller (citizen brewery cellar), a hall of some three thousand seats in an eastern suburb of Munich. Hitler, deciding on a sudden improvisation, drew his best long coat from the wardrobe, pinned on his Iron Cross, and drove through the city toward the hall, turning in the car to the astonished Anton Drexler with the words, “Toni, can you keep silence? We are not driving to Freising today. At half past eight I strike.” His storm troopers, the Stoßtrupp Hitler (shock troop Hitler), surrounded the brewery and posted machine guns; when Hitler burst into the packed hall, pistol in hand, and fired a shot at the ceiling, he looked to one witness like a man entirely beside himself. He sprang on a chair, shouted that the nationale Revolution (national revolution) had broken out, that the hall was surrounded by six hundred armed men, that no one might leave, and that the barracks of the Reichswehr and the state police were already in their hands — a claim that was false.
Under an escort he carried Kahr, Lossow and the police chief Colonel von Seißer into a side room and there forced on them the shape of the new government: a Bavarian regency under Kahr, Pöhner as minister-president with dictatorial powers, Ludendorff at the head of the national army, Lossow as Reichswehr minister, Seißer as police minister, and himself as the political leader of the provisional national government. “Reich government Hitler, national army Ludendorff,” he thrust out; the “drummer” had thrown off the mask. To break their resistance he raised the pistol and spoke of four shots — three for his staff if they deserted him, the last for himself — and promised that if he was not victorious by the next afternoon he would be a dead man. Kahr answered with the only dignity in the room: Hitler could have him shot, but no bullet would force a political decision from him. In the hall Hitler, returning to the crowd, announced that the three men had agreed, and the assembly, released from its alarm, broke into jubilation. Kahr, Lossow and Seißer, released on their word, slipped away as soon as they could and set about undoing the whole business.
The march and the collapse
Through the night Hitler’s following grew — from the few hundred of the evening to several thousand by morning, far stronger at the decisive point than the forces of the state. What the Kampfbund lacked was not numbers but, as Heiden puts it, twenty-four costly hours: the barracks, the railway stations, the telegraph offices had never been seized. In the early hours the triumvirate recovered itself, rallied the Reichswehr in the infantry barracks, and repudiated the forced agreements; Lossow’s officers swore to defend their garrisons to the last cartridge. On the morning of 9 November Hitler and Ludendorff resolved on the old gesture — a march through the centre of Munich to the Feldherrnhalle (hall of the commanders), in the hope of carrying the city and the army with them. The columns moved up from the Bürgerbräu, the swastika banners to the fore, Ludendorff in his general’s greatcoat at the head of the second rank. At the closed line of state police across the Odeonsplatz the marchers pressed on; a volley rang out; Hitler, his arm linked with a fallen comrade — the Blutzeuge (blood witness) who died that day, in the movement’s later canon — went down with a dislocated shoulder, and the column dissolved. Some threw themselves flat, some ran. Hitler was carried away in the confusion and driven off, the first figure of the collapse, while the army and police swept up the prisoners. The Feldherrnhalle, scene of the morning’s disaster, would become the holy place of the Nazi martyrs’ cult.
The trial and the fortress
The failure of the march ended the putsch, but not its consequences. Hitler was arrested, tried before a sympathetic Munich court early in 1924, and used the dock as a platform, turning a prosecution for high treason into a national advertisement for himself and the movement. Ludendorff, acquitted on his own plea, began the separation from Hitler that the two men would never fully repair. Hitler himself was condemned to a short term in the fortress of Landsberg, where he served only months of it. It was behind those “comfortable walls,” as Heiden calls them, that he dictated the first volume of Mein Kampf to his secretary Rudolf Hess — at once a settlement of accounts with the age and a programme for seizing it, fixing in the party’s foundational text the doctrine of the völkisch state, the Führer principle and the demand for Lebensraum in the East. From the ruins of the putsch Hitler drew a tactical conclusion that the next decade would vindicate: power was not to be stormed but awaited, through the state and the ballot. The movement dissolved, then was refounded; the “seven years on the magic mountain” began.
Sources

















SourceTreatmentheiden-adolf-hitler-1936The principal contemporary account of the putsch (chapters 9–10): the Bavarian crisis, Kahr as General State Commissioner, the coup in the Bürgerbräukeller, the collapse of the march on the Feldherrnhalle, Hitler’s flight, the trial, Landsberg and the writing of Mein Kampf.hitler-mein-kampf-1925-26Hitler’s own retrospective: the book dictated at Landsberg after the failure, the autobiographical “settlement of accounts,” and the doctrinal core of race, the Führer principle and Eastern policy.

events/berlin-olympics-1936.title: Berlin Olympics, 1936
events/berlin-olympics-1936.content:
Berlin Olympics, 1936
1–16 August 1936.
The Games and the State
In the summer of 1936 the eyes of the world turned upon Berlin. From 1 to 16 August the German capital was the seat of the eleventh Olympic Games, the largest gathering of nations and athletes the modern festival had yet seen, and the regime made the occasion the great public display of its first Olympiad in power. The Olympic flame, the stadium, the floodlit ceremonies and the ordered thousands of spectators were not merely the setting of a sporting contest; the National Socialist state presented them as the evidence of its order, its peace, and its recovered place among the powers. The official documentary record of the year, compiled by Axel Friedrichs for the Dokumente der deutschen Politik, numbers the Games among the defining events of 1936 — set beside the remilitarization of the Rhineland and the launch of the Four Year Plan — and treats them as a demonstration to the foreign visitor of the new Germany.
The Games came to Berlin at the height of the regime’s international rehabilitation. Barely five months earlier the Reich had remilitarized the Rhineland; in the same year it was to sign the Anti-Comintern Pact with Japan and proclaim the second Four Year Plan. The Olympic festival allowed the regime to present the face it chose for the world: an orderly, hospitable, athletic nation, at peace and eager to receive its guests. The stadium built for the occasion, on the model of the ancient Greek festival grounds, gave monumental form to the claim, and the ceremonial of the opening and closing days — the procession of the nations, the flags, the greeting of the host — cast the Reich as the peaceful and accomplished centre of the international community.
The Sportpalast of the Nations
The Games were, in the regime’s handling, an act of the state as much as of sport. The celebrations of the year had already given the Reich its calendar of public spectacle — the National Day of the German People called by Goebbels in April, the party congress at Nuremberg in September — and the Olympics took their place in this sequence of controlled and choreographed national festivals. The athletes who competed under the German banner were the agents of a state that identified physical prowess with national strength, and the victories won in the Berlin stadium were recorded in the official account as triumphs of the German people. The world’s acceptance of the invitation, the arrival of the delegations of the powers, and the reports that carried the Games to every country were themselves read by the regime as the acknowledgment of its place among the nations.
The same summer saw the regime’s domestic measures proceed alongside the festival: Himmler had been appointed Chef der deutschen Polizei (chief of the German police) in June, and the law amending the Defence Law on the active military service of Jews was enacted at the end of June, weeks before the opening of the Games. The state that received the world was thus the state that had already legislated the exclusion of the Jew from its army and was completing the apparatus of the police state. The two faces of the regime — the festival of the nations and the consolidation of the racial and police order — ran together through the summer of 1936, and the Games served the one even as the other advanced.
The Festival and Its Meaning
The Olympics of 1936 were, in the German record, an act of peace — the Führer’s peace plan of March had offered the powers a new European security, and the Games were the visible proof of Germany’s good faith and peaceful intentions. The official volume gives the festival this place in the narrative of the year: Germany, having recovered its sovereignty and demanded its equality, stood ready to take its seat among the great powers of the world in a spirit of sport and concord. The foreign guests who thronged Berlin carried home with them the image the regime had designed, and the international acceptance of the Games lent to the Reich a legitimacy that no treaty and no negotiation could have conferred.
Yet the festival was inseparable from the state that staged it. The same weeks in which the world’s athletes ran and leapt in the new stadium saw the Reich’s leaders set in motion the economic and military reordering of the German people — the Four Year Plan was proclaimed in October, within two months of the closing ceremonies, and the machinery of rearmament was already running at full speed. The Games stood to the rearmament as the smiling face of the same body: the one opened the gates of the world to the Reich, the other prepared the Reich for the war the world did not yet see coming. In the German record of 1936 the Olympic summer is remembered as the moment when the Third Reich, having seized its sovereignty in the Rhineland, displayed to the world the order, strength and peace it claimed to embody.
Sources

events/biennio-rosso-1919-20.title: The Red Biennium (1919–1920)
events/biennio-rosso-1919-20.content:
The Red Biennium (1919–1920)
1919–1920
In the two years after the war Italy was swept by the greatest wave of labour unrest in its history — the biennio rosso (the red biennium). Strikes spread from factory to factory, the peasants of the Po valley rose against their landlords, and in the autumn of 1920 the metalworkers of the north occupied the great factories of Milan and Turin and held them for weeks under the red flag. The revolution that the workers proclaimed in their own ranks never came; the paralysis of the state that it revealed, and the reaction it provoked, gave the Fasci their opportunity and their mission. The Fascist chroniclers called the period the “red insurrection” — the proof of what awaited Italy if the liberal order failed.
The wave of strikes
The movement had been gathering since the end of the war. Prices rose, the soldiers returned to find no work, and the unions, swollen with confidence after the Russian revolution, pressed their advantage. Businelli, in the chapter he calls “the tragic year of recovery,” lists the strikes and the “red wave” that broke over the country in 1919 and 1920. Farinacci, opening his account of the red insurrection, calls it “a revolt without ideas and without leaders” — strikes economic and revolutionary, tumults in the cities, the episode of Cremona, the incidents of Trieste, the agrarian riots in the countryside. In the provinces the peasants demanded the land, and the hunt for the landowner’s agent and the blackleg became a regular feature of the Po valley. The state seemed to look on powerless: the ministries of Nitti and then Giolitti, in the Fascist telling, surrendered to the pressure rather than govern. Nitti’s government fell amid the anarchy; Giolitti returned with his policy of conciliation, waiting for the storm to break of itself.
The occupation of the factories
The crisis came to a head in September 1920. The metalworkers, organised in the FIOM, fought the lockout of the factories and turned it into an occupation: in Milan, Turin and the industrial cities the workers took possession of the great plants and ran them under the red flag, printing revolutionary proclamations and hoisting barricades. Farinacci’s chapter on the occupation is the centre of his whole account — the agitation of the metalworkers, obstructionism and lockout, the “attempted blackmail of the Government,” the closing of the Romeo works, and then the occupation itself, with its “tragicomic episodes” and the technical incapacity of a workers’ management that could not make the factories run. For a few weeks it seemed that Italy might follow Russia. But the workers, led by the Socialists who themselves feared the revolution, hesitated; Giolitti, instead of ordering the army to fire, let the occupation run its course and then mediated, securing a wage rise and the workers’ evacuation in exchange for the promise of factory councils. Farinacci calls the settlement the “false mirage of Moscow” and an “expedient for dictatorship” — the state, he wrote, had abdicated. Volpe records the same episode as the reaction against the occupation of the factories, the moment that turned the middle classes and the ex-servicemen against the red movement for good.
The turn of the tide
The occupation ended in stalemate, not revolution, and the failure broke the red movement’s spell. The Fasci, founded the year before, seized the moment. Businelli places in this same chapter the “Fascist reaction” and the “second adunata of the Fasci”; Farinacci’s second part, “the victory of the Fasci,” narrates the riscossa — the resurgence — that followed the autumn of 1920: the first nuclei of squadrist reaction, the rising of Trieste, the “bulwark of Italianness” against Slavs and Socialists, the devastation of the Lavoratore, the punitive expeditions, and above all the establishment of Fascism in the agricultural provinces of the Po valley. The chronicles linger on the blood of the transition — the massacre of Molinella, the episode of Palazzo d’Accursio at Bologna in November, where a bomb thrown into the Fascist ranks gave the excuse for the “surgical” violence of the squadre. Meanwhile the Socialist movement tore itself apart: at the congress of Livorno in January 1921 the maximalists, reformists and the new Communists quarrelled over adherence to Moscow, and the party split, the Communist Party of Italy breaking off — a division Farinacci treats as the self-destruction of the red cause.
By the spring of 1921 the reaction had become a general counter-offensive. The Fasci multiplied; the squadre d’azione carried their punitive expeditions across the provinces; and when Giolitti dissolved the Chamber and called elections in May 1921, the Fascists entered the lists with him in the National Blocs. The red biennium was over. The strikes had exhausted themselves, the factories had returned to their owners, and the state, having failed to master the anarchy, had handed the initiative to the movement that promised to restore order by force. The two years that began with the red flag over the factories ended with the blackshirts masters of the road.

events/blomberg-fritsch-crisis-1938.title: Blomberg–Fritsch Crisis, 1938
events/blomberg-fritsch-crisis-1938.content:
Blomberg–Fritsch Crisis, 1938
26 January – 4 February 1938.
The Fall of the Commanders
In the last week of January 1938 the two men at the head of the German armed forces fell. Field Marshal Werner von Blomberg, the Reich War Minister and Commander-in-Chief of the Wehrmacht, and General Werner von Fritsch, the Commander-in-Chief of the Army, were removed from their posts in the course of a few days, and with them fell the last barrier between the Führer and the personal command of the German military machine. The crisis that bore their names brought about, within a single week, a reconstruction of the entire high command and a reshuffle of the foreign ministry that concentrated in Hitler’s hands the direction of both the army and the foreign policy of the Reich. The official documentary record of 1938, compiled by Hans Volz for the Dokumente der deutschen Politik, records the event in the documents of 4 February — the decree establishing a Secret Cabinet Council, the Führer’s letter of thanks to the dismissed Foreign Minister Freiherr von Neurath, and the announcement of Joachim von Ribbentrop’s appointment as Reich Foreign Minister.
The occasion of the crisis, in the public German record, was a personal scandal. Blomberg, a widower, married a young woman early in January; when the marriage proved, in the eyes of the regime, incompatible with the honour of the War Minister, he was compelled to resign. Fritsch, whose fall followed within days, was charged with a moral offence, a charge that the official documents do not elaborate but that brought down the commander of the army as swiftly as the scandal had brought down the War Minister. In the account the regime published, the two commanders went because their persons were no longer acceptable to the standards the state required of the leaders of the Wehrmacht. Behind this surface, however, the crisis removed at a stroke the military men who still stood between Hitler and the command of the army, and cleared the path for the aggressive policy that the year was to unfold.
The Reconstruction of 4 February
On 4 February 1938 the new order was proclaimed. The high command was reorganized and Hitler himself took over the supreme command of the Wehrmacht, uniting in his own person the functions that Blomberg had held and making the armed forces directly subordinate to him. The generals who were thought loyal to the old army leadership were displaced; the offices of the supreme command were refashioned so that there was no longer any commander above the Führer but himself. At the same time the foreign ministry was delivered to Ribbentrop, whose long mission to London and whose advocacy of an alliance with the revisionist powers had made him the natural instrument of the new policy. Neurath, the last of the old conservative diplomats, was thanked and retired, and the German ambassadors in London, Rome, Tokyo and Vienna were recalled — a gesture that announced to the world that German foreign policy was being made anew.
The documents of 4 February that Volz reproduces give the shape of the reconstruction. The creation of a Secret Cabinet Council appeared to assemble a body of advisers around the Führer, but its real effect was to remove the old channels of military and diplomatic counsel and to leave Hitler, with Ribbentrop and the new high command, in sole control. The letter to Neurath was courteous and grateful; the announcement of Ribbentrop’s appointment was formal and final. Together the three documents record a coup within the state — bloodless, conducted by decree, and complete — by which the Führer gathered into his own hands the two instruments, the army and the foreign office, with which he was to make the annexations of the year.
The Concentration of Power
The crisis was the decisive event of the opening of 1938, and it defined the character of the year that followed. Within six weeks of the reconstruction of the command, German troops marched into Austria; within nine months the Sudetenland was ceded at Munich. The removal of Blomberg and Fritsch was the removal of the last serious voices of caution in the German military leadership — the men who had still conceived of the army as an instrument of the state rather than of the Führer’s will. In their place Hitler placed commanders who owed their positions to him alone, and the Wehrmacht, which had sworn its oath to him in 1934, was bound to him now by a chain of command that had no other summit.
The year 1938 was thus, in the German official record, the year in which the Führer-state completed its hold on the machinery of war. Volz’s volume opens with the crisis and closes with the Sudetenland; the two are the frame of the same story. The reconstruction of 4 February made the German state one in which the army, the foreign ministry and the party were all the instruments of a single will, and it was this concentrated power that carried out the reunion of the German lands. The Blomberg–Fritsch crisis, in the record the regime published, appears not as a scandal but as a necessary reordering — the fitting of the Wehrmacht and the diplomatic service to the leadership that was to lead the German people to its greatest territorial expansion since the foundation of the Reich.

events/cartel-des-gauches-1924.title: The Cartel des Gauches (May 1924 – April 1925)
events/cartel-des-gauches-1924.content:
The Cartel des Gauches (May 1924 – April 1925)
May 1924 – April 1925
The electoral victory and government of the Left Cartel (Cartel des Gauches) in 1924 — the alliance of the Radical and Socialist parties that swept the parliamentary election of May 1924, drove out the majority of the Bloc National, and brought a Radical ministry under Édouard Herriot to power in the name of the “republican defence” of the regime against its nationalist and clerical opponents. For the Third Republic, Zévaès’s committed history records, the elections of 1924 and the Cartel government that followed marked the decisive turn of the postwar years — the moment when the Republic, which had governed through the war and its nationalist aftermath, swung back toward the Left, before the financial crisis of 1925 broke the coalition apart.
The balance after the war
The Cartel des Gauches must be understood against the majority it displaced. In the election of November 1919 the Bloc National — the wartime and postwar coalition of the nationalist and moderate Right — had carried the Chamber. The socialist historian Zévaès, and the electoral geographer Siegfried alike, saw in that result the governing mood of the immediate aftermath of the war. In 1919, Siegfried observed, the recent image of war impressed the country less than the menacing shadow of bolshevism that terrified the bourgeois; there was a resentment of the combatants against the deputies, an antiparliamentary effluvia in the air more insistent than at any time since Boulangism or the Panama affair, and a feeling that the political militant had lost prestige to the technician — the creation of the war who, under the name of expert, was to reappear in innumerable international conferences. The Left, which stood for the worker, the deputy and the militant, suffered by solidarity, and the Right’s slogan taunted it with the war itself: “La guerre ne vous a donc rien appris?” (Has the war then taught you nothing?).
The Bloc National Chamber of 1919–1924 sat with 617 deputies — the Left reduced to 180 (68 socialists, 24 socialist republicans, 88 radical-Socialists), the Centre to 216, and the Right holding 221 (185 progressists and 36 independents). The union of the wartime majority had given the nationalist and conservative parties the largest bloc, and for four years they governed the Republic.
The making of the Cartel
Against this majority the Left gathered itself. The Cartel des Gauches (Left Cartel) was the electoral and parliamentary alliance that united the Radical and Radical-Socialist party with the Socialists (the SFIO) and the smaller groups of the republican Left — a combination of the two great families of the French Left, which in Siegfried’s analysis rested on the permanent tension of the French political temper. For the old parliamentary republic, Siegfried argued, the Frenchman was politically on the left but socially conservative: “son cœur est à gauche, mais sa poche est à droite” (his heart is on the left, but his pocket is on the right). Every Frenchman, he said, has a pocket, so that a deferred prudence, his interest, comes sooner or later to contradict the extremist ideology in which he delights; the Don Quixote of the Left is always accompanied by a Sancho Panza. The Cartel — the alliance of the Socialists with the Radicals of the republican middle — was the practical expression of this republican coalition of the heart and the pocket, of the working-class party and the party of the small proprietors of the country.
The Cartel stood, in the idiom of the Third Republic, for the défense républicaine (republican defence) — the defence of the secular, parliamentary Republic against the nationalism and clericalism of the postwar majority. Its programme was one of the old battles of the regime: the enforcement of laicism, the restoration of the Chamber’s authority, and the rectification of the financial policy of the Bloc National. Zévaès, whose history moves in these same terms, treats the campaign of 1924 as the republican Left’s recovery of the initiative it had lost in 1919 — the return of the working-class and radical alliance to the centre of the parliamentary stage.
The election of May 1924
In the election of 11 May 1924 the Cartel des Gauches won a decisive victory. The new Chamber of 1924–1928 seated 582 deputies, and the balance of the parties was reversed. The Left now held 328: 105 united socialists, 42 socialist republicans, 140 radical-Socialists and 41 of the radical Left; the Centre was reduced to 80; the Right to 146 (104 of the democratic republican Union, 14 democrats, 28 independents); and 28 Communists sat at the extreme Left, outside the Cartel. The majority that had governed since the war was turned out, and the Republic had passed, in a single electoral stroke, from the union of the nationalist Right to the union of the republican Left.
The formation of the government fell to the leader of the Radical-Socialist party, Édouard Herriot. Herriot’s ministry, formed in June 1924, drew its strength from the Cartel’s parliamentary coalition and its programme from the republican defence that the election had vindicated. The Radical premier embodied the marriage of the two Lefts that the Cartel represented — a man of the party of the small proprietors and of the secular school, governing with the support of the Socialist party that for the first time in its postwar history stood behind a Radical-led majority.
The fall of the Cartel
The Cartel government proved short-lived, and its undoing was the great theme of the old Republic: the question of money. In April 1925 the Herriot ministry fell, broken by the financial crisis that the postwar deficits and the flight of capital had brought to a head — the moment when, as the conservative-radical reaction of the later decade was to show, the pocket of the Frenchman reasserted itself over his heart. The parliamentary arithmetic of the Cartel had already proved fragile: in June 1924 the Chamber had overthrown the last ministry of the Bloc National, the cabinet of François-Marsal, by a vote of 327 to 217; and in April 1925, on the financial question, the coalition that had carried Herriot to power divided against him. Zévaès, closing his history in the very season of the failure, records the election and the government as the last great event of the Republic’s postwar story — the Left’s victory that raised the secular and parliamentary France of the old parties to power once more, only to founder on the same economic forces that the financial stabilisation of the later 1920s would turn to the advantage of the Centre and the Right.
The fall of the Cartel in April 1925 did not destroy the alliance, but it ended its governing hour. The Republic would pass, in Siegfried’s cycle of the parties, into the regime of Poincaré and the conservative-radical cabinets of the later decade — the sequel that revealed, in the balance of the French parties, the permanent oscillation between the leftward heart and the conservative pocket that the Cartel had for a single year brought together.

events/collectivization-of-agriculture.title: The Collectivisation of Agriculture (1929–1934)
events/collectivization-of-agriculture.content:
The Collectivisation of Agriculture (1929–1934)
1929–1934
The collectivisation of agriculture was the campaign by which the Communist Party and the Soviet government brought the scattered individual holdings of the village into collective farms — the колхоз (kolkhoz) — uniting the land, the livestock and the implements of the peasants in the common economy of the producers. It was the sequel to the socialist industrialisation of the Five-Year Plans, and it rested on the decision, proclaimed by the party in 1929, to abandon the earlier policy of restricting the kulaks and to pass to the liquidation of the kulaks as a class (раскулачивание). Carried through in the years 1929–1934, the campaign transformed the countryside: whole villages and districts entered the kolkhozes, the tractors of the machine-tractor stations came to the fields, and the socialist system of agriculture was established alongside the socialist industry of the towns. The party’s own account of these years — the Short Course of party history, the biography of Stalin and the school textbook of Shestakov — presents the collectivisation as a necessary and victorious stage of the construction of socialism, undertaken against the resistance of the kulak and of the oppositionists who had defended him.
The course of the Fifteenth Congress
The Fifteenth Congress of the party, meeting in December 1927, had adopted the course on the collectivisation of agriculture. Socialist industrialisation had advanced, but agriculture lagged behind: the small, scattered individual holdings could not supply the growing towns and industrial centres, and the kulak — the prosperous peasant who hired labour and held back the surplus grain — stood in the way of the socialist supply of the country. The congress resolved on the all-round extension of the collectivisation of agriculture and laid down a plan for the expansion and strengthening of the network of kolkhozes and совхозов (state farms). The growth of socialist industry, which had begun the mass production of tractors and machines for agriculture, supplied the material base; the decisive struggle against the kulaks during the grain-collection campaigns of 1928 and 1929, the growth of agricultural co-operation, and the good experience of the first kolkhozes and sovkhozes together prepared the transition to the collective economy. The peasants, broken into petty and scattered individual holdings, without tolerable implements and draught power, and ground down by poverty and isolation, found in the union of the small farms into collectives, in the tractor and in the help of the state, the road to a better life and the liberation from the kulak yoke.
The turn to the liquidation of the kulaks
Until the end of 1929 the Soviet government had conducted a policy of restricting the kulak elements — taxing the kulak, requiring the sale of his grain to the state at fixed prices, and limiting the size of the kulak holding by the laws on land rent and hired labour — but not of liquidating the kulaks as a class. The kulaks answered the advance of the party with resistance: they refused in masses to sell their surplus grain to the Soviet state, conducted terror against the kolkhoz members and the party and Soviet workers in the villages, and set fire to the kolkhozes and the state grain-collection points. Stalin, addressing the conference of agrarian-Marxists in December 1929, laid down the new policy: with the growth of the kolkhozes and sovkhozes, which could now replace the kulak grain production by their own, the party could pass from the policy of restricting the kulak elements to the policy of liquidating the kulaks as a class on the basis of wholesale collectivisation. At the end of 1929 the Soviet government made the sharp turn: it abolished the laws on land rent and on hired labour, thus depriving the kulak of both land and hired workers; it removed the prohibition on razkulachivanie; and it permitted the peasants to confiscate the cattle, the machines and the implements of the kulaks in favour of the kolkhozes. The kulak class was expropriated as the capitalists had been expropriated in 1918, with the difference that the means of production of the kulaks passed this time not into the hands of the state but into the hands of the united peasants, of the kolkhozes.
The policy was fixed in the historic decision of the Central Committee of 5 January 1930, “On the rate of collectivisation and the measures of state aid to the kolkhoz construction,” which took full account of the varying conditions of the regions of the USSR. The Central Committee divided the country into three groups: the principal grain regions, best prepared, with the most tractors, sovkhozes and experience, were to complete collectivisation in the main by the spring of 1931; a second group of grain regions — the Ukraine, the Central Black Earth region, Siberia, the Urals and Kazakhstan — by the spring of 1932; the remaining regions, territories and republics could stretch the terms to the end of the Five-Year Plan, that is to 1933. The party simultaneously required the further acceleration of the building of the tractor and combine factories, while demanding a resolute rebuff to the tendencies that undervalued the role of horse traction in the current stage of the kolkhoz movement.
The kolkhoz movement and the correction of its distortions
On the basis of the liquidation of the kulaks and the establishment of wholesale collectivisation (сплошная коллективизация) a powerful kolkhoz movement unfolded. The peasants entered the kolkhozes by whole villages, districts and regions, sweeping the kulak from the land and freeing themselves from the kulak yoke. But alongside the great successes there began to appear shortcomings in the practice of the party workers — distortions (искривления) of the party’s policy in the kolkhoz construction. Despite the warning of the Central Committee, many party workers artificially forced the collectivisation, disregarding local conditions and the degree of preparedness of the peasants, and in a number of regions the principle of voluntariness was replaced by compulsion under threat of razkulachivanie and the loss of electoral rights. The Central Committee moved at once to correct the errors: by its decision the article of Stalin “Dizzy with Success” (Головокружение от успехов) was published on 2 March 1930, warning all those who, carried away by the successes, had fallen into crude errors and had sought to drive the peasants on the kolkhoz road by administrative pressure, and reasserting with full force the principle of voluntariness and the account of the diversity of the regions. The decision of 15 March 1930, “On the struggle with the distortions of the party line in the kolkhoz movement,” struck a further blow at the errors, and the article of 3 April 1930, “Reply to the kolkhoz comrades,” pointed to the root of the mistakes — the wrong approach to the middle peasant and the violation of the Leninist principle of voluntariness. By these measures the party achieved the liquidation of the distortions of its line in the kolkhoz movement.
The victory of the collective-farm system
The corrected movement advanced to its completion. In January 1933 the Central Committee resolved on the organisation of political departments at the machine-tractor stations (машинно-тракторные станции) serving the kolkhozes, and sent into the countryside seventeen thousand party workers for work in the political departments. In two years, 1933 and 1934, the political departments of the MTS did great work in removing the shortcomings in the life of the kolkhozes, in training the kolkhoz activists and strengthening the collective farms, and in clearing them of hostile, kulak and wrecking elements. The fulfilment of the Five-Year Plan in four years brought the victory of socialism on the whole front, and the Seventeenth Congress of the party, held in 1934, fixed the results: the collectivisation of agriculture, together with socialist industrialisation, had completed the construction of the foundation of socialist society. The school textbook of Shestakov taught the children of the Soviet land that socialist industry and the collective farms were the marks of the land of victorious socialism. The campaign of 1929–1934 was thus presented in the official accounts as the second great reconstruction of the country’s economy — the completion, in the village as in the town, of the building of socialism.

events/coup-of-25-july-1943.title: The Coup of 25 July 1943
events/coup-of-25-july-1943.content:
The Coup of 25 July 1943
24–25 July 1943
The removal of Benito Mussolini in the space of two days by the Crown and the armed forces, at the very moment the Fascist Party itself had turned against its leader. Summoned by the King to a palace audience on the afternoon of Sunday 25 July 1943, the Duce who had ruled Italy for over twenty years was stripped of office, placed under arrest in a motor ambulance, and driven to a Carabinieri barracks; the Crown appointed Marshal badoglio, the army’s first soldier under the regime, to head a new government pledged to carry on the war. The regime that Fascism’s own chroniclers had celebrated as the irreversible conquest of the state collapsed without a shot fired in its defence — “like a rotten pear,” in the new Prime Minister’s phrase — and left Italy facing the Germans she had promised to fight alongside, and the Allies she had resolved in secret to join.
The conspiracy of the leading Fascists
Through the spring of 1943 the ruin of the war in Tunisia, in Russia and in the Mediterranean had turned the inner ring of the Fascist regime against its master. As badoglio reconstructs it, a section of the Party’s own leadership, convinced that the country could be governed without the Duce, began during the first two weeks of July to lay a plan for summoning the Fascist Grand Council (Gran Consiglio del Fascismo) and voting against Mussolini. Ciano, the former favourite who had been deposed as Foreign Minister and made Ambassador to the Holy See, had rebelled more or less openly; Grandi, deprived of the Ministry of Justice but still President of the Chamber, had retired into the background; Bottai, still Minister of Education, was an open “frondist.” The conspirators did not intend that the Party should abandon the reins of government: they had chosen three members of the Council to form a triumvirate — the names given to Badoglio were Ciano, Grandi and Federzoni — and to assume power, with Mussolini’s fate left vague, some wishing him to disappear altogether and others proposing that he be given some post without power. Their resolution, Grandi’s, asked the King to resume the effective command of the armed forces and to restore all the organs of state.
The Grand Council
On the morning of 24 July a rumour spread through Rome that the Council had insisted Mussolini should summon it for that evening; the news was received with considerable incredulity, and there was even talk of a plot that might lead to violence. The Council met, and the discussion continued to a very late hour. The next morning, Sunday 25 July, came the sensational news that the Grand Council had demanded Mussolini’s resignation, his most bitter assailants said to be Ciano, Grandi, De Bono and Bottai. Badoglio reproduces the text of the resolution, which saluted the heroic combatants and the noble Sicilians defending the historic tradition of the armed forces, proclaimed the sacred duty of all Italians to defend the unity, independence and liberty of the country “which are the fruits of the sacrifices of four generations from the Risorgimento,” affirmed the necessity of the spiritual and material union of all Italians, and declared that with this aim the immediate restoration of all the organs of state was essential, inviting the Government to beg the King to assume the effective command of the Army, Navy and Air Force. Nineteen members signed it; seven voted against; Farinacci presented a resolution of his own which was not voted upon; and Suardo abstained. In the city the excitement was intense; violent arguments led to brawls in the streets, and Fascists were roughly handled.
The audience at the Villa Savoia
That afternoon, about five o’clock, the Minister of the Royal Household came to Badoglio to say that the King wished to see him urgently, and to tell him that Mussolini had gone to His Majesty to inform him of the result of the Council meeting. The King had forced him to resign, and as he left the palace he had been arrested and taken to a Carabinieri barracks. Badoglio went at once to the Villa Savoia, the royal residence on the outskirts of Rome, where the King was calm and told him what had happened almost word for word. Mussolini had asked for an interview, fixed for four o’clock; he told the King that the Grand Council had passed a vote of censure on him, but he believed the resolution was not in order. Badoglio answered that he did not agree: the Grand Council was an organ of state which Mussolini himself had created by a law passed by the Chamber and the Senate, and therefore every decision of the Council was valid. “Then according to Your Majesty I ought to resign,” said Mussolini with considerable violence. “Yes,” the King answered, “and I forthwith accepted his resignation.” When he heard this, Badoglio records, Mussolini collapsed as if he had received a blow over the heart; “Then my ruin is complete,” he muttered hoarsely. Taking leave of the King, he went out and, not seeing his car, was directed by an officer to where it stood in the shade at the side of the Villa — and suddenly found himself surrounded by secret police, who asked him to get into a motor ambulance. Asked where he was being taken, he was told, “To a place where you will be quite safe,” and was conveyed to a Carabinieri barracks. The arrest had been planned and carried out by the Minister of the Royal Household with the co-operation of the General Commanding the Carabinieri, with the King’s consent; the military conspiracy of Ambrosio and Badoglio, which had agreed that arrest was necessary, had in the event been by-passed.
The appointment of Badoglio
The King then asked Badoglio to become Head of the Government. He accepted, “very conscious of my lack of political experience,” and put forward a list of the politicians who had promised to collaborate — Bonomi for Internal Affairs, Casati for Education, with Soleri, Bergamini and Einaudi among the rest. The King was entirely opposed to the plan: Badoglio must act with great rapidity and energy, internally and in relation to the Germans, and must not be surrounded by politicians — “You must have a Ministry of experts, who will carry out your orders efficiently.” When Badoglio objected that he would be cut off from public opinion, the King answered that the whole country was with him and handed him a list of the new ministers. The King was determined to have his own way, and Badoglio agreed. The two proclamations announcing that the war would go on had already been printed, drawn up with the help of Senator Vittorio Orlando; it was decided that, in view of the precarious position, Italy could not announce that she would ask for peace, which would have provoked an immediate and violent German reaction that the government, not yet in existence, could not have faced.
As Badoglio made his way home an enormous and delirious crowd made it difficult for him to get in, and cheering crowds paraded the streets of Rome all night, with occasional firing as Fascist headquarters were attacked and sacked. At two o’clock in the morning he was summoned to the Ministry of War, where a crisis had arisen: General Galbiati, Chief of Staff of the Fascist Militia, had apparently decided to resist, but Badoglio’s peremptory order to place himself under the command of General Armellini had the desired effect, and Galbiati resigned. Badoglio wrote at once to the imprisoned Mussolini assuring him that he need not fear for his personal safety, that his confinement had been necessary to save him from the fury of the people; the fallen Duce replied on a scrap of paper that he was very pleased the war was to continue and thanked him warmly for securing his safety. “So ended this historic day.”
The fall of a regime
The King had struck one resolute blow at their leader, and without any resistance or violence the whole Fascist structure collapsed. On 26 July, Badoglio notes, one did not see a single person in Rome wearing the Fascist badge. The leading Fascists had been convinced that without Mussolini they could continue to run the country, which showed, in Badoglio’s judgement, how completely out of touch they were with a public opinion now expressing itself clearly and forcibly. “Fascism fell, as was fitting, like a rotten pear.” Only one shadow lay over the settlement in the new Prime Minister’s eyes: the failure of the King to abdicate. Badoglio had argued, through the Minister of the Royal Household, that the people blamed the King for the continuance of the Fascist Party in power and for the present tragedy, and that he should, like Charles Albert after Novara, abdicate in favour of Prince Umberto; the Minister was entirely opposed, insisting that only the King had the experience and energy to deal with a situation so fraught with unknown dangers. The decision was deferred — and with it, the constitutional question that would pursue the monarchy to the eve of the liberation of Rome.

events/defense-of-madrid-1936.title: The Defense of Madrid, November 1936
events/defense-of-madrid-1936.content:
The Defense of Madrid, November 1936
8–23 November 1936.
The Harpoon in the Suburbs
At the beginning of November 1936 the Nationalist columns, pressing up the road from Toledo, stood five kilometres from the suburbs of Madrid, and the fall of the capital seemed a matter of hours. Aznar, the Nationalist historian, describes the escort of the assault columns preparing their kit on 5 November to enter the city and quarter themselves in their houses, seized by the Reds since 18 July; only Franco, and General Varela, it seemed, had discerned the transformation the war was undergoing. Madariaga closes the purely national phase of the war on precisely this frontier: on 8 November the march on Madrid was broken before the city, and the foreign infiltration of the conflict began. The assault failed, and the failure was a turning point of the war — a arpón clavado in the suburbs, “a harpoon stuck fast” in the flank of the capital, which the Nationalist command, for reasons of morale more than of tactics, would refuse ever to withdraw.
The Decisive Turn
The encirclement had been long prepared. Franco, commanding the Army of Africa, had paused on his march in late September to relieve the Alcázar of Toledo — the decision, made against those who urged haste toward the capital, that “Spain will go to Toledo” and its cadets, women and Guardia Civil who had held the fortress through sixty-eight days of siege. From Toledo the army turned north again for the “maneuver of approach to Madrid,” and by early November the battle front of the encirclement stood before the city’s southern parks. Tusell reads this moment as the decisive military turn of the war: the direct assault on Madrid failed, the war of columns — of loose armed nuclei without a precise front — was exhausted as the fronts consolidated, and the popular militias, at least on the defensive, grew more efficient. Franco’s response was coherent and strategic: he abandoned the direct assault for a flanking manoeuvre that would draw the adversary onto open ground, where the Nationalist superiority had been shown.
The Casa de Campo
The first assault went in on 8 November. Columns under Lieutenant-Colonels Tella and Barrón reached the houses of Carabanchel and Villaverde and there halted, checked by a “very dense fire of automatic weapons”; Asensio Cabanilles and Castejón carried the attack into the wooded grounds of the Casa de Campo, the old royal estate west of the Manzanares, tearing a breach in its wall and pouring among the oaks. The prisoners taken in the woods revealed the secret of the unexpected resistance: the defenders were the 1st and 11th International Brigades, formed of ex-combatants of several European armies, commanded by Czech, Austrian and Russian colonels, supported by a mass of artillery and by hundreds of machine-guns. The promised crossing of the Manzanares and the entry into the Ciudad Universitaria — the university city on the western bluffs — proved a chimera. The river, an “apprentice river,” was shallow, but its banks were steep; the tanks could not pass; the assault of the 9th enlarged the foothold and took the Garabitas height but gained no decision. The Nationalists had no reserves, and the loss of officers was eating the columns alive.
The Defence of the Capital
The Republican government had already abandoned Madrid for Valencia, leaving a Junta of Defence in the capital under General Miaja, with a communist-dominated Defence Committee behind him. In three days some 12,000 men of the International Brigades had entered the city, joined to 12,000 Spanish front-line combatants, together forming two well-armed divisions; a third division lay in reserve in the centre of the city. The “General Kleber” — the adventurer, in Aznar’s hostile phrase, who “served the designs of other technicians come from Russia” — commanded among them. On 15 November Asensio forced the river: a company of Moorish Regulares of the Tetuán group jumped the Manzanares at mid-morning and entered the Moncloa park and the first grounds of the Ciudad Universitaria, followed by the whole of the grouping behind them. The attackers seized the Moncloa palace, the Casa de Velázquez, the Hospital Clínico on its commanding height, and made themselves strong in them; but the exhausted assault column now numbered no more than 1,500 men, and two hundred red machine-guns swept the approaches.
The War Changes Sign
The Nationalist command, its head at Salamanca, saw the problem clearly. Only eight or ten fresh, well-armed units could carry the centre of a hostile city of over a million inhabitants, and no such units existed. Franco ordered the positions in the Ciudad Universitaria fortified and held — the harpoon to stay lodged in the capital’s side, threatening the vital centre of the red army’s organization and resistance. In a civil war, Aznar insists, moral elements carry extraordinary weight, and the command subordinated many technical decisions to them; never in the whole war, for reasons of morale as much as of policy, would the Nationalists abandon a position once taken. Around the university city, the Casa de Campo and Carabanchel the struggle settled into the daily, indecisive combat of the new war — Lister and “El Campesino” commanding the red units that faced Tella and Barrón, the International Brigades strung around the Ciudad Universitaria, the sectors of Húmera and Pozuelo. The assault on Madrid was renounced, the frontal assault at least. “The war has changed sign,” Aznar writes; a great phase had ended and another, much greater and harder, had begun. Tusell notes the consequence: Franco, turning from the direct attack, would now draw the enemy onto open ground — and the war’s centre of gravity would move, first to the Jarama, then to Guadalajara, and at length to the north.
