events/dictatorship-of-primo-de-rivera-1.title: The Dictatorship of Primo de Rivera (1923–1930)
events/dictatorship-of-primo-de-rivera-1.content:
The Dictatorship of Primo de Rivera (1923–1930)
13 September 1923 – 28 January 1930.
The Pronunciamiento
On the night of 13 September 1923, Miguel Primo de Rivera, the Captain-General of Catalonia, proclaimed martial law in Barcelona and declared that the constitutional order had failed. The monarchy, exhausted by the Moroccan disaster of Annual, the social war in the cities, and the discredit of the parliamentary turno — the rotation of the old liberal and conservative parties — offered no resistance. King Alfonso XIII, who had seen the constitution suspended before and who preferred to stand at the head of a governing general than to lose the throne, accepted the coup. On 15 September he entrusted Primo de Rivera with the formation of a Military Directory (Directorio militar), a government of generals in place of a ministry of parliamentarians. The pronunciamiento — the barracks rising that had punctuated Spanish politics for a century — had at last delivered the country into the hands of a soldier, and the liberal regime that had held since the Restoration collapsed without a blow in its defence.
The new head of government was an Andalusian aristocrat and artillery general of the old school, at once traditionalist and impatient, who presented himself less as a tyrant than as a cirujano de hierro — an “iron surgeon” — summoned to cut away the corruption of the politicians. His first decrees dissolved the provincial corporations, suspended the constitutional guarantees, and instituted a summary censorship of the press. The aged institutions of parliamentarism, already hollowed out, were set aside; Spain was to be governed, in the general’s phrase, by the Army and the truth.
The Years of the Directory
The first years of the Dictatorship were its most vigorous and its most popular. Primo de Rivera threw himself against the Catalan question he had once seemed to court: he suppressed the Catalanist symbols and the regional statutes, subordinated the province to a military government, and proclaimed the unity of Spain. Against the old politics he set his Unión Patriótica (Patriotic Union), a movement of official notables raised to replace the parties of the turno. The socialists he sought to conciliate, drawing their trade-union wing into a collaboration that startled the revolutionary left; the syndicalists of the anarchist CNT he crushed with a police terror and the ley de fugas — the law of flight — by which arrested men were shot while “escaping.”
The great enterprise of these years was Morocco. The disaster of Annual in 1921 had left the Rif in the hands of Abd-El-Krim and Spain in a state of national humiliation. In 1924 the Dictatorship began a new policy of concentration and retrenchment; in 1925, in cooperation with the French under Marshal Pétain, it staged the landing at Alhucemas (desembarco de Alhucemas) on the Rif coast, the first amphibious operation of modern Spanish warfare. The landing broke the power of Abd-El-Krim, who surrendered to the French in 1926, and closed the Moroccan problem that had poisoned Spanish politics for a quarter of a century. It was the Dictatorship’s single undisputed triumph, and for a time it made Primo de Rivera the most admired man in Spain.
From Military to Civil Government
In December 1925 Primo de Rivera dissolved the Military Directory and formed an ordinary government of civilians, the first step in a slow attempt to give his rule a constitutional and civilian face. The Directorio civil (civil directory) gathered monarchists, ex-liberals and men of the Unión Patriótica, and proclaimed the intention of returning to a reformed parliamentarism. Yet the Dictatorship could not rest on institutions it had destroyed. A plebiscite in 1926, conducted with official pressure, approved the idea of a consultative assembly; in 1927 the National Consultative Assembly (Asamblea Nacional Consultiva) was convoked, a handpicked chamber of appointed notables whose drafting of a new constitution remained stillborn. The regime drifted between the old constitutionalism it had killed and a fascist-style corporate state it refused to embrace, borrowing gestures from Mussolini’s Italy — a journey to Rome in 1923 had brought Primo de Rivera and the Duce face to face — without ever adopting its party or its revolution.
Opposition gathered from both extremes. Republican exiles and intelectuales — Unamuno, exiled and later confined; the student generation that would carry the Republic — were driven to the margin and then, as the regime hardened, into conspiracy. The Sanjuanada of 1926 and the Ciudad Real pronunciamiento of 1929, artillery conspiracies against the Dictator, failed, but they revealed the army’s disaffection. The socialists, courted at first, turned against the regime as the world crisis of 1929 struck; the peseta collapsed and the financial house the Dictatorship had built began to tremble. The great expositions of Seville and Barcelona in 1929, designed to display a regenerated Spain, masked a treasury in crisis and a regime whose popularity had drained away.
The End of the Dictatorship
By the winter of 1929 the Dictatorship was visibly dying. The Constitution of 1812, whose centenary fell that year, was invoked against him; the students struck against the university statute; the army, whose confidence he had once commanded, fell away. On 28 January 1930 Primo de Rivera, consulting the captains-general and finding them against him, presented his resignation to the king. Alfonso XIII accepted it and entrusted power to General Dámaso Berenguer, charged with leading Spain back toward constitutional normality. The Dictator withdrew to Paris and died there within weeks, in March 1930, a broken and embittered man.
The Dictatorship had not been a monarchy in exile nor a republic born; it was a parenthesis in which the old regime’s ailments were suppressed but not cured. Madariaga’s balanced judgment, written as the dictatorship was liquidated, held that it had left Spain in a situation equal or worse than the one it found: the constitutional monarchy had been so thoroughly discredited that it could not be restored, while the social and political forces the Dictatorship had denied — the republicans, the workers, the regional nationalisms — emerged more radical and more determined than before. The very suspension of politics had made the return to politics violent. When Berenguer called the constitutional machinery back to life, there was little left to govern; the throne that had survived the Dictatorship by sheltering under it would not survive the attempt to restore a normal monarchy. The parenthesis of 1923–1930 opened the road that led, within fifteen months, to the proclamation of the Republic.

events/end-of-the-civil-war-1939.title: The End of the Civil War (February – 1 April 1939)
events/end-of-the-civil-war-1939.content:
The End of the Civil War (February – 1 April 1939)
February – 1 April 1939
The closing offensive of the Spanish Civil War, in which the Nationalist forces of the Generalísimo overran the remaining republican zone in the centre and south of Spain, and the proclamation of victory read on the radios of the victorious Spain on 1 April 1939. The final weeks were marked less by the resistance of the Republic than by its internal disintegration — the coup of March against the government of Juan Negrín, the refusal of the victors to negotiate with its successors, and the unconditional surrender that ended the war that had begun on 18 July 1936.
The last maneuver of the Generalísimo
The conquest of Catalonia in the early weeks of 1939 left the Republic confined to the central and south-eastern provinces — Madrid, Valencia, the Mediterranean coast and the Andalusian south — cut off from the frontier and from any further hope of foreign help. Aznar’s Tomo III opens the account of the war’s close with what he calls the great final maneuver of the Generalísimo, the descent upon the remaining zone with the whole weight of the Nationalist army now concentrated for the last stroke. The campaign of late February and March carried the Nationalist columns through the central region toward Madrid and the coast, meeting an opposition that, in the victor’s telling, was less a defence than the collapse of an already defeated state. By the end of March the last military objectives had been reached and the Red army, in Aznar’s phrase, destroyed.
The Nationalist command, however, refused to treat the closing phase as a negotiation. Franco, determined to finish not only the communists but the whole Popular Front, would accept nothing short of surrender, and the final offensive was pressed to the complete occupation of the national territory.
The collapse of the Popular Front
The end of the war was, in the judgement of the modern historian, a phenomenon of disintegration affecting all sectors and protagonists of the Popular Front rather than an interweaving of conspiracies — but it was the conspiracy that delivered the coup de grâce. The centre of resistance, and of the last political struggle, was Madrid. Colonel Casado, the defender of the capital, had for months judged the prolongation of the war a crime against humanity, describing the Popular Front zone as a dictatorship in the service of a foreign power, Russia; and in the last days he acted on that judgement. Negrín, returned from France, sought to reorganise the resistance and to impose a command disposed to continue the war, replacing non-communist commanders such as Casado with men, in large part communist, who were the only party that at this point seemed willing to resist. The change never took effect. On 4–5 March 1939, as the last hopes of negotiation died, Casado formed the National Defence Council in Madrid, its manifesto drafted by Julián Besteiro denouncing the “catastrophist fanaticism” of the head of government, who had already left the country. The communist attempt to resist the coup was crushed in a short, bloody struggle in the capital; the Cartagena rising of the fleet against Negrín’s authority had already collapsed in confusion. The government of the Republic was finished, its authority gone, its leader abroad and without power.
The unconditional surrender
The National Defence Council, having taken power in the name of peace, sought a settlement with the victors — only to discover that Franco, who wanted to finish not merely the communists but the whole Popular Front, refused to negotiate. The final offensive was pressed against a Republic that had ceased to command itself. The remaining zones surrendered in the last days of March: Madrid fell, the coastal and southern provinces were overrun, and the Nationalist forces completed the occupation of the whole of Spain. The mediation that Madariaga records as having begun with the war itself — the efforts to end the conflict by negotiation, with all their suspicions and misapprehensions — had failed; the war ended, as the victor insisted, in unconditional surrender.
The end came on 1 April 1939. At a quarter past eleven on the night of 1 April the habitual announcer of the victorious Spain read the last official war bulletin — number 982 — over the radios of the nation: «cautivo y desarmado el Ejército rojo» — captive and disarmed the Red Army — and the troops of the Generalísimo had reached their last military objectives. The vivas that accompanied the bulletin were directed, as the less-remembered part of the record, to the exterior allies of the three preceding years — Portugal, Italy and Germany. The war was over. What followed for the defeated was the repression and the exile that closed the conflict and opened the long dictatorship of the man who had won it.

events/fall-of-barcelona-1939.title: The Fall of Barcelona (26 January – 10 February 1939)
events/fall-of-barcelona-1939.content:
The Fall of Barcelona (26 January – 10 February 1939)
26 January – 10 February 1939
The capture of Barcelona by the Nationalist army on 26 January 1939 and the completion of the occupation of Catalonia in the first days of February — the decisive defeat of the Spanish Republic in the second great campaign of the final year of the Civil War. The fall of the Catalan capital, the seat of the republican government since the transfer of the seat from Valencia, ended the last organized resistance in the eastern zone and drove the leadership of the Republic into exile across the French frontier. For many sympathisers of the Popular Front, as the scholarly record observes, the fall of Catalonia simply meant the end of the war.
The Battle of Catalonia
The Battle of Catalonia, which carried the Nationalist army from the Ebro to the French frontier, grew directly out of the exhaustion left by the summer’s great struggle. The Army of the Ebro, spent by its four months on the river, had recrossed to the north bank on 16 November 1938 with its strength gone; the Republic had no second instrument with which to meet the offensive that Franco now prepared. Aznar’s Tomo III opens the account of the campaign with the collapse of the resistance along the Segre and the descent of the Nationalist forces on the Catalan plain, the battle unfolding as the generalísimo turned the whole weight of his army, now reinforced by the contingents released from the Mediterranean front, upon the truncated republican zone.
The Nationalist offensive of late December 1938 broke through the line in the opening days and, by the second half of January, had shattered the last organized republican front. The retreat became a rout: the broken Army of the Ebro, the new levies called out in the desperation of the final weeks, and the mass of the civilian population streamed northward before the advancing columns. By the third week of January the way to Barcelona lay open. The Nationalist forces entered the city on 26 January 1939, taking possession of the capital that had been the centre of the republican war effort and the seat of the government of Juan Negrín.
The republican collapse
The fall of Barcelona unravelled the Republic at a stroke. The government, which had moved its seat to the Catalan capital in the last years of the war, had already abandoned the city in the retreat; with its fall the political authority of the Republic ceased to function as a territorial power. For the leadership of the Popular Front, as Tusell observes, the capture of Catalonia meant simply the end, ratified almost at once by the immediate recognition of Franco by France and Great Britain — the great powers shedding the fiction of non-intervention to accept the victor’s fait accompli. Azaña, the president of the Republic, crossed the frontier into France in the first days of February, closing the life of the Republic’s leading spirit in the exile that was to end with his death in 1940.
The first concrete testimony of the disintegration was the surrender of Menorca in the first days of February 1939. The island and the naval base of Mahón, which had played no important part in the war, gave themselves up by an initiative that arose, in the judgement of the historian, from the simple spectacle of the collapse of the republican state, with a British warship involved in the transaction. What remained of the Republic in the center — Madrid, Valencia, the Mediterranean coast — held on only by clinging to the fiction that the war might yet be prolonged or negotiated.
The last resistance and the exodus
The end of January and the first days of February saw the mass exodus of the defeated population across the Pyrenees. The columns of refugees, with the remnants of the republican army, poured over the frontier at the French customs posts, the great éxodo that was to mark the close of the Spanish war as the beginning of the long exile. The Nationalist forces, pressing northward through Catalonia, took the last towns of the province in the opening days of February and reached the frontier at Puigcerdà and the passes, completing the conquest of Catalonia by 10 February 1939.
The campaign had decided the war. The Republican army that had resisted so long at the Ebro was gone, and with it the will and the means to continue the struggle on the scale the war demanded. Negrín, who had crossed into France with the retreat, spoke to the military commanders at Los Llanos in the days after the fall of Catalonia of his central conviction — that as the enemy would not make peace, the only solution was to resist. But the authority to act on that conviction had slipped from his hands. The fall of Barcelona, followed by the surrender of Menorca and the flight into France, left the Republic no territory in the east, no capital, and a government abroad whose orders the remaining commanders were already preparing to disobey.

events/fiume-expedition-1919.title: The Fiume Expedition (September 1919 – December 1920)
events/fiume-expedition-1919.content:
The Fiume Expedition (September 1919 – December 1920)
12 September 1919 – 27 December 1920
In the autumn of 1919 the poet and war-hero Gabriele d’Annunzio marched at the head of a band of legionaries from Ronchi to the Adriatic city of Fiume and seized it in the name of Italy, defying both the Allies and his own government. For fifteen months the city held out as a free commune under a “regency of Carnaro,” until the state, having signed the Treaty of Rapallo with Yugoslavia, expelled it by force at Christmas 1920. The Fascist chroniclers came to regard the expedition as the model and prophecy of their own revolt — the first open refusal of the official Italy, and the seed of the March on Rome.
The ideal origin
The enterprise grew out of the Adriatic settlement that the war was supposed to have decided. By the Pact of London Italy had been promised Dalmatia; at the peace conference the American president Wilson refused it, and the government under Orlando seemed to submit. Farinacci records the “ideal origin of the Fiume undertaking” in the surrender at Paris — the Wilsonian utopia, the Adriatic question left wounded, the violations of Italian right. Fiume, an Italian city on the Croatian coast, had been claimed by the new Yugoslavia, and as the peacemakers fumbled the city became the symbol of the denied victory. The humiliation, for the interventionists and ex-servicemen who had won the war, was complete. Pini and Bresadola set the whole question under the heading “months of shame,” and d’Annunzio’s gesture as the answer of the war-generation to a state that would not defend its own.
The march of Ronchi
In the night of 11–12 September 1919 the poet put himself at the head of some hundreds of mutinous soldiers, sailors and Arditi at Ronchi, on the border of the still-disputed zone, and marched on Fiume. Farinacci calls the episode the “epic of Ronchi”; Businelli, the “Fiume rebellion and the Ronchi march of d’Annunzio.” The Italian grenadiers of the garrison, instead of resisting, went over to the legionaries, and the city opened its gates. d’Annunzio proclaimed the annexation of Fiume to Italy, and for a moment the mutiny had no answer: the official Italy of Prime Minister Francesco Nitti was helpless before it. “Fiume contro Roma” — Fiume against Rome — became the cry of the undertaking, the city set up in open rebellion against the government that had abandoned it. For the Fascists the lesson was plain. Mussolini, who had hesitated, threw the weight of his paper behind the legionaries, and the Fasci made the defence of Fiume their own cause; the undertaking hardened the conviction that the state must be seized, not begged of.
The regency of Carnaro
For more than a year the city lived outside the law. d’Annunzio governed as a dictator-poet, gathering veterans and adventurers, and gave his free city a constitution of his own invention, the Carta del Carnaro (Charter of Carnaro), drawn up with the syndicalist Alceste De Ambris — a document of corporative fancy that mixed the rights of the individual with the authority of a charismatic head. Farinacci’s account of the closing phase records the Reggenza del Carnaro (the Regency of Carnaro) that d’Annunzio proclaimed, styling himself the commander of a state that no power recognised. The undertaking drew much of the militant Right to the city; from Fiume came some of the language and the gesture that the Fascist movement would absorb — the black shirts, the Roman salute, the declamatory heroism of the anti-parliamentary leader.
The Natale di sangue
The end came when the state at last recovered its nerve. Nitti fell; Giolitti returned to power determined to settle the Adriatic by negotiation. At Rapallo in November 1920 the government made peace with Yugoslavia, conceding that Fiume should become a free state — a solution d’Annunzio refused to accept. Farinacci, in the volume on the “red insurrection,” narrates the fulfilment of the tragedy: Giolitti’s accommodation, the ultimatum of General Caviglia, the declaration of a state of war, and the full powers d’Annunzio extracted from the Fiumans. On 24 December 1920 the royal navy and army opened fire on the defiant city, and after days of fighting — the Natale di sangue, the “bloody Christmas” — d’Annunzio surrendered and Fiume submitted. The poet withdrew, wounded in pride and body, to his estate; but the undertaking had done its work. What the legionaries had begun at Ronchi, the Fasci would complete at Rome two years later; the state that had fired on Fiume would be swept away by the movement Fiume had inspired.

events/founding-of-the-fasci-1919.title: The Founding of the Fasci di Combattimento (23 March 1919)
events/founding-of-the-fasci-1919.content:
The Founding of the Fasci di Combattimento (23 March 1919)
23 March 1919
In a hall in Piazza San Sepolcro, Milan, a few hundred interventionists, ex-servicemen, Futurists and Arditi gathered to found the Fasci di combattimento (fighting bands) — the movement that in three years would remake the Italian state. Mussolini presided over the meeting as the whole country, having won the war, seemed to be losing the peace; the Fascist chroniclers of the next two decades would look back on the adunata as the seed of the revolution, and on the twenty-third of March as a sacred date.
The troubled peace
The months after the armistice had drained the victory of its meaning. The demobilised soldiers returned to find a country that had changed while they were at the front: prices rising, the Socialists triumphant in the cities, the government at Paris under Vittorio Orlando apparently surrendering what the war had been fought to win. Farinacci’s party history opens its account of 1919 with the “collapse of the ruling class” — the verbose and irresolute Orlando at the peace conference, the League of Nations as the “ideal instrument of an iniquitous peace,” and the strength of the country diminished and offended by its own government. The neutralists, who had opposed the war, raised their heads again; the Socialists prophesied the Russian example for Italy; the Russian revolution had set a current running across Europe that the timid Italian parliament seemed unable to meet. Pini and Bresadola compress the season into two phrases — “troubled months” and “the defeat at Versailles.” Out of that double humiliation, at home and abroad, the new movement was struck.
The meeting at San Sepolcro
The impulse came from the men of the war and of the interventionist struggle. Volpe calls what Mussolini created a deliberate “anti-party,” a reaction against the whole mass politics of the postwar, built on youth, impulse and faith rather than on programme. Around him stood the survivors of the trench and the assault squads — the Arditi (the daring ones), the demobilised officers and officer-students, the Futurists of Marinetti who had carried the banner of intervention in 1915. Farinacci stresses the episode of Dalmine, the metalworkers’ occupation in the early months of 1919, as one of the sparks that convinced the war-veterans that only force could answer the red wave; and he records the intervention of the Arditi in creating the Fasci. On the morning of 23 March the founders came together at the meeting-hall in Piazza San Sepolcro. Businelli, himself a young squadrist who had served under Marinetti in the Roman days of 1919, calls it the adunata of Piazza San Sepolcro — the first victory, the constituent assembly of interventionism.
From the meeting issued a programme that was at once revolutionary and national: anti-monarchical in its republicanism, anti-clerical, hostile to the great landowners and the banks, insistent on the rights of the war-winners, demanding a constituent assembly. Its temper, in the words the movement would long repeat, was that of the trincerocrazia — the aristocracy of the trenches, the men who had fought, who felt themselves betrayed by a state that was already failing before their eyes.
The founding in the crisis
The Fasci were not yet a party. They were, in Volpe’s phrase, a movement — a mood and a weapon rather than an organisation, a “policy of the masses” answered with the passion of the few. From the first they placed themselves against both the red internationalism of the Socialists and the timid moderation of the liberal ministries. In the weeks after San Sepolcro the new bands made themselves felt in the streets. In April the first open collision came in Milan: the assault on the offices of Avanti!, the Socialist daily, an act Farinacci records as the beginning of the civil war and the “prologue of the long drama,” the moment the Fasci answered the insult of defeat with force. The movement would go through the elections of November 1919 with a single deputy — Mussolini himself, elected in Milan — a handful of votes beside the Socialist flood, and yet the chroniclers insisted that the seed had been sown.
Businelli closes the chapter on the founding with the phrase that frames the whole Fascist self-understanding: the movement, born in the ruin of the peace, would not wait on the liberal state to save the nation. Out of the hall in Piazza San Sepolcro, with its few hundred believers, came the forces that would fight the red biennium, raise Fiume, and march on Rome.

events/german-polish-non-aggression-pact.title: The German–Polish Non-Aggression Pact (26 January 1934)
events/german-polish-non-aggression-pact.content:
The German–Polish Non-Aggression Pact (26 January 1934)
26 January 1934
The declaration signed in Berlin on 26 January 1934 by which the German and Polish governments agreed to regulate their mutual relations directly, to renounce the use of force in the settlement of any disputes between them, and to base their understanding on the renunciation-of-war principles of the Pact of Paris. Published as the first fruits of the new Germany’s “peace policy,” the Nichtangriffspakt (non-aggression pact) with Poland marked the most striking reversal of the Weimar years — a settlement of accounts with the country that the National Socialists had once named their principal enemy, and the regime’s most emphatic early demonstration that it meant to undo the Versailles order by agreement rather than by arms.
The peace policy of the new Germany
The pact belonged to a wider diplomatic offensive that the regime’s own documentary record of 1934 presents under the heading of German peace policy. The months before and after Hitler’s appointment had produced a stream of German memoranda and declarations — the memorandum of 18 December 1933, the disarmament memorandum of 19 January 1934 — in which the Reich protested its peaceful intentions, demanded equality of rights, and offered non-aggression arrangements to its neighbours. In the official compilation these documents are set out as the foreign policy of a Germany that sought, in the editor’s framing, the preservation of peace through the conclusion of non-aggression pacts and disavowed any thought of war as an instrument of policy. The agreement with Poland stood at the head of this record as its most concrete achievement: the proof, as the volume’s commentary puts it, that a direct understanding between states could open “a new phase in the political relations between Germany and Poland.”
The declaration
The text of the declaration is short and general. Both governments, it opens, consider the moment come to open a new phase in their relations through a direct understanding from state to state. They proceed from the fact that the maintenance and assurance of a lasting peace between their countries is an essential precondition of general peace in Europe, and they are therefore resolved to base their mutual relations on the principles contained in the Pact of Paris of 27 August 1928 — the pact by which the signatory states renounced war as an instrument of national policy — and to define the application of those principles more exactly as between Germany and Poland. Each government affirms that the international obligations it has already undertaken do not hinder the peaceful development of their mutual relations, do not contradict the present declaration, and are not affected by it; and each declares that the declaration does not extend to questions which, under international law, are exclusively the internal affairs of the one or the other state. The operative core follows: both governments declare their intention to consult directly on all questions touching their mutual relations, of whatever kind; and should disputes arise between them whose settlement by direct negotiation cannot be achieved, they will in each particular case, by mutual agreement, seek a solution through other peaceful means — while undertaking that in no circumstances will they resort to force for the settlement of such disputes. The peace guarantee created by these principles, the declaration closes, will ease the great task of both governments in finding solutions for problems of a political, economic and cultural kind, on a basis of a just and fair balance of their mutual interests.
Origins: Lipski and Pilsudski
The regime’s own annotation of the treaty records its carefully prepared origins. The Polish envoy, Lipski, had sought out the Führer on 15 November 1933, and in the announcement of that meeting it was already stated that an agreement had been reached between the two governments “to renounce all application of force in their relations to one another.” On 27 November 1933 the German envoy in Warsaw held a conversation with Marshal Pilsudski. From these exchanges the declaration of 26 January followed. The Führer, the notes add, gave the agreement its full due in his speech of 30 January 1934 — the first anniversary of his assumption of the chancellorship — presenting it as the model of a policy that sought peace with Germany’s neighbours.
The meaning
For the regime the pact with Poland was a double demonstration. In its own telling it proved the sincerity of German peace policy: here was the Reich, on the morrow of a bitter frontier dispute and against the expectations of its critics, concluding a renunciation-of-force agreement with the state it had once reviled. And it showed the German hand free: the settlement with Poland, the loudest of the grievances bequeathed by Versailles and the corridor question, was taken out of the field of the great powers and negotiated over their heads, state to state, in the manner the National Socialists insisted was the only honest way. The diplomacy of Locarno and the League, the regime implied, was superseded by the direct understanding of equals. Whatever its later fate — the pact would not survive the years it was meant to govern — in January 1934 it stood as the leading evidence of a Germany that claimed to have renounced force, and the first great treaty of Hitler’s foreign policy.

events/great-patriotic-war-1941-45.title: The Great Patriotic War of the Soviet Union (22 June 1941 – 3 September 1945)
events/great-patriotic-war-1941-45.content:
The Great Patriotic War of the Soviet Union (22 June 1941 – 3 September 1945)
22 June 1941 – 3 September 1945
The Great Patriotic War (Великая Отечественная война) was the war of the Soviet people against fascist Germany and its allies, begun by the perfidious attack of Hitler’s Germany on 22 June 1941 and brought to an end by the unconditional surrender of Germany on 9 May 1945 and of Japan on 2 September 1945. In the official account, gathered in the collected wartime utterances of Stalin published in 1946, the war was a just, patriotic and liberating war: the German invasion, violating the non-aggression pact of 1939, had thrown the whole Soviet people against the aggressor, and the Red Army, bearing the whole weight of the war in the absence of a second front in Europe, routed the fascist armies and carried the banner of victory to Berlin and to the Far East. Stalin, who became People’s Commissar of Defence and Supreme Commander-in-Chief, appears in the record as the military and political head of the war; the party and the Soviet people, in the wartime self-account, were the true bearers of the victory.
The perfidious invasion
The German attack of 22 June 1941 came without the declaration of war, in perfidious violation of the non-aggression pact concluded between Germany and the USSR in 1939. In his first radio address to the people, of 3 July 1941, Stalin announced that the war had begun, explaining the initial Soviet retreats by the fact that Germany, as a country already at war, had been fully mobilised, its 170 divisions brought up to the frontiers in complete readiness, whereas the Soviet forces had still to mobilise; and by the sudden and perfidious breach of the pact, which the peace-loving Soviet state, unwilling to take upon itself the initiative of breaking the treaty, could not answer with treachery. The address set the war in the frame of the historic defeats of the supposedly invincible armies of Napoleon and of Wilhelm II, which had been broken in their turn, and declared that the German-fascist army of Hitler could and would be broken likewise. It called for the reorganisation of all work on a military footing, for the partisan war in the occupied regions, for the destruction of supplies rather than their surrender to the enemy, and for the total patriotic war of the whole people; and it announced the formation of the State Committee of Defence (Государственный Комитет Обороны), in whose hands all power in the state was now concentrated. “Our cause is just,” the address concluded — “the enemy will be broken, victory will be ours.” On 7 November 1941, on the twenty-fourth anniversary of October, Stalin spoke at the Red Army parade on Red Square in besieged Moscow, proclaiming his confidence in victory and the certainty that the German invaders were standing before the abyss.
The first period of the war
The first period of the war, surveyed in the order of 23 February 1942, was the period of the German blitzkrieg (молниеносная война). Taking advantage of the absence of a second front in Europe, the Germans and their allies threw all their reserves into a single southwestern direction, broke the Soviet front in the summer, and in the autumn of 1941 advanced to the very approaches of Moscow. The order of 23 February 1942 recorded the defeat of the German plan for a blitzkrieg and the rout of the German forces before Moscow, where the Red Army, having beaten off the attack on the capital, took the initiative into its hands, passed to the offensive and drove the Germans to the west, liberating a whole series of regions of the country. The defensive battles of the first year — the heroic defence of Moscow and Tula, of Odessa and Sevastopol, of Leningrad and Stalingrad — were presented as the schooling of the Red Army, whose soldiers and commanders, lacking previous military experience, learned to beat the enemy for certain and to destroy his men and material. The enemy, the order declared, had already felt the power of the Red Army’s resistance; it would yet learn the force of its shattering blows.
The turning of the war
In the summer of 1942 the position on the front worsened. Taking advantage again of the absence of a second front in Europe, the Germans and their allies gathered all their reserves, broke the Ukrainian front and, at the cost of enormous losses, advanced in the south, placing Stalingrad, the Black Sea coast, Grozny and the approaches to the Transcaucasus under threat. The plan of the German command to pass round Moscow from the east and strike it from the rear was frustrated by the firmness and courage of the Red Army; the enemy was halted at Stalingrad. The order of 7 November 1942 announced the turn: the Red Army, having worn down the enemy, prepared its shattering blow, and on 19 November the counter-offensive at Stalingrad opened. The battle of Stalingrad — the greatest battle in the history of wars at the walls of the city — ended with the encirclement and liquidation of an enormous picked German army of three hundred and thirty thousand men and the taking of about a third of the encircled troops prisoner. The order of 28 February 1943, for the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Red Army, recorded the destruction of the German forces at Stalingrad and the beginning of the mass expulsion of the enemy, and the order of 7 November 1943, surveying the year, fixed the turning point of the war: from Stalingrad the Red Army never again let the initiative out of its hands, and the winter and summer campaigns of 1942–1943 — the battles of Stalingrad and of Kursk and the forcing of the Dnieper — predetermined the defeat of the German forces. “Stalingrad was the sunset of the German-fascist army,” ran the official verdict; after the Stalingrad massacre the Germans could no longer recover.
The expulsion of the enemy and the liberation of Europe
From the turning point of Stalingrad the Red Army advanced through 1943 and 1944 to the complete expulsion of the German forces from Soviet territory. The order of 23 February 1944 recorded the final expulsion of the German armies from the Soviet land; the order of 20 August 1944 saluted the troops who had completed the expulsion and had advanced to the frontiers of the country; and the order of 7 November 1944 marked the entry of the Red Army into the war of liberation of the peoples of Europe. In 1945 the war was carried onto the territory of the enemy. The order of 21 April 1945 saluted the troops on the approach to Berlin, the order of 1 May 1945 the troops who had captured the German capital and raised the banner of victory over the Reichstag, and the address of 27 April 1945 the historic meeting of the Soviet and Anglo-American forces in Germany. On 9 May 1945, with the signature of the unconditional surrender of Germany, Stalin addressed the people, saluting the Soviet people — “a people of extraordinary patience” — as the true bearers of the victory, and the order of the same day declared 9 May the day of victory over Germany. At the Kremlin reception of 24 May 1945 the toast on the Russian people, as the most outstanding nation of all the nations forming the Soviet Union, closed the European war.
The victory over Germany and Japan
The war with Japan followed. On 19 August 1945 the order for the day of victory over Japan and of the liberation of the Far East marked the defeat of the Japanese aggressor, and on 2 September 1945 the Japanese instrument of surrender was signed in Tokyo. In his address of 2 September Stalin declared the victory over Japan, and the final order of 3 September 1945 declared 3 September the victory day over Japan and saluted the victorious troops, bringing to an end the whole war. In the official account of the years 1941–1945, the Great Patriotic War vindicated the Soviet order: the war was a severe test of the strength and firmness of the Soviet system, and the socialist state, the collective-farm order and the friendship of the peoples of the USSR emerged from it victorious. The party’s history and the biography of Stalin place the war at the centre of the Stalinist narrative — the war in which Stalin, as Supreme Commander and then Generalissimus of the Soviet Union, led the Red Army to the rout of fascist Germany and to the victory that the Soviet people had won by their self-sacrifice and their unshakable faith.

events/great-terror-1936-38.title: The Great Terror: The Trials and the Liquidation of the Enemies of the People (1936–1938)
events/great-terror-1936-38.content:
The Great Terror: The Trials and the Liquidation of the Enemies of the People (1936–1938)
1936–1938
The political trials of the years 1936–1938 were the series of judicial processes by which the Soviet state exposed and liquidated the “enemies of the people” (враги народа) — the remnant of the Trotskyist and Bukharinist oppositions, which, in the account of the party, had degenerated into a band of spies, wreckers and murderers in the service of the foreign intelligence services. The trials followed the murder of S. M. Kirov, the secretary of the Leningrad party organisation, shot on 1 December 1934 in the Smolny; the investigation established that the murder had been prepared by a concealed counter-revolutionary terrorist organisation descended from the old opposition, and the processes that followed — the trial of Zinoviev, Kamenev and their accomplices in 1936, the trials of Pyatakov, Radek and others, of Tukhachevsky, Yakir and others, and finally of Bukharin, Rykov, Krestinsky and Rozengolts in 1937–1938 — laid bare, according to the official account, a conspiracy against Lenin, the party and the Soviet state that had run through twenty years, directed from abroad by Trotsky and executed for foreign intelligence services. The party’s history and the biography of Stalin present these years as the completion of the purge of the party and the strengthening of Bolshevik vigilance that the enemies of socialism had made necessary.
The murder of Kirov
The murder of S. M. Kirov was the deed that opened the period. On 1 December 1934, in the Smolny in Leningrad, Kirov — the favourite of the party and of the working class, whose murder caused the greatest anger and deep sorrow of the toilers of the country — was killed by a revolver shot. The investigation established that in 1933–1934 there had been formed in Leningrad, from among former participants of the Zinovievite opposition, an underground counter-revolutionary terrorist group at the head of the so-called “Leningrad centre,” which set itself the murder of the leaders of the Communist Party, with Kirov as the first victim; the members of the group, as their evidence showed, were connected with representatives of the foreign capitalist states and received money from them. Soon the existence of an underground counter-revolutionary “Moscow centre” was established, and the investigation and the court brought out the vile role of Zinoviev, Kamenev, Evdokimov and the other leaders of the organisation in cultivating terrorist moods among their fellow-thinkers and in preparing the murder of members of the Central Committee and of the Soviet government. The double-dealing of these men reached such a point that Zinoviev, one of the organisers and inspirers of the murder of Kirov, who had urged the assassin to hasten the deed, wrote a eulogistic obituary on Kirov’s death and demanded its publication. The murder, as became clear later, was committed by the united Trotskyist-Bukharinist band; and within a year it became known that the true, direct and effective organisers of the murder of Kirov, and the organisers of the preliminary steps toward the murder of other members of the Central Committee, were Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev and their accomplices. The Central Committee, in its letter to the organisations of the party issued on the occasion of the murder, drew the lesson of the events: the party organisations must liquidate their own political blindness and carelessness and raise their Bolshevik vigilance, the vigilance of all members of the party.
The trial of 1936
The trial of Zinoviev, Kamenev and their accomplices followed in Moscow in 1936. Brought before the court were Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bakaev, Evdokimov, Pikel, I. N. Smirnov, Mrachkovsky, Ter-Vaganian, Reingold and others. Caught red-handed, the criminals were obliged to acknowledge publicly, before the court, that they had organised not only the murder of Kirov but had prepared the murder of all the remaining leaders of the party and government. The investigation established further that these villains had set out upon the path of organising diversions and of espionage. The most monstrous moral and political fall of these men, the lowest-grade vileness and betrayal covered by double-dealing protestations of loyalty to the party, were laid bare in the course of the trial. The principal inspirer and organiser of the whole band of murderers and spies was the “Judas” Trotsky; the assistants of Trotsky and the executors of his counter-revolutionary instructions were Zinoviev, Kamenev and their Trotskyist following. They were preparing the defeat of the USSR in the event of an attack upon it by the imperialists; they became defeatists in relation to the workers’ and peasants’ state; they became the contemptible servants and agents of the German and Japanese fascists. In connection with the murder of Kirov, the party had already undertaken the thorough verification and the exchange of the old party documents for new ones, begun after the murder and added to the purge of the party ranks that had been started in 1933 — the cleansing of the party of the hangers-on and alien elements that the double-dealers had sheltered.
The trials of 1937
The year 1937 brought new data concerning the monsters of the Bukharinist-Trotskyist band. The judicial process in the case of Pyatakov, Radek and others, the judicial process in the case of Tukhachevsky, Yakir and others, and finally the judicial process in the case of Bukharin, Rykov, Krestinsky, Rozengolts and others — all these processes showed that the Bukharinists and Trotskyists had long ago constituted one common band of enemies of the people under the name of the “right-Trotskyist bloc” (право-троцкистский блок). The processes showed that these dregs of the human race, together with the enemies of the people Trotsky, Zinoviev and Kamenev, had been in conspiracy against Lenin, against the party and against the Soviet state from the very first days of the Great October Socialist Revolution. The provocative attempts to break the Brest peace at the beginning of 1918; the conspiracy against Lenin and the collusion with the Left SRs for the arrest and murder of Lenin, Stalin and Sverdlov in the spring of 1918; the villainous shot at Lenin and his wounding in the summer of 1918; the revolt of the Left SRs in the summer of 1918; the deliberate sharpening of disagreements in the party in 1921 in order to shake and overthrow the leadership of Lenin from within; the attempts to overthrow the leadership during Lenin’s illness and after his death; the betrayal of state secrets and the supply of espionage information to the foreign intelligence services; the villainous murder of Kirov; wrecking, diversion and explosions; the villainous murder of Menzhinsky, Kuibyshev and Gorky — all these and similar crimes, according to the account of the trials, had been committed over twenty years with the participation or under the direction of Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin, Rykov and their hangers-on, by the assignments of the foreign bourgeois intelligence services.
The liquidation of the remnants
The trials and the investigation of 1937–1938 completed the liquidation of the remnants of the Bukharinist-Trotskyist spies, wreckers and traitors to the motherland. The party presented these measures as the necessary defence of the socialist state: the construction of socialism and the adoption of the new Constitution of 1936, the first Constitution of the land of victorious socialism, had been threatened by the concealed band that sought to serve the foreign intelligence services against the Soviet people. The biography of Stalin records the political trials and the liquidation of the “enemies of the people” among the achievements of the period in which the general line of the party triumphed, and the Short Course of party history sets beside the story of the trials the party’s course on developed intra-party democracy and the preparation of the elections to the Supreme Soviet of the USSR. In the official account, the terror of 1936–1938 was not the persecution of innocents but the final cleansing of the party of its enemies — the extension of the Bolshevik vigilance that had been demanded after the murder of Kirov, and the condition of the further advance of the country along the road of socialism.

events/july-1936-coup.title: The Military Rising of 18 July 1936
events/july-1936-coup.content:
The Military Rising of 18 July 1936
17–20 July 1936.
The Alzamiento
On the night of 17 and the morning of 18 July 1936 the Spanish Army rose against the Republic. In the Moroccan protectorate the garrison of Melilla and then of Ceuta and Tetuán declared themselves first; within hours the rising — the alzamiento (the “raising” of the Army in revolt) — had spread across the peninsula, and Spain was at war with herself. Madariaga dates the purely national phase of the Civil War from precisely this moment: “the sublevación of Morocco” of 17–19 July opening the conflict, and the failure of the Nationalist assault on Madrid on 8 November closing it. The rising was not, the Nationalist military historian Aznar insisted with great force, a pronunciamiento — not the classic nineteenth-century barracks coup by which a handful of officers toppled a ministry. It was, in his telling, a military and popular movement, an “action and reaction of the national army,” which the failure of the first days would not have broken because it rested not on the professional habits of a clique but on the adhesion of the nation itself.
The Plane Inclined
The rising did not spring from a void. Tusell traces the long “plano inclinado” — the inclined plane — down which the Republic slid through the spring and summer of 1936, when the violence and political paralysis brought the state to the point of the military conspiracy. The February elections had returned the Popular Front to government; Azaña, who had presided over the Republic’s reforming years, headed a cabinet that could neither command the streets nor reconcile the right. Armed factions on both flanks collided in the pueblos; the monarchist, Falangist and traditionalist parties had sought help abroad, the republican authorities publishing the pacts the monarchists had made with Mussolini in 1934 to expose the plot. The conspiracy itself had been long in preparation, and its centre lay in the north. The Director of the plot, General Mola, working from Pamplona among the Carlist requetés of Navarre, wove the network of garrisons into a design for a simultaneous rising of the Army and of the national parties.
The Murder of Calvo Sotelo
The final precipitant was political assassination. On 13 July 1936, five days before the rising, José Calvo Sotelo, the leader of the monarchist right and the man Aznar would call the great martyr of the cause, was killed in Madrid. His murder, carried out by men of the state security forces, removed the last hopes of a constitutional rallying of the right and delivered the argument into the hands of the plotters. Aznar, writing from within the Nationalist camp, sets beside this death the years of accumulated grievance — the army blamed and persecuted since the loss of Cuba, the Republic’s military reforms that had broken the old officer corps, the “monstrous exaggeration” of a political system that had taught the army to see itself as the axis and living spring of Spanish life. “It is the spinal column of the Patria,” Calvo Sotelo had said of the army, in the phrase Aznar recalls at his murder; it was that same army which now, in July 1936, rose to seize the State.
The Division of Spain
The rising succeeded in much of the north and in the provincial capitals, and failed in Madrid and Barcelona and along the Mediterranean coast. The great cities — the capital, the Catalan industrial world, the Levante — remained loyal to the Republic; the garrisons of Old Castile, Navarre, Aragón, Galicia and much of Andalusia declared for the movement. The two zones of the war took shape within days: the Republic holding Madrid, the central tableland and the Mediterranean littoral, the Nationalists commanding the northern meseta, the Pyrenean borderlands and the Army of Africa. The fleet, in large part, stayed with the government, and it was the passage of that Army of Africa — the Legion and the Moorish Regulares — across the Strait from Morocco in the weeks that followed that first turned the rising into a war. Madariaga’s framing of the phases of the conflict rests on this division: the first, purely national phase, fought between Spaniards, running from the alzamiento to the first winter, gave way in time to a phase of foreign infiltration and then of foreign domination, as the forces Franco and his lieutenants had summoned to their aid — and the Soviet advisers, the International Brigades and the whole weight of the intervention — came in from without.
The War Declared
Within a week the rising had become a civil war. The Nationalist junta at Burgos gathered the authority of the rebel zone; the generals of the peninsula — Mola in the north, Queipo de Llano in the south from his audacious seizure of Seville, Franco assuming the command of the Army of Africa — emerged as the movement’s leaders. From the Republic’s side, the government was forced to arm the popular militias to meet the columns advancing on Madrid, and the revolution of the rear-guard began almost immediately, as the proletarian masses who had not risen against the government yet would not obey it set about a syndical revolution in the name of the struggle against fascism. Azaña’s retrospective verdict, which Tusell records, held that the republican government faced henceforward two enemies at once — the military movement marching on the capital and the insurrection of the masses — and that its chief task through the whole war would be to reduce those masses to discipline. On 18 July 1936 the first of these enemies had already struck; the long effort to contain the second, and the long war that followed, had begun.

events/liberation-of-rome-1944.title: The Liberation of Rome (4 June 1944)
events/liberation-of-rome-1944.content:
The Liberation of Rome (4 June 1944)
4 June 1944
The entry of the Allied armies into Rome on 4 June 1944, which broke the German hold on the capital almost a year after the armistice of 8 September 1943. For the cobelligerent Italian government of Marshal badoglio, driven from Rome to Brindisi and then to Salerno during the German occupation, the fall of the city was both the military end of a long advance up the peninsula and the signal for the constitutional settlement of the monarchy: on the very day of liberation the King, at Ravello, signed the decree handing the royal power to his son as Lieutenant of the Realm, and within days the wartime government resigned to make way for a democratic administration led by the anti-Fascist parties gathered at last in the liberated capital.
The collapse of the Gustav line
The advance that broke into Rome was the fruit of a change of plan by the Allied commander, General Alexander, who had made a profound study of his operations in Italy and recognised the causes of his lack of success. He had radically changed his plans, concentrating all his available resources in one area: he left a thin covering force in the Adriatic sector, of obviously secondary importance, and by a carefully co-ordinated and rapid manoeuvre massed his two armies in front of the “Gustav” line. He chose as the spearhead of the attack the French Corps, consisting chiefly of Moroccan troops, and the Polish Corps, both imbued with the spirit of the offensive; the British and Americans were on either flank of Cassino. After a bitter resistance the Germans began to fall back, losing one strong position after another. Marshal Kesselring, the German commander, then threw all his remaining reserves into the battle, which in Badoglio’s judgement was his most serious mistake: he had no forces left to cover the inevitable withdrawal, and only postponed for a few days the very rapid collapse of the line. The Americans on the west established contact with the troops on the Anzio beachhead, who then went over to the attack.
Badoglio hastened to send his warmest congratulations to General Alexander, telling him of the ardent desire of the Italian Corps of Liberation (Corpo italiano di liberazione) to be sent to the front as soon as possible. Alexander welcomed the request, saying he had always been very pleased with the conduct of the Italian detachments in the front line, and gave orders for the army corps to go into action at once; it began the attack in the mountain sector and met with complete success. The advance of the Allied troops became more rapid, and shortly afterwards the government was informed that the advance guard had entered Rome — 4 June 1944, as the translator’s note records.
The King and the Lieutenant of the Realm
The liberation coincided with the final act of the constitutional question that had shadowed the monarchy since the coup of 25 July 1943. General Mason-MacFarlane, the Allied chief in Italy, came to Badoglio and asked him to go with him to see the King at Ravello. On the way he explained that, as the Allied troops had now entered Rome, it was essential that the King should at once sign the decree handing over the royal power and prerogatives to the Lieutenant of the Realm (Luogotenente del Regno). It was impossible, he added, to grant the King’s request to go to Rome: for reasons of security the Allied authorities could not consent until the enemy had been compelled to retreat some distance from the city, which would take days, and such a delay would antagonise public opinion in England and the United States and arouse doubts as to the validity of the royal proclamation.
At Ravello, General Mason-MacFarlane explained all this to the King and asked him to sign the decree. But the King declared he would not sign it unless he were given a letter, signed by the Head of the Government, informing him officially that the Allies refused to allow him to proceed to Rome immediately. With Mason-MacFarlane’s agreement Badoglio at once wrote and signed the letter, stating that notwithstanding the earnest and frequently expressed desire of the King to reach Rome by any means available, the Allied Supreme Command could not accede to the request, and therefore it was unavoidable that the decree should be signed. His Majesty then appended his signature at Ravello, appointing his son Prince Umberto Lieutenant-General of the Realm, conferring the royal prerogatives on him in perpetuity, and Badoglio countersigned. “So ended the reign of a King who, for forty-four years in good and evil fortune, had guided the destinies of Italy.” victor-emmanuel-iii, the sovereign who had appointed Mussolini in 1922 and dismissed him in 1943, thus surrendered the effective crown in the hour of the capital’s liberation.
The resignation of the government
Now that the Lieutenant of the Realm had taken up his office, Badoglio hurriedly consulted the experts in the Cabinet office as to whether, according to constitutional practice, the Cabinet should resign. The answer was that, as the transfer of powers was irrevocable, the Cabinet should resign in order to leave the Lieutenant free either to confirm it in office or to choose new ministers. Badoglio called a meeting of the Cabinet and informed the members of what had happened at Ravello, and of the advice he had received — that it was necessary to resign; the Lord Privy Seal, Signor Arangio Ruiz, speaking as a legal expert, maintained that this was not the case. But the next day, when Badoglio was going to Naples to see the Lieutenant and receive his instructions, Mason-MacFarlane asked him to come to his office on the way. He told Badoglio that during the morning he had sent for Dr. De Nicola, who had given the same opinion as the experts — that the whole Cabinet must resign. Mason-MacFarlane added that it was not advisable to increase the Cabinet by creating other ministries; it would be better for Badoglio to go to Rome without a Cabinet, so that he could include in the new Government the politicians who were in Rome, leaving behind the members of the resigning Cabinet. There was no time to return to Salerno to consult the Cabinet; as it was Tuesday he had only Wednesday to publish the news of the resignation and arrange a meeting of the political leaders in Rome for Thursday, and Badoglio and six ministers, one for each political party, were to leave by air for Rome on Thursday morning.
The democratic government
The Lieutenant-General, who had already been coached by Mason-MacFarlane, accepted the resignation of the Cabinet and invited Badoglio to form a new Government to include the politicians in Rome. On Thursday morning Badoglio and the six ministers flew to Rome; at the Grand Hotel they found the leaders of the six parties and Signor Bonomi waiting — Casati for the Liberals, Ruini for Democratic Labour, De Gasperi for the Christian Democrats, Nenni for the Socialists, Cianca for the Action Party, and Togliatti for the Communists. Badoglio gave a brief account of the situation, Croce and Sforza adding a few words, and begged the leaders to discuss their future line of action and to meet him again at six o’clock to tell him what they had decided.
At six the proceedings began. Ruini stated that his party considered that, if the Government was to be really and completely democratic, it must have a head who was not a soldier, and that this head should be Signor Bonomi; similar declarations were made by Casati, De Gasperi and Cianca without comment, and Nenni said he was of the same opinion, adding that he did not approve of the enlargement of the Cabinet by ministers without portfolios, since the new Government, to act effectively and rapidly, should not consist of more than seven or eight ministers. Togliatti said the Communists wished to act with the other parties and therefore supported Ruini’s motion, though he would regret being separated from Badoglio, with whom they had worked so harmoniously. Badoglio rose and shook Togliatti’s hand, thanking the leaders for expressing their views so clearly: “I have served my country to the best of my ability, and I willingly resign my post into the more expert hands of my friend Bonomi.” He added a pointed reminder — “It is not because of any action on your part that you have met round this table in Rome; you were in hiding or living safely with friars in convents. The man who has done the work, who has shouldered the heaviest responsibilities, is that soldier, who, as Ruini has said, does not belong to any party.” He then went to see the Lieutenant, who had arrived in Rome during the day, and suggested that he should at once send for Bonomi; the next day Badoglio returned to Salerno, and the wartime government of Marshal Badoglio, which had carried Italy from the coup of July 1943 through the armistice and the cobelligerence, gave way to the government of democratic unity of Ivanoe Bonomi.

events/march-on-rome-1922.title: The March on Rome (24–29 October 1922)
events/march-on-rome-1922.content:
The March on Rome (24–29 October 1922)
24–29 October 1922
The concentration of the Fascist squads upon the capital and the seizure of the State that followed — the adunata (gathering) of Naples, the proclamation of the quadrumvirate of action, the mobilisation of the Blackshirts through a central Italy that fell without a blow, and the King’s refusal to sign the decree of siege, which delivered the premiership to mussolini. The march was the revolutionary act that closed the phase of squadrism and opened the one of power; for the regime’s own historians it was the passage from the Italy of the Parliament to the Italy of Vittorio Veneto.
The preparations and the gathering of Naples
Throughout the summer and autumn of 1922 the Fascist leadership prepared a stroke, and the ministry of Facta drifted without perceiving it. Volpe records that after the victory over the general strike of August the revolutionary current in the Party swelled rather than the moderate one; the government “by right” had never been more passive and the government “by fact” more firmly implanted. In September the Fascists moved in the Alto Adige, seizing Bolzano and Trento under De Stefani, Giunta, Farinacci and Starace, and the cry ran through the country that this was a stage of that march on Rome which men sensed was not far off. Mussolini announced a concentration of Blackshirts at Naples for 24 October, and at Udine on the 20th of September spoke of Rome as “the palpitating heart of imperial Italy,” declaring that the regime could be changed and the monarchy left untouched — “we must have the courage to be monarchical.”
The plan was settled in secrecy. On the 29th of September the Directorat e of the Party met at Rome and Mussolini traced the lines of the movement; on 16 October at Milan, in the seat of the Fascio primogenito, he gathered the generals Fara and Ceccherini with De Vecchi, Bianchi and Balbo and, refusing all further delay, named a quadrumvirato (quadrumvirate) — De Bono, De Vecchi, Balbo and Bianchi — with full powers from the beginning of the revolutionary action. The colonels of the squadre fixed the points of concentration twenty or thirty kilometres from the capital: Santa Marinella and Monterotondo for the columns of the centre and north, Tivoli for the forces from the Abruzzi, a reserve at Foligno, and the Perugia command, while the southern legions under Captain Padovani were to hold the Volturno and mask the movement of troops.
At Naples the plan was rehearsed before the crowd. On 24 October, before the adunata of some forty thousand Fascists and thirty thousand workers, Mussolini spoke at the San Carlo theatre: “We are at the point where the arrow must leave the bow, or the over-stretched string of the bow must break.” In the Piazza San Ferdinando, as the columns filed past after a three-hour march, he gave the crowd its formula — “we shall be given the government or we shall take it, advancing on Rome” — and the cry went up, “To Rome, to Rome.” The congress that followed was, in Businelli’s frank phrase, a “lustra,” dust thrown in the eyes of the timid men of Rome; Bianchi hurried the speakers along with the historical remark, “Fascists, at Naples it is raining — what are you doing here?”
The mobilisation
On the evening of 26 October secret orders went out to the principi and triari for an immediate mobilisation, and by midnight the plans were in execution. A proclamation, signed by the quadrumvirate, recalled the anniversary of the Piave offensive: “Today, the army of the Blackshirts affirms the mutilated victory and, advancing at all costs on Rome, will bring back the glory of that victory to the Capitol.” It called on the army to stand outside the struggle, which was “against a political class of weaklings which for four years has not known how to rule the nation.” In the great cities the Fascists took possession of the public offices, the post and telegraph offices, the prefetture and questure, and seized the arms where they could; there was bloodshed at Casale Monferrato, Cremona and in the Bolognese, but in general, as Volpe writes, astute and audacious action took the public forces by surprise and left them unable to react. The columns of Igliori, Perrone and Bottai moved upon Monterotondo, Santa Marinella and Tivoli; the Quadrumvirate directed operations from Perugia, which had fallen after the Prefect surrendered to avoid bloodshed.
The ministry met at the Viminale on the evening of the 26th and placed its portfolios at the disposal of the President; Facta remained to keep order. The King, who had been at San Rossore, returned to Rome on the evening of the 27th, acclaimed by Fascists and Nationalists at the station, and accepted the resignation of the Cabinet. But the fallen ministry did not die quietly. That night it sat in permanence, strung barbed wire across the bridges of the Tiber, set cannon on Monte Mario, and resolved to proclaim the stato d’assedio (state of siege) throughout the Kingdom from noon of 28 October, publishing a message that spoke of its duty “to maintain order by every means and at any cost.” Facta had been egged on by his most anti-Fascist ministers, Taddei and Amendola.
The King’s refusal
The decree of siege was submitted to the King on the morning of 28 October, in the certainty that he would sign it. He did not. Farinacci, the squadrist historian, casts the moment as the working of a royal education and of history itself — Victor Emmanuel, who had forced the Salandra ministry into the war in May 1915 against the majority of the Chamber, would not now sign the decree that declared civil war against the Italians who had wanted that war. The King declared the measure “neither serious nor opportune.” Facta returned to press him, pleading that the proclamation had already been given to the press and the measures partly taken; the King refused again — “the state of siege, no.” At 12.40 on the 28th the Stefani agency announced that the proclamation had no more force. Pini records the King’s words to De Vecchi at the Quirinal: “I desire that the Italians should know that I did not wish to sign the state of siege.” In Rome a great crowd gathered under the Quirinal crying “Viva il Re”; the nightmare of a river of blood had passed. Volpe, writing from within the regime, draws the larger meaning: there was no defection of the army, which had been the nation’s flower and carried the traditions of the war; it simply adapted itself to the new situation and did not open fire on comrades in grey-green.
The call to power
The refusal of the siege decided the issue, but not yet the form. A ministry of Salandra, with the participation of the best Fascists, was floated in the corridors and pressed upon Mussolini, who was holding himself deliberately at a distance, at Milan, with rifle in hand behind the barricades of the Popolo d’Italia. The reply was instantaneous and absolute: “It was not worth mobilising the Fascist army, making a revolution, having our dead, for a Salandra–Mussolini solution and four portfolios. I do not accept.” He refused even to come to Rome to discuss the “resolution of the grave political moment” unless the King formally and publicly entrusted him with the formation of the new government. On the evening of the 29th, invited to the capital, he left Milan. On 30 October, before the King, he pronounced the ritual words, “Maestà, vi porto l’Italia di Vittorio Veneto” — Majesty, I bring you the Italy of Vittorio Veneto — and presented the list of his ministry, which included General Diaz and Admiral Thaon di Revel. A hundred thousand Blackshirts massed in the Villa Borghese, filed past the Duce, rendered homage at the Altare della Patria and marched to the Quirinal to salute the King, before the order for demobilisation came down on 31 October and the squadre returned to their homes.
The March on Rome was, in the phrase Pini closes his chapter with, the most revolutionary act the history of Italy could boast — not because it had been almost bloodless, but because it was a sovvertimento of laws, customs and mentality, the opening rather than the closing of the Fascist revolution. The old Italy had been swept aside; the work of consolidating the State still lay ahead.

events/matteotti-crisis-1924.title: The Matteotti Crisis (June–November 1924)
events/matteotti-crisis-1924.content:
The Matteotti Crisis (June–November 1924)
10 June – November 1924
The murder of the socialist deputy Giacomo matteotti on 10 June 1924, and the political crisis that followed — the violent press campaign against Fascism, the resignation of Cesare Rossi and the arrest of his associates, the secession of the opposition deputies upon the Aventine, and the long, disciplined wait of the provincial Blackshirts that finally forced the Duce back upon the offensive. The regime’s own historians called it the prova (the trial), the proof that would reveal what the March on Rome had not yet completed; for the opposition it was the moment when the parliamentary State reasserted the moral question against the government.
The summer’s discontent
The spring of 1924 had seen Fascism at its apparent height. The elections of April had returned a great Fascist majority, and in May the Duce made a triumphal tour of Sicily. Yet beneath the surface there was unease. Volpe records a wave of discontent and restlessness within the Party and, more still, in the great mass outside it; the Corriere della Sera of Milan and the Stampa of Turin directed their fire upon the whole work and doctrine of Fascism, demanding a return to “normality,” the reintegration of the parliamentary system, and the end of the form of government Fascism had introduced. Pini, writing from within the movement, traces the weakness differently: the opposition was regaining courage from the longanimity of the Duce, the provincial Fascists distrusted a central leadership in which, he insisted, unworthy and insufficient men had lodged themselves, and the police and the bureaucracy remained men of the Nitti and Giolitti era, largely inscribed in Freemasonry. On 7 June Mussolini spoke to the Chamber of the need for fraternal collaboration among all Italians; his appeal was substantially rejected by the constitutional and socialist oppositions alike. For the constitutionalists Amendola spoke, calling for the abolition of the Militia and the regular functioning of parliament; for the socialists, in an acridly hostile tone, spoke Matteotti, just returned from France and England.
The crime of 10 June
On the afternoon of 10 June 1924 Matteotti was set upon and seized on the outskirts of Rome by a group of determined men and killed in the struggle. The squadristi who had done the deed concealed the body, so that on the 11th only the disappearance of the socialist deputy was known; Montecitorio was in an uproar and the socialist group agitated. Pini, the regime’s chronicler, insists that the assassination was an error before it was a crime — carried out by individuals who had boasted of their squadrist past and struck up friendships with the obliqui personages whose presence in the high spheres of the Party, he had argued, was proving so nefasta; they had even borrowed the automobile from the director of one of the so-called Fascist newspapers of Rome. The Duce at once issued the severest orders that the light should be made and the guilty arrested; the police and the magistrature searched feverishly but did not find the body, and, driven by the fever of the inquest and the frenzy of the opposition press, went further and involved men of faith who, Pini insists, had nothing to do with the affair — it would take two years to discover it. Cesare Rossi, one of the triumvirs of the directorate, resigned and was arrested after a few days of hiding; Marinelli, “absolutely ignorant of everything,” was also arrested. The body was found only later, at the Quartarella near Rome; the finding did not quiet the campaign, which continued, in the words of the hostile chronicle, “indisturbed and implacable.”
The press campaign and the Aventine
The murder became, in Pini’s phrase, the pretesto for unchaining all the anti-Fascist hatred that had been smouldering under the ashes of Roman political journalism. The Duce had words of execration in the Chamber — “only an enemy who had thought of something diabolical against me for long nights could have carried out this crime” — but the opposition would not let the occasion slip. Matteotti was not the true aim; the true aim was to bring down Mussolini and Fascism. Volpe, the academic apologist, records the same storm from the other side: the crime was made the very most of in the country and abroad in order to destroy the credit and power of Fascism, and the whole movement was defamed “from the leader to the last-joined member.” A hundred deputies from the various branches of the opposition left Parliament as a protest, hoping by this action to lower the legal status of the Chamber and impede its functioning; they were, in Volpe’s account, “the true and legitimate representation of the nation.” It was the Aventino (the Aventine) against Montecitorio — the secession of the parliamentary oppositions, so named after the hill to which the plebeians of ancient Rome withdrew.
There was, Volpe admits, a check in the moral and numerical development of Fascism — a “profound moral oscillation in the mass of the people,” as he quotes Mussolini himself admitting. Among Fascists and sympathisers there was uncertainty, perplexity, even the beginning of a break-away; many who had prudently kept contact with both camps turned their backs, as did many university professors and intellectuals, a large part of the ministerial bureaucracy, and the greater part of Freemasonry. Government activity was checked and even foreign policy affected.
The provincial riscossa
The salvation of the regime, in Pini’s account, came from the provinces. “This is your hour, O Blackshirts of the provinces!” — the cry of the intransigent Fascists. From Bologna, the city of 8 August and 21 November, came the imperious call to assembly; on 19 June fifty thousand Fascists gathered in the city, with music and song, before the Palazzo d’Accursio, where Grandi told them that it was not the fate of a party but of the whole nation that was at stake, and that the counter-offensive began that day. On the 22nd the provincial leaders of the Po valley renewed their oath. Two legions of the most faithful Blackshirts, the Francesco Ferruccio of Florence and the Ferrarese, were sent to Rome. In early August the National Council of the Party met in Rome; the intransigent programme, urged by the journals of the provinces such as L’Assalto of Bologna, Il Selvaggio of Colle Val d’Elsa and La Conquista dello Stato of Rome, won its first success, and the Duce closed with the watchword “Vivi pericolosamente!” — live dangerously. He told the oppositions to exhaust themselves; he imposed on the Fascists the command, Mani in tasca (hands in your pockets), to endure the campaign without reply — but an endurance, he warned, that was not weakness, only an awaiting.
So passed the summer and autumn of 1924. The oppositions continued their insidious campaign; the liberals met at Livorno and went over to decided opposition, as did the Combattenti at Assisi; Giovanni Amendola called the season “an estate di maturazione,” a summer of ripening, believing victory was maturing for the oppositions. It was to prove otherwise. The crisis had separated the true Fascists from the false friends, had revealed the weakness of a movement that had neither a true press nor a purified leadership. For the regime’s own historians the Matteotti crisis was the proof that showed what had to be corrected, and it set the stage for the counter-stroke of 3 January 1925, when the Duce, in Volpe’s words, showed that he was ready to take again the helm of the ship of State and to engage in a decisive battle — the end of the Aventine and the beginning of the open dictatorship.
