events/munich-agreement-1938.title: The Munich Agreement (29–30 September 1938)
events/munich-agreement-1938.content:
The Munich Agreement (29–30 September 1938)
29–30 September 1938
The conference of the four powers in Munich on 29–30 September 1938 at which Germany, Great Britain, France and Italy agreed to the cession of the Sudetenland to the Reich, and the Czechoslovak government, summoned to accept their decision, submitted under protest. The agreement that ended the Sudeten crisis by sacrificing Czechoslovakia to the peace of Europe — the high point of the policy of appeasement, the greatest territorial triumph yet of hitler’s diplomacy, and the moment the German documentary record would present as the establishment of Greater Germany. For France, the anxious chronicle of Daniel Halévy records, the crisis brought Europe to the very brink of war, and Munich postponed the war without dissolving the threat.
The crisis
The crisis gathered through the spring and summer of 1938, when the annexation of Austria in March had already enlarged the Reich and left Czechoslovakia, with its large German minority in the borderlands — the Sudetengebiet (Sudeten territory) — as the next object of German pressure. The agitation of the Sudeten German Party under Henlein, the refusal of the Prague government to concede the autonomy demanded, and the steady drumbeat of German propaganda worked on each other through the summer months. Halévy, chronicling the year as it passed, records first the deceptive calm — the euphorie estivale (summer euphoria) of a Europe that hoped, against the evidence, that war might after all be avoided — and then the abrupt descent into crisis in September. The tension mounted week by week; France and Britain mobilised in alarm; and as the month wore on the Czechoslovak question flew, in Halévy’s phrase, toward the very brink of war. Hitler’s speech to the Nuremberg party congress in September, and his demand for the return of the Sudetenland, brought the confrontation to its head.
The four-power conference
At the last moment the great powers moved to avert the catastrophe. The British prime minister, Chamberlain, had already flown twice to see Hitler in Germany in September, and now proposed a conference of the powers concerned. On 29 September 1938 the four heads of government met at Munich — Hitler for Germany, Chamberlain for Great Britain, Daladier for France and Mussolini for Italy; Czechoslovakia was not admitted to the meeting, only to the acceptance of its outcome. The Italian account, recorded by Foreign Minister Ciano in his speech to the Chamber in Rome on 30 November, gives the shape of the proceedings: it was the Duce, he said, who brought the exchange of views onto practical ground, putting forward a proposal which the German government had already accepted in principle and which, apart from unavoidable changes of form, was adopted as the final solution; it was the Duce, too, who raised the question of the Polish and Hungarian minorities and proposed the immediate formation of the executive commission. Chamberlain himself, in his speech to the House of Commons on 3 October, acknowledged Mussolini’s contribution as “very remarkable and perhaps decisive,” and gave thanks to the chief of the Italian government for his work toward a peaceful solution.
The agreement
The agreement reached in Munich rested on the cession of the predominantly German districts of the Sudetenland. Germany, the United Kingdom, France and Italy, taking account of the understanding on the cession that had already been reached in principle, agreed on the conditions and modalities of the transfer and declared themselves individually responsible for securing its execution. The evacuation was to begin on 1 October and be completed by 10 October, without the destruction of any existing installations, the Czechoslovak government bearing responsibility that the evacuation was carried out without damage to the designated institutions. The modalities were to be fixed by an international commission composed of representatives of Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Italy and Czechoslovakia. The occupation of the predominantly German territory by German troops was to proceed in stages, the four zones marked on the annexed map being occupied in order — the first zone on 1 and 2 October, the second on 2 and 3, the third on 3, 4 and 5, the fourth on 6 and 7 — while the remaining territory of predominantly German character, to be fixed by the international commission, would be occupied by 10 October. The commission was also to determine the areas in which a plebiscite was to be held, these areas to be occupied by international formations until the vote was completed. The Czechoslovak government, under Beneš, met at noon on Friday 30 September and accepted the Munich decisions of the four great powers, in full awareness, its official report stated, of the historical responsibility, and with the consent of the responsible factors of the political parties — while at the same time raising protest against the one-sided decision taken without its participation.
The establishment of Greater Germany
The German record of the year closes the account in its own terms. In the weeks that followed Munich the transfer was completed and legalised: the German-Czechoslovak declaration on the protection of the mutual Volksgruppen (national groups) of 20 November, the final delimitation of the German-Czechoslovak frontier of 21 November, and the law on the reunion of the Sudeten German territories with the German Reich of 21 November, followed by the introduction of Reich labour service and the Nuremberg race laws into the new territories. The Sudetenland, added to the Austria already annexed in March, made the Third Reich “Greater Germany” — the territorial triumph the volume celebrates, and the frontier on which the enlarged Reich now pressed against the truncated rump of Czechoslovakia.
The aftermath
Halévy, writing as a Frenchman at the moment, gives the other face of the event. The September mobilisation had brought France and Europe to the edge of war; Munich turned back from that edge, and the relief was real and general. But the relief was shadowed, in his telling, by the knowledge of what had been bought with the sacrifice of an ally and by the shame of the peace that had been purchased. His closing chapter, “the last eddies,” records the final disturbances of the autumn and the calm of December — the year turning toward 1939 with the threat of war postponed but not dissolved. The agreement that had averted the immediate catastrophe had not resolved the crisis that produced it; the peace of Munich was, in the chronicler’s implied judgement, a reprieve rather than a settlement.

events/night-of-the-long-knives-1934.title: The Night of the Long Knives (30 June 1934)
events/night-of-the-long-knives-1934.content:
The Night of the Long Knives (30 June 1934)
30 June 1934
The action of 30 June through 2 July 1934 in which hitler, striking with the SS and the Gestapo, broke the leadership of the storm detachments and settled a wider account of blood — the deposition and murder of the SA chief of staff Ernst roehm, the shooting of General von Schleicher and of gregor-strasser, and the killing of others across the Reich that the regime would present as the suppression of a plot and retrospectively legalise as Staatsnotwehr (state self-defence). The purge removed the last internal force that stood between the Führer and absolute rule, and fixed the dictatorship in a month of murder.
The crisis of the storm detachments
Through the first months of 1934 the SA — the brown-shirted Sturmabteilung (storm detachment), two or three million strong — pressed against the limits the new regime had set it. Its chief of staff, Ernst Röhm, an old comrade of Hitler and the builder of the force, wanted the SA to be the nucleus of a new army of the revolution; the professional officers of the Reichswehr, who had helped put Hitler in power, demanded the SA’s reduction and the preservation of the army’s monopoly of arms. Heiden, writing a year later, describes the summer as an “unplanned dictatorship” sliding toward catastrophe: Röhm’s advances met with evasion, then with hostility; the Reichswehr leadership, with the field marshal President von Hindenburg behind it, made the demotion of the SA a condition of its continued support. Meanwhile voices around Röhm spoke openly of a “second revolution” that would complete what the first had left undone — a revolution that would sweep away the old officers, the conservatives and the men of the first hour who now stood in the way. The SA chief, whose “unfortunate disposition” the regime’s own documents would later cite, pressed his claims without discretion and entered, Heiden records, into dangerous contacts with General von Schleicher, the former chancellor, who had his own score to settle with the men who had displaced him.
The purge
On 30 June Hitler struck. He flew to Munich, then to the country retreat where Röhm and the SA leaders had gathered, and the arrests began; in Berlin, in the provinces, the SS and the secret police rounded up the brownshirt commanders through the night and shot many of them on the spot. Heiden’s chapter on the 30th of June is a catalogue of what an armed state does when it turns on its own party: the armoured cars and the pistol, the shootings of the SA men, the settling of accounts that had nothing to do with Röhm at all. General von Schleicher, shot in his house with his wife, was killed for the conspirator he had been or was alleged to be; Gregor Strasser, the fallen rival of the party’s left, was murdered in prison; conservative figures who had spoken against the regime — Heiden notes the Marburg speech and the resentment it drew — were swept up in the same bloodbath. Röhm himself was taken, and after Hitler refused to order his execution by his own hand, was shot in his cell on the following day. The purge ran on into the night of the first and the second of July, and the dead included, by the official tally later published, among others the SA chief of staff and a former Reich Chancellor.
The state’s account
The regime’s own documentary record of 1934 tells the event from the victor’s side, and it is instructive. The decree of 30 June deposed Röhm as chief of staff and expelled him from the SA and the party, and appointed the Obergruppenführer Lutze in his place; the Führer’s letter to Lutze spoke of the “gravest failings” of his predecessor. The published commentary enumerated those who had been shot — nineteen senior SA leaders, thirty-one SA leaders and men, three SS leaders, thirteen SA leaders and civilians who resisted arrest, and five party comrades, among them Röhm and General Schleicher — and set out the official charge: that the chief of staff, in collaboration with outside elements, had prepared a high-treasonous rising, and that the Führer and the government had been forced to the sharpest intervention. The law on measures of state self-defence of 3 July declared the measures taken on 30 June, 1 and 2 July to be “lawful as state self-defence” (als Staatsnotwehr rechtens); Hindenburg’s telegrams of 2 July thanked Hitler and conveyed the satisfaction of the President and the army; and in his speech to the Reichstag on 13 July Hitler, having described the plot, assumed full responsibility for the shootings and declared that during those twenty-four hours he had been the supreme court of the German people. The Reichswehr minister von Blomberg, in the cabinet, thanked Hitler for having saved the German people from civil war.
The meaning of the massacre
The two sources of the event could not diverge further, and the contrast is the history. For the regime the purge was a justified act of self-defence, the crushing of a treacherous plot by the SA leadership, crowned by Hindenburg’s approval and the applause of the army. For Heiden, writing from exile, it was a settling of accounts that revealed the nature of the power that had been built: an “end with terror,” the murder of the SA leaders who had served Hitler’s rise, of the prince who had once stood at his side, of Schleicher and Strasser and of nameless men shot for scores that had nothing to do with any plot. Heiden closes his biography not with the great victims but with a Munich lawyer, Dr. Glaser, shot by three SS men on the evening of 30 June — the ashes of the unknown German who fell victim, in his phrase, to the highest responsibility assumed on that day. The purge had done its work: the SA was tamed under Lutze, the army was bound to Hitler, and two months later, on the death of Hindenburg, the Führer united in his own person the offices of President and Chancellor, and the Wehrmacht swore its oath to him.

events/nuremberg-laws-1935.title: Nuremberg Laws (15 September 1935)
events/nuremberg-laws-1935.content:
Nuremberg Laws (15 September 1935)
15 September 1935 — the Reichstag, summoned to Nuremberg during the party congress, passed the Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour, together with the Reich Flag Law. The three laws, adopted unanimously, gave statutory form to the racial programme that had stood at the head of the party’s platform since 1920 and defined the place of the Jew in the German state.
The setting
The congress at which the laws were proclaimed was the Reich Party Congress of the year, which had assembled on 11 September and was named, on account of the recovery of the military sovereignty (Wehrhoheit), the “Party Congress of Freedom” (Parteitag der Freiheit). Its high points, beside the proclamation of the Führer, were Goebbels’ speech against Bolshevism on 13 September, the day of the Labour Service and the SA, the great march of the Hitler Youth, the Führer’s cultural address, and the closing speech. On 15 September the Reichstag, which had been summoned to Nuremberg, was to pass the laws. Goebbels’ speech of the 13th against Bolshevism, delivered in this setting, set the tone of the congress’s racial vocabulary — the rejection of the “internationalism” that was alleged to dissolve the natural bonds of nation and race, and the claim that the National Socialist state upheld race, personality and nation against the forces that would destroy them.
The Reich Citizenship Law
The Reichsbürgergesetz (Reich Citizenship Law) distinguished between the state subject and the citizen of the Reich. A state subject (Staatsangehöriger) was one who belonged to the protective union of the German Reich and was specially obligated to it; nationality was acquired under the Reich and State Citizenship Law. But the Reich citizen (Reichsbürger) was only the state subject of German or kindred blood who by his conduct proved that he was willing and able to serve the German people and Reich in loyalty, and the right of Reich citizenship was acquired through the grant of the Reich Citizen’s Certificate (Reichsbürgerbrief). The Reich citizen alone was the bearer of full political rights in accordance with the laws. The official footnote traced the law to the ideas developed by Hitler in the third chapter of the second book of Mein Kampf, and to point 4 of the party programme: only a national comrade (Volksgenosse) could be a citizen, only one of German blood could be a national comrade without regard to confession, and therefore no Jew could be a national comrade. The first implementing ordinance of 14 November 1935 gave the final definition of who was a Jew; the second ordinance of 21 December concerned Jewish officials and the holders of public office.
The Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour
The second law was prefaced by the declaration that, penetrated by the knowledge that the purity of German blood was the precondition for the continued existence of the German people and animated by the unyielding will to secure the German nation for all future, the Reichstag had unanimously resolved the law. It forbade marriages between Jews and state subjects of German or kindred blood, declaring even marriages contracted abroad to evade the law void, with the action for annulment reserved to the public prosecutor. Extra-marital intercourse between Jews and such state subjects was forbidden. Jews were forbidden to employ in their households female state subjects of German or kindred blood under the age of forty-five. Jews were forbidden to fly the Reich and national flag or to show the Reich colours, while the showing of the Jewish colours was permitted under state protection. The penalties ranged from penal servitude for the forbidden marriage to imprisonment of up to a year and a fine for the lesser contraventions; the law took effect on the day after its promulgation, except for the clause on the employment of women, which entered into force on 1 January 1936.
The programme fulfilled
In the compilation of Büttner the Nuremberg Laws stand as the realisation of the programmatic points on land and colonies, on racial citizenship, and on the treatment of non-citizens as guests under aliens law — the whole second and third blocks of the party’s 1920 platform. The Reichsbürgergesetz and the Blood-Protection Law of 15 September were followed in the party’s own documentary record by the implementing ordinances of 1935 to 1939, by the law on Jewish cultural associations of 1938, the ordinance on identity cards and passports of Jews of 5 October 1938, the ordinance against the possession of arms by Jews of 11 November, and the ordinances of November 1938 excluding Jews from German economic life. The Reich Flag Law of the same day made the swastika flag of the party the national flag of the Reich. The exclusion begun in Nuremberg in 1935 — the denial of citizenship to the Jew, the criminalisation of the “mixed” marriage, the segregation of the races — supplied the legal frame upon which the successive measures of the following years built, down to the forced emigration and the deportations of the war years.

events/occupation-of-the-factories-1920.title: The Occupation of the Factories (September 1920)
events/occupation-of-the-factories-1920.content:
The Occupation of the Factories (September 1920)
September – October 1920
The seizure of the metalworks of Italy by their workers in September 1920, at the height of the biennio rosso — the lockout of the Romeo works, the occupation of the Milan factories by night, the armed life of the red-guard garrisons, and the eventual evacuation on the promise of a workers’ control that was never to be given. Farinacci called it the most dangerous, the most intense and the most vast of the convulsive movements of the Italian postwar; for the Fascist historians it proved the incapacity of the revolutionaries and, more than anything else, persuaded the Italian middle classes that a new force was needed to hold the State. It was the decisive defeat that opened the way for the Fascist reaction.
The crisis of the metalworkers
The autumn of 1920 found Italy in the grip of the “red two years,” a wave of strikes, agrarian unrest and revolutionary expectation that the governments of nitti and then giolitti had let run its course. Farinacci, the Cremona ras, sets the scene in a country where the rising cost of living and the example of the Bolshevik victories in Russia had fired the industrial world: a typical Milanese worker’s family saw its weekly cost of living rise from 124 lire in January to 155 in July and toward 190 in December; wholesale prices had climbed from 100 in 1913 to 500. The metalworkers, the metallurgici, the best organised and most combative element of the red unions, had already won a great strike in the summer of 1919, and in May 1920 their federation, the F.I.O.M. (Federazione Italiana degli Operai Metallurgici), asked the employers’ association for a revision of wages — an increase of 7.50 lire a day on a pre-existing average of 18, and twelve days’ paid holiday a year.
Negotiations dragged on for two months. The employers refused in a body; the metalworkers answered on 20 August with ostruzionismo (obstructionism), the slow, scrupulous, ostentatious execution of work “according to the rules,” a strain of the machine of production, and warned that if the industrialists proclaimed the lockout the workers would force their way into the plants. On 30 August the direction of the Romeo firm at Milan proclaimed, on its own initiative, the serrata (lockout) of the Officine del Portello, denouncing indiscipline, threats and thefts. That same evening, without consulting the central committee, the F.I.O.M. agitation committee meeting at the Camera del Lavoro of Milan resolved on the occupation of the metalworks: “no one abandon the shops, and each remain with the precise aim of working until the lockout is lifted in every establishment.”
The occupation
At the hour of exit the commissions internes notified the factory directors that they were taking possession in the name of the workers, and the operai occupied the offices, cut the telephone lines and manned the doors. In some plants, like the Isotta Fraschini, the Breda and the Riva, the directors were sequestered; in others the technicians and engineers were allowed out only on a written undertaking to return. On the night of 31 August 160 establishments were occupied at Milan and the principal metalworks at Turin. On 1 September the industrialists proclaimed the general lockout and closed the works in Lombardy, Liguria and Naples; the workers invaded them, and so, following occupation or invasion, almost all the metallurgical plants of Italy passed under the command of the operai. On 9 September, incited by the direction of the socialist party, the anarchists and the communists, the occupations were extended to non-metallurgical establishments, above all in Lombardy and the Piedmont. At Genoa, Businelli notes, the occupation had begun earlier and spread little by little across all Italy; the Fasci di combattimento, watching, issued their own order of the day on 6 September, denouncing the “scioperomania” of the workmen and calling on the government to name a commission of enquiry into the future of the Italian iron and steel industry.
The factories became armed camps. Pini describes how every industrial plant was transformed into a barrack of rebels, a fortified place with sentinels, guard posts and barbed-wire fences, watched over by young fanatics who believed themselves able to resist any attack of the public force. Farinacci’s account is a catalogue of the garrisons’ life: the red flag and the Soviet emblem and the black banner of the anarchists hoisted over the gates; the plants rebaptised — the Fiat the “Fiat Soviet,” the Breda the “comuniste” mechanical works; the watchmen’s cry “Sentinella all’erta” echoing in the night; the machine shops turned to the manufacture of arms, with helmets, rifles, bombs, machine-guns and knives; the tribunals improvised to judge the disobedient, with their own prisons — at Breda a wooden hut “solidly barred,” at one Sesto San Giovanni works a hen-house inaugurated by two workers caught rifling the director’s desk. Red guards patrolled by day and night; the whole spectacle, Farinacci remarks with savage irony, was at once a game of war and a game of revolution, in which the workers’ technical incapacity and their inexperience stood naked.
Blood in Turin
The occupation was most violent at Turin, where, in Farinacci’s telling, the methods of Russia and Hungary were felt as an affair of honour and of doctrinal proof. There the sequestrations went beyond directors and technicians to officers of the army, to passers-by seized near the Fiat-Centro and set to work at the furnaces; there the streets ran with blood through the latter part of September — a guard killed riding past in a bicycle, a vice-brigadier shot, a child of eight killed in a doorway. The most infamous episode was the fate of Costantino Scimula and Mario Sonzini. Scimula, recognised as a warder of the Turin gaols, was dragged into the Bevilacqua works, where his captors debated not his guilt but the manner of his death — the furnaces, the revolver, or the cellar; four shots killed him, and Sonzini, a nationalist and a decorated war volunteer, shortly after. Pini tells the same story as the work of the factory councils, who took them in the street, judged them before a parody of a tribunal and riddled them with revolver-fire. The occupation, by then “emptied of every ideal content,” closed at Turin with, by Farinacci’s count, twenty dead and hundreds wounded.
The settlement
The collapse was inevitable, and came from within. The workers had no money, no raw materials and no technical direction; the engineers and technicians in their great majority refused service; the banks closed their credit and the production stopped as supplies ran out. “The enemy they could never have overcome,” Farinacci concludes, “was within them — their incapacity.” The intransigence of the movement, however, would not let it end in an unconditional surrender. Giolitti had kept the government ostensibly neutral — going himself on holiday to Bardonecchia while the garrisons stood — and his intervention at the end rescued the leaders from the “extreme humiliation.” By his presidential decree of 15 September he named a commissione paritetica (a paritary commission) charged to formulate proposals for a controllo sindacale (workers’ control) of the industries. The two sides could not agree on a common project, the workers seeking to extend the principle of control and the industrialists to limit it; and in the end the control, in Farinacci’s judgement, was an expedient — a “Greek gift,” as Pini calls it — imposed by the government on the industrialists and given to immature workers, that would come to nothing. The workers obtained increased wages and the appearance of victory, and evacuated the factories at the end of September. “The occupation ended in appearance with a workers’ victory: wages increased and the control of the plants, which no one knew well what it meant,” writes Pini. “The flagrant offence against property — armed garrisons settled for tens of days in the cities — had provoked a grave impression through all Italy.” It was that impression, more than anything, that the Fascist historians set at the origin of the counter-revolution: the State had shown itself impotent, and the middle classes began to look for the force that would restore it.

events/october-1934-insurrection.title: October 1934 Insurrection
events/october-1934-insurrection.content:
October 1934 Insurrection
4 – 6 October 1934.
The Crisis of the Second Biennium
In the autumn of 1934 the Spanish Republic, three years old, tore itself apart in the bloodiest crisis of its peacetime existence. The government of the centre-right had governed through the second, conservative biennium under the coalition of the Radical Party of Alejandro Lerroux and the CEDA — the Confederación Española de Derechas Autónomas, the great Catholic confederation of José María Gil Robles. On 4 October the CEDA entered the government in force, taking several ministries. To the socialists, who had been driven from power in 1933 and who saw in Gil Robles a Spanish Dollfuss preparing a clerical counter-revolution on the Austrian model, the admission of the CEDA to the cabinet was the signal for insurrection. The revolutionary committees of the PSOE — the Partido Socialista Obrero Español — and its trade-union wing the UGT had been preparing for this hour since the defeat of 1933, when the party’s sense of abandonment had turned its leadership toward revolution. On 4 October they declared a general strike against what they called the fascist threat, and the insurrection of October 1934 began.
The strike was general in name but uneven in fact. In Madrid it was contained and soon broken; in most of the provinces it flickered and died. It was in the mining basin of Asturias that the rising took fire. There the miners and the workers of the cuenca — the coal valley — rose in arms, seized Oviedo and the surrounding towns, and held the region for nearly two weeks under a revolutionary junta. The government answered with a brutal military campaign, bringing Moorish troops from the colonial army to the peninsula and turning the repression of Asturias into a siege; General Franco, commanding the operations, made the reconquest of the mining basin a byword for the savagery that could attend the defence of the Republic. The Asturian revolution — the Revolución de Asturias — was crushed in blood, and the Republic that had begun in the clean idyll of 1931 found itself, three years later, governing a province by fire.
The Catalan Revolt
In Barcelona the insurrection took a different and, in its way, more fateful course. The president of the Generalidad — the autonomous government of Catalonia — was Lluís Companys, the Catalanist leader who had succeeded Macià. On the night of 6 October, fearing that the entry of the CEDA portended the destruction of the autonomy statute and the triumph of the centralizing right, Companys proclaimed from the balcony of the palace in Barcelona the Estat Català — the Catalan State — “within the Federal Republic of Spain.” The proclamation, answered by the shouts of the crowds below, was an act of regional defiance aimed as much at the government of Madrid as at the threat it invoked.
The Republic’s government responded with the declaration of a state of war in Catalonia. The army of Barcelona, commanded by General Domingo Batet, moved against the Generalidad, and within hours the Catalan rising was over. The Generalidad — the Generalitat — was dissolved, its statute suspended, and Companys and the Catalan ministers were arrested and tried for rebellion. The revolt that the government denounced as an act of sedition in the rear of a besieged state was, to its authors, a desperate attempt to defend the democratic and regional gains of the Republic against a reaction they believed imminent. Both sides claimed the constitution; both had, in some measure, abandoned it. The Republic, in crushing the Catalan proclamation, had reasserted the unity of the state, but at the price of making enemies of the very forces that had done most to bring it into being.
The Arrest of Azaña
The repression that followed the October rising reached beyond the rebels to the man many held to be their hidden instigator: Manuel Azaña, the former prime minister who had directed the reformist biennium and remained the most prominent republican statesman in Spain. Azaña had come to Catalonia in the summer of 1934, to the waters of the region, for his health, and had been in Barcelona when the revolt broke. On 8 October he was arrested and charged with rebellion — accused, though he had counselled the Republic against the insurrection, of having fomented it. He was taken aboard the prison ships Uruguay and Ciudad de Cádiz in the port of Barcelona, and later the Barcaiztegui, and held through the winter.
From these ships Azaña wrote his defence, Mi rebelión en Barcelona — “My rebellion in Barcelona” — a title that answered his indictment with irony. The book is at once a memoir of his detention and a political testament: he insisted that he had no part in any conspiracy, that his enemies were persecuting him not as a defeated statesman but as a hated one, and he traced the campaign against him — which public men who were not his partisans protested in an open letter was “not opposition but annihilation” — to the determination of the right to destroy him. Azaña’s conduct during the October events had in fact been that of a moderate: Tusell records that his preference lay with the legal order, with the king’s ministers against the rebels. The charge against him collapsed; in 1935 the Supreme Court decreed the sobreseimiento libre — the free dismissal of his case — finding no evidence that he had participated in the proclamation of the Catalan State. He was released, vindicated in law, but marked in reputation: his enemies had made him the living symbol of the rebellion he had opposed.
The Aftermath of October
The insurrection of October 1934 left the Republic changed. The government of Lerroux and the CEDA survived, but its legitimacy was damaged; it had repressed its own people with the colonial army, and the left, defeated but unreconciled, remembered the two weeks of Asturias as a wound. The suspension of the Catalan statute and the trials of the Catalan leaders, along with Azaña’s own prosecution, deepened the regional and personal resentments that had been latent since 1931. The “interminable agony” of the second biennium dragged on through 1935, the radical-cedista coalition slowly disintegrating as scandals and divisions consumed it.
Yet October also reshaped the left. The socialists, divided between the reformism of Indalecio Prieto and the revolutionary rhetoric of Largo Caballero, were radicalised by the defeat; the failure of the revolution drove them toward the alliance that would, in the following year, reunite the left as the Popular Front. Azaña, released from the ships and vindicated, emerged from the crisis as the natural head of a reunited opposition, the victim whose persecution had cleansed his reputation. The Republic that had crushed the insurrection of October had, in doing so, prepared the coalition that would win the elections of February 1936 — and the road that led from Asturias and the Catalan proclamation to the Civil War of July 1936 ran straight through the hatreds and alliances that October had created.

events/popular-front-1936.title: Popular Front and the Elections of February 1936
events/popular-front-1936.content:
Popular Front and the Elections of February 1936
16 February 1936 – July 1936.
The Reconstruction of the Left
In the elections of 16 February 1936 the Spanish left, which had been routed in 1933 and driven into the wilderness of the second biennium, returned to power in a landslide. The coalition that won was the Frente Popular — the Popular Front — a pact of the republican left, the socialists, the communists, and the Catalan and other regional lefts, concluded in January 1936 in the shadow of the repression that had followed the insurrection of October 1934. Its programme was not the revolution its enemies feared but a restoration: the amnesty of the prisoners of Asturias and Catalonia, the reinstatement of the Catalan statute, the resumption of the reforms of the first biennium. The left that had been split in 1933, when Azaña’s republican-left position had been volatilised in seats though less in votes, had recomposed itself; the fear of a reaction on the Austrian model, and the memory of the two weeks of Asturias, had driven even the revolutionary wing of socialism into the electoral alliance.
The campaign was fought against a right that was itself divided, between the Catholic mass of the CEDA and the monarchists and the nascent Falange. The result was a victory for the Popular Front — a decisive majority in the Cortes, carried by the great cities and the agrarian south. The Republic had swung back to the left, but the swing, as Madariaga observed, changed opinion less than appearances suggested: the country remained deeply and bitterly divided, and the coalition that had won the election had not won the nation. The Popular Front had come to power by uniting against a common enemy, and it carried within itself the contradictions of that union — the reformist republicans, the revolutionary socialists of Largo Caballero, the disciplined communists, all harnessed together for the contest, none agreed on what the victory was to produce.
The Popular Front in Government
On 19 February Azaña formed a government of the republican left — the moderate wing of the coalition — with the socialists supporting but not yet joining the cabinet. The new government moved at once to the promises of the pact: the amnesty freed the prisoners of October, the Catalan statute was restored and Companys reinstated, the social and agrarian reforms of the first biennium were resumed. But the government was from the first caught between two fires. On one side the revolutionary left, and above all the anarchist CNT and the radicalised socialists, pressed for a transformation the moderate cabinet neither could nor would deliver; the land was occupied in the countryside, strikes multiplied in the cities, and churches were burned in a renewal of anticlerical fury. On the other side the right, seeing its worst fears confirmed, hardened into resistance and conspiracy; the Falange and the monarchists turned to violence, and the army, already humiliated by the reforms and now alarmed by the return of the republicans, began to plot.
The Republic that the Popular Front governed slid rapidly toward chaos. The two anti-republican extremes — the monarchist right and the anarchist-revolutionary left — had always pressed upon the democratic regime from opposite directions; now, in the spring of 1936, the pressure became intolerable. Street violence rose to a daily level of assassination and revenge, in Madrid and the provinces; each killing answered another, and the state, increasingly impotent, could neither restrain its own revolutionary supporters nor disarm its enemies. The middle ground of the Republic — the constitutional republicans who had founded it and still governed it — shrank before a country that was polarising into two armed camps.
The Inclined Plane
The months from the February election to the military rising of July formed what Tusell called the plano inclinado — the inclined plane — toward the Civil War. Yet the metaphor, Tusell insisted, must not be read as inevitability: until nearly the last moment the war could have been avoided, and the claim that it was fated from the elections was a retrospective illusion of those who had lived through it. The responsibility lay in acts and failures of will rather than in an irreversible destiny. The government of Casares Quiroga, who had succeeded Azaña when the latter was elected president of the Republic in May, refused to credit the mounting evidence of a military conspiracy; a different behaviour, a different minister of war, might have disarmed the plotters. The polarisation, the violence, the paralysis of authority prepared the ground; the conspiracy of the generals — Mola, Sanjurjo, Franco — exploited it.
Azaña, chosen president of the Republic in the spring, presided over a state that he watched being torn apart. The parties of the Popular Front fought among themselves as the right armed; the socialists of Largo Caballero talked of revolution while the Falangists and the military plotted counter-revolution. In the first days of July 1936 the assassination of the monarchist deputy Calvo Sotelo by the police answered the earlier killing of a republican officer, José Castillo, and the cycle of revenge seemed to close around the state. On 17–18 July the army of Morocco and then the garrisons of the peninsula rose against the Republic. The Civil War had begun — the war that the February elections had not made inevitable but that the months of the Popular Front government had done nothing to prevent. The Republic that had been proclaimed in the radiant spring of 1931, and that the Popular Front had restored to power five years later, entered its long agony; the inclined plane had reached its foot.

events/popular-front-france-1936.title: The French Popular Front (May 1936 – June 1937)
events/popular-front-france-1936.content:
The French Popular Front (May 1936 – June 1937)
May 1936 – June 1937
The French Popular Front (Front populaire) of 1936 — the electoral and governing coalition of the Socialists, Communists and Radicals, built to meet the double threat of fascism at home and war abroad, that carried the parliamentary election of May 1936 and brought the Socialist Léon Blum to power at the head of the first government of the French Left to be led by a Socialist. The high tide of the French republican and working-class alliance of the interwar years, celebrated for its social legislation — above all the agreements of the matignon that conceded the forty-hour week and paid holidays — and doomed by the financial pressure and the gathering war that, within little more than a year, brought the first Blum government to its fall.
The alignment of the French parties
The Popular Front drew on a party system whose permanent shape Siegfried had charted six years before. The French Republic of the centre rested, in his analysis, on the intimate contradiction of the Frenchman — politically on the left, socially conservative, “son cœur est à gauche, mais sa poche est à droite” (his heart is on the left, but his pocket is on the right). The fan of the parties spread from the united Socialists and the Radical-Socialists of the Left and the republican middle, through the Centre, to the nationalist Right; and the balance of the Chamber, he had shown, swung in great cycles between the leftward and the conservative majorities — the Bloc National, the Cartel des Gauches, the regime of Poincaré. The Popular Front of 1936 was the most complete expression yet of the leftward coalition of the French parties: the union, this time, not merely of the Radicals and the Socialists but of the Socialists with the Communists, the party that had stood outside the Cartel of 1924 and that now entered, in the anti-fascist emergency, into alliance with the parliamentary Left.
The anti-fascist coalition
The Popular Front was forged in the years of the rise of the European dictatorships. The victory of the Fascist and National Socialist movements, and above all the spectre of a fascism on the French Right itself, pressed the parties of the French Left together in a union of defence. The object of the alliance, in its own account, was to bar the road to fascism in France — to unite the working-class parties and the party of the small republican proprietors in a common front against the enemy that threatened the Republic from within and from without. The coalition stood, in the language of the French Left, for the défense républicaine carried to its furthest extent: not the old alliance of the Radicals and Socialists alone, but the union with the Communist party that had refused to sit within the parliamentary Republic’s majority a decade before.
The election of May 1936 and the Blum government
In the election of May 1936 the Popular Front won a decisive victory, and the government fell to the leader of the Socialist party, Léon Blum. Blum’s government, formed in June 1936, was the first French ministry to be led by a Socialist and the first to count Communist support within the Popular Front majority — though the Communists, in a decision that marked the limits of the coalition, supported the government from outside rather than entering the ministry. Blum brought to power the alliance that Siegfried had described in the very structure of the French parties: the union of the working-class party with the party of the small proprietors, of the heart of the Left with the republican middle.
The immediate demand of the summer of 1936 was social. In the great strike wave that followed the election, the workers occupied the factories, and the government pressed the employers to concede. The accords Matignon (Matignon agreements) of June 1936 — signed between the employers and the trade unions under the aegis of the state — granted the forty-hour week, paid holidays, and the recognition of the workers’ right to organise and to collective bargaining. For the working class these measures were the charter of the Popular Front: the leisure and the security that the socialist movement had demanded for a generation.
The era of tyrannies in the liberal mirror
Élie Halévy, the liberal historian of the state, had diagnosed the deeper movement of the age against which the Popular Front defined itself. The era of the new tyrannies, he wrote, dated from the month of August 1914 — from the outbreak of the First World War, which by its strain and its total character had set in motion the forces of total war and total revolution. Italian Fascism, German National Socialism and, in its own fashion, Russian Bolshevism were not, in his argument, simple reactions against the French Revolution and its liberal inheritance, but continuations and transformations of the revolutionary era under the new conditions of the war: the organised, and in Russia the totalitarian, state mobilised the whole nation for war and revolution alike. It was against this closing of the world that the French Popular Front stood as the contrary pole — the democratic, parliamentary and libertarian heritage of the old Left defending the individual against the state of mass and series that the totalitarian movements embodied. The coalition that the Halévy brothers chronicled and analysed was, in the diagnosis of the age, the last great stand of the French republican tradition in its classic parliamentary form.
The fall of the first Blum government
The Popular Front’s hour was short, and its undoing was once again the question of money — the same force that had broken the Cartel a decade before. The financial pressure on the franc, the flight of capital from a government of the Left, and the mounting cost of the war preparations bore down on the coalition through 1936 and 1937. The Radicals of the governing majority, the party of the small proprietors, grew restive under the social expenditure and the financial strain; and in June 1937 the first Blum government fell. The sequel, as the chronicler Daniel Halévy was to record of the following year, was the drift and inaction of the regime in the face of its deepening crisis — the pratique du rien (the practice of nothing), the parliamentary and ministerial paralysis as the financial and diplomatic problems accumulated, and the turn, in April 1938, from the Popular Front’s programme toward a ministry of Daladier pledged to restore the authority of the state. The Popular Front had raised the alliance of the French Left to power and given it its greatest social legislation; but it could not hold together the union of the working-class party and the party of the pocket against the financial and martial pressure of the age — and the year of Munich would open on the wreckage of its promises.

events/proclamation-of-the-republic-1931.title: Proclamation of the Republic (1931)
events/proclamation-of-the-republic-1931.content:
Proclamation of the Republic (1931)
14 April 1931.
The Fall of the Monarchy
On the morning of 14 April 1931, Spain was a republic. The municipal elections of the previous Sunday, 12 April, held as the first clean and contested vote in the memory of living Spaniards, had returned a sweeping republican and socialist majority in the great cities of the kingdom. Within hours the news ran from Madrid to the provinces; in Barcelona and Valencia the Republic was proclaimed from the balconies before the capital had acted. By mid-day the monarchy was a ruin. King Alfonso XIII, whose reign of almost thirty years had ended without a shot fired in its defence, convened his last Council of Ministers, heard from the generals that the Army would not march to save him, and prepared for flight. That evening, from the ministry of the Interior, a provisional government of the Republic was announced, and the king departed for the port of Cartagena and exile. The proclamación de la República — the proclamation of the Republic — had been accomplished almost without bloodshed, the cleanest of the revolutions that had overthrown the crowned heads of Europe after the war.
The Republic was not born of the April vote alone. It had been prepared through the year that followed the Dictatorship’s fall. The Pact of San Sebastián of August 1930 had united the republican parties, the socialists, and the Catalan regionalists in a revolutionary committee, resolved to end the monarchy by whatever means presented itself. In December 1930 the garrison of Jaca rose under Captains Fermín Galán and Ángel García Hernández and marched on the capital of Aragon, a premature alzamiento — rising — that the government crushed and whose leaders it shot. The executions made martyrs of the two captains and turned the republican cause from a conspiracy into a national emotion. The abortive flight over Madrid from the Cuatro Vientos airfield followed, and the revolutionary committee, its hand strengthened by the general sympathy, awaited its hour. Berenguer’s attempt to restore a normal constitutional monarchy — the dictablanda, the “soft dictatorship” — satisfied no one, and his fall left a last royalist government under Admiral Aznar to face the municipal elections it was compelled to call.
The Municipal Elections
The elections of 12 April 1931 were municipal only, and had been designed by the monarchy to give it a measured victory in the villages while the cities, it was hoped, would be neutralized. Instead they became a plebiscite. In Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Zaragoza and the other capitals, the republican-socialist coalition swept the field; the great urban centres, where the consciousness of the new Spain lived, declared against the Crown almost to a man. The republican leaders, taken by surprise at the completeness of their triumph, hesitated, but the street did not. Crowds gathered, the tricolour flag — the bandera tricolor of republican Spain, red, yellow and purple — appeared over public buildings, and the revolutionary committee, seeing that it could either lead the movement or be swept aside by it, acted.
On 14 April the committee installed itself as the provisional government at the ministry of the Interior under Niceto Alcalá-Zamora, and proclaimed the Republic. Alfonso XIII, in a last act of kingcraft, declined to abdicate outright, choosing instead to suspend the exercise of the royal power and to leave Spain, hoping perhaps to return. The decision satisfied no one fully, but it spared the country a contested civil succession. As he left, the king addressed his people with a resignation that acknowledged the verdict: the elections had shown that the monarchy no longer counted on the love of the people. The provisional government, gathering republicans of every shade — Alcalá-Zamora, Azaña, the socialists Indalecio Prieto and Fernando de los Ríos — received the power and, in the radiant days that followed, the trust of a country that greeted the Republic as a deliverance.
The Idyll of Spring
Madariaga, an exile who had believed the Republic could not come without a military conspiracy and found himself proved wrong, recorded the opening of the regime as a spontaneous overflow of joy — Spain, in those first splendid days, was rebosante de alegría, brimming with a happiness like that of nature in spring. The revolution had been clean, almost untainted by the excesses that usually marked dramatic moments; there was no reign of terror, no settling of scores, only an immense relief and a vast hope. The crowds that filled the streets of Madrid were not merely celebrating a change of government but hailing what they believed to be the dawn of a new epoch, in which the land, the schools, the workers and the regions would at last receive justice.
The provisional government set about the first tasks with a fervour that matched the mood: an amnesty, a statute of Catalonia, the preparation of elections to a Constituent Cortes. Yet even in the spring idyll the divisions that were to rend the Republic were latent. The monarchy had fallen not because a nation had agreed but because a coalition of the disaffected had momentarily united; the republicans were not one party but several, ranging from the moderate Alcalá-Zamora to the anticlerical Azaña to the socialists, and the burning questions of the church, the land and the army lay unresolved beneath the surface of celebration. The Republic had been proclaimed against a monarchy that had forfeited its legitimacy; it would now have to build a legitimacy of its own, and the forces it had summoned to bring the Crown down — the workers who expected revolution, the Catalan and Basque nationalists who expected autonomy, the anticlericals who expected the destruction of the Church — could not all be satisfied at once.
Tusell’s later scholarship insisted that the democratic experience of 1931 was the coming of the masses to Spanish public life, something never seen before under the oligarchic liberalism of the Restoration and not to be seen again until the transition of the 1970s. The proclamation of April 1931 was thus not merely the substitution of one regime for another but the admission of the Spanish people to their own politics — a transformation that the Dictatorship had delayed and then made abrupt. The Republic was the Spanish democratic experiment par excellence, and its opening on 14 April 1931 was the moment at which a people that had been governed without its consent took hold of the state. Whether the leaders who now held power would choose well, neither Tusell nor the men of 1931 could presume; but the Republic had begun, and for a season it carried the hopes of Spain.

events/reichstag-fire-1933.title: The Reichstag Fire (27 February 1933)
events/reichstag-fire-1933.content:
The Reichstag Fire (27 February 1933)
27 February 1933
The burning of the Reichstag building in Berlin in the fourth week of hitler’s chancellorship — the fire that the regime laid at the door of an alleged communist arsonist, Marinus van der Lubbe, and used to suspend the constitution, arm the party’s storm detachments as auxiliary police, and complete the seizure of power in the weeks before the elections of 5 March. The event and its use stand at the hinge of the National Socialist revolution: the moment the new government turned a deed of uncertain authorship into the legal instrument of dictatorship.
The burning
On the evening of 27 February 1933 the Reichstag went up in flames. The fire was discovered in the great plenary chamber of the German parliament building in Berlin, and by the time it was controlled the assembly hall lay gutted, the cupola blackened over a charred ruin. The young Dutchman Marinus van der Lubbe, a drifter of vaguely communist sympathies, was taken near the building, and the government proclaimed at once that the fire was the work of the communists — the opening of an insurrection, the signal for a red rising that had to be crushed without mercy. Heiden, writing from exile and treating the affair as the centre of the first months of power, is explicit that this theory of a communist arsonist does not survive scrutiny. The communists had no interest in burning the parliament of a regime they were bent on destroying by other means, and the evidence pointed elsewhere.
The Ernst document
Heiden’s account turns on a document that he weighs carefully without wholly accepting — the so-called Ernst document, a written confession attributed to Karl Ernst, the SA group leader of Berlin, who was himself shot in the purge of 30 June 1934. By this account the fire was a Nazi deed from the first. The idea, it says, was goering’s — to detonate a great Wahlbombe (election bomb), a political coup that would terrify the country on the eve of the poll; goebbels proposed the Reichstag itself as the target. The role of the young Dutchman van der Lubbe, the confession goes on, was to serve as the decoy, the patsy on whom the guilt could be fixed. Heiden is careful to mark the limits of his evidence: the document may not be Ernst’s own work, and the technical particulars it gives may be the inventions of a well-informed writer rather than the recollection of a participant. But the shape of the account, he notes, agrees too closely with what had long been suspected to be dismissed, and the direction of the truth — that the real arsonists are to be sought among the National Socialists themselves — could no longer be doubted. The fire, in this reading, was struck by the party’s own hand, and the government’s cry of a communist insurrection was the instrument for which the deed had been done.
The decree and the seizure
Whatever the authorship, the political harvest was immediate and was reaped by the regime. On the strength of the fire the Reich government induced the aged President hindenburg to sign the decree für den Schutz von Volk und Staat (for the protection of people and state), which suspended the constitutional guarantees of personal liberty, the freedom of the press, of assembly and of association, and delivered into the hands of the Reich government the power to take control of any state that failed to restore public order. The paper constitution of the republic, already bent by the emergency practice of the last years, was set aside with a signature. Göring, as Prussian minister of the interior, called the SA and SS into service as auxiliary police; Heiden records the passage by which “the streets of Adolf Hitler” were handed to the brownshirts and the practical power of the state passed into party hands beyond the reach of law. The fire thus accomplished in a night what weeks of legal manoeuvre might not have done: it gave the regime the cover to arrest and terrorise its enemies, to close the communist and social-democratic press, and to fight the election of 5 March with the state and the police as weapons. The National Socialists won their plurality in that poll, and from it the Enabling Act followed in March, delivering legislation into the government’s hands and ending the party state.
The trial
The guilty man was found, or the men were found guilty. Van der Lubbe, tried with the communist leaders Dimitrov, Torgler and others before the Reichsgericht at Leipzig, was condemned and beheaded, while his co-defendants — above all Dimitrov, who turned the trial into a platform against the prosecution — were acquitted. The verdict of the court disposed of the charge that the fire had been a communist insurrection; the German judges, in Heiden’s dry summation, pronounced the communist-arson theory untrue without naming the true authors, who, he concludes, must be sought among the National Socialists. The fire did its work and the trial drew the line under it: the republic was gone, the dictatorship was building, and the deed itself had been absorbed into the fog of the seizure of power.

events/reintroduction-of-conscription-19.title: Reintroduction of conscription (16 March 1935)
events/reintroduction-of-conscription-19.content:
Reintroduction of conscription (16 March 1935)
16 March 1935 — the Reich government proclaimed the reintroduction of general military service and, by the law for the building of the Wehrmacht, laid the basis for the armed forces whose enlargement was to follow. The step abolished the military clauses of the Treaty of Versailles at a stroke and gave the regime the legal foundation of its rearmament.
The proclamation
The proclamation of the Reich government, addressed to the German people, justified the step as the answer to a promise broken. Germany, it argued, had laid down its arms in November 1918 trusting in the fourteen points of Wilson; it had accepted the disarmament of the Versailles treaty in the belief that its own compliance would be answered by a general international disarmament. Instead, the treaty’s disarmament clauses had been fulfilled by Germany — as the inter-allied control commission confirmed — while the promised general disarmament never came, leaving the nation under a perpetual discrimination and an assertion of inferiority. The proclamation rehearsed the inventory of destruction imposed on the German forces: nearly sixty thousand guns and barrels, a hundred and thirty thousand machine guns, over six million rifles and carbines, and tens of millions of rounds of ammunition and shell. In the face of a rearming world, the government declared, Germany’s own restoration of its military power had become unavoidable.
The Wehrgesetz
The law for the building of the Wehrmacht of 16 March fixed the German defence sovereignty (Wehrhoheit) by statute. The deeper framework came in the Defence Law (Wehrgesetz) of 21 May 1935, which became the fundamental law of the German military system. The Wehrmacht was defined as the bearer of arms and the soldierly training school of the German people, composed of the army (Heer), the navy (Kriegsmarine) and the air force (Luftwaffe). Supreme command lay with the Führer and Reichskanzler, with the Reich War Minister exercising command under him as Commander-in-Chief of the Wehrmacht. Military service ran from the completed eighteenth year of life to the end of March following the forty-fifth year; in time of war all conscripts were to hold themselves at the disposal of the Wehrmacht and the interests of the Wehrmacht were to take precedence over all others. Blomberg, the Reich War Minister, set out the official gloss on 20 March in the Völkischer Beobachter, arguing that the German army under general conscription was not aimed at conquest but represented the fulfilment of the best German military traditions. The proclamation itself, followed by the building of the Wehrmacht on this legal foundation, was cast in the official record as the recovery of the nation’s Wehrhoheit (military sovereignty) — the outward freedom that the law of 16 March had secured.
The reaction of the powers
The reintroduction of conscription was answered by protest. Great Britain, France and Italy addressed protest notes, and representatives of the three powers met soon after at Stresa to concert their attitude toward the German step. An ill-considered declaration of the Stresa conference on a German move concerning the Eastern pact gave the Reich government occasion on 14 April to restate with all sharpness its attitude to the proposed Eastern security pact. France had appealed to the League of Nations, and on 17 April the League adopted a resolution declaring that the German government, by reintroducing general conscription, had broken its obligations toward the community of states. The German government answered on 20 April with a note to the member states of the League Council, protesting the decision as a renewed discrimination against Germany and denying the participating governments the right to sit in judgment over it.
A peace plan
Two months after the proclamation, on 21 May 1935, the same day on which the Wehrgesetz was enacted, Hitler laid before the Reichstag a great German peace plan for a European reordering, setting out in thirteen points the principles on which he proposed that a new European peace system might be founded. In the meantime France and Soviet Russia had concluded their pact of 2 May 1935, which the German government denounced as a breach of the Locarno treaty because it allowed the two powers to determine the aggressor without the intervention of the League; a German memorandum of 25 May set the German view before the Locarno powers. The proclamation of conscription thus stood, in the regime’s own presentation, not as a break with the peace but as the prerequisite of a peace negotiated between equals. It opened the military expansion that the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of June was to canalise on the sea, and that rearmament on land, sea and air was to pursue for the rest of the decade.

events/remilitarization-of-the-rhineland.title: Remilitarization of the Rhineland, 1936
events/remilitarization-of-the-rhineland.content:
Remilitarization of the Rhineland, 1936
7 March 1936.
The Stride of Sovereignty
On the morning of 7 March 1936 German troops entered the Rhineland, the demilitarized zone on the western bank of the Rhine that the Treaty of Versailles had stripped of all German armed force. In a single stroke the Reich government restored the military occupation of its own border country and tore up the last of the territorial restraints the peace settlement of 1919 had laid upon it. The step was at once a repudiation of the Locarno treaties of 1925 and a proclamation that the Reich no longer held itself bound by the clauses of Versailles that had left its western frontier defenseless. The regime’s official documentary record of the year, compiled by Axel Friedrichs for the Dokumente der deutschen Politik, presents the event as the highest act of the year — the recovery of Souveränität (sovereignty) over German soil after fifteen years of standing as a power among powers with its own territory at the mercy of its neighbours.
The German argument, as the state documents set it out, rested on the claim that the system Locarno had founded was already broken. Germany had offered to sign non-aggression pacts with all her western and eastern neighbours; those offers, the government maintained, had been met with the Soviet–French mutual assistance pact, which the Reich refused to regard as compatible with Locarno. The Reichstag was summoned to the Kroll Opera House, and there Hitler, addressing the assembled deputies and the world, announced that Germany regarded the Locarno treaty as void because its partners had broken its spirit, and that the Reich government had thereupon restored full sovereignty over the Rhineland. At the same sitting he dissolved the Reichstag and threw the question before the German people in a general election called for 29 March. The official statement of 12 March amplified the declaration: the remilitarization was presented not as aggression but as the completion of Germany’s claim to equality, the counterpart to the peace plan the Führer laid before the powers, by which the Reich offered to guarantee the borders of the West and to enter a new European security system.
The Locarno Question
The legal pivot of the action was the question whether Germany, as a party to the Locarno treaties of 1925 — by which the Reich, France, Belgium, Great Britain and Italy had guaranteed the inviolability of the Franco-German and Belgian–German frontiers and the permanent demilitarization of the Rhineland — could unilaterally set them aside. The Reich government answered that it could, because the maintenance of the demilitarized zone presupposed a condition of equal rights that the Franco-Soviet pact had destroyed. Ribbentrop, whom the regime sent to London, carried this case to the council of the League of Nations in March, where he protested against the Soviet pact, restated the German reading of Locarno, and unfolded the German peace plan as the foundation on which a new order might be built. The German note to the Locarno powers of 7 March and the peace plan of 31 March were the two documents in which the Reich set its position on paper: the one declaring the old treaties dissolved, the other offering the new structure of guarantees in their place.
The claim to the Rhineland rested deeper than the treaties, in the regime’s own telling, on the natural right of a great power to the defense of its own soil. Büttner’s party-authorized compilation of the same decade groups the step under the second point of the NSDAP programme — equal rights for the German people and the abrogation of the treaties of Versailles and St. Germain — and lays beside it the other documents of the same claim: the declaration of the former German rights, the withdrawal from the League of Nations in 1933, the peace plan of 1935, the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of June 1935. In this reading the remilitarization was the last and most complete of the acts by which the Reich reclaimed the status of a sovereign great power, and the peace plan of 31 March 1936 was its constructive face, offered to the powers as the price of a new stability.
The West in the Balance
The other powers made no military answer. France, whose treaty rights and whose security the demilitarization had been designed to protect, was bound to the League covenant and to its own alliances, but did not march. Great Britain, party to Locarno, entered into negotiation. The German government, with the troops already on the Rhine and the election already proclaimed, held the field and waited upon events; the official record notes the election result of 29 March, which returned the regime an overwhelming mandate. The diplomatic exchanges of the spring — the German front-fighters’ answer to the French of 16 May, the notes on Spain and the German rivers through the summer and autumn — show the Reich, having taken the step, moving immediately to the next claims upon the European order.
Within Germany the act was celebrated as the restoration of the Wehrmacht’s freedom of movement and of the Reich’s equality among the powers. General von Blomberg, the War Minister, spoke on Heroes’ Memorial Day, 8 March, the day after the entry, of the recovered honour and security of the Reich. The demilitarized zone, emptied of German troops since the end of the war, became once more the terrain of the German army. The remilitarization of the Rhineland closed the first phase of the German revolt against the territorial settlement of 1919 and opened the second: the Reich, having armed itself within its own borders and freed its western frontier, turned next toward the reunion of the German lands beyond them. The event stands in the German record as the decisive stride by which the Third Reich ceased to be a power that accepted its confinement and became a power that dictated its own place in Europe.

events/saar-plebiscite-1935.title: Saar plebiscite (13 January 1935)
events/saar-plebiscite-1935.content:
Saar plebiscite (13 January 1935)
13 January 1935 — the inhabitants of the Saar territory went to the ballot for the third option written into the Treaty of Versailles, and returned the basin to the German Reich by an overwhelming majority. The vote closed the fifteen years in which the Saar had stood outside Germany under the League of Nations, and it handed the National Socialist regime its first great external triumph.
The mandated territory
The Saar had been separated from the Reich by the Treaty of Versailles against the current of the national demand. The territory’s coal mines had been ceded to France in reparation; the government of the basin itself had been placed under a Governing Commission appointed by the League of Nations, and the whole arrangement was to run for fifteen years, at the close of which the population was to be asked to choose between three courses: the maintenance of the status quo created by the treaty, union with France, or union with Germany. Should the vote favour Germany, the Versailles text obliged the Reich to buy back the French property in the Saar mines in gold at the full price. The interwar record of the mandated land was one of estrangement and grievance. The Governing Commission and the Plebiscite Commission that was to organise the vote held the actual power in the territory. The French troops, though the treaty required their withdrawal, remained until June 1927, and the small inter-allied railway guard of some eight hundred Frenchmen, Englishmen and Belgians was only removed in December 1930. The plan for a Franco-German economic approach to the Saar, agreed in principle at Thoiry in 1926, collapsed and left the questions of the mines and the administration unresolved.
The two nations’ bid
Hitler had proposed in his Reichstag speech of 30 January 1934 that Germany and France should settle the Saar problem in advance of the ballot, arguing that it was the only territorial question still open between the two countries, that the outcome of the vote was never in doubt, and that a premature campaign could only rekindle national passions on both sides. The offer came to nothing, and the campaign that followed was fought on the ground. In the territory the parties that demanded the return to the Reich drew together into the Deutsche Front (German Front), and all the parties of the mandate dissolved themselves in its favour, the Marxists and Communists alone standing apart. The German Front demanded a clear vote for reunion and campaigned under the cry that put an end to party quarrelling in the face of a great duty — “Schluß mit allem Parteihader! … Der Sieg wird unser sein! Es lebe die Deutsche Front!” (an end to all party quarrelling … victory will be ours! Long live the German Front). Against it stood the status-quo camp and the pro-French camp, and the émigré circles abroad who worked against the German return. The campaigners themselves, before the ballot, reckoned on at least eighty-five per cent of the electorate for the immediate return.
The three days of decision
The vote was held on 13 January 1935. Bürckel, speaking on the radio as the campaign’s victorious leader, put the result in round and graphic form: 528,000 Germans had cast their valid votes, and of these 89.05 per cent had declared for the fatherland. The Berndt collection’s eyewitnesses dwell on the scenes of the polling — the old and the dying brought to the urn, the wife who sank dead in a polling station after casting her vote for Germany, the mother who travelled sixteen days from China through Siberia to be present when her homeland answered the question of its German character, the ninety-two-year-old who marched eighteen kilometres on the icy road to do his German duty. The vote was presented in the triumphant press as a thousand-year struggle brought to an end, and its closing cry was the claim that “the Rhine is Germany’s stream and not Germany’s frontier.”
Reincorporation
The formal reincorporation followed on 1 March 1935. The protocol of 1 March recorded Germany’s reintegration into the government of the Saar territory, and the law of 30 January 1935 had already provided for the provisional administration of the Saarland. Frick, the Reich Minister of the Interior, spoke at the reunion; Bürckel was installed as Reichskommissar and took his oath to carry the Saarland’s cause as the cause of the whole nation, under the Führer’s authority. The Reich bought back the mines and folded the territory back into the Reich administration. For the National Socialist state the recovery of the Saar was the first outward proof of its claim to have undone the injustices of Versailles, and it was celebrated in the official record of the year as the precondition of the steps that followed — the proclamation of conscription in March and the rearmament that the Saar’s return had made possible. For the empire’s own historians the episode closed the chapter that the treaty of 1919 had opened.
Sources

events/wolfram-crisis-1943-44.title: The Wolfram Crisis (1943–1944)
events/wolfram-crisis-1943-44.content:
The Wolfram Crisis (1943–1944)
1943–1944
The diplomatic confrontation of 1943–44 in which the Western Allies, and above all the United States, brought the full weight of their wartime leverage to bear upon Franco’s Spain to cut off the export of tungsten — in Spanish, wolframio, hence the crisis del wolfram — to Germany. The mineral, indispensable for the hardening of steel in the manufacture of armour and armour-piercing projectiles, had become one of the Reich’s most valuable imports from the only European source the Allies could reach; and the refusal of the Spanish government to halt the traffic, under persistent German pressure, made the wolfram question the central issue of Allied policy toward Spain through 1943 and into 1944.
The mineral and the trade
Wolfram — tungsten — held a peculiar place in the war economy of the Reich. The ores of the Iberian peninsula, mined in the Spanish provinces of the northwest, were a principal source of a metal vital to the German armaments industry, and their sale to Germany a principal source of the foreign exchange and influence on which the Franco regime drew. Throughout the early war years the export continued under the cover of Spain’s policy of non-belligerency, the traffic feeding the German war machine while the Spanish government balanced its professions of friendship to the Axis against the demands of its neutrality. The American ambassador, Carlton Hayes, who reached Spain in 1942, found in the wolfram traffic one of the chief obstacles to his mission to keep Spain from the Axis and to win Allied facilities; and the struggle to cut off the exports grew through his term into a full crisis of Spanish-American relations.
The pressure turned to crisis as the war turned against Germany. With the Allied landings in North Africa in late 1942 and the progress of the campaign in the Mediterranean, the importance of keeping Spain neutral — and of denying the Reich the Spanish ore — mounted for the Allies, while the German embassy in Madrid redoubled its own pressure on the Spanish government to maintain the trade. The wolfram question became, in Hayes’s account of the opposing currents of his third chapter and the progress of neutrality of his sixth, the test case of Spain’s wartime policy, the point at which Allied determination met German insistence in the corridors of Madrid.
The American ultimatum
By 1944 the United States resolved to break the impasse. The American government, dissatisfied with the partial measures and the calculated delays of the Spanish authorities, pressed the question to the point of ultimatum, threatening the most damaging of all the measures at its disposal — the total stoppage of the supply of petroleum to Spain. The threat was made real by the dependence of the Spanish economy upon American oil, which the blockade of the Axis and the Allied control of the seas made irreplaceable; and it confronted the Franco government with a choice between the German ore-trade and the fuel on which the whole of Spanish life and industry depended.
The crisis brought the two governments to the edge of rupture in the early months of 1944. Hayes’s chapter on the wolfram records the tension and the negotiation as the American ambassador, with the full support of his government, pressed the Spanish foreign minister to a settlement; the outcome was an agreement by which Spain suspended the export of wolfram to Germany. The mineral trade, so long a symbol of the regime’s Axis leanings, was brought to an end under the pressure of the Allied embargo, and the crisis passed. The settlement of the wolfram question marked, in Hayes’s account of the “benevolent neutrality” of his eighth chapter, the decisive advance of Allied influence in Spain.
The hesitant path to neutrality
The wolfram crisis belongs to a wider movement of Spanish policy that Tusell periodises as the titubeante camino hacia la neutralidad — the hesitant path toward neutrality of 1942–45. The displacement of Serrano Suñer, the most interventionist of Franco’s ministers, and the appointment of Jordana at the Foreign Ministry had begun the shift; yet the government still gave assurances to the Axis even as its policy turned. Against the claim of later Francoist propaganda that Germany pressed and Franco resisted, Tusell holds that from the German victory over France there had been an absolute identification of the Spanish leaders with the Axis cause, prolonged with nuances into 1944 — the very years in which Hayes, from the American side, was laboriously extracting from that government the facilities and, finally, the wolfram halt. The wolfram crisis was the hinge of that hesitant course: the moment when the Allied victory, made certain by the progress of the war, tipped the balance of Spanish policy decisively toward the Allies, and the regime that had so long inclined to the Axis submitted to the demand that the German ore-trade should cease.
Sources
