index.title: Rest of Europe 1919–45
index.content:
Rest of Europe 1919–45
A narrative-research knowledge base on continental European history from the end of the First World War and the Paris Peace Conference through the interwar republics, the rise of fascism, and the Second World War. The United Kingdom is treated separately in its own wiki. Pages are grounded in the deposited source corpus — German Weimar and National Socialist documentary and biographical sources, Italian Fascist party histories, Spanish Second Republic and Civil War accounts, French Third Republic analyses and the eyewitness of its collapse, and the Soviet official history of the Stalin era.
Total pages: 169 · 41 sources · 49 entities · 43 events · 36 concepts
Narrative arc
The Great War ended the old order and opened the era the sources of this wiki survey. Weimar Germany was born of the November revolution of 1918 and died in 1930, its republic undone by the burdens of Versailles, the Ruhr crisis and inflation, and the failure of its guardians — the story Rosenberg tells from the left, Heiden from the democratic side. In the wreckage arose the National Socialist movement: Hitler’s Mein Kampf supplied the doctrine of race, the Führerprinzip and Lebensraum; the Beer Hall Putsch of 1923 and the years of reconstruction led to the seizure of power in 1933, the Enabling Act, the Gleichschaltung of state and society, the Nuremberg racial laws of 1935, the remilitarization of the Rhineland of 1936, and the annexations of 1938 — the arc recorded step by step in the regime’s own Dokumente der deutschen Politik.
Italy travelled the parallel road of Fascism: born of interventionism and the Fasci di combattimento of 1919, it passed through the biennio rosso, squadrism, Fiume and the March on Rome of 1922 to the corporate state — the story told from within by Businelli, Volpe, Farinacci and Pini — and ended in the disasters of the Second World War and the coup of 25 July 1943, recorded by Badoglio, and in the testimony of Primo Levi’s Se questo è un uomo.
Spain descended from the dictatorship of Primo de Rivera into the Second Republic (1931), whose reforms and crises — the agrarian and Catalan questions, the October 1934 insurrection, the Popular Front of 1936 — plunged the country into the Civil War, the internationalised conflict of the three Franciscos that ended in Franco’s victory of 1939 and the long dictatorship. Madariaga, Azaña, Chaves Nogales, Fernández Almagro, Aznar and Hayes record it from every side.
France, the old parliamentary Republic of the centre, drifted through the Bloc National and the Cartel des Gauches to the Popular Front and the crisis of 1938 — the “practice of doing nothing” of Daniel Halévy’s chronicle — and collapsed in the strange defeat of 1940, dissected by Bloch, while Élie Halévy diagnosed the era of tyrannies and the Soviet sources told the parallel story of the building of socialism, the purges and the Great Patriotic War.
How to read

Start with major events: the founding of the Fasci (1919), the March on Rome (1922), the Beer Hall Putsch (1923), the seizure of power and Enabling Act (1933), the Nuremberg laws (1935), the Anschluss and Munich (1938), the Spanish Civil War campaigns (1936–39), the coup of 25 July 1943, the Great Patriotic War (1941–45).
Read entities as continuous political biographies tied to those crises.
Use concepts for structures that span decades: national-socialism, fascism-italian, the totalitarian-state and era-of-tyrannies, the second-spanish-republic, the third-republic-france, weimar-republic.
Every entity/event/concept page ends with a Sources section pointing at the underlying books.
Native-language glosses follow on first use of each technical term.

sources-map.title: Sources Map
sources-map.content:
Sources Map
This page maps the wiki’s source pages by what they cover. It will grow as sources are ingested.
Russia / Soviet Union

Pokrovsky — Russian History in the Briefest Outline (4th ed., 1933) — Soviet Marxist survey, earliest times to the 1905 revolution; Part III on the revolutionary period 1897–1917 and the defense of October.
Short Course of the History of the VKP(b) (1945) — official Stalin-era party history, twelve chapters from 1883 to 1937; the obligatory text of party and civic education.
Shestakov (ed.) — Short Course of the History of the USSR (1937) — school textbook (3rd–4th grades) surveying Russian and Soviet history from antiquity to the 1936 Constitution.
Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin: A Short Biography (2nd ed., 1948) — official biographical portrait of Stalin, from his birth in Gori (1879) through the Great Patriotic War and post-war reconstruction (1946).
Stalin — On the Great Patriotic War of the Soviet Union (1946) — Stalin’s collected wartime speeches, orders and allied correspondence, 3 July 1941 to 3 September 1945; the primary documentary record of the war.

Germany / Weimar Republic & Third Reich

Rosenberg — History of the German Republic (1935) — an exile history of the Weimar Republic by the left-socialist historian Arthur Rosenberg, from the 1918 revolution to the death of the republic in 1930.
Volz (ed.) — From Great Power to World Power 1937 (1938) — Band 5 of the official Nazi Dokumente der deutschen Politik: 81 German state documents of 1937 — laws, decrees, speeches, notes and protocols — recording the consolidation of the Third Reich and its foreign policy on the eve of the 1938 annexations.
Volz (ed.) — Großdeutschland 1938, Band 6 Teil 1 (1940) — Band 6, Part 1 of the official Nazi Dokumente der deutschen Politik: 85 German state documents of 1938 — the Blomberg–Fritsch crisis and Ribbentrop’s appointment as Foreign Minister, the Anschluss of Austria, the Sudeten crisis and Munich Agreement, and the reordering of the enlarged state.
Büttner (ed.) — The Road to the National Socialist Reich (1943) — a party-authorized documentary compilation realizing the 25-point program of the NSDAP point by point: the recovery of the Saar, Austria, the Sudetenland, Memel, Danzig and Eupen–Malmedy, the abrogation of Versailles and St. Germain, the Nuremberg racial laws and the exclusion of Jews from the economy, and the labour, agrarian and tax legislation of 1933–1940.
Berndt & Kriegk (eds.) — We Experience the Liberation of the Saar (1935) — six German journalists’ eyewitness reports of the Saar campaign and the plebiscite of 13 January 1935, written at the moment of the Saar’s return to the Reich.
Friedrichs (comp.) — The National Socialist Revolution 1933, Band 1 (3rd ed., 1938) — the opening volume of the official Nazi Dokumente der deutschen Politik series of the German Academy for Politics: the principal laws, decrees, speeches and documents of the Nazi seizure of power in 1933 — from Hitler’s appointment on 30 January through the Enabling Act and the end of the party state, to the rebuilding of state, economy, culture and law.
Friedrichs (comp.) — Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934, Band 2 (3rd ed., 1938) — the second volume of the official Nazi Dokumente der deutschen Politik series and direct companion to Band 1: 92 German state documents of 1934 recording the completion of the Führer-state — the Röhm purge of 30 June, Hitler’s assumption of the head-of-state office on Hindenburg’s death and the plebiscite of 19 August, the German–Polish Non-Aggression Pact, the Saar campaign, and the reordering of state, people, economy, culture and law.
Friedrichs (comp.) — Deutschlands Weg zur Freiheit 1935, Band 3 (3rd ed., 1938) — the third volume of the official Nazi Dokumente der deutschen Politik series and direct companion to Bands 1, 2 and 4: 52 German state documents of 1935 — the recovery of the Saar, the reintroduction of general conscription and the building of the Wehrmacht, the Anglo-German Naval Agreement, the Nuremberg racial laws, and the reordering of state, people, economy, culture and law.
Friedrichs (comp.) — Deutschlands Aufstieg zur Großmacht 1936, Band 4 (2nd ed., 1938) — the fourth volume of the official Nazi Dokumente der deutschen Politik series and direct continuation of Bands 1, 2 and 3: 64 German state documents of 1936 — the remilitarization of the Rhineland and repudiation of Locarno, the Berlin Olympics, Himmler’s appointment as Chef der deutschen Polizei, the German–Austrian agreement of 11 July, the Anti-Comintern Pact with Japan, and the second Four Year Plan — recording the regime’s consolidation and outward assertion.
Geisow — The Soul of the Third Reich (1933) — a völkisch racial-ideological tract written in February 1933, in the weeks after Hitler’s appointment as Reich Chancellor; the unofficial, party-side voice of the Nazi revolution in its first months.
Speer — Erinnerungen (1969) — the autobiography of Hitler’s architect and, from 1942, Reich Minister for Armaments and War Production, from his youth and party entry in 1931 through the Third Reich and the war to his capture, the Nuremberg trial and his postwar reflection on responsibility; an insider’s account of Hitler’s circle and the armaments economy.
Heiden — Adolf Hitler: Eine Biographie (1936) — the first full-length biography of Hitler, written in exile by the German-Jewish journalist Konrad Heiden and published in Zurich in 1936: from Hitler’s Austrian birth, youth and the “lost years” in Vienna and Munich, through the founding of the NSDAP, the Beer Hall Putsch of 1923 and the writing of Mein Kampf, the years of reconstruction and electoral advance after 1925, to the seizure of power in 1933 and the Night of the Long Knives of 30 June 1934; the critical-democratic German case in “the age of irresponsibility,” counterpart to the regime’s own documentary compilations and to Geisow’s völkisch tract.
Hitler — Mein Kampf (Band I 1925, Band II 1926) — the foundational text of National Socialism, dictated in Landsberg prison after the failure of the Beer Hall Putsch and published in two volumes (Eine Abrechnung, 1925; Die nationalsozialistische Bewegung, 1926): the autobiography of Hitler’s Austrian origins, Vienna years and wartime service, and the doctrinal and programmatic core — race and the völkisch state, the Führer principle, propaganda, and the foreign-policy chapters demanding Lebensraum in the East and the destruction of Soviet Russia; the regime’s own foundational text.

Italy / Fascism

Businelli — Rivoluzione fascista: Origini e sviluppi del movimento delle camicie nere (1933) — a narrative history of the rise of Italian Fascism written from within the movement by the Fascist educator Alberto Businelli, with a preface by F. T. Marinetti: from the Balkan Wars and the intervention crisis, the founding of the Fasci at Piazza San Sepolcro (1919) and the biennio rosso, to the March on Rome of 1922; the Fascist regime’s own account of its origins and victory.
Volpe — Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) — the collected wartime-and-Fascist political journalism of the historian Gioacchino Volpe, from 1916 through the Great War, the postwar crisis and the Fascist consolidation of the mid-1920s: morale pieces written for the VIII Armata, essays on France, England, Egypt, regionalism, the school question and Machiavelli, and the explicitly Fascist pieces of 1921–1928; how a professional academic historian of the national school wrote for the interventionist and Fascist press and framed Fascism within Italy’s longer history.
Levi — Se questo è un uomo (1947) — the first edition of the most celebrated Italian testimony of the Holocaust: Primo Levi’s account of his deportation from Fossoli to Auschwitz in February 1944 and his survival to the liberation in January 1945 — the arrival and the tattooing of Häftling 174517, the Ka-Be and the selections, the “drowned and the saved,” the chemistry examination, and the closing Storia di dieci giorni; the Italian-Jewish victim’s voice standing at the far end of the fascism the regime sources celebrate.
Volpe — History of the Fascist Movement (1936) — the English translation of Volpe’s continuous narrative history of the Fascist movement, published in Rome in the Fascist year XIV (1935–1936): from interventionism and the Fasci d’azione, the founding of the Fasci di combattimento and the movement’s transformation into a party, the March on Rome, Fascism at the helm and the reform of the state, to a closing chapter placing “Fascist Italy” in Europe; the canonical mid-1930s regime historiography of Fascism’s origins by the regime’s foremost academic historian.
Farinacci — Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. I (Il 1919) (1937) — the first volume of the party history of the Fascist Revolution by the Cremona ras Roberto Farinacci: a polemical insider account of the crisis year 1919 in sixteen chapters and two parts (“Lo sfacelo della classe dirigente,” “La disfatta diplomatica”) — the interventionist split, the founding of the Fasci di combattimento (23 March), the fatti di Milano, the Fiume undertaking (September) and the elections of 16 November.
Farinacci — Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. II (L’Insurrezione Rossa e la Vittoria dei Fasci) (1938) — the second volume of Farinacci’s party history, covering 1 January 1920 – May 1921: the “red biennium” of strikes, factory occupations and agrarian unrest (L’Insurrezione Rossa) answered by the squadrist reaction and the electoral triumph of the National Blocs (La Vittoria dei Fasci).
Farinacci — Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. III (La Marcia su Roma) (1939) — the third and final volume of Farinacci’s party history, covering May 1921 – October 1922: from the end of the Giolittian system (Part I, Cap. XXXII–XXXV) through the March on Rome (Part II, Cap. XXXVI–XXXIX) to the formation of the Fascist government.
Pini & Bresadola — Storia del Fascismo: Guerra – Rivoluzione – Regime (1928) — a continuous, regime-published chronicle of the rise of Italian Fascism by Giorgio Pini and Federico Bresadola (Libreria del Littorio, Roma 1928): from the fall of Crispi after Adua and the precursor movements, through Nazionalismo e Sindacalismo and the Libyan conquest, interventionism and the Great War, the founding of the Fasci (23 March 1919), Fiume, squadrism and the March on Rome, the Matteotti crisis, the “conquest of the state” (1925–27) and Fascist Italy in the world.
Badoglio — Italy in the Second World War: Memories and Documents (1948) — the memoirs of Marshal Pietro Badoglio, the Fascist general who succeeded Mussolini as Prime Minister after the coup of 25 July 1943: Italy in the Second World War from the fall of the regime to the cobelligerence — Mussolini’s April 1939 memorandum to Hitler, the declaration of war of June 1940, the war disasters, the coup d’état of 25 July 1943 and the arrest of Mussolini, the armistice of 8 September 1943, the flight to Brindisi, the cobelligerent government and the liberation of Rome in June 1944; the Allied-side counterpart to the regime’s own histories of Fascism.

France / Third Republic

Siegfried — Tableau des partis en France (1930) — a contemporary political geography and sociology of the French party system of the Third Republic, written in 1930 by the founder of French electoral geography: the French character (Part I) and the determining factors of domestic (Part II) and foreign (Part III) policy, the cycles of the postwar Bloc National and Cartel des Gauches (Part IV), the fan of parties from Left to Right (Part V), the closing comparison of Latin and Anglo-Saxon democracy (Part VI), and two statistical appendices on the strength of the parties in the Chamber and the principal votes of 1924–1930; the French case from within the old parliamentary republic of the centre, on the eve of the crises of the 1930s.
Halévy — L’ère des tyrannies (1938) — the posthumous essay collection of the historian of English liberalism Élie Halévy, with Célestin Bouglé’s preface: “Sismondi” and the Saint-Simonian economic doctrine, the English policy of social peace, the problem of workers’ control, the present state of the English social question, the interpretation of the world crisis of 1914–1918 (towards revolution, towards war, war and revolution), socialism and democratic parliamentarism, and the closing “L’ère des tyrannies” (1936) — the argument that Fascism, Nazism and Bolshevism are continuations of the revolutionary era transformed by total war and total revolution into the era of the organised, totalitarian state; the French liberal-democratic diagnosis of the totalitarian state, the counterpart to the German, Italian and Russian sources presented from the totalitarian side.
Zévaès — Histoire de la Troisième République (1926) — a committed narrative history of the French Third Republic from 1870 to 1926 by the Socialist deputy and historian Alexandre Zévaès: the 4 September 1870, the National Defence and the Commune, the monarchist crisis and the Constitution of 1875, Boulangism and the Panama scandal, the Dreyfus affair, the separation of Church and State, the prewar ministries, the Great War, and the postwar Bloc National and Cartel des Gauches, closing with a Conclusion and annexes tabulating the Presidents, ministries and principal dates of the Republic; the French parliamentary republic told from within by a man of the Left.
Daniel Halévy — 1938: Une année d’histoire (1938) — a contemporary month-by-month chronicle of the crisis year 1938 by the historian and man of letters Daniel Halévy, brother of Élie Halévy: the January reopening of the Chamber, his portrait of parliamentary drift and inaction (“la pratique du rien”), a Socialist statesman come to power, the fall of Blum and the ministry of Daladier, the deceptive calm of the summer, the mounting Sudeten crisis and the approach of war, and the closing aftermath of Munich — the French moderate-liberal diary of the year of the Munich Agreement, written at the moment before 1939.
Bloch — L’Étrange Défaite (1940) — the celebrated eyewitness account of the collapse of France in 1940 by the historian Marc Bloch, co-founder of the Annales school, written “en pleine rage” in the weeks after the disaster (July–September 1940) and published posthumously in 1946: the presentation of the witness, the deposition of a defeated man from the Intelligence staff of the 1st Army, and the examination of conscience of a Frenchman indicting the military caste, the political class and the whole society that had failed to prepare for total war; the volume appends Bloch’s Testament (18 March 1941) and the clandestine essays written under Vichy (Pourquoi je suis républicain, Sur la réforme de l’enseignement); the French case from the side of the victim and the analyst — the internal diagnosis of the “strange defeat” from a citizen-soldier of the Republic’s academic elite.

Spain / Second Republic & Civil War

Madariaga — España: Ensayo de historia contemporánea (1950) — the contemporary history of Spain by the Spanish liberal diplomat and writer Salvador de Madariaga, 1950 Buenos Aires fifth edition (first published in English as Spain 1930, in Spanish 1931): Libro Primero, from the land, people and empire (Chs. I–VIII), the elements of Alfonso XIII’s reign — the agrarian, labour, church, army, Catalan (three chapters), Basque and Galician, Portuguese, Moroccan, Hispanoamerican and foreign questions (Chs. IX–XXI) — and the reign of Alfonso XIII itself, the prewar, the Great War, postwar liberal crisis, the dictatorship of Primo de Rivera and its liquidation, to the situation of 1930 (Chs. XXII–XXVII); Libro Segundo, the Republic of 1931 through its left and right phases and the Popular Front (Chs. I–VII), the Civil War — the battle of the three Franciscos, the national phase and the phases of foreign infiltration and domination, the role of the Spanish Communist Party and Russian influence, and the war’s end (Chs. VIII–XI) — and Franco’s early dictatorship, its interior and foreign policy and the éxodo (Chs. XII–XV), closing with five appendices (Memoria personal; the Stalin letter to Largo Caballero; the Companys letter to Negrín; and two articles on Azaña and on civil war from Ahora, March 1935) and the name and general indexes; the Spanish liberal-democratic case from within — the victim-analyst of the Civil War, in the manner of Bloch on the French defeat, the peninsular counterpart to the regime sources and the French and Italian pages.
Chaves Nogales — A sangre y fuego: Héroes, bestias y mártires de España (1937) — nine stories of the Spanish Civil War written in exile in Paris in 1937 by the Sevillian liberal journalist Manuel Chaves Nogales (first published 1937): the author’s prologue (Montrouge, January–May 1937) and the nine novelas — ¡Masacre, masacre!, La gesta de los caballistas, Y a lo lejos, una lucecita, La columna de hierro, El tesoro de Briesca, Los guerreros marroquíes, ¡Viva la muerte!, Bigornia and Consejo obrero — each drawn, per the author’s NOTA, from a rigorously veridical fact; the literary testimony of the war itself from the liberal “third Spain” that refused solidarity with the assassins of either side.
Fernández Almagro — Historia del reinado de Alfonso XIII (4th ed., 1977) — the Spanish monarchy-centered institutional chronicle of the whole reign of Alfonso XIII, 1902–1931, by the Granada historian and critic Melchor Fernández Almagro (4th ed., Montaner y Simón, Barcelona, 1977): a strictly political and external history in six Parts — I. Liquidación de la Regencia (1902–1906), II. Intentos de renovación (1907–1912), III. Equilibrio inestable (1912–1917), IV. Conatos revolucionarios (1917–1923), V. La Dictadura (1923–1930) and VI. Capitulación de la Monarquía (1930–1931) — each government and each royal intervention from Sagasta through the Moroccan wars, the Juntas de Defensa and the general strike of 1917, the pistolerismo of Barcelona, the disaster of Annual, the Dictatorship of Primo de Rivera, and the monarchy’s fall in the municipal elections of 12 April 1931; the antecedent to the republic and Civil War covered by Madariaga and Chaves Nogales.
Azaña — Mi rebelión en Barcelona (1935) — the prison memoir of the October 1934 events written by the liberal republican statesman Manuel Azaña (former prime minister, 1931–1933) while held, first aboard the Uruguay and then aboard the prison ships Ciudad de Cádiz and Barcaiztegui, 2nd edition 1935, dedicated to Ángel Ossorio: the title answering his own indictment for rebellion, and six sections of narrative (Barcelona in November aboard the Galiano, through December aboard the Barcaiztegui) giving his account of the general strike, the proclamation of the Catalan State by the Generalidad and its crushing under martial law, and his own arrest and imprisonment; the volume adds his parliamentary speech of 25 June 1934 on the Catalan law of land-cultivation contracts, his address to the Catalan republicans of 10 August 1934, and a legal appendix reproducing the papers of his prosecution — the cipher telegram of 10 October 1934 recording his detention, the fiscal’s dictamen, the statement of HECHOS (the proclamation of the Estado Catalán on the night of 6 October and the state of war), and the numbered juridical studies (El estado de guerra, La garantía de las setenta y dos horas, Un delito patente) — closing with the Supreme Court’s sobreseimiento libre; the accused statesman’s own voice at the moment the Republic’s internal crisis broke in Catalonia.
1940) — the Nationalist side’s own authorized military history of the Spanish Civil War by the war correspondent and propagandist Manuel Aznar Zubigaray (1940; dedicated to his three sons “combatientes de España”): thirty-four chapters across three volumes tracing the war as a sequence of campaigns and maneuvers — the alzamiento of 18 July 1936, the march on Madrid and the failed assault, the isolated strongholds (Alcázar, Oviedo, Santa María de la Cabeza), Málaga, the Jarama, Guadalajara, the northern front and the conquest of Bilbao, Brunete, Santander, Asturias, Teruel, the great battle of the Ebro, the Battle of Catalonia and the fall of Barcelona, and the final offensive of 1939 — closing with a summary of the reasons for Franco’s victory; the regime’s military-strategic voice on the 1936–39 war, complementary to Madariaga’s liberal history and to Chaves Nogales’s testimony.
Hayes — Misión de Guerra en España, 1942–1945 (1945) — the memoir of Carlton J. H. Hayes, the Columbia historian who served as U.S. Ambassador to Franco’s Spain from May 1942 to January 1945 (Spanish translation of Wartime Mission in Spain, 1942–1945, Macmillan 1945): nine chapters on his double mission to counter Axis pressure on Spain and keep it out of the war while winning Allied facilities — his appointment and first contacts, the struggle with Spanish non-belligerency, the winning of facilities, the opposing currents of Axis agents, the progress of Spanish neutrality, the wolfram crisis, Spain’s growing benevolent neutrality, and his departure in January 1945; the American ambassador’s Allied-side eyewitness account of Spain’s wartime neutrality, covering the war years 1942–45 beside Tusell’s chapters on the same period.
Tusell — Historia de España en el siglo XX, II. La crisis de los años treinta: República y guerra civil (2000) — continuous scholarly history of the Second Republic and the Civil War by Javier Tusell (UNED), volume II of his four-volume Historia de España en el siglo XX (2000; ePubLibre edition): society and economy at the height of 1930 (the agrarian and urban world, everyday life, the impact of the world crisis, the coming of mass democracy), the Republic from the 1931 experience through the Constitution, the reformist biennium (military, religious, agrarian, social and economic reforms), the «República en una tenaza», the conservative biennium of radicals and cedistas, the October 1934 insurrection and its aftermath, the split of the socialists, Spanish fascism, the Popular Front of 1936 and the “plano inclinado” toward war, and then the Civil War from conspiracy and the balance of forces through revolution, repression, the church, the column-war, Madrid, internationalisation, the northern campaign, the two armies, Franco’s political unity, the Popular Front’s internal confrontation, Negrín, Teruel, the Ebro and the war’s end, closing with society and culture in wartime and a long bibliography; the Republic-and-Civil-War companion to the wiki’s Tusell volume III, the modern Spanish scholarly backbone for the crisis years the wiki’s contemporary Spanish sources (Aznar, Chaves Nogales, Hayes, Azaña, Madariaga) enter from within. Volume IV (La transición democrática) belongs with Rest of Europe 1946–present when processed.
Tusell — Historia de España en el siglo XX, III. La dictadura de Franco (2000) — continuous scholarly history of Franco’s dictatorship by Javier Tusell (UNED), volume III of his four-volume Historia de España en el siglo XX (2000; ePubLibre edition): from the last war bulletin of 1 April 1939 to Franco’s death in November 1975 — the dictator, the regime as dictatorship, repression and exile, fascist temptation and wartime foreign policy 1939–45, isolation and autarky, Concordat and US pacts of 1953, developmentalism and opposition 1951–65, tardofranquismo of Carrero and Arias Navarro; the modern Spanish analytical backbone for the Franco years the wiki’s contemporary Spanish sources enter only in part. Volume IV (La transición democrática) belongs with Rest of Europe 1946–present when processed.

World War II / Espionage

Singer — Spies and Traitors of World War II (1945) — a wartime journalistic survey of espionage in the Second World War by the American writer Kurt Singer, published by Prentice-Hall in 1945: twenty-six spy stories and network profiles ranging across the secret services of both sides — Admiral Wilhelm Canaris and the German Abwehr, Lavrenti Beria and the Soviet secret service at Lubianka Street, the Japanese networks, the saboteurs landed in the United States, the Nazi weather-station espionage in the Arctic, German and Japanese illicit radio, the Nazi spy web in Denmark, agents in neutral Ireland, Baltic espionage, Canaris’s hand in the Arab world and his agents hunting Maurice Mercier through Spain and Portugal, the De Gaulle agents in Africa, and the secret plan for a postwar Nazi underground in Argentina; written partly from the author’s own work exposing Axis agents since 1933, with names of Allied agents still at work concealed and some incidents reconstructed — the Allied-side, secondary account of the secret war that the regime and memoir sources in this wiki describe from within.

sources/a-sangre-y-fuego-chaves-nogales-.title: Manuel Chaves Nogales — A sangre y fuego: Héroes, bestias y mártires de España (1937)
sources/a-sangre-y-fuego-chaves-nogales-.content:
Manuel Chaves Nogales — A sangre y fuego: Héroes, bestias y mártires de España
Full bibliographic citation — Manuel Chaves Nogales (1897–1944). A sangre y fuego: Héroes, bestias y mártires de España. — First published 1937 (this edition: Austral Edición Especial, January 2011; © Herederos de Manuel Chaves Nogales, 2006; © of the prologue, Ana R. Cañil; © Espasa Libros, S.L.U., 2011). The work first appeared in exile, the author’s prologue being dated “Montrouge (Seine), enero-mayo de 1937.”
Manuel Chaves Nogales, the Sevillian liberal journalist — editor of the republican daily Ahora during the first months of the war — wrote these nine stories in exile in Paris, where he had fled after the government’s departure for Valencia. His prologue is the manifesto of the “small bourgeois liberal” who, antifascist and antirevolutionary alike, refused solidarity with the assassins of either side: “my only and humble truth was an insuperable hatred of stupidity and cruelty,” against the seed of which “the fertile earth of Spain made the ancestral stupidity and cruelty pavorously prolific.” The nine novelas that follow are, by his own statement in the closing NOTA, “not works of imagination and pure fantasy” — “each of its episodes has been faithfully drawn from a rigorously veridical fact; each of its heroes has a real existence and an authentic personality,” veiled only because of the proximity of the events.
The text is 3,057 lines (~424,000 characters), extracted from the EPUB container (12 content sections), clean text layer, no OCR required.
Content Summary
Front matter. The EPUB opens with the title page, edition and copyright notices, then the prologue of this Austral edition by Ana R. Cañil, “La (imposible) tercera España,” which opens with the author’s own words — “«Cuento lo que he visto y lo que he vivido más fielmente de lo que yo quisiera»” — and places the work in the spring of 1937. The author’s own Prólogo del autor follows (Montrouge, January–May 1937): the testament of a liberal who served the workers of his newspaper after a consejo obrero seized it, who “luché contra el fascismo con el arma de mi oficio,” and who left when “ya no había nada que salvar,” choosing exile over the choice between “un abisinio desteñido” (Franco’s Spain) and “un kirguís de Occidente” (Bolshevism). The NOTA closes the front matter, asserting the veridical basis of the nine stories.
The Nine Stories
1. ¡Masacre, masacre! Opens: “Al sol de la mañana la bomba de aviación que cae es una pompita de jabón que en un instante raya el cielo azul de arriba abajo.” A tale of the aerial bombing of a town — Valero, an incorruptible revolutionary investigator, learns that his own retired-military father is on the day’s list of detainees, and must weigh personal feeling against revolutionary duty. The story closes with the official part: 222 dead, a hundred identified by name, and the line “«Los ciento veinticinco cadáveres restantes no han sido identificados».”
2. La gesta de los caballistas. Opens with the four Jerezano ponies of the young señoritos “cogidas del diestro por Currito, el espolique del marqués.” The heroic charge of a cavalry squadron of gentlemen against the red-held town square — the marqués’s men ride against the revolutionaries, barricade themselves in the town hall, hold the women and children found in the cellars as hostages, and end reduced to two dozen able men; the survivor bears the stigma of being Spanish and yet carries on — “¡Con todo! Y aún tuvo alma para levantar la cabeza y seguir adelante.”
3. Y a lo lejos, una lucecita. Opens: “La calle era una sima honda, larga y negra.” Jiménez, a milicianos’ responsible, with his thick-lensed spectacles, bursts into the elegant bedroom of Señorita Carmina on a doomed raid; at the story’s close he is shot and carries away “clavada en ellos… la imagen de aquella lucecita distante,” while the dying Pedro, “en la guerra y la revolución era difícil dormir. ¡Pero qué a gusto se dormía al final!”
4. La columna de hierro. Opens: “Se dobló sobre la barandilla del palco y echando el cuerpo fuera dijo algo que no entendió nadie.” The anarchist Iron Column and the struggle between the Chino’s men, who “para hacer la justicia revolucionaria que vosotros no habéis sabido hacer” would shoot fascist prisoners, and the committee’s authority (“Aquí no hay más autoridad que la del comité”); the closing air attack cuts down even the slender standing miliciana.
5. El tesoro de Briesca. Opens: “Testarudo y valiente, aquel hombrín insensato se obstinaba en seguir haciendo, bajo el bombardeo de las baterías rebeldes, el inventario del tesoro artístico.” The artist Arnal, of the Junta de Incautación y Conservación del Tesoro Artístico Nacional, sent “—Salve usted todo lo que buenamente pueda,” salvages Castilian art under fire; a dead miliciano’s imprecise sketch lines sell to an American journalist for five dollars of Red Aid — “valía por dos obras maestras del Greco.”
6. Los guerreros marroquíes. Opens with the surrender of Mohamed — “—Paisa, por Dios Grande, no tirar. Yo estar rojo.” — the Moroccan soldiers of Franco’s forces and their relationship with the Spanish milicianos who meet them; the caíd’s parting words — “Moro sabe que tú estar amigo aunque mates. Moro también mataría. Estar cosa de guerra y de hombres. ¡Alá es grande!” — and the prisoners lined against the wall and cut down with a machine gun.
7. ¡Viva la muerte! Opens with a captain and two lieutenants pacing the deserted station platform, and the great fascist parade in the Plaza Mayor of Valladolid — the pedritos and flechas, uniformed children, the señoras with veil and mantilla cheering the saviours of Spain. The falangist’s obsessive refrain over Rosario — “¡Cómo lloraba! Lloraba como una chiquilla.”
8. Bigornia. Opens: “Le llamaban Bigornia, y era un ogro jovial y arrabalero.” The jovial ogre of the suburb who, instead of eating children, produces them with indecent fertility; his tank rescues a terrified mother and her little ones from the roadside, carrying the mother asleep on his shoulder; the burnt and monstrous figure that reaches the Madrid hospital lives a few hours more — “Sucumbió sintiendo llorar a ambos lados de su cama a dos pobres mujeres.”
9. Consejo obrero. Opens with a man rising furiously: “—Pido la palabra. —No hay palabra —respondió el presidente.” The workers’ council that seizes a factory and the anguish of the bourgeois technician forced to train his own replacements — “esperando y a veces deseando que las milicias fuesen de una vez por él” — until the communist’s verdict: “un pobre diablo sin conciencia revolucionaria… Para ir a morir al frente servía, sin embargo. Le pusieron en una mano un plato de comida y en la otra un fusil.” Daniel, converted into a miliciano of the revolution, “luchó como los buenos. Y murió batiéndose heroicamente por una causa que no era suya.”
Key Data Points









































AttributeDetailAuthorManuel Chaves Nogales (1897–1944)TitleA sangre y fuego: Héroes, bestias y mártires de EspañaPublishedFirst ed. 1937 (exile, Paris); this text from the Austral/Espasa ed. of January 2011SourceEPUB container (12 sections: cubierta, sinopsis, título, info, prólogo, prologue, NOTA, 9 stories)Raw filewiki/raw/a-sangre-y-fuego-chaves-nogales-1937.txtLines3,057Sections/ChaptersFront matter (edition prologue by A. R. Cañil; Prólogo del autor; NOTA) + 9 storiesSignificanceThe liberal-journalist’s eye on the Civil War from the inside — an antinomic middle voice that refuses both “blancos y rojos,” the civilian counterpart to Madariaga’s political history and to the regime sources, giving the wiki its Spanish literary testimony of the war itself
Relationship to the Wiki
Chaves Nogales gives the wiki its second Spanish source and its first literary testimony of the Civil War itself, seen not from the vantage of the regime or the political history of the Republic but from the desk of a republican editor who served the workers after his newspaper was seized and then left for exile. His is the “third Spain” — liberal, antifascist and antirevolutionary alike — that refused solidarity with the assassins of either side. Read against Madariaga’s political chronicle, Aznar’s Nationalist military history, Azaña’s 1934 prison memoir, Tusell’s volume II on the Republic and Civil War, and his later scholarly history of the dictatorship born of the war, it extends the Spanish section into the lived war, complementing the French pages of Bloch on the defeat and the regime testimonies elsewhere in the wiki. Its nine stories, each “extraído fielmente de un hecho rigurosamente verídico,” bring the maelstrom of 1936–37 to the raw corpus from the pen of a Spanish liberal in exile.
Naming Convention

sources/badoglio-italy-in-the-second-wor.title: Badoglio — Italy in the Second World War: Memories and Documents (1948)
sources/badoglio-italy-in-the-second-wor.content:
Badoglio — Italy in the Second World War: Memories and Documents (1948)
Author: Marshal Pietro Badoglio (1871–1956)
Publisher: Oxford University Press, London, 1948 (English translation by Muriel Currey of L’Italia nella seconda guerra mondiale); reprint by Greenwood Press, Westport, Connecticut, 1976. Library of Congress catalog card 75-28658; ISBN 0-8371-8485-1. (Digitized copy from the Baker College–Flint library, via Internet Archive, oclc 61198029.)
Preface: dated “Cava dei Tirreni, July 1944” — “I have written this book because I believe that the Italian people have the right to know the course of events which led to their ruin. I do not wish to try to justify myself. Only the man who acts makes mistakes.”
Character
The memoir of Marshal Pietro Badoglio, the Army Chief of Staff under the Fascist regime who led the Italian conquest of Ethiopia and commanded in the Greek and North African theatres, and who in July 1943 became Prime Minister after the King’s coup against Mussolini. Written at Cava dei Tirreni in the summer of 1944 — between the liberation of Rome and the end of the war — it is at once an apologia for Badoglio’s own conduct and a denunciation of the Fascist political and military leadership that he held responsible for Italy’s ruin. It is the testament of the man who dismantled the Fascist state from within, negotiated the armistice with the Allies, and presided over the cobelligerent government at Brindisi, Salerno and Rome. Where the other Italian sources in this wiki are regime-side narratives of Fascism’s rise, this is the Allied-side account of Fascism’s fall and of Italy’s wartime ordeal, told by the regime’s own military commander who turned against it.
Structure
Two parts, eighteen chapters (numbered I–VI, VIII–XIX; the number VII is skipped in the text), followed by six appendix documents. Part I covers the road to war and the fall of the regime (1939 – 8 September 1943); Part II covers the armistice, the Brindisi government and the cobelligerent period (September 1943 – June 1944).


Part I (chs. I–VI, VIII–IX) — 1939 to the Armistice

Ch. I (1939) — Mussolini’s memorandum of April 1939 to Hitler (the “rich vs. poor nations” war thesis); the character of Mussolini and Hitler
Ch. II — Mussolini decides on Intervention — the Polish campaign, the decision of 10 June 1940 and Italy’s declaration of war
Ch. III — At War — the command of the armed forces, the campaign against France and the early war years
Ch. IV — The Dictatorship ‘in extremis’ — Badoglio’s resignation as Chief of the General Staff, the war disasters and the crisis of the regime
Ch. V — The ‘Coup d’état’ — the conspiracy, the meeting of the Grand Council (24–25 July 1943), the arrest of Mussolini and the King’s appointment of Badoglio
Ch. VI — A Review of the Situation — the reasons for continuing the war, negotiations with the Allies
Ch. VIII — The Armistice — the negotiations with the Allies and the armistice of 8 September 1943 (the number VII is not used)
Ch. IX — From Rome to Brindisi — the flight of the King, Badoglio and the government from Rome to the Allied lines at Brindisi



Part II (chs. X–XIX) — the Cobelligerent Government, September 1943 – June 1944

Ch. X — First Days at Brindisi
Ch. XI — Military Problems — the Anglo-American strategy in Italy, the co-belligerent Italian armed forces
Ch. XII — The Difficulties Increase
Ch. XIII — The Government extends its Jurisdiction — the transfer to Salerno, the re-establishment of administration
Ch. XIV — The Pact with Russia: Roosevelt’s Declaration — the Soviet recognition of the Italian government
Ch. XV — The New Provinces: The Allied Control Commission: The Elimination of Fascism
Ch. XVI — The Constitutional Compromise — the debate over the King’s position and the Crown
Ch. XVII — The Government of Democratic Unity — the formation of the six-party government under the anti-Fascist parties
Ch. XVIII — The Liberation of Rome: The Lieutenant-Generalship: The New Government — the fall of Rome (June 1944), the Prince’s lieutenant-generalship, Badoglio’s resignation
Ch. XIX — Italy and the Allies — a summing-up of the cobelligerence



Appendixes — six documents

Document 1 — The Royal Italian Army (its war record and reorganisation)
Document 2 — The Royal Italian Navy
Document 3 — The Royal Italian Air Force
Document 4 — The Government and the Patriots — the guerrilla/partisan movement and the decision to support it
Document 5 — The Prisoners of War
Document 6 — Internal Reconstruction



OCR Quality
Clean embedded text layer (LuraDocument PDF, Roman type) — no re-OCR required. Isolated slips only, chiefly in the printed front matter and Contents (e.g. the catalog-card and title-page ornamentation lines 1–50, “The Coup @ état” for “coup d’état”, “Furisdiction” for “Jurisdiction”, “reladl” for “relations”, “Alhes” for “Allies”); the body text is readable throughout.
Coverage
The Second World War as experienced by Italy’s wartime government, from April 1939 (Mussolini’s memorandum to Hitler) through Italy’s declaration of war in June 1940, the campaigns in France, Greece, North Africa and the Soviet Union, the fall of Mussolini and the coup of 25 July 1943, the armistice of 8 September 1943, the German occupation and the establishment of the cobelligerent government at Brindisi and Salerno, to the liberation of Rome in June 1944. It is the counterpart to, and refutation of, the Fascist-side accounts of the rise of the regime: where Businelli, Volpe, Farinacci and Pini narrate Fascism’s victory, Badoglio narrates its collapse and Italy’s passage to the Allied side.
Cross-references

Companion Italian sources on the rise of Fascism (the regime side): Businelli, Rivoluzione fascista (1933); Volpe, Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) and Volpe, History of the Fascist Movement (1936); Farinacci, Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vols. I–III (1937–39); Pini & Bresadola, Storia del Fascismo (1928). Badoglio stands at the opposite pole of the same political history — the account of the regime’s military commander who overthrew it.
Companion German memoir: Speer, Erinnerungen (1969) — the analogous insider’s memoir of a defeated dictatorship written after its fall.

sources/bloch-l-etrange-defaite-1940.title: Marc Bloch — L'Étrange Défaite (1940)
sources/bloch-l-etrange-defaite-1940.content:
L’Étrange Défaite
Marc Bloch — L’Étrange Défaite (Strange Defeat). Written July–September 1940; first published posthumously by Éditions Franc-Tireur, Paris, 1946; the digital edition used here (Feedbooks) reproduces the full volume, which appends to L’Étrange Défaite proper the Testament de Marc Bloch and the Écrits clandestins. The celebrated eyewitness account of the collapse of France in 1940 by one of the foremost French historians of the century.





























AuthorMarc Bloch (1886–1944) — French medieval historian, co-founder with Lucien Febvre of the Annales school and the journal Annales d’histoire économique et sociale (1929); author of Les Rois thaumaturges (1924), Les Caractères originaux de l’histoire rurale française (1931) and La Société féodale (1939–40); veteran of both World Wars — corporal in 1914, mobilised again as a captain of the Intelligence staff (3e Bureau) in 1939; after the defeat a professor at Montpellier, deprived of his chair by the Vichy racial laws, who entered the Resistance under the pseudonym “Narbonne,” was captured, tortured and shot by the Germans on 16 June 1944 near LyonEditionFeedbooks digital reproduction of the full Franc-Tireur volume; L’Étrange Défaite written in a few weeks between July and September 1940 (the manuscript closes “Guéret-Fougères (Creuse): juillet-septembre 1940”), published 1946 with an avant-propos by Georges Altman; the volume also contains Bloch’s Testament (Clermont-Ferrand, 18 March 1941) and the posthumous Écrits clandestins; 7,553 lines / ~460,000 characters of extracted textStructureAvant-propos by Georges Altman + Partie 1, L’Étrange Défaite (3 chapters: “Présentation du témoin,” “La déposition d’un vaincu,” “Examen de conscience d’un Français”) + Partie 2, Le Testament de Marc Bloch + Partie 3, Écrits clandestins (6 essays, chiefly dating from 1941–43)PeriodThe French collapse of May–June 1940 and its causes, judged at the moment of the defeat (July–September 1940); the appended clandestine essays written under Vichy, 1941–1943NoteThe testimony of a professional historian writing “en pleine rage” (in a fury) in the weeks after the disaster, who declares he writes not his memoirs but a procès-verbal (an official report) of the year 1940 for future researchers. For this wiki it supplies the French case from the side of the victim and the analyst — the internal diagnosis of the “strange defeat” from a citizen-soldier of the Third Republic’s academic elite, standing at the opposite pole from the German, Italian and Russian sources presented from the totalitarian side
Contents. Georges Altman’s avant-propos praises the work as “un récit, une explication, un réquisitoire” (a narrative, an explanation, an indictment) without equal in France on 1940, and the voice of “un grand civil martyr, mort sans avoir jamais douté de l’aube” (a great civilian martyr, dead without ever having doubted the dawn). L’Étrange Défaite itself, dated July–September 1940, is divided into three chapters. “Présentation du témoin” (Presentation of the Witness) gives Bloch’s état civil as a witness: thirty-four years a historian, twice a soldier, and the first duty of the historian, in his master Pirenne’s phrase, to be interested “à la vie” (in life). “La déposition d’un vaincu” (The Deposition of a Defeated Man) — the longest chapter, written first and in the heat of the moment — recounts the collapse as Bloch saw it from the Intelligence staff of the 1st Army: the unreadiness of the high command, the confusion, the rout, the extraordinary slowness of the French command to grasp the war that the Germans were fighting. “Examen de conscience d’un Français” (A Frenchman’s Examination of Conscience) — written with more distance after the armistice — turns from the army to the nation: the responsibility of the professional military caste, of the political class, of the bourgeoisie, of the educational system, of the whole French society that had failed to prepare for total war. Partie 2 is Bloch’s Testament (18 March 1941): his instructions for his own burial, his refusal of religious ceremony, his affirmation that he was born a Jew, never sought to deny it and found no reason to be tempted to do so, and his declaration that throughout his life he felt himself “avant tout et très simplement Français” (above all and very simply French). Partie 3, the Écrits clandestins, gathers seven essays written under Vichy: “Pourquoi je suis républicain,” “L’alimentation humaine et les échanges internationaux,” “La vraie saison des juges,” “Un philosophe de bonne compagnie,” “À propos d’un livre trop peu connu,” “Sur la réforme de l’enseignement,” and the closing reflection on the France of the Resistance.
Character of the source. A first-person testimony and self-examination written in the weeks immediately following the catastrophe of 1940, by a man who combined the exacting method of the professional historian with the lived experience of two wars. Bloch is explicit about his purpose: “Je n’écris pas ici mes souvenirs” (I am not writing my memoirs here) — he writes a witness’s report, intended to lie hidden until the day France “verra de nouveau s’épanouir… la liberté de pensée et de jugement” (again sees the freedom of thought and judgment blossom), when researchers may profit from “ce procès-verbal de l’an 1940” (this report of the year 1940). It is at once a narrative of defeat, an analysis of its causes reaching into the deepest structures of French society and the French military mind, and a moral examination of conscience. His enemies are the routine of the military caste, the mental timidity of the ruling classes, the “vieux démon” of the bourgeoisie, and the intellectual smugness that left France unprepared; his heroes are the common people of France — the miners of the Nord and the Pas-de-Calais whom he names the best warriors of 1914–18, “une aristocratie” of honesty and courage. Written in the present tense of its own moment, it is a contemporary source of the first rank for the defeat of 1940 and the French reaction to it.
Quality. Good. Extracted from the clean HTML of a Feedbooks EPUB (no OCR required); French text clean and continuous, with the usual EPUB ligatures and spaced dashes carried over. Structure verified against the EPUB table of contents and the in-file “Chapitre N” and “Partie N” markers; the three-part division of the volume (L’Étrange Défaite / Testament / Écrits clandestins) confirmed.

Avant-propos de Georges Altman (Preface by Georges Altman)
Georges Altman’s preface praises the work: “il n’a pas paru à ce jour en France, sur 1940, un récit, une explication, un réquisitoire d’une pensée aussi lucide, d’un dessin aussi net” (there has appeared to this day in France, on 1940, no narrative, explanation or indictment of so lucid a thought, of so clear a design). Bloch wrote the text, he says, “en pleine rage” (in a fury) — “la belle rage d’un grand esprit qui n’admet pas” (the fine fury of a great mind that does not accept). Altman stresses the second part, the examen de conscience: “la bouleversante confession d’un grand intellectuel français qui se penche sans merci sur un monde et sur une caste” (the overwhelming confession of a great French intellectual who bends without mercy over a world and a caste). He closes by citing Bloch’s tribute to the common people: “Je n’ai pas connu en 1914-1918 de meilleurs guerriers que les mineurs du Nord ou du Pas-de-Calais” (I knew no better warriors in 1914–1918 than the miners of the Nord or the Pas-de-Calais), with the single exception of a man who proved to be a jaune, a non-unionised strike-breaker — evidence, for Bloch, that political choice, not class, made the soldier.
Partie 1 — L’Étrange Défaite (Strange Defeat)
The main work, written July–September 1940.
Chapitre 1 — Présentation du témoin (Presentation of the Witness)
Bloch declares he has decided to write, though the pages will long be unknown save “sous le manteau” (under the cloak): “Un témoignage ne vaut que fixé dans sa première fraîcheur” (a testimony is worth only fixed in its first freshness). He gives his état civil — “Écrire et enseigner l’histoire: tel est, depuis tantôt trente-quatre ans, mon métier” (to write and teach history: such has been, for some thirty-four years now, my trade) — and the first duty of the historian, in Pirenne’s phrase, to be interested in life: “sans se pencher sur le présent, il est impossible de comprendre le passé” (without bending over the present, it is impossible to understand the past). He was twice a soldier: he began the first war in August 1914 as a sergeant of infantry, “presque au niveau du simple soldat” (almost at the level of the simple soldier), and rose through chef de section, officer of intelligence, to captain; in 1939, twenty-one years later, he was mobilised again into the Intelligence staff.
Chapitre 2 — La déposition d’un vaincu (The Deposition of a Defeated Man)
“We have just suffered an incredible defeat. Whose fault is it? The parliamentary regime, the troops, the English, the …” — so the second chapter opens, listing the rival recriminations. The account of the collapse from within the Intelligence staff of the 1st Army: the high command’s unreadiness, its “extraordinary slowness” to grasp the nature of the war the Germans were fighting, the confusion and the rout, the collapse of communications and command, the breakdown of the army as a fighting institution. Bloch the historian applies to the present the same habits of criticism, observation and honesty he had brought to old documents: he is a witness who also explains, measuring the “strange defeat” against the standards of military history and of the German conduct of war.
Chapitre 3 — Examen de conscience d’un Français (A Frenchman’s Examination of Conscience)
The closing chapter, written with greater distance after the armistice, turns from the army to the nation: “Dans une nation, jamais aucun corps professionnel n’est, à lui seul, responsable” (in a nation, no professional body is ever alone responsible). The failure of the professional military caste, of the political class, of the bourgeoisie and its “vieux démon,” of the educational system and the whole society that had not prepared itself for total war; the “examen de conscience” of a Frenchman who refuses the facile explanation and indicts the deep structure of the Third Republic. The manuscript closes: “Guéret-Fougères (Creuse): juillet-septembre 1940.”
Partie 2 — Le Testament de Marc Bloch (The Testament of Marc Bloch)
Bloch’s testament, dated “Clermont-Ferrand, le 18 mars 1941.” He leaves to his wife, or failing her to his children, the care of his funeral: “Ce seront des obsèques purement civiles” (they will be purely civil obsequies), with no Hebrew prayers despite their cadences having accompanied so many of his ancestors and his father himself — his whole life he had striven “vers une sincérité totale de l’expression et de l’esprit” (towards a total sincerity of expression and spirit), and he held complaisance in lying to be the worst leprosy of the soul; his device is “Dilexit veritatem” (he loved truth). But it would be more odious still that any see in this act of probity a cowardly renunciation: “J’affirme donc, s’il le faut, face à la mort, que je suis né Juif” (I affirm then, if need be, in the face of death, that I was born a Jew) — the generous tradition of the Hebrew prophets, taken up and widened by Christianity in its purest, remains “une de nos meilleures raisons de vivre, de croire et de lutter” (one of our best reasons to live, to believe and to fight). “Étranger à tout formalisme confessionnel comme à toute solidarité prétendument raciale, je me suis senti, durant ma vie entière, avant tout et très simplement Français” (a stranger to all confessional formalism as to all supposedly racial solidarity, I have felt myself, during my whole life, above all and very simply French) — “je meurs, comme j’ai vécu, en bon Français” (I die, as I lived, a good Frenchman). He asks that his five military citations be read at his grave.
Partie 3 — Écrits clandestins (Clandestine Writings)
Seven essays written under Vichy and gathered in this posthumous volume.
Chapitre 1 — Pourquoi je suis républicain (Why I Am a Republican)
“Asking me why I am a republican, is that not already to be one? Is it not to admit that the form of power can be an object of choice maturely deliberated by the citizen, that the community therefore does not impose itself on man…” — Bloch’s republican confession under the Vichy regime that had abolished the Republic.
Chapitre 2 — L’alimentation humaine et les échanges internationaux (Human Food and International Exchanges)
An essay on food supply and international trade, reflecting Bloch’s wartime and blockade-era concerns.
Chapitre 3 — La vraie saison des juges (The True Season of Judges)
On law, judgment and the judges — written under a regime that had made law a weapon.
Chapitre 4 — Un philosophe de bonne compagnie (A Philosopher of Good Company)
A literary-philosophical essay, presumably on a figure of French thought.
Chapitre 5 — À propos d’un livre trop peu connu (On a Book Too Little Known)
A note drawing attention to a neglected work.
Chapitre 6 — Sur la réforme de l’enseignement (On the Reform of Education)
Bloch’s notes “pour une révolution de l’enseignement” (for a revolution in education), written for the Cahiers politiques of the resistance: “Tout malheur national appelle, d’abord, un examen de conscience” (every national misfortune calls, first, for an examination of conscience), then a plan of renovation. He demands a reasoned revision of values throughout — an historical and geographical teaching “largement conçu” and, for history at least, “totalement refondu” (totally recast), giving the young a truthful and comprehensive image of the world; a warning against reducing history to the purely political events of a Europe temporally close to us — “le passé lointain inspire le sens et le respect des différences entre les hommes” (the distant past inspires the sense and respect of differences between men) — and it matters more to a future French citizen to form a just image of the civilisations of India or China than to know by heart the succession of measures by which the “autoritaire Empire” became the “libéral Empire.” The tradition française, “incorporée dans un long destin pédagogique,” is dear to him; they intend to preserve its most precious goods — its taste for the human, its respect for spiritual spontaneity and liberty, the continuity of the forms of art and thought that are the very climate of the French spirit — knowing that to be truly faithful to it commands them to prolong it towards the future.

sources/businelli-rivoluzione-fascista-1.title: Businelli — Rivoluzione fascista: Origini e sviluppi del movimento delle camicie nere (1933)
sources/businelli-rivoluzione-fascista-1.content:
Rivoluzione fascista: Origini e sviluppi del movimento delle camicie nere (1933)
Identity
Rivoluzione fascista: Origini e sviluppi del movimento rivoluzionario delle camicie nere (The Fascist Revolution: Origins and Development of the Movement of the Blackshirts) is a narrative history of the rise of Italian Fascism by Alberto Businelli (1902–1944), a young Fascist educator — described in the preface as “il giovane e geniale educatore fascista” — and a diciannovista (veteran of the Fascist movement of 1919). It was published by R. Bemporad & Figlio, Firenze, in 1933 (the tenth year of the Fascist era, 1933-XI). The book opens with a preface by Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, of the Accademia d’Italia, dated Roma, 24 Gennaio 1933-XI, which salutes the work and sets out the futurist-squadrista temper of the movement.
It is the first Italian-language source in this wiki, and the first to give the Fascist side’s own account of the movement’s origins — covering the years from the Balkan Wars and the Sarajevo assassination through the intervention crisis, the First World War, the Fasci di combattimento founded at Piazza San Sepolcro, the biennio rosso and the March on Rome of 1922. Where the German sources document the parallel Nazi seizure of power, Businelli’s book offers the Italian counterpart: the Fascist movement’s own narrative of its founding, its struggles, and its victory, written from within the movement at the height of the regime.
Character of the source
A partisan, movement-insider narrative written at the height of the Mussolini regime, sympathetic to and celebratory of the Fascist revolution it describes. It is the work of a committed participant — Businelli was himself a squadrista who had served under Marinetti and the Futurist Arditi in the Roman days of 1919 and contributed to the Mostra della Rivoluzione Fascista. The tone is elegiac, martial and loyalist, glorifying the “squadrist” and futurist energies of the movement and framing the March on Rome as the triumph of a “bollente fede italiana.” Marinetti’s preface is itself a primary document of the Fascist–Futurist synthesis. The book is therefore valuable less as a detached history than as a specimen of how the Fascist regime’s own activists narrated and mythologised the movement’s origins in the celebratory year of 1932–1933.
Contents (structure)
The narrative is organized into seven chapters (the seventh an appendix), tracing the movement chronologically from the Balkan crisis of 1912–1914 to the March on Rome of October 1922. Chapter and subsection headings follow the printed Indice:

Capitolo I — Dalle guerre balcaniche alla lotta per l’intervento (pp. 1–28): the Balkan powder-keg, the Congress of Berlin and the danger of German predominance; the declaration of Italian neutrality in August 1914; the founding of Il Popolo d’Italia and Mussolini’s turn to interventionism; his arrest; and the campaign for Italian entry into the war
Capitolo II — Mussolini e la guerra (pp. 29–36): Mussolini’s own war record — “I galloni di caporale erano sufficienti alla mia ambizione” (the corporal’s stripes sufficed to my ambition) — alongside the wartime action of Il Popolo d’Italia and the rebuttals to Avanti!
Capitolo III — L’epica lotta contro la bestia ritornante (pp. 37–64): the “epic struggle against the returning beast”; the constituent assembly of interventionism; the errors of post-war policy; the Fiume rebellion and the Ronchi march of d’Annunzio; the adunata of Piazza San Sepolcro (23 March 1919); the first victory; the ministerial crises; the elections; and Il Popolo in 1920
Capitolo IV — Il tragico anno della ripresa (pp. 65–99): the “tragic year of recovery,” 1920–1921: strikes and the red wave; the student Avanguardie; the second adunata of the Fasci; the bilancio of the Nitti government; the occupation of the factories; Lenin’s twenty-one points; the Fascist reaction; the Treaty of Rapallo; and the “Natale di sangue” (bloody Christmas) of 1920
Capitolo V — L’anno del martirio e della gloria (pp. 100–118): 1921, “the year of martyrdom and glory”: the Fasci begin their syndical organization; the stillicidio di sangue (the drip of blood); the tregua; the Ispettorato generale delle squadre; the delineation of the Fascist victory; and the new elections
Capitolo VI — L’anno della vittoria (pp. 119–133): 1922, “the year of victory”: the agony of the anti-national parties; the plan of insurrection; the adunata of Naples (24 October); and the action in the provinces and the March on Rome (28 October)
Capitolo VII — Appendice: Il movimento futurista e la rivoluzione fascista (pp. 134–137): Marinetti’s account of the Italian Futurist movement and the Fascist Revolution, from the founding Manifesto del Futurismo (published in Le Figaro, 20 February 1909) through the Futurist participation in the Fasci and the March on Rome

The volume closes with the printed Indice and the word FINE at p. 137; the text ends there (the physical book is a short octavo of 137 printed pages).
OCR / extraction quality
Source is a PDF scan (154 physical pages) delivered as a clean embedded text layer produced by ABBYY FineReader 12. The book is set in Roman (Antiqua) type, and the Italian text layer is clean, fluent and fully readable — including proper accented forms (e.g. “l’occupazione”, “trattato”, “Roma”) with only the occasional ligature/hyphenation artifact and isolated OCR slips (e.g. “LVsnuLioùe” for “L’Assunzione”, “Le nqove elezioni” for “Le nuove elezioni”). Per protocol the embedded text layer is the extraction source (the scan carries no image pages requiring a re-OCR pass). Result: a clean Italian transcription assembled with pdftotext -layout (4,258 lines; 136 page-form-feeds across the 137 printed pages, the shortfall being blank front-matter leaves). The structure above has been reconstructed from the printed Indice and cross-checked against the body chapter headings.
Cross-references

Companion Italian source: Pini & Bresadola, Storia del Fascismo: Guerra – Rivoluzione – Regime (1928) — the regime-published full-length chronicle of the same rise of Italian Fascism (from the 1890s to the mid-1920s), the broad continuous didactic counterpart to this compact movement-insider origin-story.
Companion Italian source: Volpe, Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) — the collected wartime-and-Fascist political journalism (1916–1928) of the historian Gioacchino Volpe, which complements this movement-insider origin-story by recording how a professional academic historian wrote for the interventionist and Fascist press through the Great War, the postwar crisis and the Fascist consolidation. This wiki’s Italian-language entries stand alongside the German Dokumente der deutschen Politik series as the Fascist (Italian) counterpart to the Nazi (German) regime documentary record.
Companion Italian sources: Volpe, History of the Fascist Movement (1936) and Farinacci, Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. I (1937) — the mid-1930s English translation of Volpe’s narrative and the exhaustive documentary party-history of the crisis year 1919.
Regime’s own vantage (German): Friedrichs (comp.), Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Bands 1–4; Geisow, Die Seele des Dritten Reiches; Büttner (ed.), Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich (all in this wiki) — parallel examples of regime-authored revolutionary histories.
Contrast with the Soviet sources (Pokrovsky, VKP(b) Short Course, Stalin) as the third revolutionary regime’s official self-account.

sources/daniel-halevy-1938-une-annee-d-h.title: Daniel Halévy — 1938: Une année d'histoire (1938)
sources/daniel-halevy-1938-une-annee-d-h.content:
1938: Une année d’histoire
Daniel Halévy — 1938: Une année d’histoire (1938: A Year of History). Éditions Bernard Grasset, Paris, 1938; sixth edition, printed by Imprimerie Floch, Mayenne, finished 29 December 1938. A contemporary chronicle of the French and European political year 1938, written month by month in the manner of Halévy’s earlier Courrier de Paris and Courrier d’Europe — a diary of the crisis year that ended in the Munich Agreement.





























AuthorDaniel Halévy (1872–1962) — French historian and essayist, brother of the liberal historian Élie Halévy; Dreyfusard, biographer of Nietzsche, Péguy and Michelet, author of La Fin des Notables and La République des Ducs (his history of the early Third Republic), Décadence de la Liberté, and the political chronicles Courrier de Paris (1932) and Courrier d’Europe (1933); a conservative-liberal observer of the Third Republic’s declineEdition1938, Éditions Bernard Grasset, 61 rue des Saints-Pères, Paris; sixth edition; printed by Imprimerie Floch, Mayenne, finished 29 December 1938 (University of Victoria Library copy digitised by the Internet Archive)Structure7 chapters in the form of a running chronicle of the year: “La séance est suspendue,” “La pratique du rien,” “Un Socialiste homme d’État,” “Daladier au pouvoir,” “Euphorie estivale,” “La Guerre en vue,” “Derniers remous” + a Table des Matières; 1,450 lines / ~71,000 characters of extracted textPeriodThe calendar year 1938 in France and Europe, chronicled from the January opening of the Chamber to the year’s end: the successive crises of the Popular Front’s final months, the fall of Blum, the ministry of Daladier, the summer of illusion, the mounting threat of war through the Sudeten crisis, and the Munich AgreementNoteA contemporary diary of the crisis year 1938 by a historian of the Third Republic, written in the genre of the political chronicle that Halévy had practised through the 1930s. For this wiki it supplies the French moderate-liberal record of the year of Munich — the civilian counterpart to the military and totalitarian sources of the German, Italian and Russian sides, and the sequel in time to Élie Halévy’s diagnosis of “the era of tyrannies”
Contents. The book follows the political year 1938 as it unfolded. The opening chapter, “La séance est suspendue,” records the January reopening of the Chamber — Herriot re-elected president, the fragile parliamentary arithmetic of the Popular Front’s winter. “La pratique du rien” is Halévy’s portrait of the drift and inaction of the regime in the face of the deepening crisis. “Un Socialiste homme d’État” considers a leading Socialist figure come to the exercise of state power. “Daladier au pouvoir” marks the coming to power of Édouard Daladier in April and the attempt to restore the authority of the state. “Euphorie estivale” evokes the deceptive calm of the summer of 1938, between the Austrian Anschluss and the Sudeten storm. “La Guerre en vue” chronicles the escalating crisis of the autumn — the September mobilisations, the flight of the Czech crisis toward war, and the diplomatic parleys. “Derniers remous” closes the year with the aftermath of the Munich Agreement and the December calm, ending as the year turns toward 1939.
Character of the source. A contemporary, month-by-month political chronicle of the year 1938 by a historian and man of letters of the moderate Right, deeply attached to the Third Republic yet increasingly pessimistic about its capacity to face the totalitarian threat. Halévy writes in the intimate, allusive style of the Parisian man of letters — sharp portraits of the leading figures (Herriot, Blum, Daladier, the Socialist ministers), a running commentary on parliamentary manoeuvre and public mood, and an undercurrent of foreboding about the drift of Europe toward war. It is the record of a participant-observer writing at the moment, before the outcome of 1939–1940 was known; its value for this wiki lies in the immediacy of a French voice registering the crisis year as it happened.
Quality. Fair. Extracted from a 72-page Internet Archive PDF scan (University of Victoria Library copy) via pdftotext -layout with a clean text layer; the body text from the opening of chapter I through the Table des Matières was retained and the title pages, “Du même auteur” bibliography, publisher advertisements and library front matter stripped. French text readable, with some OCR noise on the ornamental title pages and a scattering of character misreadings in the body.
