I. — « La séance est suspendue »
The January reopening of the Chamber of Deputies. Herriot, re-elected president, thanks his colleagues in a speech at once animated and charming, “musical as a song,” a powerful nightingale in the chair, closing with the plea that every difficulty can be mastered by a common will to wisdom. The chronicle opens the year with the parliamentary scene of the Popular Front’s final winter.
II. — La pratique du rien
Halévy’s diagnosis of the regime’s drift and inaction — the practice of doing nothing as the governing art of the Third Republic in crisis, the parliamentary and ministerial paralysis as the financial and diplomatic problems accumulate.
III. — Un Socialiste homme d’État
Portrait of a Socialist statesman — the figure of a leading socialist come to the exercise of power, examined as one of the central political facts of the year.
IV. — Daladier au pouvoir
The coming to power of Édouard Daladier in April 1938 and the attempt to restore the authority of the state after the fall of the Blum government — the new ministry, the financial emergency, the turn away from the Popular Front’s programme.
V. — Euphorie estivale
The deceptive calm of the summer of 1938 — the mood of relaxation and hope between the Anschluss of March and the gathering Sudeten crisis, the sense that war might after all be avoided.
VI. — La Guerre en vue
The escalating crisis of the autumn: the Sudeten German agitation, the September tension and mobilisation, the flight of the Czechoslovak question toward the brink of war, and the diplomatic parleys that preceded Munich.
VII. — Derniers remous
The closing chapter of the year: the aftermath of the Munich Agreement of 29–30 September, the final disturbances of the autumn and the December calm, the year turning toward 1939 with the threat of war postponed but not dissolved.

sources/der-aufbau-des-deutschen-fuehrer.title: Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934 — Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Band 2 (3rd ed., 1938)
sources/der-aufbau-des-deutschen-fuehrer.content:
Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934 (Band 2, 3rd ed. 1938)
Identity
Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934 (The Construction of the German Leader-State, 1934) is Band 2 of Dokumente der deutschen Politik — the official documentary series of the Deutsche Hochschule für Politik (German Academy for Politics). It was compiled by Axel Friedrichs, under the general editorship of Paul Meier-Benneckenstein (Regierungsrat, President of the Hochschule für Politik), and published by Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin. Title-page copyright 1936; this is the 3rd edition, 1938 (print by Hofbuchdruckerei C. Dünnhaupt, Dessau).
The volume collects the principal laws, decrees, speeches and public documents of the year 1934, presented as the construction of the Führer-state — the consolidation of power completed in the second year of the regime. It is the direct companion to Friedrichs’ Band 1 (Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933, in this wiki), the next volume of the same official series after the 1933 volume and before Volz’s 1937 and 1938 volumes.
Character of the source
A government-sponsored source book, identical in character to Band 1: an internal, regime-sanctioned compilation of authoritative state documents — laws, decrees, party orders, Hitler’s and other leaders’ speeches — with framing commentary from the editor. The year 1934 is the year in which the Führer-state was completed: the Night of the Long Knives (30 June–2 July), the death of Reich President Hindenburg and Hitler’s assumption of the head-of-state office (2 August), the plebiscite of 19 August, and the Reich-reform legislation that abolished the Reichsrat and centralized the German federal structure. It complements the other regime-published documentary volumes in the Germany group.
Contents (structure)
The volume is organized into three parts, with 92 numbered documents (some subdivided: 36a/b, 41a/b/c, 44a/b, 49/50, 70a). Main structure:

A. Der Aufbau des Führerstaates — the construction of the Führer-state (documents 1–27): Hitler’s New Year’s call to the party (1 Jan 1934); the Reichstag speech of 30 January 1934; Heß’s Cologne radio speech (25 June); Blomberg on the Wehrmacht in the Third Reich (29 June); the Röhm purge — Hitler’s decree deposing and expelling SA chief of staff Röhm (30 June), the letters and commands to his successor Lutze, the Hindenburg telegrams of 2 July, the law on measures of state emergency (“Staatsnotwehr”) of 3 July; Hitler’s Reichstag speech of 13 July 1934 on the purge; the law on the head of state (1 August), the soldiers’ oath of 2 August, the Reich government’s proclamation to the German people (2 August), Hindenburg’s political testament (11 May, published 15 August); the result of the plebiscite of 19 August; Hitler’s thanks to party and people (20 August); the law of 20 August on the oath of civil servants and soldiers; the law of 16 October on the oath of Reich ministers; the “Heimtückegesetz” against malicious attacks on state and party (20 December 1934)
B. Die deutsche Friedenspolitik — German peace policy (documents 28–43): the German memorandum of 18 December 1933; the disarmament memorandum (19 January 1934); the German–Polish Non-Aggression Pact (26 January 1934); the Saar campaign — the German Front’s call (1 March), Goebbels’ “Tag der Saar” speech (6 May), Bürckel’s speeches and decrees, Pirro’s calls of November 1934, Heß’s Bochum speech of 8 December; the Venice communiqué on the Hitler–Mussolini meeting (15 June); Hitler’s Gera Gau-tag speech (17 June); the Papen mission to Vienna (July); the Eastern Pact communiqué (10 September); the Memel Landtag’s protest (13 December 1934)
C. Die Neuordnung von Staat, Volk, Wirtschaft, Kultur und Recht — the reordering of state, people, economy, culture and law (documents 44–92), in six thematic sections:

Die Begründung der Reichseinheit (44–51): the law on the reconstruction of the Reich (30 January 1934), the abolition of the Reichsrat (14 February), the transfer of the administration of justice to the Reich, the Göring–Hitler correspondence on uniting the Prussian and Reich interior ministries
Die Rassen- und Bevölkerungspolitik (52): Frick’s speech before the diplomatic corps on racial legislation (15 February 1934)
Neubau von Volk und Wirtschaft (53–76), subdivided into a) the struggle for the worker and the new social constitution (the law on the ordering of national labour, 20 January 1934; the German Labour Front decree, 24 October), b) the rebuilding of the economy (Schacht’s speeches; the law for the preparation of the organic construction of the German economy, 27 February; the law on the regulation of labour deployment, 15 May; the Anleihestockgesetz, 4 December), c) the new regulation of foreign trade (Schacht’s speeches; the German–English transfer agreement, 4 July; the law of 3 July on the settlement of foreign payment obligations), and d) peasant and agrarian policy (Darré’s speeches; the law on the ordering of the grain economy, 27 June; Darré’s proclamation of the production battle, Goslar, 11 November)
Der Arbeitsdienst (77–79): Hierl’s speeches and the law on voluntary labour service (13 December 1934)
Der Neubau der Kultur (80–87): the constitution of German art (7 February); Goebbels’ speeches to film and press; Rosenberg’s Kroll Opera and Nuremberg party-congress speeches; the establishment of the Reich Ministry for Science, Education and Culture (1 May); the State Youth Day agreement between Rust and Schirach
Die Neuschaffung des deutschen Rechts (88–92): Frank’s radio address; the law amending criminal law and procedure (24 April); the law on the Academy for German Law (11 July) and its statutes; Göring’s speech before the Academy (13 November)



Back matter: Zeittafel und Chronologie der wiedergegebenen Dokumente (chronological table, p. 327) and Sach- und Namen-Gesamtregister (general name and subject index, p. 337).
OCR / extraction quality
Source is an Internet Archive scan (Kahle/Austin Foundation funding, 2019; identifier deraufbaudesdeut0002frie; Trent University Library copy, shelfmark DD253 .A66; 372 pages). The PDF’s embedded text layer was a garbled low-quality OCR because the book is set in Fraktur type. Per protocol, the full 372 pages were re-OCR’d with tesseract 5.5.2, -l deu+script/Fraktur --psm 3 at 300 dpi gray. A sample-page comparison confirmed the Fraktur model clearly outperformed plain deu (correct “abseits/Unbelehrbaren/selbst” vs deu’s “abjetts/Unbelchrbaren/felbit”). Result: clean, readable Fraktur transcription (19,563 lines; 367 page-form-feeds; the 5-page shortfall is blank illustration/library plates). The opening pages of the Inhaltsverzeichnis OCR partially fragmented (dense small Fraktur, Roman numerals split), but the body text and document headings are high quality; the structure above has been reconstructed and cross-checked against the printed TOC and body headings. The closing Sach- und Namen-Gesamtregister, as in Band 1, OCRs partially garbled (dense small Fraktur) but is present.
Cross-references

Companion official volumes: Friedrichs (comp.), Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933, Band 1 (in this wiki) — this volume is its immediate predecessor — Deutschlands Weg zur Freiheit 1935, Band 3 (in this wiki) — this volume’s immediate sequel covering 1935 — and Deutschlands Aufstieg zur Großmacht 1936, Band 4 (in this wiki) — covering 1936; Volz (ed.), Dokumente der deutschen Politik 1937 and Großdeutschland 1938, Band 6/Teil 1 (in this wiki).
Party-authorized program compilation: Büttner (ed.), Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich (in this wiki).
Regime’s own vantage: Geisow, Die Seele des Dritten Reiches; contrast with the exile-left Rosenberg history and Speer’s insider memoir.

sources/der-weg-zum-nationalsozialistisc.title: Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich — Dokumente zur Verwirklichung des Programms der NSDAP (Teil 1, 1943)
sources/der-weg-zum-nationalsozialistisc.content:
Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich
Dr. Johannes Büttner (comp. and ed.) — Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich: Dokumente zur Verwirklichung des Programms der NSDAP (The Road to the National Socialist Reich: Documents on the Realization of the Program of the NSDAP), Teil 1. Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin, 1943; released by the Zentralverlag der NSDAP, Franz Eher Nachf., Munich, on 9 March 1943. A party-authorized documentary compilation that sets out the 25-point program of the NSDAP (proclaimed 24 February 1920) and reproduces the German laws, decrees, treaties, speeches and official declarations of 1933–1940 by which each demand of the program was fulfilled — from the recovery of the Saar, Austria, the Sudetenland, Memel, Danzig and Eupen–Malmedy, the abrogation of Versailles and St. Germain, the racial Nuremberg Laws and the exclusion of Jews from the economy, to labour, agrarian and tax legislation.

































Compiler/EditorDr. Johannes Büttner, who assembled and edited the documentsPublisherJunker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin, 1943; released (freigegeben) for the publisher by the Zentralverlag der NSDAP, Franz Eher Nachf., Munich, 9 March 1943; copyright 1943 by Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin; printed by Clemens Landgraf Nachf. W. Stolle, Dresden-Freital; binding by Horst MichelEditionTeil 1 (v. 1), 1943; dedicated “to my dear, brave mother” by the compiler; scanned from the Northwestern University Library copy (call number 943.085 N276w v.1)StructureOrganized by the 25 program points (Punkte) of the NSDAP; this volume reproduces the documents realizing Punkte 1–14, with a Vorbemerkung (preface) quoting Hitler’s Mein Kampf on the program and his Munich speech of 24 February 1941; 23,983 lines of extracted textPeriodDocuments dated 1918–1940, realizing program points proclaimed in 1920 — chiefly the years of the Third Reich 1933–1940NoteA companion party-side compilation to the Volz and Friedrichs Dokumente der deutschen Politik volumes (Bände 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, also in this wiki): while Volz and Friedrichs reproduced documents of a single year in chronological order, Büttner organizes the documents thematically, point by point, to demonstrate that the party program of 1920 had been fulfilled
Contents. The volume sets each demand of the 25-point program at the head of a section and reproduces the official documents realizing it. Punkt 1 (reunion of all Germans in a Greater Germany on the basis of national self-determination) documents the recovery of the Saarland (the Saar reunification protocol of 1 March 1935, the law on the provisional administration of the Saar of 30 January 1935), the Anschluss of Austria (from Emperor Karl’s manifesto of 16 October 1918 and the notes of the First World War’s end, through the failure of the 1931 Austro-German customs-union plan, to the Reichsstatthalter arrangement, the law of reunion of 13 March 1938 and Hitler’s speech at Linz), the Sudetenland (the Karlsbad demands, the Munich Agreement of 29 September 1938, the law of reunion of 21 November 1938), the Memel territory (the German–Lithuanian treaty of 22 March 1939), the Polish Corridor and Danzig (the German–Polish declaration of 26 January 1934, the British–Polish agreements and the German proposals of 28 August 1939, the reunion of Danzig with the Reich on 1 September 1939), and Eupen–Malmedy–Moresnet (the Führer’s decree of reunion of 18 May 1940), together with the Umsiedlung (resettlement) and the Auslandsorganisation der NSDAP. Punkt 2 (equal rights for the German people, abrogation of the treaties of Versailles and St. Germain) documents the Five-Power declaration of 11 December 1932, the Reich government’s proclamation of 1 February 1933, Hitler’s speech of 17 May 1933, the German withdrawal from the League of Nations (14 October 1933), the German peace plan of 21 May 1935, the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 18 June 1935, the remilitarization proposals of 7 March 1936, and the law reorganizing the Reichsbank and Reichsbahn of 10 February 1937. Punkte 3–5 (land and colonies; the racial definition of the Staatsbürger/Reichsbürger; and the treatment of non-citizens as guests under aliens law) reproduce the Reichsbürgergesetz (15 September 1935) and its implementing ordinances of 1935–1939, the law on Jewish cultural associations of 28 March 1938, the passport, arms and economic-exclusion ordinances of October–November 1938, and the foreigner legislation. Punkte 6–14 cover the people’s right of co-determination, work and welfare (labour service and the struggle against unemployment), the prevention of further non-German immigration, equal rights and duties of citizens, the primacy of the common good over self-interest, the breaking of interest slavery and the abolition of unearned income (with the taxation laws), the nationalization of trusts, profit-sharing in large enterprises, and old-age provision — reproducing the relevant labour, agrarian, and corporation-tax legislation through 1940.
Character of the source. An official party publication of the National Socialist state, issued with the release of the Zentralverlag der NSDAP (Franz Eher Nachf.) during the Second World War, and dedicated to demonstrating — through the original texts of laws, decrees, treaties, speeches and official communiqués — that the party program of 24 February 1920 had been fulfilled point by point. It is a primary source in the strictest sense: it reproduces verbatim the founding program itself, the Nuremberg racial laws and their ordinances, the German–Austrian, German–Lithuanian and German–British instruments, and the official texts of the Saar, Austrian, Sudeten, Memel and Danzig reunions. It is the regime’s own self-justifying account of the realization of its program, and is at once a record of fact (the texts of the instruments are authoritative) and a document of propaganda (the framing, that every demand was fulfilled). It stands alongside the Volz volumes as an official documentary voice of the Third Reich, and opposite the exile history of Rosenberg, also in this wiki.
Quality. Good. Extracted from a 598-file paginated text dump (Northwestern University Library scan) by concatenating the numbered page files in order. The text uses the long-s (ſ) of Fraktur; the OCR layer preserves the original spelling of laws, decrees, treaties and speeches with footnotes. Program-point headings and document titles verified against the printed Inhaltsverzeichnis (table of contents), which lists all 25 Punkte; this bound volume (Teil 1 / v. 1) reproduces the documents for Punkte 1–14, ending within the corporation-tax legislation. The scan closes with the library’s date-due card (barcode 35556009652967).
Raw text: wiki/raw/der-weg-zum-nationalsozialistischen-reich-1943-buettner.txt.

Punkt 1 — Reunion of all Germans in a Greater Germany
Saarland
The recovery of the Saar: the Saar reunification protocol of 1 March 1935; the law on the provisional administration of the Saarland of 30 January 1935; and the incorporation of the Saar into the Reich administration.
Österreich (Austria)
From the end of the Habsburg Monarchy to the Anschluss: Emperor Karl’s manifesto of 16 October 1918; the German-Austrian armistice notes to President Wilson; the proclamation to the Austrian people of 12 November 1918 and the law on the state form of German-Austria; the notes of the Allied and Associated Powers of 2 September 1919 and the Geneva Protocol of 4 October 1922; the failed Austro-German customs-union plan of March–September 1931; Hitler’s Reichstag speech of 30 January 1934; the radio appeals of Dr. Seyss-Inquart and Hitler’s speech at Linz of 12 March 1938; and the Federal Constitutional Law and the law of 13 March 1938 on the reunion of Austria with the German Reich.
Sudetenland
The Karlsbad demands of the Sudeten German Party; the Munich Agreement between Germany, Great Britain, France and Italy of 29 September 1938; and the law of 21 November 1938 on the reunion of the Sudeten German territories with the German Reich.
Memelland
The German–Lithuanian treaty of 22 March 1939 and the law of 23 March 1939 on the reunion of the Memel territory with the German Reich.
Der Korridor und Danzig (The Corridor and Danzig)
The German–Polish declaration of 26 January 1934 and the minorities declaration of 5 November 1937; the British–Polish guarantees of 6 April and 25 August 1939; Hitler’s Reichstag speech of 28 April 1939, the German memorandum to Poland and the German proposals of 28–30 August 1939; the law on the reunion of the Free City of Danzig with the German Reich of 1 September 1939; the Reich government’s memorandum of 3 September 1939; and the Wehrmacht communiqué on the Polish campaign of 24 September 1939.
Eupen, Malmedy und Moresnet
The German declaration of 13 October 1937; the Reich government’s memorandum to the Belgian government of 9 May 1940; and the Führer’s decree of 18 May 1940 on the reunion of Eupen, Malmedy and Moresnet with the German Reich.
Die Umsiedlung; Die Auslandsorganisation der NSDAP
The resettlement of German populations and the role of the NSDAP’s Foreign Organization in upholding the unity of Germans abroad.
Punkt 2 — Equal rights for the German people; abrogation of Versailles and St. Germain
The Five-Power declaration of 11 December 1932; the Reich government’s proclamation of 1 February 1933; Hitler’s speech of 17 May 1933; the call for Germany’s withdrawal from the League of Nations (14 October 1933); the Reich government’s memorandum on disarmament and equal rights (18 December 1933); the German peace plan of 21 May 1935; the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 18 June 1935; the proposals of 7 March 1936 and the peace plan of 31 March 1936; the note of 14 November 1936 on the international river commissions; and the law reorganizing the Reichsbank and German Reichsbahn of 10 February 1937.
Punkte 3–5 — Land and colonies; racial citizenship; aliens under the law
Punkt 3 (land and soil, colonies, for the nourishment of the people); Punkt 4 (only a Volksgenosse of German blood — no Jew — can be a citizen); Punkt 5 (non-citizens live in Germany only as guests under aliens law): the Reichsbürgergesetz and the law for the protection of German blood of 15 September 1935; the implementing ordinances (First, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Eighth and Tenth) of 1935–1939; the law on Jewish cultural associations of 28 March 1938; the ordinance on identity cards and passports of Jews (5 October 1938); the ordinance against Jewish possession of arms (11 November 1938); the ordinance excluding Jews from German economic life (12 November 1938) and its first implementing ordinance (23 November 1938).
Punkte 6–14 — Co-determination, work, welfare, taxation
Punkt 6 (the right of the people to determine its leadership and laws); Punkt 7 (the state must above all provide work and livelihood for its citizens); Punkt 8 (prevention of further non-German immigration); Punkt 9 (equal rights and duties of all citizens); Punkt 10 (the first duty of every citizen is to labour, mentally and physically); Punkt 11 (abolition of unearned income, breaking of interest slavery); Punkt 12 (in view of the sacrifices of blood and goods of every war, personal gain from war is a crime); Punkt 13 (nationalization of existing trusts); Punkt 14 (profit-sharing in large enterprises); reproducing the Reich Labour Service legislation, the employment and unemployment measures, the hereditary-tenant (Erbhof) and agrarian laws, the breaking of interest slavery and the corporation-tax legislation of 1934–1940 by which these demands of the program were realized.

sources/deutschlands-aufstieg-zur-grossm.title: Deutschlands Aufstieg zur Großmacht 1936 — Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Band 4 (2nd ed., 1938)
sources/deutschlands-aufstieg-zur-grossm.content:
Deutschlands Aufstieg zur Großmacht 1936 (Band 4, 2nd ed. 1938)
Identity
Deutschlands Aufstieg zur Großmacht 1936 (Germany’s Rise to Great Power, 1936) is Band 4 of Dokumente der deutschen Politik — the official documentary series of the Deutsche Hochschule für Politik (German Academy for Politics). It was compiled by Axel Friedrichs, under the general editorship of Paul Meier-Benneckenstein (Regierungsrat, President of the Hochschule für Politik), and published by Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin. Title-page copyright 1937; this is the 2nd edition, 1938. The volume collects the principal laws, decrees, speeches, notes and public documents of the year 1936 — the year of the Rhineland remilitarization, the Berlin Olympics, the Four Year Plan and the Anti-Comintern Pact.
It is the direct continuation of Friedrichs’ Band 1 (Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933), Band 2 (Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934) and Band 3 (Deutschlands Weg zur Freiheit 1935, all in this wiki): it covers the year between Band 3 and Volz’s 1937 volume (Band 5), and is the Dokumente der deutschen Politik volume in the wiki covering the pivotal year 1936, when the regime combined the staging of the Olympic Games with the remilitarization of the Rhineland and the launching of the Four Year Plan.
Character of the source
A government-sponsored source book, identical in character to Bands 1 and 2: an internal, regime-sanctioned compilation of authoritative state documents — laws, decrees, party orders, Hitler’s and other leaders’ speeches, and diplomatic notes — with framing commentary from the editor. The year 1936 was the regime’s annus mirabilis of consolidation and external assertiveness: the remilitarization of the Rhineland (7 March) and the repudiation of Locarno, the overwhelming Reichstag election of 29 March, the Berlin Olympics, the appointment of Heinrich Himmler as Chef der deutschen Polizei (17 June), the German–Austrian agreement of 11 July, the recognition of Italian Abyssinia and of Franco’s government, the Anti-Comintern Pact with Japan (25 November), and the proclamation of the second Four Year Plan (18 October). It complements the other regime-published documentary volumes in the Germany group.
Contents (structure)
The volume is organized into three parts, with 64 numbered documents:

A. Der nationalsozialistische Staat und die nationalsozialistische Bewegung — the National Socialist state and movement (documents 1–6): Goebbels’ speech at the Berlin Gau-tag on the work of the state and party (17 January); Lutze’s speech before the Diplomatic Corps on the nature and tasks of the SA (24 January); the Führer’s decree appointing a Chef der deutschen Polizei and naming Heinrich Himmler to the office (17 June); the Führer’s proclamation opening the 8th Party Congress, the “Parteitag der Ehre,” at Nuremberg (9 September); Goebbels’ and Rosenberg’s party-congress speeches on the world danger of Bolshevism and the decisive world struggle (10 September)
B. Der Kampf um den Frieden und die deutsche Ehre — the struggle for peace and German honour (documents 7–32): Hitler’s interview with Bertrand de Jouvenel on Franco-German relations (21 February); Hitler’s Reichstag speech on the restoration of German sovereignty over the Rhineland and his plan for European peace (7 March); the Reich government’s memorandum to the Locarno signatory powers and the decree dissolving the Reichstag (7 March); Blomberg’s Heroes’ Memorial Day speech (8 March); the official statement on the German step and peace plan (12 March); Ribbentrop’s speech and protest before the League of Nations Council in London on the Soviet pact, Locarno and the German peace plan (19 March); the result of the Reichstag election (29 March); the Reich government’s peace plan (31 March); the German front-fighters’ answer to the French (16 May); the German–Austrian agreement of 11 July; the note to François-Poncet on non-intervention in the Spanish Civil War (17 August); the decree on the two-year term of service (24 August) and the NSK communiqué justifying it as self-defence against Soviet imperialism; the notes on the Spanish Civil War, Abyssinia and the German rivers; the recognition of the Franco government (18 November); Ribbentrop’s note to Vansittart on Germany’s accession to the U-boat-warfare agreement (23 November); the Anti-Comintern Pact with Japan (25 November) with the declarations of Goebbels and Ribbentrop; the answer to the Anglo-French mediation proposals on Spain (12 December); and Ribbentrop’s Anglo-German Fellowship speech on colonial equality (15 December)
C. Die Neuordnung von Staat, Volk, Wirtschaft, Kultur und Recht — the reordering of state, people, economy, culture and law (documents 33–64), in five thematic sections:

Staatsordnung, Verfassung und Verwaltung (33–36): Heß’ speech before the civil service on officialdom in the National Socialist state (4 June); Frick’s speeches on the rebuilding of communal administration (14 September) and “Neubau des Reiches” at the Ordensburg Vogelsang (19 November); the law on the constitution and administration of the Reich capital Berlin (1 December)
Bevölkerungs- und Rassenpolitik (37–38): the law amending the Defence Law on the active military service of Jews (26 June); Frank’s speech on Judaism in legal science (3 October)
Neubau der wirtschaftlichen und sozialen Ordnung (39–51), subdivided into a) the struggle for the worker and the new social constitution (Goebbels’ call for the National Day of the German People, 25 April; the decree on the Reich Labour Service, 26 September; the Winterhilfswerk law, 1 December) and b) the rebuilding of the economy and the Four Year Plan (Schwerin von Krosigk’s speech on financial policy, 6 February; Schacht’s declaration on currency policy, 30 September; Heß’ Hof speech on Germany’s struggle for economic freedom, 11 October; the Führer’s decree implementing the Four Year Plan, 18 October; Göring’s Sportpalast speech on the second Four Year Plan, 28 October; the law appointing a Reich Commissioner for Price Formation, 29 October; the law against economic sabotage, 1 December; Reinhardt’s speech on tax reform, 3 December; Schacht’s Frankfurt lecture, 9 December; and Schacht’s article “Deutschlands Kolonialproblem” in Foreign Affairs, December)
Neubau der Kultur (52–57): Rust’s Heidelberg speech on “Nationalsozialismus und Wissenschaft” at the university’s 550th anniversary (29 June); Goebbels’ decree on the reform of art criticism (26 November) and his speech to the Reichskulturkammer (27 November); the Hitler-Jugend law (1 December) with Schirach’s declaration and press speech (2 and 7 December)
Neugestaltung des Rechts (58–64): Frank’s theses on the position of the judge (14 January) and his speech on the foundations of the National Socialist conception of law (29 January); the law on the People’s Court (18 April); Frank’s speech opening the German Jurists’ Day at Leipzig (16 May); the law against kidnapping for ransom (22 June); the law re-establishing a Supreme Court of the Wehrmacht (26 June); and Gürtner’s essay on “Die Erneuerung des deutschen Strafrechtes” (5 November)



Back matter: Zeittafel und Chronologie der wiedergegebenen Dokumente (chronological table, p. 358) and Sach- und Namen-Gesamtregister (general name and subject index, p. 367), the latter a series-wide register referencing all four volumes (I–IV) of the Dokumente der deutschen Politik.
OCR / extraction quality
Source is a University of Florida Library scan (Smalthers Libraries; shelfmark DD253 .A6 Bd. 4, 1938) delivered as a 404-file paginated text dump (Anna’s Archive). The book is set in Fraktur type; the embedded text layer is a Fraktur OCR of good but not perfect quality — clean and fully readable, though it shows the characteristic Fraktur-model misreadings (e.g. “Luke” for Lutze, “Gesek/Gesez” for Gesetz, “deursche” for deutsche, “Aufsak/Aufsah/Aussak” for Aufsatz). Per protocol this is the extraction source (the dump carries no image pages, so no re-OCR pass was possible). Result: clean, readable German transcription assembled from the 404 ordered page files (18,216 lines; 403 page-form-feeds; no page gaps — the printed text closes with the series register at physical p. 380, followed only by blank leaves and the library date-due card). The structure above has been reconstructed and cross-checked against the printed Inhaltsverzeichnis and body headings.
Cross-references

Companion official volumes: Friedrichs (comp.), Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933, Band 1, Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934, Band 2, and Deutschlands Weg zur Freiheit 1935, Band 3 (all in this wiki) — this volume is their direct sequel; Volz (ed.), Dokumente der deutschen Politik 1937 (Band 5) and Großdeutschland 1938 (Band 6/Teil 1, both in this wiki) follow it.
Party-authorized program compilation: Büttner (ed.), Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich (in this wiki).
Regime’s own vantage: Geisow, Die Seele des Dritten Reiches; contrast with the exile-left Rosenberg history and Speer’s insider memoir.

sources/deutschlands-weg-zur-freiheit-19.title: Deutschlands Weg zur Freiheit 1935 — Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Band 3 (3rd ed., 1938)
sources/deutschlands-weg-zur-freiheit-19.content:
Axel Friedrichs (comp.) — Deutschlands Weg zur Freiheit 1935 (Germany’s Road to Freedom 1935), Band 3 of Dokumente der deutschen Politik (Documents of German Politics), edited by Paul Meier-Benneckenstein, president of the Hochschule für Politik (Academy for Politics), Berlin. Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin, 3., umgearbeitete Auflage 1938 (copyright 1936). An official Nazi compilation of 52 German state documents of the year 1935 — laws, decrees, speeches, notes and protocols — recording the great outward and internal advances of the regime: the recovery of the Saar, the reintroduction of general conscription and the building of the Wehrmacht, the Anglo-German Naval Agreement, the Nuremberg racial laws, and the reordering of state, people, economy, culture and law.
| Title | Deutschlands Weg zur Freiheit 1935 (Germany’s Road to Freedom 1935) |
| Series | Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Band 3 (3rd volume of the series, which covered the years 1933 to 1936 in the annual Friedrichs compilations and continued with Volz’s Band 5 for 1937) |
| Editor | Axel Friedrichs (series ed. Paul Meier-Benneckenstein) |
| Publisher | Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin, 3., umgearbeitete Auflage 1938 (copyright 1936) |
| Documents | 52 German state documents of the year 1935, in 3 parts |
| Note | A companion to the other Dokumente der deutschen Politik volumes in this wiki — the Friedrichs-compiled Band 1 (Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933), Band 2 (Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934) and Band 4 (Deutschlands Aufstieg zur Großmacht 1936), and the later Volz Band 5 (Von der Großmacht zur Weltmacht 1937) and Band 6 (Großdeutschland 1938); reproduced from the 3rd edition with the original German text of laws, decrees and official communications preserved verbatim |
Character of the source. An official documentary publication of the National Socialist state, reproducing the original texts of German laws, decrees, speeches, notes and protocols of the year 1935 in the German original, published in Berlin in 1938 by the party-supporting Junker und Dünnhaupt house. It is a primary source in the strictest sense — the laws themselves (the Wehrgesetz, the Nuremberg racial laws, the Reichsarbeitsdienstgesetz), the verbatim official communications of the Reich government (the answer to the London communiqué, the protest against the League of Nations resolution on conscription, the memorandum to the Locarno powers), and the speeches of Hitler, Göring, Goebbels, Frick, Schacht, Darré, Heß and others as officially released. Edited from within the regime with the aim of documenting the state’s own account of its activity, it is at once a record of fact and an instrument of propaganda; read alongside the exile histories (such as Rosenberg’s History of the German Republic, also in this wiki), it supplies the official internal voice of the German dictatorship in the year of the Saar’s return and the proclamation of rearmament.
Quality. Good. Re-OCR of a 372-page Internet Archive scan (Internet Archive/LuraDocument text layer garbled and unusable) by rendering each page at 300 dpi and running Tesseract with the deu+script/Fraktur model, which preserves the long-s (ſ) of the Fraktur type. Laws, decrees, official notes and speech texts are preserved verbatim with footnotes; minor OCR artifacts (e.g. “Gefeg” for Gesetz, “Reihs” for Reichs) are typographical, not substantive. Document headings and dates verified against the printed Inhaltsverzeichnis (table of contents). The volume closes with the Zeittafel und Chronologie (pp. 333–337), the Sach- und Namen-Gesamtregister (pp. 339–360), and the library’s date-due card (DD253 .A1 D6 Bd. 3), confirming Band 3.
Contents. The 52 documents are arranged in three parts.
A. Nationalsozialistische Staatspolitik (docs 1–7). Goebbels’ speech at the Nuremberg party congress against Bolshevism (13 September); the Reichsflaggen-gesetz of 15 September; Hitler’s and Göring’s speeches to the Nuremberg Reichstag of 15 September on the three laws of the Nuremberg Reichstag; the ordinance on the state emblem of the Reich (5 November); the Führer’s decree to the Wehrmacht introducing the new Reich war flag (7 November); the dissolution of the Stahlhelm (Hitler’s letter to the Bundesführer Seldte and Seldte’s reply, 7 November); and Himmler’s speech on the SS as an anti-Bolshevik combat organization at Goslar (12 November).
B. Der Kampf Deutschlands um Frieden und Gleichberechtigung (docs 8–22). Bürckel’s radio speech on the victory in the Saar territory (13 January); the Reich government’s answer to the London communiqué (14 February); the protocol of 1 March on Germany’s reintegration into the government of the Saar territory; Frick’s speech at the reunion of the Saar with Germany (1 March); the Reich government’s proclamation on the reintroduction of general conscription (16 March); the law for the building of the Wehrmacht (16 March); Blomberg’s essay on German conscription in the Politischer Beobachter (20 March); the communiqué on Germany’s attitude to the Eastern pact (14 April); the German protest against the League of Nations resolution of 17 April on the reintroduction of conscription (20 April); Hitler’s Reichstag speech on German peace policy and the Wehrgesetz (21 May); the German memorandum to the Locarno powers on the incompatibility of the Soviet pact with the Locarno treaty (25 May); Rust’s speech on Volkstumspolitik as peace policy at the VDA meeting in Königsberg (9 June); the Anglo-German Naval Agreement (18 June); the Luftschutzgesetz (26 June); and the declaration of the German Memel directorate to the Landtag (10 December).
C. Die Neuordnung von Staat, Volk, Wirtschaft, Kultur und Recht (docs 23–52).
1. Reichseinheit — Verfassung und Verwaltung (docs 23–24): the Reichsstatthaltergesetz and the Deutsche Gemeindeordnung (both 30 January).
2. Rassen- und Bevölkerungspolitik (docs 25–30): Rust’s decree on the establishment of separate Jewish schools (10 September); the Reichsbürgergesetz and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour (both 15 September); the law for the protection of the hereditary health of the German people (18 October); and the first implementing ordinances to the Reichsbürgergesetz and to the Blood-Protection law (both 14 November).
3. Neubau der wirtschaftlichen und sozialen Ordnung (docs 31–42). a) Die Arbeitsordnung: the agreement between the German Labour Front and the commercial economy (21 March); Ley’s appeal to working Germany (26 March); Ley’s speeches at the constitution of the Reichsarbeitskammer (31 August) and at the Nuremberg party congress on the tasks of the Labour Front (13 September); Schacht’s speech at the third annual meeting of the German Labour Front (14 September). b) Umbau der Wirtschaft: Schacht’s radio speech on National Savings Day (29 October); Schwerin von Krosigk’s speech on National Socialist financial policy in Kiel (27 November); Schacht’s speech on the reform of the companies law before the Akademie für Deutsches Recht (30 November); and Schacht’s speech on Germany and the world economy (7 December). c) Agrar- und Bauernpolitik: Darré’s speech at the Nuremberg party congress on the foundations of National Socialist agrarian policy (12 September); Darré’s speech at the Reichsbauerntag in Goslar on the tasks and aims of agrarian policy (17 November); and Heß’s speech at Goslar on the production battle as an anti-Bolshevik weapon (17 November).
4. Der Arbeitsdienst (doc 43): the Reichsarbeitsdienstgesetz (26 June).
5. Kultur- und Kirchenpolitik (docs 44–48): Schirach’s speech on the nature and structure of the Hitler Youth before the Auslandspolitisches Amt (12 May); the law for the securing of the German Evangelical Church (24 September) and Kerrl’s first implementing ordinance (3 October); Kerrl’s speech on the position of church and religion in the National Socialist state before the Wirtschaftsrat of the German Academy (16 October); and Goebbels’ speech at the annual meeting of the Reichskulturkammer in the Berlin Philharmonie (15 November).
6. Neugestaltung des Rechts (docs 49–52): the state act on the transfer of the Länder justice to the Reich (Göring’s, Gürtner’s and Frick’s speeches, 2 April); the Leitsätze zum nationalsozialistischen Strafrecht; Gürtner’s speech at the 11th International Criminal Law and Prison Congress in Berlin on the idea of justice in German criminal-law renewal (19 August); and Frank’s speech at the congress of the NSDAP on “Die Neugestaltung des Deutschen Rechts” (14 September).

sources/die-nationalsozialistische-revol.title: Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933 — Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Band 1 (3rd ed., 1938)
sources/die-nationalsozialistische-revol.content:
Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933 (Band 1, 3rd ed. 1938)
Identity
Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933 is Band 1 (Teil 1) of Dokumente der deutschen Politik — the official documentary series of the Deutsche Hochschule für Politik (German Academy for Politics). It was compiled by Axel Friedrichs, under the general editorship of Paul Meier-Benneckenstein (Regierungsrat, President of the Hochschule für Politik), and published by Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin. Title-page copyright 1935; this is the 3rd edition, 1938 (print by Hofbuchdruckerei C. Dünnhaupt, Dessau).
The volume collects the principal laws, decrees, speeches and public documents of the Nazi seizure of power in 1933, presented as the realization of the “national socialist revolution.” It is the opening volume of the same official series as Volz’s Großdeutschland 1938 (Band 6) already held in this wiki, and stands alongside Büttner’s party-authorized program compilation.
Character of the source
A government-sponsored source book. The German Academy for Politics, in its prefatory Geleitwort, presents the volume as the start of a documentary record meant to make the nature and scope of the 1933 “revolutionary transformation of the state” clear to contemporaries. It is therefore an internal, regime-sanctioned compilation — the texts (laws, decrees, party orders, Hitler’s and other leaders’ speeches) are reproduced as authoritative state documents, with framing commentary from the editor. It complements, from the state’s own vantage point, the party-history and memoir sources in the Germany group.
Contents (structure)
The volume is organized into four parts, each subdivided by theme, containing numbered documents (1–79). Main structure:

I. Die Eroberung der Macht durch den Nationalsozialismus — the conquest of power

A. Vom 30. Januar 1933 bis zum Tag von Potsdam — 30 January 1933 (Hitler’s appointment as Chancellor; the Reichstag fire decree “Zum Schutz von Volk und Staat”; the 5 March 1933 Reichstag election and its result) to the Potsdam state ceremony
B. Der erste Reichstag des Dritten Reiches — the first Reichstag of the Third Reich (including Hitler’s speech against Abg. Wels on 23 March 1933 and the Enabling Act)
C. Das Ende des Parteienstaates — the end of the party state (law against the formation of new parties, 14 July 1933)
D. Ausbau und Befestigung der Macht — Partei und Staat — consolidation of power, party and state


II. Der Kampf um den Frieden — the struggle for peace (incl. Hitler’s Reichstag speech on national-socialist peace policy, 17 May 1933)
III. Der Kampf um den deutschen Arbeiter — the struggle for the German worker (Goebbels’ call, the “Arbeitsschlacht”/battle for work, the law on Treuhänder der Arbeit 19 May 1933)
IV. Der Neubau von Staat, Wirtschaft, Kultur und Recht — rebuilding state, economy, culture and law

A. Staat und Verwaltung — state and administration (1. Beamtentum und Staatsaufbau; 2. Auf dem Wege zur Reichseinheit: Reich und Länder, incl. the Reichsstatthalter law and Gleichschaltung of the Länder)
B. Bevölkerungs- und Rassenpolitik — population and racial policy (incl. the 14 July 1933 law on German citizenship)
C. Wirtschaftspolitik — economic policy (1. Allgemeiner Neubau der Wirtschaft; 2. Außenwirtschaft; 3. Agrarpolitik, incl. Reichsernährungsminister Darré)
D. Arbeitsdienst — labour service (Staatssekretär Hierl; the student work service)
E. Neubau der Kultur — rebuilding of culture (Propaganda Ministry tasks, 30 June 1933; the Reichskulturkammer law, 22 September 1933; the book-burning speech)
F. Die Kirchenpolitik des Dritten Reiches — the church policy of the Third Reich



Back matter: Zeittafel (chronology of 1933) and name/subject registers.
OCR / extraction quality
Source is an ABBYY-scanned PDF (University of California scan, barcode 35556009652967; 424 pages). The PDF’s embedded text layer was garbled because the book is set in Fraktur type. Per protocol, the full 424 pages were re-OCR’d with tesseract 5.5.2, -l deu+script/Fraktur --psm 3 at 300 dpi. A sample-page comparison confirmed the Fraktur model clearly outperformed plain deu (correct “Jahre/Vertrag/können/Frankreich/Saargebiet” vs deu’s “Yedes/Sahre/Dertrag/Sranfreicd)”). Result: clean, readable Fraktur transcription (22,357 lines; 424 page-form-feeds). A handful of pages (p0003, p0006, p0009, p0022, p0396, p0406, p0421, p0423, p0424) are genuine blank illustration plates. The closing index/register pages OCR partially garbled (dense small Fraktur), but the body and TOC are high quality. Roman numerals in the TOC are partially fragmented by the OCR (e.g. “B. Der erste Reichstag des Dritten Reiches”); the structure above has been reconstructed and cross-checked against body headings.
Cross-references

Companion official volumes: Friedrichs (comp.), Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934, Band 2 (in this wiki) — the direct sequel covering 1934 — Deutschlands Weg zur Freiheit 1935, Band 3 (in this wiki) — covering 1935 — and Deutschlands Aufstieg zur Großmacht 1936, Band 4 (in this wiki) — covering 1936; Volz (ed.), Großdeutschland 1938, Band 6/Teil 1 (in this wiki); Volz (ed.), Dokumente der deutschen Politik 1937 volume.
Party-authorized program compilation: Büttner (ed.), Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich (in this wiki).
Regime’s own vantage: Geisow, Die Seele des Dritten Reiches; contrast with the exile-left Rosenberg history and Speer’s insider memoir.

sources/espana-ensayo-de-historia-contem.title: Salvador de Madariaga — España: Ensayo de historia contemporánea (1950)
sources/espana-ensayo-de-historia-contem.content:
Salvador de Madariaga — España: Ensayo de historia contemporánea
Full bibliographic citation — Salvador de Madariaga (1886–1978). España: Ensayo de historia contemporánea. — 5th edition, published August 1950 (“Año del Libertador General San Martín”). Editorial Sudamericana, Buenos Aires, 1950. Copyright 1950, Editorial Sudamericana, S.A. First Spanish edition Aguilar, January 1931; the work first appeared in English as Spain: A Modern History, February 1930.
Salvador de Madariaga, the Spanish liberal diplomat, writer and historian, wrote España in English in 1929 for a collection of monographs on contemporary nations, published it in that language in February 1930, then gave it to his mother tongue in the Spanish edition of January 1931. The 1950 Buenos Aires fifth edition here presented carries prologues to the fourth (Oxford, June 1943), third (Oxford, February 1942), second (Paris, September 1933) and first (Gibraltar, 1 January 1931) editions, in which Madariaga corrects errors, revises his figures for Italian and German forces in the Civil War, and records how the book grew: the second edition restored four opening chapters on the land, the people and the history that the first Spanish edition had judged superfluous for a Spanish public. The work is a contemporary history of Spain told from within — the author’s stated aim being to adapt the Spanish character’s insolidarity to “la era de la solidaridad” — running from the land and people through the empire, the nineteenth century and the reign of Alfonso XIII, into the Republic, the Civil War and the first years of Franco’s dictatorship.
The text is 29,493 lines, extracted from a 840-file paginated OCR text dump (Rutgers University / Douglass College library copy, call no. DP26 .M33 1950), set in Roman type, no re-OCR required.
Content Summary
Front matter. Title page and imprint; prologue to the fourth edition (Oxford, June 1943) — rectifications of two points attributed to Don Diego Martínez Barrio and corrected figures for Italian (≥100,000 men) and German (the Condor Legion, first air support 31 July 1936) intervention in the Civil War; prologue to the third edition (Oxford, February 1942), written amid the Civil War’s aftermath, announcing the planned second book on the Republic and Franco; prologue to the second edition (Paris, September 1933); “Al lector” (Gibraltar, 1 January 1931), the first-edition note on the work’s English origin and its debts to Altamira, Fernando de los Ríos, Pellicena, Valls y Taberner, Cambó and Palacios.
Libro Primero — Tierra, pueblo, historia; los elementos del reinado; el reinado de Alfonso XIII
Parte Primera — Tierra, pueblo, historia (Chs. I–VIII)
Capítulo I — La Tierra. Madariaga opens: “El hecho esencial sobre la tierra española es su inaccesibilidad. España es un castillo.” The land as a fortress — the mean altitude of ~700 metres, the surrounding cordilleras and the Pyrenees, the Meseta Central as the citadel, the Guadalquivir valley as the only gradual gate, and the interior compartments cut by ranges and deep depressions.
Capítulo II — El Pueblo. “Varia, pero una, la tierra; vario, pero uno, el pueblo.” The anthropological complexity of the Spanish people — zones of round heads from Santander to La Coruña, the mixture of physical types, the racial variety beneath national unity.
Capítulo III — El Imperio español. “La historia moderna de España puede dividirse en dos períodos de duración aproximadamente igual”: the rise and fall of the Spanish empire (1492–1700) and the Bourbon restoration, new rise and new decline of Spain as a world power.
Capítulo IV — Auge y decadencia del imperio. “Toda la corriente de nuestra historia interna ilustra lo que hasta ahora queda dicho.” The Habsburg kings as, in Oliveira Martins’s image, pharaohs; the religious unity of the country as their chief idea, and the internal history that carried the empire from its height to its decay.
Capítulo V — Nuevo pueblo, nueva dinastía, nueva España. “España había perdido su vocación.” The passing of the religious atmosphere in which that vocation had manifested itself, the intellectual self-description of the century, and the court no longer frequented by ardent friars and active bishops.
Capítulo VI — El siglo XIX. “Sólo puede concebir nuestro siglo XIX como un período caótico y turbulento, sin sentido alguno, quien no comprenda que en la historia de España este siglo constituye una era de reconstitución nacional desde el mismo suelo.” The nineteenth century as an age of national reconstitution, from the collapse onward.
Capítulo VII — Escuela y despensa. “En su esencia, el problema de España consiste en adaptar su psicología nacional a las condiciones del mundo moderno.” The modern law of solidarity against the Spaniard’s rebellious individualism; the two ways of restraining the tendency — school and bread, the title’s escuela y despensa.
Capítulo VIII — Galdós y la generación del 98. “Mientras… constituía Giner el etos de la nación, Galdós reconstruía vigorosamente su epos.” Giner de los Ríos forming the national ethos and Galdós rebuilding the national epic; the generation of 1898 and its relation to the loss of empire.
Parte Segunda — Los elementos del reinado (Chs. IX–XXI)
Capítulo IX — El Rey. “El reinado de Alfonso XIII puede interpretarse como el esfuerzo para hacer penetrar en la conciencia del pueblo español las lecciones del despertar intelectual y económico” of the second half of the nineteenth century. The king’s reign and its reading of the modern awakening.
Capítulo X — La cuestión agraria. “La base de la vida nacional de España es su agricultura.” Agriculture as the base of national and social life; the obstacles raised by a defective agricultural organization in inextricable combination with a defective political system.
Capítulo XI — La cuestión obrera. “En el plano material, la nota típica del siglo xx en España ha sido un rápido desarrollo de su vida económica” — the industrial centres of the Basque country, Catalonia, Asturias and Valencia, and the emergence of the labour question.
Capítulo XII — La Iglesia. El clericalismo. “El clericalismo es un mal que desconocen los países protestantes.” Clericalism as a malady of Catholic countries, and Spain as a nation where it stands as a rigid enemy; the church question.
Capítulo XIII — El Ejército. Militarismo. “La palabra militarismo no corresponde muy exactamente al fenómeno español que pretende describir.” The Spanish military phenomenon distinguished from the Prussian-style militarism; the army question.
Capítulo XIV — La cuestión catalana: I. Aspecto psicológico. “La cuestión catalana, y en menor grado las que plantean los movimientos de resurgimiento de conciencia local en Vasconia y Galicia, son quizá las más difíciles, pero también las más fértiles en la vida pública contemporánea de España.” The psychological aspect of the Catalan question.
Capítulo XV — La cuestión catalana: II. Aspecto histórico. “La historia, dice una frase española, es una dehesa de aprovechamiento común.” The historical aspect; how the Catalanist historian exploits the common past more readily than the Castilian.
Capítulo XVI — La cuestión catalana: III. Orígenes de la situación actual. “A principios del siglo XIX, el espíritu nacional de Cataluña está muerto.” The death of the Catalan national spirit at the century’s opening — the peasantry speaking the language, an ignoble corruption of it in the urban crowd — and the origins of the modern situation.
Capítulo XVII — La cuestión vascongada. La cuestión gallega. Conclusión. The language criterion less sure a guide for the Basque question; the Galician question; the conclusion of the regionalist survey.
Capítulo XVIII — Portugal. “Las relaciones entre España y Portugal se ajustan a la regla que rige las relaciones entre los demás pueblos peninsulares.” The double wall of pride, bristling on the Portuguese side with suspicion of Spanish ambitions, obstructing an essentially simple reality.
Capítulo XIX — Marruecos. “Hay en el Quijote un episodio dentro de un episodio que arroja más luz sobre las raíces históricas de la política marroquí de España que toda la literatura técnica sobre la materia.” The captive’s tale in Don Quixote as the key to Spain’s Moroccan policy; the Moroccan question and its wars.
Capítulo XX — Hispanoamericanismo. “Las relaciones entre España y las naciones hispanoamericanas se han transformado durante los siglos XIX y XX, siguiendo una evolución gradual” — from domains of the crown, through the Cortes of Cádiz and the Constitution, to the modern Hispanoamericanism.
Capítulo XXI — Relaciones exteriores. “Basta una ojeada al mapa para mostrar que las ventajas estratégicas naturales de España son tales, que, si fuerte, ha de representar en el mundo un papel de primer plano.” Spain’s strategic position and the foreign relations of the reign.
Parte Tercera — El reinado de Alfonso XIII (Chs. XXII–XXVII)
Capítulo XXII — La preguerra. “El 17 de mayo de 1902, un adolescente que había cumplido aquel día los dieciséis años se preparó para asumir los deberes regios.” Alfonso XIII’s assumption of the throne at sixteen; the political world of the prewar years.
Capítulo XXIII — La guerra. “Los acuerdos de Cartagena firmados en 1907, y las conversaciones de 1913 entre M. Poincaré y el conde de Romanones” — the Entente agreements on the Mediterranean and African coasts; Spain and the Great War, neutrality and its strains.
Capítulo XXIV — Desde el fin de la guerra hasta el fin de la Constitución. “Al estallar la paz sopló sobre España un viento de liberalismo.” The postwar liberal wind, the Romanones government and the course from 1918 to the end of the constitutional regime — the mounting crisis, Morocco, the social struggle, the lead-up to the 1923 coup.
Capítulo XXV — La dictadura. “Gobernar no es cosa fácil para un rey. Alfonso XIII hubiera preferido ser el verdadero dictador de la nueva situación.” The king’s relation to the dictatorship of Primo de Rivera, established 1923; the military government.
Capítulo XXVI — La liquidación de la dictadura. “No es posible un juicio exacto, ni siquiera aproximado, de la dictadura sin formarse una opinión equilibrada sobre el régimen que se complació en llamar ‘antiguo’.” The liquidation of the dictatorship and a balanced judgment on it against the “old regime.”
Capítulo XXVII — Situación en 1930. “En las páginas siguientes se describe la situación tal y como se presentaba en 1930, cuando, ya caída la dictadura, no había caído todavía la Monarquía.” The political-historical landscape of Spain on the eve of the monarchy’s fall; “En lo esencial, la dictadura dejó a España en una situación igual o peor que la que encontró.”
Libro Segundo — La República, la Guerra Civil, y lo que va de mal vivir la dictadura de Franco
Al lector. “No es éste libro que se escriba por gusto o con gusto. Pero era menester escribirlo.” Spain as one of the world’s key nations, geographically and through its American ties; the need for an objective examination of the events of 1931–1941 “escrito con reconocimiento íntimo que sólo la consanguinidad puede aportar.” This second book studies “la corta vida y larga muerte de la segunda República y lo que lleva de mal vivir la dictadura del General Franco.”
Parte Primera — La República (Chs. I–VII)
Capítulo I — Caída de la monarquía. “Al comenzar el año de 1930 la monarquía estaba en peligro mortal.” The king’s lapse into the daily struggle of parties and sects; his personal responsibility (recalled to him by the presidents of the Senate and Congress after the Primo de Rivera coup); the fall of the monarchy and the advent of the Republic.
Capítulo II — La niña bonita. “España, en aquellos primeros días esplendorosos de la República, estaba rebosante de alegría – una alegría espontánea, como la de la naturaleza en primavera.” The early idyll of the Republic — the revolution so clean and untainted by the excesses that usually mar dramatic moments.
Capítulo III — Idealistas e irrealistas. “El 14 de julio de 1931 (delicado homenaje a la República francesa) se reunió por primera vez la Asamblea Constituyente en Madrid.” The Constituent Assembly of 14 July 1931 and the elections of 28 June; the idealists and the unrealists who were to shape the Republic’s course.
Capítulo IV — Primera fase. Izquierda. The left phase — the autonomous problems (Catalan, Basque, Galician), the religious problem, the military problem, the agrarian problem, the labour problem, teaching, and political events. Opens with Barcelona’s proclamation of the Republic and Macià’s “En nom del poble de Catalunya, proclamo l’Estat Català.”
Capítulo V — Segunda fase. Derecha. “Las fuerzas de la derecha, estimuladas por los errores de la izquierda más que por su propia virtud, habían ido creciendo durante los dos años primeros de la República” and uniting under José María Gil Robles, the young professor and militant Catholic founder of CEDA.
Capítulo VI — Tercera fase. Izquierda. “Cambiaba la opinión, pero, como iba a probarlo el tiempo, no cambiaba mucho, pese a las apariencias.” The swing back to the left through the oscillations of politics — the Popular Front and the approach of July 1936.
Capítulo VII — Política extranjera de la República. “La primera indicación de lo que iba a ser la política extranjera de la República fué la designación de don Alejandro Lerroux como ministro de Estado del Gobierno Provisional.” The Republic’s foreign policy from its first minister of state.
Parte Segunda — La Guerra Civil (Chs. VIII–XI)
Capítulo VIII — La batalla de los tres Franciscos. “La controversia que en el oeste reflejó en un cielo de papel nuestra Guerra Civil de sangre en una Guerra Civil de tinta.” The paper war in the West that mirrored the Spanish war of blood — how the disputants forgot the deeply Spanish nature of the conflict to stress its international aspect, and the “orgía de ‘donjulianismo’” by which both sides begged foreign help, the right convincing the fascist world the left was communist and the left convincing the democracies it was not.
Capítulo IX — Las dos primeras fases de la Guerra Civil. “La fase puramente nacional de la Guerra Civil comienza el 17–19 de julio de 1936, con la sublevación de Marruecos, y termina el 8 de noviembre del mismo año con la salida a [luz]…” I. La fase nacional; II. La fase de infiltración extranjera.
Capítulo X — La fase de dominación extranjera. “…esta fase de la Guerra Civil se caracteriza por el aumento del poder del partido comunista español y de la influencia rusa.” The phase of foreign domination, marked by the growth of the Spanish Communist Party and Russian influence, and the mounting intervention.
Capítulo XI — El fin de la Guerra Civil. “La idea de terminar la guerra por mediación había comenzado con la guerra misma.” The efforts to end the war by mediation, their suspicions and misapprehensions, and the war’s close.
Parte Tercera — Entre la Guerra Civil y la Guerra Mundial (Chs. XII–XV)
Capítulo XII — Asuntos interiores. “Tres son los aspectos de la obra que el general Franco tenía por delante al encargarse de la jefatura del Estado español: rehacer el alma nacional; rehacer el cuerpo nacional; llevar la nave del Estado en peligroso rumbo.” Franco’s interior work — remaking the national soul and the national body in the first years of the dictatorship.
Capítulo XIII — Política extranjera. “La política extranjera del general Franco resultó ser en su conjunto menos mala que su política interior.” Franco’s foreign policy between the Civil War and the world war — its limits and determining forces.
Capítulo XIV — El éxodo. “Hasta cierto punto puede decirse que desde el principio de la Guerra Civil se había producido ya una especie de éxodo” — the refugee movements, the embassies in Madrid sheltering fugitives from the anarchic terror of the first months, and the mass exile at the war’s end.
Capítulo XV — Al borde del porvenir. “¿Qué rumbo tomará la vida de España más allá de las tormentas de la hora presente? Huelgan las profecías…” Spain’s course beyond the present storms; the closing reflection at the edge of the future.
Apéndices. Five appendices: I. Memoria personal (Madariaga’s account of himself at the abdication — in Mexico as an extraordinary professor, living outside Spain since 1916, and his error in believing the Republic could not come without a military conspiracy); II. Carta de Stalin (a confidential letter in French to Largo Caballero at Valencia, on Soviet aid to the Spanish government); III. Carta de Don Luis Companys a Don Juan Negrín (on the morale of the Catalonian rear guard); IV. and V. Artículos publicados en Ahora (20 March 1935, on Manuel Azaña; 13 March 1935, on “Guerra civil” and the fulanista republicans). The volume closes with the Índice de nombres and the Índice general, and the colophon (“Se terminó de imprimir el doce de agosto de mil novecientos cincuenta”).
Key Data Points









































AttributeDetailAuthorSalvador de Madariaga (1886–1978)TitleEspaña: Ensayo de historia contemporáneaPublished5th ed., Editorial Sudamericana, Buenos Aires, 1950 (1st Spanish ed. Aguilar 1931; English Spain 1930)Source libraryRutgers University / Douglass College Library (DP26 .M33 1950)Raw filewiki/raw/espana-ensayo-de-historia-contemporanea-madariaga-1950.txtLines29,493Sections/Chapters2 books; Libro Primero 27 chs. (3 parts), Libro Segundo 15 chs. (3 parts) + 5 appendicesSignificanceThe Spanish liberal-democratic case from within — a contemporary history of Spain from the land and empire through the monarchy, Republic, Civil War and Franco’s early dictatorship, the peninsular counterpart to the regime sources and the French/Italian/German cases already in the wiki
Relationship to the Wiki
Madariaga gives the wiki its first Spanish source and its fullest non-Iberian-adjacent case from the liberal-democratic centre, complementing the French pages of Siegfried, Halévy and Zévaès. Read against the fascist and communist sources already ingested, it presents the Spanish republic of the 1930s as seen by one of its most prominent liberal exiles — the victim-analyst of the Civil War from the democratic side, in the manner of Bloch on the French defeat and Badoglio’s Allied-side Italian counterpart. Its survey of the Spanish land, the imperial past, the agrarian, labour, church, army and regional questions, and the Republic’s descent through left and right phases into the Civil War and foreign intervention extends the wiki’s geography of interwar Europe westward to the Iberian peninsula. His closing parts on the early dictatorship sit beside Aznar’s Nationalist military history, Hayes’s wartime embassy memoir, Tusell’s volume II on the Republic and Civil War, and his continuous scholarly arc of the Franco regime from 1939 to 1975.
