sources/farinacci-storia-della-rivoluzio.title: Farinacci — Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. I (Il 1919) (1937)
sources/farinacci-storia-della-rivoluzio.content:
Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Volume I — Il 1919 (1937)
Identity
Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista (History of the Fascist Revolution) is a multi-volume history of the rise of Italian Fascism by Roberto Farinacci (1892–1945), the Cremona ras (provincial Fascist boss), former squadrist leader and later Secretary of the National Fascist Party (1925–1926). This is Volume I, subtitled Il 1919 — the year of the founding of the Fasci di combattimento. It was published by the Stabilimento Tipografico Soc. Ed. «Cremona Nuova», Cremona, 1937 (Year XV of the Fascist era), the press of Farinacci’s own home province. The archive.org scan is a copy held by the Biblioteca Civica di Varese (N. 1018543), with the stamp of the Fascist-era Scuola di Mistica Fascista “Sandro Italico Mussolini” (Sezione Storia della Rivoluzione) bound at the back.
It is the third Italian-language source in this wiki, and the most substantial yet: a full documentary-political narrative of the single most important year in Fascism’s origin-story, 1919 — the year of the interventionist crisis, the founding of the Fasci at Piazza San Sepolcro (23 March), the fatti di Milano of April, the Fiume undertaking of September, and the elections of 16 November. Where Businelli’s Rivoluzione fascista (1933) is a compact movement-insider origin-story running 1912–1922, and Volpe’s Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) is the collected journalism of an academic fellow-traveller, Farinacci’s is the authoritative party-history written by the movement’s own most ruthless organizational boss and — uniquely — it opens with the claim (on the first pages) that it is the history of the Fascist Revolution as witnessed from within its most violent and decisive phase.
Character of the source
A partisan, polemical and self-consciously authoritative party history written by a central figure of the movement at the height of the Mussolini regime. Farinacci was not a neutral chronicler: he was the leader of the squadrist Fascism of the Po valley, the organizer of the Cremona Fasci, and one of the two dominant figures (with Italo Balbo) of the violence that marked the movement’s rise. The volume’s rhetorical posture is accusatory — its two parts are titled “Lo sfacelo della classe dirigente” (The Collapse of the Ruling Class) and “La disfatta diplomatica” (The Diplomatic Defeat) — and it repeatedly indicts the liberal governments of 1919 (Orlando, Nitti), the “Messia americano” Wilson and the Paris Peace Conference, the Socialists, and the moderates for the national humiliation that, in Farinacci’s telling, made the Fascist reaction necessary and justified. The book is therefore less a detached history than a primary document of how the radical-squadrist wing of the regime narrated the crisis year of 1919 and the Fasci’s founding as the patriotic answer to it.
Contents (structure)
The volume is organized into two parts and sixteen chapters, tracing the political crisis of Italy in 1919 month by month. Chapter headings and page numbers follow the printed Indice del Volume I:

Parte I — Lo sfacelo della classe dirigente (The Collapse of the Ruling Class)

Cap. I — Lo stato degli animi in Italia dopo la cessazione delle ostilità (p. 9): the war and the victory; the “mirabile gioventù italiana”; testimonies of valour; the pride and the disillusion of the combatants; Mussolini’s warning
Cap. II — Orlando alla Conferenza della pace a Parigi (p. 31): the verbose and irresolute man; a compliant submission; the League of Nations as the “ideal instrument of an iniquitous peace”; the strength of the country diminished and offended by the Italian government
Cap. III — La rivoluzione russa e le sue ripercussioni in Italia (p. 51): on the road of despair; the oppressions and violences of the Tsars; the first signs of revolt; the unfolding of the drama; the ignorance of the Italian parliamentarians
Cap. IV — La classe dirigente cerca nella liquidazione della guerra la salvezza e prepara la rivolta (p. 71): a bitter truth; the last masterpiece; the betrayal of the state; a decisive act of accusation
Cap. V — Dissidio fra interventisti e offensiva neutralista (pp. 79–108, in three parts): Part I — anguished questions, the insufficiency of government, Wilson and eternal justice, the transformation of political values, the split among the interventionists; Part II — the dispersal of the national forces, the Giolittians and the “parecchio,” the accusations of the neutralists, Lenin’s prophecy, the nefanda joy of the socialists; Part III — universal Christianity, a great experiment, Christian democracy, the birth of the Partito Popolare
Cap. VI — La costituzione dei Fasci di Combattimento (p. 109): Mussolini’s character and orientation; the situation in Italy — the reds and the whites; the last proof; a dramatic alternative; the attitude of the industrialists; the episode of Dalmine; the intervention of the Arditi; the creation of the Fasci


Parte II — La disfatta diplomatica (The Diplomatic Defeat)

Cap. VII — L’inizio della guerra civile (p. 195): a memorable date; the Constituent Assembly of Interventionism; the prologue of the long drama; the assault on Avanti!; promises kept; Fascists and interventionists; Mussolini’s faith
Cap. VIII — La resa a discrezione del Governo italiano alla Conferenza di Parigi (p. 151): the Adriatic question; the American Messiah; the Wilsonian utopia and the violations of Italian right; Orlando and the road of dishonour; the ideal origin of the Fiume undertaking; the submission to the Allies
Cap. IX — La disfatta tedesca e la caduta dell’Impero in Germania (p. 167): fatal resignation; the revolutionary movements; the flight of Wilhelm II; the shattering of German pride; the signing of the “peace”; the provvida sventura
Cap. X — I tumulti del caroviveri fra le delusioni di Versailles e i tentativi di riforme (p. 181): the political crisis of the postwar; the first phase of the dissolutive process; the government twice guilty; the assault on the shops; the general strike of July; Mussolini’s incitement; the “electoral reform”
Cap. XI — L’inchiesta su Caporetto (p. 199): the insufficiency of the rulers; the monstrous trial; the action of the socialists; the episodes of the Ravenna and the Catanzaro; exasperation and paroxysm; the will of the Fascists — to save the truth and defend the victory
Cap. XII — L’Impresa di Fiume (p. 231): political imbecility; the entry of the Granatieri; the cowardice of official Italy; the anguished hours of the holocaust city; the epic of Ronchi
Cap. XIII — Fiume contro Roma (p. 249): the cowardice of Nitti; the inertia of the government; the resumption of the march of Vittorio Veneto; war on official Italy; a comment by Mussolini; the will of the Legionaries; a paradoxical situation
Cap. XIV — I Partiti politici nella lotta elettorale del 1919 (p. 257, in two parts): Part I — the Socialist congress, the framing of the electoral struggle, the Partito Popolare against the war, Sturzo’s report on the party programme, the skilful political tactics; Part II — the congress of the Fasci at Florence, programmatic postulates, the Giolitti–Salandra polemic, the participation of the Fascists in the elections, the result
Cap. XV — Il commento dei Partiti alle elezioni del 1919 (p. 269): exceptions and reservations; miserable excuses; universal distrust; examinations of conscience; the miseries of the bourgeoisie; the involuntary ally; a courageous confession
Cap. XVI — L’equivoca azione dei socialisti moderati (p. 283): the masculine voice of Italy; the fatti di Roma; ambiguity of thoughts and attitudes; the shepherd of the mad sheep; the nullism and the responsibilities of the revolutionaries



The volume closes with the printed Indice del Volume I (pp. 295–296 of the scan). Bound at the back is the Fascist-era library form of the Scuola di Mistica Fascista “Sandro Italico Mussolini,” Sezione Storia della Rivoluzione — a printed document of the school’s plan for compiling a history of the Revolution, with its reading-project instructions (periodization from Avanti! 1914 through 1922; sections on doctrine, organization, chronicle, foreign judgments; the obligation of monthly articles for “Dottrina fascista” and “Libro e moschetto”). This is part of the scan but not of Farinacci’s text.
OCR / extraction quality
Source is the archive.org _djvu.txt full-text of the scan of the Biblioteca Civica di Varese copy (identifier farinacci-roberto.-storia-della-rivoluzione-fascista.-vol.-1-ocr-1937), delivered as a text file of the OCR’d pages. The book is set in Roman (Antiqua) type, and the OCR is clean, fluent and fully readable across the body of the work — proper accented Italian forms, footnote apparatus with source attributions (e.g. “Vedi: M. Toscano, Il Patto di Londra, Zanichelli, 1934”), and printed page numbers are all present and legible. Only isolated OCR slips appear (e.g. “La Costituenie dell’Interventismo” for “La Costituente,” “L’Impresa di Finme/Fiume,” ligature and stray-dash artifacts in the front matter and the facsimile library form). Per protocol the embedded/full-text OCR layer is the extraction source. Result: a clean Italian transcription saved as wiki/raw/farinacci-storia-della-rivoluzione-fascista-1937.txt (14,181 lines). The structure above has been reconstructed from the printed Indice del Volume I and cross-checked against the body part and chapter headings.
Cross-references

Companion Italian source, same author and series: Farinacci, Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. II (L’Insurrezione Rossa e la Vittoria dei Fasci) (1938) — Vol. I treats 1919; Vol. II continues the same party history into the “red biennium” of 1920–21 and the squadrist reaction, with the same publisher, provenance (Biblioteca Civica di Varese) and editorial apparatus.
Companion Italian source: Businelli, Rivoluzione fascista (1933) — the movement-insider origin-story of Fascism (1912–1922), including the founding of the Fasci in 1919 which Farinacci here treats in exhaustive documentary detail.
Companion Italian source: Volpe, Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) — the collected wartime-and-Fascist political journalism (1916–1928) of the academic historian Gioacchino Volpe, the intellectual counterpart to Farinacci’s organizational-boss narrative.
These stand alongside the German Dokumente der deutschen Politik series (Friedrichs Bands 1–4; Volz Bands 5–6) and the German regime-vantage sources (Geisow; Büttner) as the Fascist (Italian) counterpart to the Nazi (German) documentary record, and against the Soviet sources (Pokrovsky, VKP(b) Short Course, Stalin) as the third revolutionary regime’s official self-account.

sources/farinacci-storia-della-rivoluzio.title: Farinacci — Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. II (L'Insurrezione Rossa e la Vittoria dei Fasci) (1938)
sources/farinacci-storia-della-rivoluzio.content:
Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Volume II — L’Insurrezione Rossa e la Vittoria dei Fasci (1938)
Identity
Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista (History of the Fascist Revolution) is a multi-volume history of the rise of Italian Fascism by Roberto Farinacci (1892–1945), the Cremona ras (provincial Fascist boss), former squadrist leader and later Secretary of the National Fascist Party (1925–1926). This is Volume II, subtitled L’Insurrezione Rossa e la Vittoria dei Fasci (The Red Insurrection and the Victory of the Fasci). It was published by the Stabilimento Tipografico Soc. Ed. «Cremona Nuova», Cremona, 1938 (Year XVI of the Fascist era) — the volume’s colophon reads “Finito di stampare il 12 aprile XVI con i tipi della Società Editoriale «Cremona Nuova» - Cremona” — the press of Farinacci’s own home province. As with Volume I, the archive.org scan is a copy held by the Biblioteca Civica di Varese (Mod. 347 stamp).
It continues directly the narrative of Volume I (1937): where Vol. I treated the crisis year 1919 (the founding of the Fasci, Fiume, the elections), this volume covers the period 1 January 1920 – May 1921 — the two years of the “red biennium” and of the squadrist reaction. It is the fourth Italian-language source in this wiki, and it documents the crucial turn from the parliamentary-political phase of 1919 to the violent, extra-legal phase of squadrism (the squadre d’azione and their punitive expeditions) that culminated in the electoral victory of the National Blocs in May 1921.
Character of the source
A partisan, polemical and self-consciously authoritative party history written by the movement’s most violent provincial boss at the height of the Mussolini regime. Its subtitle announces the two-fold argument: the “Red Insurrection” of the workers’ and peasants’ movements in 1920 (the strikes, the occupation of the factories, the agrarian unrest) and the “Victory of the Fasci” as the patriotic, anti-Bolshevik answer to it. In the Avvertenza (prefatory note) Farinacci states that the volume follows an ideal rather than chronological criterion — each Part and Chapter develops a single argument or historical moment — and that doctrinal discussions and the Fascist congresses have deliberately been omitted, to be treated in a later volume examining the Fascist Congress of Rome. The rhetorical posture is accusatory throughout: the liberal governments (Nitti, then Giolitti), the Socialists and the “ruling class” are indicted for the anarchy and national humiliation that, in Farinacci’s telling, made the Fascist reaction necessary and justified. It is thus a primary document of how the radical-squadrist wing of the regime narrated the “red biennium” and its own violent triumph.
Contents (structure)
The volume is organized into two parts and fifteen chapters, continuing the chapter numbering of Volume I (which ended at Cap. XVI). Chapter headings and page numbers follow the printed Indice del Volume II:

Parte I — L’Insurrezione Rossa (The Red Insurrection)

Cap. XVII — La rivolta senza idee e senza capi (p. 9, in two parts): Part I — odious arrogance, economic and revolutionary strikes, the episode of Cremona, the tumults of Viareggio, the essay (trial) of the occupation of the factories, the cowardice of the ruling class, the incidents of Trieste; Part II — in the countryside, the desire for land, the rivalry between Socialists and Popolari, the clerical party, the agrarian riots, the hunt for the carabiniere and the blackleg, the conflicts between partisans of the extreme parties
Cap. XVIII — Nitti al Governo (p. 41): the “blackmail-note” of Wilson; Nitti’s programme, the ideal man of the ruling class; peace at any price; the prayers of a Prefect; the massacre of via Nazionale in Rome
Cap. XIX — La caduta di Nitti (p. 52): the slow transformation of minds; the sad agony of the ruling class; Mussolini’s warning; the tragedy of socialism; Nitti the bourgeois chief; the blindness of the Turatians
Cap. XX — Giolitti al potere (p. 64): the mortal crisis; the decadence of liberalism; the vain warnings; the dictator and corrupter of political struggle in Italy; Giolitti’s astuteness; a suicidal formula
Cap. XXI — L’abbandono dell’Albania (p. 77): the return of the dictator; the resumption of seditious unrest; conflicts, rebellions and assassinations; the facts of Piombino and Ancona; the destruction of the conscience of the law; the democratic draft-laws
Cap. XXII — L’occupazione delle fabbriche (p. 91, in three parts): Part I — resumption of the riots, the agitation of the metalworkers, obstructionism and lockout, the attempted blackmail of the Government, the struggle of the FIOM and the closing of the “Romeo”; Part II — tragicomic episodes, the technical incapacity and obstacles of workers’ management, intrinsic impotence, sequestrations and homicides, the “Scimula and Sonzini” affair; Part III — the false mirage of Moscow, the interests and rights of all sacrificed to Giolittian opportunism, demagogy of changed colour, an expedient for dictatorship
Cap. XXIII — Il Natale di sangue (p. 129, in two parts): Part I — Yugoslav resistance, Giolitti’s accommodation, the negotiations of Rapallo, Italy rising stronger from the denied victory, the mission to Fiume, the Reggenza del Carnaro; Part II — the pact not recognized by the nationalists, Caviglia’s ultimatum, the state of war, the full powers obtained by d’Annunzio from the Fiumans, the fulfilment of the tragedy
Cap. XXIV — Gli avvenimenti in Europa dopo la Pace di Versaglia e la politica estera del Governo italiano (p. 153, in two parts): Part I — honest aspirations, the isolation of France and English realism, the anxieties of Paris, a salutary truth, the reservations of London, the economic peace, confessions of carelessness, the error of a peace, the occupation of the Ruhr, the plebiscite in Upper Silesia; Part II — the Anglo-French intervention in Russia, the Russo-Polish war, France’s action and the Franco-English dissension, Giolitti’s and Nitti’s programme — peace at any cost, England and Italy, Greece and Turkey, the purposes of conciliation, a policy of suicide, Italian resignation, the appearance of defeat


Parte II — La Vittoria dei Fasci (The Victory of the Fasci)

Cap. XXV — La riscossa fascista (p. 193, in three parts): Part I — the process of development, the anarchy of the piazza, the shattered myth, the intuition and energy of a Leader, the humiliation of the middle classes, the first nuclei; Part II — the rising of Trieste, bulwark of Italianness, against the arrogance of Slavs and Socialists, an open wound, desperation and exasperation, the burning of the Balkum, the shadow of defeat, the flaring of passions; Part III — the energetic reaction of the Fascists of Venezia Giulia, barricades and massacres, a speech by Mussolini, the mystification of politicians, the devastation of the “Lavoratore,” the beginning of the reaction, the administrative elections
Cap. XXVI — L’«epicentro» della riscossa fascista (p. 214, in two parts): Part I — the capital of agricultural Bolshevism, the massacre of Molinella, the propaganda against the war, the religion of the land, the dominion of the red organizations, the surrender of the proprietors and the arrogance of the lega-bosses; Part II — the tragic episode of Palazzo d’Accursio (Bologna), the installation of the communal Council, the killing of Giordani, the rise of the new state of mind, the cowardice of the leaders, the toscin
Cap. XXVII — La scissione dei socialisti (p. 224, in two parts): Part I — the inconsistency of Italian political life, the climate before the Socialist congress, the regional congress of the Fasci at Cremona, episodes of blood, a vast tide of energies, the Socialist victory of Ferrara, the mobilization of the Fascists; Part II — the quarrels among the factions at the congress of Livorno, the three red tendencies at grips, the fault of the war, the reformist chorus and the anger of the Communists, to avoid the split, the victory of the maximalist unitarians
Cap. XXVIII — L’inizio della bufera (p. 240, in two parts): Part I — the parliamentary discussions on Fascism, historical deafness, the tragic process of Italian political life, the reproach of the reformists and the invectives against the bourgeoisie; Part II — the red insurrection in the Puglie, the martyrdom of R. Barbera and G. Berta, the massacre of Empoli, savage scenes, the Diana massacre, Turati’s tears and the cynicism of the Communists
Cap. XXIX — Le squadre d’azione e le rappresaglie (p. 248): the multiplication of the Fasci; the end of the strength of the State; the punitive expeditions; the cowardice of the revolutionaries; Giolitti’s incapacity; surgical necessity
Cap. XXX — Lo scioglimento della Camera (p. 264, in two parts): Part I — the extreme attempt and Giolitti’s manoeuvre, the reasons for the dissolution, a perfect field of manoeuvre, democratic politics, the sad dictator, the work of seduction; Part II — the anger of the parties and the eternal lie of the Socialists, Treves’s whining, the historical energy of the war, Turati’s act of contrition, the malady of the bourgeoisie, infecundity and incapacity
Cap. XXXI — La lotta durante le elezioni (p. 275, in two parts): Part I — the constitution of the National Blocs, useless resistances, a phase of the civil war, the language of Mussolini, the “sottocoda” manoeuvre, the peace of the victors, the new State of Italy; Part II — the bloody spread of the civil war, assassinations and reactions, the law of the talion, a bloody dripping, the hopes of the Giolittians and their speculation on corpses, a nauseating amalgam, the tragic May, the lie of the regime; the rovent atmosphere of the “electoral battle,” the new Risorgimento, the blindness of Giolitti, cold decision, hatred calling hatred, the living process of history, the attitude of the Popolari, the balance-sheet of the “battle”



The volume closes with the printed Indice del Volume II and the colophon “Finito di stampare il 12 aprile XVI con i tipi della Società Editoriale «Cremona Nuova» - Cremona.”
OCR / extraction quality
Source is the archive.org _djvu.txt full-text of the scan of the Biblioteca Civica di Varese copy (identifier farinacci-roberto.-storia-della-rivoluzione-fascista.-vol.-2-ocr-1938). The book is set in Roman (Antiqua) type, and the OCR is clean, fluent and fully readable across the body of the work — accented Italian forms, footnote apparatus and printed page numbers all present and legible. Only isolated OCR slips appear (e.g. “vos1SIISÙI” for the reverse of a title page, “GVERRA” artifacts in ornamental front matter, “ebbandono” for “abbandono,” the reading of the Indice’s scattered page-number column). Per protocol the embedded/full-text OCR layer is the extraction source. Result: a clean Italian transcription saved as wiki/raw/farinacci-storia-della-rivoluzione-fascista-1938.txt (21,420 lines). The structure above has been reconstructed from the printed Indice del Volume II and cross-checked against the body part and chapter headings (Cap. XVII at the opening, Part I “L’Insurrezione Rossa,” Part II “La Vittoria dei Fasci,” Cap. XXXI as the closing chapter).
Cross-references

Companion Italian sources, same author and series: Farinacci, Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. I (Il 1919) (1937) and Vol. III (La Marcia su Roma) (1939) — Vol. I treats 1919 and Vol. III continues the same party history into May 1921 – October 1922 (Cap. XXXII–XXXIX), with the same publisher, provenance (Biblioteca Civica di Varese) and editorial apparatus; this volume (Cap. XVII–XXXI) is the central volume of the trilogy.
Companion Italian source: Pini & Bresadola, Storia del Fascismo: Guerra – Rivoluzione – Regime (1928) — the regime-published full-length chronicle of the rise of Fascism, whose later chapters (the occupation of the factories, squadrism, the May 1921 elections) cover the same ground as this volume.
Companion Italian source: Businelli, Rivoluzione fascista (1933) — the movement-insider origin-story of Fascism (1912–1922), including the 1920–21 phase Farinacci here treats in exhaustive detail.
Companion Italian source: Volpe, Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) — the collected wartime-and-Fascist political journalism (1916–1928) of the academic historian Gioacchino Volpe, the intellectual counterpart to Farinacci’s organizational-boss narrative.
These stand alongside the German Dokumente der deutschen Politik series (Friedrichs Bands 1–4; Volz Bands 5–6) and the German regime-vantage sources (Geisow; Büttner) as the Fascist (Italian) counterpart to the Nazi (German) documentary record, and against the Soviet sources (Pokrovsky, VKP(b) Short Course, Stalin) as the third revolutionary regime’s official self-account.

sources/farinacci-storia-della-rivoluzio.title: Farinacci — Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. III (La Marcia su Roma) (1939)
sources/farinacci-storia-della-rivoluzio.content:
Farinacci — Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. III (La Marcia su Roma) (1939)
Author: Roberto Farinacci
Publisher: Stabilimento Tipografico Soc. Ed. «Cremona Nuova», Cremona, 1939 (Year XVII; colophon “Finito di stampare… XVI” [?]; Biblioteca Civica di Varese copy, with the “Sala” and library stamps)
Archive.org: identifier farinacci-roberto.-storia-della-rivoluzione-fascista.-vol.-3-ocr-1939 (full text, tesseract Roman-type OCR)
Character
The third and final volume of the party history of the Fascist Revolution written by the Cremona ras Roberto Farinacci at the height of the regime, published by his own provincial press at Cremona. This volume carries the subtitle “La Marcia su Roma” and treats the decisive phase of the Fascist seizure of power: from the elections of May 1921 (the immediate post-electoral situation with which Vol. II had closed) through the collapse of the Giolittian, Bonomi and Facta parliamentary systems and the party’s rise to national power, to the March on Rome of October 1922, the King’s refusal of the military response, and the victory of the “Blackshirts.” It is the account of the Fascist consolidation of state power written from the insider vantage of the Cremona ras, a prominent squadrist leader who stood at the centre of the events he describes.
Structure
Two parts, eight chapters (Cap. XXXII–XXXIX, continuing the numbering of Vols. I and II):


Parte I — La fine del sistema giolittiano (The End of the Giolittian System), Cap. XXXII–XXXV

Cap. XXXII — La fine della vecchia dittatura (The End of the Old Dictatorship) — the results of the electoral struggle and the fall of Giolitti
Cap. XXXIII — Speranze e propositi di Mussolini (Mussolini’s Hopes and Purposes)
Cap. XXXIV — Bonomi al Governo (Bonomi in Government) — the Bonomi ministry and the Sarzana bloodshed, the pact of pacification
Cap. XXXV — Crisi di sviluppo (Crisis of Development) — the Fascist congresses and the transformation of Fascism into a party



Parte II — La Marcia su Roma (The March on Rome), Cap. XXXVI–XXXIX

Cap. XXXVI — Il Partito Nazionale Fascista (The National Fascist Party)
Cap. XXXVII — Socialismo democratico e socialismo rivoluzionario (Democratic Socialism and Revolutionary Socialism) — English, French and Italian revolutions compared; the Risorgimento and the Statuto
Cap. XXXVIII — La catastrofe della economia italiana e lo sviluppo del Fascismo (The Catastrophe of the Italian Economy and the Development of Fascism); Facta al Governo (Facta in Government) — the Facta ministry and the fall of Bonomi
Cap. XXXIX — A Roma (At Rome) — the state of mind of October 1922, the Congress of Naples, Mussolini’s proclamation, the March on Rome, the King’s conduct, and the “victory of the Blackshirts”



The volume closes with the printed Indice del Volume III.
OCR Quality
Clean Roman-type OCR layer (tesseract), readable throughout — no re-OCR required. Isolated slips only: fragmented title-page ornament (lines 1–27), “PARTE Il” for “Parte II,” “Banomi”/“Bonomi” alternation, “verchia” for “vecchia,” “neinire”/“nainra” for the Dante quotation “La natura delle cose altro non è che nascimento di esse,” and run-together running heads in the printed Indice.
Coverage
The third and final volume completes the Farinacci trilogy: Vol. I (1937) = the crisis year 1919; Vol. II (1938) = the “red biennium,” 1 January 1920 – May 1921; Vol. III (1939) = May 1921 – October 1922, ending with the March on Rome and the formation of the Fascist government.
Cross-references

Companion Italian sources, same author and series: Farinacci, Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. I (Il 1919) (1937) and Vol. II (L’Insurrezione Rossa e la Vittoria dei Fasci) (1938) — this volume (Cap. XXXII–XXXIX) is the direct sequel of Vol. II (Cap. XVII–XXXI), with the same publisher, provenance (Biblioteca Civica di Varese) and editorial apparatus; the trilogy ends here with the March on Rome.
Companion Italian sources: Pini & Bresadola, Storia del Fascismo: Guerra – Rivoluzione – Regime (1928) — the regime-published full-length chronicle, chapter XIII of which treats the same March on Rome; Businelli, Rivoluzione fascista (1933); Volpe, Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) and Volpe, History of the Fascist Movement (1936).
These stand alongside the German Dokumente der deutschen Politik series (Friedrichs Bands 1–4; Volz Bands 5–6) and the German regime-vantage sources as the Fascist (Italian) counterpart to the Nazi (German) documentary record of the interwar revolutionary seizure of power.

sources/geisow-die-seele-des-dritten-rei.title: Die Seele des Dritten Reiches (1933)
sources/geisow-die-seele-des-dritten-rei.content:
Die Seele des Dritten Reiches
Hans Geisow — Die Seele des Dritten Reiches (The Soul of the Third Reich), 2nd edition, Armanen-Verlag, Leipzig, 1933 (title page dated 1933; preface signed Frankfurt a. M., February 1933). A völkisch tract on the racial and spiritual foundations of the National Socialist revolution, written in the weeks immediately after Hitler’s appointment as Reich Chancellor on 30 January 1933 and before the seizure of absolute power later that year. 93 pages.

































AuthorHans Geisow (the name is OCR’d “Hans Beifow” on the scan); a völkisch author of the Armanen circlePublisherArmanen-Verlag, Leipzig (Hofpitalstraße 10), the occultist-völkisch house founded by Guido von List’s successor and associated with the “Armanen” racial-mystical school; 2nd edition (Zweite Auflage)Edition1933, Armanen-Verlag, Leipzig; printed by Pierer’sche Hofbuchdruckerei Stephan Geibel & Co., Altenburg, Thür.; title page carried the note “Zweite Auflage”StructureA preface (Vorwort) and fourteen chapters of continuous völkisch argument on race, soul, history, liberalism, economics, family, church, art and education; 2,742 lines of extracted textPeriodThe weeks around February 1933 — a contemporary record of the mood of German völkisch nationalism at the moment of Hitler’s appointment, treating the revolution as “a piece of religion”NotePublisher’s advertisement for the Armanen “Neue Bücher zur Staats- und Kulturpolitik” series appears on the final page of the scan and is not part of the text
Contents. The book is an essay in racial-mystical politics, arguing that German history and German decline must be understood through race and “the soul of the people.” The preface opens with Hitler’s appointment of 30 January 1933 and the promise of a Volksgemeinschaft (national community) overcoming class divisions. The opening chapter, “Weltenwende” (Turn of the Age), holds that history is a piece of nature and that the forces of race and blood are the true currents beneath political events. The chapters then move through the crisis of the present age (“Unsere Zeit und ihre Krankheit”), the racial idea (“Der Rassegedanke”), the origins of mankind (“Vom Ursprung der Menschheit” — drawing on the researches of Hermann Wirth), the creativity of the Nordic man (“Das Schöpfertum des nordischen Menschen”), race-specific thought (“Das arteigene Denken”), the psychic current in German history (“Der seelische Kraftstrom in der deutschen Geschichte”), and a long polemic against liberalism (“Der Liberalismus”) as an alien, Jewish-masonic mode of thought born of the French Revolution. The second half applies the argument to economic life (“Das Wirtschaftsleben”), the family (“Die Familie”), the church (“Die Kirche”), art, and education (“Die Erziehung”), ending with the conviction that God, not man, makes world history and that the German’s struggle for his right to life is a piece of religion.
Character of the source. A primary document of German völkisch-nationalist ideology at the moment of the National Socialist seizure of power, written by a party-adherent author and published by the Armanen occultist-völkisch house in the spring of 1933. It belongs to the same family of racial-theoretical texts that supplied the ideological accompaniment to the Nazi revolution, and it shows the theological-racial vocabulary — blood, soul, Nordic race, the enemy Jew and freemasonry, the rejection of liberalism and individualism — in which that revolution presented itself to its German public in its first months. As a window on the mental world of the movement’s own adherents in 1933 it complements the official document collections of the same period (such as Volz’s Von der Großmacht zur Weltmacht, also in this wiki), being the unofficial, party-side voice rather than the state record.
Quality. Moderate. The original scan carries a garbled Google ABBYY text layer (the Fraktur text misread almost beyond use); the raw text here was produced by a fresh tesseract OCR pass in German (-l deu, PSM 3) at 300 dpi over all 63 pages, which recovers the text cleanly. Some Fraktur OCR errors remain throughout (e.g. “Don Hans Beifow” for “Von Hans Geisow”, “Die $Samilie” for “Die Familie”, “Die Kicche” for “Die Kirche”, scattered s/f/r substitutions), and the Roman chapter numerals are misread (duplicated and gap-ridden: II, IV, V, VI twice, VII, X, XI twice, XIV). The chapter headings given in the Contents above are identified from the recovered text by content; the exact numeral sequence of the original is not reliably recoverable from this scan. Chapter breaks at 2142–2547 covering church, art and education are continuous in the source and are attributed to their chapters by content.

Vorwort (Preface)
Signed Frankfurt a. M., February 1933. Opens with the appointment of Adolf Hitler as Reich Chancellor on 30 January 1933 and the advent of a movement whose goal is a Volksgemeinschaft overcoming class antagonisms.
I. Weltenwende (Turn of the Age)
History is a piece of nature; the path of nature is never straight. Race and blood, not political arrangement, are the deep currents beneath events. God makes world history through the nature and blood He gives to men and peoples.
II. Unsere Zeit und ihre Krankheit (Our Time and its Sickness)
The present age is diseased; the roots of the German people’s health lie in its own inherited being. The task of the time is to learn the soil and life-sap from which the people draws its strength.
III. Der Rassegedanke (The Racial Idea)
The racial idea as the governing principle of German renewal. (Heading misread by OCR; chapter content identified by position.)
IV. Vom Ursprung der Menschheit (On the Origin of Mankind)
Draws on the researches of Hermann Wirth to extend the history of mankind some fifteen to twenty thousand years back, and reads the Bible — including the figure of Jesus — in the light of Nordic racial prehistory.
V. Das Schöpfertum des nordischen Menschen (The Creativity of the Nordic Man)
Creative spirit as a chief psychic mark of the Nordic man; the creative capacity of the race as the source of German culture.
VI. Das arteigene Denken (Race-Specific Thought)
Thought is race-bound; the German must think out of his own inherited being rather than alien categories.
VII. Der seelische Kraftstrom in der deutschen Geschichte (The Psychic Current in German History)
The hidden spiritual current that carried German history — from the struggles of the Reformation (Luther, Münzer) to the call to become a people. (Chapter numeral misread by OCR.)
VIII. Der Liberalismus (Liberalism)
The central polemic: liberalism as an alien, artfremd way of viewing life, an instrument of Jewish-masonic forces behind the French Revolution; the “freedom, equality, fraternity” of the Revolution as deception; the organic people as against the dismembering, individualist liberalism.
IX. (On the arts under liberalism)
The dissolving effect of liberalism on art, the university and culture; the loss of the people’s rootedness in its homeland; against “world literature” as against great creative individual spirits. (Heading misread; content recovered.)
X. Das Wirtschaftsleben (Economic Life)
The economy must be restored to its bond with the people; against liberal economics, world economy and the argument for autarky in a seventy-million nation; the economy exists for life, not life for the economy.
XI. Die Familie (The Family)
The family as the innermost cell of a people’s life; the state’s task in strengthening it; the man’s duty as father and example in the circle of wife and children.
XII. Die Kirche (The Church)
The churches and the racial renewal: the brown fighters for Hitler’s German renewal are forbidden to enter into disputes of belief; the Catholic church knows no democracy; Luther’s work not yet complete; the need for the church to grasp the blood-bound, God-given order of the people.
XIII. (Art)
Architecture, poetry, music and the other arts in the service of the people; the artist’s great responsibility; art must find again the soil from which it springs. (Heading misread; content recovered.)
XIV. Die Erziehung (Education)
The renewal of life is above all a work of education of the German people; the reconciliation of age and youth; the excesses of revolutionary movements pass like a pendulum; God, not man, makes world history — to be German is to be a whole man, and the fight for German Lebensrecht is a piece of religion.

sources/grossdeutschland-1938-volz.title: Großdeutschland 1938 — Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Band 6 Teil 1 (2nd ed., 1940)
sources/grossdeutschland-1938-volz.content:
Großdeutschland 1938
Hans Volz (ed.) — Großdeutschland 1938 (Greater Germany 1938), Band 6 / Teil 1 of Dokumente der deutschen Politik (Documents of German Politics), founded by the Hochschule für Politik (Academy for Politics) and continued by the Deutsches Auslandswissenschaftliches Institut (German Institute for Foreign Affairs), edited by Prof. Dr. F. A. Six. Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin, 2nd edition 1940 (first edition 1939). An official Nazi compilation of 85 German state documents of the year 1938 — laws, decrees, speeches, notes and protocols — recording the most decisive year of the Third Reich: the Blomberg–Fritsch crisis and the reconstruction of the Wehrmacht command, the annexation of Austria, the Sudeten crisis and the Munich Agreement, and the reordering of the enlarged state.

































EditorDr. Hans Volz (1904–1978), head of the library of the Hochschule für Politik, Berlin; series continued under Prof. Dr. F. A. Six, director of the Deutsches Auslandswissenschaftliches InstitutSeriesDokumente der deutschen Politik, Band 6 (following Band 5, Von der Großmacht zur Weltmacht 1937, also in this wiki; the earlier volumes Band 1, Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933, and Band 2, Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934, are likewise held); Band 6 is issued in two parts, of which this scan is Teil 1Edition2. Auflage 1940 (first edition 1939), Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin; copyright 1940, printed in Germany by Clemens Landgraf Nachf. W. Stolle, Dresden-Freital; the University of Florida Libraries copy (OCLC 6853113)Structure85 numbered documents in three main parts, with a Zeittafel und Chronologie (chronological table), Personenregister and Sachregister (name and subject indexes); 18,884 lines of extracted textPeriod1938: documents dated January–December 1938, covering the sixth year of the National Socialist regime and the territorial expansion that made the Third Reich “Greater Germany”NoteThe filename of the source file reads “Belarus, 1940” — this is erroneous archive metadata; the title page confirms Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin, 2. Auflage 1940. A companion to the other Dokumente der deutschen Politik volumes in this wiki — the Friedrichs-compiled Bände 1, 2, 3 and 4 (1933, 1934, 1935 and 1936) and Volz’s Band 5 for 1937 — reproducing the original German text of laws, decrees and official communications verbatim
Contents. The volume documents the decisive year 1938 of the Third Reich in three parts. Part A (documents 1–20) records the National Socialist state and movement: the creation of the Secret Cabinet Council and the dismissal of Neurath and appointment of Ribbentrop as Foreign Minister (4 February 1938) at the height of the Blomberg–Fritsch crisis; Hitler’s Reichstag speech of 20 February 1938; the decree on a Reich Chancellery office for the Sudeten question; Goebbels’ speech “Democracy and Bolshevism” at the Nuremberg party congress (10 September 1938); Hitler’s speeches at Saarbrücken, Weimar and the Munich Bürgerbräukeller (October–November 1938); and the decree instituting the Cross of Honour of the German Mother (16 December 1938). Part B records foreign policy: Germany’s relations with Italy, Hungary, Japan and Manchukuo. Part C records the establishment of Greater Germany — the Anschluss of Austria (the German march into Austria of 12 March 1938, the law of reunion of 13 March 1938, the plebiscite of 10 April 1938) and the annexation of the Sudetenland (the Munich Agreement of 29 September 1938 and the law on the reunion of the Sudeten territories of 21 November 1938), closing with a reprinted Czech account of the Munich cession.
Character of the source. An official documentary publication of the National Socialist state, reproducing the original texts of German laws, decrees, speeches, notes and protocols of the year 1938 in the German original, published in Berlin by the party-supporting Junker und Dünnhaupt house under the auspices of the Deutsches Auslandswissenschaftliches Institut (directed by F. A. Six, an SS-Brigadeführer). It is a primary source in the strictest sense — the laws themselves (the law of reunion with Austria, the law on the reunification of the Sudeten territories), the verbatim official communications of the Reich government, and the speeches of Hitler, Goebbels, Frick and Göring as officially released. Edited from within the regime to document the state’s own account of its expansion, it is at once a record of fact and an instrument of propaganda; it supplies the official internal voice of the German dictatorship in the year of its greatest territorial triumph, standing opposite the exile histories (such as Rosenberg’s History of the German Republic, also in this wiki).
Quality. Good. Extracted from a 432-file paginated text dump (University of Florida scan) by concatenating the numbered page files in order. Text is clean and continuous; laws, decrees, official notes and speech texts are preserved verbatim with footnotes. Section and document headings and dates verified against the printed Inhaltsverzeichnis (table of contents). The scan closes with the library’s date-due card (barcode 31262043259190), confirming the volume ends at the Sudetenland documents.
Raw text: wiki/raw/grossdeutschland-1938-volz.txt.

A. Der nationalsozialistische Staat und die nationalsozialistische Bewegung (The National Socialist State and the National Socialist Movement)
Dokumente 1–20
The consolidation of the regime in the year of expansion. The decree establishing a Secret Cabinet Council and the Führer’s letter of thanks to Freiherr von Neurath (4 February 1938); the official announcement of Ribbentrop’s appointment as Reich Foreign Minister and the recall of the German ambassadors in London, Rome, Tokyo and Vienna (4 February 1938); Hitler’s Reichstag speech in the Kroll Opera House (20 February 1938); the amnesty for party jurisdiction (27 April 1938); Hitler’s speeches at the Berlin Olympiastadion and Lustgarten on 1 May 1938; the Blood Order award (30 May 1938); Hitler’s proclamation to the “Party Congress of Greater Germany” at Nuremberg (6 September 1938); Goebbels’ speech “Democracy and Bolshevism” (10 September 1938); Hitler’s speech at Saarbrücken (9 October 1938); his speeches at Weimar and to his old comrades in the Munich Bürgerbräukeller (6 and 8 November 1938); and the decree instituting the Cross of Honour of the German Mother (16 December 1938).
B. Deutschlands Außenpolitik (Germany’s Foreign Policy)
I. Deutschlands Verhältnis zu Italien, Ungarn, Japan und Mandschukuo (Germany’s Relations with Italy, Hungary, Japan and Manchukuo)
Germany’s relations with the Axis and its partners as officially documented in 1938: the treaties and communiqués with Italy (the Rome–Berlin Axis), the recognition of Manchukuo, and the strengthening of relations with Hungary and Japan in the year of the Anti-Comintern front.
C. Die Errichtung des Großdeutschen Reiches (The Establishment of Greater Germany)
I. Der Anschluß Österreichs (The Anschluss of Austria)
The German annexation of Austria as officially documented: the entry of German troops on 12 March 1938; the law of 13 March 1938 on the reunion of Austria with the German Reich; the Reich governor arrangements; the ordinance introducing the Nuremberg race laws into Austria (20 May 1938); the plebiscite of 10 April 1938 and its result; the administrative incorporation of the “Ostmark” into the Reich.
II. Der Anschluß des Sudetengebietes (The Annexation of the Sudetenland)
The Sudeten crisis and its resolution as officially documented: the German-Czechoslovak declaration on the protection of the mutual Volksgruppen (20 November 1938); the final delimitation of the German-Czechoslovak frontier (21 November 1938); the law on the reunion of the Sudeten German territories with the German Reich (21 November 1938); Hitler’s speech at the Sudeten supplementary elections in Reichenberg (2 December 1938) and their result (4 December 1938); the ordinances introducing Reich Labour Service and the Nuremberg race laws into the Sudeten territories (6 and 27 December 1938). The volume closes with the reprinted text of the Munich Agreement of 29 September 1938 and a Czech account of the cession of the Sudetenland.
Zeittafel und Chronologie (Chronological Table), Registers
The volume closes with a Zeittafel und Chronologie of the reproduced documents month by month, together with Personen- and Sachregister (name and subject indexes) and maps drawn by Alois Moser (pp. 224 and 368) of the territorial changes of 1938.

sources/halevy-l-ere-des-tyrannies-1938.title: Élie Halévy — L'ère des tyrannies (1938)
sources/halevy-l-ere-des-tyrannies-1938.content:
L’ère des tyrannies : études sur le socialisme et la guerre
Élie Halévy — L’ère des tyrannies: études sur le socialisme et la guerre (The Era of Tyrannies: Studies on Socialism and War). Librairie Gallimard, Paris, 1938, with a preface by Célestin Bouglé. A posthumous collection of essays and lectures by the historian of English liberalism, brought together after his sudden death in 1937, on the relation between socialism, war and the rise of dictatorial government.





























AuthorÉlie Halévy (1870–1937) — French historian and philosopher, professor at the École Libre des Sciences Politiques, famed for the six-volume Histoire du peuple anglais au XIXe siècle and La Formation du radicalisme philosophique; a liberal who spent his life analysing the growth of the state and the evolution of socialism in England and EuropeEdition1938, Librairie Gallimard, Paris (copyright Gallimard 1938); printed by Imprimerie Chantenay, Paris, 21 June 1938; 65 numbered copies on alfa paper + 10 hors commerce; 257 printed pages. The text is taken from the Gallica scan of the Bibliothèque nationale de FranceStructurePreface (Bouglé) + 9 essays in chronological-thematic sequence; 11,450 lines / ~744,000 characters of extracted textPeriodThe history of socialism, the state and war from the early nineteenth century (Sismondi, Saint-Simon) through the crisis of 1914–1918, the problem of workers’ control, and the rise of the totalitarian dictatorships (Fascism, Nazism) as analysed up to Halévy’s death in 1937NoteA philosophical-historical essay collection, not a narrative chronicle — Halévy’s object is to trace how socialism, which began as the enemy of the state, ended in alliance with a strengthened and dictatorial state, and how war and revolution together brought on “the era of tyrannies.” For this wiki it supplies the French liberal-democratic analysis of the very forces the Russian, German and Italian sources present from the revolutionary, National Socialist and Fascist sides — the diagnosis of the totalitarian state from within the democratic tradition, on the eve of the Second World War
Contents. A series of essays on the evolution of socialist doctrine and the state, from the industrial-crisis economics of Sismondi, through the Saint-Simonian school, to the great question of the twentieth century. “Sismondi” treats the Genevan economist’s critique of industrial optimism and his anticipation of the socialist analysis of crises. “La doctrine économique saint-simonienne” analyses the economic doctrine of Saint-Simon himself and then of his disciples, closing with a conclusion on their social system. “La politique de paix sociale en Angleterre” surveys the English movement of social peace and state intervention. “Le problème du contrôle ouvrier” examines the debate over workers’ control of industry, chiefly in England. “État présent de la question sociale en Angleterre” gives a present-state analysis of the English social question. “Une interprétation de la crise mondiale de 1914-1918” offers Halévy’s famous interpretation of the world crisis — towards revolution, towards war, and the mutual reinforcement of war and revolution. “Le socialisme et le problème du parlementarisme démocratique” is the 1934 lecture to the Société française de Philosophie on socialism and democratic parliamentarism. The closing essay, “L’ère des tyrannies,” the celebrated piece of 1936, argues that after the French and English revolutions the era of the new “tyrannies” — Italian Fascism, German National Socialism and Russian Bolshevism — is that of the “organised” (and in Russia the totalitarian) state.
Character of the source. A contemporary liberal diagnosis of the totalitarian danger, written across the two decades of 1914–1937. Halévy was a liberal (in the English sense) who had made his name studying the growth of the state and the history of English liberalism and socialism. The collection shows him treating socialism’s movement from hostility to the state to the use of the state, and warning that the post-1914 world, in which war and revolution had combined, had produced a new kind of organised and totalitarian tyranny that recalled the old tyrannies of the ancient world and the French Revolution. The title essay’s thesis — that Fascism and National Socialism are not reactions to the French Revolution but continuations of the “era of revolutions,” transformed by the total war and total revolution of 1914–1918 into the era of totalitarian states — makes it a key text of interwar democratic political thought.
Quality. Good. Extracted from a 265-page PDF scan (Gallica / Bibliothèque nationale de France) with a clean embedded text layer via pdftotext -layout; continuous prose throughout. French text clean and readable; the running page headers (PRÉFACE, SISMONDI, LA POLITIQUE DE PAIX SOCIALE…, LE PROBLÈME DU CONTRÔLE OUVRIER, etc.) are carried inline in the body and were identified as such; a few OCR slips and typographical artefacts noted (e.g. “socialis?ne” for “socialisme”, “Va doctrine” for “La doctrine”). The complete Table des Matières was recovered from the end-of-text pages and cross-checked against the body section headings.
