Préface (Preface) — Célestin Bouglé
Bouglé’s preface, dated from the Société française de Philosophie, explains the genesis of the volume after Halévy’s sudden death in August 1937. His friends sought to save the unfinished part of his work — the great Histoire du Peuple Anglais had not been brought from 1848 up to 1895. Alongside that teaching at the École Libre des Sciences Politiques ran a separate course on socialism and the state, and from these studies the Société française de Philosophie had drawn the essays and lectures here collected. Bouglé recounts that at a session of the Société in the autumn of 1936, Halévy had presented a paper — “L’ère des tyrannies” — and that, in the discussion, objections had been raised: there is socialism and socialism, it was said, and against Saint-Simon stood Fourier and Proudhon, and the democracies had not yet said their last word. The objections were not resolved before Halévy’s death; in offering the texts to public discussion the editors fulfil “un pieux devoir envers la mémoire de l’ami qui nous a été enlevé” (a pious duty towards the memory of the friend who has been taken from us).
Sismondi — Critique de l’optimisme industrialiste (Sismondi: Critique of Industrialist Optimism)
A study of Jean-Charles-Léonard Simonde de Sismondi (1773–1842), the Genevan economist whom Halévy presents as “le premier annonciateur des crises” (the first announcer of crises) — the earliest critic of the optimist faith that industry and free competition would spontaneously bring general prosperity. Halévy traces Sismondi’s life and formation: born in Geneva, the old holy city of Calvin; his family exiled and ruined, the Simonde fleeing to Florence; his education and his turn to economics against Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations. Sismondi’s Nouveaux principes d’économie politique (1819) argued that the indefinite expansion of production, without regard to consumption, would produce periodical crises and the distress of the working class, and that the remedy lay not in letting the market alone but in the deliberate action of the legislator. Halévy shows how Sismondi, who “se sent français” (feels French) despite Geneva, came to stand for a middle path between the political economy of the optimists and the nascent socialism, anticipating themes later developed by the socialist school while himself remaining a cautious reformer and friend of liberty. The essay closes with Sismondi’s death and the arrival of “de Cologne à Paris” of the manuscripts and papers that mark the transition to the socialist question proper.
La doctrine économique saint-simonienne (The Saint-Simonian Economic Doctrine)
1. — La doctrine économique de Saint-Simon (The Economic Doctrine of Saint-Simon)
The economic doctrine of Saint-Simon himself, considered as the founder of the school — his plan for the reorganization of society on the basis of industry and the “capacities,” and his conception of a new order in which the producers, the industrialists and the savants would replace the old feudal and military ruling classes.
2. — La doctrine économique des saint-simoniens (The Economic Doctrine of the Saint-Simonians)
The economic doctrine of Saint-Simon’s disciples — the school that carried his ideas into a systematic social and economic programme, the cult of industry and association, and the early socialist conceptions of property and of the state.
Conclusion
The concluding synthesis of the Saint-Simonian social and economic system — its place in the history of socialism, and its anticipations of later doctrines.
La politique de paix sociale en Angleterre (The Policy of Social Peace in England)
An essay on the English policy of “social peace” — the tradition, running through the nineteenth century, by which the English state and the English governing classes sought to reconcile the classes and to pre-empt revolutionary discontent through legislation and social reform, in contrast to the continental pattern of revolution. Halévy draws on his mastery of English history to show how England, from the factory legislation of the 1830s and 1840s through the later social reforms, sought the peaceful, gradual improvement of the condition of the working class.
Le problème du contrôle ouvrier (The Problem of Workers’ Control)
On the problem of workers’ control of industry. Halévy notes that the question “n’a pris d’importance dans les” [the problem only took on importance in the] — the text opens mid-sentence at the essay head — the debate over whether the workers should control the factories and industries in which they work, a question that gained urgency with the syndicalist and Guild-Socialist movements in England and the postwar revolutionary ferment on the continent. Halévy analyses the arguments for and against industrial democracy, and the relation of the control question to the larger socialist programme of the conquest of the state.
État présent de la question sociale en Angleterre (The Present State of the Social Question in England)
A “present-state” survey of the English social question as it stood in the interwar years — the condition of the English working class, the state of labour legislation and social policy, the decline of the old industries and the problem of unemployment, and the evolution of English socialism and trade unionism since the war.
Une interprétation de la crise mondiale de 1914-1918 (An Interpretation of the World Crisis of 1914–1918)
1. — Vers la révolution (Towards Revolution)
Halévy’s famous interpretation begins with the revolutionary dynamic of the war years — how the strain of the world war drove the European states, and above all Russia, towards revolution.
2. — Vers la guerre (Towards War)
The complementary movement towards war — how the crisis of the pre-war decades and the war itself produced the conditions in which the totalitarian movements and states could arise.
3. — Guerre et révolution (War and Revolution)
The synthesis of the essay — the mutual reinforcement of war and revolution in 1914–1918, and Halévy’s argument that the modern crisis is not a simple reaction against the French Revolution but a new and distinct phenomenon born of the combination of total war and revolution. This is the conceptual core of the collection, the thesis that underlies the closing study of the tyrannies.
Le socialisme et le problème du parlementarisme démocratique (Socialism and the Problem of Democratic Parliamentarism)
The lecture delivered to the Société française de Philosophie on socialism and the problem of democratic parliamentarism. Halévy examines the tension within socialism between its democratic, parliamentary and libertarian heritage and its revolutionary and authoritarian impulses — and how the socialist movement, in the age of the war and the dictatorships, came to face the question whether parliamentary democracy and socialism could be reconciled, or whether the one must yield to the other.
L’ère des tyrannies (The Era of Tyrannies)
The celebrated closing essay, the text of Halévy’s 1936 lecture to the Société française de Philosophie, which gives the volume its title. Halévy begins by dating the new era: “L’ère des tyrannies date du mois d’août 1914” (the era of tyrannies dates from the month of August 1914) — in other words, from the outbreak of the First World War, which by its strain and its total character set in motion the forces of total war and total revolution. He argues that the modern tyrannies — Italian Fascism, German National Socialism and, in its own fashion, Russian Bolshevism — are not simple reactions against the French Revolution and its liberal inheritance, but continuations and transformations of the revolutionary era under the new conditions of 1914–1918: the “organised” state (and in Russia the totalitarian state) mobilises the whole nation for war and revolution alike. The essay thus gives the collection its thesis — that the twentieth century’s dictatorships represent a new kind of state power, distinct both from the old absolutisms and from the liberal order of the nineteenth century, born of the convergence of war and revolution.
Table des matières (Table of Contents)
The end-of-text table of contents lists the essays and their printed page numbers: Préface 7; Sismondi 15; La doctrine économique saint-simonienne 30 (1. La doctrine économique de Saint-Simon 30, 2. La doctrine économique des saint-simoniens 60, Conclusion 90); La politique de paix sociale en Angleterre 95; Le problème du contrôle ouvrier 134; État présent de la question sociale en Angleterre 152; Une interprétation de la crise mondiale de 1914-1918 171 (1. Vers la révolution 171, 2. Vers la guerre 181, 3. Guerre et révolution 189); Le socialisme et le problème du parlementarisme démocratique 200; L’ère des tyrannies 213. Colophon: “Imp. CHANTENAY, 15, Rue de l’Abbé-Grégoire, PARIS · 21-6-38.”

sources/heiden-adolf-hitler-1936.title: Konrad Heiden — Adolf Hitler: Das Zeitalter der Verantwortungslosigkeit. Eine Biographie (1936)
sources/heiden-adolf-hitler-1936.content:
Adolf Hitler: Das Zeitalter der Verantwortungslosigkeit. Eine Biographie
Konrad Heiden — Adolf Hitler: Das Zeitalter der Verantwortungslosigkeit. Eine Biographie (Adolf Hitler: The Age of Irresponsibility. A Biography). Europa-Verlag, Zürich, 1936. The first full-length biography of Hitler, written in exile by the German-Jewish journalist and critic of National Socialism, from Hitler’s birth and youth in Austria to the Night of the Long Knives of 30 June 1934.





























AuthorKonrad Heiden (1901–1966) — German-Jewish journalist and political writer; as a reporter on the Bavarian political scene he attended National Socialist meetings from 1922 and followed the movement from within; author of the earlier Geschichte des Nationalsozialismus (1932) and Geburt des Dritten Reiches (1934); emigrated in 1933 and wrote this biography from SwitzerlandEdition1936, Europa-Verlag G. m. b. H., Zürich; printed in Switzerland (Druckerei-Genossenschaft Aarau); preface dated Zürich, 20 August 1935; a volume of the publisher’s exile list, issued in the third year of the regime it chroniclesStructurePreface + 20 chapters in 3 parts; 19,465 lines / ~968,000 characters of extracted textPeriod1889–1934: from Hitler’s birth at Braunau am Inn and his youth in Linz and Vienna, through the First World War, the founding of the NSDAP and the Beer Hall Putsch, the years of reorganisation and electoral advance, to the seizure of power in 1933 and the purge of 30 June 1934NoteThe book’s subtitle, “Das Zeitalter der Verantwortungslosigkeit” (the age of irresponsibility), supplies its thesis: that Hitler’s rise was the product of an epoch in which the German middle classes abandoned responsibility, and that the biography is at once a portrait of the man and an explanation of “this present-day Germany,” in Heiden’s words from the preface; based on fifteen years of study, observation from close range, and the use of confidential informants some of whom remained active near Hitler
Contents. A critical biography of Hitler, from his birth and formative years to the consolidation of the dictatorship. The three parts trace his Austrian childhood and the “lost years” in Vienna and Munich, his war service and the discovery of his political vocation; the founding and early growth of the National Socialist movement, its propaganda and organisation, the Beer Hall Putsch of 1923, the imprisonment and writing of Mein Kampf, and the seven years of reconstruction and electoral advance after 1925; and finally the Hitler of power — his personality and private life, his entourage, the Reichstag fire, and the massacre of 30 June 1934, with which the book closes. Heiden presents Hitler less as a master of events than as the creation of his age, the “great inferior one” who rose because the responsible classes failed.
Character of the source. The principal non-Nazi biographical portrait of Hitler written during the Third Reich, by a contemporary who had observed the movement from inside since 1922. Heiden’s standpoint is that of the independent democratic opponent of National Socialism: he neither heroises nor demonises, describing Hitler as “neither a superman nor a bogeyman, but a very interesting contemporary and, numerically considered, the greatest mass-agitator in world history.” Written in exile and published in Switzerland, it draws on observation from close range and on confidential informants, several of whom remained in the Führer’s entourage. For this wiki it supplies the German case from the critical-democratic side — the counterpart to the regime’s own documentary compilations (the Dokumente der deutschen Politik volumes) and to the völkisch racial tract of Geisow, all of which treat the same rise from within the National Socialist camp.
Quality. Good. Re-OCR’d from a 454-page PDF scan via Tesseract at 300 dpi (deu model; the German Antiqua/Fraktur text rendered cleanly), since the PDF’s embedded Scribe text layer was unusable; continuous prose throughout. Chapter headings, running titles and page numbers verified against the book’s own table of contents. A few hyphenation artefacts and scattered OCR misreads of headings noted; the opening and closing scan pages (endpapers) were stripped.
Raw text: wiki/raw/heiden-adolf-hitler-1936.txt.

Vorwort (Preface)
Dated Zürich, 20 August 1935. States the book’s genesis in the need “to say what is,” impossible in Germany where the interests of the state stand against objective research; describes the basis of the work in fifteen years of study, observation from close range, and the use of all accessible sources open and confidential, including informants still active near Hitler; notes that objectivity is not freedom from standpoint — the hero is neither a superman nor a bogeyman but “a very interesting contemporary and, numerically considered, the greatest mass-agitator of world history”; closes with the epigraph from Goethe’s Dichtung und Wahrheit on the demonic.
Erster Teil (First Part)
1. Kapitel: Heimat und Herkunft (Home and Origins)
Hitler’s Austrian birth and childhood. The “Schicklgruber-Hitler” family, the failed examination and the early failure in Linz; the years in Vienna — the encounter with the working class, the Jews, and Karl Lueger the anti-Semitic mayor of Vienna as the model; the departure from Vienna for Munich.
2. Kapitel: Der Krieg als Erlöser (The War as Redeemer)
The First World War as Hitler’s deliverance from an aimless life: his gratitude for the war, the Iron Cross, the unrecognised leader, the front as home; Heiden’s account of “Hitler’s world-historical error” and the failure of Pasewalk (the alleged discovery of his political mission in the field hospital).
Zweiter Teil (Second Part)
3. Kapitel: Umkehr in der Sackgasse (The Turning in the Cul-de-sac)
The failed revolutionary and the “strike of the individual” in postwar Munich: a useless talent, the stairway into nothingness, the devaluation of the parties, illusions against interests, the failure of the revolution of 1918–19.
4. Kapitel: Der Aufbruch (The Departure)
The beginnings of the movement: Dietrich Eckart in search of a leader, the “iron fist” of Röhm, and the early slogan of “breaking the bondage of interest” (Brechung der Zinsknechtschaft).
5. Kapitel: Der Klassenkampf der Intellektuellen (The Class Struggle of the Intellectuals)
Hitler’s obscure vocation and the “illusion-bourgeois”; “Jewish Marxism”; the development of anti-Semitism from a social game into a mass madness; the Pan-Germans and the Fatherland Party; “the privilege of race”; member No. 7, Karl Harrer, Dietrich Eckart’s advice, and the program assembly.
6. Kapitel: Propaganda und Organisation (Propaganda and Organisation)
The instruments of the movement’s growth: wit, logic and insolence; the refuted theories; the symbols; the listener as collaborator; the art of oratory; “Hitler always says the same thing…”; the Führerprinzip (leadership principle).
7. Kapitel: Der Weg in die Gesellschaft (The Way into Society)
How the movement entered respectable society: the question of Hitler’s livelihood, “in the circle of beautiful women,” the struggle for the salons, at tea and biscuits — the courtship of the upper middle classes.
8. Kapitel: Stufen zur Macht (Steps to Power)
The Bavarian fronde and the Kapp Putsch; the tireless organiser; the emergence of “the Führer”; the beginnings of the SA, terror, the Black Reichswehr; word of honour and the consecration of flags; the break with the Reichswehr.
9. Kapitel: Der Putsch (The Putsch)
The Beer Hall Putsch of November 1923: the General State Commissioner von Kahr against Berlin, Lossow’s 51 percent, Hitler’s panic at the closing door; the shot in the Bürgerbräukeller, the march to the Feldherrnhalle, the collapse, Hitler’s flight — and the question “was Hitler permitted to flee?“
10. Kapitel: Die Rückkehr zum Herrn Präsidenten (The Return to the Lord President)
The aftermath of the putsch: an attempted suicide, the judicial comedy of the trial, Hitler and Dimitroff, the separation from Ludendorff, Gürtner’s rescue of Hitler, behind comfortable walls in Landsberg; the dissolution of the movement; the writing of Mein Kampf; the first brown shirt, the release, “peace with Rome,” the whip; the refounding of the party, the first break with Röhm, and the appearance of Hindenburg.
11. Kapitel: Sieben Jahre auf dem Zauberberg (Seven Years on the Magic Mountain)
The years of reconstruction 1925–1932, named for Thomas Mann’s novel: the writer in Haus Wachenfeld, the Straßer–Goebbels rivalry, riots and trials, Goebbels’ desertion of Straßer, the blood flag and the advertisements, the homosexuals, Heines’ expulsion, the terror of the offices, the lawsuit over Prince Rupprecht, idyll and intrigue, and how the bourgeoisie capitulated.
12. Kapitel: Der große Minderwertige (The Great Inferior One)
Heiden’s analysis of Hitler’s character and social base: from the life of a good-for-nothing; collapsing classes, the desecration of property, the reactionary revolution, privilege and irresponsibility, the defection of all classes; “Hitler’s ripened field.”
13. Kapitel: Die diplomatische Periode (The Diplomatic Period)
The movement’s courtship of power and money: Göring’s return, Otto Dietrich’s mission, foreign money, heavy industry, the incapable reaction, “the magnet before the dungheap,” the break with Otto Strasser, Pfeffer’s fall, the “military-political association,” courting the Reichswehr, and the 107 parliamentary seats.
14. Kapitel: Der Einbruch in den Staat (The Break-in into the State)
The assault on the republic: Röhm’s return, “the Bohemian corporal,” the “System!,” disunited opponents, the sham struggle against Hindenburg, the reserve army of the Junkers, and how Röhm overthrew Brüning.
15. Kapitel: Der Wettlauf mit der Katastrophe (The Race with the Catastrophe)
The final crisis of the republic: the decay of Social Democracy, the mistakes of the Communists, Severing yielding to force, the blow with the walking-stick, the descent; in Schleicher’s pincers, Gregor Strasser’s last struggle, a weary proletariat, a weary capitalism, the Cologne alliance, mines and countermines, Schleicher’s fall — “at the goal,” the transfer of power to Hitler in January 1933.
Dritter Teil (Third Part)
16. Kapitel: Die beiden Hitler (The Two Hitlers)
The Hitler of power: egoist or altruist, the “wonderful double nature,” the mask, “le style c’est l’homme,” his relation to the intellect, inclinations and habits, the road upward, the inner voice.
17. Kapitel: Die Frauen (The Women)
Hitler and women: an opaque eroticism, a puritanical man, a failed love, “Alf and Geli” (the suicide of Geli Raubal), “Adolf Hitler’s secret.”
18. Kapitel: Die Begleitfiguren (The Companion Figures)
The entourage: the vanished founders, two accomplices, the confessor, the ornament of the movement, the powerless cleverness, a Caesar without ambition, Cheka and anti-Cheka, a disappointment, subservient youth, Julius Streicher “the true Hitler,” the Pettenkofer system.
19. Kapitel: Am schwankenden Steuer (At the Shaky Helm)
The first months of power: the burning of the Reichstag, the atrocities, the licence to kill, “the streets of Adolf Hitler.”
20. Kapitel: Der 30. Juni (The 30th of June)
The Night of the Long Knives: an unplanned dictatorship, Röhm’s failed advances, the Marburg speech, Schleicher against “the criminals,” Röhm’s encirclement, the corporal and the generals, on a knife’s edge, Hitler contradicting himself; with armoured cars and pistol, shooting at homosexuals; legend and reality, at the wall, Göring and the prince, the bloodbath, “end with terror.” The book closes with the account of Dr. Glaser of Munich, shot by three SS men on the evening of 30 June, and the urn of ashes handed to his brother — “the ashes of the unknown German who fell victim to the highest responsibility assumed on 30 June.”

sources/historia-del-reinado-de-alfonso-.title: Melchor Fernández Almagro — Historia del reinado de Alfonso XIII (4th ed., 1977)
sources/historia-del-reinado-de-alfonso-.content:
Melchor Fernández Almagro — Historia del reinado de Alfonso XIII
Full bibliographic citation — Melchor Fernández Almagro (1893–1966). Historia del reinado de Alfonso XIII. — 4th edition. Montaner y Simón, S. A., Barcelona, 1977. © Montaner y Simón, S. A.; ISBN 84-274-379-8; Depósito legal B. 19.049-1977 (Gráficas Román, S. A.). The edition is the mature synthesis of a historian-critic of Granada, a member of the Real Academia de la Historia, whose chronicle of the political history of contemporary Spain Azorín praised as “minucioso, exacto y sugestivo”.
Fernández Almagro’s Historia del reinado de Alfonso XIII is a strictly political and external history of Spain from the accession of Alfonso XIII (17 May 1902) to the proclamation of the Republic (14 April 1931). In his Nota preliminar the author declares the work’s method and scope: “Ha aspirado a hacer historia. Esto es: a contar las cosas como han sido” — to tell things as they were, “ni el vejamen ni la apología de nada ni de nadie” (neither the vilification nor the apology of anything or anyone). He insists that the difficulty of writing contemporary history lies not in any lack of perspective but in the poverty of Spanish sources — the scarcity of memoirs, the destruction of family papers, the State’s own failure to preserve archives or publish documents — and affirms that perspective can be obtained “a despecho de la cronología, mediante un esfuerzo moral”. He identifies the work as “política y externa”, political and external, giving the general march of the State as the skeleton to which internal history (culture, economy, customs) must be attached, and observes that between 1902 and 1931 the society of Spain was so thoroughly renewed that “la sociedad y el Estado… siguieron caminos distintos” — two Spains joined only by an ascending line of wealth and enlightenment. The body is a continuous narrative chronicle, built as a sequence of dated sections and governments rather than thematic chapters, divided into six Parts.
The text is 25,299 lines, extracted directly from the embedded text layer of the 508-page PDF (a Boston Public Library copy, call no. 3 9999 00803 745 7), set in Roman type; the OCR text is clean apart from isolated slips (e.g. “XIH” for XIII, “paicia-Udad” for parcialidad), and no re-OCR was required.
Content Summary
Front matter. Decorated title leaf (the print title is only partly legible in the scan); imprint leaf identifying the fourth edition, © Montaner y Simón, S. A., ISBN and Depósito legal; then the Nota preliminar (pp. 5–11), the author’s statement of method and a synthesis of the whole reign as five successive periods: the liquidation of the regency (1902–1906), the renewal intents of Maura and Canalejas (to 1912), the unstable equilibrium of the war years (to 1917), the revolutionary attempts (1917–1923), and the Dictatorship (1923–1930), closing in the monarchy’s capitulation (1930–1931).
Part I — Liquidación de la Regencia (1902–1906)
1. Sagasta (1902). “17 de mayo de 1902. — Sagasta, presidente. — Primer Consejo de ministros.” The king’s first ministry and its enmities — palatines, enemies of the régime, socialism, Canalejas’s resignation and propaganda — the royal journey, Sagasta and the new problems, the religious associations, public instruction, the crisis and Sagasta’s fall.
2. Silvela (1902–1903). Two governments: Silvela’s — Morocco, the liberals, Unión Republicana, the Salamanca events, the Marina conflict, Villaverde’s resignation, elections, the king and Maura, the twenty-six dead, the opening of the Cortes — then the Villaverde government, Alcalá del Valle, Silvela’s withdrawal, the Bilbao strike, the king and the military, and Villaverde’s fall.
3. Maura (1903–1904). First Maura government — the budget, the press, the Nozaleda question, the removal of Admiral Beránger, republican propaganda, the moderating power, the Vigo meeting of William II and Alfonso XIII, the Franco-English accord and the Franco-Spanish treaty, the agreement with Rome, the king in Barcelona, Catalan politics, the attempt on Maura, the royal visit to the Balearics, África and Andalusia, the scandalous crisis and the succession to the Throne.
4. Dos puentes (1904–1905). The interlude governments of Azcárraga and Villaverde — the ministerial declaration, whether toward a coup d’état, official favour, procuring the Cortes, famine in Andalusia, the students and La Cierva, the sinking of the third depot, the king’s journey to France and England, the attempt in Paris, London, Maura and Villaverde, and the rise of the villaverdistas.
5. Cinco gobiernos liberales (1905–1907). Five liberal ministries — Montero Ríos (the Barcelona events, military imposition, royal intervention, his fall), Moret (the king’s military policy, the Algeciras conference, the Law of Jurisdictions, the king’s marriage, the attempt by Morral against the royal couple), López Domínguez (anticlerical policy, the Bishops’ protest, Canalejas’s note, the Law of Associations), the “relámpago” (lightning) government, and Vega de Armijo — the “papelito” crisis and the fall into Maura’s second accession.
Part II — Intentos de Renovación (1907–1912)
1. Gobierno largo de Maura (1907–1909). The long Maura government — a new style, the movement toward the right, terrorism, Solidarios and antisolidarios, the republicans and Salmerón, the Cartagena meeting of Edward VII and Alfonso XIII, the general elections and the liberals’ withdrawal, the Catalan theme, five laws and the Rull affair, the local-administration project, Cambó and the Lliga, the Escuadra law, the anti-terrorism project, the king in Barcelona; then the “año memorable” — Morocco and its antecedents, the occupation of the Restinga and Cabo de Agua, the action of 9 July, the Beni-Bu-Ifrur mines, the call-up of reservists, La Cierva’s attitude, the battle of the Gurugú and the Barranco del Lobo, the “Semana trágica” of Barcelona, the trial and execution of Francisco Ferrer Guardia and the Escola Moderna, the foreign protests and the “mito” Ferrer, Moret against Maura, and the parliamentary crisis.
2. Paréntesis. The Moret government — the republican-socialist conjunción, Maura’s “implacable hostilidad”, the “¡Maura, sí!”, Morocco, and militarism.
3. Canalejas (1910–1912). Canalejas’s presidency — his programme, the new Cortes, republicans and socialists in the Senate, the royal message, Maura, Pablo Iglesias and an attempt, social questions, the Bilbao strike, the religious question, Morocco, the Cullera events and the Kert campaign, the battle of 27 December and the death of El-Mizzian, the Cullera trial, the crisis, the law of the Mancomunidades provinciales, the railway strike, the mobilisation of reservists, and the assassination of Canalejas.
Part III — Equilibrio Inestable (1912–1917)
1. Romanones (1912–1913). Two aspirants to Canalejas’s succession; the interlude of García Prieto, then Romanones president of the Council — the Franco-Spanish treaty on Morocco and its ratification, Maura’s retirement and the conservative party, the republicans applauding the king, liberal concessions, the occupation of Tetuán, Alfonso XIII in Paris, Poincaré in Madrid and Cartagena, the Mancomunidades in the Senate, the total crisis, the adhesion of the reformists to the monarchy, and Dato’s accession to power.
2. Dato (1913–1915). A typical conservative — Maura at Guisando, Sánchez-Guerra in Gobernación, “idóneos” and “mauristas”, the king’s unwillingness to be spoken to sharply, the king and the Army, the king and the left, Morocco, the Mannesmann brothers, Lyautey in Madrid, the Decree of the Mancomunidades and the Mancomunidad of Cataluña, general elections, the Liga de Educación Política and Ortega y Gasset, the Spanish neutrality in the European war, “neutralidades que matan”, the king at the ready, Lerroux as interventionist, the Junta de Iniciativas, the German-maritime-blockade note, the sinking of Spanish ships, Catalan separatism, and the “crisis del susto”.
3. Segundo gobierno romanonés (1915–1917). Romanones’s second ministry — the new ministry, Basque and Catalan nationalisms, general elections and Azcárate’s defeat, the royal message, the railway conflict, a German submarine at Cartagena, French pressures and the sinking of Spanish ships, the pro-German press, diplomatic notes and the blockade declaration, the law of authorisations, a conference on Morocco and the attempt at a general strike, the torpedoing of the San Fulgencio, and the total “crisis verdadera”.
Part IV — Conatos Revolucionarios (1917–1923)
1. García Prieto: las Juntas de Defensa. García Prieto president, ratification of neutrality, the note to Germany, the military movement and its antecedents, the constitution of the Juntas de Defensa, the 1 June exposition, the king, Weyler and the Juntas, the approval of Article 1, a national crisis, the mauristas and the king, revolutionary stimuli, and the beginnings of the Russian revolution.
2. Dato: la Asamblea de parlamentarios y la huelga de agosto (1917). Dato’s second government, approval of the Junta regulation, the revolutionary accord of republicans and socialists, the Asamblea de parlamentarios in Barcelona, the general revolutionary strike — in Madrid, in the provinces, in Barcelona — the Juntas and the revolution, the message to the king, the lanzamiento (overthrow) of Dato, the eight-day crisis, the Asamblea at the Ateneo of Madrid, Cambó in the palace, toward a minimal renovation.
3. Primer gobierno de concentración (1917–1918). García Prieto’s concentration government — ministerial dissonance, municipal elections, the lure of Russia, public order and subsistence, La Cierva and his military policy, general elections, the grant by royal decree of military reforms, another crisis, the civil Juntas, the postal and telegraph strike, plans of military dictatorship, an idea of Romanones, and the national government.
4. Gobierno nacional (1918). A moment of illusion and a minimum programme — the end of the communications strike, reticence against the Army, nationalism in the Cortes, the debate on the August strike, the anti-espionage law and the left, torpedoed ships and Spain’s reclamation, the Germanophile ballast, the confiscation of six German ships, meetings, strikes and the influenza, the new ministry of Abastecimientos, Cambó’s project and Alba’s plans and resignation, the total crisis and the eve of the armistice.
5. Gobiernos y gobiernos: el sindicalismo (1918–1921). A sequence of short ministries — García Prieto again; Romanones (the Catalan question, the parliamentary withdrawal of the catalanistas, the Sindicato Único, the “La Canadiense” strike, strikes throughout Spain, José Moróte’s mediation, Ángel Pestaña and the Noi del Sucre, the Juntas expelling the civil governor and police chief of Barcelona); Maura (the telegraph strike, the dissolution of the Cortes, the consecration of Spain to the Sacred Heart, the left against Maura); Sánchez de Toca (social war, the Federación Patronal, Bravo Portillo, the students of the Superior War School); Allendesalazar (the military revolt in Zaragoza, Milans del Bosch and Salvatierra de Álava, Weyler in Barcelona, the budget); and Dato again (the creation of the Labour ministry, Joffre in Barcelona, the recrudecimiento of the social war, Tafersit and Xauen, Martínez Anido governor of Barcelona, the CNT and the UGT, the “ley de fugas”, the theme of repression in the Congress) — ending with Dato’s assassination and Bugallal as interim president.
6. Annual (1921–1922). The Moroccan catastrophe — the government and Martínez Anido, terrorism in the Congress and in action, the king’s Córdoba speech, the crisis of socialism and the formation of the communist party, the collapse of the Melilla command, Berenguer and Fernández Silvestre, the king and Silvestre, Abd-El-Krim, Monte Abarran, the disaster of Igueriben and the disaster of Annual, the stupefaction of Spain, the defence of Melilla, the “República del Rif”, the fall of the government; then Maura (confidence in Berenguer, the Picasso inquiry, the spirit of the public, the advance, Tizza, the macabre landscapes, Gomara, the informative commissions, Dar-Drius, the Pizarra conference, Unamuno against the king); and Sánchez-Guerra (restoration of constitutional guarantees, terrorism in Barcelona, Tazarut, responsibilities and rewards, the Picasso expediente in the Supreme Council of War and Navy, Berenguer’s prosecution and resignation, the Congress debate, the dissolution of the Juntas, the destitution of Martínez Anido and Arlegui, fascism, the parliamentary commission and the expediente Picasso).
7. Ultimo gobierno constitucional (1922–1923). The liberal Concentration in power — a royal decree of Romanones, general elections, military unease, the rescue of prisoners, the artillerymen, civil responsibilities, terrorism and the assassination of the Noi del Sucre, the transport strike, Alcalá-Zamora’s resignation, Martínez Anido commander-general of Melilla, Primo de Rivera in Madrid, the attitude and thought of the king, the denounced conspiracy, the commission of twenty-one deputies, a government plan for Morocco, the siege of Tifaruin, the sedition in Málaga, the Central Staff memorandum, the king’s consultation with Maura, the date of the pronunciamiento, the Captaincy-General of Cataluña, the king and Alba, Aizpuru and Primo de Rivera, the government’s isolation, Primo de Rivera’s impatience — and Primo de Rivera on the way.
Part V — La Dictadura (1923–1930)
1. Directorio militar (1923–1925). The dictator and the naming of the Military Directory — opinions and attitudes, Primo de Rivera and Catalanism, the first measures of the Dictatorship, Martínez Anido subsecretary of Gobernación, the dictator and the socialists, against the politicians, the journey to Rome and Mussolini and Primo de Rivera, the Tánger Statute, the municipal statute, the exile of the Marqués de Cortina and the sanctions against the Duque de San Pedro de Galatino, the Caoba episode, the confinement of Unamuno and Soriáno, the responsibilities of 1921 and the amnesty, the Unión Patriótica, Morocco and the line of the Lau, the general rising of the cabilas, Lyautey’s declarations and the fear of another Annual, the evacuation, Abd-El-Krim against the Raisuli and against France, the Hispano-French conference of Madrid, Primo de Rivera and Pétain, the landing at Alhucemas, the operations, the hour to leave power, the students and the attempt of Colonel Segundo García, and the substitution of the military Dictatorship by a civil one.
2. Gobierno de hombres civiles (1925–1930). The civil ministry — the new ministers and first measures, the flight of the Plus Ultra, sanctions on La Época, the foundation of Alianza Republicana, the “Sanjuanada”, the extraordinary fines, the 1926 spring campaign in Morocco, the battle of the Loma de los Morabos, the surrender of Abd-El-Krim, the artillery pronunciamiento, Spain in the League of Nations, the plebiscite toward a consultative Assembly, the Prats de Molló intent, the “raid” of Commander Capaz; 1927 — the end of the campaign, the convocation and opening of the National Consultative Assembly, the exile of Sánchez-Guerra; 1928 — the social question, schools, the socialists thinking of the end of the Dictatorship, the debates in the Assembly, the ministerial council at Coruña; 1929 — Sánchez-Guerra in Valencia, the Ciudad Real pronunciamiento and the failure of the movement, the dissolution of the Artillery, the death of Doña María Cristina, the student strike against Article 53 of the University Statute, the Sevillian and Barcelona Expositions, the constitutional draft, the depreciation of the peseta, the enemies of the Dictatorship; and 1930 — the preparation of a pronunciamiento in Cádiz, the result of the consultation to the Army, the abortive pronunciamiento, the end of the Dictatorship, Berenguer the new head of government, and the last official note of Primo de Rivera.
Part VI — Capitulación de la Monarquía (1930–1931)
1. Berenguer. The old parties and the new ministers, toward constitutional normality, the last acts and death of Primo de Rivera, the Unión Monárquica Nacional, Sánchez-Guerra’s speech at the Zarzuela, Alcalá-Zamora’s speech at Valencia, Unamuno in Madrid, Ossorio demanding the king’s abdication and Sánchez Román’s bill of indictment, the military-republican association’s circular, the syndicalists, the communists, the catalanistas and the intellectuals of Madrid, the republicans, the decree on regional flags, the electoral-census renewal, Cambó and Alba and the king, the peseta, the Pact of San Sebastián, propaganda, counter-propaganda and strikes, the impatience of the CNT, the abortive movement, the general strike in Madrid, the military rebellion at Jaca, Captain Galán and Anzánigo–Ayerbe–Cillas, the execution of Galán and García Hernández, the manifesto of the provisional government of the projected Spanish Republic, the Cuatro Vientos airfield, renewed conspiracy and the Agrupación al Servicio de la República, the parties before the electoral convocation, general abstention, and the total crisis.
2. La Monarquía, sitiada. “La realidad puede más que la realeza” — consultations, Sánchez-Guerra called to power, the meeting at the ministry of War, the Aznar government and its ministerial declaration, the council of war at Jaca and at Madrid, the revolutionary committee freed, the opening of a credit at the Morgan Bank, the Madrid faculty-of-Medicine events, the amnesty, the Centro Constitucional, before the municipal elections, the municipal elections of 12 April, the triumph of the republican-socialist coalition, the eviction of the monarchy, the interview of Romanones and Alcalá-Zamora, the proclamation of the Republic, the last Council of Ministers, the provisional government of the Republic at the ministry of Gobernación, and the departure of Don Alfonso.
The volume closes with the Índice (table of contents, pp. 480–488) and the 1977 jacket text on the character, the epoch and the author.
Key Data Points













































AttributeDetailAuthorMelchor Fernández Almagro (1893–1966), historian, essayist and critic of GranadaTitleHistoria del reinado de Alfonso XIIIPublished4th ed., Montaner y Simón, Barcelona, 1977 (© Montaner y Simón; ISBN 84-274-379-8)Source libraryBoston Public Library (3 9999 00803 745 7)Raw filewiki/raw/historia-del-reinado-de-alfonso-xiii-fernandez-almagro-1977.txtLines25,299Sections6 Parts, 22 numbered sections; Nota preliminar; Índice; jacket textScopePolitical history of Spain 1902–1931, from the accession of Alfonso XIII to the proclamation of the RepublicSignificanceA Spanish conservative-institutional chronicle of the whole reign, the monarchy-centered counterpart to the liberal-republican sources of Madariaga and the revolutionary accounts already in the wiki, extending coverage from the colonial disaster of 1898 through the Moroccan wars, the Juntas, the Dictatorship of Primo de Rivera and the fall of the Crown
Relationship to the Wiki
Fernández Almagro’s reign-history is the closest thing in the wiki to an institutional Spanish history of the years 1902–1931: it is written from the standpoint of a Spanish historian who took the monarchy’s constitutional machinery as its subject, tracing each government, each crisis and each royal intervention from Sagasta to the exit of Don Alfonso. It therefore complements the wiki’s existing Spanish sources — Madariaga’s exile liberal case, Chaves Nogales and Aznar on the Civil War, Azaña on 1934, Hayes on wartime neutrality, Tusell on the Republic and Civil War, and Tusell on the Franco dictatorship that closed the monarchical and republican sequences — by supplying the preceding monarchical era and its long Moroccan and domestic crises, and it connects to the interwar themes already present: the Russian revolution’s echo (the Juntas, the general strike of 1917), the rise of fascism (the Mussolini–Primo de Rivera encounter), and the collapse of the liberal order that the European sources describe from their own national standpoints.

sources/historia-espana-siglo-xx-ii-cris.content:
Javier Tusell — Historia de España en el siglo XX, II. La crisis de los años treinta: República y guerra civil
Full bibliographic citation — Javier Tusell Gómez (1945–2005). Historia de España en el siglo XX, volume II, La crisis de los años treinta: República y guerra civil. — First published 2000. This text from the ePubLibre digital edition (ePUB r1.3, JeSsE, 6 February 2014; UUID e6d70ae1-5e32-42f8-bb91-60437555f4ef; hash 8e15882a1410ffd7a2485eb09611e5c3). The four-volume series covers the Spanish twentieth century; volume II studies the crisis of the decisive thirties, in which the Second Republic and the Civil War marked the lives of Spaniards. It is the Republic-and-Civil-War companion to volume III (La dictadura de Franco), already held in this wiki.
Javier Tusell, catedrático of Contemporary History at the UNED and a leading Spanish political historian of the twentieth century, wrote the volume as a full-scale scholarly synthesis of the Republic and the Civil War — not a memoir or a party history, but a modern secondary survey. It opens on society and economy before politics: the agrarian and urban world, daily life, the impact of the world economic crisis, and the coming of mass democracy. It then traces the democratic experience of the Second Republic from the 1931 elections through the Constitution, the reformist biennium (military, religious, agrarian and social reforms), the «República en una tenaza» of monarchists and anarchists, the conservative biennium of radicals and cedistas, the insurrection of October 1934 and its aftermath, the split and radicalisation of the socialists, Spanish fascism, the Popular Front of 1936, and the “plano inclinado” toward the Civil War, before turning to the war itself — conspiracy, balance of forces, revolution and repression, the church, the column-war, Madrid, internationalisation, the northern campaign, the formation of the two armies, Franco’s political unity, the Popular Front’s internal divisions, Negrín’s government, Teruel and the march to the Mediterranean, the Ebro, and the end of the war — closing with society and culture in wartime and a long bibliography.
The text is 16,164 lines, extracted from the EPUB container (clean text layer; no OCR required). Alpha-character ratio ≈ 0.94; no Fraktur or garbled OCR layer.
Content Summary
Front matter. Title page: Historia de España en el siglo XX / II. La crisis de los años treinta: República y guerra civil; ePUB r1.3 (JeSsE 06.02.14); original title note; Javier Tusell, 2000; digital-editor credits. Publisher’s blurb: divided into four volumes, the series spans the twentieth century and its two decisive Spanish events — the Civil War and the Transition — while Spanish culture reached a level from early in the century comparable with the Golden Age; this second volume studies the crisis of the transcendent thirties, in which the Second Republic and the Civil War marked the lives of Spaniards. “Una obra fundamental para entender la España de hoy.”
Part I — Sociedad y economía
Plenitud y crisis de los años treinta
Tusell’s framing chapter on why the thirties carry an almost impossible-to-exaggerate weight in Spanish contemporary history: the density of the period, the sense that its events refuse to be narrated like any other era, and the claim that Spain’s twentieth-century peculiarity derives from these years. The democratic experience of 1931 onward was not an ordinary phenomenon, however comparable to parts of Eastern Europe in the first postwar, because the Second Republic’s reforming social and participatory political purposes went far deeper than any such parallel.
Medio rural y urbano
The agrarian and urban social world of 1930s Spain — the latifundist and smallholding countryside, the growing cities and their class structure — as the setting for the political conflicts to come.
El ritmo de la vida cotidiana
Everyday life in the thirties: work, wages, prices, leisure, housing and the material texture of daily existence in a society still largely poor and unequally distributed.
El impacto de la crisis económica
The impact of the world economic crisis of the early 1930s on Spain — slower to arrive than elsewhere but with grave social consequences — and its role in sharpening the agrarian and labour problems the Republic inherited.
La democracia de masas: Movilización política y experiencia de la democracia
Essential to the republican years was a decisive change in the way politics was lived: the Republic was not merely a change of regime but the advent of the masses to public life, which Primo de Rivera’s dictatorship had hidden and then made abrupt. Tusell insists the Second Republic was the Spanish democratic experience par excellence before 1977 — never before (under oligarchic liberalism) nor after had Spain mass participation in public life on the pattern of the democracies. This affirms a fact, not a value-judgment, and does not presume the republican leaders always chose well.
Part II — La República
La experiencia democrática republicana
The founding democratic experience of 1931: the elections, the fall of the monarchy, the provisional government and the hopes and divisions of the opening of the regime.
La elaboración de la Constitución
The drafting of the 1931 Constitution in the constituent Cortes — its separation of church and state, territorial and social provisions, and the political alignments that produced it.
La reforma militar
The reformist biennium’s military reform under Azaña — the prestige his ministerial work earned him, and the restructuring of an over-large officer corps and army. The religious question, dividing the provisional government in the Cortes, imposed a new governing formula and opened what Tusell calls the reformist biennium, directed by Azaña.
La cuestión religiosa
The religious question as the sharpest anticlerical-clerical cleavage of the republican years — very acute in the first biennium, less so later — and the Church’s place in a society where, whatever the cultural and educated middle classes had become, the whole of Spain could not be said to have ceased being Catholic.
La reforma agraria y la agitación social en el campo
The agrarian reform as the most ambitious problem facing the new regime, appearing before the constitution was drafted and, like the religious question, decisive in alienating a large part of the population. Even with the timidity of its content and application it confronted a multisecular problem made urgent by the economic crisis, social expectations and a growing population the labour market could not absorb; the accompanying social agitation in the countryside.
La pluralidad española
The regional and linguistic pluralism of Spain — Catalan and Basque questions in particular — as a defining problem of the Republic and its territorial organisation.
La política económica y las reformas sociales
The Republic’s economic policy and social reforms: legislation on labour, wages, social insurance and welfare, and their limits in the crisis conditions of the early thirties.
La «República en una tenaza»: monárquicos y anarquistas
The Republic “in a pincer” between monarchists on the right and anarchists on the left — the two anti-republican extremes that, from opposite directions, pressured and destabilised the democratic experiment.
La crisis del bienio reformista y las elecciones de 1933
The crisis of the reformist biennium and the 1933 elections that ended it — the disintegration of the centre-left coalition and the shift of power that brought the conservative biennium.
Radicales y cedistas: el comienzo de la colaboración
The beginning of the collaboration between the Radical Party of Lerroux and the CEDA (Confederación Española de Derechas Autónomas) that governed the second, centre-right biennium.
La insurrección de octubre de 1934
The October 1934 insurrection — the socialist and Catalan revolt against the entry of the CEDA into government, opened here through the figure of Ricardo Samper who briefly headed the caretaker cabinet and was respected by neither right nor left. The PSOE’s sense of abandonment after 1933 as background to the rising; Azaña’s preference for «el rey y sus ministros» against the rebels.
Las secuelas de octubre y la agonía inacabable del segundo bienio
The aftermath of October and the “interminable agony” of the second biennium — repression, the suspension of Catalan autonomy, and the slow disintegration of the radical-cedista coalition through 1935.
División y radicalización de los socialistas españoles
The split within Spanish socialism — reformists versus revolutionaries (Prieto against Largo Caballero) — and its radicalisation that pushed the party toward revolution, a course with consequences for the Republic’s stability.
Fascismo en España
The curious parallel between far-right and far-left: direct communist and fascist influence in Spain was quite small until the outbreak of the Civil War, even though totalitarian styles seemed to pervade political life. The fascist extreme, divided and nearly without parliamentary representation, was a negligible social and political force at the start of 1936 — even more marginal than the communists — its one success being in university student circles.
El Frente Popular y las elecciones de 1936
The Popular Front and the February 1936 elections: the recomposition of the left (Azaña’s republican-left position volatilised by 1933 in seats though less in votes) and the election that returned the Popular Front to government.
El Frente Popular en el Gobierno
The Popular Front in government: the programme and personnel of the new cabinet, its early measures and the quickening of social and political conflict under it.
El plano inclinado hacia la Guerra Civil
The “inclined plane” toward the Civil War — the spring and summer of 1936, the accelerating polarisation, violence and political paralysis that brought the Republic to the point of the military rising, with the argument that until nearly the last moment the war could have been avoided.
Política exterior española en los años treinta
Spanish foreign policy in the thirties: the Republic’s place in the Europe of the League of Nations and the dictatorships, and the neutrality and relations that framed the approach of 1936.
Plenitud y crisis en los medios culturales
Spanish culture in the republican years as a period of “plenitude and crisis”: the twenties vanguard had reached only small minorities, but the thirties produced a project of cultural modernisation rooted in Madrid and Barcelona and diffused to urban and partly rural media — the Republic as, in many senses, the beginning of the tradition of modernity in Spanish cultural history (urbanism, quality theatre in the capital, the diffusion of the plastic-arts vanguard, supporting legislation).
Part III — La Guerra Civil
La Guerra Civil española
Tusell’s framing of the war as one of only two moments when Spain played a protagonist role in twentieth-century world history (the other being the Transition), and a warning against the interpretive axis that makes all Spanish contemporary history an inevitable road to the conflict between two death-gripped sectors of society. The war was not inevitable; it could have been avoided until nearly the last moment. Eyewitnesses, especially those with major political responsibility, tended to deny this, perhaps to exculpate themselves, but they refer only to the final stretch — the proof that it could have been avoided lying in how different behaviour by Casares Quiroga, or his earlier replacement, might have averted it.
La conspiración contra la República
The conspiracy against the Republic: although the war’s outbreak cannot be attributed to external factors despite Italy’s aid to monarchists, traditionalists and falangists — that help neither sufficed to finance the rising nor grew at the moment of it — the extreme-right groups had sought Italian fascist help. The republican authorities published the monarchists’ 1934 pacts with Mussolini to show an early conspiracy, but Italian aid was only decisive from July 1936 onward.
Un primer balance de fuerzas: España dividida en dos
A first balance of forces at the outset of the war — Spain divided in two: the geographic, military and material resources of each side in July 1936 and the initial prospects of the conflict.
La revolución y sus consecuencias
The revolution and its consequences, opened with Azaña’s retrospective verdict that after the rising the republican government faced both the military movement advancing on Madrid and the insurrection of the proletarian masses who, without directly attacking the government, did not obey it — who wanted to make a syndical revolution to combat fascism — and that the government’s chief task through the whole war was to “reduce those masses to discipline.” The social revolution in the republican zone and its consequences for the war’s conduct.
La represión en la retaguardia
An immediate consequence of the war’s becoming irreversible was that individuals on both sides demonised the adversary and judged it most urgent to exterminate him physically. Initial tolerance or pacts of neutrality soon gave way; the repression was both the testimony that the Civil War had begun and a contributor to making it irreversible — once the blood flowed, an abyss opened between the belligerents that could not close. Terror, not social revolution or the restoration of traditional principles, came first on both sides.
El catolicismo ante la Guerra Civil
Catholicism before the Civil War: the religious factor’s enormous weight in social and political life. Against Azaña’s claim that Spain had ceased to be Catholic, Tusell finds arguments both ways — the cultural world and much of the educated middle classes had ceased to be, but the claim cannot extend to the whole society, and the very sharpness of the clerical-anticlerical contrast shows the question was not indifferent to Spaniards.
La guerra de columnas
The first military phase as a war of columns: successive clashes between not-very-large groups without a precise front, in which disparity of numbers and quality made one side almost always defensive; the heterogeneous composition of these armed nuclei mixing the military and the revolutionary.
La batalla en torno a Madrid. La guerra en el mar
The failure of Franco’s direct assault on Madrid in November 1936 as a decisive military turn — the column-war exhausted as fronts consolidated and the popular militias grew more efficient, at least on the defensive. Franco’s coherent response: abandoning the direct assault for a flanking manoeuvre that would draw the adversary onto open ground where his superiority had been shown. The naval war and the blockade that accompanied the fight around Madrid.
La internacionalización de la Guerra Civil
The internationalisation of the war: though internal in origin, the war made Spain the “centre of the world’s passions and disappointments.” Without foreign aid the crossing of the Strait, the defence of Madrid, Guadalajara and Franco’s maritime hegemony cannot be understood; both contenders sought help because the Spanish army was badly equipped materially. The international conjuncture of the moment was already tense.
Las potencias y la guerra española
The powers and the Spanish war: the stance and interest of the major European (and some American) states from the conflict’s outset — the Non-Intervention Committee and its limits, and the balance of aid to each side.
La campaña del norte
Franco’s decision, despite initial resistance, to move the war’s centre of gravity to the northern zone at the end of March 1937 — a sound decision involving a “detour” to his final objectives but yielding, at the conflict’s “critical point,” a victory decisive for its end. The war was resolved in the northern campaign: from April to October the rebel army successively conquered Vizcaya, Santander and Asturias, transforming the initial balance of July 1936.
Aspectos económicos de la guerra
Economic aspects of the war: finance, production, blockade, scarcity and the economic management of both zones during the conflict.
La formación de dos Ejércitos y la conducción de la guerra
The formation of the two armies — the Popular Army in the republican zone and the regular command structure in the rebel zone — and the conduct of the war as each side’s forces professionalised.
Unidad política en torno a Franco
Political unity around Franco: like the Popular Front, the first result of the rising in the rebel zone was the fragmentation of political authority — but here, without bloodshed, a high degree of unity was achieved over time, explained by the peculiar mentality of the rebels, who sought above all to prevent the triumph of a revolution they felt as imminent though neither prepared nor with a capable political group. A preventive counter-revolution whose result was a revolution of disparate contents.
El enfrentamiento en el seno del Frente Popular
The confrontation within the Popular Front: the political crisis of the republican zone in 1937 — the conflict between the anarchist and communist-influenced currents, Largo Caballero’s government and its fall, and the growing communist role.
El gobierno Negrín
The Negrín government: Azaña and Prieto as the true authors of the political resolution, not any of the named groups. Azaña had deplored Largo Caballero’s presence in power, judging his performance in the harshest terms («ineptitud delirante aliada con la traición»), sought to rid himself of him, and was decisive in selecting Juan Negrín, in whom he saw a “tranquil energy” against Prieto’s «altibajos» and «repentes». Prieto made clear to Largo Caballero that the communists’ withdrawal from the cabinet meant the inevitable political crisis.
Teruel y la marcha hacia el Mediterráneo
Teruel and the march to the Mediterranean: the end of the northern front could make observers think the war nearly over. Apart from the rebels’ material and military superiority on land, Soviet supplies were hindered by Italian submarines and the fall of Blum’s government in France; the republican fleet, after losing the Jaime I by accident, acted strictly defensively; the USSR, pressured by Far Eastern events, reduced its aviators in Spain. Everything seemed to favour Franco, yet the fighting was prolonged — at Teruel and the Ebro the German ambassador twice wrote to Hitler that the Spanish conflict had no military solution.
La batalla del Ebro y sus consecuencias: Colapso en Cataluña
The Ebro battle and its consequences — collapse in Catalonia. During the Maestrazgo offensive the Popular Army rebuilt its organisation and effectives when months earlier it had been near disintegration; it prepared a modest offensive that showed its “inconsistency” but revived the desire to resist. Reconstitution drew on new intakes from the “quinta del biberón” (eighteen-year-olds) to reservists over forty — 17 intakes against Franco’s 12. The Army of the Ebro was rebuilt on strict, necessarily political discipline; as Azaña noted, «casi todo el Ejército del Ebro es comunista» — the command (Modesto) and the discipline of the units reflecting it.
Alternativas finales de la política exterior sobre la guerra
Final alternatives of foreign policy on the war: the shifting interventionism of each power and a balance of the aid received by both belligerents in a rapidly changing international conjuncture. The Non-Intervention Committee’s control plan for Spain of early 1937 soon proved ineffective; from April, via the so-called Fagioli agreement, Mussolini’s Italy ceded two submarines — the pattern of covert aid that persisted.
El fin de la guerra
The end of the war: for many Popular Front sympathisers the fall of Catalonia simply meant the end, ratified by France’s and Britain’s immediate recognition of Franco. The final phase is better judged as a phenomenon of disintegration affecting all sectors and protagonists of the Popular Front, who acted in sensibly different ways, than as an interweaving of conspiracies. The first testimony was the surrender of Menorca in the first days of February 1939 — the island and Mahón base had played no important part in the war, the initiative for surrender arising from the simple spectacle of the republican state, with a British warship involved.
Sociedad y cultura en tiempos de guerra
Society and culture in wartime: the polarisation of Spanish society into two or three hard-to-reconcile redoubts was not characteristic of the whole of Spanish history but of the war period and after, since before it divergence had not excluded coexistence. The war opened a deep division destined to last. The decisive factor was partly class, but strictly cultural factors — conceptions of man and of life — probably weighed more than social-sector characterisations; the latifundist aristocracy stood with one side, and culture was mobilised and torn by the conflict.
Mapas de la Guerra Civil española
A section of maps of the Civil War, occupying the transition into the bibliography.
Bibliografía
Bibliography of the Republic and Civil War. The text signals especially original recent monographs with an asterisk (*). Opens with sources for Spanish society at the height of 1930 (Bahamonde and Otero on Madrid’s Restoration society, Borrás Llop on childhood 1834–1936, Castillo on mutual-aid solidarity, Cuesta on compulsory social insurance, Díez de la Guardia on secondary education, the Basque cooperative movement, Mujer y sociedad en España, Palacio Morena on the institutionalisation of social reform, Romeu on the working classes, Tuñón de Lara on living standards), a bibliography commented on the Second Republic 1931–1936 (works 1940–1992), and the claim that the most recent global study is Stanley Payne, La primera democracia española. La Segunda República, 1931–1936 (Paidós, 1995), together with a wide selection of general works of very varied ideological significance (de la Cierva, Arrarás, Carr, Jackson, and others).

Relationship to the Wiki
Tusell’s volume II gives the wiki the continuous scholarly history of the Second Republic and the Civil War, the two subjects the wiki’s Spanish contemporary sources approach from within. Where Madariaga surveys Spain from the liberal exile’s standpoint, Chaves Nogales brings the war’s lived texture from the liberal middle, Aznar narrates the campaigns from the Nationalist side, Azaña speaks from inside the 1934 events as the imprisoned accused, Hayes records the American embassy’s view of wartime neutrality, and Fernández Almagro traces the monarchical era that preceded the Republic, Tusell supplies the full analytic arc — the Republic from its 1931 foundation through its reforms, crises, the conservative biennium and October 1934 to the Popular Front of 1936, and the Civil War from conspiracy and revolution through the campaigns, foreign intervention, the internal politics of both zones and the war’s end. His chapters on the revolution, repression and the church sit directly beside Chaves Nogales and Aznar; his analysis of the internationalisation and the powers’ roles beside the German, Italian and Russian wartime sources and Hayes’s American witness; his treatment of the reformist biennium, October 1934 and the Catalan question beside Azaña’s prison memoir. Together with volume III (already held), it makes Tusell the wiki’s scholarly spine for the whole crisis-and-dictatorship sequence of the Spanish twentieth century. Volume IV of the same series (La transición democrática) belongs with the Rest of Europe 1946–present collection when processed.

Javier Tusell — Historia de España en el siglo XX, III. La dictadura de Franco
Full bibliographic citation — Javier Tusell Gómez (1945–2005). Historia de España en el siglo XX, volume III, La dictadura de Franco. — First published 2000 (publication date in this edition 6 March 2000). This text from the ePubLibre digital edition (ePUB r1.3, JeSsE, 6 February 2014; UUID 03d3ce49-7a2a-4822-ad87-f6f39849e113; hash cbda17f72963c6e02278ac5597cfe884). The four-volume series covers the Spanish twentieth century; volume III is the continuous political, social and cultural history of Franco’s dictatorship from the last war bulletin of 1 April 1939 to the dictator’s death in November 1975. Volume IV (La transición democrática) continues the series beyond this wiki’s terminal date.
Javier Tusell, catedrático of Contemporary History at the UNED and a leading Spanish political historian of the twentieth century, wrote the volume as a full-scale scholarly synthesis of the Franco regime — not a memoir or a party history, but a modern secondary survey that treats the dictator, the regime as a dictatorship, the repression and exile of 1939, the fascist temptation and wartime foreign policy of 1939–45, the postwar isolation and autarky of the 1940s, the years of consensus and economic opening (1951–65), and the tardofranquismo of 1966–75 (succession, Carrero, Arias Navarro, opposition unity, decolonisation of Guinea and the Sahara, and Spain at Franco’s death). The author’s generation, as the closing biography notes, was obsessed with why democracy failed under the Second Republic and what the Franco dictatorship and the later restoration under Juan Carlos meant for Spanish democracy.

Content Summary
Front matter. Title page: Historia de España en el siglo XX / III. La dictadura de Franco; ePUB r1.3 (JeSsE 06.02.14); original title note; Javier Tusell, 2000; digital-editor credits. Publisher’s blurb: “Una obra fundamental para entender la España de hoy.”
Opening block — El dictador, el régimen y la sociedad
Opens on the night of 1 April 1939: at a quarter past eleven the habitual announcer Fernando Fernández de Córdoba reads the last official war bulletin (no. 982) on the radios of the victorious Spain — “cautivo y desarmado” the Red Army, Franco’s troops have reached their last military objectives — and the less-remembered vivas that accompanied it to the exterior allies of the three preceding years, Portugal, Italy and Germany. The block frames the volume’s three subjects: the person of the dictator, the regime as a dictatorship, and the society that lived under it.
Franco: biografía y praxis política de un dictador
Against the tendency to reduce the regime to a psychological portrait of its founder, Tusell sets Franco’s biography and political practice — the traits that the regime itself made the centre of rumour and expectation, and that the historian must neither inflate into pure personalism nor dissolve into impersonal structure. Covers origin, military career, rise during the Civil War, and the long praxis of rule to 1975.
El franquismo como dictadura
Defines the Spanish regime of 1939–1975 as a dictatorship without making it a Spanish peculiarity: Franco’s conceptions and behaviour expressed a wider European type rather than a unique national path. Typology of the regime against fascist, authoritarian and personal-dictatorship models.
Vencedores y vencidos: Los desastres de la guerra y la represión
From Cambó’s wartime diary reflection that the “Año triunfal” forgot the torrents of blood, the destruction of wealth and the sediment of rancour, through the disasters of the war and the repression that fell on the defeated after 1 April 1939.
El exilio y el comienzo de la posguerra en el interior
The exile of 1939 as a rupture in Spanish history — larger, longer and more severed from interior reality than earlier Spanish emigrations — and the beginning of the postwar inside Spain for those who remained.
La tentación fascista y la supervivencia (1939–1951)
Periodising frame for the first long phase: economic policy makes 1959 a key date, but the decades themselves differ sharply; 1939–51 is the phase of fascist temptation, wartime alignment, cosmetic adaptation after 1945, isolation, and the “noche oscura” of autarky.
El «Nuevo Estado» y la «fascistización» fallida
From the end of the Civil War to the summer of 1940 — when world war seemed decided and Fascist Italy entered — Spain’s internal and institutional drift toward homologation with the Axis (Anti-Comintern adhesion, exit from the League of Nations) and the limits of that “fascistisation.”
La tentación intervencionista y la lucha interna (1940–1942)
Against the late-franquista propaganda claim that Germany pressed and Franco resisted, Tusell holds that from the German victory over France there was an absolute identification of Spanish leaders with the Axis cause, prolonged with nuances into 1944; internal struggle (Serrano Suñer and others) and the interventionist temptation of 1940–42.
Un titubeante camino hacia la neutralidad (1942–1945)
Serrano Suñer’s displacement and Jordana at Foreign Affairs; the hesitant path toward genuine neutrality as the world war turned, still giving Axis assurances while government policy shifted — the years that Hayes’s embassy memoir covers from the American side.
El cambio cosmético: La política del régimen entre 1945 y 1951
At the close of the world war the regime faced simultaneous dangers: uncertainty of internal course, an opposition aiming at rupture or peaceful transition, and external isolation born of its wartime stance. Cosmetic adaptation without substantial change.
La oposición de los supervivientes: La izquierda desde 1939 a 1951
The left opposition of the survivors — opened with the figure of Manuel Cortés, the socialist mayor of Mijas who reappeared in 1969 after thirty years hidden in his house — from 1939 through guerrilla and exile politics to 1951.
El gran momento de la alternativa monárquica
Prieto’s readiness to deal with the monarchists; Western democratic powers’ preference for a monarchical path of reconciliation; the high moment of the monarchical alternative as a possible substitute for Franco.
Franco, aislado
Post-1945 isolation did not begin only with the Allied victory but became severe then; Tusell assigns primary responsibility to Franco’s maintenance of the political system, not only to wartime Axis collaboration.
La «noche oscura»: Autarquía y racionamiento en la década de los cuarenta
The coherence of early postwar interior and exterior policy; when the European environment changed, the political system did not, adapting only cosmetically. Autarky, rationing and the economic “dark night” of the 1940s.
Cultura y sociedad en la primera posguerra
From the “Edad de Plata” of Spanish letters at the Civil War’s outbreak to culture and society under the first postwar — rupture, exile of talent, and the official cultural order.
Los años del consenso: el apogeo del régimen (1951–1965)
The central years as plenitude and apogee: a dictatorship stable enough that passive social acceptance could be called consensus — explained by repression and the dismantling of opposition. By 1951 the worst immediate postwar pressure had been passed.
El final definitivo del aislamiento internacional: El concordato y los pactos con Estados Unidos
The almost coincident Concordat with the Holy See (1953) and the pacts with the United States as the definitive end of international isolation — anachronistic Concordat, strategic American interest, and consolidation of the regime abroad.
España ante Europa. La descolonización: Marruecos
European democratic memory of the Civil War versus American strategic distance; Spain before Europe; the decolonisation of Morocco.
La política del régimen y la oposición hasta 1956
Interior politics without major convulsions through the mid-1950s; limited opposition capacity; the significance of that quiet.
Una nueva oposición política
A new political opposition whose path diverged from official politics and only episodically affected it (most decisively at the Munich meeting of 1962); links to cultural evolution.
Por o contra la Falange: La vida política del régimen entre 1956 y 1965
From 1956 the first serious attempt at institutionalisation (Franco allergic to “constitutionalisation”); blue revival versus technocratic course; the nine years that prepared the clearer turn after the 1965 cabinet.
El alivio de la autarquía y el cambio en la política económica
Early-1950s growth of national income; end of the ration book in 1951; Spain catching the European postwar “miracles” after exceptional backwardness; industrial growth and the relief of autarky (road toward the 1959 Stabilisation Plan).
De la oposición política a la oposición social
After 1962 (Munich; ministerial change) a new stage in which social protest outweighs strictly political opposition; limits of the earlier small symbolic groups.
La cultura durante el franquismo intermedio
Intermediate-franquismo culture: opening abroad, will to modernise, identification of much of the cultural world with opposition, yet contact with official circles.
La cultura popular y el ocio
Cinema, popular arts and leisure as defining marks of the epoch; the porous border between high culture and mass entertainment.
Desarrollo económico, apertura y tardofranquismo (1966–1975)
The last decade dominated more than any earlier phase by Franco’s person in decline; zones of indifference left to ministers shrink as succession and crisis concentrate on the aging dictator.
La modernización de la sociedad española
Economic growth paired with deep social transformation; from a 1950s profile comparable to parts of Spanish America to a late-franquista Spain already clearly Western European in structure.
El cambio en el catolicismo español
Reception of Vatican II; the Church as both mirror and motor of mental and political change, given its enormous social power in the 1950s and its early role in founding the regime’s legitimacy.
La apertura (1965–1969)
“Apertura” as loosening of controls without substantial transformation of the regime; optimism from growth and weak opposition; Press Law and younger politicians of imprecise affiliation.
La decisión sucesoria. Matesa y la división interna del régimen
Juan Carlos named successor — López Rodó’s “Operación Salmón” with Carrero; the last institutionalising decision taken with sufficient unity of the ruling class; the Matesa scandal and internal division.
La protesta laboral. El terrorismo
Rising opposition in the final phase: labour protest and terrorism; the regime coexisted with both; historical weight lies as much in that coexistence as in the pressure itself.
El tardofranquismo: Carrero Blanco, presidente
Franco past seventy-five; failure of the old arbitral role among the victorious families; foreign visitors’ portraits of an old man who scarcely spoke; Carrero as president of the government.
El tardofranquismo: el Gobierno Arias Navarro
Continuity in Franco’s physical decline after Carrero; Fraga’s sense that he “escuchaba, pero no oía”; López Rodó’s last interviews; Arias Navarro’s government in the final crisis.
Actividad de la oposición: el camino hacia la unidad
Social protest rising slowly to 1967, sharply from 1973, peaking in the months after Franco’s death; not by itself able to overthrow the regime, but the backdrop of late politics; path toward opposition unity.
España y el mundo occidental
External context of the final phase; Spain’s peculiar place in Western Europe and Western defence; the last Moroccan/Saharan crisis in the regime’s final weeks.
La descolonización tardía: Guinea y el Sahara
Carrero against decolonisation, Castiella promoting it (partly with Gibraltar in view); Sahara and Guinea declared provinces 1958–59, then the retreat — Guinea first, Sahara in the terminal crisis.
¿Una cultura comprometida?
Late-franquismo culture: less simple increase of cultural belligerence than development of culture and society beside the political system, with periodic conflict.
España a la muerte de Franco
Last year of Franco’s life — pathos and esperpento; July 1974 thrombophlebitis from hard gift shoes; re-learning to speak and walk by narrating the Moroccan campaigns; obstinacy in remaining in power until death in November 1975.
Bibliografía
Selective bibliography with asterisks for especially original recent monographs. Opens with Stanley Payne, El régimen de Franco, 1936–1975 (Alianza, 1987) as the best overall study, and the contrasting Biescas–Tuñón de Lara antifranquista synthesis; continues through specialised works on politics, economy, Church, opposition, culture and foreign relations. The digital edition closes with a short author biography of Tusell (Barcelona 26 August 1945 – 8 February 2005).
Key Data Points
