La dictadura de FrancoSeriesFour volumes; III = dictatorship 1939–1975; IV = democratic transition (not in this wiki)Published2000 (this text: ePubLibre ePUB r1.3, 2014)SourceEPUB container; clean text layer; hash cbda17f72963c6e02278ac5597cfe884Raw filewiki/raw/historia-espana-siglo-xx-iii-dictadura-franco-tusell-2000.txtLines19,406StructureOpening block (dictator / regime / society) + three long period-parts (1939–51; 1951–65; 1966–75) with titled sections + bibliographyCoverageFranco Spain from the last war bulletin (1 April 1939) to Franco’s death (November 1975); wartime foreign policy 1939–45; isolation, autarky, Concordat and US pacts; developmentalism and tardofranquismoSignificanceFull modern Spanish scholarly synthesis of the dictatorship — the analytical backbone for the Franco years that the wiki’s contemporary sources (Aznar’s Nationalist military history, Hayes’s 1942–45 embassy memoir, Madariaga’s early-dictatorship chapters) record from inside their own moments
Relationship to the Wiki
Tusell gives the wiki its continuous scholarly history of Franco’s Spain from the end of the Civil War to the dictator’s death. Where Aznar narrates the war’s campaigns from the Nationalist side, Chaves Nogales the war’s human texture from the liberal middle, Madariaga the Republic and early dictatorship from exile, Azaña the 1934 Catalan crisis from prison, Fernández Almagro the reign of Alfonso XIII that preceded the Republic, and Hayes the American embassy’s view of wartime neutrality 1942–45, Tusell supplies the full arc of the regime those sources enter only in part. His volume II (Republic and Civil War) gives the continuous scholarly history of the crisis years from the 1931 Republic through the war’s end; the present volume III continues that arc across the dictatorship. His chapters on the failed fascistisation, the interventionist temptation of 1940–42 and the hesitant neutrality of 1942–45 sit directly beside Hayes and the European war sources; his repression, exile and early-postwar chapters continue Madariaga’s closing parts; his later sections (1951–75) run past this wiki’s 1945 terminal date and are held here because the volume is a single argument from 1939 and because the Spanish cluster already anchors the Iberian case in this wiki. Volume IV of the same series (La transición democrática) belongs with the Rest of Europe 1946–present collection when processed.

sources/historia-militar-guerra-espana-a.title: Manuel Aznar Zubigaray — Historia militar de la Guerra de España, Tomos I–III (1939/1940)
sources/historia-militar-guerra-espana-a.content:
Manuel Aznar Zubigaray — Historia militar de la Guerra de España, Tomos I–III
Full bibliographic citation — Manuel Aznar Zubigaray (1894–1975). Historia militar de la Guerra de España. — Tomo I (1940), Tomo II (1940), Tomo III (1939/1940). This text from the ePubLibre digital editions (ePub r1.0, “Titivillus,” 2018). Dedication: “A mis hijos Manuel, Javier y José María, combatientes de España.”
Manuel Aznar Zubigaray, the Navarrese journalist who became the Nationalist side’s principal war correspondent and propagandist (and grandfather of the future prime minister José María Aznar), wrote this as the authorized military history of the Nationalist war effort. His NOTA PREVIA explains the work’s aim — to place before the general reader “un relato sistemático… de la guerra de liberación de España,” to show that an army is “un sistema nacional en marcha,” and to “vulgarize the thoughts and plans that were born in the mind of the Generalísimo Franco to attain victory.” It covers only the operations of the Army of the land; the maritime and air war and the interior politics are touched upon only in passing. It is the Spanish national case — the military chronicle of the war from the side that won it, written while the fighting had barely ended, the direct counterpart to Madariaga’s liberal political history and to the regime sources elsewhere in the wiki.
The three volumes run ~37,000 lines combined (Tomo I: 13,883; Tomo II: 11,977; Tomo III: 12,194), extracted from EPUB containers, clean text layer, no OCR required.
Content Summary — Tomo I (1936–1937)
Opening with the author’s manifesto of purpose, the volume covers the outbreak and first year of the war:

Cap. Primero — Acción y reacción del Ejército nacional. The Movimiento of 18 July 1936 as military and popular, argued (citing Ortega y Gasset’s “Epílogo para ingleses”) not to be a mere pronunciamiento.
Cap. II — El alzamiento del Ejército y de los partidos nacionales. Popular support for the army; the mobilization of Falange Española.
Cap. III — Situación estratégica general; problema de las comunicaciones. Strategy of the war, and the communications problem on land, sea and air.
Cap. IV — Maniobras sobre las fronteras de Portugal y Francia; marcha hacia Madrid. Operations along the two frontiers and the early march on Madrid.
Cap. V — Sobre la frontera francesa. The frustrated relief of the San Sebastián garrison and combats in the north.
Cap. VI — La guerra en los frentes llamados secundarios: Aragón, Baleares, Andalucía, Santander y Asturias. The “secondary” fronts.
Cap. VII — Comienza la maniobra para el cerco y asalto de Madrid. The opening of the encirclement and assault on Madrid.
Cap. VIII — Tres centros aislados de resistencia: el Alcázar de Toledo, Oviedo, Santa María de la Cabeza. The three isolated strongholds.
Cap. IX — Conversión del frente nacional para la liberación de Toledo y maniobra de aproximación a Madrid.
Cap. X — El ataque frustrado sobre Madrid; un arpón clavado en los suburbios; la guerra cambia de signo. The failed assault on Madrid and the turning of the war.
Cap. XI — Final del año 1936; Franco Generalísimo de los Ejércitos y Jefe del Estado; notas sobre la situación general.

Content Summary — Tomo II (1937–1938)

Cap. Primero — Año 1937. La batalla del cerco de Madrid. The battles for the encirclement of Madrid.
Cap. II — La batalla de Málaga. The fall of Málaga (February 1937); the siege operations shifting to the right wing; the Red reaction in Asturias.
Cap. III — Continúan las operaciones del cerco de Madrid. The great battles on the banks of the Jarama and the cutting of the road.
Cap. IV — Operaciones de Guadalajara y sus consecuencias militares y políticas. The Guadalajara battle (March 1937) and its consequences.
Cap. V — La campaña del Norte; conquista de Bilbao. The northern campaign and the conquest of Bilbao (June 1937).
Cap. VI — Batalla de Brunete. The Red army’s first great strategic diversion (July 1937).
Cap. VII — La maniobra sobre Santander. The advance on Santander (August 1937).
Cap. VIII — Belchite; el frente de Aragón durante el año 1937. The second Red strategic diversion against Zaragoza (September 1937).
Cap. IX — Reconquista de Asturias por Franco; «El frente norte ha desaparecido». The reconquest of Asturias and the end of the northern front (October 1937).
Cap. X — Pausa, planes en Aragón, preparación de una nueva ofensiva nacional en Guadalajara y gran ataque general del Ejército rojo en Teruel. The pause and the approach of the Teruel battle.
Cap. XI — Año 1938. Gran batalla de Teruel y del Alfambra. The great battle of Teruel (December 1937–February 1938) fought in the snow.
Cap. XII — Martirio y gloria de la ciudad de Huesca. The siege and defense of Huesca.

Content Summary — Tomo III (1938–1939)

Cap. Primero — La batalla de Aragón o «Gran batalla de Franco». The Aragon offensive; the Generalísimo’s strategy widening its scope (spring 1938).
Cap. II — Desarrollo y triunfo de la batalla de Franco o de Aragón; cinco Cuerpos de Ejército y cinco marchas.
Cap. III — Continúa el relato de la batalla de Aragón; segundo tiempo de la ofensiva. Operations north and south of the Ebro, toward Catalonia and the Mediterranean.
Cap. IV — Campaña de Teruel y de Castellón de la Plana; reacción roja en el Segre.
Cap. V — Batalla hacia Sagunto y Segorbe. The National operation in Extremadura; the Red strategic diversion on the Ebro.
Cap. VI — Gran batalla del Ebro. The great battle of the Ebro (July–November 1938), including the Red plan per the Orden general de operaciones número 2.
Cap. VII — Gran batalla del Ebro (fases tercera y cuarta; desgaste y contraofensiva).
Cap. VIII — Episodios en el río Segre y en Extremadura; intermedio de dos batallas.
Cap. IX — Gran batalla de Cataluña. The Battle of Catalonia (December 1938–February 1939) and the fall of Barcelona.
Cap. X — La gran maniobra final del Generalísimo. The final maneuver; the last objectives reached; the Red army destroyed; the end of the war (April 1939).
Cap. XI — Resumen y consideraciones generales sobre la victoria nacional. The reasons for Franco’s victory.

Key Data Points













































AttributeDetailAuthorManuel Aznar Zubigaray (1894–1975), Nationalist war correspondent and propagandistTitleHistoria militar de la Guerra de España, Tomos I–IIIPublishedTomo I 1940; Tomo II 1940; Tomo III 1939/1940; this text from ePubLibre digital editions (2018)Dedication”A mis hijos Manuel, Javier y José María, combatientes de España”SourceEPUB containers (3 volumes); clean text layerRaw fileswiki/raw/historia-militar-guerra-espana-tomo-i-aznar-1939.txt, ...-tomo-ii-aznar-1940.txt, ...-tomo-iii-aznar-1939.txtLinesTomo I 13,883; Tomo II 11,977; Tomo III 12,194CoverageThe Civil War as a military campaign, 18 July 1936 – end of March 1939SignificanceThe Nationalist side’s own authorized military history of the war it won — the regime’s complementary voice to Madariaga’s liberal account and to the testimony of Chaves Nogales, giving the wiki its military-strategic narrative of the 1936–39 war
Relationship to the Wiki
Aznar gives the wiki the national military history of the Spanish Civil War, written from within the victor’s camp while the fighting had barely ended. Its eleven-plus-twelve-plus-eleven chapters trace the war as a sequence of campaigns and maneuvers — the march on Madrid, Málaga, Guadalajara, the northern front, Brunete, Teruel, the Ebro, Catalonia, the final offensive — narrated from the perspective of the Generalísimo’s staff. Read against Madariaga’s political chronicle of the Republic and Civil War, Chaves Nogales’s literary testimony from the liberal middle, the Azaña prison memoir of 1934, and Tusell’s continuous scholarly history of the dictatorship that followed the victory Aznar celebrates and his companion volume II on the Republic and the war’s politics (revolution, repression, the church, the internationalisation) that Aznar treats from the staff viewpoint, it completes the Spanish cluster with the military-strategic voice of the winning side, complementary in the Spanish section to how the German, Italian and Russian regime sources anchor their national clusters elsewhere in the wiki.

sources/hitler-mein-kampf-1925-26.title: Adolf Hitler — Mein Kampf (Band I 1925, Band II 1926)
sources/hitler-mein-kampf-1925-26.content:
Adolf Hitler — Mein Kampf (Band I 1925, Band II 1926)
Source
Adolf Hitler, Mein Kampf. Erster Band: Eine Abrechnung (1925); Zweiter Band: Die nationalsozialistische Bewegung (1926). First published by Franz Eher Nachfolger, the central publishing house of the NSDAP, in Munich. EPUB reproduction of the full German text (2016 digital edition, uncredited original); 780 printed pages in the standard edition.
Description
The foundational text of National Socialism, dictated by Hitler in Landsberg prison after the failure of the Beer Hall Putsch of 9 November 1923 and written out by his secretary Rudolf Hess, published in two volumes in 1925 and 1926. It is at once an autobiography, a confession of faith (the subtitle of the first volume, Eine Abrechnung, “a settlement of accounts,” announces its polemical purpose), and a programme for the movement and, ultimately, the state.
The first volume traces Hitler’s origins in Braunau and Linz, his years of poverty in Vienna (1909–1913), his discovery of the “Jewish question,” and his wartime service as a Gefreiter in a Bavarian regiment, and ends with the collapse of 1918 and his “political awakening” in Munich. The second volume sets out the National Socialist doctrine proper — Weltanschauung und Partei, Der Staat, race and the völkisch state, the organization of the movement, the place of propaganda and the spoken word, and the closing chapters on foreign policy (Deutsche Bündnispolitik nach dem Kriege, Ostorientierung oder Ostpolitik, Notwehr als Recht) that give the book its infamous programmatic core: the demand for Lebensraum in the East and the destruction of Soviet Russia.
The book sold slowly at first (the first volume appeared in two printings in 1925–1926), but became a best-seller and a standard gift after 1930, and was the compulsory wedding gift in the Third Reich. It is the single most important contemporary statement of the ideology whose triumph this wiki’s interwar collection documents; it sits alongside Heiden’s contemporary critical biography as the Nazi text that Heiden analyses from outside.
Context
Dictated in the fortress-prison of Landsberg am Lech between 1924 and 1925, after the failed putsch of November 1923 and the trial at Munich in early 1924 that made Hitler nationally known. It was therefore composed at the moment of the movement’s apparent ruin and reconstitution — the period in which Hitler decided to seek power through the state and the ballot rather than through insurrection, the strategy that carried the NSDAP through the later 1920s to the breakthrough of 1930 and the seizure of power in January 1933.
Within this collection it is the central primary source of the German section: the canonical statement of Nazi racial doctrine, anti-Marxism, the Führer principle, and the Eastern programme that the other German sources — the Geisow tract, the Junker & Dünnhaupt yearbooks, Rosenberg, and Heiden’s biography — refract in different ways. It is the regime’s own foundational text, the “programme” against which the course of the Third Reich is measured.
Contents
Erster Band: Eine Abrechnung (1925)



Kapitel: Im Elternhaus — the family home: Hitler’s ancestry in the Waldviertel, his father Alois, his mother, his childhood in Braunau, Passau and Linz, his early dreams and the quarrel over the career of a civil servant.




Kapitel: Jahre der Lehre und der Leidenszeit in Wien — the years of study and suffering in Vienna: the death of his mother, his rejection by the Academy of Fine Arts, his poverty in the men’s hostels, his work as a draughtsman, and the Vienna that taught him, in his telling, the Jewish question and the bankruptcy of the Habsburg state.




Kapitel: Allgemeine politische Betrachtungen aus meiner Wiener Zeit — general political reflections from his Vienna years: on the Austrian Reichsrat, the nationalities, pan-Germanism (Schönerer) and the Christian-socialist mayor Karl Lueger.




Kapitel: München — Munich, 1913–1914: the move to the German city, the appeal of the German imperial idea.




Kapitel: Der Weltkrieg — the World War: volunteering in August 1914, service as a runner on the Western Front, the Iron Cross, and the wounding.




Kapitel: Kriegspropaganda — war propaganda: the failure of the German leadership’s propaganda and the power of the English and the Entente’s.




Kapitel: Die Revolution — the revolution: the collapse of November 1918, the sailors’ mutiny and the Bavarian revolution, which Hitler experienced in the hospital at Pasewalk, blinded by gas.




Kapitel: Beginn meiner politischen Tätigkeit — the beginning of his political activity: the course for returned soldiers in Munich, the encounters with the revolution, the discovery of the German Workers’ Party, and his entry as the seventh member.




Kapitel: “Die Deutsche Arbeiterpartei” — the German Workers’ Party and its early meetings.




Kapitel: Ursachen des Zusammenbruchs — causes of the collapse: the November criminals, Marxism, the Jewish influence, the armistice and the “stab in the back.”




Kapitel: Volk und Rasse — people and race: the foundations of the racial doctrine, the hierarchy of races, the state as the means of preserving the race, and the Jewish people as the contrary principle.




Kapitel: Die erste Entwicklungszeit der Nationalsozialistischen Deutschen Arbeiterpartei — the early development of the party: the growth of the movement, the red flag, the swastika, the SA, the programme and the “twenty-five points.”



Zweiter Band: Die nationalsozialistische Bewegung (1926)



Kapitel: Weltanschauung und Partei — worldview and party.




Kapitel: Der Staat — the state: the völkisch state, race as the foundation, the rejection of the democratic and parliamentary state.




Kapitel: Staatsangehöriger und Staatsbürger — subject and citizen: the racial qualifications of citizenship.




Kapitel: Persönlichkeit und völkischer Staatsgedanke — personality and the völkisch idea of the state: the Führer principle against the principle of the majority.




Kapitel: Weltanschauung und Organisation — worldview and organization.




Kapitel: Der Kampf der ersten Zeit — Die Bedeutung der Rede — the struggle of the first period and the importance of the spoken word.




Kapitel: Das Ringen mit der roten Front — the struggle with the red front.




Kapitel: Der Starke ist am mächtigsten allein — the strong man is mightiest alone.




Kapitel: Grundgedanken über Sinn und Organisation der SA — the fundamental ideas on the meaning and organization of the SA.




Kapitel: Der Föderalismus als Maske — federalism as a mask.




Kapitel: Propaganda und Organisation — propaganda and organization.




Kapitel: Die Gewerkschaftsfrage — the trade union question.




Kapitel: Deutsche Bündnispolitik nach dem Kriege — German alliance policy after the war: the demand for Lebensraum, the rejection of colonial and trade policy in favour of territorial conquest in Europe.




Kapitel: Ostorientierung oder Ostpolitik — orientation toward the East: the alliance with England and Italy, the war against Soviet Russia, the destruction of the “Asiatic” threat and the conquest of land in the East.




Kapitel: Notwehr als Recht — self-defence as a right: the justification of the movement’s methods and the closing summons to the party.



Access

Raw text: hitler-mein-kampf-1925-26.txt (18,877 lines; ~1.58 million characters) — the complete body text of both volumes extracted from the EPUB (HTML converted to text, page-markers and the front-matter alphabetical index omitted), from “Erster Band. Eine Abrechnung” through the end of Band II. All 27 chapters present.
Notes on extraction: the EPUB (2016 digital reproduction, uncredited original) carries the full German text as clean HTML; no OCR required. Chapter boundaries confirmed against both the front-matter table of contents and the in-body “N. Kapitel” markers.

sources/istoriya-vkpb-kratkij-kurs-1945.title: History of the CPSU(b). Short Course (1945 reprint)
sources/istoriya-vkpb-kratkij-kurs-1945.content:
History of the CPSU(b). Short Course
Комиссия ЦК ВКП(б) — История ВКП(б). Краткий курс (History of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks). Short Course). Approved by the Central Committee of the CPSU(b) in 1938; this printing, OGIZ / Gospolitizdat, Moscow, 1945. A reprint of the canonical Stalin-era party history.





























AuthorCollective commission of the Central Committee of the CPSU(b) — the official party history issued under Stalin’s direct editorship (commonly attributed to Stalin and the Central Committee commission); approved by the CC CPSU(b) 1938Edition1945 reprint (OGIZ / Gospolitizdat, Moscow) of the text first approved in 1938; FB2 electronic edition (librusec-id 655522) prepared 2018StructureIntroduction + 12 chapters + Conclusion; canonical Short Course ending; 4,703 lines / ~810,000 characters of extracted textPeriod1883–1937: from the rise of Russian social democracy to the completion of socialist construction and the adoption of the 1936 ConstitutionNoteIncludes the Stalin “Antaeus” parable from On the Shortcomings of Party Work; Lenin quotations cited by volume and page (т. XXV, XXVII)
Contents. The canonical Short Course of party history. The introduction frames the study of party history as the study of the struggle of the revolutionary proletariat; the work then narrates the formation of Russian social democracy from the abolition of serfdom and the rise of the industrial proletariat, the narodnik movement and Plekhanov’s Emancipation of Labour group, the beginning of Lenin’s revolutionary activity, and the creation of the “Iskra” newspaper. It treats the formation of the RSDRP at the Second Congress and the split into Bolsheviks and Mensheviks; the party in the Russo-Japanese War and the first Russian revolution (Bloody Sunday, the Potemkin mutiny, the October general strike, the December armed uprising, the Duma); the party in the Stolypin reaction and its formation into an independent Marxist party at the Prague conference; the party in the years of the labour upsurge before the First World War; the party in the imperialist war and the February revolution; the preparation and conduct of the October socialist revolution; the party in the period of foreign military intervention and civil war; the transition to peaceful work and the restoration of the national economy; the struggle for socialist industrialization; the struggle for the collectivization of agriculture; and the completion of the construction of socialist society with the adoption of the new Constitution. The conclusion states the chief lessons of the historical path of the Bolshevik party.
Character of the source. The official Soviet party history of the Stalin period, approved by the Central Committee in 1938 and for decades the obligatory text of party and civic education. Written from a strict Bolshevik standpoint, it presents the party’s history as the history of the struggle of the Marxist-Leninist line against its internal opponents (economists, Mensheviks, Trotskyists, “rightists,” Bukharinists) and against the enemies of the revolution. Its chapter structure — twelve chapters from 1883 to 1937 — is the authoritative periodisation of Soviet history adopted throughout the Stalin era. A companion volume in this folder — Shestakov’s Short Course of the History of the USSR (1937), a school textbook covering the same years — has its own source page.
Quality. Good. Extracted from an FB2 e-book via regex stripping of the markup; continuous prose throughout. Cyrillic text clean; chapter and section headings verified. Non-breaking spaces after numbered section headings (U+00A0) noted during extraction.
Raw text: wiki/raw/istoriya-vkpb-kratkij-kurs-1945.txt.

Введение (Introduction)
The study of the history of the party of the Bolsheviks as the study of the struggle of the revolutionary proletariat; the party of a new type; the worldwide significance of the history of the CPSU(b).
Глава I. Борьба за создание социал-демократической рабочей партии в России (1883–1901 годы)
The struggle for the creation of a social-democratic workers’ party in Russia, 1883–1901. The abolition of serfdom and the development of industrial capitalism in Russia; the appearance of the modern industrial proletariat; the first steps of the workers’ movement. Narodism and Marxism in Russia; Plekhanov and his “Emancipation of Labour” group; Plekhanov’s struggle against narodism; the spread of Marxism in Russia. The beginning of Lenin’s revolutionary activity; the Petersburg “Union of Struggle for the Emancipation of the Working Class.” Lenin’s struggle against narodism and “legal Marxism”; the Leninist idea of the alliance of the working class and the peasantry; the First Congress of the RSDRP. Lenin’s struggle against “economism”; the appearance of the Leninist newspaper “Iskra.”
Глава II. Образование Российской социал-демократической рабочей партии. Появление внутри партии фракций большевиков и меньшевиков (1901–1904 годы)
The formation of the RSDRP and the appearance within the party of the Bolshevik and Menshevik factions, 1901–1904. The rise of the revolutionary movement in Russia in 1901–1904. The Leninist plan of building a Marxist party; the opportunism of the “economists”; the struggle of “Iskra” for the Leninist plan; Lenin’s book What Is to Be Done?; the ideological foundations of the Marxist party. The Second Congress of the RSDRP; the adoption of the programme and statute and the creation of a united party; disagreements at the congress and the appearance of two currents in the party — Bolshevik and Menshevik. The splitting actions of the Menshevik leaders and the sharpening of the struggle inside the party after the Second Congress; the opportunism of the Mensheviks; Lenin’s book One Step Forward, Two Steps Back; the organisational foundations of the Marxist party.
Глава III. Меньшевики и большевики в период русско-японской войны и первой русской революции (1904–1907 годы)
The Mensheviks and Bolsheviks in the period of the Russo-Japanese War and the first Russian revolution, 1904–1907. The Russo-Japanese War; the further rise of the revolutionary movement; strikes in Petersburg; the demonstration of workers at the Winter Palace on 9 January 1905; the shooting of the demonstration; the beginning of the revolution. Political strikes and workers’ demonstrations; the growth of the peasant revolutionary movement; the mutiny on the battleship “Potemkin.” Tactical disagreements between Bolsheviks and Mensheviks; the Third Congress; Lenin’s Two Tactics of Social-Democracy in the Democratic Revolution; the tactical foundations of the Marxist party. The further rise of the revolution; the all-Russian political strike of October 1905; the retreat of tsarism; the tsar’s manifesto; the appearance of Soviets of Workers’ Deputies. The December armed uprising and its defeat; the retreat of the revolution; the First State Duma; the Fourth (Unity) Congress. The dissolution of the First Duma; the convocation of the Second Duma; the Fifth Congress; the dissolution of the Second Duma; the causes of the defeat of the first Russian revolution.
Глава IV. Меньшевики и большевики в период столыпинской реакции. Оформление большевиков в самостоятельную марксистскую партию (1908–1912 годы)
The Mensheviks and Bolsheviks in the period of the Stolypin reaction; the formation of the Bolsheviks into an independent Marxist party, 1908–1912. On dialectical and historical materialism. The Bolsheviks and Mensheviks in the years of the Stolypin reaction; the struggle against the liquidators and otzovists. The Bolshevik struggle against Trotskyism; the August anti-party bloc. The Prague party conference of 1912; the formation of the Bolsheviks into an independent Marxist party.
Глава V. Партия большевиков в годы подъема рабочего движения перед первой империалистической войной (1912–1914 годы)
The party of the Bolsheviks in the years of the upsurge of the workers’ movement before the first imperialist war, 1912–1914. The rise of the revolutionary movement in 1912–1914. The Bolshevik newspaper “Pravda”; the Bolshevik faction in the Fourth State Duma. The victory of the Bolsheviks in the legal organisations.
Глава VI. Партия большевиков в период империалистической войны. Вторая революция в России (1914 – март 1917 года)
The party of the Bolsheviks in the period of the imperialist war; the second revolution in Russia, 1914 – March 1917. The origin and causes of the imperialist war. The theory and tactics of the Bolshevik party on questions of war, peace and revolution. The defeat of the tsarist troops at the front; economic ruin; the crisis of tsarism; the February revolution.
Глава VII. Партия большевиков в период подготовки и проведения Октябрьской социалистической революции (апрель 1917 – март 1918 года)
The party of the Bolsheviks in the period of the preparation and conduct of the October socialist revolution, 1917. The beginning of the crisis of the Provisional Government; the April conference of the Bolshevik party. The party’s course on the preparation of the armed uprising; the Sixth Congress. The Kornilov plot and its defeat; the transfer of the Soviets in Petrograd and Moscow to the side of the Bolsheviks; the October armed uprising. The struggle for the consolidation of Soviet power; the Brest peace; the Seventh Congress.
Глава VIII. Партия большевиков в период иностранной военной интервенции и гражданской войны (1918–1920 годы)
The party of the Bolsheviks in the period of foreign military intervention and civil war, 1918–1920. The beginning of the foreign military intervention; the first period of the civil war. The military defeat of Germany; the revolution in Germany; the formation of the Third International; the Eighth Congress. The attack of the Polish gentry on the Soviet country; the sortie of General Wrangel; the failure of the Polish plan; the rout of Wrangel; the end of the intervention.
Глава IX. Партия большевиков в период перехода на мирную работу по восстановлению народного хозяйства (1921–1925 годы)
The party of the Bolsheviks in the period of the transition to peaceful work on the restoration of the national economy, 1921–1925. The Soviet country after the liquidation of the intervention and civil war; the difficulties of the restoration period. The discussion in the party on the trade unions; the Tenth Congress; the defeat of the opposition; the transition to NEP. The first results of NEP; the Eleventh Congress; the formation of the USSR; Lenin’s illness; Lenin’s co-operative plan; the Twelfth Congress.
Глава Х. Партия большевиков в борьбе за социалистическую индустриализацию страны (1926–1929 годы)
The party of the Bolsheviks in the struggle for the socialist industrialisation of the country, 1926–1929. The difficulties in the period of socialist industrialisation and the struggle with them; the formation of the Trotskyist-Zinovievist anti-party bloc; the anti-Soviet pronouncements of the bloc; the defeat of the bloc. The successes of socialist industrialisation; the lag of agriculture; the Fifteenth Congress; the course on the collectivisation of agriculture; the rout of the Trotskyist-Zinovievist bloc; political double-dealing. The offensive against the kulaks; the Bukharin-Rykov anti-party group; the adoption of the first five-year plan; socialist emulation; the beginning of the mass collective-farm movement.
Глава XI. Партия большевиков в борьбе за коллективизацию сельского хозяйства (1930–1934 годы)
The party of the Bolsheviks in the struggle for the collectivisation of agriculture, 1930–1934. The international situation in 1930–1934; the economic crisis in the capitalist countries; the seizure of Manchuria by Japan; the coming of the fascists to power in Germany; two seats of war. From the policy of restricting the kulak elements to the policy of liquidating the kulaks as a class; the struggle with distortions of the party’s policy in the collective-farm movement; the offensive against the capitalist elements on the whole front; the Sixteenth Congress. The plan for the reconstruction of all branches of the national economy; the role of technology; the further growth of the collective-farm movement; the political departments of the machine-tractor stations; the results of the fulfilment of the five-year plan in four years; the victory of socialism on the whole front; the Seventeenth Congress. The degeneration of the Bukharinites into political double-dealers; the degeneration of the Trotskyist double-dealers into a White-guard band of murderers and spies; the villainous murder of S. M. Kirov; the measures of the party to strengthen Bolshevik vigilance.
Глава XII. Партия большевиков в борьбе за завершение строительства социалистического общества и проведение новой Конституции (1935–1937 годы)
The party of the Bolsheviks in the struggle for the completion of the construction of socialist society and the adoption of the new Constitution, 1935–1937. The international situation in 1935–1937; the temporary easing of the economic crisis; the beginning of a new economic crisis; the seizure of Abyssinia by Italy; the German-Italian intervention in Spain; the invasion of Central China by Japan; the beginning of the second imperialist war. The further rise of industry and agriculture in the USSR; the early fulfilment of the second five-year plan; the reconstruction of agriculture and the completion of collectivisation; the significance of cadres; the Stakhanovite movement; the rise of popular welfare; the rise of popular culture; the strength of the Soviet revolution. The Eighth Congress of Soviets; the adoption of the new Constitution of the USSR. The liquidation of the remnants of the Bukharinist-Trotskyist spies, wreckers and traitors to the motherland; the preparation for elections to the Supreme Soviet of the USSR; the party’s course on developed intra-party democracy; the elections to the Supreme Soviet of the USSR.
Заключение (Conclusion)
The chief lessons of the historical path of the Bolshevik party: the party of the working class is the leading force of the revolution; the party grows stronger by cleansing itself of opportunist elements; the party is strong through its bond with the people, who are the source of its strength. Includes the “Antaeus” parable. Text ends: “Such are the chief lessons of the historical path traversed by the Bolshevik party.”

sources/kratkij-kurs-istorii-sssr-1937.title: Shestakov (ed.) — Short Course of the History of the USSR (1937)
sources/kratkij-kurs-istorii-sssr-1937.content:
Shestakov (ed.) — Short Course of the History of the USSR
Professor A. V. Shestakov (editor) — Краткий курс истории СССР (Short Course of the History of the USSR), a school textbook for the 3rd and 4th grades, edited by Prof. A. V. Shestakov and approved by the All-Union Government Commission for the compilation of the history textbook. Uchpedgiz, Moscow, 1937. Print run 5,000,000 copies.





























AuthorEdited by Prof. A. V. Shestakov, under a government commission convened to prepare a standard Soviet history textbook for the schools; approved by the All-Union Government CommissionEdition1937, Uchpedgiz (Moscow). Print run 5,000,000, first run 115,000. Colophon: 10.61 author sheets plus 9 inserts (“vkleeki”)StructureOne volume, 250 scan pages; introduction (Введение) + fifteen chapters (I–XV), each divided into numbered sections (§1–§65), followed by a chronological table and table of contents; ~9,177 OCR linesPeriodFrom the earliest times (the ancient Slavs, Kievan Rus) through the formation and growth of the Russian state, the imperial period, and up to the 1936 Constitution of the USSR — i.e., a full history from antiquity to the mid-1930sNoteThe companion textbook to the Short Course of the History of the VKP(b) (1945) also in this folder; together they represent the two canonical Stalin-era textbooks of Soviet history. Approved by a government commission as the standard school history
Contents. A compressed survey of the whole of Russian and Soviet history written for the elementary grades (3–4). The introduction, “Our Motherland,” presents the basic patriotic and materialist premises of the textbook. Chapter I covers the remote past of the homeland — the life of early man, the transition from clan to state, the earliest states in the country, and the Slavs. Chapter II treats the Kievan state: the first Russian princes, Olga and Svyatoslav, the introduction of the new faith and of laws, spontaneous popular uprisings, the Novgorod land and Suzdal Rus. Chapter III deals with Eastern Europe under the Mongol conquerors — the Tatar-Mongol yoke, Moscow and the first Moscow princes, Tamerlane and the decline of the Golden Horde. Chapter IV treats the creation of the Russian national state (Ivan III and the end of the yoke); Chapter V the expansion of the Russian state (Ivan IV); Chapter VI the peasant wars and uprisings of oppressed peoples in the 17th century (Razin, the Ukraine, Siberia, culture); Chapter VII Russia in the 18th century as an empire of landlords and merchants (Peter I, Pugachev, Catherine II). Chapter VIII treats “Tsarist Russia, the gendarme of Europe” — from the French Revolution and the war of 1812 through the Decembrists, the Caucasus, 1848 with Marx and Engels, and the eve of the 1861 reform. Chapter IX covers the growth of capitalism (the abolition of serfdom, the Polish uprising, the Paris Commune, the workers’ movement of the 1870s–90s and V. I. Lenin). Chapter X is the first bourgeois revolution in Russia (1905). Chapter XI the second bourgeois revolution (the world war and the overthrow of tsarism in February 1917). Chapter XII the Great October Socialist Revolution; Chapter XIII the military intervention and civil war (Brest, the intervention, the revolutions in Western Europe, Kolchak/Denikin/Yudenich, Poland/Wrangel). Chapter XIV the transition to peaceful work of rebuilding the national economy and the creation of the USSR; Chapter XV “the USSR — the land of victorious socialism” (socialist industry and the kolkhozes, the new Constitution of 1936).
Character of the source. The Stalin-era Soviet school textbook of Russian history, prepared under a government commission and published in an enormous print run (five million copies) for the elementary schools. It presents Soviet history in the orthodox form canonized in the mid-1930s — the narrative of backwardness and oppression under the tsars, the class struggle and peasant wars, the revolutionary movement, and the triumphant building of socialism culminating in the 1936 Constitution. Written in simplified language for young readers, it nonetheless gives the complete Soviet periodisation of the national past. It is the school-level companion to the party-oriented Short Course of the History of the VKP(b) (1945) and complements the adult survey of Pokrovsky’s Russian History in the Briefest Outline (1933) also in this folder.
OCR. Good quality. The volume had no embedded text layer, so it was rendered page-by-page (ddjvu) and OCR’d with Tesseract (-l rus). Typical Cyrillic OCR errors present (e.g. “Моековскаго” for “Московскаго”, “царекой” for “царской”, “ХУШ” for “XVIII”, garbled Roman numerals such as “ТХ”/“ХГ”/“УШ” for IX/XI/VIII in the table of contents). Headings and chapter structure checked against the table of contents at the end of the volume.
Raw text: wiki/raw/kratkij-kurs-istorii-sssr-1937.txt.

Introduction. Our Motherland (Введение)
1. Our Motherland
The opening chapter of the textbook: an elementary presentation of the homeland — its territory, peoples, natural wealth, and the basic concepts of the history of the USSR taught to schoolchildren.
I. Our homeland in the remote past
2. How people lived in the remote past
3. From the clan to the state
4. The earliest states in our country
5. The Slavs
The first chapters of the survey: the life of primitive man, the emergence of the clan and the transition to the state, the earliest states on the territory of the country, and the settlement and life of the Slavs.
II. The Kievan state
6. The first Russian princes
7. Princess Olga and Prince Svyatoslav
8. The Kievan princes introduce a new faith and laws
9. Spontaneous popular uprisings
10. The Novgorod land
11. Suzdal Rus
The formation of the Kievan state and the early Russian princes; the introduction of Christianity and of written law; peasant and popular revolts against the princes; the separate lands of Novgorod and Suzdal.
III. Eastern Europe under the power of the Mongol conquerors
12. The Mongol conquerors and the Tatar-Mongol yoke
13. Moscow and the first Moscow princes
14. Tamerlane and the decline of the Golden Horde
The Mongol invasion and the establishment of the Tatar-Mongol yoke over the Russian lands; the rise of Moscow under its first princes; Tamerlane and the weakening and decline of the Golden Horde.
IV. The creation of the Russian national state
15. The expansion of the Muscovite state under Ivan III and the end of the Tatar-Mongol yoke
The annexation of Novgorod, the liberation of the Muscovite state from the authority of the Tatar khan, and the consolidation of the unified Russian national state under Ivan III.
V. The expansion of the Russian state
16. The strengthening of the Muscovite state. The conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan
17. Ivan IV (“the Terrible”) and the struggle against the boyars
18. The liberation of Moscow from the Polish invaders
The expansion of the Russian state in the 16th–early 17th centuries: the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan, the reign of Ivan IV and his struggle with the boyars, and the expulsion of the Polish invaders from Moscow.
VI. Peasant wars and uprisings of oppressed peoples in the 17th century
19. The peasant war at the beginning of the 17th century
20. The struggle of the Russian people against the Polish and Swedish invaders
21. The peasant war led by Stepan Razin
22. The Ukraine. The Bogdan Khmelnitsky uprising
23. The annexation of Siberia
24. Culture in the 17th century
25. (unverified section)
26. (unverified section)
The 17th-century peasant wars and national uprisings: the peasant war of the early 17th century, the struggle against the Polish and Swedish invaders, the rising of Stepan Razin, the Ukrainian revolt of Bogdan Khmelnitsky and the annexation of the Ukraine, the conquest of Siberia, and 17th-century culture.
VII. Russia of the 18th century — an empire of landlords and merchants
27. The wars of Peter I and popular uprisings
28. The establishment of factories and of a regular army
29. Peter I’s reforms and the building of Petersburg
30. The peasant war led by Pugachev
31. Russia under Catherine II
32. (unverified section)
The 18th century: the wars and reforms of Peter I, the building of the new capital Petersburg and the creation of factories and a regular army, the peasant war of Pugachev, and the empire of the landlords and merchants under Catherine II.
VIII. Tsarist Russia — the gendarme of Europe
33. The bourgeois revolution in France and Catherine II’s and Paul I’s struggle against it
34. The war of 1812
35. The Decembrists
36. The Caucasus
37. 1848. Marx and Engels
38. Tsarist Russia — the gendarme of Europe
39. Tsarist Russia before the reform of 1861
The reactionary empire of the first half of the 19th century: the struggle of Catherine II and Paul I against the French Revolution, the war of 1812, the Decembrist uprising, the conquest of the Caucasus, the revolution of 1848 and the founders of Marxism, and the conditions in the tsarist empire on the eve of the 1861 reform.
IX. The growth of capitalism in Tsarist Russia
40. The abolition of serfdom in Russia
41. The Polish uprising of 1863
42. The First International and the Paris Commune
43. The growth of capitalism in Russia
44. The working-class movement in the 1870s–1890s. V. I. Lenin
The post-reform era: the abolition of serfdom in 1861, the Polish uprising of 1863, the First International and the Paris Commune, the growth of industrial capitalism, and the rise of the workers’ movement with V. I. Lenin.
X. The first bourgeois revolution in Russia
45. On the eve of the revolution
46. The beginning of the revolution
47. The December armed uprising
48. The defeat of the revolution
49. The new upsurge of the revolutionary movement
50. (unverified section)
The revolution of 1905: its preconditions and outbreak, the October general strike and the December armed uprising, the defeat of the revolution and the subsequent new upsurge of the revolutionary movement.
XI. The second bourgeois revolution in Russia
51. The world imperialist war
52. The overthrow of tsarism
The First World War and the defeats of Russia; the February revolution of 1917 and the overthrow of tsarism.
XII. The Great October Socialist Revolution in Russia
53. The Bolsheviks prepare the socialist revolution
54. The Great October Socialist Revolution
The preparation of the revolution by the Bolsheviks and the October Revolution of 1917, the establishment of Soviet power.
XIII. Military intervention. The civil war
55. The Brest peace. The German occupation of the Ukraine
56. The military intervention of the Entente
57. The revolution in Western Europe
58. Kolchak, Denikin, Yudenich
59. The war against Poland. The rout of Wrangel
The civil war and foreign intervention: the Brest peace and the German occupation of the Ukraine, the Entente intervention, the revolutions in Western Europe, the White generals Kolchak, Denikin and Yudenich, and the war against Poland and the rout of Wrangel.
XIV. The transition to peaceful work of rebuilding the national economy
60. The restoration of the national economy and the creation of the USSR
61. Lenin’s death. “Lenin is dead, but his cause lives on”
The transition to peaceful construction after the civil war: the restoration of the national economy, the creation of the USSR, and the death of Lenin with the slogan that his cause lived on.
XV. The USSR — the land of victorious socialism
62. Socialist industry. Collective farms (kolkhozes) in agriculture
63. The USSR — a land of socialism
64. Enemies and friends
65. The new Constitution of the USSR
The building of socialism in the 1930s: the construction of socialist industry and the collectivisation of agriculture, the USSR as a land of socialism, its enemies and friends, and the adoption of the new Constitution of 1936.
Chronological table
A table of the principal dates of Russian history from the treaty of Oleg with the Greeks (911) and the baptism of Rus (988) through the later period, closing with the entries for the Soviet era — the elementary chronology for the school text (physical p. ~241).
Table of contents (Оглавление)
The end-of-volume table of contents listing the introduction and all fifteen chapters with their numbered sections (physical p. 242–245).

sources/levi-se-questo-e-un-uomo-1947.title: Primo Levi — Se questo è un uomo (1947)
sources/levi-se-questo-e-un-uomo-1947.content:
Primo Levi — Se questo è un uomo (1947)
Source
Primo Levi, Se questo è un uomo, F. De Silva, Turin, 1947. PDF scan of the first edition; 133 printed pages (64 PDF pages).
Description
The first edition of the most celebrated Italian testimony of the Holocaust — the account of Primo Levi, an Italian Jewish chemist from Turin and a partisan, deported to Auschwitz in February 1944 and liberated in January 1945. It was published in the autumn of 1947 by the small Turin firm of F. De Silva and sold poorly (some 1,500 copies) before being reissued in the much-expanded and now-canonical Einaudi edition of 1958, by which point Levi had become world-famous.
This 1947 text is the true original: the sixteen chapters stand as Levi first wrote them, in the order of urgency he describes in his Preface rather than in a strictly chronological sequence. Its closing pages are the original Storia di dieci giorni (story of ten days) recounting the ten days between the Germans’ abandonment of the camp and the arrival of the Red Army, with the sick left in the infirmary (the Ka-Be) and Charles and Levi for a time alone among the dying.
The book is framed by the opening poem “Voi che vivete sicuri” (You who live secure), which gives the book its title and its summons — “Considerate se questo è un uomo” (Consider whether this is a man) — and by a Preface dated “dalla prigionia” in which Levi insists that none of the facts is invented and that the book is not a new indictment but “documents for a calm study of certain aspects of the human soul.”
Context
Levi, born in Turin in 1919 into a liberal Jewish family, graduated in chemistry in the summer of 1941 (under the Fascist racial laws of 1938, which had barred Jews from academic employment). He joined the resistance after 8 September 1943, was arrested in the Val d’Aosta in December 1943, and was sent to the Fossoli transit camp near Modena before being transported with his fellow Italian Jews to Auschwitz in a freight train on 22 February 1944 — the journey he records at the opening of the book.
The book is the Italian-Jewish voice of the Holocaust, the counterpart within this collection to the Fascist and Nazi sources that produced the catastrophe: it stands at the far end of the interwar Europe the wiki surveys, as the endpoint of the racial laws and deportations documented in the regime sources. Unlike the official Fascist histories of Italy in the collection, Levi writes as the victim, a prisoner in the Lager.
Contents

Prefazione — the Preface, written in prison; the book as “a calm study of certain aspects of the human soul”; none of the facts invented; the chapters written not in logical succession but in order of urgency, “mainly for the purpose of inward liberation.”
Voi che vivete sicuri — the dedicatory poem, “Se questo è un uomo.”
Il viaggio — the deportation: the carriage, the journey from Fossoli to Auschwitz, the arrival, the first selection, the shaving and tattooing, the transformation into “Häftling” 174517.
Sul fondo — on the bottom: the division into Arbeitskommandos, the daily struggle for bread and soup, the initiation into the camp’s rules.
Ka-Be — the Krankenbau (infirmary): the camp’s limited “care” for the sick, the selection of those to be gassed, the precarious balance of staying alive.
Le nostre notti — our nights: the dreams of home, the “dream of the unattainable,” the nightmare of the soup.
Il lavoro — the work: the labor details, the Buna works, the cold, the exhaustion.
Una buona giornata — a good day: a day without blows, without selections; a day of relative ease and of the exchange of bread for extra soup.
Al di qua del bene e del male — on this side of good and evil: the camp’s ethics, the moral degradation imposed by hunger and cold.
I sommersi ed i salvati — the drowned and the saved: the camp hierarchy, the “Prominents,” the Primos who survive by privileged posts, and the mass who drown; the distinction that gives the title of Levi’s last book.
Esame di chimica — the chemistry examination: how Levi, as a chemist, was steered toward a laboratory post (the Buna “Kommandos”) and so toward survival.
Il canto di Ulisse — the song of Ulysses: the famous chapter in which Levi tries to recall Dante’s Inferno, Ulysses’ speech on the pursuit of knowledge, in a moment of shared humanity with the young Frenchman Jean.
I fatti dell’estate — the events of the summer: the summer of 1944, the arrival of the Hungarians, the crematoria working at full capacity, the approach of the front.
Ottobre 1944 — October 1944: the great selection of 20 October 1944, in which a quarter of the camp’s prisoners were sent to the gas chamber; Levi was saved.
Kraus — the portrait of one prisoner who drowns.
Die drei Leute vom Labor — the three men from the laboratory: Levi’s comrades in the chemical Kommando.
L’ultimo — the last one: the last day.
Storia di dieci giorni — story of ten days: the original closing chapter, from the abandonment of the camp by the SS to the arrival of the Soviet army, Levi and Charles in the infirmary among the dying, “the complicated miracles of the aerial duels” overhead.

Access

Raw text: levi-se-questo-e-un-uomo-1947.txt (2,822 lines; ~359,000 characters) — the full clean text extracted from the PDF’s embedded text layer (Adobe Acrobat Pro DC Paper Capture); form-feed page markers removed.
Notes on extraction: the PDF carries a usable embedded OCR text layer produced by Adobe Acrobat’s Paper Capture plug-in; the layer is legible throughout with isolated OCR slips (e.g. “I944” for “1944,” scattered misread characters); no re-OCR was required. Structure (Preface, poem, sixteen chapters, closing Storia di dieci giorni) confirmed against the printed running heads and page numbers (pp. 11–133).

sources/mi-rebelion-en-barcelona-azana-1.title: Manuel Azaña — Mi rebelión en Barcelona (1935)
sources/mi-rebelion-en-barcelona-azana-1.content:
Manuel Azaña — Mi rebelión en Barcelona
Full bibliographic citation — Manuel Azaña (1880–1940). Mi rebelión en Barcelona. — 2nd edition, 1935. “Propiedad del autor. Copyright by Manuel Azaña, 1935.” Imprenta “Sáez Hermanos”, Martín de los Heros 65, Madrid. The volume gathers Azaña’s prison memoir of the events of October 1934 — the proclamation of the Catalan State within the Spanish Federal Republic by the Generalidad and the crushing of it under martial law — together with two of his parliamentary and public addresses and a legal appendix reproducing the documents of his prosecution.
Manuel Azaña, the liberal republican statesman who had been prime minister of the Republic from 1931 to 1933 and its most prominent parliamentary figure, was detained at Barcelona on 8 October 1934, four days after the general strike and the Catalan revolt that his enemies charged him with instigating. He wrote Mi rebelión en Barcelona while held, first aboard the Uruguay and then the prison ship Ciudad de Cádiz off Barcelona, and aboard the Barcaiztegui in December; the title answers his own indictment for rebellion. The book is dedicated “Al Excmo. Señor D. Ángel Ossorio.” Its narrative is a defence of his conduct in the autumn of 1934 and a rebuke to the campaign against him, and it closes with the Supreme Court’s free dismissal of his case.
The text is 10,739 lines, extracted from a 319-page PDF whose embedded text layer was clean (Microsoft Word-generated), no re-OCR required.
Content Summary
Front matter. Title page; dedication to Ángel Ossorio; “A la opinión pública” — an open letter signed by public men who were not Azaña’s co-partisans, protesting that what was being done against him was not opposition but persecution: “No se aspira a vencerle, sino a aniquilarle.” The colophon records the second edition and the copyright of 1935.
Mi rebelión en Barcelona (six sections, I–VI)
The memoir proper, written in the first person from aboard the ships of his detention.
I — Barcelona, noviembre a bordo del “Galiano”. Azaña opens: “De pronto, cuando tenía a mano el sosiego y empezaba a retupir la tela sensible, hollada hasta la urdimbre, una ocurrencia singular me fuerza a mover la pluma por desazones políticas.” Detained and afloat, he resolves to give his account of the political storms that had carried him there.
II. “Finando julio vine a Cataluña en demanda de ciertas aguas para descansar y curarme.” His arrival in Catalonia in late July for his health, the months before the October events, and the ironies of his being charged as a conspirator for the very journey he had made to recover from illness.
III. “La buena fortuna nos deparó al otro día un cielo radiante.” The narrative of the days leading to the revolt and his position amid the Catalan crisis.
IV — “Hombre sospechoso”. The charge of being a suspect man — his status as one watched and calumniated, and his account of the summer of 1934 when, he insists, he had no part in any conspiracy.
V. “En los días postreros de septiembre supimos en Madrid que don Jaime Carner había muerto.” From the death of Carner and the gathering tension of late September to the eve of the October rising.
VI — Barcelona, diciembre a bordo del “Barcaiztegui”. “La huelga general me recluyó en el hotel desde la mañana del viernes.” The general strike that confined him to his hotel, the revolt, his arrest, and his conveyance to the ships — the closing of the narrative aboard the Barcaiztegui in December.
El Gobierno de la República y la ley catalana de Cultivos
A parliamentary speech in the Cortes, 25 June 1934: “Señores diputados: Me hago cargo de la indicación del señor Presidente de la Cámara y voy a molestar brevísimos momentos vuestra atención.” Azaña’s defence of the Republic’s government and its relation to the Catalan law of land-cultivation contracts.
Discurso a los republicanos catalanes
A public address at Barcelona, 10 August 1934: “Entre las adhesiones a este acto que se han recibido y leído figura una que ya recibí esta mañana personalmente: la de un veterano correligionario barcelonés, que se suscribe con el nombre de ‘superviviente de la primera República’.” Azaña’s speech to the Catalan republicans weeks before the October rising.
Apéndices
A legal dossier reproducing the papers of his prosecution: the certification of the secretario de Gobierno del Tribunal Supremo (Luis Cornide Quiroga) of the case formed on the “rebelión de la Generalidad de Cataluña”; the cipher telegram of 10 October 1934 recording Azaña’s detention aboard the Uruguay on 8 October; the dictamen del señor fiscal of 12 October; the statement of HECHOS — the proclamation of the Estado Catalán on the night of 6 October and the declaration of a state of war by the Republic’s government; the juridical argument (“La inmunidad parlamentaria”, “La detención ilegal”, “Por qué está preso el testigo”) and numbered appendix studies: II. El estado de guerra, III. La garantía de las setenta y dos horas, IV. Un delito patente. The dossier closes with the auto ordering the sobreseimiento libre of the case, the Court holding that the investigation showed no participation by the querellados — Luis Bello Trompeta and Manuel Azaña — in the proclamation of the Catalan State.
The volume closes with the Índice and a list of Azaña’s published works.
Key Data Points









































AttributeDetailAuthorManuel Azaña (1880–1940)TitleMi rebelión en BarcelonaPublished2nd ed., Imprenta “Sáez Hermanos”, Madrid, 1935 (copyright Manuel Azaña, 1935)Source fileMi rebelión en Barcelona -- Manuel Azaña, -- 442ba64e7df33b1865e2d95e3f606cd1 -- Anna's Archive.pdf (319 pp.)Raw filewiki/raw/mi-rebelion-en-barcelona-azana-1935.txtLines10,739SectionsMemoir (6 sections, I–VI) + 2 speeches + legal appendix (HECHOS + 4 numbered studies)SignificanceThe accused statesman’s own account of the October 1934 Catalan revolt and his arrest — the liberal-republican voice of the period set against the Catalanist and authoritarian sources, the Spanish counterpart in the wiki’s interwar set to Madariaga’s history and the A sangre y fuego chronicle of the Civil War
Relationship to the Wiki
Azaña gives the wiki the testimony of the imprisoned liberal statesman at the moment the Spanish Republic’s internal crisis broke in Catalonia in October 1934. Where Madariaga surveyed Spain from exile, Chaves Nogales chronicled the Civil War, Aznar the Nationalist campaigns, Hayes the wartime embassy years, Tusell volume II the Republic and Civil War, and Tusell volume III the full arc of the Franco dictatorship, Azaña speaks from inside the 1934 events — as the accused, writing his own “rebellion” against the charge of rebellion. His parliamentary and public speeches and the appended legal record of the sobreseimiento libre document the Republic’s constitutional crisis and the Catalan question from the pen of the man who had led the Republic at its height.

sources/mision-de-guerra-en-espana-hayes.title: Carlton J. H. Hayes — Misión de Guerra en España, 1942–1945
sources/mision-de-guerra-en-espana-hayes.content:
Carlton J. H. Hayes — Misión de Guerra en España, 1942–1945
Full bibliographic citation — Carlton J. H. Hayes (1882–1964). Misión de Guerra en España, 1942–1945. — Spanish translation of Wartime Mission in Spain, 1942–1945 (New York: Macmillan, 1945). The author was U.S. Ambassador to Spain from May 1942 to January 1945.
Carlton J. H. Hayes, the Columbia University historian of Europe who served as Franklin Roosevelt’s Ambassador to Franco’s Spain during the Second World War, wrote this as a personal memoir of his three-year mission. The task, as the publisher’s note states, was “contrarrestar las presiones del Eje sobre la España de Franco y conseguir que permaneciera al margen de la guerra, concediendo facilidades y auxilio a los Estados Unidos y sus aliados” — a double commission, both to keep Spain from joining the Axis and to encourage it to resist any German advance across the Peninsula (vital for the planned North African invasion). The book is his account of how, over three years, Spain granted the Allies an increasing number of facilities, at first under severe German threats and later more readily as the Allied victory became certain.
His NOTA PRELIMINAR (dated Jericho Farm, Afton, New York, 15 September 1945) declares it “un relato personal,” neither an official book nor an apology for an ambassador, a State Department, or Spain, but “el relato sencillo y real de un historiador de lo que vio y aprendió por sí mismo,” based on a detailed personal diary, remembered conversations, private correspondence with the President, and a memory “entrenada para la historia” — deliberately avoiding State Department documents so that the manuscript needed no departmental review. It is the American ambassador’s eyewitness account of Spain’s wartime neutrality from the Allied side, the diplomatic counterpart to the Nationalist military history of Aznar and the regime sources.
The text is 13,684 lines, extracted from the EPUB container, clean text layer, no OCR required.
Content Summary
Opening with the front matter and the author’s NOTA PRELIMINAR (his personal-narrative method and his refusal of State Department censorship), the book proceeds in nine chapters tracing his mission from appointment to departure:

Se me nombra Embajador en España. Hayes’s Columbia professorship and internationalism, the coming of the Second World War, and his appointment as Ambassador to Spain in the spring of 1942.
Primeros contactos e impresiones. His first contacts and impressions of Spain on arrival.
En brega con la no-beligerancia española. Struggling with Spain’s policy of non-belligerency, the early period of Axis pressure.
Obtenemos facilidades. The winning of facilities from the Spanish government for the Allies.
Corrientes opuestas. The opposing currents — Axis agents and their influence in Spain, set against the Allied mission.
Progresos de la neutralidad española. The progress of Spanish neutrality as the war turned.
La crisis del wolfram. The tungsten (wolfram) crisis — the Allied struggle to cut off Germany’s crucial wolfram exports from Spain.
La benévola neutralidad española. Spain’s growing “benevolent neutrality” toward the Allies as victory approached.
De cómo dejé a España. His departure from Spain in January 1945 and his assessment of the mission.

Key Data Points













































AttributeDetailAuthorCarlton J. H. Hayes (1882–1964), Columbia historian, U.S. Ambassador to Spain 1942–45TitleMisión de Guerra en España, 1942–1945 (orig. Wartime Mission in Spain, 1942–1945)PublishedMacmillan, New York, 1945; this text from a Spanish translationSourceEPUB container; clean text layerRaw filewiki/raw/mision-de-guerra-en-espana-hayes-1945.txtLines13,684Chapters9 (appointment → first contacts → non-belligerency → facilities → opposing currents → neutrality → wolfram crisis → benevolent neutrality → departure)CoverageSpain’s wartime diplomacy and neutrality, May 1942 – January 1945SignificanceThe U.S. ambassador’s firsthand account of Franco Spain’s wartime neutrality — the Allied diplomatic voice on the Spain of 1942–45, complementary to Aznar’s Nationalist military history and to the wider European sources
Relationship to the Wiki
Hayes gives the wiki its source for the late period of Franco Spain — the three war years 1942–45 seen from the American Embassy in Madrid. As the ambassador who worked to keep Spain neutral and to extract Allied facilities and (eventually) the wolfram halt from the Spanish government, he is the Allied-side diplomatic observer of the Spain that Aznar’s Nationalist military history celebrates, that Madariaga’s retrospective history judges, and that Tusell’s volume II (Republic and Civil War) and volume III (the dictatorship) synthesise. His memoir, written immediately after the war (September 1945), extends the Spanish cluster into the Second World War period and sits beside Tusell’s chapters on the interventionist temptation of 1940–42 and the hesitant neutrality of 1942–45; it complements the German, Italian and Russian wartime sources in the wiki with an American witness on the Iberian periphery.

sources/pini-storia-del-fascismo-1928.title: Pini & Bresadola — Storia del Fascismo: Guerra – Rivoluzione – Regime (1928)
sources/pini-storia-del-fascismo-1928.content:
Storia del Fascismo: Guerra – Rivoluzione – Regime (1928)
Identity
Storia del Fascismo (History of Fascism) is a narrative history of the rise and consolidation of Italian Fascism by Giorgio Pini (1899–1987) and Federico Bresadola, published by the Libreria del Littorio, Roma, 1928 (Year VI of the Fascist era). Giorgio Pini — who had already published the mass-market biography Benito Mussolini. La sua vita fino ad oggi (1926, eight editions, 190,000 copies, Dutch translation) — here writes with Bresadola a full-length, regime-published chronicle of the Fascist revolution, from its nineteenth-century precursors to the established regime of the mid-1920s. The archive.org scan is a copy held by the University of Michigan (shelfmark DG 571 .P65), a gift of Prof. M. Levi, bound in the full leather-and-gilt library form and carrying a sculpted portrait plate of “Il Duce” (by Cleto Tomba) as its frontispiece.
It is the fourth Italian-language source in this wiki. Where Businelli’s Rivoluzione fascista (1933) is a compact movement-insider origin-story running 1912–1922, Volpe’s Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) is the collected journalism of an academic fellow-traveller, and Farinacci’s Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista (1937) is the exhaustive documentary party-history of the single crisis year 1919 — Pini & Bresadola’s is the broad, continuous, didactic chronicle running from the 1890s to the mid-1920s, covering in one sweep the whole arc announced in its subtitle: Guerra – Rivoluzione – Regime (War, Revolution, Regime).
Character of the source
A partisan, didactic and self-consciously foundational history written from within the movement and published by the Fascist state’s own book distributor (Libreria del Littorio). The preface declares the authors’ aim — directed “ai giovani” (to the young) — to form a real and ideal historical consciousness through “pagine modeste” on the advent of the regime: the state formed “fatally” over the old political situation, by popular adhesion, the dedication of martyrs and the “genial and victorious will of Benito Mussolini.” The narrative is organized into chapters that read as a running title of Fascism’s own self-justification — the collapse of the liberal order after Adua, the red menace of Socialism and the “settimana rossa,” interventionism and the war, the founding of the Fasci (23 March 1919), the Fiume undertaking, squadrism and the “convulsione insanguinata,” the March on Rome, the “prova” of the Matteotti murder, and the consolidation of the regime. It is therefore less a detached history than the regime’s canonical early account of its own origins and victory, written while the consolidation was still fresh.
Contents (structure)
The volume is organized into a Prefazione, seventeen chapters and a Conclusione, in chronological sequence. Chapter headings and page numbers follow the printed Indice:

Prefazione (p. v): the authors’ didactic programme; Proudhon (1863) on Italy’s future, Oriani (1890) on the national conscience, Sorel (1912) as the intellectual prologue
I. Il Tempo dei Precursori (1896–1900) (p. 3): the fall of Crispi after Adua; Masonic democracy; the volunteers at Domokos and the sailors in China; the assassination of the King
II. Nazionalismo e Sindacalismo (1900–1910) (p. 23): the Socialist tide; the policy of compromise; a new generation; the liberal method; pacifist Italy in the Triple Alliance
III. La Conquista Libica (1911–1912) (p. 47): the minority that drags the people along; the people fight; the origins of the world war; immaturity; the two souls of Socialism
IV. Rivolta Prematura (1913–1914) (p. 69): universal suffrage; Mussolini; the “settimana rossa”
V. Interventismo (1914–1915) (p. 89): between past and future; Mussolini the interventionist; the “radiose giornate di maggio”
VI. La Guerra (1915–1918) (p. 113): the war of the liberals; vain alarm; Caporetto; Vittorio Veneto
VII. Fondazione dei Fasci (1919) (p. 143): troubled months; 23 March; the defeat at Versailles
VIII. Governo senza Fede (1919–1920) (p. 169): the Nitti ministry; D’Annunzio’s gesture; months of shame
IX. L’Impresa di Fiume (1919–1920) (p. 193): the Adriatic question; the March of Ronchi; Fascism for Fiume; the Carta del Carnaro; the Natale di sangue
X. Convulsione Insanguinata (1920) (p. 239): Giolitti reappears; the beginning of the resurgence; 21 November
XI. Controffensiva Nazionale (1921) (p. 265): the bitter struggle; Fascism in the provinces; Giolitti abandons power
XII. Le Camicie Nere (1921) (p. 285): squadrism; Fascism organizes; Sarzana and Modena; the exhaustion of the liberal government
XIII. Marcia su Roma (1922) (p. 319): political dissolution; the extreme anti-Fascist proof; the ideal revolt
XIV. Formazione del Regime (1922–1924) (p. 353): Corfù; the opposition resumes; backward work
XV. La Prova (1924) (p. 385): the Matteotti crime; Avanti!; the Aventine; provincial Fascists, forward!; new intransigence
XVI. Conquista dello Stato (1925–1927) (p. 413): 3 January; the works of the regime; the Fascist economy; syndical organization; the reorganization of the armed forces; the party reform; the Circolare ai prefetti; the Carta del Lavoro
XVII. L’Italia Fascista nel Mondo (p. 453): the struggle for expansion; the reconquest of the colonies; the Adriatic settlement; toward the future
Conclusione (p. 507): the Roman Empire that was caesarean and Catholic must renew itself after the conquest of national unity; the Fascist state as the latest-formed of the European states, certain and already realizing its imperial future

The volume closes with the printed Indice (pp. 539–543 of the scan) listing all chapters and the Conclusione. Back matter includes the plate “Il Duce” (frontispiece), the author’s prior works, the Prefazione, and the library’s gift and date-due cards. The text of the body itself ends at printed p. 503 (scan p. 531), followed by the Conclusione and the Indice.
OCR / extraction quality
Source is the Anna’s Archive dump of the University of Michigan scan (folder 39015057193826, 554 numbered TXT page files), delivered as a ZIP of the OCR’d pages. The book is set in Roman (Antiqua) type, and the OCR is clean, fluent and fully readable across the body of the work — proper accented Italian forms, printed page numbers and running heads are all present and legible. Only isolated slips appear (e.g. the fragmented “INDICE” page 539 with its interleaved stray text, “GVERRA” for “GUERRA” and “RIVOLV ZIONE” for “RIVOLUZIONE” on the back cover plate, and short scattered fragments on some plate/divider pages). Per protocol the embedded full-text OCR layer is the extraction source. Result: a clean Italian transcription saved as wiki/raw/pini-storia-del-fascismo-1928.txt (554 pages, 553 form feeds, 13,648 lines). The structure above has been reconstructed from the printed Indice and cross-checked against the body chapter headings.
Cross-references

Companion Italian source: Businelli, Rivoluzione fascista (1933) — the movement-insider origin-story of Fascism (1912–1922), a more compact account of the same rise that Pini & Bresadola here narrate at full length.
Companion Italian source: Volpe, Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) — the collected wartime-and-Fascist political journalism (1916–1928) of the academic historian Gioacchino Volpe, published the same year.
Companion Italian source: Volpe, History of the Fascist Movement (1936) — the English translation of Volpe’s continuous narrative of the Fascist movement, the canonical mid-1930s regime historiography of the same arc.
Companion Italian source: Farinacci, Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. I (1937) — the exhaustive documentary party-history of the single crisis year 1919, which here forms chapter VII of the present chronicle.
These stand alongside the German Dokumente der deutschen Politik series (Friedrichs Bands 1–4; Volz Bands 5–6) and the German regime-vantage sources (Geisow; Büttner) as the Fascist (Italian) counterpart to the Nazi (German) documentary record, and against the Soviet sources (Pokrovsky, VKP(b) Short Course, Stalin) as the third revolutionary regime’s official self-account.

sources/pokrovsky-russkaya-istoriya-v-sa.title: Pokrovsky — Russian History in the Briefest Outline (4th ed., 1933)
sources/pokrovsky-russkaya-istoriya-v-sa.content:
Pokrovsky — Russian History in the Briefest Outline
Mikhail Nikolaevich Pokrovsky (1868–1932) — Русская история в самом сжатом очерке (Russian History in the Briefest Outline). Fourth (combined) edition, Partizdat, Moscow, 1933. Print run 200,000 copies.





























AuthorM. N. Pokrovsky — the leading Soviet Marxist historian of the 1920s; deputy people’s commissar of education of the RSFSR; head of the Institute of Red Professors; author of the standard Marxist survey of Russian historyEditionFourth, 1933 (Partizdat). The text of all three parts printed without changes from the 10th edition (Parts I–II) and the 4th edition (Part III), reviewed and corrected by the author for press in his lifetime; editor’s note added after his death (d. 10 April 1932)StructureThree parts bound as one volume + two appendices + subject index + maps and plans; 623 scan pages; ~38,138 OCR linesPeriodParts I–II: from the earliest times to the end of the 19th century; Part III: the revolutionary period, 1897–1917, centered on the 1905 revolution (with the introduction framing 1897–1929 and the defense of the October Revolution)NoteVolume includes a biographical sketch of Pokrovsky and Lenin’s letter to Pokrovsky praising the work; maps by Prof. N. V. Kudryashov
Contents. The canonical Soviet Marxist survey of Russian history. Part I begins with general concepts of historical materialism (“why we need to know the past,” class struggle as the motor of history, nature and economy), then the first centuries of Russian history: the Scythians and Slavs, Kievan Rus and the “Russian Truth,” feudal Russia, the Mongol invasion, the formation of the Moscow state, Moscow’s struggle with Novgorod, the decomposition of Moscow feudalism, and the oprichnina; the “peasant revolution” of the Time of Troubles (the False Dmitrii, Bolotnikov, Minin and the fall of Moscow); the Romanov state and the schism; the Northern War and the Russian Empire. Part II (capitalism) treats the serf-owning state, commercial capitalism, the Decembrists, the populist (narodnik) revolution — Herzen, Chernyshevsky, Bakunin, Lavrov, the “Going to the People,” the People’s Will and the assassination of Alexander II — and the rise of the workers’ movement, the growth of the proletariat in the 1880s–90s, strikes, the first Marxist circles, Plekhanov and the Emancipation of Labour group. Part III covers the revolutionary period: the economy of the revolutionary era, the industrial crisis and the workers’ movement, the beginning of mass peasant movement, the Russo-Japanese War, “9 January and the Potemkin,” the peasant uprisings, the general strike and the armed uprising of October–December 1905, the “constitutional efforts” of the bourgeoisie and the Duma, the 1905 revolution in the borderlands (Caucasus, Poland, the Baltic, Finland), and the Stolypin era (“Stolypinshchina”) with its agrarian policy and state coup of 3 June 1907.
Character of the source. The definitive Soviet Marxist narrative, written by the most influential Bolshevik historian of his generation and endorsed by Lenin. Written from a strict class-struggle and historical-materialist standpoint; reflects the orthodoxy of the Soviet historical profession in the early 1930s, before the later Stalin-era attack on the “Pokrovsky school.” Part III in particular is a memoir-historian’s account of a revolution in which Pokrovsky himself participated. A companion volume in this folder — Shestakov’s Short Course of the History of the USSR (1937), a Stalin-era school textbook covering the Soviet period — has its own source page.
OCR. Good quality. This volume had no embedded text layer, so it was rendered page-by-page (ddjvu) and OCR’d with Tesseract (-l rus). Typical Cyrillic OCR errors present (e.g. “армiя” variants, Ѣ/Е confusion in pre-reform spellings, garbled Roman numerals). Headings and chapter structure checked against the table of contents.
Raw text: wiki/raw/pokrovsky-russkaya-istoriya-v-samom-szhatom-ocherke-1933.txt.

Biographical sketch and Lenin’s letter
Introductory matter: a biographical note on Pokrovsky and the text of Lenin’s letter to Pokrovsky (from the sanitarium of the People’s Commissariat for Education, December 1920), in which Lenin asked him to write the “Russian history in the briefest outline” and warmly endorsed the projected work (“I ask you to undertake this, and we would then have a work… worthy of our attention”).
Part I. From the earliest times to the end of the 19th century
Chapter: General concepts of history
Why we need to know the past; the changeability of the world and of human life; knowledge of the past as power over the future; the “laws of history”; peasant revolutions before and now, worker revolutions; class struggle as the development of history, classes and economy, materialism; the bourgeois and proletarian understanding of history; the influence of nature — climate, seas, mountains — on culture and political development; nature and economy in Russia; the dependence of man on nature; “at the basis of history lies not nature but labour”; class struggle and the development of technique.
Chapter: The first centuries of Russian history
The Scythians; the Slavs and Slavic colonization; the life of the ancient Slavs; the accounts of foreign writers; the Russian princes, the Varangians and the Khazars; the “foundation of the Russian state”; the princes as slave-owners and slave-traders; the “Rus” and the “Russian Truth,” judicial customs, classes and class struggle reflected in it; the Novgorod commune and the “veche”; the causes of the decline of the ancient Russian cities; the “crusades”; the Tatar invasion; the transformation of Kievan Rus into a rural country; the culture of old Rus; the “Tale of Igor’s Campaign” and the chronicles; the baptism of Rus and the significance of Christianity as a class phenomenon.
Chapter: The formation of the Moscow state
Russian feudalism; the lord (boiarin) and the peasant; the forms of peasant obligations; the appanage order and the destruction of appanage fragmentation; the prerequisites of the national monarchy; why unification occurred around Moscow; the Orthodox church and its alliance with the Tatar khan and the Moscow prince; the economic ground of unification; the growth of the city of Moscow; the separation of craftsmen and merchants, the formation of the bourgeoisie; the struggle of Moscow with Novgorod (Zavoloch’e, furs and silver, European connections, the composition of the population, the outcome — Moscow as the all-Russian commercial centre); the decomposition of Moscow feudalism — commodity economy, the formation of the market, money, barter, corvée, serfdom; class struggle in the Muscovite state; the publicists, Peresvetov; the alliance of the small landowner and commercial capital; Kazan and Astrakhan; the Livonian War; the crisis of the service-land system and the coup of 1584 — the oprichnina and its class meaning; predatory economy, the flight of peasants, famine; the fugitives and the colonization of the southern borderland; the Cossacks; the growth of revolutionary mood; the False Dmitrii.
Chapter: The peasant revolution
