The uprising against Godunov; Russian emigration and the Polish landlords; the Cossacks; the False Dmitrii; his victory and legislation; the conspiracy of Shuiskii; Shuiskii as the merchant-boyar tsar; the uprising of the southern Ukraine; Bolotnikov and the peasant revolution; the second Cossack revolution — Tushino; the class stratification of the revolution; the bourgeois upper layers of Tushino and commercial capital; the dethronement of Shuiskii; the alliance of the Poles with the propertied classes of Russia and its bankruptcy; the city bourgeoisie at the head of the struggle — Minin; the Nizhnii Novgorod militia takes Moscow; the candidacy of the Romanovs as the result of a new alliance of the bourgeoisie; the class meaning of the Romanov monarchy; tsarist power and commercial capital — the “gosti”; the Muscovite state and the regular army; the development of serfdom; urban uprisings of the second half of the 17th century; the schism (raskol) and the “streltsy” disorders; the Ukraine — its economic conditions, Zaporozh’e, the Cossack revolution, Khmelnytsky and the Muscovite state.
Part II. Capitalism
The serf-owning state and commercial capital; the reforms of Peter and the northern war; the Russian Empire and the Baltic question; the peasant war of Pugachev; the crisis of serfdom in the early 19th century; the growth of the bourgeoisie.
Chapter: The Decembrists
The Russian officer corps after 1812; the officer intelligentsia; the Decembrists and the bourgeoisie; the program of the Decembrists; the Union of Welfare (Soyuz Blagodenstviya); the republican current — S. Murav’ev, Pestel; the project of agrarian reform and armed uprising; the death of Alexander I and the crisis in the tsarist family; the Decembrists forced to act; their tactics and Nicholas’s tactics; why he remained victor; the Decembrists and the popular masses; the powerlessness of the bourgeois revolution in Russia and its causes.
Chapter: The populist (narodnik) revolution
Echoes of the Decembrist uprising under Nicholas: the mood of the intelligentsia; the Third Department and the gendarmes; the Petrashevtsy affair; the 1860s — the intelligentsia breaks away from the bourgeoisie; the “raznochintsy”; the political program of the petty-bourgeois intelligentsia; the “Velikoruss”; the Polish uprising; Poland under Nicholas I; the Sevastopol defeat; the Poles and Napoleon III; Alexander II’s provocative policy; the 1863 uprising and its suppression by Murav’ev; reaction in Poland; tsarist demagogy; the bourgeoisie finally breaks from revolution; petty-bourgeois socialism — its ideology; the village commune (obshchina) — its historical meaning and the hopes attached to it; Herzen; Chernyshevsky; “Young Russia”; the program of socialist revolution; Karakozovshchina and a new burst of tsarist demagogy; Lavrov, the “Historical Letters”; the philosophy and history of the petty-bourgeois intelligentsia; the practice of populism; the Chaikovskists, the Dolgushinists; “revolt” (buntarstvo), Bakunin and the Paris Commune; the “Going to the People”; its weakness — the absence of economic prerequisites for revolution; the trials; the turn in the mood of the bourgeoisie; the unfinished character of the reforms; the Turkish War; the change of tactics of the “rebels,” terror; Zhelyabov and the Executive Committee; the program of the People’s Will; Alexander II and the hunt for the “crowned beast”; the new attempt at tsarist demagogy — Loris-Melikov; 1 March 1881.
Chapter: The workers’ movement
Alexander III; the significance of the “1880s”; the economic situation — a new agrarian crisis, the revival of the “government system”; its influence on the peasantry; the “otrezki” (cut-offs), the “otrubniki”; the proletarianization of the peasantry and the unsuccessful struggle against it; the revival of serfdom — the counter-reforms of Alexander III and the role of the zemstvo; the University Statute of 1884 and the student movement; the “eighties-men” (vos’midesyatniki); the industrial proletariat and the industrial upswing of the end of the 19th century; the origin and composition of the Russian proletariat; its conditions of existence in the 1880s — housing, food, occupational diseases; its legal condition; strikes — the era of Nicholas II, the peasant reform and the proletariat; the strikes of the 1870s and the revolutionary movement; the workers’ unions; Khalturin; the industrial crisis of the beginning of the 1880s; the Morozov strike and its influence; the factory legislation of Alexander III in theory and practice; the industrial upswing of the 1890s and a new wave of strikes; Russian Marxism; Plekhanov; the Emancipation of Labour group; the first social-democratic organizations in Russia; the social-democrats and the People’s Will; economic agitation and political struggle; the unions of struggle for the emancipation of the working class.
Part III. The revolutionary period (1897–1917), centered on 1905
Introduction
“The last period of Russian history, which we still have to study (1897–1929), is entirely taken up with the preparation and immediate consequences of one great event — the Great Russian Revolution.” The introduction frames the 1905 revolution and the defense of the October Revolution of 1917, warning of the continuing threat of bourgeois intervention. In contrast to Parts I–II (which dealt with the irrevocable past), Part III explains the author’s own present.
Chapter I. The economy of the revolutionary period
Chapter II. The industrial crisis and the workers’ movement
Chapter III. The beginning of the mass movement in the countryside
Chapter IV. 9 January and the “Potemkin”
The shooting of the peaceful procession of workers to the Winter Palace (“Bloody Sunday,” 9 January 1905) under the leadership of Father Gapon; the mutiny of the battleship “Prince Potemkin Tauride” in June 1905, its course (the shooting of officers, the raising of the red flag, Odessa, Constanta) and its significance.
Chapter V. The Russo-Japanese War
The Japanese war of 1904–05, the defeats at Mukden and Tsushima, and their revolutionary consequences.
Chapter VI. The peasant uprisings
Chapter VII. The general strike and the armed uprising
The October general strike of 1905; the formation of the first Soviet of Workers’ Deputies in Petersburg; the December armed uprising in Moscow (Presnya) and its defeat.
Chapter VIII. The “constitutional efforts” of the bourgeoisie
The attempts of the liberal bourgeoisie to obtain a constitution; the Manifesto of 17 October 1905; the Duma; the differences between the revolution and the liberalism of the propertied classes.
Chapter IX. The 1905 revolution in the borderlands
The revolution in the Caucasus, Poland, the Baltic provinces, and Finland; the pogroms in Odessa and elsewhere; the national revolutionary movement at the edge of the empire.
Chapter X. The Stolypin era (Stolypinshchina)
Stolypin as minister of internal affairs; the state coup of 3 June 1907; the dissolution of the Second Duma and the new electoral law; the Stolypin agrarian reform and its effect on the peasantry.
Appendices
Appendix 1. On Russian feudalism, the origin and character of absolutism in Russia
Pokrovsky’s article arguing the reality of Russian feudalism and analyzing the origin and class character of Russian absolutism in connection with commercial capital.
Appendix 2. The role of the working class in the 1905 revolution
Text of Pokrovsky’s speech to the activists of the Krasnopresnensky district of Moscow (11 December 1930), comparing the 1905 revolution with the Great French Revolution and analyzing the continuing revolutionary struggle.

sources/rosenberg-geschichte-der-deutsch.title: Arthur Rosenberg — History of the German Republic (1935)
sources/rosenberg-geschichte-der-deutsch.content:
History of the German Republic
Arthur Rosenberg — Geschichte der deutschen Republik (History of the German Republic). Verlagsanstalt »Graphia«, Karlsbad, 1935. A history of the Weimar Republic from the November revolution of 1918 to its death in 1930, written by a left-socialist historian in exile after the Nazi seizure of power.





























AuthorArthur Rosenberg (1889–1943) — German-Jewish historian of antiquity and of the modern German revolution; a left-wing Independent Social Democrat (USPD) who sat in the Reichstag 1924–1928 and taught at the University of Berlin until 1933; dismissed by the Nazis and emigratedEdition1935, Verlagsanstalt »Graphia« G. m. b. H., Karlsbad (Czechoslovakia); copyright 1935, printed in Czechoslovakia; a volume in the publisher’s exile series; dedicated to Wolfgang RosenbergStructurePreface + 9 chapters + appendices of notes and documents (“Anmerkungen und Dokumente”); 10,723 lines / ~651,000 characters of extracted textPeriod1918–1930: from the revolution of 9 November 1918 and the birth of the German Republic to the Reichstag elections of 14 September 1930 and the death of the Weimar RepublicNoteWritten in exile after 1933, drawing on the newly available sources of the decade — Stresemann’s Vermächtnis (Legacy), Wentzcke on the Ruhr struggle, Volkmann’s revolutionary history, and the unpublished protocols of the Council of People’s Deputies of November–December 1918; a companion volume to Rosenberg’s earlier Die Entstehung der Deutschen Republik (1928), which closed at 10 November 1918
Contents. A critical narrative history of the German Republic, from its birth out of the revolution of 1918 to its destruction. Rosenberg, himself a participant on the left of the revolution, recounts the November revolution, the government of the Council of People’s Deputies, the Spartacus rising and the Noske terror, the National Assembly at Weimar and the drafting of the constitution, the Kapp Putsch, the era of the “Catholic democracy” (1920–1922), the Ruhr occupation and inflation (1923), the stabilisation under Stresemann (1924–1928), and the end (1928–1930), closing with the Reichstag’s capitulation to the Brüning dictatorship in October 1930, which he calls “the death-hour of the Weimar Republic.” A substantial appendix of notes and documents follows the nine chapters.
Character of the source. A major exile history of the Weimar Republic, written from a left-socialist, explicitly critical standpoint between the seizure of power and the war. Rosenberg’s central thesis is that the bourgeois republic of 1918 was the work of the working class, that the bourgeoisie either fought the nascent republic or supported it only lukewarmly, and that the republic perished in 1930 because its fate was entrusted to the hands of the bourgeoisie while the workers — three-quarters of the people — were too divided, in ideals and in tactics, to save it. It is at once a work of history and of political reckoning by a participant, and the first major scholarly account to make systematic use of the documentary and memoir material that appeared in the decade after the revolution (Stresemann’s legacy, the Council of People’s Deputies protocols). For the interwar period it supplies the German case that this wiki’s Soviet sources (the Stalin biography and wartime collection) treat from the opposing side of the political divide.
Quality. Good. Extracted from a 264-page PDF scan with a clean ABBYY FineReader text layer (Fraktur OCR’d to Antiqua) via pdftotext -layout; continuous prose throughout. German text clean; chapter headings, page headers and document dates verified. The page header of the final narrative pages (“DER REICHSTAG KAPITULIERT”) is carried inline in the body text; a few hyphenation artefacts of OCR noted.
Raw text: wiki/raw/rosenberg-geschichte-der-deutschen-republik-1935.txt.

Vorwort (Preface)
Explains the genesis of the book as the continuation of Rosenberg’s 1928 work Die Entstehung der Deutschen Republik, which closed at 10 November 1918 for lack of accessible sources; surveys the documentary material that has since become available — the Feme (political murder) committee of the Reichstag of 1926–27, Stresemann’s Vermächtnis for 1923–1929, Wentzcke on the Ruhr struggle, Volkmann’s revolutionary history, and the unpublished protocols of the Council of People’s Deputies of November–December 1918; and states the author’s effort to avoid one-sided judgements shaped by his own political activity of 1919–1928.
Erstes Kapitel. Nach dem 9. November 1918 (After 9 November 1918)
The birth of the German Republic. The Berlin workers’ and soldiers’ councils elect the new republican government in the Circus Busch on 10 November 1918; the fall of the monarchy and the structure of revolutionary power in Berlin; the first acts of the revolution.
Zweites Kapitel. Die Regierung der Volksbeauftragten (The Government of the People’s Deputies)
The rule of the Council of People’s Deputies in November–December 1918 and January 1919, governing with dictatorial power; its composition from the three Social Democrat (SPD) deputies and the three Independent (USPD) deputies until the end of December; the internal conflicts of the revolution.
Drittes Kapitel. Spartakus und Noske (Spartacus and Noske)
The Spartacus League congress of 30 December 1918 and the founding of the Communist Party of Germany (Spartacusbund); the January rising of 1919 and its suppression under the minister Gustav Noske; the murder of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht.
Viertes Kapitel. Die Nationalversammlung in Weimar (The National Assembly at Weimar)
The elections of 19 January 1919 and the National Assembly at Weimar, summoned to give the republic its constitution and to show the revolution new paths; the drafting and adoption of the Weimar constitution.
Fünftes Kapitel. Der Kapp-Putsch (The Kapp Putsch)
The reaction after the revolution: the disappointment of popular expectations; the counter-revolutionary Kapp Putsch of March 1920, the general strike that defeated it, and the consequences for the republic.
Sechstes Kapitel. Die Zeit der katholischen Demokratie, 1920–1922 (The Era of the Catholic Democracy, 1920–1922)
The political ascendancy of the Centre party and its democratic- Catholic coalition partners in the early years of the republic; the growing burdens of the Entente’s demands and the reparations question.
Siebentes Kapitel. Ruhrbesetzung und Inflation, 1923 (Ruhr Occupation and Inflation, 1923)
The fall of the Wirth government in November 1922 and the formation of a government of high finance under the shipping magnate Cuno; the French occupation of the Ruhr, the policy of passive resistance, and the catastrophic inflation of 1923.
Achtes Kapitel. Stabilisierung und Stresemann, 1924–1928 (Stabilisation and Stresemann, 1924–1928)
The American financial power that had emerged from the war as the first power of the earth; the stabilisation of the currency, the Dawes Plan and the era of Gustav Stresemann as the period of the republic’s consolidation.
Neuntes Kapitel. Das Ende, 1928–1930 (The End, 1928–1930)
The delayed decision of the struggle waged by the generals and capitalists against the democratic workers; the crisis of the late 1920s, the rise of the National Socialists (the election gains of 14 September 1930), the Brüning dictatorship and its “toleration” by the Social Democrats; the capitulation of the Reichstag on 18 October 1930 — “the death-hour of the Weimar Republic”; the conclusion that the bourgeois republic, the work of the working class, perished because its fate was entrusted to the bourgeoisie while a divided working class could not save it.
Anmerkungen und Dokumente (Notes and Documents)
The appendix of source notes and documents for the nine chapters, citing the published protocols, memoirs and document collections used — the protocols of the Council of People’s Deputies, Rosa Luxemburg and the January action (Paul Levi), the background of the Baltic adventure, the workers’ government question of 1923, Stresemann’s Vermächtnis, America and the Dawes Plan, and the politics of 1928/29 — together with bibliographic indications. The volume closes with the publisher’s announcement of the exile series of which it forms a part.

sources/siegfried-tableau-des-partis-en-.title: André Siegfried — Tableau des partis en France (1930)
sources/siegfried-tableau-des-partis-en-.content:
Tableau des partis en France
André Siegfried — Tableau des partis en France (Picture of the Parties in France). Éditions Bernard Grasset, Paris, 1930; a volume in the series “Les Écrits” directed by Jean Guéhenno. A contemporary political geography and sociology of the French party system of the Third Republic, written at the height of the interwar period by the founder of French electoral geography.





























AuthorAndré Siegfried (1875–1959) — French political geographer and sociologist, professor at the Collège de France and the École Libre des Sciences Politiques, founder of the electoral-geographical school; author of Tableau politique de la France de l’Ouest sous la troisième République (1913), L’Angleterre d’aujourd’hui (1924) and Les États-Unis d’aujourd’hui (1927); a former parliamentary candidate who turned from candidacy to the systematic study of French politicsEdition1930, Éditions Bernard Grasset, 61 rue des Saints-Pères, Paris; a volume in the collection “Les Écrits” under the direction of Jean Guéhenno; sixth of the second series; printed by Imprimerie Arrault, Tours, 15 September 1930StructurePreface + 6 parts + 2 appendices, the parts divided into numbered sections; 11,259 lines / ~241,000 characters of extracted textPeriodThe Third Republic from the mid-nineteenth century to the interwar years, analysed from the standpoint of June 1930: the elections of 1919 (Bloc National), 1924 (Cartel des Gauches) and 1928, and the cabinets of the late 1920s (Poincaré, Tardieu, Chautemps)NoteA contemporary analytic essay, not a narrative history — Siegfried’s object is to explain what the French parties are and how the French political temperament works, in the tradition of the philosophical-medical “tableau.” He writes explicitly as a sympathetic observer: “mon cœur est à gauche, mais ma poche est à droite” (his heart is on the left, his pocket on the right). For this wiki it supplies the French case that the Russian, German and Italian sources treat from the revolutionary, National Socialist and Fascist sides — the picture of the old parliamentary republic of the centre from within, on the eve of the crises of the 1930s
Contents. A systematic portrait of the French party system and of the temperament underlying it. Part I sketches the permanent French character — France’s place in the contemporary world, the social and economic circumstances that form the French temperament, French civisme (civic-mindedness) and the challenge of industrial evolution. Part II analyses the permanent traits and determining factors of domestic politics: the parties as issuing from the French Revolution and as determined by the Industrial Revolution, and the spirit of French politics (the split between a heart on the left and a pocket on the right). Part III turns to the determining factors of foreign policy — the traditional place of external affairs in French preoccupations, the new internationalist orientation since the Dreyfus affair and the Franco-Russian alliance, and the postwar position. Part IV recounts the cycles of domestic politics since the war: how the balance of parties is struck in France, the Bloc National and the Cartel des Gauches, the Poincaré regime and its comment. Part V spreads out the fan of parties and groups — the Left, the Centre and the Right — and asks where political inspiration in France comes from. Part VI contrasts Latin and Anglo-Saxon democracy: the French conception of government and its survivals from the past, the spirit of the regime under the Third Republic, and the closing comparison of French and Anglo-Saxon democracy, concluding in defence of the individual against the world of mass and series. Two appendices tabulate the relative strength of the parties in the Chamber since the war and the principal votes of 1924–1930.
Character of the source. A contemporary, sympathetic-internal analysis of the Third Republic’s party system, written in 1930 by the man who founded the electoral-geographical study of French politics. It is not a party-aligned tract but the analytical essay of an academic who had himself stood for parliament and abandoned candidacy for the study of politics — “I decided therefore to continue to occupy myself with politics, but in the form of study and observation.” Siegfried’s thesis is that France, an old-formed country complete in its personality since the end of the eighteenth century, faces an industrial world of mass, series and the team that challenges its very individualist civilisation; that the Frenchman is politically on the left and socially conservative; and that the regime’s permanent spirit mixes popular sovereignty, an incorrigible penchant for absolutism and a latent Bonapartism, against which French democracy stands as an effort of liberation of the individual. His stated masters are Seignobos, Robert de Jouvenel, Alain, Étienne Fournol and Albert Thibaudet.
Quality. Good. Extracted from a 262-page PDF scan (Internet Archive copy) with a clean embedded LuraDocument text layer via pdftotext -layout; continuous prose throughout. French text clean and readable; the running page headers (LES PARTIS EN FRANCE, LE CARACTÈRE FRANÇAIS, POLITIQUE ÉTRANGÈRE) are carried inline in the body text and were identified as such; a few OCR splits and hyphenation artefacts noted. The complete Table des Matières was recovered from the end-of-text pages and cross-checked against the section headings in the body.
Raw text: wiki/raw/siegfried-tableau-des-partis-en-france-1930.txt.

Préface (Preface)
Explains the genesis and method of the book: Siegfried’s earlier Tableau politique de la France de l’Ouest sous la troisième République (1913), intended as the first of a series of regional studies toward “une psychologie politique de la France, basée sur la géographie” (a political psychology of France, based on geography), interrupted by the war; his own experience as a defeated parliamentary candidate (“j’étais un étranger, un exotique”) which taught him the rules of the game by seeing men rather than books; his acknowledgement of his masters — Charles Seignobos, Robert de Jouvenel (La République des camarades), Alain (Essai d’une doctrine radicale), Étienne Fournol, Albert Thibaudet (La République des professeurs) — and of his instinctive sympathy for the regime, even when criticising it; and his closing confession: “La volupté de comprendre me paraît aussi belle que l’ivresse de l’action” (the voluptuousness of understanding seems to me as beautiful as the intoxication of action).
I. Le caractère français (The French Character)
An account of the permanent national temperament that Siegfried holds to underlie the parties.
1. — La France dans le monde actuel (France in the Present-Day World)
France resembles no other country: its conceptions of production, property and individual life are its own, little understood and often isolated in a contemporary world whose code of values is transforming. Economically France is not contemporary with the countries that now set the tone (the United States, Germany, even England are countries of recent economic formation), for the French personality was already complete by the end of the eighteenth century — peasant and artisan come from the middle ages, and “tout l’essentiel était déjà là au moment de la Révolution” (everything essential was already there at the moment of the Revolution). The industrial revolution and the non-European development that displaces the centre of gravity of the planet raise the almost tragic problem of whether France, conceived and built for other circumstances, must change its character and its old political ideology, or whether there is still room for traditional France, including in that tradition the whole development of 1789.
2. — Circonstances sociales qui contribuent à la formation du caractère français (Social Circumstances Contributing to the Formation of the French Character)
The social circumstances — family, the individual, the role of the peasantry — that shape the French temperament and with it the national political disposition.
3. — Circonstances économiques qui contribuent à la formation du caractère français (Economic Circumstances Contributing to the Formation of the French Character)
The economic circumstances — the small producer, the artisan, the protectionist who thinks chiefly of the home market — that form the French character and its politics.
4. — Le caractère français (The French Character)
The synthesis of the French character itself: France as essentially adult, “dure comme ce qui est vieux” (hard as what is old), individualist, set in a world of youth and renewal.
5. — Le civisme français (French Civic-Mindedness)
The peculiar French form of civic spirit and patriotism.
6. — La France devant l’évolution industrielle contemporaine (France Before Contemporary Industrial Evolution)
France before the contemporary industrial evolution: the individual, the team and the series, and the permanent traits of the national temperament that the politics of the Third Republic reflects.
II. Les facteurs déterminants de la politique intérieure (The Determining Factors of Domestic Politics)
The permanent traits and historical determinants of French domestic politics.
1. — Quelques traits permanents (Some Permanent Traits)
The permanent traits of French political behaviour.
2. — Les partis en tant qu’issus de la Révolution française (The Parties as Issuing from the French Revolution)
The parties as issuing from the French Revolution — the founding division of the party system traced to the Revolution and its legacy.
3. — Les partis en tant que déterminés par la Révolution industrielle (The Parties as Determined by the Industrial Revolution)
The parties as determined by the Industrial Revolution — the newer social-economic division superimposed on the revolutionary inheritance.
4. — L’esprit de la politique française (The Spirit of French Politics)
The intimate contradiction of the Frenchman: “son cœur est à gauche, mais sa poche est à droite” (his heart is on the left, but his pocket is on the right) — every Frenchman has a pocket, so that a deferred prudence, his interest, comes sooner or later to contradict the extremist ideology in which he delights; this Don Quixote is always accompanied by a Sancho Panza who never leaves his side. Hence the “toujours à gauche” works only in symbolic gestures, and why France is more really democratic in spirit than the least radical, why foreigners call the French dangerous revolutionaries when they speak and petty bourgeois when they act.
III. Les facteurs déterminants de la politique étrangère (The Determining Factors of Foreign Policy)
The place of external affairs in French politics and its evolution.
1. — Place traditionnelle de la politique extérieure dans les préoccupations françaises (The Traditional Place of Foreign Policy in French Preoccupations)
The traditional place of foreign policy in French preoccupations: economically France is not turned outward — the producer is a protectionist who thinks of the home market, the voter bounded in his local horizon; the export agent, the sailor, the internationally-minded financier are rare exceptions; French deputies, unlike English MPs who take the boat to the Empire, have scarcely travelled the world, and French commercial negotiations think more of defending the market than conquering new ones.
2. — Nouvelle orientation depuis l’affaire Dreyfus (A New Orientation Since the Dreyfus Affair)
The new internationalist orientation since the Dreyfus affair: Michelet’s prophecy that in the twentieth century France would “declare peace to the world” is not the origin of the new ideology, which is foreign — France is losing the ideological initiative it had held unchallenged since the eighteenth century; the Franco-Russian alliance marks an important landmark in the history of political ideas in France.
3. — L’après-guerre (The After-War)
The postwar: the war did not create but amplified existing tendencies; what is truly new since the armistice is that external problems have imposed themselves on France “avec la force irrésistible des questions de salut public” (with the irresistible force of questions of public safety), in Seignobos’s phrase.
IV. Les cycles de notre politique intérieure depuis la guerre (The Cycles of Our Domestic Politics Since the War)
The succession of majority coalitions in the decade after the Great War.
1. — Comment se fait en France la balance des partis (How the Balance of the Parties Is Struck in France)
The mechanism by which the parliamentary balance of parties is produced in France, in light of the intimate contradiction of the Frenchman, politically on the left and socially conservative.
2. — Le bloc national et le cartel des gauches (The National Bloc and the Left Cartel)
The two great majority cycles of the 1920s. In 1919, the recent image of war impressed less than the menacing shadow of bolshevism that terrified the bourgeois; there was a resentment of the combatants against the deputies, antiparliamentary effluvia in the air more insistent than since Boulangism or the Panama affair, and a feeling that the political militant had lost prestige to the technician — the creation of the war who, under the name of expert, was to reappear in innumerable international conferences. The Left, which stood for the worker, the deputy and the militant, suffered by solidarity — “La guerre ne vous a donc rien appris?” (Has the war then taught you nothing?). Against this stands the Cartel des Gauches of 1924.
3. — Le régime Poincaré (The Poincaré Regime)
The regime of Raymond Poincaré — the stabilisation and the conservative-radical governments of the later 1920s.
4. — Commentaire (Commentary)
A general commentary drawing together the significance of the postwar cycles.
V. L’éventail des partis et des groupes (The Fan of the Parties and Groups)
After the balance of forces, “il nous reste à envisager la couleur des opinions” (we have still to envisage the colour of the opinions): the fan of parties spread across the political spectrum.
1. — La gauche (The Left)
The Left — the socialists and radicals of the republican spectrum.
2. — Le centre (The Centre)
The Centre — the moderate republican and radical-Socialist middle of the spectrum.
3. — La droite (The Right)
The Right — the conservative and nationalist parties of the spectrum.
4. — D’où vient l’inspiration politique en France (Whence Comes Political Inspiration in France)
Where political inspiration in France comes from — the sources of doctrine and opinion that feed the parties.
VI. Démocratie latine et démocratie anglo-saxonne (Latin Democracy and Anglo-Saxon Democracy)
The closing comparison of the French with the Anglo-Saxon conception of democracy.
1. — Conceptions de gouvernement et survivances du passé (Conceptions of Government and Survivals of the Past)
The French, it is said, renounce their past — in words; and yet that past survives: the trace of the old regimes is everywhere in French conceptions of government, so that to analyse them is to make a retrospective exhibition.
2. — L’esprit du régime sous la troisième république (The Spirit of the Regime Under the Third Republic)
Three persistences and three adaptations or reactions determine the permanent factors of the regime. The persistences: the affirmation of popular sovereignty (to be considered irrevocable); an incorrigible penchant for absolutism, the tenacious virus of the past that reappears nine times out of ten in those who administer or govern (“le pouvoir, dit Alain, est toujours monarchique” — power, says Alain, is always monarchical); and the Bonapartist spirit, this nostalgia for power in a regime that systematically enervates power — hence a latent antiparliamentarism, a paradoxical spectacle in a country that precisely willed parliamentarism to be everything. The adaptations or reactions are as vigorous as the causes that provoke them: because the people wish to be everything, their elected delegate must become the essential piece of the system — hence the supremacy of the deputy, of universal suffrage; and because government is enervated by its very nature…
3. — Démocratie française et démocratie anglo-saxonne (French Democracy and Anglo-Saxon Democracy)
The closing comparison. The end pursued by the French in democracy is essentially to emancipate the individual — intellectually by laicism, politically by resistance to “tyranny”: the will of each not to let himself be dominated by some other individual whose right to command is contested. In the popular preoccupation it remains secondary whether the regime produces more well-being, more comfort, a higher standard of living. Here touches the very essence of the Latin conception: democracy, like the gospel, becomes above all a state of mind, a will to liberation always awake, “un effort continuel, qui détruit à chaque instant un peu de monarchie renaissante” (a continual effort, which destroys at each instant a little of the re-born monarchy). The book closes by defending this old French political mystique — with its ridicules, its insufficiency of social output — as justified and explained only by an instinctive will to preserve the individual, the vital instinct that France will, no doubt, never renounce: should the question of the individual, his rights and the imprescriptible freedom of his springing-forth become again a preoccupation of men, it is not with a vocabulary of vacuum cleaners, frigidaires and calculating machines that the world will be raised — the French ideology, its dynamism intact, will recover all its power.
Appendice I. Force respective des partis à la Chambre depuis la guerre (The Respective Strength of the Parties in the Chamber Since the War)
Statistical tables of party strength in the three postwar Chambers: the Bloc National Chamber of 1919–1924 (617 deputies — Left 180: 68 socialists, 24 socialist republicans, 88 radical-Socialists; Centre 216; Right 221: 185 progressists, 36 independents); the Cartel Chamber of 1924–1928 (582 deputies — Left 328: 105 united socialists, 42 socialist republicans, 140 radical-Socialists, 41 radical Left; Centre 80; Right 146: 104 democratic republican Union, 14 democrats, 28 independents; 28 Communists); and the Chamber of 1928–1932 (611 deputies, groups at their June 1930 strengths — Left 271: 107 united socialists, 114 radical-Socialists, 16 socialist republicans, 14 members of the Socialist Party…).
Appendice II. Quelques scrutins importants 1924–1930 (Some Important Votes, 1924–1930)
A record of the principal division votes of 1924–1930: the overthrow of the François-Marsal cabinet (10 June 1924; Left 327, Centre and Right 217); the weakening of the Herriot cabinet (9 April 1925; for Herriot 290 in the “petit cartel,” against 242, the radical Left abstaining); the Caillaux vote of confidence (12 July 1925); the fall of the Tardieu ministry (17 February 1930) and of the Chautemps cabinet (25 February 1930), and other decisive scrutinies of the period.

sources/speer-erinnerungen-1969.title: Albert Speer — Erinnerungen (1969)
sources/speer-erinnerungen-1969.content:
Erinnerungen (Memoirs)
Albert Speer — Erinnerungen (Memoirs). Propyläen Verlag / Verlag Ullstein GmbH, Frankfurt am Main and Berlin, 1969. The autobiography of Hitler’s architect and, from 1942, Reich Minister for Armaments and War Production, covering his youth, his rise inside the National Socialist leadership, the war years and his postwar imprisonment.





























AuthorAlbert Speer (1905–1981) — German architect, a member of the NSDAP from 1931, Hitler’s favourite architect and planner of the Berlin “world capital” Germania project, and from February 1942 Reich Minister for Armaments and War Production; convicted at Nuremberg in 1946 and sentenced to twenty years’ imprisonment, released from Spandau on 1 October 1966Edition1969, Propyläen Verlag / Verlag Ullstein GmbH, Frankfurt am Main and Berlin; copyright 1969; first edition September 1969, with four further impressions through December 1969; the edition carries 78 partly unpublished plates of images and documentsStructureVorwort + 35 chapters in three parts and an epilogue + Nachwort + Anmerkungen (notes) + Register (index); 30,405 lines / ~1,740,000 characters of extracted textPeriodFrom Speer’s ancestry and youth in the first decades of the century, through his party career from 1931 and the twelve years of the Third Reich, to the war’s end, his captivity (Flensburg, Mondorf, Versailles, Kranzberg, Nuremberg) and the postwar reflection on his sentence; the memoir’s writing is dated by the author to March 1953 – December 1954, completed during his Spandau imprisonment, and finished for publication after his release on 1 October 1966NoteDictated and written in prison from over two thousand pages of his own material, combined with documents of his ministerial office preserved in the Federal Archives at Koblenz; the conversation partners of two years, Wolf Jobst Siedler (head of the Ullstein and Propyläen publishing houses) and Joachim C. Fest, prompted many of the book’s general reflections
Contents. An autobiographical account of a central figure of the National Socialist regime, from the inside. Speer recounts his middle-class upbringing, his architectural training under Heinrich Tessenow and his entry into the party after the election of 14 September 1930; his ascent as Hitler’s architect, the rebuilding of Berlin and the designs for the Nuremberg party-grounds; the daily world of the Obersalzberg and the new Reich Chancellery; the war years, his appointment as Armaments Minister after the death of Fritz Todt in February 1942, the organisation of the armaments economy, the bombing war, the crisis of the last years and the crumbling of the leadership around him; and finally the end, his flight from Berlin, his capture, the Nuremberg trial, and his postwar reflections on responsibility, the technocracy and his own fate.
Character of the source. The memoir of the highest-ranking technocrat of the National Socialist state, written in prison and published three years after his release. It offers an insider’s view of Hitler’s circle — the Führer’s daily life, the architecture of power, the rivalries of Bormann, Goebbels, Göring and Himmler — and an account of the armaments economy in the second half of the war. For this wiki it supplies a leading German-state perspective from the Nazi side on the era of the Third Reich, complementing the exile-left history of the republic (Rosenberg) and the official Nazi state record (Volz), and standing in explicit contrast to the Soviet sources (the Stalin biography and wartime collection) with which the period’s other side is documented. It is also a record of Speer’s own highly contested self-presentation of distance from the regime’s crimes, including his account of the June 1944 “Walküre” affair and his late claims of ignorance of the concentration-camp labour and the murder of the Jews.
Quality. Good. Extracted from an Internet Archive text layer produced with ABBYY FineReader OCR; continuous prose throughout, clean German text, chapter headings, the Vorwort, Nachwort, Anmerkungen and Register all present and verified. The index note records that Adolf Hitler was omitted from the register because of his frequent mention in the text. Minor OCR artefacts (a small number of ligature and punctuation slips, and the use of ordinary quotation marks for the book’s special quotation marks) noted.
Raw text: wiki/raw/speer-erinnerungen-1969.txt.

Vorwort (Preface)
The author explains that with this book he intended not only to depict the past but also to warn against the future; that his detailed written records, begun in the first months of captivity in Nuremberg, were a means of relieving the pressure of events, continued in studies and notes of 1946–47 until he decided in March 1953 to write his memoirs connectedly; that he closed the manuscript on 26 December 1954; and that after his release from Spandau on 1 October 1966 he worked over two thousand pages of his own material, together with the documents of his ministerial office held in the Federal Archives at Koblenz, into the present autobiography. He thanks his conversation partners of two years, Wolf Jobst Siedler and Joachim C. Fest.
Erster Teil — 1. Kapitel. Herkommen und Jugend (Origin and Youth)
Speer’s ancestry — Schwabians and poor farmers of the Westerwald, with roots in Silesia and Westphalia; his childhood, schooling, architectural study and the inflation years; his assistantship with Heinrich Tessenow in Berlin; his marriage. His path to architecture before the political events that would give him his great commission.
Erster Teil — 2. Kapitel. Beruf und Berufung (Vocation and Calling)
An offer from Afghanistan; an architect without commissions; walking tours; the election of 14 September 1930; National Socialism and the technical university; his first meeting with Hitler and Goebbels at the Sportpalast; his entry into the party.
Erster Teil — 3. Kapitel. Weichenstellung (Setting the Course)
His first party commission in Berlin; return to Mannheim; with Hitler to the Berlin rally; the rebuilding of the party’s district house and the Propaganda Ministry; the design of the May 1933 demonstration; Hitler as building client; first time privately at Hitler’s.
Erster Teil — 4. Kapitel. Mein Katalysator (My Catalyst)
Hitler as a catalyst; a guest in Hitler’s apartment; Göring as building client; travelling with Hitler; Hitler’s intellectual ancestry; his understanding of art; the old fighters; on the Obersalzberg; mountain tours with Eva Braun; jubilation and obsession; the architect of Hitler.
Erster Teil — 5. Kapitel. Gebaute Megalomanie (Built Megalomania)
The “Röhm-Putsch”; Papen driven from his house; Hindenburg’s funeral; the first great Nuremberg commission, the Zeppelinfeld; the theory of ruin value; the light-dome; foundation stones; actors of their own drama; drives through the country; the master plan for Nuremberg; world-power architecture.
Erster Teil — 6. Kapitel. Der grösste Auftrag (The Greatest Commission)
Plans for Berlin; Vienna and Paris as rivals; Hitler and his architects; the German pavilion at the Paris world exhibition; neoclassicism as a phenomenon of the age; an interrupted journey to France; Neurath’s refusal.
Erster Teil — 7. Kapitel. Obersalzberg
Bormann and Hitler; the daily routine on the Obersalzberg; tea-table conversations: the Germanic cult, the Church, the Greeks, hunting, Ribbentrop; one of Hitler’s fits of rage; Linz as his retirement seat; the confidences of the entourage; Hitler’s conversation with Cardinal Faulhaber.
Erster Teil — 8. Kapitel. Die neue Reichskanzlei (The New Reich Chancellery)
The commission; Hitler’s illness; Morell; the events of 1938 — the reshuffle (Revirement), Austria, the Munich Conference, 9 November 1938; the Bismarck bust shatters; Hacha in the New Reich Chancellery.
Erster Teil — 9. Kapitel. Ein Tag Reichskanzlei (A Day in the Reich Chancellery)
The reception; the eccentric Hess; the level of the leadership stratum; the radicals Bormann and Goebbels; Hitler’s jokes; conferences; monotonous evenings; Hitler and music.
Erster Teil — 10. Kapitel. Entfesseltes Empire (Unchained Empire)
“You have all gone completely mad”; the layout of the grand avenue: triumph squares, the Soldiers’ Hall, the Reichsmarschall office, the Hess building; megalomania; construction deadlines; costs; the boom in architecture; Hitler’s sketches; the Goebbels–Baarova affair; incognito to Italy; Hitler’s fiftieth birthday; at the Wagner family in Bayreuth; Frau Goebbels.
Erster Teil — 11. Kapitel. Die Weltkugel (The Globe)
Hitler’s power centre; the largest hall in the world; a Reichstag for 140 million; Hitler’s palace; precautions against uprisings; the Empire style; the globe as a new symbol.
Erster Teil — 12. Kapitel. Beginn der Talfahrt (The Beginning of the Descent)
The conclusion of the pact with Moscow; “northern lights” over the Obersalzberg: “This time there will be blood”; reluctance for war; the war and peace parties; Hitler goes to war; at headquarters; the armistice; with Hitler in Paris; Berlin’s buildings declared the most important war task.
Erster Teil — 13. Kapitel. Das Übermass (The Excess)
Victory parades under the triumphal arch; Hess’s flight to England; Hitler and Göring as collectors of paintings; Liszt’s “Les Préludes” and the war against the Soviet Union; the pencil-stroke at the Urals; captured weapons for the grand avenue; Trondheim and the eastern cities; his last art journey; the supply catastrophe in Russia; the second man.
Zweiter Teil — 14. Kapitel. Start ins neue Amt (Start in the New Office)
Flight to Dnjepropetrowsk; flight to headquarters; discussions with Hitler and Todt; Todt’s crash; audience with Hitler and his appointment as Minister; Göring’s appearance; his first official acts; in the Reich cabinet hall. Speer’s account of his assumption of the Armaments Ministry in February 1942 after the death of Fritz Todt.
Zweiter Teil — 15. Kapitel. Organisierte Improvisation (Organised Improvisation)
The new organisation scheme; Göring’s threat of resignation; architect and technology; the origins of their “idea of self-responsibility”; the organisation of the ministry; successes.
Zweiter Teil — 16. Kapitel. Versäumnisse (Omissions)
The technical war; attempts to mobilise all forces; the party leadership refuses sacrifices; more raw steel for the war economy; the bankruptcy of the Reichsbahn; the neglected atomic bomb.
Zweiter Teil — 17. Kapitel. Oberbefehlshaber Hitler (Commander-in-Chief Hitler)
Armament conferences with Hitler; his system of specialists; Hitler’s technical understanding; weapons demonstrations; visits to southern Russia; the capture of Elbrus and its consequences; Hitler’s situation conferences; the American landing in North Africa; Göring and the catastrophe of Stalingrad.
Zweiter Teil — 18. Kapitel. Intrigen (Intrigues)
Bormann; cabinet sessions again; on simplifying life; Goebbels’s Stalingrad speech; plans to reactivate Göring; alignments of fronts — with Göring and Goebbels, against Bormann, Keitel, Lammers; Bormann’s system of personal devaluation; with Goebbels at the Führer headquarters, with Göring in Berlin; the fiasco; Himmler’s threat.
Zweiter Teil — 19. Kapitel. Zweiter Mann im Staat (Second Man in the State)
Goebbels allies himself with Bormann; Hitler rebukes Goebbels; no prisoners in the Kursk salient; the building of positions and the bridge to Asia; Guderian and Zeitzler agree; the takeover of naval armament and war production.
Zweiter Teil — 20. Kapitel. Bomben (Bombs)
The third front; Göring’s illusionism; the attack on the Ruhr dams; “area attacks”; the attacks on Hamburg; the ball-bearing industry; the strategic errors of the enemy; the air offensive on Berlin; Hitler’s errors; Galland against Göring; reality lost.
Zweiter Teil — 21. Kapitel. Hitler im Herbst 1943 (Hitler in the Autumn of 1943)
Changes; Hitler’s rigidity, his over-tiredness; the daily routine; Hitler and his dog; taciturnity; a prisoner of himself; Hitler insults the General Staff; Hitler’s attitude to West and East; the Prince of Hesse; Mussolini freed and betrayed.
Zweiter Teil — 22. Kapitel. Abstieg (Decline)
The extension of armament to occupied territories; the agreement with Bichelonne; Sauckel’s reaction; a Reich executive demanded; the Gauleiter speech; the Mangandiskurs (manganese memorandum); estrangements; the journey to Lapland; the infantry programme; difficulties with Sauckel; Göring’s birthday.
Dritter Teil — 23. Kapitel. Krankheit (Illness)
An attempt to remove him; convalescence; the founding of the Jägerstab (fighter staff); Hitler’s emotion and a new estrangement; candidates for his ministerial office, intentions to resign; back on the Berghof; Hitler gives way; the Observer article.
Dritter Teil — 24. Kapitel. Den Krieg dreifach verloren (The War Lost Threefold)
Return to office; the strategic air war against the fuel basis; memoranda; Rommel and the coastal defence; the beginning of the invasion; the takeover of air armament; Hitler’s speech before industry.
Dritter Teil — 25. Kapitel. Fehldispositionen, Wunderwaffen und SS (Misjudgements, Wonder-Weapons and the SS)
Jet fighters as bombers; Peenemünde; concentration-camp prisoners in the armaments industry; Himmler intrudes into the rocket research; plans for an SS economic concern; the theft of workers; Auschwitz.
Dritter Teil — 26. Kapitel. Unternehmen Walküre (Operation Valkyrie)
Conversations with the conspirators; Goebbels receives news of the assassination attempt; at the centre of the counter-actions; the cordoned-off Bendlerstrasse; the meeting with Fromm; Himmler with Goebbels; the visit of Kaltenbrunner; on the ministerial list of the conspirators of 20 July; after-effects; arrests in his own circle; film showings of the executions.
Dritter Teil — 27. Kapitel. Die Welle von Westen (The Wave from the West)
Goebbels gains power; Hitler’s loss of authority; Himmler’s advance; “levée en masse”; his own front visits; military impotence, September 1944; Hitler’s intentions of destruction; outwitted and cancelled; the chromium shortage; armament runs out; wonder-weapons and propaganda.
Dritter Teil — 28. Kapitel. Der Absturz (The Crash)
The armament organisation splits apart; the emergency armament programme; the journey to the Ardennes offensive; to Upper Silesia; a memorandum; “The war is lost!”; the reaction to Yalta; gas against Hitler’s bunker.
Dritter Teil — 29. Kapitel. Die Verdammung (The Condemnation)
Concern for the postwar period: counter-activities; a new memorandum for securing the substance of the people; Hitler’s answer: “The German people may go under”; the planned catastrophe on the Saar; Hitler’s death-sentence over industry.
Dritter Teil — 30. Kapitel. Hitlers Ultimatum (Hitler’s Ultimatum)
The Ruhr district threatened; feverish journeys; the sabotage of orders; Hitler’s twenty-four-hour ultimatum; the ordered certainty of victory; an unread letter; Hitler gives way again.
Dritter Teil — 31. Kapitel. Fünf Minuten nach zwölf (Five Minutes after Twelve)
A prevented radio broadcast; the finale of the Götterdämmerung; Roosevelt’s death; Ley invents death-rays; Eva Braun; preparations for flight; the suicide intentions of the responsible men; Hitler’s last delusions; the “rebel speech”; cooperation with Heinrici; Berlin is not defended.
Dritter Teil — 32. Kapitel. Die Vernichtung (The Annihilation)
Hitler’s condition; fear and pity; his last birthday; Göring goes to Berchtesgaden; Speer’s flight; in the Hamburg radio bunker; his last flight to Hitler; the situation conference; farewell from Magda Goebbels and Eva Braun; for the last time with Hitler; flight to Rechlin; Himmler and his ideas; Dönitz suppresses Hitler’s cabinet list; the weeping fit; responsibility.
Epilog — 33. Kapitel. Stationen der Gefangenschaft (Stations of Captivity)
Flensburg, Mondorf, Versailles, Kranzberg; encounters with the victors; in the Nuremberg prison.
Epilog — 34. Kapitel. Nürnberg (Nuremberg)
The interrogations; the two parties; overall responsibility; the cross-examination.
Epilog — 35. Kapitel. Folgerungen (Conclusions)
The verdict, the technocracy and his own fate; scepticism.
Nachwort (Afterword)
Explains the genesis of the book: the purpose not only to depict the past but to warn the future; his detailed written records begun in Nuremberg, the studies and notes of 1946–47, the decision of March 1953 to write the memoirs connectedly, the completion of the manuscript on 26 December 1954, and its working-up with the documents of his ministerial office in the Federal Archives at Koblenz after his release on 1 October 1966.
Anmerkungen (Notes)
The endnotes to the thirty-five chapters, keyed to the text, citing his own documents and the archive material of his ministerial office, and serving the accounts of the armaments economy, the buildings, and the events recounted.
Register (Index)
The name and subject index to the volume. The note at its close records that, because of his frequent mention in the text, Adolf Hitler was not included in the register. The volume closes with the Bildnachweis (acknowledgement of the plates).

sources/spies-and-traitors-ww2-kurt-sing.title: Singer — Spies and Traitors of World War II (1945)
sources/spies-and-traitors-ww2-kurt-sing.content:
Singer — Spies and Traitors of World War II (1945)
Author: Kurt Singer, American journalist and writer on espionage, author of Duel for the Northland.
Publisher: Prentice-Hall, Inc., 70 Fifth Avenue, New York, 1945. Copyright 1945 by Prentice-Hall, Inc. (Digitized copy from the Mount Union College library, via Internet Archive, 2023; archive.org/details/spiestraitorsofwOO0Okurt.)
Preface: dated from Bronxville, N.Y. — “In Spies and Traitors of World War II I have attempted to portray the workings of modernized espionage during the second great World War.” Singer notes that ninety-five per cent of the names and incidents are “taken from well-substantiated documents,” that some names had to be changed or suppressed “to protect Allied agents still at work,” and that here and there he reconstructed incidents or dialogue where documentary proof was unavailable.
Character
A contemporary journalistic survey of the secret war, published in 1945 while the Second World War was still ending. It is not a memoir or a scholarly history but a popular wartime account by an informed American newspaperman, written from an openly Allied, anti-Axis standpoint and conceived partly as a warning for the postwar world. Singer presents the great spymasters and their networks as personalities — above all Admiral Walter Wilhelm Canaris, chief of the German Abwehr, who threads through the whole book and whom Singer calls “the mystery man of German espionage” — and as organized systems of the great powers. His preface frames the subject in terms that reach back to the biblical Delilah and forward to a feared postwar espionage: “There will always be human material for spies and traitors.” Where the rest of this wiki’s sources are primary documents and regime narratives, this is a secondary, journalistic synthesis written at the end of the conflict it describes, on the Allied side.
Structure
Twenty-six chapters, each a self-contained spy story or network profile, plus a Preface and Contents. The chapters are loosely arranged around the German Abwehr and its enemies, from Canaris’s appointment on 1 September 1939 to the secret planning for a postwar Nazi underground in Argentina.

Ch. I — The Admiral Who Never Wears a Uniform — Canaris’s promotion to Admiral on the morning of 1 September 1939; his character and obscurity as head of the German Secret Service
Ch. II — The Admiral’s New Spy Technique — the Mata Haris of World War II and the women agents of the Abwehr
Ch. III — The Master Mind of Lubianka Street — Lavrenti Beria and the Soviet secret service in Moscow
Ch. IV — A Beautiful “Pacifist” — largely autobiographical; Singer’s own work against Axis agents in the United States
Ch. V — The Very Complicated Story of Friedrich Ege — an individual German agent and his case
Ch. VI — Shots Are Fired at the Admiral — the ripping apart of Canaris’s network, quislings and foreign agents, sabotage
Ch. VII — Battles for Weather Stations — the Nazi weather-station espionage in Greenland and the Arctic
Ch. VIII — Espionage Rides the Air Waves — German and Japanese illicit radio stations and the war of the airwaves
Ch. IX — The Man Who Really Sank the Royal Oak — the sinking of HMS Royal Oak at Scapa Flow in October 1939
Ch. X — Beauty Treatment a la Japan — Japanese espionage and the saboteurs landed in the United States
Ch. XI — The “King of Belize,” a Submarine Tipster — an espionage entrepreneur running submarine information
Ch. XII — A Screen of Twittering Canaries — a counter-espionage screen against enemy agents
Ch. XIII — The Nazi Spy Web in Denmark — the Abwehr’s Danish network
Ch. XIV — The King of Saboteurs — the saboteur Wollweber
Ch. XV — A Spy in Every Port — Baltic espionage as the Russians entered Estonia
Ch. XVI — The Parachutist Who Spread Mischief in Ireland — enemy agents parachuted into neutral Ireland
Ch. XVII — Pelving’s Mistress — a spy case set against the former Reich Chancellery
Ch. XVIII — The Case of the Talking Dolls — an espionage case involving dolls concealing messages
Ch. XIX — Hirohito in Harlem — Japanese agents in the United States, in Harlem
Ch. XX — The Hand of Canaris in the Arab World — the Abwehr’s attempt to raise a Moslem uprising
Ch. XXI — “On to Delhi” — the Slogan of India’s Quisling — the Indian quisling Subhas Chandra Bose and the Axis drive toward India
Ch. XXII — How America’s Code Fell Into Germany’s Hands — the Tyler Kent affair and the compromise of American codes
Ch. XXIII — Fake Refugees — enemy agents posing as refugees
Ch. XXIV — De Gaulle Agents in Africa — Free French agents in Africa in 1943
Ch. XXV — Member of the Jockey Club — Canaris’s agents searching Spain and Portugal for the vanished Maurice Mercier
Ch. XXVI — The Secret Plan for a Nazi Underground Movement — postwar Nazi underground planning in Argentina

OCR Quality
Clean embedded text layer (scanned from the Mount Union College library copy); no re-OCR required. The body text is readable throughout. The garbled passages are confined to the front matter — the library bookplate, title page, preface and Contents (lines 1–410), where broken column lines scramble words (e.g. “THE ADMIRAL’s NEw Spy TECHNIQUE”, “Dr GAULLE”, “SHots ARE FIRED AT THE eee”). Chapter headings inside the body are likewise split across column lines but the chapter titles themselves are recoverable from context.
Coverage
Espionage and the secret services of the Second World War, 1939–1945, on a global stage that repeatedly touches the countries of this wiki: the German Abwehr and Admiral Canaris across Europe, the Nazi spy web in Denmark, German and Japanese radio espionage, saboteurs in neutral Ireland, Baltic espionage, the Soviet secret service under Beria, the Abwehr’s operations in the Arab world and Iberia (Canaris’s agents hunting Maurice Mercier through Spain and Portugal), the Free French in Africa, and the Axis drive on India. It is a wartime, Allied-side journalistic account — the obverse of the regime and memoir documents that make up much of the rest of this wiki, and a complement to Badoglio, Italy in the Second World War (1948) as an Allied-camp view of the war.
Cross-references

Badoglio, Italy in the Second World War (1948) — the other Allied-side account in this wiki, of the Italian theatre rather than the secret war.
The regime documents of the German and Italian sources in this wiki (Heiden’s Adolf Hitler, Mein Kampf, the Fascist histories) are the political records of the powers whose secret services Singer describes; Singer supplies the espionage underside of the same war.

sources/stalin-kratkaya-biografiya-1948.title: Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin: A Short Biography (2nd ed., 1948)
sources/stalin-kratkaya-biografiya-1948.content:
Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin: A Short Biography
Институт Маркса — Энгельса — Ленина при ЦК ВКП(б) — Иосиф Виссарионович Сталин. Краткая биография (Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin. A Short Biography). Second edition, corrected and enlarged, OGIZ — State Publishing House of Political Literature, Moscow, 1948. The official short biography of Stalin issued during his lifetime.





























AuthorThe Institute of Marx–Engels–Lenin under the Central Committee of the CPSU(b); the named contributors to this electronic edition are G. F. Aleksandrov, M. R. Galaktionov, P. N. Pospelov, M. B. Mitin, V. S. Kruzhkov and V. D. MochalovEditionSecond, corrected and enlarged, 1948 (OGIZ / State Publishing House of Political Literature, Moscow); FB2 electronic edition (librusec-id 668549) prepared 2019 from an OCR scan; print run 3,000,000, signed to press 24 December 1947StructureTitle page + 11 numbered chapters (I–XI) + closing encomium; no separate table of contents; 636 lines / ~232,000 characters of extracted textPeriod1879–1946: from Stalin’s birth in Gori to the post-war reconstruction and the elections to the Supreme Soviet of February 1946NoteThe FB2 gives Stalin’s birth date as 21 December 1879 (the official dating used in this period, before the later change to 1878); quotations from Lenin cited by volume and page; the text is the canonical hagiographic portrait of the Stalin era
Contents. The official short biography of Stalin published in his lifetime and closed to the cult of the leader. It narrates his birth in Gori, his schooling at the Gori religious school and the Tiflis theological seminary, his early conversion to Marxism in the Georgian social-democratic milieu and the “Mesame-dasi” group, and his work as a revolutionary organiser in the Caucasus. It treats his successive arrests and exiles and his role in the underground of the Transcaucasus, his participation in the party congresses, his work on “Pravda” and in the Duma faction, and his exile to Turukhansk. It covers the February and October revolutions, the Brest peace, his work during the civil war and foreign intervention, and the transition to the New Economic Policy and the formation of the USSR. It then treats the struggle for socialist industrialisation, the collectivisation of agriculture, the adoption of the 1936 Constitution, and the political trials of the 1930s, closing with the Great Patriotic War of 1941–1945 and the post-war reconstruction. Throughout, the biography presents Stalin as the disciple and successor of Lenin and the architect of Soviet power, and it closes with the standard encomium of the Stalin era: “Stalin is Lenin today.”
Character of the source. The official biographical portrait of Stalin issued under the Institute of Marx–Engels–Lenin during the high tide of the cult of the personality (1948). Written from a strict Bolshevik standpoint, it presents Stalin’s life as inseparable from the history of the party and the building of socialism, and it narrates the political struggles of the 1920s and 1930s in the standard terms of the Stalin era — the defeat of the Trotskyists, the “rightists” and the Bukharinists, and the liquidation of the “enemies of the people.” Its date of 1948 places it before any qualification of the cult, and it therefore reflects the Stalinist periodisation of Soviet history at its fullest. It is a companion volume in this folder to the Short Course of the History of the VKP(b) (1945) and Shestakov’s Short Course of the History of the USSR (1937), with whose periodisation it is fully consistent.
Quality. Good. Extracted from an FB2 e-book via structured parsing of the FictionBook XML; continuous prose throughout. Cyrillic text clean; the 11 numbered chapter headings verified; numbered source references (footnotes) preserved inline as bracketed numbers, though the footnote text itself is not carried in the FB2 body.
Raw text: wiki/raw/stalin-kratkaya-biografiya-1948.txt.

Глава I (Chapter I)
Stalin’s birth in Gori (21 December 1879), his family and Georgian peasant origins; schooling at the Gori religious school and the Tiflis theological seminary; the spread of Marxism in the Transcaucasus and Stalin’s conversion at fifteen; his work in the “Mesame-dasi” group and the revolutionary underground; his exclusion from the seminary (1899) and his arrest and first exile. Period: 1879–1904.
Глава II (Chapter II)
Stalin’s years of prison and exile amid the rising revolutionary movement; the Second Congress of the RSDRP and the Bolshevik–Menshevik split; Stalin’s escape from exile (January 1904) and his revolutionary work in the Caucasus, in the 1905 revolution, and at the Stockholm (Fourth) and London (Fifth) Congresses. Period: 1904–1907.
Глава III (Chapter III)
The defeat of the first Russian revolution and the years of reaction; the building of the Bolshevik party of a new type in the underground; Stalin’s work of organisation and consolidation through the decade between the two revolutions. Period: 1908–1912.
Глава IV (Chapter IV)
The Prague party conference (1912), its prediction of a new revolutionary upsurge and the measures to meet it; Stalin’s work on “Pravda” and with the Bolshevik Duma faction; his arrest and exile to the Turukhansk region; the February revolution of 1917 and Stalin’s return. Period: 1912 – March 1917.
Глава V (Chapter V)
The return of Lenin to Russia (April 1917); the Bolshevik course toward the armed uprising; the October socialist revolution and the consolidation of Soviet power; the Brest peace and the defence of the Bolshevik strategy and tactics against Trotsky. Period: April 1917 – 1918.
Глава VI (Chapter VI)
The foreign military intervention and civil war; Stalin’s role as an organiser of defence and of the Red Army on the key fronts; the rout of the intervention and of the White armies. Period: 1918–1920.
Глава VII (Chapter VII)
The transition to peaceful construction after the civil war; the restoration of the national economy and the New Economic Policy; the formation of the USSR; Lenin’s illness and death and Stalin’s succession as leader of the party; the struggle against the oppositions; a portrait of Stalin as the model leader of party and people. Period: 1921–1925.
Глава VIII (Chapter VIII)
The struggle for socialist industrialisation in historically the shortest possible time; the first five-year plan; the offensive against the capitalist elements; the national and colonial question and the “great friendship” of the peoples of the USSR. Period: 1926–1929.
Глава IX (Chapter IX)
Stalin’s address to the conference of agrarian-Marxists (December 1929); the fight for the collectivisation of agriculture and the liquidation of the kulaks as a class; the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Congresses; the murder of S. M. Kirov and the measures to strengthen Bolshevik vigilance. Period: 1929–1934.
Глава X (Chapter X)
The continuing growth of industry and agriculture under the general line of the party; the fulfilment of the second five-year plan and the Stakhanovite movement; the adoption of the new (1936) Constitution; the political trials and the liquidation of the “enemies of the people”; the approach of war and the interruption of peaceful construction in June 1941. Period: 1935 – June 1941.
Глава XI (Chapter XI)
The Great Patriotic War: the German attack of 22 June 1941; Stalin as Supreme Commander; the great defensive and offensive battles, the rout of fascist Germany and the raising of the banner of victory over Berlin; the war against Japan; the dissolution of the Comintern (May 1943); the post-war reconstruction and the elections to the Supreme Soviet of February 1946; the closing encomium of Stalin as the leader, teacher and Generalissimo. Period: 1941–1946.

sources/stalin-o-velikoj-otechestvennoj-.title: J. V. Stalin — On the Great Patriotic War of the Soviet Union (1946)
sources/stalin-o-velikoj-otechestvennoj-.content:
On the Great Patriotic War of the Soviet Union
И. Сталин — О Великой Отечественной Войне Советского Союза (J. V. Stalin, On the Great Patriotic War of the Soviet Union). Ukrainian State Publishing House, 1946. A collected volume of Stalin’s wartime speeches, radio addresses, Supreme Commander orders and allied correspondence covering the whole of the Great Patriotic War.





























AuthorIosif Vissarionovich Stalin (Иосиф Виссарионович Сталин, 1879–1953) — General Secretary of the Central Committee of the CPSU(b) and, from August 1941, Supreme Commander-in-Chief (Верховный Главнокомандующий) of the Red Army, elevated to Generalissimus of the Soviet Union in 1945Edition1946, Ukrainian State Publishing House (Украинское Государственное издательство); electronic text of the litru.ru library (book 25660)Structure31 documents — radio addresses, speeches, People’s Commissar of Defence and Supreme Commander orders, replies to foreign correspondents and messages to allied leaders — arranged chronologically from 3 July 1941 to 3 September 1945; 1,110 lines / ~258,000 characters of extracted textPeriod1941–1945: the Great Patriotic War of the Soviet Union against fascist Germany and JapanNoteThe documents include Stalin’s addresses to the people of 3 July 1941, 9 May 1945 (victory over Germany) and 2 September 1945 (victory over Japan); the Red Square parade speech of 7 November 1941; the annual May Day, 23 February and 7 November Supreme Commander orders; and his 1945 toast on the Russian people (“the most outstanding nation of all the nations forming the Soviet Union”)
Contents. A chronological collection of the principal wartime utterances of the Soviet leader. It opens with the first radio address to the people of 3 July 1941, announcing the German invasion, condemning the violation of the 1939 non-aggression pact, and setting the war in the frame of the historic defeats of the “invincible” armies of Napoleon and Wilhelm II. It closes with the order of 3 September 1945 on the victory over Japan, following the signature of the Japanese instrument of surrender in Tokyo on 2 September. In between the volume gathers the Red Army parade speech of 7 November 1941, the People’s Commissar of Defence and Supreme Commander orders issued on the anniversaries of the Red Army (23 February), May Day (1 May) and the October Revolution (7 November) through 1942–1945, the orders accompanying the great campaigns, and the replies to Western correspondents (James Cassidy of the Associated Press) and messages to President Roosevelt and British and Allied figures. The closing address of 9 May 1945 salutes the Soviet people as the true victors, and the final order of 3 September 1945 marks the end of the war with Japan.
Character of the source. The primary wartime record of the Soviet leadership, as presented in the persona of Stalin himself. The collection is at once a personal testament of the war years and a deliberate instrument of the wartime cult of the Supreme Commander: each order is signed “Верховный Главнокомандующий, Генералиссимус Советского Союза, И. Сталин,” and the whole is framed to affirm the thesis that the Soviet people and their leader waged a just, patriotic war against the fascist aggressor. It complements the biographical portrait in this folder — A Short Biography of J. V. Stalin (1948), which narrates the same war in prose — while resting on the documentary basis that the biography describes. For the interwar background of the war, the Short Course of party history (1883–1937) and Shestakov’s textbook provide the preceding periodisation.
Quality. Good. Extracted from a plain-text electronic edition (litru.ru) via stripping of the library header and normalisation of line endings; continuous prose throughout. Cyrillic text clean; document headings and dates verified. Minor spacing artefacts in a few compound headings (e.g. “ПРИКАЗНАРОДНОГО” for “ПРИКАЗ НАРОДНОГО”) noted during extraction.
Raw text: wiki/raw/stalin-o-velikoj-otechestvennoj-vojne-1946.txt.

1941
ВЫСТУПЛЕНИЕ ПО РАДИО — 3 июля 1941 года (Radio address, 3 July 1941). The first address to the people after the German invasion; announces the attack begun 22 June, explains the initial Soviet retreats by German mobilisation and the surprise violation of the 1939 pact, and calls for a total patriotic war, partisan resistance in occupied territory, and the destruction of supplies rather than their surrender to the enemy.
РЕЧЬ НА ПАРАДЕ КРАСНОЙ АРМИИ — 7 ноября 1941 года на Красной площади в Москве (Speech at the Red Army parade on Red Square, 7 November 1941). Delivered on the 24th anniversary of October at the parade in besieged Moscow; proclaims confidence in victory and the certainty that the “German invaders are standing before the abyss.”
1942
ПРИКАЗ НАРОДНОГО КОМИССАРА ОБОРОНЫ — 23 февраля 1942 года, № 55, Москва (Order of the People’s Commissar of Defence No. 55, 23 February 1942). Order for the 24th anniversary of the Red Army; recounts the first period of the war, the defeat of the German plan for a blitzkrieg, and the rout of the German forces before Moscow.
ПРИКАЗ НАРОДНОГО КОМИССАРА ОБОРОНЫ — 1 мая 1942 года, № 130, Москва (Order of the People’s Commissar of Defence No. 130, 1 May 1942). May Day order; sets the tasks of the second period of the war, calls for the creation of reserves and the organisation of a summer offensive.
ОТВЕТ г-ну КЭССИДИ — 3 октября 1942 года (Reply to Mr. Cassidy, 3 October 1942). Reply to James Cassidy of the Associated Press on the Allied second front and the course of the war.
ПРИКАЗ НАРОДНОГО КОМИССАРА ОБОРОНЫ — 7 ноября 1942 года, № 345, Москва (Order of the People’s Commissar of Defence No. 345, 7 November 1942). Order for the 25th anniversary of October; announces the transition of the initiative, opening with the counter-offensive at Stalingrad.
ОТВЕТЫ КОРРЕСПОНДЕНТУ — 13 ноября 1942 года (Replies to the correspondent, 13 November 1942). Reply on the Allied campaign in Africa.
1943
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 28 февраля 1943 года, № 95, Москва (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 95, 28 February 1943). Order for the 25th anniversary of the Red Army; records the destruction of the German forces at Stalingrad and the beginning of the mass expulsion of the enemy.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 1 мая 1943 года, № 195, Москва (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 195, 1 May 1943). May Day order; surveys the winter campaign of 1942–43 and sets the tasks of the coming offensive.
ОТВЕТ — 4 мая 1943 года (Reply, 4 May 1943). Reply on the abolition of the Communist International.
Президенту РУЗВЕЛЬТУ — 9 мая 1943 года (To President Roosevelt, 9 May 1943). Message concerning the dissolution of the Comintern.
Господину КИНГУ — 28 мая 1943 года (To Mr. King, 28 May 1943). Message on the dissolution of the Comintern.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 7 ноября 1943 года, № 309, Москва (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 309, 7 November 1943). Order for the 26th anniversary of October; marks the turning point of the war and the rout of the German forces at Kursk and the Dnieper.
1944
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 23 февраля 1944 года, № 16, Москва (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 16, 23 February 1944). Order for the 26th anniversary of the Red Army; records the final expulsion of the German forces from Soviet territory.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 1 мая 1944 года, № 70, Москва (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 70, 1 May 1944). May Day order; surveys the winter campaign and the tasks of driving the enemy beyond the frontiers.
ОТВЕТ — 13 июня 1944 года (Reply, 13 June 1944). Reply to a foreign correspondent on the course of the war and the opening of the second front.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 20 августа 1944 года, № 152, Москва, Кремль (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 152, 20 August 1944). Order saluting the troops who have completed the expulsion of the German forces from Soviet territory and the advance to the frontiers.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 7 ноября 1944 года, № 220, Москва (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 220, 7 November 1944). Order for the 27th anniversary of October; marks the entry of the Red Army into the war of liberation of the peoples of Europe.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 19 ноября 1944 года, № 225, Москва, Кремль (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 225, 19 November 1944). Order marking the anniversary of the beginning of the counter-offensive at Stalingrad.
1945
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 23 февраля 1945 года, № 5, Москва (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 5, 23 February 1945). Order for the 27th anniversary of the Red Army; surveys the victories of 1944 and the entry of the war onto the territory of the enemy.
ПРИКАЗ — 21 апреля 1945 года (Order, 21 April 1945). Order of the Supreme Commander saluting the troops on the approach to Berlin.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 27 апреля 1945 года, № 346 (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 346, 27 April 1945). Order on the meeting of the Soviet and Allied forces.
ОБРАЩЕНИЕ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО МАРШАЛА СОВЕТСКОГО СОЮЗА И. В. СТАЛИНА К КРАСНОЙ АРМИИ И ВОЙСКАМ СОЮЗНИКОВ — 27 апреля 1945 года (Address of the Supreme Commander Marshal of the Soviet Union J. V. Stalin to the Red Army and the Allied forces, 27 April 1945). Address on the historic meeting of the Soviet and Anglo-American forces in Germany.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 1 мая 1945 года, № 20, Москва (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 20, 1 May 1945). May Day order; salutes the troops who have captured Berlin and raised the banner of victory over the Reichstag.
ОБРАЩЕНИЕ тов. И. В. СТАЛИНА К НАРОДУ — 9 мая 1945 года (Address of Comrade J. V. Stalin to the people, 9 May 1945). Victory address to the people on the unconditional surrender of Germany, saluting the Soviet people — “a people of extraordinary patience” — as the true bearer of the victory.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО ПО ВОЙСКАМ КРАСНОЙ АРМИИ И ВОЕННО-МОРСКОМУ ФЛОТУ — 9 мая 1945 года, № 369 (Order of the Supreme Commander to the Red Army and Navy No. 369, 9 May 1945). Order declaring 9 May the day of victory over Germany.
ЗАСТОЛЬНАЯ РЕЧЬ — 24 мая 1945 года (Toast speech, 24 May 1945). Speech at the reception in the Kremlin in honour of the commanders of the Red Army; the celebrated toast on the Russian people as the “most outstanding nation of all the nations forming the Soviet Union.”
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 22 июня 1945 года, № 370 (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 370, 22 June 1945). Order marking the fourth anniversary of the outbreak of the war and the victory parade.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО — 19 августа 1945 года, № 51, Москва (Order of the Supreme Commander No. 51, 19 August 1945). Order for the day of victory over Japan and of the liberation of the Far East.
ОБРАЩЕНИЕ тов. И. В. СТАЛИНА К НАРОДУ — 2 сентября 1945 года (Address of Comrade J. V. Stalin to the people, 2 September 1945). Address to the people on the signature of the Japanese instrument of surrender in Tokyo on 2 September, declaring the victory over Japan.
ПРИКАЗ ВЕРХОВНОГО ГЛАВНОКОМАНДУЮЩЕГО ПО ВОЙСКАМ КРАСНОЙ АРМИИ И ВОЕННО-МОРСКОМУ ФЛОТУ — 3 сентября 1945 года, № 373 (Order of the Supreme Commander to the Red Army and Navy No. 373, 3 September 1945). Final order declaring 3 September the victory day over Japan and saluting the victorious troops; ends the volume.

sources/volpe-guerra-dopoguerra-fascismo.title: Volpe — Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928)
sources/volpe-guerra-dopoguerra-fascismo.content:
Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928)
Identity
Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (War, Postwar, Fascism) is a collection of essays and occasional pieces by the Italian historian Gioacchino Volpe (1876–1971), gathered and published by «La Nuova Italia» Editrice, Venezia, 1928 in the series Storici antichi e moderni directed by G. Maranini. As the preface explains, it collects “una serie di piccoli e mezzani scritti” — a series of small and middle-sized writings — published over the preceding ten or twelve years (that is, from 1916 to 1928) in Il Popolo d’Italia, Politica, La Sera di Milano, Il Corriere della Sera, Gerarchia, and elsewhere, together with others of lesser account. They concern political events, manifestations of Italian public opinion, and problems debated in the press and in Parliament.
