Volpe was one of the most distinguished Italian historians of his generation (a specialist in medieval Italian history, later a senator of the Kingdom), who during and after the First World War lent his pen to the nationalist and then the Fascist cause. He writes that he published these pieces “dal 1916 ad oggi” — from 1916 to the present — in a period “che si presenta come ben circoscritto e con caratteri di continuità,” and that he had “non dovuto superare grandi «crisi» di animo o di pensieri per aderire a quella nuova realtà italiana … sollecitata dalla guerra” — he had not had to overcome great crises of spirit or thought in order to adhere to that new Italian reality solicited by the war. The book is therefore the wartime-and-Fascist political journalism of a professional academic historian, republished as a document of the Fascist consolidation.
It is the second Italian-language source in this wiki. Where Businelli’s Rivoluzione fascista (1933) tells the internal story of the squadrist movement’s origins from within the movement itself, Volpe’s volume is the collected commentary of a nationalist-liberal academic who came to Fascism: it records how a learned historian of the national tradition wrote for the interventionist and Fascist press from the middle of the Great War through the postwar crisis to the consolidation of the regime.
Character of the source
A collection of occasional, explicitly political journalism by a leading academic historian writing from the nationalist and then Fascist side. The pieces range from short wartime morale essays addressed to soldiers of the VIII Armata (for which Volpe served as an officer attached to the army command) through essays on France, England, Egypt, Italy’s foreign relations, regionalism, the school question, and Machiavelli, to the explicitly Fascist pieces of the mid-1920s — open letters to Mussolini, “Per la nuova Italia,” “Fascismo e monarchia,” “Giovane Italia,” a look at the new Chamber (1924), reflections on the Fascist congress (1925), and “La classe dirigente.” The tone is that of a learned, earnest, and admiring fellow-traveller of the regime rather than a rank-and-file agitator. As a source it is valuable as a specimen of how a professional historian of the national school articulated the case for Fascism and framed it within Italy’s longer history (the essays on Machiavelli and on Ferrari are of literary-historical interest), and as a chronological record of the transition from wartime nationalism to Fascist adherence across 1916–1928.
Contents (structure)
The volume is organized as a single run of essays in three broad clusters, without formal part divisions, closing with an appendix and the printed Indice. Groupings follow the printed Indice (pp. 1–463):

Wartime writings (1916–1918, pp. 1–175) — the First World War section: “I maestri e la nazione” (1916, from L’Azione), “Il militarismo prussiano” (L’Azione, 15 Feb 1916), “Crisi di ministero” (L’Azione, 15 June 1916), “Propaganda nell’VIII Armata” and the short pieces on inspiring confidence in the soldiers, “Patria e religione,” “I cattolici e la guerra,” the Italians abroad, “Idee da diffondere,” “I soldati e il canto,” “Rievocazioni di morti,” “La grandezza dell’America,” “Fiducia, certezza, ansia,” “Diritti,” “Doveri,” “Nord e sud,” “Per gli Alpini,” “Wilson, Wilson, Wilson! America, America!” and “Le attività della guerra” (Guerra e democrazia; Guerra pacifista; Gli Inglesi grandi cose si aspettano)
Postwar and foreign pieces (1919–1924, pp. 105–233) — “Uscir fuori di casa, conoscere il mondo,” “Tornando dalla Dalmazia” (La Sera di Milano, 21 April 1919), the Egypt group (“Egitto ed Italiani d’Egitto,” “Nuova vita nel vicino Oriente,” “L’Egitto e la sua indipendenza,” “Ombre e luci dell’Egitto d’oggi,” “Italiani d’Egitto”), “Decadenza italiana?,” “Il nostro avvenire,” the France group (“Bella storia, la storia di Francia!” in Gerarchia, March 1923; “Tradizioni e missioni francesi”; “Pacifismo francese”; “A crisi superata, constatazioni e previsioni” in Gerarchia, Oct 1923), the Italo-English group (“Crisi di rapporti italo-inglesi,” “L’amicizia italo-inglese,” “Inghilterra, Francia e Italia,” “L’Italia e l’opinione pubblica europea”), and “Regionalismo e Federalismo” (La Sera di Milano, 12 July 1920), “Unità e regionalismo”
Fascist essays (1921–1928, pp. 233–431) — “Ritorno di Ferrari?,” “Un assente: La scuola” (Il Risorgimento di Milano, 1921), “Lettere aperte a Benito Mussolini,” “Per la nuova Italia,” “Fascismo e monarchia,” “Giovane Italia,” “Onore ad un Italiano ed all’Italia” (Il Popolo d’Italia, 8 July 1923), “Un’occhiata alla nuova camera” (Gerarchia, April 1924), “Commento al discorso della Corona,” “Lo stato e le sette segrete,” “Politica estera e coltura,” “Ripensando al congresso fascista” (Gerarchia, Aug 1925), “La classe dirigente,” “Il gran consiglio fascista,” “La politica di Machiavelli,” and “Niccolò Machiavelli: Nel quarto centenario della sua morte”
Appendice (pp. 441–463) — “Proclami agli ufficiali dell’VIII Armata” (Vittoria; Congedo; Saluto): Volpe notes his own part in drafting these proclamations, as officer attached to the army command, was minimal, and he reprints them “quasi a integrazione dei documenti ripubblicati nel capitolo «Propaganda all’VIII Armata»”; the last item is the New Year address of the Commanding General of the 8ª Armata, Ten. Gen. Caviglia, to the young officers, welcoming the 1919 that dawned

The volume closes with the printed Indice (on the final two pages, pp. 465–470); the text of the essays ends at p. 468.
OCR / extraction quality
Source is a ZIP of 492 numbered TXT page files (Anna’s Archive paginated text dump, folder 89099998890), delivered as a clean embedded text layer. The book is set in Roman (Antiqua) type, and the Italian text layer is clean, fluent and fully readable, including proper accented forms and scholarly apparatus (footnote source attributions such as “Ne L’Azione di Milano, 15 febbr. ‘16”). Per protocol the embedded text layer is the extraction source; no image pages exist and no re-OCR pass is required. Result: a clean Italian transcription assembled by concatenating the 492 page files in numeric order with per-page form-feeds (15,696 lines; 491 page-form-feeds). The physical scan carries front-matter library stamps (University of Wisconsin copy, “Library of the University of Wisconsin,” accession 14437/443802) and closes with the library date-due card; the printed text proper runs to p. 470. The structure above has been reconstructed from the printed Indice and cross-checked against the body essay headings and their dated source attributions.
Cross-references

Companion Italian source by the same author: Volpe, History of the Fascist Movement (1936) — the English translation of Volpe’s continuous narrative history of Fascism, published by Edizioni di Novissima, Roma (A. XIV); the present volume collects his journalism, the later work his consecutive narrative history.
Companion Italian source: Pini & Bresadola, Storia del Fascismo: Guerra – Rivoluzione – Regime (1928) — the regime-published full-length chronicle of the rise of Fascism, published the same year as Volpe’s collection.
Companion Italian source: Businelli, Rivoluzione fascista (1933) — the movement-insider narrative of Fascism’s origins (1912–1922). Volpe’s collection (1916–1928) complements it: a contemporary academic-nationalist commentary running through the Great War, the postwar crisis and the Fascist consolidation, reaching further forward (into the mid-1920s) than Businelli’s origin-story.
Regime’s own vantage (German): Friedrichs (comp.), Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Bands 1–4; Geisow, Die Seele des Dritten Reiches; Büttner (ed.), Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich (all in this wiki) — the parallel example of regime-side revolutionary historiography and documentary record.
Contrast with the Soviet sources (Pokrovsky, VKP(b) Short Course, Stalin) as the third revolutionary regime’s official self-account.

sources/volpe-history-fascist-movement-1.title: Volpe — History of the Fascist Movement (1936)
sources/volpe-history-fascist-movement-1.content:
History of the Fascist Movement (1936)
Identity
History of the Fascist Movement is the English translation of a study of Fascism by the Italian historian Gioacchino Volpe (1876–1971), published by Edizioni di Novissima, Roma, in the Fascist-era year A. XIV (that is, 1935–1936 by the Gregorian calendar, the Fascist era having begun on 29 October 1922). The book carries the author’s note dated two years after the original Italian study appeared, reviewing what “two important years in the history of Fascism and of Italy” had added — the Littoriali of culture at Florence (spring 1934), the Balbo squadron flight to the United States, mother-and-child welfare, the bonifica integrale land reclamation, the new cities of Littoria (inaugurated 18 December 1932) and Sabaudia (21 April 1934), the Bologna–Florence railway, colonial development in Libya, and above all the corporate organisation of 1933–34. The English text thus reflects the state of Fascism’s self-presentation in the mid-1930s.
Volpe, a specialist in medieval Italian history and a senator of the Kingdom, was the most distinguished academic historian to have lent his pen to the Fascist regime, and the author of the companion volume Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) already held in this wiki. Whereas that volume collects his occasional wartime-and-Fascist journalism, the present work is a continuous narrative history of the Fascist movement from its origins to the consolidation of the corporate state.
Character of the source
A continuous, admiring narrative history of the Fascist movement written from within the regime by its foremost academic historian. It traces the movement from the interventionism of 1914–15, through the founding of the Fasci d’azione, the transformation of the movement into a party, the March on Rome, Fascism at the helm, and the reform of the state, closing with a chapter placing “Fascist Italy” in Europe. The tone is celebratory but sober — that of a learned regime apologist constructing the official history of the movement’s rise. As a source it is valuable as the canonical mid-1930s regime historiography of Fascism’s own origins, complementing the insider narratives of Businelli and Farinacci with the perspective of the professional national historian.
Contents (structure)
The volume comprises eight chapters, preceded by the Author’s Note:

Author’s Note — Volpe’s preface written two years after the original Italian study, surveying what 1933–34 had added to Fascism (the Littoriali, the Balbo flight, the demographic and reclamation policy, the new cities, and above all the corporate organisation, including the National Council of Corporations authorized by law of 3 April 1926 and the Labour Charter)
Ch. I — Interventionism and the «Fasci d’azione» — the interventionist split of 1914–15; Mussolini and the Fasci compared to Bissolati and the Radicals; the patriotic and social content of interventionism; Fiume and Dalmatia and the Pact of London
Ch. II — The Fascist «Movement» — the postwar “policy of the masses”; Mussolini’s founding of the “anti-party,” the Fasci di combattimento (23 March 1919); the Caporetto repercussions; the movement as youth, impulse, faith, pragmatism; the demobilised officers and officer-students; the Fiume question and the French colonial troops incident; the programme of Florence; the reaction against the occupation of the factories
Ch. III — From «Movement» to «Party» — the internal strife between the two Mussolinis; the nationalist wing and the Popolo d’Italia (2 February 1922); the monarchy-or-republic question; the anti-socialist economic stance
Ch. IV — The National Fascist Party — the year 1921; the would-be peace with the socialists; the Party and the squadre as one; fascist syndicalism and the Confederations (the Lavoro d’Italia, founded April 1922, directed by Rossoni); the national bloc elections; the Bologna cry against a government incapable of governing; the battles of local expurgation (ejection of mayors and socialist communal councils); the general strike of August 1922 and its discomfiture
Ch. V — The «March on Rome» — the victory of August and the Pacification Pact of summer 1921; the Bianchi memorandum on the Alto Adige; the Milan meeting of the Fasci (16–18 October) with Mussolini, Bianchi, De Vecchi, Balbo, General De Bono, Generals Fara and Ceccherini; the quadrumvirate of action with dictatorial mandate; the concentration points twenty or thirty kilometres from the capital; the order for demobilisation on 31 October as 100,000 Blackshirts massed in the Villa Borghese
Ch. VI — Fascism at the Helm — Mussolini’s rise by revolutionary means; the Party, the Militia and the quasi-constitutional union; the restoration of order; the balance of the State budget restored; public works and agriculture (the battaglia del grano); foreign policy — debts, reparations, the question of Italy’s place among the nations; Dino Grandi as Minister for Foreign Affairs; the check of May–June 1924 and the Aventine
Ch. VII — The Reform of the State — the new phase of activity; the law of 24 December strengthening the office of the President of the Council as Prime Minister; the Prefects as supreme transmitters of government; the law authorizing dismissal of civil and military dependents who did not give guarantees; the syndical law of 3 April 1926 (drawn up with Giuseppe Bottai) and the Corporations; the corporate structure as an accord between liberty and authority; the unresolved question of appointing a successor Head of Government
Ch. VIII — Fascist Italy and Europe — Fascism as a civilising mission and a “revolution” offering itself to Europe; the theme of “anti-Europe” until a New Europe has learnt from Fascism; the observation that foreign Fascisms are mostly conservative nationalism; the question whether Fascism will appear European and universal

The volume closes with a short glossary of names and terms (including the note on Sturzo and the Popolare party — repudiated by the Holy See and dissolved by the Fascist government in 1925 — and “THE NIGHT OF RONCHI”), followed by the library date-due card and the Marygrove College Library stamp (shelfmark 945.09 V88).
OCR / extraction quality
Source is a 156-page PDF of the English translation, scanned from the Marygrove College Library copy with a clean embedded text layer (recoded by LuraDocument PDF v2.68). The text is set in Roman (Antiqua) type, and the embedded layer is clean, fluent and fully readable English, with only isolated OCR slips (e.g. “ma\e” for “make,” “rapresents” for “represents,” “uiken” for “taken,” “af” for “of”). Per protocol the embedded text layer is the extraction source; no re-OCR pass is required. Result: a clean English transcription via pdftotext -layout (4,711 lines; 156 page-form-feeds), written to wiki/raw/volpe-history-fascist-movement-1936.txt. The structure above has been reconstructed from the page-initial chapter headings (“I. INTERVENTIONISM…”, “II. THE FASCIST «MOVEMENT»”, “III. FROM «MOVEMENT» TO «PARTY»”, “IV. THE NATIONAL FASCIST PARTY”, “V. THE «MARCH ON ROME»”, “VI. FASCISM AT THE HELM.”, “VII. THE REFORM OF THE STATE”, “CHAPTER VIII. FASCIST ITALY AND EUROPE”) and cross-checked against the body.
Cross-references

Companion Italian source by the same author: Volpe, Guerra, dopoguerra, fascismo (1928) — the collected wartime-and-Fascist journalism; the present work is Volpe’s continuous narrative history of the movement, written (in its English form) in the mid-1930s.
Companion Italian source: Pini & Bresadola, Storia del Fascismo: Guerra – Rivoluzione – Regime (1928) — the regime-published full-length chronicle of the rise of Fascism, a broad continuous account of the same arc that Volpe here condenses into eight chapters.
Companion Italian sources: Businelli, Rivoluzione fascista (1933) and Farinacci, Storia della Rivoluzione Fascista, Vol. I (1937) — insider narratives of Fascism’s origins. Volpe represents the official academic-regime historiography of the same story.
Regime’s own vantage (German): Friedrichs (comp.), Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Bands 1–4; Geisow, Die Seele des Dritten Reiches; Büttner (ed.), Der Weg zum nationalsozialistischen Reich (all in this wiki) — the parallel example of regime-side revolutionary historiography.
Contrast with the Soviet sources (Pokrovsky, VKP(b) Short Course, Stalin) as the third revolutionary regime’s official self-account.

sources/volz-dokumente-der-deutschen-pol.title: Von der Großmacht zur Weltmacht 1937 — Dokumente der deutschen Politik, Band 5 (1938)
sources/volz-dokumente-der-deutschen-pol.content:
Von der Großmacht zur Weltmacht 1937
Hans Volz (ed.) — Von der Großmacht zur Weltmacht. 1937 (From Great Power to World Power. 1937), Band 5 of Dokumente der deutschen Politik (Documents of German Politics), edited by Paul Meier-Benneckenstein, president of the Hochschule für Politik (Academy for Politics), Berlin. Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin, 1938. An official Nazi compilation of 81 German state documents of the year 1937 — laws, decrees, speeches, notes and protocols — recording the internal consolidation of the National Socialist state and the conduct of German foreign policy in the year before the Anschluss and the Munich crisis.

































EditorDr. Hans Volz (1904–1978), head of the library of the Hochschule für Politik, Berlin; series edited by Paul Meier-Benneckenstein, president of the academy; a publication of the Hochschule für Politik / BerlinSeriesDokumente der deutschen Politik, Band 5 (5th volume of the series, which began in 1935 with the documents of 1933 and thereafter covered each year of the National Socialist regime)Edition1938, Junker und Dünnhaupt Verlag, Berlin; copyright 1938, printed in Germany; the University of Florida Libraries copy (OCLC 5135115)Structure81 numbered documents in three main parts with a Zeittafel (chronological table of the documents), an overview of the Führer’s speeches of 1937, and name and subject indexes; 22,426 lines of extracted textPeriod1937: documents dated January–December 1937, covering the fourth year of the National Socialist regime and the eve of the great annexations of 1938NoteA companion to the other Dokumente der deutschen Politik volumes in this wiki — the earlier Friedrichs-compiled Band 1 (Die nationalsozialistische Revolution 1933), Band 2 (Der Aufbau des deutschen Führerstaates 1934), Band 3 (Deutschlands Weg zur Freiheit 1935) and Band 4 (Deutschlands Aufstieg zur Großmacht 1936), and the later Volz Band 6 (Großdeutschland 1938); reproduced from the Hochschule für Politik edition with the original German text of laws, decrees and official communications preserved verbatim
Contents. The volume documents a single year of the Third Reich, 1937, in three parts. Part A (documents 1–11) records the National Socialist state and movement: Heß on the essence of the party, Hitler’s Reichstag speech of 30 January 1937 on the fourth anniversary of the seizure of power, the Reich cabinet memorial session, the award of the Order of the German Eagle, Rosenberg’s congress speech, and the reconstruction of the Reich cabinet of 26 November 1937 (the removal of Blomberg, Fritsch and Neurath and the beginning of Hitler’s personal command of the Wehrmacht). Part B (documents 12–46) records foreign policy: the German replies on the volunteers and control question in the Spanish Civil War, the Non-Intervention Committee speeches of Ribbentrop, relations with Italy and Japan (Mussolini’s visit to Berlin of September 1937, Italy’s adherence to the Anti-Comintern Pact of 6 November 1937), Germany’s relations with her neighbours (Switzerland, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Hungary, Poland, the Anglo-German naval agreement, Belgium’s inviolability), and the colonial demand of 1937. Part C (documents 47–81) records the reordering of state, people, economy, culture and law: the Greater Hamburg law and administrative reforms, the German Civil Service law and police law, population and race policy, economic policy, social policy (the Winterhilfswerk, the Ley-Cianetti agreement), labour service and the Wehrmacht, cultural and church policy, and the reform of law, ending with the law of 5 November 1937 on inheritance restrictions for those acting contrary to the community.
Character of the source. An official documentary publication of the National Socialist state, reproducing the original texts of German laws, decrees, speeches, notes and protocols of the year 1937 in the German original, published in Berlin in 1938 by the party-supporting Junker und Dünnhaupt house. It is a primary source in the strictest sense — the laws themselves (the German Civil Service law, the police law, the inheritance-restriction law), the verbatim official communications of the Reich government (the notes on Spain, Belgium’s inviolability, the Anglo-German naval agreement), and the speeches of Hitler, Heß, Göring, Goebbels, Rosenberg, Schacht and others as officially released. Edited from within the regime with the aim of documenting the state’s own account of its activity, it is at once a record of fact and an instrument of propaganda; read alongside the exile histories (such as Rosenberg’s History of the German Republic, also in this wiki), it supplies the official internal voice of the German dictatorship in the interwar period.
Quality. Good. Extracted from a 494-file paginated text dump (University of Florida scan) by concatenating the numbered page files in order. Text is clean and continuous; laws, decrees, official notes and speech texts are preserved verbatim with footnotes. Section and document headings and dates verified against the printed Inhaltsverzeichnis (table of contents).

A. Der nationalsozialistische Staat und die nationalsozialistische Bewegung (The National Socialist State and the National Socialist Movement)
Dokumente 1–11
The internal consolidation of the regime in 1937. Heß on the essence and work of the NSDAP before officers (16 January 1937); Hitler’s Reichstag speech of 30 January 1937 on the fourth anniversary of the National Socialist revolution; the law extending the Enabling Act; the appointment of a chief of the party’s Foreign Organisation; the Reich cabinet memorial session; the reconstruction of the Reich cabinet of 26 November 1937 (Blomberg, Fritsch, Neurath — the foundation of Hitler’s personal command of the Wehrmacht); the Order of the German Eagle; Rosenberg’s congress speech on the struggle between creation and destruction (8 September 1937); Bohle’s speech in London (1 October 1937); Hitler’s speech at the Harvest Festival on the Bückeberg (3 October 1937).
B. Deutschlands Außenpolitik (Germany’s Foreign Policy)
I. Deutschland und die Spanienfrage (Germany and the Spanish Question) — Dokumente 12–26
The German intervention in the Spanish Civil War as officially documented: the reply notes of the Reich government to the French and British demarches on the volunteer question (7 and 25 January 1937); the German notes on the intervention and control system; Ribbentrop’s speeches before the London Non-Intervention Committee (30 July and 16 October 1937); Goebbels’ speech “The Truth about Spain” at the Nuremberg party congress (9 September 1937); the attack on the Deutschland and the German bombardment of Almería; the German decision to leave the control system; the evacuation of volunteers.
II. Deutschlands Verhältnis zu Italien und Japan (Germany’s Relations with Italy and Japan) — Dokumente 27–32
Mussolini’s visit to Berlin and his speech on the Maifeld (28 September 1937) and Hitler’s answering speech; Neurath on the meaning of German-Italian friendship; the German reply to Belgium’s invitation to the Brussels Nine-Power Conference; the protocol of Italy’s adherence to the German-Japanese Anti-Comintern Pact (6 November 1937); the official German declaration on Italy’s withdrawal from the League of Nations (12 December 1937).
III. Deutschland und seine Nachbarn (Germany and her Neighbours) — Dokumente 33–38
Hitler’s declaration to the former Swiss Federal Councillor Schultheß on Germany’s relations with Switzerland (23 February 1937); Neurath’s visits to Belgrade, Sofia and Budapest (June 1937); the German-Polish agreement on Upper Silesia (14 July 1937); the Anglo-German naval agreement of 17 July 1937 and the exchange of information on fleet construction; the German note on Belgium’s inviolability (13 October 1937); the German-Polish minorities agreement of 5 November 1937 and Hitler’s reception of the Polish minority representatives.
IV. Deutschlands Kolonialforderung (Germany’s Colonial Demand) — Dokumente 39–46
The German colonial demand of 1937 as officially stated: Hitler’s Reichstag speech of 30 January 1937, his proclamation at Nuremberg and his speech at the Harvest Festival; Ribbentrop on the Four-Year Plan and world trade; Schacht at the opening of the German House at the Paris World Exhibition; Göring at the opening of the International Chamber of Commerce congress in Berlin; Epp on Germany’s legal claim to her colonial property and on “the significance of space and raw materials.”
C. Die Neuordnung von Staat, Volk, Wirtschaft, Kultur und Recht (The Reordering of State, People, Economy, Culture and Law)
I. Staatsordnung, Verfassung und Verwaltung (State Order, Constitution and Administration) — Dokumente 47–51
The Greater Hamburg law and other territorial adjustments (26 January 1937); Frick’s speech on the law; the Hessian law abolishing the provinces of Starkenburg, Upper Hesse and Rheinhessen; the law on the constitution and administration of the Hanseatic city of Hamburg; Himmler’s broadcast on the tasks of the German police (15 January 1937); the German Civil Service law and the Reich disciplinary code (26 January 1937); the German Police Officer law (24 June 1937); Frick on party and state in the Civil Service law; the law on the Reichsbank and the Reichsbahn (10 February 1937); the law on the term of office of the municipal self-government bodies; the second implementing ordinance of the Reich flag law.
II. Bevölkerungs- und Rassenpolitik (Population and Race Policy) — Dokumente 52–54
Reinhardt on the early marriage of officials at the Reich meeting of the Reich League of Large Families (Frankfurt, 5 June 1937); the law on measures in the former Upper Silesian plebiscite area (30 June 1937); Reinhardt’s article “On the Way to the Reich Family Fund” (December 1937).
III. Wirtschaftspolitik (Economic Policy) — Dokumente 55–62
The law on joint-stock and limited partnerships (the Stock Corporation law) of 30 January 1937; Hitler at the International Automobile and Motorcycle Exhibition; Ribbentrop on the Four-Year Plan and world trade; Göring on measures to increase agricultural production and his speeches at the International Chamber of Commerce congress and before the party’s Foreign Organisation; Göring’s ordinance on the union of mining rights; Funk at the East Fair in Königsberg; Darré on four years of National Socialist agrarian policy; Reinhardt on the German economy under National Socialist leadership; Schacht at the German savings-bank congress in Essen; the table of unemployment at each month-end 1933–1937.
IV. Sozialpolitik (Social Policy) — Dokumente 63–67
The constitution of the Winterhilfswerk (24 March 1937); Goebbels’ report on the Winterhilfswerk 1936/37; Heß on wages and prices (6 June 1937); the Ley-Cianetti agreement (24 June 1937); Ley’s report to the fifth annual meeting of the German Labour Front at Nuremberg and his account of the “Strength through Joy” achievements.
V. Arbeitsdienst und Wehrmacht (Labour Service and the Wehrmacht) — Dokumente 68a–68c
The decree on the Reich Labour Leader (30 January 1937); the law amending the Reich Labour Service law (19 March 1937); the decree on the summer and winter strength of the Reich Labour Service and the labour service for female youth (24 November 1937); the defence tax law (20 July 1937).
VI. Kultur- und Kirchenpolitik (Cultural and Church Policy) — Dokumente 69–78
The decree on the Adolf Hitler Schools and the Ley-Schirach declaration; the decree on a General Building Inspector for the Reich capital; the foundation of a German National Prize for Art and Science and Goebbels’ proclamation of its first holders at the Nuremberg culture congress; the decree convening a constitutive general synod of the German Evangelical Church; Scheel on the tradition and future of the German student body; the German note to the Holy See (29 May 1937); the German protest against the intervention of the Oxford World Church Conference; the decree establishing a College for Politics; Goebbels’ speech at the annual meeting of the Reich Chamber of Culture; Rust at the foundation-laying of the Military-Technical Faculty; Hitler’s speeches at Munich and on the foundation-laying of the faculty; Schirach on German-foreign youth exchange.
VII. Neugestaltung des Rechts (The Reformation of Law) — Dokumente 79–81
Schlegelberger on the reordering of the so-called civil law (Heidelberg, 25 January 1937); the law on inheritance restrictions for those acting contrary to the community (5 November 1937), restricting the compulsory portion of heirs who married Jews or Jewish half-breeds after 1935.
Zeittafel und Chronologie (Chronological Table), Registers
The volume closes with a Zeittafel und Chronologie of the reproduced documents month by month, an overview of the Führer’s speeches in 1937, and Personen- and Sachregister (name and subject indexes), together with a map of the territorial reorganisation of Greater Hamburg and a list of illustrations.

sources/wir-erleben-die-befreiung-der-sa.title: Wir erleben die Befreiung der Saar — Sechs Berichte deutscher Schriftleiter (1935)
sources/wir-erleben-die-befreiung-der-sa.content:
Wir erleben die Befreiung der Saar
Alfred-Ingemar Berndt and Dr. Otto Kriegk (eds.) — Wir erleben die Befreiung der Saar: Sechs Berichte deutscher Schriftleiter (We Experience the Liberation of the Saar: Six Reports by German Journalists). Verlag August Scherl GmbH, Berlin SW 68, copyright 1935. A German propaganda collection written at the moment of the Saar plebiscite of 13 January 1935, in which the Saar territory voted to return to the German Reich, and of the formal reincorporation of the Saar on 1 March 1935. Six German journalists who had been active in the Saar campaign (the “German Front” against the status quo and the French option) give eyewitness accounts of the years of preparation, the months of the campaign, and the three days of the vote.

































EditorsAlfred-Ingemar Berndt (1905–1945) and Dr. Otto Kriegk, who also each contributed a chapter; the other reporters were Hanns Manfred Grosser, Gräfin Erda Rödern, Karl Bartz and Karl MagesPublisherVerlag August Scherl GmbH, Berlin SW 68, 1935; printed by August Scherl GmbH, Berlin SW 68; copyright 1935 by August Scherl GmbH; 75 illustrations from photographs, 6 drawings and a map; the majority of illustrations supplied by Scherls Bilderdienst, others by PBZ Presse-Illustration Hoffmann, Wentz-Bischmisheim and the New York TimesDedication”To the head of the Reich Association of the German Press, SA-Gruppenführer Wilhelm Weiß, as a sign of the National Socialist comradeship under which the work of the German journalists at the Saar stood”StructureEinleitung (introduction) and six reports; 3,686 lines of extracted textPeriodThe book was written immediately after the Saar plebiscite (13 January 1935) and the return of the Saar to the Reich (1 March 1935); it recounts the years 1919–1935NoteAn official-adjacent press account of the Saar question: it stands alongside the Büttner and Volz volumes in this wiki as the voice of the triumphant German nationalist side, focused on a single event — the recovery of the Saar — told as a heroic national campaign
Contents. Einleitung (Introduction): the six reporters explain their purpose — to record not the Saar’s well-known history but their own experience of the campaign, the thinking of the years of preparation, the feeling of the months of struggle, and the jubilation of the three days of decision, “to bring the pictures of the Saar territory to life” for German youth. Von 1919 bis 1934 (From 1919 to 1934, by Dr. Otto Kriegk): the history of the Saar under the League of Nations mandate after the Treaty of Versailles — the Governing Commission, the French mining interest in the Saar mines, the failure of the plan for a Franco-German economic approach agreed at Thoiry (1926), and the situation of the 850,000 Germans at the Saar up to the eve of the plebiscite. Das Volk (The People, by Hanns Manfred Grosser): the endurance of the Saar population in the German cause. Die Fremden (The Foreigners, by Gräfin Erda Rödern): the author’s work at Geneva — reporting the intentions of the Governing Commission and Plebiscite Commission that exercised the actual power in the Saar territory — and the international and émigré dimension of the campaign. Der Plan (The Plan, by Karl Bartz and Karl Mages): the organization of the German electoral campaign for the return to the Reich. Der Kampf (The Struggle): the campaign itself — the rallies (“Schluß mit allem Parteihader! … Es lebe die Deutsche Front!”), the “German Front” of the parties united for the return, against the status-quo and pro-French camps. Der Sieg (The Victory, by Alfred-Ingemar Berndt): the plebiscite of 13 January 1935 and the celebration of the Saar’s return to Germany.
Character of the source. A primary source of the German nationalist / National Socialist side, written by six journalists directly involved in the Saar campaign and published within weeks of the plebiscite and the Saar’s reincorporation into the Reich. It is at once reportage — the eyewitness account of how the campaign and the vote unfolded — and propaganda, presenting the Saar’s return to Germany as the inevitable, heroic fulfilment of a national demand and a model for German youth. It gives the Nazi regime’s own framing of the Saar question: the recovery of the territory after “a thousand years” is depicted as righting the wrongs of Versailles. As such it complements the official documentary volumes of Volz and Büttner (also in this wiki) with the partisan, lived-experience press voice of the campaign, and stands opposite the exile history of Rosenberg. The editor Alfred-Ingemar Berndt later served in the Nazi press and propaganda apparatus (and died in 1945).
Quality. Good. Extracted from a 144-file paginated text dump (Ohio State University Library scan, presented by Gordon H. Walker) by concatenating the numbered page files in order. The text uses the long-s (ſ) of Fraktur; the OCR layer is clean and legible, preserving the German spelling of the period. Chapter headings and authors verified against the printed Inhaltsangabe (table of contents). The scan closes with the library date-due card (barcode 32435011143609).
Raw text: wiki/raw/wir-erleben-die-befreiung-der-saar-1935-berndt.txt.

Die Herausgeber — Einleitung (The Editors — Introduction)
The purpose of the book: to record, around the well-known pictures of the Saar territory, the reporters’ own experience of the years of preparation, the months of the campaign, and the three days of the decision; a working community of German journalists, joined indirectly by some twenty more, all of whom “truly experienced with the whole German people the time of struggle and victory”; the book is presented as “work for German nationhood and the best instruction for German youth.”
Von 1919 bis 1934 (From 1919 to 1934) — Dr. Otto Kriegk
The Saar under the League of Nations mandate after the Treaty of Versailles: the Governing Commission and Plebiscite Commission holding actual power; the French interest in the Saar mines; the years of separation from the Reich; the proposed Franco-German plan for the Saar agreed at Thoiry in 1926 and its collapse; and the condition of the German population on the eve of the plebiscite.
Das Volk (The People) — Hanns Manfred Grosser
The endurance and steadfastness of the Saar population in the German cause during the years of the mandate and the campaign: “Das Volk blieb fest” (the people stood firm).
Die Fremden (The Foreigners) — Gräfin Erda Rödern
The international dimension of the Saar question seen from Geneva: the author’s use of her diplomatic experience to report the intentions of the Governing Commission and Plebiscite Commission to the German campaigners, and the interplay of the powers over the territory.
Der Plan (The Plan) — Karl Bartz and Karl Mages
The organization of the German campaign for the Saar’s return to the Reich: the political and propagandist preparations, and the mobilization of the Saar population for the vote.
Der Kampf (The Struggle)
The campaign before the plebiscite: the rallies and the “German Front” uniting the parties that demanded the return to the Reich — against the status-quo and pro-French options — “Schluß mit allem Parteihader! Wir haben die große Pflicht … Der Sieg wird unser sein! Es lebe die Deutsche Front!”
Der Sieg (The Victory) — Alfred-Ingemar Berndt
The plebiscite of 13 January 1935 and the celebration of the Saar’s return to Germany; the reincorporation of the Saar into the Reich on 1 March 1935, closing the chapter opened by Versailles.

sources/zevaes-histoire-de-la-troisieme-.title: Alexandre Zévaès — Histoire de la Troisième République (1926)
sources/zevaes-histoire-de-la-troisieme-.content:
Histoire de la Troisième République (1870–1926)
Alexandre Zévaès — Histoire de la Troisième République (1870–1926). Les Éditions Georges-Anquetil, Paris, 1926. A single-volume narrative history of the French Third Republic from the fall of the Second Empire to the mid-1920s, written by a Socialist lawyer, journalist and historian who had himself sat in the Chamber of Deputies.





























AuthorAlexandre Zévaès (1873–1953), born Alexandre Bourson — French lawyer, journalist and historian of the socialist movement; deputy of the Parti Ouvrier Français and later of the SFIO, sitting in the Chamber from 1898 to 1914; author of Le Socialisme en France depuis 1871 (1908) and Le Syndicalisme contemporain; in the 1920s a prolific popular historian, publisher and polemicist, the founder-editor of the Éditions Georges-AnquetilEdition1926, Les Éditions Georges-Anquetil, Paris; printed by Imprimerie Amiard, 259 Faubourg Saint-Martin, Paris; a single volume of ~643 printed pages (HathiTrust scan of the Indiana University Library copy)StructurePréface + 20 chapters + Conclusion + Annexes (indexes of the Presidents of the Republic, the ministries, the principal dates, and the names cited) + Bibliographie; 26,768 lines / ~1,223,000 characters of extracted textPeriodThe Third Republic from 1870 to 1926: the 4 September 1870, the National Defence, the Commune, the monarchist crisis and the Constitution of 1875, the years of the Ordre moral and the Republic’s consolidation, Boulangism, the Panama scandal, the Dreyfus affair, the separation of Church and State, the prewar ministries, the Great War, and the postwar years to the Cartel des GauchesNoteA sympathetic, Socialist-minded narrative history of the Republic written in the mid-1920s, from the fall of the Empire to the brink of the postwar crises. Unlike the analytical Tableau des partis en France of Siegfried, this is a committed chronological history of the parliamentary republic by a man of the Left who lived much of it from the floor of the Chamber. For this wiki it supplies a French-authored, French-perspective narrative of the regime that the Russian, German and Italian sources approach from the revolutionary, National Socialist and Fascist sides
Contents. A chronological narrative in twenty chapters. Chapter I opens with the 4 September 1870 and the proclamation of the Republic at the fall of the Second Empire; Chapter II recounts the Government of National Defence and the war against Prussia; Chapter III treats the Commune, its causes and its repression; Chapter IV asks whether the Republic will survive, amid the economic recovery and the monarchist agitations; Chapter V covers the Ordre moral and the Constitution of 1875; Chapter VI (continuing the consolidation) the establishment of the Republic; Chapter VII the Republic in danger under Boulangism; Chapter VIII the Panama scandal; Chapters IX and X the Dreyfus affair and its consequences; Chapters XI and XII the Republican consolidation under Waldeck-Rousseau and the separation of Church and State; Chapter XIII the radical ministries; Chapter XIV the prewar foreign policy and domestic crises; Chapters XV–XIX the Waldeck-Rousseau and Combes ministries, the prewar years, and the Great War; Chapter XX the postwar years with the Bloc National, the Cartel des Gauches and the elections; and a Conclusion draws the balance of the Republic. A set of annexes tabulates the Presidents of the Republic, the ministries, the principal dates, and the names cited, and a bibliography closes the volume.
Character of the source. A committed, narrative history of the Third Republic written from within by a Socialist deputy and historian, favourable to the Republic and to the Left but engaging at length with the monarchist, nationalist and clerical opponents of the regime. Zévaès writes in the tradition of the engaged republican historiography of the early twentieth century; his sympathy is with the revolutionary heritage and the working-class movement, and his account of the Commune, the Dreyfus affair and the separation of Church and State reflects that standpoint. As a parliamentary memoirist-historian he brings first-hand acquaintance with many of the figures and episodes he narrates. The book is a work of popular synthesis rather than archival scholarship, aimed at a wide republican readership.
Quality. Fair-to-good. Extracted from a 658-page HathiTrust page-per-file dump (Indiana University Library scan) of the 1926 Georges-Anquetil edition, concatenated in page order from the Préface (page 7) through the Table des Matières (page 643); the library’s front-matter and shelf-mark pages were stripped. The embedded OCR is largely clean French with occasional misreadings (running headers such as HISTOIRE DE LA III RÉPUBLIQUE and the printed page numbers are carried inline in the body text); hyphenation and a few character-level OCR errors noted.
Raw text: wiki/raw/zevaes-histoire-de-la-troisieme-republique-1926.txt.

Préface — Pour qu’on sache… (So That One May Know…)
Justifies the book: no period of history is more living, more ardent, more tangled than that which runs from 1870 to the present — the war against Prussia, the Commune, the Seize-Mai, Boulangism, the Panama scandal, the social battles of Fourmies, Decazeville and Carmaux, the Dreyfus affair, the war of 1914–18 and its consequences. The preface presents the work as a record of that history for the general reader.
Chapitre Premier — Le 4 Septembre 1870
The Second Empire, the republican opposition, the declaration of war on Prussia, Sedan and the proclamation of the Republic. The Empire had begun with the Deux-Décembre (the coup of 2 December 1851); the government of the great landed property, the nobles and emigrant hobereaux, had given way to the July Monarchy governed by and for the bankers and high finance; and the césarisme of Soulouque now presented itself as the government and salvation of the propertied. The Empire dates the fashionable Paris, city of luxury and pleasure, capital of the revellers; the press is muzzled by the caution-money system and administrative suppression, books seized, and the most cynical and fantastic police arbitrariness prevails with the mouchard (spy) everywhere. The chapter traces the coming of war and the fall of the regime.
Chapitre II — La Défense nationale
Organisation of the new government, the struggle against the invader, the meeting of the National Assembly at Bordeaux, and the peace treaty.
Chapitre III — La Commune
The moral, political and economic causes of the Commune; the 18 March; the battle of the streets and the repression; the Commune in the provinces.
Chapitre IV — La République vivra-t-elle?
The economic recovery; the precarious political situation; the monarchist agitations; the republican campaign of Gambetta; the Barodet election; the Vingt-quatre mai (the fall of Thiers).
Chapitre V — L’Ordre moral; la Constitution de 1875
The Marshal (MacMahon), the ministry of the duc de Broglie, the religious crisis and the pilgrimages; the making of the Constitution of 1875.
Chapitres VI–VIII — Consolidation, Boulangisme, Panama
The establishment of the Republic; the Republic in danger under Boulangism; the Panama scandal and its political consequences.
Chapitres IX–XII — L’affaire Dreyfus et la consolidation
The Dreyfus affair and its consequences; the Waldeck-Rousseau and Combes ministries; the law on associations, the dispersal of the religious congregations and the separation of Church and State.
Chapitres XIII–XIV — Les ministères radicaux et l’avant-guerre
The Sarrien, Clemenceau and Aristide Briand ministries; the strikes; the viticultural movements in the Midi and Champagne; proportional representation and the three-year law; foreign policy — Tangier, Casablanca, Agadir — and the state of mind in Germany.
Chapitres XV–XIX — La Guerre
Waldeck-Rousseau and Combes; the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente, the drama of Sarajevo, the declarations of war; the violation of the Belgian and Luxembourg neutralities; the retreat from Charleroi and the battle of the Marne; Verdun; the Aisne and the Yser; the offensive of 16 April 1917 and the general offensive of 1918; the wartime ministries and the wartime foreign policy, the collaboration of the socialists in government and the elaboration of the Treaty of Versailles.
Chapitre XX — L’Après-guerre et la Conclusion
The electoral reform, the Bloc National and the Cartel des Gauches, the legislative elections and the elections to the Presidency of the Republic; the Conclusion draws the balance of the Republic over more than half a century.
Annexes et Bibliographie
Indexes of the Presidents of the Republic, the ministries, the principal dates of the Third Republic, and the names cited; a bibliography of works on the period; and the Table des Matières.
